Zhiqiu Yuan and co-authors speed up batch searches for disjoint paths in networks, in a 2025 paper. Disjoint paths share no middle points, so they give backup routes. Transport and network routing issue many such queries at once. Handling each query alone wastes repeated work.

Simple extensions of path listing explode in cost. Single-query methods convert the graph but cannot share effort. Their algorithm, ShareDP, merges the converted graphs across queries. Computation and storage are then shared. That sharing cuts the batch cost while keeping the disjointness guarantee. The work serves planners who need many safe route options at once, such as in chip wiring or freight.
arxiv-2502-16706:
Jonathan Light and co-authors offer, in a 2025 paper, a way to let a language model split a hard task into steps on its own. Many ways to scale up test-time work break a task into fixed steps, then sample tries and keep the best next step. Fixed step sizes, set by hand or by rule, can waste compute on easy parts and starve hard parts. The method here, named DISC, cuts the trace as the work goes on.

Hard steps get split into smaller parts and get more samples, while easy steps move fast. Tests on code and math bench sets, named APPS, MATH, and LiveCodeBench, show clear gains. Error rates fell by about 5 to 11 percent against fixed cuts. The gain held for token, sentence, and whole-step cuts as the base.
arxiv-2502-16806:
Duc Anh Le, Tu Vu, and colleagues transfer reasoning skill between language models that cut text into different tokens in a 2025 study. Distillation trains a small student on a large teacher's behavior to cut deployment cost, and chain-of-thought distillation passes along the teacher's step-by-step reasoning, not just answers. A hidden obstacle is tokenization: teacher and student often split the same sentence into different pieces, so their reasoning chains do not line up step for step.

Optimal transport supplies the alignment, matching pieces across the two tokenizations by similarity. Aligned distillation should let small models inherit reasoning from teachers built on foreign vocabularies.
arxiv-2502-16906:
Nine authors led by Qin Zhu breed logic puzzles by code to grade the thought grit of language models. Pick-one tests let models guess, which puffs their scores and makes them jump by luck. Their breeder writes open puzzles with code-checked keys and set grit grades. A twin-tongue bench of such puzzles forms the test ground for the field.

Eight new models took the bench, with scores spread from thirty-five to seventy-three percent. That spread runs far wider than the thin band on the source pick-one set. Breed scraps that fail the code check feed back as train stock in the same loop. True thought grit thus parts from test luck in the grades.
arxiv-2502-17006:
Shixin Zhao and six co-authors present a 2025 paper on CMSwitch, a compiler for computing-in-memory chips. These chips can both store data and compute on it, promising speed for neural networks. Most compilers ignore that the hardware can flip between memory and compute modes. That flipping matters for modern networks, especially large language models, whose memory and compute needs vary by layer. The team builds mode choice into the compiler's search space.

A new optimization pass picks which network segments run in which mode and how resources split between them. It uses dynamic and integer programming to find good plans. Results are expressed through a general operator form that fits many chips. On benchmarks, CMSwitch ran about thirty percent faster than the best existing compilers. The authors present it as a fuller use of dual-mode hardware.
arxiv-2502-17406:
Lintao Li and eight colleagues present a 2025 quantum optics study wiring single atoms into the fiber network the world already uses. Quantum computers will need quantum links, and photons at telecom wavelengths travel farthest through fiber with least loss. The team entangled ytterbium-171 atoms, prized for processors and clocks, with photons born directly in that band.

The atom's nuclear spin and the photon's arrival-time encoding formed a Bell pair with fidelity about zero point nine five after correction. By imaging the atom array onto a fiber array, the team ran many links in parallel, multiplying the entanglement rate. They also kept a memory qubit coherent while its neighbors did the networking. The authors call it a step toward high-rate quantum networks.
arxiv-2502-17606:
Viraj Thakkar, Qi Lin, Kenanya Keandra Adriel Prasetyo, Raden Haryosatyo Wisjnunandono, Achmad Imam Kistijantoro, Reza Fuad Rachmadi, and Zhichao Cao let a large language model tune database engines by itself. Their 2025 paper concerns LSM-based key-value stores, the storage backbone of many modern systems. These engines expose a huge configuration space covering compaction, flushing, and caches, all competing for the same CPU, memory, and storage.

Human tuning is slow and expert-bound; earlier auto-tuners assumed one workload and touched few knobs. Their framework, ELMo-Tune-V2, uses the model's reasoning to characterize workloads on its own, tune broadly across parameters, and adjust settings live as conditions change. The paper argues language models can carry real systems work, not just text tasks.
arxiv-2502-18406:
Jaron Maene and Luc De Raedt present a study from twenty twenty-five on how a unifying frame for logic based sums also covers learning. Algebraic model counting adds up the worth of logic forms with ring like math tools. It joins many inference tasks in one view. The pair ask if the same view can join learning methods too.

They show that gradients and backpropagation stretch to new rings in the same way. Traits of a ring, like when terms cancel or rank, can cut the memory cost of the backward pass. That yields fresh forms of top gradient methods for logic based chance models. Tests show clear speed gains over past routes. They also note why second order methods gain less here.
arxiv-2502-19206:
Zsolt Vizi and co-authors present in 2025 a method for finding which age groups matter most in epidemic models. Such models split the public into age bands and use a contact matrix to say how much each band mixes with the others. Those matrices are hard to measure, since age groups answer surveys in different ways, and the errors blur forecasts.

Their method runs the model many times with sampled contact values, then ranks which age bands sway the results most. A new summing step adds up each band's total share of the sway across key outcomes. Bands with the biggest sway are also the biggest source of doubt in the model. Aiming surveys and studies at those bands should sharpen forecasts the most. The authors offer the method as a guide for cheaper, better timed public health action.
arxiv-2502-19306:
Daniele Nantes-Sobrinho and three co-authors solve generalization problems in logic in twenty twenty-five. Generalization means finding the most common structure shared by expressions. In languages with binders, bound variable names can be renamed, which complicates the search. Such problems often have no single least general solution.

Using nominal techniques with atom-variables, the team had earlier removed redundant solutions. That gave unique least general generalizations in the plain case. This work extends the approach to equational theories. It handles associative, commutative, and combined forms of equality. Their algorithm is sound and weakly complete, producing finite sets of generalizations. A key hurdle is solving equivariance problems under those same theories.
arxiv-2502-19406:
Hsiang-Ku Lin and three co-authors present a 2025 study of decoding for a family of quantum error-correcting codes called generalized bicycle codes. These codes carry extra check equations by design, and the team asks how few rounds of checks are needed to correct errors well. They built many related codes and tested three of them under two kinds of noise.

Decoding from a single round of checks lost a lot of accuracy. Using just two rounds nearly matched the accuracy of using many rounds. The extra check equations clearly helped at every setting. The results suggest that these codes can correct errors with far less waiting, which matters for real quantum hardware.
arxiv-2502-20006:
Sanjay Shukla, writing alone, simulates turbulence in superfluids that pull on themselves through gravity, in a 2025 paper. The model equations also describe dark matter halos around galaxies. Without gravity, the simulated superfluid shows the classic energy spectrum of ordinary turbulence.

Adding gravity changes the picture. Matter gathers into structures, from flat sheets to round collapsed clumps. Their sizes leave a dip in the energy spectrum. The system settles early into a steady statistical state. Energy in the compressible part of the flow follows a thermal pattern. The structures suggest that particles drift from small scales to large ones through an inverse cascade. That drift offers a mechanism for building large structures like the dark matter halo around the Milky Way.
arxiv-2502-20106:
Joris Weeda and co-authors present a robot navigation method that pushes through clutter in this 2025 paper. Blocked paths force a robot to move obstacles aside. Classic planners assume obstacles stay fixed or are simply movable or not. Real objects fall on a spectrum of movability.

Their framework joins a global semantic visibility graph with a local predictive controller. Simulated rollouts test push actions in a physics engine before the robot commits. The planner scores paths by success and by contact force, favoring gentle pushes. A continuous movability estimate replaces the old binary label. Tests beat the binary based paradigm on success rate and total contact force. Code was released with the paper.
arxiv-2502-20306:
Lingyu Du and co-authors build the first shield against backdoor attacks on gaze estimation, in a 2025 paper. Eye-tracking models steer driver alerts and hands-free control, and they train on data often scraped or outsourced. A poisoned set can plant a trigger: the model reads eyes truly until a set mark appears, then swings the gaze where the attacker wants. No defense had faced this risk for gaze, whose output is a smooth direction, not a label.

Their SecureGaze hunts the backdoor's shape by reverse-building the trigger function, using tells that mark a rigged gaze model. Once rebuilt, the trigger can be spotted and the trap disarmed. Tests in screen and real-world settings beat seven defenses borrowed from image classification, across a spread of attack styles. The authors frame gaze as a safety surface in cars, and their shield as a first lock on it.
arxiv-2502-20906:
Tingting Wang, Bilel Selmi, and Zhiming Li worked in 2025 on the math of multifractals, shapes whose rough texture varies from spot to spot. A key gauge for such shapes is topological entropy, a count of how much new pattern shows as one zooms in. Their paper studies two refined forms of that gauge. Each form is tuned by two dials and built on classic cover ideas from Bowen and from packing theory.

They chart the traits of both gauges and ask when each can be measured in the strict math sense. They tie the packing form to plain entropy on level sets, the slices where local texture is fixed. The packing form's reach covers the whole local entropy spectrum, they show. That gives the field fresh tools.
arxiv-2502-21106:
Youngjin Yoo and co-authors build an AI model for head injury scans in a 2025 paper on emergency care. Head CT scans are rising in number while radiologists are scarce, so fast, accurate sorting of urgent cases matters. Their model reads three-dimensional scans without contrast dye and flags a wide range of trauma findings.

To train it, the team used language models to label scans at scale. Smaller networks first learned to outline bleeding types and brain anatomy, and those skills were folded into the main model. Against expert labels, the model sorted major findings such as bleeding and brain shift with strong accuracy. It also caught rarer urgent signs. Overall scores across sixteen conditions were high, and the authors offer the model as a benchmark for the field.
arxiv-2502-21206:
Songrun He and co-authors train language models that know only what was public by each past date, in this 2025 paper. Models trained on later text can leak future facts into studies of the past, spoiling backtests. Their pair of models accept only text available at each point in time.

Despite the strict cutoff, the models scored on par with standard peers on language benchmarks and stayed close to far larger open models. In a stock test, next-day return forecasts from news matched a much larger model's risk-adjusted gains. The authors conclude the look-ahead leak is modest here, and offer a workable recipe for clean tests.
arxiv-2502-21306:
Dana Kirchem and co-authors wrote an energy study in 2025 on homes that both make and use solar power. Such homes have roof panels and batteries, and they deal with the power grid in new ways. The team asked how the price rules set for these homes shape their choices and the grid.

They ran a linked pair of open computer models of the German power market. They tested flat prices against prices that change by the hour. They also tested prices set by zone against prices set at each grid point. Zone prices drew more roof panel uptake than point prices. Flat prices held uptake back. Local sun levels mattered more than any price rule. Grid strain from these homes stayed small in the model.
arxiv-2503-00106:
William McClymont and co-authors use high-resolution simulations to watch galaxies flicker, in a 2025 paper. Galaxies in the early universe sit on a main sequence relating their mass to star formation rate, but how steadily they form stars was unclear. THESAN-ZOOM simulations show the sequence's level rising with redshift more steeply than observations suggest.

The team reproduces the flatter observed trend by leaving out weakly star-forming galaxies, implying surveys miss a lulling population or overstate rates. On short timescales, star formation is burstier at earlier times. Two burst engines appear: external ones, where rapid inflows of gas trigger long, extreme episodes, and internal, where small galaxies cycle gas out and back in. Both operate at all epochs, but the extreme external mode grows commoner early on, driving the burstiness. Results recast the early sequence as a flickering, hidden population.
arxiv-2503-00206:
Naveen Mysore measures breaks in the Markov assumption inside noisy reinforcement learning in this 2025 paper. Learning agents assume each observation fully shows the state. Sensor noise and missing variables break that promise quietly. His method pairs a causal discovery algorithm with a new score for multi step dependence.

Three classic control tasks serve as test beds. Added noise sometimes left little trace in the score, even at high levels. Dropping key variables hurt both returns and the score sharply. Removing angular velocity from two tasks was especially damaging. Other dropped dimensions mattered far less. The score tells engineers which sensors to protect first, rather than treating all noise alike.
arxiv-2503-00806:
Cui Zhao and co-authors predict the solar cycle with a deep learning model in 2025. Sunspot counts rise and fall in a cycle that shapes the space weather near Earth. Most models predict many steps at once, but this team predicts one step at a time.

Each new prediction is fed back into the input to build the next one. Tests on smoothed monthly sunspot data fit past cycles well, with small average errors. The team predicts the current cycle peaked in late 2024 at a set height. They compare their result with other methods and judge it more sound than most.
arxiv-2503-01006:
Sampling from a lopsided probability landscape, knowing only its unnormalized heights, is a core chore in statistics and physics. Denis Blessing and co-authors build samplers from underdamped diffusion bridges. These paths carry a simple starting distribution into the target, with noise acting on only part of the state, like momentum in mechanics.

Their framework proves that the usual training objective still bounds the likelihood in this setting. Learning the whole density path, rather than fixing a noising schedule, buys accuracy. Across many sampling problems the method beat alternatives while taking fewer, larger steps and no tuning. The authors credit the underdamped motion's better convergence and its fit with accurate integrators.
arxiv-2503-01306:
Pooya Mohammadi Kazaj and nine co-authors built a fair test frame in two thousand twenty-five to compare model families for medical image segmentation. Many new architectures claim top scores, yet a strong baseline called nnU-Net still proves hard to beat. Their open frame, nnUZoo, extends that baseline to host convolutional, transformer, and Mamba-based models under one roof.

They also added five fresh hybrid designs that mix those building blocks. Tests spanned six data sets across microscopy, ultrasound, CT, MRI, and PET, covering many organs. Classic convolutional models stayed both fast and accurate. The frame lets readers check grand claims against shared evidence.
arxiv-2503-01506:
Xiangyu Xi and nine co-authors present SampleMix in 2025, a new way to build training data for large language models. The usual method picks shares for each topic area first, then samples evenly within each area. That plan misses overlap between areas and treats all samples in an area as equal.

SampleMix works from the bottom up instead. It grades each sample for quality and for how much new variety it adds, then samples across all areas at once. In tests, the method beat the usual topic-based plans on many tasks. It also needed far fewer training steps to match the older methods, which saves time and cost.
arxiv-2503-01606:
Zhanghao Hu and co-authors present an embedding-level framework for open-domain question answering. Their 2025 system, called EmbQA, aims to cut the cost and wobble of prompt-heavy pipelines. Such pipelines lean on many rounds of instructions to the model.

Query vectors are refined by light linear layers trained without labels, by a contrastive goal. That step re-ranks found passages so answer-bearing ones rise. A second trick widens the model's inner space to spawn varied candidate answers. An entropy rule then picks the most confident one. Tests span three models, three retrievers, and four benchmarks. Gains in both accuracy and speed over recent rivals are reported.
arxiv-2503-01906:
Hugo Chateau-Laurent and Rufin VanRullen build a reasoning model inspired by brain theory in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Global workspace theory holds that the brain routes information through a shared space between specialized parts. Their model copies that design to chain simple operations in sequence.

A controller learns to send information through modules for input, incrementing, and output, in the right order to add two numbers. They test a hand-built version and a learned version that reads handwritten digits. The workspace model, with fewer parameters, beat standard recurrent and transformer models on unseen additions. The authors see promise for stronger reasoning in deep learning.
arxiv-2503-02406:
Magnetic geodesics are paths that bend under a magnetic force, much as charged particles curve in a field. Peter Albers, Gabriele Benedetti, and Levin Maier study these paths on odd-dimensional spheres carrying the standard contact form as the magnetic potential. They compute the Mañé critical value, an energy threshold central to the theory.

The team shows that an energy level sits above the threshold exactly when every pair of points on the sphere can be joined by a magnetic geodesic at that energy. Their proof uses submanifolds fixed by the flow and symmetry maps they define for magnetic systems. A conserved angle also lets them view the flow as blending two known flows, the contact geodesic flow and the Reeb flow.
arxiv-2503-03006:
Rachid El Aitouni and co-authors study electron tunneling in graphene under laser light in a 2025 physics paper. Graphene's electrons behave like massless particles, which makes their tunneling through barriers unusual. Adding a scalar potential and exchange fields, plus a laser, gives several knobs to control that tunneling.

The team examines the Hartman effect, where tunneling time seems to stop growing with barrier width. Laser assistance can reshape that timing. Understanding such effects matters for future graphene devices that switch or sense at ultrafast speeds, where the tunneling current is the working signal.
arxiv-2503-03106:
Yurui Chang, Bochuan Cao, and Lu Lin present Monitoring Decoding, a method that catches a language model mid-answer when it starts to hallucinate. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Models often state falsehoods with full confidence. Checking whole answers after the fact is slow, and repeated sampling fails when errors are consistent.

A monitor watches the partial answer as it forms and scores its factuality. Tokens that look prone to hallucination get flagged on the spot. A tree-based search then revises just those risky tokens before the answer moves on. The method skips the cost of many full drafts. Tests beat self-consistency rivals on both accuracy and speed. Factual gains came with far less computation. The work suits live assistants where latency matters.
arxiv-2503-03206:
Binxu Wang and Cengiz Pehlevan build an analytic theory of spectral bias in diffusion models in two thousand twenty-five. Diffusion models learn to undo noise step by step. The team asks how the made distribution shifts as training runs. A Gaussian equivalence trick lets them solve the training flow for simple denoisers.

Their law says each mode's match time scales against its variance. Big, coarse modes are thus learned far sooner than fine detail. Weight sharing in deep nets speeds rates but keeps the bias. Local convolution acts in a distinct way, with many modes rising at once. Tests on fake and real image data back the law.
arxiv-2503-03306:
Gabriele Torri, Rosella Giacometti, and Gianluca Farina model credit losses when defaults spread like infections. One firm's collapse can knock over its partners, and healthy firms differ in how well they shrug off the hit. Their model splits contagion into an attack from defaulters and a defense that can fail.

A fast recursive method then computes the whole loss distribution for a portfolio. Extensions add richer probability shapes and a shared market factor for realism. The team prices slices of a standard credit index, the synthetic CDO tranches of iTraxx, and matches market quotes across several tranches. The fit suggests the infection picture captures real default clustering.
arxiv-2503-03406:
Bingsong Long studies fast air flow of a special gas past a cone-shaped wing. His paper from twenty twenty-five uses the Chaplygin gas, a model gas with rare traits. The wing has a diamond-shaped cross section. A shock wave sits off the wing's front edges rather than on them. Flow is ruled by the steady Euler equations in three dimensions.

In this gas, all wave paths bend in a straight-line way, and shocks can run both ways. These traits let Long fix the shock's place ahead of time. The task then becomes an edge-value problem for a slanted equation in cone coordinates. He shows the equation stays well-behaved away from the rough edge. A bound on the slope comes first. Two limit methods then yield a full solution that holds across the flow field.
arxiv-2503-03606:
Anas Buhayh, Elizabeth McKinnie, and Robin Burke explore in this 2025 paper what happens if recommendation algorithms move out of the platforms they serve. In this middleware picture, sometimes called the friendly neighborhood algorithm store, users pick their own recommender rather than accept the platform's. Research on recommender ecosystems asks how such designs split value among users, item providers, and platforms.

The authors build a model of such an ecosystem with algorithm choice switched on and study its outcomes. Their interest is the spread of utility: who gains and who loses when the algorithm answers to the reader instead of the feed. The paper opens a design space the field has barely touched.
arxiv-2503-03906:
Mithun Ravisankar and co-authors explain the squash nick shot in a 2025 paper. In squash, a ball that hits the nick where wall meets floor can die at once and roll with no bounce, an unanswerable shot. The team filmed and tested the shot to learn what makes the ball give up its bounce.

The ball must strike the wall first in a narrow height band above the floor. Above all, it must touch the floor before its roll time on the wall runs out. Then the up push is canceled by what they call a mechanical frustration state. A contact model matches the filmed results and hints at roll based shock dampers.
arxiv-2503-04006:
Amin Karimi and Charalambos Poullis present a few shot image cutting method in 2025. Few shot segmentation teaches a model to cut out new object types from a handful of labeled examples. Models often fail when the few examples miss the full look of a class. The team feeds language model knowledge into the process to fill those gaps.

Their frame turns class descriptions into a semantic prompt tuned to each query image. In parallel, dense matching pairs pixels between query and example images. The two streams join to guide the final cut. Tests show firmer results when examples are scarce or unrepresentative of the target class.
arxiv-2503-04206:
Dengler (2025) revisits how light bends when it enters a material, using a particle-like picture of light. Refraction by media that do not spread colors can be modeled with compact wave packets. These packets behave like pseudo-particles. The picture is a favorite in thought experiments about which form of light momentum is correct, the long-running Abraham-Minkowski debate.

Working at an elementary level, Dengler shows how the different kinds of momentum each play their role. He shows how the bending of light follows from conservation laws applied to the particles. A special microscopic model that can be solved exactly is used as a test case. It shows where the simple particle picture and the standard wave equations for materials pull against each other. The paper aims to make the interplay concrete rather than settle the debate by decree.
arxiv-2503-04406:
Yu-Seung Roh and co-authors present a training free method for multimodal recommendation in a 2025 paper. Recommenders that use text, images, and video beat plain ones, but neural models cost much compute to train. Sparse user data also makes learning hard.

Their method builds similarity graphs for two content types plus user item interactions. A polynomial graph filter then fuses the signals, with bounds that tune which frequencies pass. Filter values are treated as settings to adjust from data, with no model training. On real benchmarks, accuracy rose by up to about a fifth over the best rival, with far faster runs.
arxiv-2503-04906:
Duarte and co-authors test a common shortcut in galaxy studies: using dust attenuation for a whole galaxy as a stand-in for extinction of a point source such as a supernova. The two differ, since galaxy light comes from many depths and scatters into the line of sight. Simulations with the SKIRT radiative transfer code cover point sources in dust clouds plus spiral and elliptical galaxies.

For a medium with a fixed intrinsic slope, the recovered attenuation slope ranged widely, from 0.5 to 7. Dust density, galaxy shape and viewing angle all mattered, with angle the strongest factor. Face-on, heavily dimmed regions came within ten percent of the true slope, but edge-on spirals did not.
arxiv-2503-05406:
Kaede Shintani, Hamada Rizk, and Hirozumi Yamaguchi wrote a paper from 2025 on solar cells that double as motion sensors, with no battery at all. Solar cells already turn light into power. The team noticed their current output also wobbles with how the wearer moves and where they walk, since light and shadow shift with each step. That wobble, they argue, is a signal worth reading directly.

Their system treats the solar cell as the only sensor. A warping matcher compares fresh current traces against a stored bank of patterns, tolerating stretches in time. From the match, the system names the user, counts steps, and pins down location. In realistic tests it counted steps with accuracy in the high eighties and identified users at about ninety percent. Location came out within about half a meter. All of it ran with no outside power and nothing worn beyond the cell itself.
arxiv-2503-05506:
Xiamiao Zhao and Yuxuan Yang hunt the sparsest graphs in which every edge sits on cycles of all lengths in a 2025 combinatorics study. Such a graph is called edge-pancyclic: pick any edge and any cycle length from a triangle up to a full loop, and some cycle of that length uses the edge. Finding the fewest edges that achieve this for a given number of vertices is a hard extremal problem with only bounds known.

The authors raise the lower bound by analyzing a new graph class and lower the upper bound with an explicit construction. Narrowing the gap guides the search for the true minimum.
arxiv-2503-05706:
Hanlin Tian and co-authors published this road safety study in 2025. Intersections are hot spots for crashes, yet one factor had been little studied: buildings blocking drivers' views. The team combined open map data with British accident records and traffic counts. They built a method that estimates how much of the road a driver can actually see at each junction. That visible share became a new variable in their accident risk model.

The visible share correlated notably with accident frequency. In their model its coefficient was strongly positive, at 1.745. Adding the visibility factor improved how well the model explained the data, by standard fit measures. The authors read the results as proof that street architecture belongs inside safety analysis. They suggest planners should weigh building placement and sight lines when designing junctions. The work opens a data-driven path for cities to fold visibility into traffic management.
arxiv-2503-05806:
Sebastian Barros compares hallucination in minds and machines in a 2025 theoretical paper. Both humans and large language models can produce output that departs from reality: people misperceive, and models state falsehoods. Barros argues that shared predictive machinery explains both, since each system guesses at the world from partial data.

In the brain, higher levels send predictions down while errors travel up to refine the model, and gaps get filled in, sometimes wrongly. Models build text by predicting the next word without firm grounding in facts. Barros proposes that a tendency to confabulate may come free with advanced intelligence, since prediction brings creativity and flexibility along with error. Lessons on feedback and grounding may transfer between the two fields.
arxiv-2503-06406:
Daniel Murphy, Anthony Mezzacappa, Eric Lentz, and Pedro Marronetti dissect the gravitational waves emitted by a collapsing star's newborn neutron star. Using three-dimensional supernova simulations, they split the signal by where in the star it originates. The stars modeled began at fifteen and twenty-five times the Sun's mass.

Early on, the strongest emission comes from surface layers shaken by infalling matter. Later, convection inside the proto-neutron star takes over as the main source. Most of the wave luminosity likewise migrates from the surface to deep inside. A mode analysis shows the high-frequency signal tracks the star's own oscillation modes as they evolve. That match helps future detectors read the waves.
arxiv-2503-06606:
Pranoy Panda and co-authors took on a quiet failure of machine learning in a 2025 study: models go stale as the data around them changes. Knowing that a model has drifted matters twice over, since teams must fix the model and can also learn from what changed. Most drift tools only raise a flag and explain nothing.

The team built a test that names the features behind a drift, using how features act together. Their method carries proof that it can catch real drift, and it works for both sorting and value-guessing tasks. On standard test sets, it beat other tools that explain drift and matched strong tools that do not. A case study showed it points at the features that truly drive the change.
arxiv-2503-06706:
Customer service bots must follow the flowchart, not improvise, and language models are bad at that discipline. Ming Zhang and co-authors build a training set straight from flowcharts. Their PFDial collection converts hundreds of process diagrams into more than twelve thousand dialogue lessons in Chinese. Each flowchart node becomes a structured teaching unit.

Small models trained on this data surprised the authors. With only eight hundred examples, a mid-sized model passed ninety percent accuracy on process dialogue tasks. A larger one beat GPT-4o on the benchmark by wide margins. Hard backward jumps in a flow, where a case returns to an earlier step, got special study. The lesson: structure in the data teaches structure in behavior.
arxiv-2503-06806:
Bianchetti and Scaringi showed in twenty twenty-five how to move euro rate deals from an old night rate to a new one with no fear of loss. The old rate was set to end at the close of twenty twenty-one. The new rate was picked as its swap by a euro bank work group.

They trace the swap's hit on a few deal kinds and on risk add-ons in full. A clean way that uses the new rate in full is sound in theory, they show. Its hit on deal worth is small in all cases tried. The trade can thus move all such deals in a safe, matched way.
arxiv-2503-07106:
Mordehai Milgrom asks whether MOND, his modified dynamics theory of gravity, must be nonlinear, in this 2025 paper. MOND explains galaxy motion without dark matter by changing the rules at tiny accelerations. Its deep-limit law ties acceleration to the square root of mass, which seems to force a nonlinear theory. That nonlinearity breaks a basic equivalence rule and creates an external-field effect.

Milgrom shows the deep-limit axioms still allow a linear, action-based formulation, possibly a unique one. The linear model changes both inertia and gravity, and it shows no external-field effect. He judges it too flawed to ground a full theory, and he cannot yet join it smoothly to Newtonian physics. Still, the model spawns families of variants and clarifies which MOND predictions are basic and which depend on the version.
arxiv-2503-07506:
Labeling data by hand is costly, so active learning picks only the most useful samples to label. Soumya Banerjee and Vinay Kumar Verma present a framework called ADROIT for that task in this 2025 paper. Good picks need a rich picture of the data, learned from both labeled and unlabeled samples. Their framework builds that picture in a self-supervised way, without extra labels.

ADROIT joins several training goals in one model based on a variational autoencoder. A helper classifier keeps the picture tied to the real task, learning from labeled data and from a self-taught signal on unlabeled data. A separate part learns to tell labeled from unlabeled samples, which guides the next picks. Knowledge from the target model is distilled back into the helper. The design aims for picks that stay sound as labeling proceeds.
arxiv-2503-07706:
Berta and co-authors take a many-wavelength census of cosmic dust in one deep sky field, in a 2025 paper. To grasp early star birth, astronomers must know how much dust young galaxies held. Cold dust glows at submillimeter wavelengths, giving a fair mass tracer that starlight-based methods can miss.

The NIKA2 camera surveyed the GOODS-N field at two millimeter wavelengths, finding sixty-five faint sources. Follow-up with sharper instruments split them into seventy-one individual galaxies and matched them across the spectrum. Tracking this sample lets the team chart how the universe's dust density has changed since redshift seven, near the dawn of galaxy building. Dust, the paper shows, was already plentiful early on.
arxiv-2503-07806:
Song and co-authors benchmark in 2025 group fairness inside the reward models used to fine tune large language models. Fairness checks usually judge only final output, and they force the same prompt questions on every group, which real use breaks. Bias can enter at pretraining or at fine tuning, and the reward model is one entry point.

Expert written texts from arXiv let them test reward models without identical prompts across groups. Results show all evaluated reward models display group fairness gaps in their setup. Locating bias at this component level should help target fixes, rather than treating the whole pipeline as one black box.
arxiv-2503-07906:
Qinghao Ye and co-authors raise the bar for detailed image captioning in a paper from 2025. Vision-language models now write long, rich captions. Judging those captions is the weak link: old metrics are blunt and reference texts are coarse.

Their benchmark, DeCapBench, pairs with a new score called DCScore. The score splits each caption into the smallest self-standing facts. Each fact is then checked for truth and coverage. Hallucinated details get caught instead of averaged away. Human raters agreed with DCScore more than with rival metrics. The benchmark also tracks public model arena standings closely. A companion training method teaches models to earn the higher score.
arxiv-2503-08006:
Zhou, Liu, Zhao, and Gong argue that multi-task learning research has worried about the wrong problem. When one model learns several tasks at once, gradient methods have focused on conflicts, where tasks pull the shared network in opposite directions. The authors show empirically that imbalance matters more: a dominant task can swamp the others even without direct conflict. Their fix, IMGrad, adds imbalance sensitivity to a standard gradient method by constraining the sizes of the projected task gradients.

They test the method on mainstream multi-task benchmarks in both supervised learning and reinforcement learning. Performance stayed competitive across the board. The authors present the work as evidence that balancing task influence, not only resolving conflict, should guide how shared models are trained.
arxiv-2503-08606:
Seungjun Ahn and co-authors built a numeric method in 2025 for tracing how exposures affect survival through chains of molecular mediators. Patients' survival often depends on proteins and genes acting as middlemen between a risk factor and death. Standard mediation tools for survival data handle one exposure and one omics layer at a time, missing how layers interact. Their method, SMAHP, handles high-dimensional exposures and mediators jointly across multi-omics data.

The method is among the first to bring the accelerated failure time model into multi-omics causal mediation for survival. Models across multiple cases were used to test its actions. Identifying true causal pathways, rather than mere links, could show drug builders exactly which molecule to push on. In proteogenomic cohorts where thousands of traits compete for focus, a principled filter like this is needed infrastructure.
arxiv-2503-08706:
Ali and a large team of co-authors published an instrumentation paper in 2025 on a new spectrometer for electron scattering at Jefferson Lab. The Super High Momentum Spectrometer serves Hall C and reaches very high particle momentum. It uses the upgraded accelerator's full beam energy. A chain of new superconducting magnets guides charged particles through tracking and identification detectors.

Shielding guards the detectors from background radiation. The whole device rides on a rotating frame, so measures can span a wide range of scattering angles. That reach opens low-rate experiments that were out of range before. The paper describes the build and how events are traced back to the target.
arxiv-2503-09106:
Chuyu Zhang and co-authors propose a simple baseline for finding new classes over time without storing old data, in a 2025 paper. The task mixes two hard problems: learning must continue, and new classes arrive unlabeled. Past methods often train from scratch or save old examples to avoid forgetting.

Their method, Freeze and Cluster, first estimates how many new classes exist using known class knowledge. It then takes features from a model trained only on the base classes, groups them with k means to make draft labels, and trains only the final classifier layer. Tests on car, bird, nature, and small image benchmarks support their claim. They also report that adding unlabeled data can harm the feature quality of pretrained models.
arxiv-2503-09506:
Sawtooth sound waves that ratchet magnetic skyrmions are proposed by Philipp Schwenke and co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. Skyrmions are tiny magnetic swirls eyed for data tools. Sound waves on a surface can push them, past work shows. A sawtooth wave, the team argues, can walk them one way even with pin spots in the way. The net drift runs across the wave's path.

A strain slope must top the pin strength to start the walk. Sims and hand sums both back the scheme. Pinned spots, once a flaw, turn into the engine here.
arxiv-2503-09606: Zengjing Chen and co-authors propose a generative model that translates structural brain images into functional ones, guided by backward stochastic differential equations. Structural and functional scans show different sides of the brain, and a translator could supply the functional view when only the structural one exists. The pack evidence for the work is thin, giving the model name and purpose without results.
arxiv-2503-09906:
Haaris Mehmood and co-authors present ValSub in a 2025 paper on tuning speech tools to one user. Tuning a phone's speech model to its owner lifts scores on rare words and accents. The risk is that the model forgets its broad training and gets worse on plain speech.

A check set from the broad data can track that loss, but full check sets are too big for phones. ValSub shrinks a large check set to a small one that still gauges the loss well. That small set then sets how many tuning rounds are ideal for each user. Its picks land closer to the picks of a 50 times larger set than random picks of the same size do. The method also stays steady across users.
arxiv-2503-10006:
A resetting integrator that grades slopes live is set out by Mahmoud Abdelgalil and Jorge Poveda in a 2025 arXiv paper. Model-free tuning steers a plant by cost reads alone. Their integrators reset at the same beat as the probe wiggle sent into the plant. That sync makes the integrator spit out true slope reads, not near guesses.

The slope error can be made as small as one likes, they show. As hybrid oracles, the integrators plug into step-wise tuners over live plants. Global calm holds for a broad cost class, past past local claims. Tests on sample plants close the case.
arxiv-2503-10606:
Mehrab Momennia and Olivier Sarbach generalize how gas falls into black holes in a paper from 2025. The classic problem drops a collisionless gas onto a Schwarzschild black hole. Real candidates may wear other geometries: modified gravity, string theory, or loop quantum gravity dresses. Accretion should betray which dress is worn.

Their work covers a broad family of static, spherical black holes. The spacetimes must settle flat far away, carry positive mass, and keep a regular horizon. Metric functions obey set monotonicity rules. The most general gas solution follows for the whole class at once. Observers comparing inflow patterns across theories get one shared yardstick. Simpler Schwarzschild results become a special case.
arxiv-2503-10706:
Pierre Sermanet, Anirudha Majumdar, and Vikas Sindhwani present a 2025 paper that turns science fiction into a test of whether AI systems share human values. They gathered key decision moments from 824 major works of science fiction across film, television, and books, where an AI or robot chose well or badly.

From each moment they built questions with the original choice and other options, scored against votes from human readers. Modern language models paired with rule sets drawn from the stories matched human values far better than the fictional agents did. The rule sets also lifted weak base models sharply and scored well on a separate real-world safety test.
arxiv-2503-10806:
Four authors wrote a cosmology paper in two thousand twenty-five on a hint that dark matter and dark energy interact. New results from the DESI survey have stirred debate about how dark energy behaves. In the standard picture the two dark components ignore each other; here they are linked by a long-range force.

In their model, dark energy is a field whose measured behavior crosses a key line, the phantom barrier, even though the field itself stays on the safe side. The crossing happens at roughly the distance era DESI points to. The authors show the model fits the DESI results within their stated uncertainty for several parameter choices.
arxiv-2503-11106:
Jiawei Wang, Xuedong Hu, and Herbert Fotso model a hole qubit in a germanium dot in this 2025 paper. Real dots sit between barriers of finite height, not the endless walls of simple models. The team treats those finite walls with care, then scans how well width, dot size, and silicon share shift the energy map.

The spin splitting factor proves sensitive to wall modeling choices and silicon content. The dot already carries some spin-orbit coupling on its own. Gate fields and leftover strain add more, and those extras matter for total coupling. That coupling is what lets electric signals steer the spin fast.
arxiv-2503-11506:
Piotr Hajłasz, Jacob Mirra, and Armin Schikorra develop the analysis of Hölder continuous mappings, functions that can bend space but only within a set limit on roughness. Their 2025 paper covers distributional Jacobians for such maps and how differential forms pull back under them. Versions of the change of variables formula and the Stokes theorem are included.

The main uses sit in the Heisenberg groups, a setting with a twist in how directions combine. There the authors give a simple proof of a generalized form of Gromov's non-embedding theorem. They also prove new results about the Hölder homotopy groups of these groups. The catalog title carries stray grant text, so the head title governs here.
arxiv-2503-11606: Juan Sebastian Numpaque-Roa wrote a mathematics paper in 2025 introducing a tensor product for quiver bundles. Quivers encode data along arrows between points, and their bundles enrich that data over a space. The new product is defined for twisted representations with relations, inside modules over the space's functions. A first payoff shows products of polystable bundles stay polystable. From there the author derives a quiver version of the classic Segre embedding. Special closed parts of certain character varieties are also identified. The paper gives the construction its first working applications.
arxiv-2503-11706:
Fabian Galis and Darian Onchis refine how features are weighted before grouping unlabeled data, in a 2025 paper. Clustering can reveal patterns with no labels to guide it. Its quality hinges on which features count most, and that varies by dataset. Equal treatment of all features often dulls the result.

Their new weights borrow a tool built to explain supervised models. Scores that explain a model's choices are reused to rate each feature for clustering. Tests across five benchmark datasets and several clustering methods followed. The explanation-based weights improved cluster quality by up to about twenty-three percent over rival schemes. Better weighting lets analysts trust the groups their data falls into.
arxiv-2503-11906:
Muhammad Awais and co-authors survey, in 2025, deep learning methods for classifying ships in radar satellite images. Such classification supports sea surveillance, but radar images are grainy and hard to read. The survey sorts the literature by model type, use of handcrafted features, radar attributes, and fine-tuning, a taxonomy the authors call a first.

Trends and pain points run through the review: scarce data, the value of public datasets and augmentation, and the need for explanations users can trust. Cross-field teamwork is urged. Future directions include new architectures, shared scoring standards, and interpretability, all aimed at more accurate and efficient ship spotting.
arxiv-2503-12406:
Binggwong Leung and co-authors give robots flexible control in a 2025 paper on animal-like machines. Neural controllers can fail badly when the world shifts beyond their training. A learning rule borrowed from biology, which adjusts links by local activity, can adapt on the fly, but it can also blow up and destabilize the network.

The team added a weight-normalizing guard and tested the design on two real robots: an eighteen-joint beetle-like walker and a sixteen-joint gecko-like one. The plastic network carried skills from simulation to the real robots with no retraining. It coped with rough ground and even with body damage. Analysis of the learned weights shows how the adaptation is organized. The authors back plastic networks for robust field robots.
arxiv-2503-12606: Federico Buseghin and Nicola Garofalo wrote a 2025 math paper on a class of wave equations with a drift term. The equations carry the name of Schrodinger, and the drift can thin out in places, which makes standard tools fail. The authors study bounds that track how waves spread in space and time.
arxiv-2503-12706:
Rahul Deshmukh and Avinash Kak build a dataset that teaches AI to match images of the same land taken from space. Space images come at wild tilts and turns, in all light and weather, as craft pass again and again. Past match sets used ground images from plain cameras, which leaves a gap. Their 2025 set gives dense true pairs for space images, pixel by pixel.

A rotation trick in the build lets the set teach matches even when two images are turned far apart. Four known match tools were trained and scored on the set. Tools trained with the rotation trick beat those trained on other sets, with accuracy gains up to 40 percent. The gap yawned most when the turn between images was large. The set is pitched as a base for space image work.
arxiv-2503-12906: Christian Puntini models how wind drives ice drift currents near the North Pole. From the basic equations of geophysical flow, he trims a system for polar drift. He then finds an exact solution in a frame that moves with the material. The solution stacks three parts: plain oscillations, a mean Ekman flow, and a geostrophic current.
arxiv-2503-13006:
Noémie Combe tackled a famous conjecture that links two giant groups of modern mathematics, in a solo paper published in 2025. One group governs shape changes of surfaces; the other governs the symmetries of the rational numbers. The conjecture says the two are in truth one group. Her proof works in the profinite world, where groups are built as limits of finite ones.

A new kind of path integral, defined for both groups at once, brings number facts into reach. It reads off when classes descend to the rationals and sets ranks for number objects. A construction she calls the Cubic Matrioshka codes each path as an endless binary string, the same for both groups. That match mirrors the underlying shape link the conjecture claims. The work speaks to deep ties between shape and number.
arxiv-2503-13406:
Parameshwar Pasnoori, Patrick Azaria, and Ari Mizel propose a superconducting circuit that hosts a protected topological phase, in a paper from 2025. At set settings, the low-energy behavior of their circuit matches a classic field theory. A discrete symmetry protects the phase, an idea prized for robust quantum devices.

The ground state comes in two forms and shows local symmetry breaking near the circuit edges, with spontaneous edge currents. Exotic zero-energy modes sit at the edges of each ground state. Extra bound states at both edges resist small bulk disorder. The authors argue the spectrum should be visible in a circuit experiment with feasible settings.
arxiv-2503-13506:
Mustafa Cavus, Katarzyna Woźnica, and Przemysław Biecek show that the knobs used to tune machine learning models also control how much equally good models disagree. Their paper appeared in 2025. This disagreement, called predictive multiplicity, matters when models judge credit, hiring, or health. The team tuned six common tabular-data models across 21 benchmark data sets and tracked how predictions scattered between top models.

Tuning improved accuracy but widened disagreement, sometimes sharply. One boosting method showed the worst instability. Specific knobs, like penalty strengths, were the main levers. The authors warn that squeezing out the last points of accuracy can buy arbitrariness: two defensible models may judge the same person differently, and the tuning diary, rarely reported, decides which.
arxiv-2503-13706:
A quantum impurity, a small system bathed in a sea of electrons, hides its behavior in tangles of many-body motion. Yuriel Núñez Fernández, Maxime Debertolis, and Serge Florens introduce a simulation method that follows that motion exactly, in a 2025 paper. Their insight is that most electron orbitals in the bath can be rotated into a do-nothing state.

After a sudden change, the count of active orbitals and the size of the state description both level off at small values. That makes the algorithm far faster and more accurate than the state of the art, tracking thousands of electrons out to the settled long-time regime. The team uses the reach to study how entanglement spreads inside the Kondo screening cloud, the shroud of electrons that gathers around a magnetic impurity.
arxiv-2503-14106:
Jef Jonkers and four co-authors give medical image tools an honest sense of doubt, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Software that marks body landmarks on scans must not only aim well but also say how unsure it is, so doctors can judge trust. Standard doubt methods lean on bell-curve guesses and tend to lowball the true spread.

Their fix uses conformal prediction, a method with a firm promise on coverage. Two new variants handle several landmark points at once and draw flexible, non-boxy regions around each guess, hugging the real spread of error. Across flat and 3D scan sets, the methods beat older ones on both honesty and tightness. The authors note the same trick could serve other many-output tasks.
arxiv-2503-14606:
Suprovo Ghosh and co-authors model how sticky neutron star matter can shift the gravitational waves from a merging pair, in this 2025 paper. As the stars spiral in, tides knead their interiors and heat them. Hyperon bulk viscosity, a friction from weak reactions, may drain real energy.

Earlier estimates said the effect could register in next-generation detectors. Ignoring it, the team now show, biases the measured squishiness of heavy neutron stars. Their phase model, built on simple orbital dynamics, plugs into standard waveforms. Full statistical recovery tests confirm the fix removes the bias. Detector templates, they argue, should carry the term.
arxiv-2503-14706:
Taishi Kotsuka and Enoch Yeung showed in 2025 how to tune the spread of outcomes in a cell without moving the outcomes themselves. Cells with few copies of key molecules behave randomly, and their results often form two or more humps. Those humps guide choices like which cell type to become. Designers may want a hump tighter or wider, but normal tweaks shift the hump as well.

Using a classic equation for chemical chance, the pair define a sharpness score for each hump. They derive rules under which sharpness can be dialed up or down while hump spots and count stay fixed. Simulations on a two-hump system confirmed the control works. The method may help synthetic biologists build cells with set levels of randomness.
arxiv-2503-14806:
Pawel Rubach presents a software engine that spreads heavy computing across clusters without expert setup, in this 2025 paper. The engine was born from protein research: after a famous model began predicting protein shapes, his team needed to hunt for knots in thousands of predicted chains. That search demanded far more computing than one machine holds.

The tool, called the Kafka Slurm Agent, links workstations and clusters managed by the common Slurm scheduler through a message broker. It is written in Python, open source, and needs no administrator rights or extra libraries on the clusters. Users send Python tasks and the engine farms them out and gathers the stream of results. Beyond the knot hunt, which found proteins with new knot types, the engine now runs the knot checks behind a public database of knotted proteins. Rubach offers it to any group whose science outgrows a single cluster.
arxiv-2503-15306: The Euclid Collaboration reports on the first quick data release from the Euclid space mission, in a paper from 2025. The part described here covers galaxy distances estimated from colors. It also covers galaxy traits derived by a processing step. That step joins Euclid data with ground based data. The head is taken up by the long author list. This note therefore rests on the title, subtitle, and catalog summary. Those sources describe a three dimensional view of the universe from billions of galaxies.
arxiv-2503-15406:
Jisu Nam and co-authors introduce Visual Persona in a 2025 paper on remaking a whole person in pictures. Given one photo of someone, the model writes them into new scenes from text prompts, keeping not just the face but the full body's look.

Training such a model needs many photos of each person, which are hard to gather. The team built a sorting pipeline that uses vision-language models to check body consistency, yielding a data set of about 580,000 paired images across 100,000 people. Their design splits the input body into regions, encodes each part, and feeds the blend into a text-to-image diffusion model. The result follows prompts for body type and scene while holding identity from head to toe.
arxiv-2503-15606:
Dongjun Li and co-authors computed the ringdown tones of spinning black holes in a changed gravity theory in a 2025 paper. When two black holes merge, the result rings like a bell, with tones that fade fast. Those tones test whether Einstein's gravity holds in the strongest fields.

The theory here, dynamical Chern-Simons gravity, adds a scalar field that twists the ring. Past tools had only just learned to handle such theories. The team worked in the slow-spin limit and derived the tone equations for both the space warp and the scalar field. Their tone tables give wave hunters a template to test against real merger signals.
arxiv-2503-15906:
Yanbin Zhu, Xiaomeng Jiang, and Yong Li solve a math problem, in a paper published in 2025, about random paths whose rules depend on the crowd of paths itself. Such equations model systems where each moving part feels the whole group's spread. Their noise source has memory, unlike the jitter in standard models, which makes the math harder.

The team compute a quantity, the Onsager-Machlup functional, that says which smooth path a random path is most likely to hug. They work out which ways of measuring closeness are valid, split by how strong the memory is. As a worked case, they handle a swinging pendulum pushed by random forces. Results of this kind help physicists and engineers judge likely paths in noisy systems with memory.
arxiv-2503-16106:
Mohamad Hassan and co-authors teach a vision language model to generalize to new domains from as little as one example per class, while still spotting unknown classes, in work from twenty twenty-five. Prompt tuning of CLIP style models falters when data is scarce. It also flags unfamiliar samples poorly.

Their framework mixes domain free prompts with cues drawn from the image itself, joined by a cross attention module. Generic visual prompts add flexibility across the two input types. For rejection, training prompts use fake unknown samples built to sit near known classes in fine detail. Those fakes sharpen the unknown detector. Across five benchmarks, the method set a new best for this combined task.
arxiv-2503-16606:
Crnogorčević and co-authors hunt for gamma rays that should accompany an extraordinarily energetic neutrino caught in 2025, in a research paper from 2025. One detector saw the event while another set tight limits on such particles, a tension needing explanation. A source placed where the first detector sees best could reconcile the two.

If the source made the neutrino through particle collisions, it should also shine in gamma rays that cascade to lower energies en route. The team modeled that cascade and scanned the sky around the event with satellite data. No matching source appeared. The blank result bounds the source's distance and the magnetic fields between us and it.
arxiv-2503-17006:
Alejandro Vigna-Gómez and co-authors ask what a close third star does to pairs of massive stars on their way to becoming merging black holes. Tight massive binaries can evolve with their chemistry staying homogeneous, a favored channel for making black hole pairs that merge in cosmic time. Most such pairs, however, have a tertiary companion nearby.

The team blends analytic triple dynamics with detailed star models. A third body can tilt orbits through the von Zeipel-Lidov-Kozai mechanism, while tides and relativity twist them back. They follow the systems at three life stages, from birth to near collapse. The verdict shapes how many gravitational-wave sources this channel really supplies.
arxiv-2503-17306:
Meisam Seikavandi and co-authors study how people copy the facial expressions of others over time, and how that copying varies by emotion, in a paper from 2025. This copying, called facial mimicry, is automatic and helps people grasp what others feel. Most past work treated mimicry as a single snapshot rather than a moving pattern.

The team coded videos into small facial action units for both the shown faces and the watchers' faces. A warping method then measured how closely the two time patterns lined up. Fear drew stronger copying than happiness, while anger drew less copying than fear. Copying also tracked modestly with traits such as extraversion and agreeableness. The authors link the findings to emotion software that reads and answers human expression.
arxiv-2503-17506:
Xinwei Liu and Vladimir Dvorkin make optimization over trained neural networks easier in this 2025 paper. Some decision problems lack neat formulas for their rules, so a neural network learns them from data instead. Optimizing with that network inside is notoriously hard in practice.

The pair rewrites the problem in a bilinear form that moves the network's switch like rules into the goal as penalties. That shape suits a difference of convex algorithm, and they give a principled way to set the penalties so the method settles at good points of the original problem. They apply it to scheduling a data center's electricity demand on a power grid, and report clear savings when the grid is congested.
arxiv-2503-17606:
Aghabazaz and colleagues merge seven long health studies to trace heart risk across adult life in twenty twenty-five. No single study follows people from youth to old age. Their pooled project fills the gaps by letting each study lend strength to the others. A layered stats model tracks many risk factors at once over time.

The model borrows across risk factors as well as across studies, which sharpens each curve. New checks test that the model keeps true links among factors as it fills gaps. The curves show risk paths shift a lot with age. They also split by subgroup and by study. The team flags key ages for prevention and watch.
arxiv-2503-17806:
Vaibhav Kumar and Marwa Chafii ask how much send power a green net that senses, talks, and feeds power needs. The work dates to 2025. Next-wave nets must sense and talk on one build. They must also feed hosts of low-power things with no wires.

The build in view uses a smart sheet that sends and bounces at once. It serves sense marks, talk users, and power users in one frame. The team sets beam forms to trim send power while set floors for each task hold. A swap-step solve gives the beam forms in closed or cone form. Sheet use cut send power next to past builds.
arxiv-2503-18006:
Zuyev and Grushkovskaya work on keeping wheeled and similarly constrained machines steady at a chosen rest point. Such systems cannot move sideways at will, so standard control rules fail. Their 2025 paper builds on earlier work in which a control rule that changes over time steadies the system, but only under a sampled notion of what counts as a solution.

Here the authors give conditions under which ordinary, smooth solutions of the closed system also settle at the rest point. That closes a gap between the math used in proofs and the paths a real machine would follow. They apply the result to a broad class of drift-free systems with several inputs. Computer runs on an example system back up the theory.
arxiv-2503-18106: Ivan So proves that any transverse link in a compact contact 3-manifold can be braided around a rational open book. Transverse links are curves that stay angled against the contact planes, and open books cut the space into pages around a binding. Earlier work by Pavelescu handled the standard case. So extends the argument so the pages may wrap with rational twisting, the looser structure called a rational open book decomposition. The result says the link can always be moved, through transverse isotopies, into braid form around that binding.
arxiv-2503-18206:
Sasindu Wijeratne and co-authors model a photonic memory array meant for very fast in-memory computing. Their 2025 paper explains that computing with light promises higher speeds and wider data paths than electronics, and that photonic static memory is a key building block. The team studies a new array design and asks how fast it can run a core workload from tensor decomposition.

They mapped that workload, a product step called MTTKRP, onto the array, including a mode that runs several wavelengths at once to raise throughput. A predictive model then estimates the sustained speed of different array layouts. In a practical layout the model gives seventeen peta-operations per second. The authors present the model as a guide for sizing such hardware before it is built, in a field where the devices themselves are still in development.
arxiv-2503-18406:
Sherry Chen, Misha Sra, and Pradeep Sen fix the training pairs behind instruction-guided image editing, in a 2025 paper. Editors that follow text commands need many before-and-after image pairs, usually faked by image generators. Those pairs often stray from the stated edit, which poisons training. Their method, Instruct-CLIP, learns the semantic shift between an original and an edit from contrastive training. It then scores and repairs the instruction text in a stock data set.

The repair yielded a large cleaned set used to retrain an editor with a fresh loss tied to their scorer. The retrained editor follows commands more closely, the team reports. Code and the cleaned data are public.
arxiv-2503-18806:
Chenyi Li and co-authors formalize in 2025 the proofs that two workhorse optimization methods converge on problems with block structure. Such problems, split into linked blocks of variables, sit at the heart of machine learning and numerical work. Paper proofs of convergence are long and error prone.

The team rebuilt the analysis of block coordinate descent and of the alternating direction method inside a proof assistant. Key ideas from nonsmooth and nonconvex analysis had to be defined in the machine's logic first. Those include generalized slopes for jagged functions and a curve condition that tames nonconvex landscapes. Machine checked proofs cannot hide a skipped step. Formal libraries like this one let later work reuse the proofs instead of redoing them.
arxiv-2503-19006:
Tahiya Chowdhury wrote a 2025 paper on an entry-level computer science course that teaches AI through computer vision. AI skill matters for students at all levels, but intro courses rarely build it. The course pairs core computing ideas with vision tasks as the setting. It also adds critical thinking about AI's social effects.

Students did hands-on projects and took part in reading talks. Surveys before and after the course tracked change. Students reported a stronger sense of belonging and confidence. Awareness of AI ethics rose as well. Reading talks showed deep engagement with hard issues in AI today. Scaling tips close the paper.
arxiv-2503-19306:
Amjad Ali and three co-authors introduce the centroid decision forest, a new ensemble method for classifying data with very many features. Their paper came out in 2025. An ensemble combines many decision trees, which are flowchart-like classifiers, into one stronger system.

Their method changes how each tree splits its data. Instead of single-feature thresholds, a separability score picks the most informative features at each node. The split then uses centroids, the average feature profile of each class, and distances to those centroids. That makes the division more flexible and keeps it representative of each class. Across twenty-three high-dimensional datasets, the method beat conventional classifiers on accuracy and on a chance-corrected agreement measure.
arxiv-2503-19606:
Deepti Madurai Muthu and three co-authors use a known image tool to count a growth mark in breast cancer cells, in one pass. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The mark, called Ki-67, guides how a tumor is classed and how it is treated. Hand counts and eye gauges vary from reader to reader. The team trains an object-spotting tool on sharp images of stained tumor slices, from the mark's hot spots. An expert marked each cell as lit or not by the stain. The set was grown and split for train, check, and test. Of the tool's forms, the mid one scored best on lit cells. The way gives a count labs can repeat.
arxiv-2503-19806:
Peyton Mullarkey and Sarah Marzen present new math for a kind of computing system in a 2025 paper. Reservoir computers feed signals into a fixed network and read the result at the output, which makes them cheap to train. Adding time delays to the network gives it more room to hold past signals, and that can boost its memory and its forecasts.

The authors derive exact formulas for how much such a system can remember and predict. The formulas rest on the spectrum of the input signal and on how the system passes signals through. Computer tests backed the formulas, even when the real system was not fully linear. The pair also checked whether using several delays helps, and found results much like those seen for messier systems. Their formulas give designers a way to judge a delayed system before building it.
arxiv-2503-20206:
Manh Mai Van and Tin Tran blend text meaning with past likes to sharpen product suggestions, in work from twenty twenty-five. Suggestion tools often learn from what users liked or bought before. That past-behaviour signal is called collaborative filtering. It can miss what an item is, since names and blurbs go unused. Text models can read those blurbs and judge how alike two items sound.

Their system, BeLightRec, feeds both signals into one graph network. One signal comes from shared user taste across items. The other comes from a BERT text model that reads item names and blurbs. The network learns weights that balance the two signals for each case. Tests are set up to weigh what each signal adds on its own. The aim is a light tool that still gives sharp, well-grounded picks. Readers get a clear recipe for mixing text and taste.
arxiv-2503-20406:
Marc Satkowski, Weizhou Luo, and Rufat Rzayev write a position paper on the misuse of affordances in augmented reality design, in two thousand twenty-five. Designers often borrow features of real objects to place digital content or give touch-like feedback. Used carelessly, those borrowed cues can confuse users and cause errors.

The authors name four fallacies in how affordances get facilitated. Affordances can be subjective, imposed on the wrong object, or reshaped by a changing setting. Copying the real world too closely is a further trap. Against each, they stress cues users can actually perceive and controls mapped to fitting physical features. The paper closes with a path toward more deliberate design.
arxiv-2503-21306:
Anunay Prasanna and co-authors pin down how a medical liquid behaves under sudden pressure, in a 2025 paper. Perfluorohexane forms the core of tiny agents that respond to sound in the body, but its basic physical data were missing, which hampered simulations of those agents. The team squeezed the liquid with shocks at pressures of a few hundred megapascals.

From the shock data they fitted a standard equation of state suited to flow simulations, using a search that balances several goals at once. They then simulated a shock wave passing through a droplet of the liquid and matched the result against real experiments. The close match supports using simulations to design these agents for clinical use.
arxiv-2503-21906:
Anand Balakrishnan and co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper on watching swarms and other spread-out cyber-physical systems for rule breaking. Their logic, STREL, states space-and-time requirements over shifting networks, like a drone flock keeping shape. The authors translate its statements into weighted alternating automata that encode both the yes-no and the graded meanings of the logic.

Those automata then drive both offline log checking and live monitoring. A simulated drone swarm shows the machinery working. The authors pitch the construction as a practical bridge between a rich spatial logic and tools that can actually run it.
arxiv-2503-22006:
Marc Brinner, Tarek Al Mustafa, and Sina Zarrieß use text written by large language models to sharpen small specialist models, in this 2025 paper. Their test domain is invasion biology, where training data are scarce. An ontology of the field's concepts anchors the approach: model generated definitions enrich it, and the small encoder learns as an ontology informed embedding model.

On a benchmark built for the domain, the method beat standard continued pretraining by a wide margin. The authors then asked whether the ontology is dispensable. Concepts pulled automatically from a small set of abstracts, linked by distributional statistics, performed about as well. That yields a fully automated pipeline that rivals pretraining on far larger corpora. The work targets low resource specialties where big data will never exist.
arxiv-2503-22106:
Granados and co-authors study how space-time couplings shape vortex light beams and their harmonics, in this 2025 paper. When an intense vortex beam hits matter, it can emit light at multiples of its base frequency. The beam's twist in space and time affects what comes out.

The team show how those couplings shape the brightness pattern and the pitch shifts of the harmonic beams. By reading the shifts they tie each harmonic trait back to a coupling in the driver. They check the process close to the source and far away, and name when the two views agree. The work aims to settle clashing readings in the field.
arxiv-2503-22306:
Francesco Sylos Labini and co-authors untangle two effects that bend the measured motions of galaxy discs. A disc can warp like a vinyl record left in the sun, or its stars can stream inward and outward. From Earth we see only the line-of-sight part of the motion, and each story can mimic the other.

Working with toy disc models, the team shows that a true warp leaves a dipolar fingerprint between the two velocity components read under a flat-disc assumption. They then scan real velocity fields from the THINGS survey and the galaxy M33. Many discs carry the fingerprint, so warps are common. Yet warps alone cannot explain all the wiggles, hinting that inner disturbances stir most discs as well.
arxiv-2503-22906:
Heng Yu and co-authors introduce SocialGen, a model that generates social interaction among several people at once, guided by language. Most earlier systems handle only pairs. SocialGen instead tokenizes the motions of any number of people in a shared format aligned with words. That alignment lets the model borrow the rich knowledge stored in pretrained language models to reason about social behavior.

Data for groups is scarce, so the team built SocialX, a multi-human interaction data set enriched with text notes. On it they set up the first broad benchmark for multi-human tasks. SocialGen reached state-of-the-art results across motion-language tests. The authors present the model and data set together as a new standard base for studying how groups of people move, react, and coordinate, with uses from animation to social robotics.
arxiv-2503-23206:
Two players sharing an entangled quantum system can sometimes win coordination games that classical players cannot. Demian Banakh and co-authors ask when that quantum edge is an illusion. They study games built from constraint satisfaction problems, where a perfect quantum strategy exists.

Their answer: any such perfect quantum win can be matched by classical players given an extra communication channel. The channel's size depends only on the shared quantum system's size and the problem's shape, not on the game's length. The proof characterizes perfect classical strategies with help channels, then rounds the quantum measurements into classical form. A side result bounds the gap between classical and quantum coloring numbers for graphs.
arxiv-2503-23306:
Youxiang Zhu, Ruochen Li, Danqing Wang, Daniel Haehn, and Xiaohui Liang wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It traces why long-context language models get distracted, to a small crew of attention heads, and finds a way to steer them.

Long inputs bury the key facts in noise. The authors spot the contextual heads, the few that set where the model looks as a whole. Distraction strikes when those heads short the key spans. Inside their key and query states sit focus directions, pushes that lift attention to the right spans without naming them. Across long-context tasks the pushes mend much of the drift. The find could guide fresh work on how long-context models are aligned.
arxiv-2503-23406:
Anbang Du, Michael Head, and Markus Brede map topic networks to show top medical journals publish less interdisciplinary work, in work from twenty twenty-five. Interdisciplinary blending drives many scientific advances forward. Prestige, though, may reward narrow depth over broad mixing. Topic correlation networks are built from journal publications. Prestigious and ordinary journals are compared on mixing measures.

Elite journals' research blends topics less than the field norm. Cancer research drives most interdisciplinarity across medicine overall. Topic correlation patterns overlap weakly between prestige tiers. Infection, nerve disease, and cancer topics differ most between tiers. Easing rigid boundaries at top journals could help science. Prestige incentives may be taxing knowledge integration quietly.
arxiv-2503-23906:
Repeating a function-based operation again and again can drift in ways that pure algebra struggles to rank.
