Angela Albanese and Héctor Ariza study those repeats for a class of ultra-smooth functions in a 2025 paper. The functions live in Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which stay closed under the Fourier swap of time and frequency.

The pair ask which input curves make the repeat chain settle into a rankable, topological form. For curves above first degree, the chain always settles in the settings they test. A stronger ranked form, though, can fail, unlike in the classic Schwartz setting. For straight-line inputs, they give a full test for both forms. The work maps where control holds.
arxiv-2503-24006:
Safa Alsaidi and co-authors test ways to match an anonymous clinic note to the right patient, in a 2025 paper. Hospitals need that match to spot duplicate records and to group a patient's notes. Long notes strain models that read text in fixed windows.

The team compared stacked attention networks, layered Transformers, a long-window model, and current BERT-style encoders. They also tried three ways to pool word scores into one patient fingerprint, plus sliding windows over long notes. BERT-style encoders won overall, above all on long texts. Mixing mean and max pooling worked best. Results held on both a public data set and a Paris hospital warehouse, which bodes well for real record rooms.
arxiv-2504-00006:
Samuel Allen Alexander asks whether an equation can draw itself, and then shows why the famous version of the question is broken. Tupper's self-referential formula went viral in 2012 for seeming to print its own formula on a graph. Alexander argues the puzzle is both meaningless, since it leans on font choices, and trivial once the trick is seen. A careful formal statement replaces the internet version.

Under the repaired definitions, a very general construction answers yes. The machinery comes from computability theory, the study of what functions machines can in principle compute. Self-description, handled honestly, turns out to be broad rather than rare.
arxiv-2504-00406:
Han, Buntine, and Shareghi build VerifiAgent, a system that checks the reasoning of large language models. Language models often produce answers that sound right but are wrong. Older checkers tend to fit one model or one subject area. VerifiAgent instead works at two levels.

The first level reviews a response for completeness and consistency. The second level picks a checking tool that fits the task, whether math, logic, or common sense. Tests show the agent beats earlier verifiers across reasoning tasks. Its feedback can also improve the model's next answer. The team reports better results with fewer samples than process reward models need.
arxiv-2504-00706:
Rakshanda Goswami and co-authors refine a key correction for lepton-proton scattering at very low energy. Their 2025 paper deals with two-photon exchange, a small effect that shapes how a lepton bounces off a proton. The work is aimed at the MUSE experiment, which needs a clean estimate of this effect.

The team works within heavy baryon chiral theory, a method for low-energy particle physics. A soft-photon shortcut turns hard loop sums into simpler ones. They use a stronger way to solve those sums and add higher-order fixes. Those fixes include how the proton's own structure changes its links to light. The result gives a model-free estimate of the charge gap between lepton and anti-lepton scattering, a value tests can check.
arxiv-2504-00906:
Saaket Agashe and co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, an agent that works a computer by its screen, with tasks split by skill. Such agents can do open user jobs on phones and desktops. Three faults dog them: clicks land off the mark, long plans drift, and one do-all model tires on mixed work. Agent S2 splits the load across broad and niche models. A mix-of-grounding step pins each screen part to its true spot. Plans are set in ranks and are reworked on the fly as the screen shifts.

On the OSWorld bench, the agent beat the best past agents by 18.9 and 32.7 percent at two step caps. It also led on Windows and Android test fields, by wide spans.
arxiv-2504-01006:
Mario Gleirscher and Philip Honnecke build controllers for safety-critical machines with provable guarantees in a 2025 study. Cyber-physical systems such as autonomous aircraft need controllers that reach goals while avoiding danger. Reinforcement learning can perform well but explains its safety poorly, which troubles high-integrity uses.

The authors revisit exhaustive search as an alternative that needs no prior training. Their model casts the setting as a hybrid game, and a dynamic programming method solves discretized games online with shielding steps. Tests use an autonomous aerial vehicle scenario. The parametric design aims for near-best performance plus guarantees a reviewer can inspect.
arxiv-2504-01106:
Jędrzej Stempin and co-authors reset quantum systems with a trick from automata theory in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. In classical automata, a synchronizing word is a rule sequence that drives any start state to one fixed state. Quantum evolution, being reversible, seems to forbid such resetting.

Their protocol gives each rule to an extra qubit, so the word lives in the quantum system itself. They design a circuit that runs the protocol on a quantum computer. A link to Kraus channels shows the trick works without reading the extra qubits' states. The authors bridge classical and quantum notions of synchronization.
arxiv-2504-01306:
Yonglin Wang, Xu-Tao Zeng, Bo Li, Cheng Su, Takanori Hattori, Xian-Lei Sheng, and Wentao Jin squeeze a layered magnet under pressure in a 2025 paper. The material is a van der Waals ferromagnet with a high Curie point. It suits spintronic devices and shrugs off air exposure. Theory said pressure would reshape its magnetism.

Neutron scattering tracked the magnet up to five gigapascals. Its ferromagnetism proved robust under that squeeze. The Curie temperature still slid steadily downward with pressure. The ordered iron moment shrank dramatically as well. No structural phase change appeared in the range. Bond shifts explain the weaker exchange forces, they argue.
arxiv-2504-01406:
Guang-Xin Pang and Yi-Cai Zhang solved a flow puzzle in a superfluid in two thousand twenty-five. A superfluid flows without friction at near-zero temperature. Their superfluid carries spin as well as mass flow. They found a steady one-dimensional solution to its flow equations. In that solution, magnetization grows in direct proportion to density. Mass and magnetic patterns are locked together.

The problem can be viewed as a particle orbiting a center. Those orbits come out elliptical in shape. A steady mass current makes the orbit precess. The three magnetization parts then cycle at mismatched periods. That mismatch is what incommensurate means here. The work shows how flow twists magnetic order in quantum fluids. It may inform cold-atom experiments with spinful gases.
arxiv-2504-01806:
Yue Wang, Haoyu Wang, and Zhaoxing Li present Quattro, a faster control framework for robots, in a paper from 2025. Robots must plan smooth paths in real time, even when their motion is complex. A classic method, called iLQR, works step by step in order, which makes it slow.

Past parallel versions needed extra rounds of math and strong hardware for small gains. Quattro uses a transformer model to predict key matrices ahead of time. That lets the steps run in parallel on modest devices. The design pairs the algorithm with the hardware it runs on. Fast path planning could help small robots react in tight, changing settings.
arxiv-2504-01906:
Mona Zavichi and four co-authors present a way to travel through virtual worlds using eyes and hands together, so users can look around freely while moving. Eye-only steering hijacks the view, hand-only steering lacks precision, and both make multitasking awkward. In their method, movement starts only when the user's gaze lands on a target the hand points at, blocking accidental drift. Speed is set by a joystick or a circle control at waist height.

Twenty volunteers tested the technique against a similar one in single-task and multitasking scenes. The gaze-hand method held its performance while improving comfort and awareness of surroundings during multitasking. The authors recommend it for virtual reality uses where eyes lead and hands must stay free for other work. They argue the design supports immersion because looking and steering stop competing for the same channel.
arxiv-2504-02106:
Xiao Wang and six co-authors present ContrastScore in two thousand twenty five. Auto grading of generated text still tracks human judgment poorly in practice. Reference based metrics correlate weakly with human scores. Language model judges help but smaller ones lag behind.

ContrastScore uses contrastive evaluation to sharpen the signal. Tests cover machine translation and summarization tasks. Correlation with human judgment beats single and ensemble baselines. Small Qwen builds outperform a larger Qwen judge here. Length and likelihood biases shrink under the method. Quality, fairness, and efficiency improve together in the results.
arxiv-2504-02606:
Jonas Teufel, Annika Leinweber, and Pascal Friederich published this machine learning paper in 2025. It concerns computer models that predict the properties of molecules, and the short explanations offered for those predictions. An explanation often names the smallest change to a molecule that would shift the predicted value most. The authors argue that such an explanation is only useful if the new value still reflects the true property.

The team proposes filtering candidate changes with an estimate of how unsure the model is about each one. Changes the model is unsure about are dropped before an explanation is chosen. In tests on both made-up and real data, simple methods such as averaging several models cut prediction error and made the explanations more truthful. The gain was largest for molecules unlike those the model was trained on.
arxiv-2504-02806:
Rajat Adak and L Sunil Chandran sharpen a classic result in graph theory, in a 2025 paper. Turán's theorem caps how many edges a graph can hold without containing a full clique of a set size. The usual cap leans only on the graph's size and that clique limit, which wastes what each point knows about its own largest clique.

For each point, the pair define its clique number from the largest clique holding it. Their new cap sums a simple fraction over all points, then halves it. They also pin down exactly which graphs meet the cap, and the family holds two extra graphs beyond the known Turán shapes. The result ties the edge limit to local structure.
arxiv-2504-03206:
Wan and four co-authors made chatbots more personal by rewarding curiosity in twenty twenty-five. Helpful, safe responses are not the same as empathetic, adaptive conversation. Existing personalization leans on long user histories, which new users lack.

Their approach plugs a user model into reinforcement learning from human feedback. The chatbot earns an intrinsic curiosity reward when its questions improve the user model's accuracy about the user's traits, so it actively learns preferences during the conversation itself. Tests covered conversational recommendation and tutoring adapted to learning styles. Personalization improved significantly in both, generalization beat standard multi-turn training, and conversation quality held up. The authors offer curiosity rewards as a route to agents that learn who they are talking to while they talk.
arxiv-2504-03806:
A. V. Minkevich reviews a gauge theory of gravity built on a spacetime with torsion in a 2025 theoretical physics study. In Riemann-Cartan geometry, spacetime can twist as well as curve, and a gauge approach treats gravity like the other fundamental forces. The author sets out the theory's place among gauge approaches and builds cosmology from a general gravitational Lagrangian with free parameters.

Consequences include a possible ceiling on energy density, gravitational repulsion under extreme conditions, and a vacuum repulsion effect. Such features could remove the initial singularity and mimic cosmic acceleration. The review weighs which of those claims survive physical scrutiny.
arxiv-2504-03906:
Abhilekh Borah, Hasnat Md Abdullah, Kangda Wei, and Ruihong Huang build a test for how AI models talk about climate change, in a 2025 paper. Climate debate fills social media, often through memes and skeptical posts, and it was unclear whether large language models boost solid answers or empty claims. The team gathered a dataset of more than two and a half thousand posts from Twitter and Reddit.

They also created a scoring yardstick with five parts, covering clarity, evidence, and how concrete a reply is, among others. Judged through three lenses, most models did fairly well on fairness and critical thinking but poorly on giving usable next steps. One named model scored highest overall. The team released the dataset and code so others can keep testing how AI handles climate talk.
arxiv-2504-04506:
Labeling data costs money, so active learning picks the examples most worth labeling by hand. It struggles when the budget allows few labels, and wobbles further when the labeler errs. Netta Shafir, Guy Hacohen and Daphna Weinshall propose Noise-Aware Active Sampling, a framework that adapts coverage-based selection to noisy labeling. Coverage methods spread chosen examples across the dataset. When a noisy example becomes a region's representative, that region ends up falsely covered.

Their framework spots those falsely covered regions and samples from them again. A simple noise filter from the same mechanism cleans labels before training. On standard image benchmarks, including a hundred-class dataset and subsets of a large photo collection, the method lifted the performance of standard active learning across noise types and noise rates. The authors present it as a practical patch for learning when labels are few and imperfect.
arxiv-2504-04606:
Deformed algebras tweak the usual rules of algebra and have been proposed as tools for quantum physics. Julio Cesar Jaramillo Quiceno and Plamen Neytchev Nechev examine those proposals with strict methods in a 2025 paper. They rebuild a special kind of integral, the Jackson integral, inside a carefully equipped space framework, using point measures where the construction allows.

Along the way, they correct mistakes and loose claims they found in earlier works they cite. Their closing analysis is cautious: real obstacles remain before deformed algebras can be applied soundly to quantum mechanics and field theory. The paper serves as both a repair job and a warning.
arxiv-2504-04906:
Linard Hoessly writes in 2025 about a widely used score for yes-or-no forecasts in medical research. The Brier score grades how close predicted chances land to real outcomes. Its meaning, though, clashes with ideas taught in standard medical statistics, so readers often get it wrong.

Hoessly sets out to name the common misreadings and clear them up. The paper explains what the score does and does not say, in terms working clinicians and researchers can use. The aim is practical: better reading of a score that appears in many clinical prediction papers, where a wrong reading can bend real choices about care.
arxiv-2504-05006:
Jiuyang Bu and four co-authors use fine tuned language models to find flaws in smart contracts in a 2025 paper. Decentralized apps rest on these contracts, and logic flaws such as price manipulation escape classic checkers. The team build a data set from hundreds of real projects with thousands of contracts, including hard cases that simple benchmarks miss.

They fine tune two open models with two methods and add a sampling trick to balance rare flaw types. Their best setup beat prompt based models and leading tools on a standard score. It was especially strong at spotting price manipulation flaws, with high precision.
arxiv-2504-05306:
Kavana Venkatesh, Connor Dunlop, and Pinar Yanardag set out a fresh task for image tools in a 2025 paper: creative editing. Plain edits follow a direct prompt, such as swapping a color. Creative edits ask for more, namely fresh and rich changes that still fit the first image and its aim.

Their system, called CREA, splits the work among a team of smart agents. The agents dream up ideas, build drafts, judge them, and polish the best ones in rounds. That loop copies how human artists work side by side. In both scored tests and plain review, the system beat top past methods on variety, fit to the prompt, and flair.
arxiv-2504-05506:
Ahmed Masry and a team of co-authors release ChartQAPro, a harder test for systems that answer questions about charts. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that charts fill reports and dashboards everywhere. Reading them well takes sharp eyes and hard thought. The older ChartQA test has grown too easy for top vision-language models.

The new set gathers charts from many sources and types, from plain plots to dashboards. Its questions span choice tasks, chat-style turns, what-if cases, and traps with no answer. The team ran a wide set of models on it. Scores fell hard versus the old test. One top model dropped from above ninety percent to the mid-fifties. Error studies map where models fail. The set aims to push chart reading toward real-world skill.
arxiv-2504-05606:
Nawapan Wattanawanichkul gives a new proof of regions where certain L-functions cannot vanish, in a 2025 mathematics paper. Zero-free regions for these functions guard deep facts about prime numbers and automorphic forms. The proof covers an L-function alone and the product of two, when the objects involved are self-dual in the stated ways.

The approach borrows the pretentious view of multiplicative functions developed by Granville and Soundararajan, as presented by Koukoulopoulos, and a notion of positive semi-definite families of automorphic representations from Lichtman and Pascadi. The author presents the metric viewpoint as a cleaner path to a classic result, joining analytic number theory with representation theory.
arxiv-2504-05706:
Fida Mohammad Thoker and co-authors stress-test how well self-taught video models travel beyond their training pond, in this 2025 paper. Video models that learn without labels shine on standard action tests, but those tests use near-identical training and scoring sets. The team broadens an earlier sensitivity study to modern transformer models, both video-only and video-text, plus older convolutional rivals. Over eleven hundred runs span eight datasets and seven tasks.

Four pressures are applied: new domains, fewer training samples, finer action classes, and new task types. No method held up across all four. Video-only transformers coped best with domain shift, plain convolutional nets won on fine-grained actions, and video-text models often lagged despite giant pretraining. Newer transformers did not reliably beat older ones.
arxiv-2504-05806:
Woo, Yun, and Kim teach neural fields to learn new scenes without forgetting old ones in a 2025 paper. Neural fields store images, sound, or scenes inside a network. When tasks arrive in a stream, old skills fade and learning crawls. The team sets this as a fresh problem and answers with a modular design plus meta-learning.

Their method rebuilds scenes with higher quality and far faster learning than prior routes. A new loss term rewards gains at each sample for light-based scene fields, with proof of sound behavior. Tests span images, audio, video, and view building across six data sets. City-scale scene rendering came with fewer parameters than rivals needed.
arxiv-2504-06206:
Some quantum models let particles hop one way around a loop more easily than the other, breaking the usual rules of Hermitian physics. Eduard Naichuk and co-authors built a two-dimensional version of such a model and added electron repulsion. They asked whether magnetic order survives in a system that can gain and lose energy.

Antiferromagnetism, with neighboring spins opposed, does form. The model keeps a combined symmetry that splits its behavior in two: a region with real energies and a broken region with complex ones. The border between them coincides with the switch from metal to insulator, tuned by the repulsion strength. Spin waves come in paired diffusive modes, one tied to gain, one to loss.
arxiv-2504-06306:
Polycarp Nalela, Deepthi Rao, and Praveen Rao use machine learning to predict survival in spread cancer in a 2025 paper. Their data set joins gene and clinical records for more than 25,000 patients across 27 cancer types.

Five models were tuned and compared on the task. A boosting model won, with a solid score for telling survivors from non-survivors. An explanation tool then showed which traits drove its calls. The number of spread sites, tumor mutation load, and the share of the genome changed ranked high. Classic survival methods backed several of these signals. The authors say such ranked risks can guide personal care plans.
arxiv-2504-06406:
Ziqian Liu and co-authors build a city scale mesh network in a 2025 paper. When disaster cuts wide area links, phones and Wi-Fi boxes still dot a city. Their system, MapMesh, links those fixed access points and moving devices into one network that routes packets among themselves and to any node that still reaches the internet, such as by satellite.

The core advance is a routing method that scales to millions of nodes, far past past mesh designs. It exploits map data on buildings, now widely available at scale, to predict which links can work. That map sense lets the protocol pick paths that dodge blocked lines of sight.
arxiv-2504-06506:
Christoph Fischbacher, Fritz Gesztesy, and Lance Littlejohn review product rules for defect numbers in a 2025 paper. The paper is largely a teaching piece. Defect numbers measure how far a closed operator sits from being fully well behaved, and they matter when operators are multiplied together. The authors gather known facts on how defect numbers behave for products.

Their tools come from the theory of semi-Fredholm operators, a class with well mapped behavior. They apply the product facts to whole-number powers of symmetric operators. They then turn to minimal Sturm-Liouville operators and to higher even-order operators, in both ordinary and partial differential form. Along the way, they flag chances that past research groups missed when similar work was compared side by side.
arxiv-2504-07106:
Adam McCabe and Matthew Chequers coin in a 2025 paper entity entropy, a measure of how scattered a topic's knowledge sits across company documents. Firms generate webs of linked content that language models struggle to search well. Some entities are simply harder to retrieve than others, and the gap was unmeasured.

Their score counts how an entity's facts spread across the document pile. On a large enterprise corpus, entropy runs heavy tailed across entities. Bigger entities tend to carry higher entropy, and content classes show set patterns. A generative model in the diffusion style is offered to explain those patterns. The upshot is entity aware retrieval for the hard cases, not a blanket fix.
arxiv-2504-07306:
Carolina Benedetti and three co-authors study an order on matroids in twenty twenty-five. Matroid quotients connect to deep questions about flag variety geometry. For lattice path matroids, earlier work characterized quotients by a simple combinatorial condition. The resulting quotient order is a graded poset whose rank polynomial refines the Catalan numbers.

The authors show this poset admits an EL-labeling. That labeling implies the order complex is shellable, a strong structural property. Shellability brings several combinatorial and topological benefits with it. They also bound the poset's Möbius function through falling chains in the labeling. Those chains are read through properties of the underlying permutations. The labeling turns out to be a Whitney labeling as well.
arxiv-2504-07406:
Yu-Hua Chen and five co-authors work on automatically transcribing amplified electric guitar recordings into notes. Amps, cabinets, and pedals reshape tone so much that models trained on narrow data fail on new rigs. Diverse training data were the first bottleneck.

They built EGDB-PG, a dataset spanning many amplifier and cabinet combinations to capture that tonal variety. Their Tone-informed Transformer adds a learned tone embedding so the model can adapt to each setup's character. Trained on the new dataset, it beat existing baselines across amplifier types. Ablation studies separated the contributions of tone and content augmentation, normalization, and the tone embedding itself.
arxiv-2504-07606:
Andrés Bell-Navas and co-authors predict not just whether a heart will fail, but when, from ultrasound videos of the beating heart. Echocardiography databases are usually too small to train deep networks well, which blocks such forecasts. Their 2025 system attacks the data problem first, using a modal decomposition method to multiply and mine the video frames, turning each study into many annotated images rich in motion features.

A vision transformer then learns from those images under a masked autoencoder scheme, mixing self-supervised pretraining with supervised fine-tuning so it can train from scratch on scarce data. The network reads echo sequences in real time and estimates the time to failure. Across tests it beat established transformer and convolutional rivals. The authors fold the code into their open ModelFLOWs software for others to use.
arxiv-2504-07906:
Takahisa Igata studies how light bends when it grazes a black hole or star in a 2025 paper. As a light ray's path nears a critical ring, its bend grows without bound in a smooth, log-shaped way. Two numbers set that growth: a slope and an offset.

Working with steady, symmetric spacetimes, Igata writes both numbers from the local curve of space at the unstable light ring. One piece gauges tidal pull, the other the local push of matter and pressure. The same numbers feed the pitch of the ring's fading tones, which ties lensing to the sounds such bodies ring with after a shake.
arxiv-2504-08006:
Petri nets are a classic tool for modeling systems that reason and act step by step, but plain nets know nothing about the meanings of the things they move. Krzysztof Pancerz blends them with ontologies, structured webs of concepts and relations drawn from the OWL 2 web language. In these nets the tokens and places carry that meaning with them.

The paper lays out the basic theory of such nets and then presents a working Python toolkit for them. Users can define both the structure of a net and how it runs, while the ontology supplies semantic links in the background. The aim is richer models for reasoning and control processes. Domain knowledge, once locked in documents, becomes part of the machine that thinks with it.
arxiv-2504-09606:
Lexington Whalen and five co-authors, including Yingyan Lin, look for sparse subnetworks inside diffusion models that appear early in training and still generate well. Training these models is expensive because every step runs many timesteps. Pruning to an early-bird ticket could cut that cost sharply.

The team first confirms that ordinary early-bird tickets exist in diffusion models. They then refine the idea: timesteps matter unequally, so sparsity should be aggressive in unimportant ranges and gentle in critical ones. Their training scheme derives such timestep-aware tickets, trains them in parallel, and merges them for generation. Experiments support the efficiency gains, and the method combines with other acceleration techniques.
arxiv-2504-09706:
Matthew Repasky and three co-authors modeled how coatings break down, in a 2025 paper. Knowing when a coating will fail guides repairs and saves material. Sensors can track wear at fine detail, but the flood of readings makes forecasting hard.

The team turned steady sensor data into a short list of wear events that keep the key traits of the full record. A process that lets past events raise the chance of new ones then models those events over time. Forecasts from this lean record beat forecasts built on the full sensor stream for picking a failure date. The authors link the method to care that is done when needed, not on a fixed clock.
arxiv-2504-09806:
Albert Schwarz asks whether quantum theory can be forced on an observer who lives inside a classical world near equilibrium. He considers Hamiltonian systems with a non-degenerate minimum at zero momentum and position, where the sum of squares of momenta and coordinates is conserved. Near that point the quadratic part of the Hamiltonian dominates everything.

Suppose a classical observer can only measure quantities tied to quadratic Hamiltonians. Schwarz argues such an observer must describe his world with the laws of quantum theory. The catalog entry buries the author inside affiliation and email text; the head byline names Albert Schwarz of the University of California, Davis.
arxiv-2504-10006:
Valentin Charvet and co-authors recast robot control problems in dimensionless form so learned controllers travel better to new settings, in a 2025 paper. Controllers trained by reinforcement learning often fail when the test setup differs from training. The team's fix trains both the world model and the policy in scaled, unit-free variables, using a classic physics scaling theorem.

Their framework extends contextual decision processes with that scaling step, which makes policies respond evenly to context changes. A model-based search method with Gaussian process models carries the approach. On simulated pendulum and cartpole systems, policies trained in one setting held up when the setting's distribution shifted.
arxiv-2504-10106:
Marc Gutiérrez-Pérez and Antonio Agudo build datasets for 3D soccer analysis in this 2025 paper. Broadcast soccer video holds rich spatial detail across many camera views. Turning that footage into 3D knowledge needs matched views and known camera settings.

Their datasets, SoccerNet-v3D and ISSIA-3D, extend older soccer sets with field-line camera calibration. Views are synced so the ball can be located by triangulation. A new task asks for the ball's 3D position from a single image. Their baseline method uses camera data and ball size to make that guess. A box refinement step aligns 2D marks with the 3D scene.
arxiv-2504-10206:
Arpan Dey, Sathish Kumar, and Devaraj prove in a 2025 math paper approximation rates for neural network sampling operators in mixed Lebesgue spaces. Mixed norms weigh functions differently along each axis of the domain. Rates are stated through an averaged smoothness gauge for bounded measurable functions.

Finiteness of that gauge is first shown for the right function subspaces. Linear operator rates in the mixed norm follow from the gauge's properties. A Jackson type theorem then characterizes the network operators' speed by the same gauge. Example activation curves, all sigmoidal, ground the abstract result in usable shapes. Both smooth and jumpy target functions are built by the operators in closing examples.
arxiv-2504-10406:
Nicholas Wawrykow, a mathematician, tackles the shape of spaces formed by sets of points on a surface, in a 2025 paper. Such point-set spaces matter in topology, the study of shapes, and in planning how robots can move without colliding. Blocky stand-in models exist for points on graphs and disks in the plane, but not for most surfaces.

Wawrykow builds the missing model for ordered sets of points on a surface that has a chosen direction. He tiles the surface with cubes and shows the true space can be bent, without tearing, into a blocky subspace of a grid of those cubes. The result gives researchers a finite, hands-on object they can compute with, instead of a smooth space that resists direct study.
arxiv-2504-10506:
Yuan Yuan, Yuheng Zhang, Jingtao Ding, and Yong Li build a worldwide open data set of human movement in a 2025 paper. Planners and health officials need such data, but privacy rules and cost leave poor regions with almost none.

Their synthetic set covers more than sixteen hundred cities in 179 countries. A diffusion based model learned from public inputs: population grids, maps of points of interest, and commuting flows between areas. It then generates day long movement paths for fake residents that behave like real ones. Checks show the paths match real world patterns at both the person and city scale. The trained model and full pipeline are released for anyone to make data for any city.
arxiv-2504-10606:
Milica Banic and co-authors present an exact way to simulate a prized quantum resource in a 2025 paper. The resource is the GKP state, a pattern of light that can correct its own errors, and its cluster form links many such states for quantum computing. Real versions are imperfect, and the standard simulation basis is too slow to cover the cases that matter.

Their method writes each resource state as a sum of Gaussian humps in phase space, which computers can handle exactly and fast. They use it to study making single GKP states by breeding cat states, and building multi-mode clusters with optical circuits and measurements. Scores from stabilizer measures match the slow standard simulations. They also test a popular noise shortcut against the exact answers and find gaps, a warning for designers who trust the shortcut.
arxiv-2504-10706:
Ram and colleagues introduce in 2025 GestureCoach, a rehearsal system that teaches speakers to gesture well using language model guidance. It was trained on how expert TED speakers move. One module spots note passages worth a gesture. Another picks a fitting gesture from a curated library. In tests, the spotter beat general-purpose models at choosing gesture moments.

Speakers rated most suggested moments and gestures as apt. Rehearsing with the system made people gesture more and with more variety, and talks felt more engaging. The authors draw lessons for future AI rehearsal tools.
arxiv-2504-10906:
Language models can fetch facts across languages, and Changjiang Gao and co-authors measure how in a 2025 paper. More than forty models faced reading tests in twelve languages, answering in one tongue from passages in another. Post-trained open models matched top closed ones at the task.

Two phases split the skill: grasping the question forms in pre-training, while fetching the answer is shaped later. Steadier phasing tracks better scores. The bottleneck sits in the last layers during the fetching phase. Knowing where cross-lingual skill lives helps builders fix it without retraining whole models.
arxiv-2504-11006:
Mingshuo Han, Shiwei Hu, Tianbai Xiao, and Yonghao Zhang present a hybrid method for simulating fast flows that break solid materials. Their 2025 paper joins two solvers at a fine scale. One handles compressible gas flow with a method rooted in molecular theory, and the other handles damage in solids without a mesh.

The two fields update together at each time step, swapping boundary data through a ghost-cell technique. Tests include a cracking plate, flow around a wing profile, supersonic flow past a cylinder, and a shock wave hitting an elastic panel. Results matched the hybrid method's aims across those varied cases. Such coupling matters in aerospace work, where high-speed flow and breaking parts meet in real failures.
arxiv-2504-11306:
Trinnhallen Brisley and co-authors improve palmprint recognition, in a paper published in 2025. Palm scanners identify people by the lines and ridges of the palm. Standard matching compares two prints directly, by angle or distance, which can miss how a score stacks up against every other identity in the database.

Their relative similarity metric judges each pair's score in the context of all scores, which suppresses false matches and false misses. Laid on top of a recent network design, it reached a near-zero error rate on a public palm dataset, beating prior methods. The gain came from the matching rule, not a bigger network. Such relative scoring could strengthen other biometric systems where one odd score can fool a fixed threshold.
arxiv-2504-11406:
Felipe Salvagnini and co-authors blend two light methods for finding salient objects in images, in a 2025 paper. Deep learning for this task usually needs many labeled images and heavy networks. That is a poor fit for medical imaging in places with modest computers. One classical method, FLIM, lets experts design image filters from hand-drawn marks.

FLIM networks can pair with a decoder to form tiny models that skip backpropagation entirely. Cellular automata, another classic tool, excel with little data but need a good starting state. The authors use each layer of a FLIM network to seed the automata states with expert knowledge. No per-image user input is needed after setup. The blend targets strong results on a small budget.
arxiv-2504-11606:
Ruoqi Zhao, Hengyuan Shen, Allen LaCour, Joseph Heindel, Martin Head-Gordon, and Teresa Head-Gordon test a romantic idea about why oil droplets in water repel: maybe electrons themselves leak from water into oil. Emulsion droplets carry negative surface charge, and its molecular origin is contested. Ions gathering at the interface are the conventional suspect. Charge transfer across weak carbon-hydrogen to oxygen contacts is the challenger.

Energy decomposition analysis delivers the verdict. Forward and backward charge flows through those weak contacts nearly cancel, leaving a negligible net transfer. Droplets charged only that way would coalesce, contradicting experiment. The same analysis explains a spectroscopic blue shift as Pauli repulsion from interfacial confinement. Neither transfer nor polarization yields the conductivity that electrophoretic mobility requires. Ions keep their crown.
arxiv-2504-11806:
Sayantan Mondal and Prasenjit Das wrote this 2025 physics paper on mixtures of two kinds of self-moving particles. Such active matter can sort itself into rich and lean zones, an effect called motility-induced phase separation. Here the two species can also turn into each other through a chemical reaction. The authors ask how that switching reshapes the sorted pattern.

Starting from the density equations for the sorting, they add a reaction rate term. When the rate is high and one species moves more, the busier species forms droplets. Domains grow with a slow one-third power law in time before settling. The final domain size shrinks as the reaction rate rises, following a clean power rule that holds regardless of the activity gap.
arxiv-2504-11906:
Katarzyna Macioszek, Farzad Sabzikar, and Krzysztof Burnecki set out tests for a class of random motion models. Their twenty twenty-five paper deals with tempered fractional Brownian motion. These models show long memory that fades, and spread that is faster or slower than normal for a while.

The tests rest on three tools that track how values link over time and how far paths wander. The authors cover three forms of the model, each with tempering built in a distinct way. Charts of quantile lines show how each form behaves. A power study shows the tests can tell apart models with distinct memory settings.
arxiv-2504-12006: Held and co-authors (2025) reply to two recent papers that challenged asymptotic safety, a candidate theory of quantum gravity. Asymptotic safety aims to give a predictive quantum theory of gravity and matter. Two works published in 2024 argued against the scenario. In this short comment, the authors state that those challenges fail at a basic level. The head of the text gives no detail on the disputed points or on the rebuttal itself, so the comment's specific arguments cannot be summarized from the evidence provided here.
arxiv-2504-12106:
Crystal bases are combinatorial skeletons of quantum group representations, and the largest of them, B(∞), carries a two-sided structure called a bicrystal. Taehyeok Heo gives a new description of that object in a 2025 paper, building on its polyhedral picture.

Heo defines fresh crystal maps on B(∞) from the polyhedral realization and proves the result matches Kashiwara's original bicrystal. The structure is then spelled out as a sliding diamond rule, a concrete recipe for how the maps move between elements. With that recipe in hand, Heo defines an extended crystal and shows it agrees with the version Kashiwara and Park introduced. The work gives algebraists a more hands-on model of a central object.
arxiv-2504-12206:
Yuping Yang proves a classification result about Nichols algebras, algebraic structures that sit at the heart of quantum group theory. The question is which of these algebras stay finite in a growth measure called Gelfand-Kirillov dimension. Yang works in a twisted category tied to a finite abelian group and a twisting function, focusing on objects that are not of diagonal type.

The main theorem says every pre-Nichols algebra of such a nondiagonal object grows without bound in that measure. From this it follows that a Nichols algebra in this setting has finite dimension of growth exactly when it is of diagonal type with a finite root system. Through a standard construction, the result classifies a family of pointed coquasi-Hopf algebras built from group-like and skew-primitive elements. The paper settles which members of this family can stay small.
arxiv-2504-12406:
Perseas Christodoulidis, Robert Rosati, and Evangelos Sfakianakis studied early universe inflation with many fields tied non-minimally to gravity in a 2025 paper. Multi-field models usually give scattered predictions, unless a strong attractor tames them. This family, motivated by rich particle spectra at high energy, turns out to have exactly that taming.

As long as one coupling to curvature is large, the single-field and many-field predictions for microwave background observables come out identical. Simple formulas give the expansion scale, the duration count, and the turn rate for any number of fields. The authors also explored how statistical priors over the fields shift the outcome spread. The result rescues a whole model family for testing against sky data.
arxiv-2504-12606:
Lv and co-authors present a 2025 computer vision paper on scene graph systems that must survive damaged images. Scene graphs list the objects in a picture and how they relate. Rain, blur, and occlusion shift image features and wreck accuracy. Their plug-in module, Robo-SGG, leans on layout, the global arrangement that corruption barely touches.

A normalization step strips domain quirks, and a restitution step rebuilds sturdy structural features. An encoder then blends layout with visual features through a learned gate. The module bolts onto existing scene graph models without redesign. Wide tests on corrupted sets show clear robustness gains. The authors pitch layout as the anchor for vision under bad conditions.
arxiv-2504-13106:
Subrata Manna settles a fifteen-year-old conjecture about how two geometric objects can overlap in this 2025 paper. The objects live in a finite projective space: a Hermitian variety, a curved shape defined over a squared finite field, and a hypersurface of a given degree. The 2010 conjecture said the overlap is largest only for one neat arrangement of flat pieces.

Manna proves the conjecture when the hypersurface has degree three and the field is not too small. In the winning arrangement, three hyperplanes fan through one shared lower space, tangent or not depending on dimension parity. The result closes a case in finite geometry with ties to coding theory. Degree three is the first degree where the pattern truly bites.
arxiv-2504-13206:
Aniket Roy and co-authors present DuoLoRA, a method to personalize image models for content and style at once, in a research paper from 2025. Users may want a subject from a few photos rendered in a style from a few others. Training split adapters for content and style, then merging them, is a promising route, but past merges treat the two as independent.

Content and style in fact intertwine. DuoLoRA merges inside the rank dimension of the adapters, cutting learnable parameters. Layer priors from the base model guide how much rank each layer gives to content or style. A cycle-consistency loss refines the merge. Tests show cleaner joint personalization from few examples.
arxiv-2504-13706:
Gray Manicom and co-authors calibrate immunity inside agent based models of disease spread. Such models guide vaccine policy, but their immunity settings are tricky. Many vaccines leak: they cut risk per exposure rather than granting full armor. So the modeler's numbers must bend with exposure pressure and with the model's own rules.

The team first builds target immunity curves from real COVID data and immune studies. They then fit lean waning curves that hit those targets inside simulations. Household spread tests link per attempt protection to the overall immunity seen. The method accounts for network shape and the code's spread rules, giving policy models a firmer base.
arxiv-2504-13806:
Roberto Vila and Helton Saulo wrote a 2025 statistics paper on two well known measures of inequality. The Theil index and the Atkinson index sum up how unevenly income or wealth is spread. When the data follow a gamma form, the standard estimators of both indices carry bias.

The authors derive exact formulas for that bias in closed form. With those formulas in hand, they build corrected estimators that remove the bias. Simulation studies then test how well the corrected forms behave. The work gives analysts a cleaner way to report inequality when their data fit the gamma family.
arxiv-2504-14006: Zoé Chatzidakis and Nicholas Ramsey work in mathematical logic. In this 2025 arXiv paper they describe a way to build Keisler measures on bounded perfect PAC fields. As a payoff, they prove a broad amenability result. Every group that can be defined inside such a field is definably amenable. The same holds in a wider class of fields, the unbounded perfect Frobenius fields. The construction grows out of their earlier work on e-free PAC fields. It also builds on a related construction by Will Johnson.
arxiv-2504-14106:
Bulat Gafarov, Matthias Meier, and José Luis Montiel Olea wrote a paper in 2025 on projection inference for structural vector autoregressions. In these models the parameters of interest are set-identified rather than point-identified. Such models trace how economic shocks, such as shifts in labor supply or demand, move through an economy. In some, the values are pinned to a set of possible values, not a point.

The paper studies the classical projection method, which builds confidence regions covering both the structural impulse-response coefficients and their identified set. The authors show that, as the sample size grows, projection inference achieves at least the nominal level in two senses at once: frequentist coverage and robust Bayesian credibility. They calibrate the region's radius so that the robust Bayesian credibility is exact for a posterior. A demand and supply model of the United States labor market illustrates the method.
arxiv-2504-14206:
Wenxin Zhang and Cuicui Luo propose a transformer framework to spot anomalies in time series, in a 2025 paper. Real sequences hold diverse, complex patterns that are hard to model directly. Methods trained on squared error also suffer when the data are noisy, which dulls their detection power.

Their framework first splits each series into parts, then learns each part with a multi scale patch transformer. A contrast step aligns the clean patterns seen at unlike patch sizes. A new loss design with a stop gradient trick speeds training and lifts scores. Tests on five public data sets beat twelve rival methods on the F1 score.
arxiv-2504-14406:
Making sense of large document sets is slow, central work for qualitative researchers. Runlong Ye and co-authors present ScholarMate, a tool that mixes AI help with human control. On a free-form canvas, users arrange text snippets by hand while the system suggests themes, builds summaries at several levels, and proposes theme names backed by evidence.

Every suggestion stays linked to its source documents, so users can check the trail. In pilot studies, users prized the balance between machine suggestions and direct handling, saying it kept the work clear and trustworthy. A case study on 24 papers showed the system handling a real analysis task. The authors frame the tool as support for human judgment, not a replacement for it.
arxiv-2504-14506:
Roberto Montemanni and Derek Smith solve a set covering problem where picked sets can clash, in a paper from 2025. Each set has a cost, each clash adds a fine, and the aim is to cover all items at the least total price.

Their route states the task as a compact mixed integer program and runs it on a free solver. On the standard bench sets used in past work, bounds and covers came out well, though short of the best known average. The solver did beat nine past best heuristic covers, a gain the authors note with care.
arxiv-2504-14706:
Shin-nosuke Ishikawa and Atsushi Yoshino test in 2025 whether large language models can act out set emotions. Public hopes for AI with feelings are rising as these models match human skill on many tasks. The team asked several leading models to answer questions while playing a given emotional state.

They set each state with a classic map of emotion that uses two scales: how pleasant it feels, and how stirred up it is. A separate sentiment tool, trained on a public set of labeled feelings, then scored the replies. The replies matched the states they were asked to play. The authors say this skill could support AI advisors that respond with a more personal touch.
arxiv-2504-14806:
Xiongwei Zhao and colleagues published a computer science paper in 2025 on robot navigation in bad weather. Self-driving systems use laser scans to recognize places they have visited. Rain, snow, and fog corrupt those scans with noise. Recognition then fails exactly when driving is hardest.

Their framework pairs a cleanup module with the recognition module. The two train together in alternating rounds. Cleaned scans help recognition stay accurate in storms. Recognition feedback, in turn, teaches cleanup what matters. Special blocks mix frequency and spatial features for the cleanup step. A semantic-aware generator rebuilds the damaged point clouds. The authors report stronger place recognition under harsh weather than earlier methods.
arxiv-2504-15206:
Sílvia Casacuberta, Parikshit Gopalan, Varun Kanade, and Omer Reingold study fairness conditions for predictors, in a paper published in 2025. Multiaccuracy asks that a predictor's averages be right within every group of interest, a weaker demand than full multicalibration. The question is how much learning power that weaker demand buys, alone or with calibration added.

Alone, multiaccuracy proves weak: no post-processing can turn such a predictor into a general weak learner. It does yield a restricted kind of learning, and only half-strength versions of certain hard-core measures. Adding global calibration changes the picture sharply. The combined condition recovers full agnostic learning and optimal hard-core measures, matching results once known only for the stronger condition. The work draws a clean line between the two fairness notions.
arxiv-2504-15506:
Paula Ferreira and co-authors map sound wave echoes from the young cosmos in sliced space data in a 2025 paper. The echo, a faint ring in how galaxies cluster, serves as a cosmic ruler, but it fades when slices are compared across distance.

They pair the standard galaxy density wobble with a newer redshift wobble in shells of distance. Forecasts show most of the ruler's news sits in the echo marks of the shell spectra. Joining the two probes boosts the news on key cosmic numbers by tenfold or more. Shell width and reach rules are mapped so surveys can plan well.
arxiv-2504-15706:
Mohammad Reza Deylam Salehi and Derya Malak study how cheaply two far-apart nodes can compute a function of their data, in this 2025 paper. Each node holds one of two correlated sources, and a receiver wants a function of both, computed almost without loss. The trick is to code the structure of the task itself, using characteristic graphs that capture which inputs must stay distinguishable.

The authors bound the best possible rate, expressed through the chromatic entropy of repeated graph products, for regular graphs and for general graphs. For cycle graphs they pin down the exact chromatic numbers and matching rate bounds. For wider classes of regular graphs they connect graph spectra to how fast the repeated products expand. For general graphs they use the Gershgorin Circle Theorem to describe the spectra and build rate bounds. The codes, they argue, compress the computation's structure in a succinct new way.
arxiv-2504-16006:
Wenlin Li, Xingli Li, Yan Li, Francesco Marzioni, Paolo Piergentili, Francesco Rasponi, and David Vitali wrote a 2025 paper on a light-and-motion device. Two thin membranes sit inside a mirrored cavity, and light bouncing inside pushes on them as they vibrate. Most studies use a simple model in which the push grows in a straight line with each membrane's shift.

The team instead worked out the full behavior, keeping the exact curved link between the light and the membranes. They compared the full model with the simple one and found where the two part ways. In some settings the simple model gives plainly wrong predictions, for linked vibration and for quantum links between the membranes. The work tells experimenters when the shortcut is safe and when it misleads.
arxiv-2504-16606:
Mai Su and seven co-authors introduce HUG in a 2025 paper on building large aerial city scenes with Gaussian splatting. The method renders new views with high realism and speed, but city-scale aerial data brings heavy memory use, slow training, and a drop in quality.

HUG stands for Hierarchical Urban Gaussian Splatting, and it splits the work into blocks. A visibility-based method cuts the scene into parts far faster than past splits. A layered neural Gaussian form then lifts the quality of each block. The aim is a full city scene that still renders well in real time.
arxiv-2504-17006:
Jalal Arabneydi and a large team set out a plan for deep learning rigs that learn with a human in the loop. Trial-and-error AI can steer hard tasks, yet real rigs gain when a human feeds hints mid-run. Their 2025 plan stacks three learning modes: self trial, copying a guide, and carry-over from past tasks. Human input comes in three forms too: score marks, set acts, and shown runs.

A drone duel tests the plan: guard drones must stop foe drones from a barred zone. The rig runs on an award-grade open tool for loop work. Loop runs trained faster and scored higher than lone runs. Hints steered the learning path and cut its shake. Too much or too little hint hurt the end grade, so dose counts. Twin stress tests, a flood and a decoy rush, also passed.
arxiv-2504-17106:
Five researchers survey software that must keep data safe while running in the cloud in a 2025 tutorial paper. Payment, booking, and business flow systems are being rebuilt for cloud use, drawn by cost and scale. Builders have tried varied frames, from microservices to actor models and live dataflow systems.

The move revives old data problems: keeping state in line, keeping records durable, and running the life cycle of an app. New problems join them, like message delivery, task timing, and auto scaling. Database research has pushed analytic and transactional systems, the authors note, but cloud apps of this kind draw little study. They map open problems for the field.
arxiv-2504-17206:
Motohiko Ezawa studies how p-wave magnets absorb elliptically polarized light, in a 2025 physics paper. The quantum geometric tensor, built from Berry curvature and the quantum metric, can be read out through optical absorption. A p-wave magnet splits its energy bands along one axis, which makes it a clean test case for these effects.

Ezawa derives formulas for the optical conductivity up to second order in the size of the Néel vector, with exact results when that vector points along each axis. The absorption depends strongly on the light's ellipticity, an effect called elliptic dichroism. When the Néel vector points along one axis, the dichroism becomes perfect, so measuring it reveals the vector's direction.
arxiv-2504-17306:
Meher Boulaabi and co-authors apply, in a 2025 paper, a deep segmentation network to the lesions diabetes stamps on the retina. Tiny bleeds, fatty deposits, and cotton-like patches each signal advancing eye disease. Marking them precisely in scans guides treatment and screening.

The team trained a separate binary model for each lesion type. Their outputs merge into one annotated image for review. Cropping and contrast enhancement on one color channel prepared the scans. Targeted augmentation stretched a limited dataset further. Accuracy reached ninety-nine percent in their tests. Separate specialists per lesion beat one generalist here, a pattern worth noting for medical imaging with scarce labels.
arxiv-2504-17406:
Marco Peruzzo and co-authors find graph conditions for steering chosen nodes in directed networks. Target controllability asks if some nodes can be driven as wished. Past criteria leave gaps and miss some valid target sets.

The authors define a new network class called Christmas trees. It widens both trees and cactus graphs into one family. For a simple subclass they characterize controllable target sets fully. Any network can be probed through spanning subgraphs of this class. That trick reveals target sets older criteria overlook. The paper also reviews past conditions and their limits. The results sharpen control theory for networked systems under partial control goals.
arxiv-2504-17806:
Sergiu Vacaru builds a nonmetric version of the Einstein-Dirac-Maxwell theory in a 2025 paper on modified gravity. Standard gravity rests on a metric that fixes lengths and angles. Nonmetric theories loosen that frame and add torsion, which opens new kinds of black holes, wormholes, and cosmos models. Yet the basic equations for mixed gravity, electric fields, and fermion matter stayed unsolved in that setting.

Vacaru offers a frame and connection method that splits the tangled equations into parts that can be solved. With it, he builds fresh classes of steady solutions shaped by Dirac and Maxwell fields and free generating functions. The set spans warped black holes, wormholes, and ring-like toroids. Some of these objects fall outside the classic black hole frame, so he turns to a generalized entropy from geometric flow theory to score their heat traits.
arxiv-2504-17906:
Shamal Faily argued in a 2025 paper for designing access control early, using asset and goal models. Who may do what in a system shapes the whole design, yet access rules are often written before, during, or after the needs they serve are captured. Knowledge about access is scattered across stakeholders, and the gaps stay invisible. The proposed technique hunts those gaps down with two simple modeling languages.

Asset models list what must be protected; goal models list what people aim to do. Together they act as boundary objects that make access concerns plain to everyone, evening out who knows what. A case study tests the approach on reusing a software component inside a new military air system, where access mistakes carry unusual weight.
arxiv-2504-18206:
Stefano Sossi-Rojas, Gissel Velarde, and Damian Zieba test which data streams help machine learning predict Bitcoin's price direction, in a 2025 paper. Earlier work hinted that the closing price alone cannot carry a forecast. The team assembled a wider set of time series and searched for the subset that sharpens directional calls.

The daily open, high, and low prices did the work, with the low price contributing most. Non-price features tied to the Bitcoin network added almost nothing. The best setup paired a gated recurrent unit network, a sequence-learning model, with a plain baseline forecast in an ensemble. Its directional accuracy matched the best published results. The authors frame the lesson as focus: a few price streams, well combined, beat a flood of extras.
arxiv-2504-18406:
Yusen Zhang and co-authors published a 2025 paper testing how well AI vision models handle very large images. Some images hold over a million pixels: tissue scans, farm fields seen from the air, telescope views. Models that mix vision and language claim to cope with such pictures. Yet no test measured that claim across many kinds of scenes.

The team's benchmark, HRScene, gathers twenty-five datasets plus two made-up test sets. Image sizes run from about a thousand pixels square to more than thirty-five thousand on a side. Ten annotators collected and re-labeled the material. The scenes range from microscope views to street photos and scanned documents. The made-up sets hide a target image among distractors to probe how models use each region. Testing twenty-eight models showed how far current models fall short.
arxiv-2504-18606:
Ryohei Miyadera and co-authors study a new twist on a coin-sliding game, in a 2025 paper. Two coins sit on a long strip of numbered squares, and players take turns sliding a coin to a lower free square. A coin pushed off the strip is lost from play. The twist adds a push move: the right coin can shove the left one as it moves.

That push makes the game hard to read, yet the team worked out formulas for its Grundy numbers, the scores that reveal who wins. With two coins alone, the first player always wins, so the game looks trivial. Joining two boards into one game restores real contest, and the formulas hand the winner a clear plan. The work adds a fresh case to the theory of impartial games.
arxiv-2504-18706:
Jamila Taaki, Athol Kemball, and Farzad Kamalabadi hunt for planets in data from the TESS space telescope, in a 2025 paper. Their detector looks for the small dips in starlight that mark a planet crossing its star. It works in a Bayesian way, learning the noise and the star's own flicker from priors it estimates as it goes, which guards against overfitting.

In injection tests the detector caught eighty percent of planted signals with a modest false-alarm rate, a hair better than a standard comparison method. On three years of real TESS data it recovered most known planet candidates. The team also ran it as an independent search for new candidates in the telescope's continuous viewing zone.
arxiv-2504-18806:
Jagrit Acharya and Gouri Ginde release BugsRepo, a curated data set of Mozilla bug reports, in a 2025 paper. Bug reports guide fixes, but vague or missing detail slows developers and weakens tools that sort, grade, and summarize reports. The data set aims to give such work a richer base.

It holds metadata and comments for 119,585 fixed or closed reports, with fields such as severity, timing, and status. A second part profiles 19,351 community members with roles and activity counts. A third part gives 10,351 well structured reports with steps to reproduce and expected versus actual behavior, further graded by a quality scale.
arxiv-2504-19006:
Benjamin Church settles a conjecture in 2025 about smooth maps and zero-free forms on four-dimensional varieties. A 1-form is a kind of differential that can vanish at points. Pulling one back from an abelian variety without zeros was conjectured to signal that the map itself is smooth.

Church proves the claim in dimension up to four: for maps to a simple abelian variety, smoothness matches exactly the existence of such a nowhere-vanishing pulled-back form. He also classifies completely the four-folds that carry a zero-free 1-form yet admit no map to an elliptic curve, closing the classification side of the problem.
arxiv-2504-19206:
Ahmed Zahari Abdou, Kol Beatrice Gamou, and Ibrahima Bakayoko classify Leibniz algebras and their Rota-type operators in a two thousand twenty-five math paper. A Leibniz algebra is a variant of a Lie algebra. In the nilpotent kind, repeated products vanish. A compatible kind has two multiplication rules that interact in a set way.

The team gives computer based methods for these structures in four dimensions. It gives full lists of the compatible nilpotent ones with size below four. They also list the matching operators, which are linear maps that meet a weighted form of a classic identity. Other researchers can use these lists to test ideas and find examples.
arxiv-2504-19306:
Jixuan Liu, Long Feng, Liuhua Peng, and Zhaojun Wang build a test for sudden shifts in large data sets. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, works when data has many parts at once. A shift point is a spot where the pattern changes. Old tests based on means can fail when data has heavy tails.

The new test uses spatial signs and medians, which resist odd values. It checks both the largest shift in one part and the sum across parts. The authors prove how the test acts when no shift is present. Tests on made-up data show strong power for both sparse and dense shifts.
arxiv-2504-19406:
Good quiz questions from a lecture video must land on the right moment and the right answer. Mengxia Yu and co-authors build a system for that job in a 2025 paper, working from real classroom recordings rather than tidy textbook text.

They first gathered a data set of questions tied to actual lectures, speech and slides together. Current generators stumbled there, picking weak context and drifting from target answers. Their framework uses a language model to select context from both the transcript and key video frames, favoring passages near the target time and relevant to the answer. The chosen pieces are then rewritten into answer-bearing knowledge statements before questions are drafted. Question quality and relevance rose clearly.
arxiv-2504-19606:
Hieu-Dai Tran, Duc-Vu Nguyen, and Ngan Luu-Thuy Nguyen build a Vietnamese coreference data set in a 2025 paper. Coreference resolution links the many phrases in a text that point to the same entity. Vietnamese is a low resource language with few labeled sets for this task. Narrative texts from the VnExpress news site form the base.

The team writes detailed labeling rules to keep entity marks consistent and accurate. They then test two large language models on the set. GPT-4 beats GPT-3.5-Turbo clearly on both accuracy and consistency of answers, they report. That makes it the more reliable tool for Vietnamese coreference work.
arxiv-2504-20006:
Sahel Sharifymoghaddam and co-authors look for a better way to grade long answers written by chatbots. Their 2025 paper starts from arena battles, where people pick the better of two replies side by side. Such votes show which reply won, but not why, and not what was missing.

The team instead breaks each answer into small facts, called nuggets, and scores how many of the key facts appear. They ran their scoring tool on about seven thousand arena battles from search tasks. The nugget scores matched human choices well. The authors argue that fact-based scoring can both explain a grade and point to what an answer left out or got wrong.
arxiv-2504-20106:
Liang and eight co-authors split help and harm aims into shift codes for model tuning in this twenty twenty-five paper. A model tuned too strict says no too much, while a loose one may do harm. Past drills bake both aims in one pot, which blurs fine control at use time.

Inside, one model is drilled per aim, and its shift from base is kept as a code. At test time those codes merge in shares the user sets by hand. New aims join the mix with no fresh drill of the whole base. Tests show help gains with no wild rise in no-said calls. Smooth knobs let a user slide the help-harm mix live as needs shift.
arxiv-2504-20306:
Teja Krishna Cherukuri and co-authors present a vision model for spotting colon polyps in a 2025 paper. Polyps are early warning signs of colorectal cancer, but scope images can miss them or leave doctors unsure where the growth sits. Their network adds a dynamic attention system that shifts focus toward the most telling regions of each image.

Rather than bolting on a separate locator, the model folds context into the classification step itself. That makes its verdicts easier to explain, since the focus map shows what drove the call. The catalog title carries footnote clutter, but the work is the attention network described here. Clearer, better-flagged images could raise early cancer detection.
arxiv-2504-20706:
Sihong Shao and Yuxuan Wu settle a case of a long-running conjecture about cycles that visit every vertex of a network exactly once. Their 2025 paper proves that every planar graph that is two-connected, where every vertex has degree three, and whose faces have at most six sides, contains such a Hamiltonian cycle. A two-connected graph has no single vertex whose removal splits it, and the graphs are drawn flat with polygonal faces.

The bound on face size cannot be loosened: six is tight, and the authors show why. The result also weakens the connectivity demanded by the Barnette-Goodey conjecture, a classic open problem about cycles in three-regular planar graphs, pushing it to the least that can be asked. The paper is a short, sharp step in structural graph theory.
arxiv-2504-21206:
Zihan Chen, Xingbo Fu, Yushun Dong, Jundong Li, and Cong Shen present FedHERO, a federated method for labeling nodes in graphs whose neighbors tend to differ. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Federated graph learning trains shared models across private data holders. Most methods assume neighbors resemble each other, as friends often share tastes.

Real graphs often break that rule: fraudsters link to honest users, and unlike nodes connect. When clients hold graphs with different mixing patterns, their local lessons clash. Merging them can wreck the global model. FedHERO's two-channel network learns the structure of each local graph as it goes. It separates the patterns that travel across graphs from those that stay local. Client models gain from both their own and the shared structural insight. The authors claim a new standard for heterophilic federated learning.
arxiv-2504-21506:
Nasipuri and Chatterjee study how exotic waves meet and merge in a coupled Boussinesq system, a model of shallow water waves. They use the Hirota bilinear method to build exact wave forms. Lump waves come first, derived from a quadratic form in the method. Then come meetings between lumps and kink waves, which yield double lump patterns. Breather waves add a further family of shapes.

Breathers were seen to spread in a diffusion-like way as they interact. They can meet periodic waves, kinks, and bright solitons for the right settings. Pairs of double breathers also interact in chains. Symbolic math and plots together reveal the behavior. The work reports patterns not seen before in this system.
arxiv-2504-21606:
Grammatikos, Mohamed Ali, and Sossan measure the hidden traits of power lines in 2025 without the fancy meters such work expects. A line's resistance and reactance shape how a local grid behaves, yet small grids rarely have phasor meters. The team first shows that with full phasor data and known voltages, the task becomes a standard flow problem with swapped unknowns.

They derive by hand the matrix that speeds solving it. With only plain meter readings, data from many time slots must pool into a best-fit estimate, and their matrix speeds those older methods too. Tests ran on a real test grid in Switzerland with true parts and loads. Knowing line traits cheaply helps small grids host more solar and batteries safely.
arxiv-2504-21706:
Saber Mehdipour, Seyed Abolghasem Mirroshandel, and Seyed Amirhossein Tabatabaei survey Vision Transformers in precision agriculture in work from 2025. Spotting plant disease early helps protect crop health and yield, but manual checks and classic learning methods scale poorly.

The survey explains how these models moved from language to vision and why they handle long-range image links well. It reviews methods, datasets, and scores across farm tasks, and compares transformer models with convolutional networks and hybrids. Challenges include data needs, computing cost, and clarity of decisions. Future paths for field use are outlined.
arxiv-2504-21806:
Rachael Boyd and Corey Bregman worked out in 2025 the shape of the space of all ways to place a Hopf link in ordinary space. A Hopf link is two rings linked once, the simplest true link. Its placement space collects every smooth way the rings can sit, up to labeling.

The pair prove that this space has the same shape, in the stretch-and-bend sense, as a known closed three-dimensional world built from a sphere. Round placements alone already carry the full shape, a helpful middle step. They give a matching answer for placements inside a sphere, tied to two copies of a projective plane.
arxiv-2505-00106:
Yuma Watanabe and four co-authors present a physics study from 2025 on a model of bosons on a ladder-like lattice. An past study had claimed a strange phase in which flow-like order and string-like order occur at once. The team tests that claim with two strong computer methods for such systems.

One method, used on finite chains, gave results that fit the claimed phase. The second method, built for endless chains, gave sharper phase lines and left no room for that phase. The work shows why the choice of method matters when teams map phases that are hard to pin down in low-dimension systems.  Their phase map is offered as a firmer guide for later theory and lab work on such ladders.
arxiv-2505-00606:
Wallace Lee and YuHao Chen estimate food intake from video in 2025. Knowing how much a person eats helps guard against obesity and diabetes. Self reports of meals are often wrong in both directions. The team rebuilds food in three dimensions from a single camera video as the meal proceeds.

Standard scene rebuilding tools plus pose tracking form the three dimensional model. Watching the model shrink shows how much food was eaten. Tests used toy foods and real items to check the approach. A state tracking method keeps the model faithful as the food changes shape on the plate.
arxiv-2505-00706:
Jorge Caravantes and three co-authors shared a new way in 2025 to tell how a parabola or a hyperbola sits next to an ellipse. The test does not need the points where the two curves cross. How two curves sit matters in robotics, in animation, in design software, and in physics. The old way finds the cross points first, and that work is slow and hard.

Their test reads the result straight from the coefficients of the implicit equations. It still works when the curves are not in canonical form. It also works when the curves lie in odd spots in the same flat plane. That makes it a strong, fast shortcut for geometry software. Staff who use such software must sort many pairs of curves, and they must do so fast and with care and with few wrong calls.
arxiv-2505-00806:
Yongtai Li, Gour Jana, and Chinedu Ekuma present a computing method in a 2025 physics paper. The head gives a second title on Rashba spin-orbit coupling in disordered two-dimensional systems. Disorder, spin-orbit coupling, and wider spatial links all shape how electrons behave in such materials, but modelling them together is costly.

The authors extend a cluster method that treats a patch of the material exactly and the rest in average terms. Their version adds the Rashba effect, which ties an electron's spin to its motion. Checks against an exact but slower method matched well. The method reproduced known signs of spin-driven delocalisation, where electrons spread instead of trapping. The authors offer it as a cheaper route to harder multi-band and strongly linked systems.
arxiv-2505-01006:
Sumit Mamtani and co-authors present a 2025 paper on spotting sarcasm without token splitting. Most language tools first split text into tokens, which can fail on odd or new words. Models that read raw bytes or characters avoid that step. The team tested two such models on sarcasm in tweets and in news headlines, against token-based rivals.

Both raw-text models beat the token-based ones in the study. They also set new top scores on both data sets. Gains were under one percent, but they held across a noisy social set and a cleaner news set. The authors say raw-text models suit messy, informal text well. Sarcasm is a hard test, since tone often flips the literal meaning.
arxiv-2505-01206:
Anna-Katharina Nitschke and co-authors published a design paper in 2025 for a digital twin to support patient care. A digital twin is a virtual copy that mirrors a patient's course through care. Such tools could tailor care to each person, but only if they fit real clinical routines. The team set out a general design not tied to one disease.

The design joins knowledge graphs with a team of learning models. It aims to reflect the whole patient journey and help doctors choose next steps. The authors list the traits they target: it should predict, come in modules, keep evolving, stay informed, and be readable and explainable. They present the design as a base for broad clinical use.
arxiv-2505-01506:
Stanisław Kurzyna and co-authors use Rydberg atoms to measure microwave fields with quantum precision while shrugging off detection losses. Quantum sensors promise unmatched sensitivity, yet photons lost at readout often erase the advantage. Rydberg atoms, with their huge dipole moments, both sense fields strongly and can process quantum information.

The team senses with an ensemble of such atoms, reaching fine microwave sensitivity. Then interactions between the atoms run an error-prevention protocol that protects the result against lost detections. Mixing sensing and computing in one atomic system is the trick. Robust quantum metrology like this matters for radar, communications, and fundamental field measurements outside the lab.
arxiv-2505-01606:
Connery Chen, Yihan Wang, and Bing Zhang published an astronomy paper in 2025 on X-ray signals from merging neutron stars. Such mergers are heard in gravitational waves and seen in light. Most past work on their light focused on gamma-ray bursts and glowing debris in visible light. The team argues X-rays give a strong extra probe of the merger's physics and shape.

They model signals from just after the merger through an afterglow lasting years. A general method computes X-ray light curves for jets seen from any angle. Shape limits from the early signal can predict when the afterglow peaks and how bright it gets. The paper also sets time windows for X-ray searches across distances and detector limits.
arxiv-2505-01706:
Sarvesh Shashidhar and co-authors probe a training method for large language models in a 2025 paper. Direct preference methods teach a model from ranked answers, but they score each whole answer at once. Real readers judge parts of an answer, since even a good reply can hold weak segments. A two dimensional scoring version was built to fix that gap. The team tests how it holds up when scores carry noise.

Their study compares win rates for the standard method and the two dimensional one on open data sets. Both work well on clean scores yet falter when labels or scores are noisy. The authors add a fix that makes the segment scores resist noise, backed by theory and lab tests. They also lay out other noise patterns that could appear in real scoring work.
arxiv-2505-01806:
