Georgios Vassos, Richard Lusby, and Pierre Pinson build a simulation of how ships' supply requests become orders. Crews file requisitions for parts and stores, shore staff process them, and buyers place orders, all while prices move and demand stays uncertain. Their discrete-event framework models each stage, from a requisition raised on board to the final order allocation, and is designed to transfer to other procurement settings.

Inside the simulation they compare two buying rules. One leans on standing contracts, as buyers often do in practice. The other watches the spot market and switches supplier when prices favor it. The spot strategy can save real money, but it risks breaking the volume promises made to contract suppliers. When spot prices react strongly to order size, both rules end up using contracts heavily, which the authors say argues for larger committed volumes.
arxiv-2505-01906: Dmitry Kerner proves a relative version of a classic theorem about the shape of complex algebraic varieties, in a 2025 paper. The classic result says a complex affine variety of complex dimension n has the homotopy type of a real space of dimension at most n. The classic form deals with one variety on its own. Kerner's version deals with maps between varieties. For a morphism from one variety to another, he proves the same kind of bound in relative form.
arxiv-2505-02206:
Lei Mao, Yuanhe Tian, and Yan Song build richer gene sequence representations in a 2025 paper. Genome models borrow language tools, treating DNA like text, but they usually fix one unit size. Real sequences carry meaning at several scales, from short blocks to grouped patterns the authors call G-grams.

Their framework, DNAZEN, mines G-grams from large genome collections without supervision and builds a vocabulary of them. During learning, matching G-grams from each sample are encoded by a dedicated Transformer and merged with the base unit encoder. A second training task sharpens the joint representation. The mixed scale design aims to catch both local motifs and longer range grammar in gene sequences.
arxiv-2505-02306:
Junfeng Jiao and co-authors introduce SafeMate, an AI helper that turns official emergency guidance into answers a layperson can act on, in this 2025 paper. Safety documents and standard procedures are written for professionals. Under stress, ordinary people cannot dig answers out of dense PDFs in time.

SafeMate uses retrieval-augmented generation: it searches trusted sources and drafts replies grounded in what it finds. Built on the Model Context Protocol, it routes each question to tools for document search, checklist building, or structured summaries. A FAISS index with cosine similarity picks the most relevant passages. The design serves both quiet preparation days and active crises. Its modular build lets new tools slot in as needs change.
arxiv-2505-02406:
Zichen Liu, Xu Zou, Gang Hua, and Jiahuan Zhou present a new part for vision models in two thousand twenty-five. Such models are often tuned with a small set of learned prompts shared by all image tokens. The shared setup treats each token the same, though tokens play quite distinct roles.

Their part, called Token Coordinated Prompt Attention, splits prompts into two kinds. One kind works only with the class token, which sums up the whole image. The other kind works with patch tokens, and a matching rule gives each patch its own prompt. Tests on many standard sets show clear gains over the shared-prompt approach.
arxiv-2505-02506:
Florian Gallusser and co-authors probe which design choices let AI weather models run for years without drifting apart in a 2025 paper. Learned forecasters shine at two weeks yet often break physical sense beyond that, while a few stay stable for decades. Three leading architectures trained on the same reanalysis data faced off.

Training steps taken at once, model size, and the choice of predicted variables were varied one by one. Some settings held a stable ten-year rollout that kept the climates statistics intact. The spherical model proved most forgiving of settings, though every model could fail on an unlucky seed. Stability, the team shows, is a design outcome, not luck.
arxiv-2505-02606:
Mikkel Bue Lykkegaard and co-authors test whether compressing sensor data harms energy demand forecasts. Their 2025 study starts from a practical problem: smart grids stream huge volumes of high-frequency data, which strain storage and networks. A case study uses a seawater supply system in Hirtshals, Denmark, driven by weather, schedules, and seasons.

The team compressed the data with wavelet methods at rates up to near-total reduction, then ran three forecasting models on the squeezed data. One model, XGBoost, proved highly robust to compression. Careful wavelet compression kept the features forecasts need. The findings suggest grid operators can store far less data without losing prediction quality.
arxiv-2505-02706:
When heavy ions collide, the droplet of quark-gluon plasma they form either settles into thermal balance or it does not, and the difference should be written in the spray of particles. Rupam Samanta and Tribhuban Parida read that writing in this 2025 paper through fluctuations in the average sideways momentum of the particles. In the most head-on lead collisions, the spread of that average drops steeply.

The authors argue the drop is a natural fingerprint of the plasma thermalizing. They also champion a differential map of the fluctuations across momentum, which behaves much like the flow patterns used to prove the plasma moves as one fluid. The measure, they say, deserves a place beside flow in probing collective behavior.
arxiv-2505-02806:
Mohammadali Mohammadi and co-authors design cell free massive antenna systems that deliver both data and wireless power to Internet of Things devices. Separate user groups need information and harvested energy. The design chooses which access points send energy and which send data, and sets their power levels jointly.

Two optimization goals are studied, maximizing total spectral efficiency and maximizing energy efficiency, under limits on per user data rates, harvested energy, and transmit power. The problems are mixed integer and nonconvex, and successive convex approximation solves them in practice. Extensions cover total harvested energy and fairness among energy users. Gains reach four to five fold in energy efficiency over random mode selection, with and without power control.
arxiv-2505-02906:
Christopher Eckner and four colleagues use neural simulation-based inference to count gamma-ray sources in the Fermi telescope sky, in a 2025 paper. Big open questions, from the glow of the isotropic background to possible dark matter signals, hinge on knowing how many faint sources hide in the data. The team analyzed fourteen years of high-latitude observations between one and ten gigaelectronvolts.

Their pipeline recovered over 98 percent of catalogued bright sources and found no unknown ones above that brightness. It also rebuilt the source-count distribution in both formula-based and free-form versions, agreeing well with earlier work. A separate anomaly check confirmed their simulator mimics the real sky closely.
arxiv-2505-03006:
Chen studies random motions of many bosons that pull on each other at a single point, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The work is the third part in a series on this gas in two dimensions. The gas model is used to test hard ideas in quantum physics. Chen aims to link the random motions to path-sum formulas.

He uses motions built in the prior part of the series as the base paths. He shows the path-sum formulas hold for any count of three or more bosons. The weights on the paths take a new form here. They come from exact solutions found in an earlier paper in the series. For two bosons, the formula is a small tweak of a known one.
arxiv-2505-03106: Kunyu Guo and co-authors prove a sharp bound for a projection operator on special harmonic function spaces, in a 2025 paper. The setting is the real unit ball in three or more dimensions, with a standard weight family. They bound the operator's size on weighted spaces by a clean power of the weight's own constant, the larger of one and a simple fraction set by the exponent. The proof borrows dyadic methods, with the main step a grid-based breakdown of the Bergman kernel.
arxiv-2505-03406:
Mohammad Shoaib Ansari and four co-authors build a lightweight decision support system for clinics in this 2025 paper. The system pairs a small language model, Llama 3.2 in its three-billion-parameter instruct form, with retrieval over hospital data, so answers draw on local records rather than the model's memory alone. A technique called QLoRA fine-tunes the model cheaply, compressing weights while protecting medical accuracy.

The authors report the system performs reasonably on several medical benchmarks and can offer basic medical suggestions. Its intended jobs include predicting disease from symptoms and history, proposing treatments, and summarizing complex reports. They discuss the ethics honestly: patient privacy, data security, and the need for strict clinical validation before real use. Because the compressed weights are light, the system can run in hospitals with modest computing resources. The paper closes with the wider promise of language models in medicine and the work still ahead.
arxiv-2505-03506:
Xiaojun Chen, Kelley, and Lei Wang prove, in a 2025 mathematics paper, a new complexity bound for gradient descent on a class of well behaved optimization problems. The functions are strongly convex, which guarantees a single bowl shape, but their gradients are only locally smooth in a weaker sense than usual. That weaker smoothness covers problems the classic theory handles poorly.

With a fixed, well chosen step size, plain gradient descent still converges. The authors bound how many steps are needed to land within a set distance of the true minimizer. The bound extends the classic result for the fully smooth case, which sits at one end of their smoothness scale. For rougher gradients, the cost grows in a controlled way that their formula makes exact. Such bounds let practitioners predict run times before they compute, and compare methods fairly on hard nonsmooth problems.
arxiv-2505-03906:
Rahman and co-authors speed up language-model code writing for high-performance computing, in a 2025 paper. They use a team of cooperating AI agents. Supercomputing code needs careful tuning for parallelism and memory that general models often miss. Their framework, MARCO, splits the work: one agent writes code and another grades its performance. A feedback loop refines the result.

A web-search agent fetches current optimization techniques from recent papers and proceedings, filling gaps in the model's training. On a standard problem set, the system cut run time by about fifteen percent against a strong model alone. Adding web search improved performance by about thirty-one percent over the base system.
arxiv-2505-04206:
Robbie Webbe and co-authors report a flaring X-ray source that may be a new magnetar in this 2025 paper. Magnetars are neutron stars with extreme magnetic fields, and only about thirty-one are known. The team hunted fast X-ray outbursts in telescope archives with a revised detection program.

The source brightened by a hundredfold within hours, glowing hardest at high energies. Its light fit a hot blackbody of a few thousand electron volts in temperature units. Checks of visible and infrared data ruled out an ordinary star, a spinning pulsar, and a known class of flare from giant stars. The outburst's speed and hardness look most like a magnetar's. More finds like it would sharpen theories of how such stars evolve.
arxiv-2505-04306:
Qiannan Fan, Zhuoyang Li, Jitong Li, and Chenyang Cao build a face reader in 2025 that works when part of the face is covered. Masks became a daily sight in epidemic years, and most face systems fail on covered faces of new types or depths. Their system uses a team of image builders, each guessing one full face from the covered one.

Since rebuilt faces vary by chance, a gating net scores how much each guess helps pin the person's identity. The guesses are then merged at the choice level. The module can plug into most face systems already in use, they note. Tests on three public sets and two wild sets beat past methods across cover types. Covered-face reading matters for phones, gates, and clinics alike.
arxiv-2505-04406:
Valeev and co-authors launch YABLoCo, a bench for long-tale code birth in vast shops. Word tools can write code, yet tests use short tales in the main. Real shops span up to scores of 1,000s of code lines. Their bench holds 215 tasks picked from four big shops. Each task is a lone task form in a big shop set. Shop facts join task past, tale tiers, tales, and call webs.

Tasks aim at task body birth in C and C-plus tongues. Those tongues lacked past bench care in long-tale work. Shops span 200K to 2,000K lines of code in the set. A scale score pipe grades the made code at low cost. A sight tool lets hands view the made code in depth. The bench thus tests tools as real shops would strain them.
arxiv-2505-04506:
Guirado and co-authors catch auroral radio emission from a cool brown dwarf, a failed star far too dim for such fireworks by older thinking. Their 2025 paper reports a year of observations at 5 gigahertz with a continent-wide radio array. The dwarf spins fast, about once every two hours.

Both the plain and polarized signals pulse with that spin, in the pattern of a known maser process. Model fits place the steady emission in rings around the poles, much like Jupiter's main auroral oval. One session caught a fully polarized flare, which hints at active longitudes in the rings. The team also nailed down the dwarf's sky motion with tenfold sharper precision, and confirmed it travels with a known companion star.
arxiv-2505-04806:
Chetan Pathade weighs in a set way how with ease top language models can be broke out of their guards. As these models spread into goods for home and work use, prompt tricks and jail breaks threat the guards meant to hold them in. The work sorts more than 1,400 prompts made to hit them. It tests them next to four models, GPT-4 and Claude 2 in that set.

The read checks rates of hits by such prompts, how plans spread through models, and the build sense in back of prompts that work. Pathade then sets out shield plans in tiers. His tip joins red team work that does not stop with sand box walls for firm guard. The text is a guard check. It maps the hit face of models in use and says guards must be built in form, not in looks.
arxiv-2505-04906:
Meng-Quan Yang, Peng Ru, and Ben-Wei Zhang propose a 2025 way to image how nuclei change parton distributions in proton-nucleus collisions. Partons are the quarks and gluons inside a proton, and inside a nucleus their spread shifts in ways that are hard to pull apart from real data.

Past work reads those shifts through a global fit of many data sets, where key traits are tangled up in each measure. The new plan images the change factors at the level of what is seen, using a joint study of processes at the Large Hadron Collider. Z-boson production is one of the probes they use.
arxiv-2505-05706:
Ali Maalaoui sets out a conformal fractional Dirac operator in a 2025 paper. The work also sets up a fractional spinorial Yamabe problem, asking for a metric that makes a related curvature value constant.

Using a Caffarelli-Silvestre type extension, he casts the nonlocal operator as a boundary map for a problem in a space with one added direction. That yields energy inequalities and a weighted Sobolev inequality for spinors. For the critical operator, local for even counts and not local for odd ones, he defines a spinorial Q-curvature, building on the old scalar notion in the spinor world.
arxiv-2505-05806:
Kaili Qi and co-authors fuse classic variational math with a U-Net to segment images, in a 2025 paper. Variational models draw precise boundaries and explain their logic. They are fussy about settings and slow to run. Deep networks learn features on their own but act as black boxes. Each side envies the other's strengths.

Their framework embeds a fourth-order Cahn-Hilliard equation inside a tailored U-Net. The equation's smoothing guides the network's edge behavior. Training data needs shrink when math supplies part of the answer. Interpretability improves over a plain network. Tests target segmentation accuracy and boundary quality. Medical and industrial imaging both need trustworthy outlines. The hybrid points to a broader merger of equations and learning.
arxiv-2505-05906:
Mamat Bake and Obulkasim Olugh study pair birth from empty space under lopsided, pulsing electric fields. Strong fields can pull matter and antimatter pairs from the vacuum, a famed quantum effect. Their field pairs split pulse spots with time pulses that chirp and shift phase.

Lopsided space layout boosts pair yield over matched layouts. Fine tuning of pulse rate and chirp boosts it more, up to near nine fold in one case. High rates give wavy momentum patterns from light like steps, while low rates give smooth hills from tunneling. The recipe fits lab reach fields.
arxiv-2505-06206:
Alexander Clow, Alfie Davies, and Neil Anderson McKay extend a game result in a 2025 combinatorics paper. A placement game on directed graphs was lately proved able to mirror any normal-play game. Games are classed by the day their values first appear, and past work built all day-two values on at most four graph points.

The team combined exhaustive and random computer searches to build all one thousand four hundred seventy-four day-three values. Each needed at most eight points, and the authors prove eight is sometimes required. They also improve bounds for day-four and day-five values. The work tightens the link between abstract game values and concrete graph constructions.
arxiv-2505-06306:
Yikun Li and co-authors describe a smart radio surface in a 2025 engineering letter. Such surfaces bounce wireless signals in chosen directions to boost coverage, and the best ones stay thin, work over a wide band, and steer smoothly. Their design adds a middle patch layer, with no extra air gap, to keep the panel slim.

A built array of ten by ten units steered beams cleanly across a wide slice of spectrum. The surface shifted signal phase smoothly over a broad range while keeping reflections strong. Tests showed stable behavior across the full band. The authors present the design as a fit for next-generation wireless systems that need flat, tunable panels on walls or towers.
arxiv-2505-06406:
Access control decides who may do what in a computer system, and the NGAC model is a modern, graph-based way to set those rules. Brian Tan and co-authors study its safety problem in this 2025 paper: can a given user ever gain a right they do not start with? Knowing whether that question is even tractable matters for trusting the model.

The team shows that, under mild assumptions, the problem is coNP-complete, so no fast general method is likely to exist. Under further realistic assumptions, they give an algorithm that beats brute force search by a wide margin. They also show that real-world patterns of mutually exclusive attributes can push their method close to its worst case, which marks where care is needed.
arxiv-2505-06606:
Ernandes and co-authors read the life story of a swallowed galaxy in its stars' chemistry in a 2025 paper. The Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus merger was the Milky Way's last big one, roughly a Large Magellanic Cloud's worth of stars, and its debris records how a dwarf galaxy lived before it fell in. Heavy elements made by different kinds of stellar explosions act as dated receipts.

Using abundances gathered in the SAGA database, the team compared ratios of europium, barium, and magnesium against those in surviving dwarf satellites. The patterns say the lost galaxy formed stars slowly for more than two billion years before the merger shut it down. Such element fingerprints can date other eaten galaxies too.
arxiv-2505-07006: Peter Heinzner and Christian Zoller proved in 2025 a structure theorem along fibers over extreme points of a momentum polytope. Their setting is a complex reductive Lie group acting on a compact Kahler manifold, with a maximal compact subgroup acting in a Hamiltonian way. Each extreme point defines an open dense part of the space, held by a parabolic subgroup. They prove a product decomposition for that subgroup's action on this part, and show a parallel statement for real reductive subgroups.
arxiv-2505-07206:
Yuncong Liu and co-authors built a tiny device that links light and motion on a chip made from silicon carbide. The stuff has strong optical and physical traits, but it is hard to shape at small scale. Past devices made from it lost too much light or lacked a built-in way to read the motion.

Their device is a small disk, hung free so it can ring, on an insulated chip base. It loses very little light and rings at a high rate with strong quality. At low light power it kept a steady hum on its own, and at higher power it made clean higher tones. Such chips could serve in small sensors.
arxiv-2505-07506:
Giacomo Canevari, Federico Luigi Dipasquale, and Bianca Stroffolini study singular patterns in a magnetic liquid crystal material. Their 2025 paper is part one of a two-part work on ferronematics. These materials mix magnetic particles into a liquid crystal base. Two linked order fields describe the crystal and the magnetization, under a shared energy.

They track critical points of that energy as a small parameter shrinks toward zero. The energy of the crystal part gathers, at leading order, on a finite set of points. They prove energy bounds and compactness results for that behavior. Those tools are built for the companion paper, which will pin down the magnetization pattern. It will also show how the two singular sets relate.
arxiv-2505-07706:
Codes made of three-symbol strings can be judged by how much any three of them clash. Anurag Bishnoi and co-authors study the largest such codes in a 2025 paper. For any three distinct strings, at least a set number of spots must show all three symbols at once.

The team proves upper and lower bounds for that largest size across ranges of the clash demand. They find the exact point where the size jumps from flat to fast-growing as the demand rises. A straight-line version of the task links to blocking sets in finite geometry, which yields builds by hand. Small cases are worked out in full, for both the plain and the straight-line task.
arxiv-2505-08106:
Jiashen Du and co-authors test whether large chat models can work through hard moral binds as well as experts, in a paper from 2025. The team built a set of close to two hundred real world binds, each with an expert take split into five parts, from scene set to key lessons. Lay human takes were also kept for the core part of each bind.

Four top models were scored on word match, edit gap, and sense match to the expert takes. On the whole the models beat lay humans on form and word fit, with one mini model the most steady of the pack. All models sagged on past roots of each bind and on fine grained fix plans. Lay takes, though loose, at times matched expert sense by gut feel.
arxiv-2505-08406:
Gayatri Ghosh studies how quantum corrections bend a symmetry in theories of neutrino mass, in a 2025 paper. Neutrinos are nearly massless particles whose tiny masses need explaining. In type II seesaw models, a heavy partner particle gives them mass, and many versions assume a symmetry between the muon and tau flavors at high energy. Running the theory down to low energy can shift that symmetry.

Ghosh follows the flavor coupling matrices as they evolve under the renormalization group equations, for both the basic mass operator and its next-order cousin. She tracks how far the couplings drift from the symmetric pattern. Collider limits on the heavy partner's mass and couplings then bound the models. The paper weighs whether the drift stays within what experiments allow.
arxiv-2505-08506:
Duy Ho and Trygve Johnsen study code hulls in a 2025 paper. A code hull is the shared part of a code and its twin code. For plain codes, past work showed the hull can be shrunk by swapping the code for a twin form.

The pair ask the same for codes judged by a rank gauge, the kind used where bursts of flaws strike in blocks. They work the case through the code kin forms, as grid codes and as long block codes. Their yield: each such code, over any field, has a twin form whose hull is empty. Code teams gain a clean base for codes that hide no self-twin part.
arxiv-2505-08706:
Ningzi Li, Shiyang Lai, and James Evans review how big data and machine learning are reshaping the study of entrepreneurship and innovation, in a book chapter from 2025. Huge streams of text, network, image, and video data now record business life as it happens. That flood brings both fresh questions and fresh traps, such as spotting true novelty.

The authors describe two uses. First, models fed on large data can build precise measures that act as observatories, watching innovation across whole societies. Second, AI models can form digital doubles of technologies and firms, giving labs for virtual tests of ideas and policies. The chapter argues that pairing big data with big models can advance how theory in this field is built and checked.
arxiv-2505-08806:
Alvarez, Bruining, and Marchesin model in 2025 how flooding a carbonate rock reservoir with low-salt water can free more oil. The method is cheap and can raise recovery, but it works only when the water chemistry and the rock minerals interact in the right way.

The authors built a combined model that links surface chemistry calculations with the flow of oil and water through rock. Their measure of oil-rock bonding feeds into flow rules inside a standard simulation tool, and they test the setup against core flooding experiments. The model helps engineers tune the injected water instead of relying on trial and error.
arxiv-2505-09206:
Zhenyu Du and colleagues set out a randomized measurement protocol to gauge non-linear traits of quantum states. Quantum mechanics is linear at its base. That makes it hard to learn non-linear traits of a state. Single-copy randomized protocols had hit best sample counts for set tasks such as purity gauges. They had not done so for broader classes of traits.

Their protocol gauges the trace of an observable times the squared density matrix. That value sits at the core of quantum computing and many-body physics. They prove a bound on its sample count and show it is best for observables with large trace norm. That set includes Pauli and local observables. For those, the protocol runs well with Clifford circuits. Tests show it needs far fewer samples than classical shadows for the same precision.
arxiv-2505-09506:
A classic child-growth model is rebuilt as a neural autoencoder by Maria Alejandra Hernandez, Oscar Rodriguez, and Dae-Jin Lee in a 2025 paper. The SITAR model bends one shared growth curve per child through shifts in timing, size, and intensity. Their deep version learns those three personal knobs with an encoder network.

A spline-based decoder then rebuilds each child's curve, as the classic model does. New children can be scored without refitting the whole study. Growth clinics track teens whose spurts come early or late; a fast learned version could update risk charts at each visit.
arxiv-2505-09606:
Steve Cabrel Teguia Kouam, Jean-Pierre Tchapet Njafa, and others benchmark fast, rough quantum chemistry methods on semiconductor molecules in a 2025 study. The GFN family of semiempirical methods promises geometries at a fraction of the cost of density functional theory, the standard workhorse. Four variants, from tight-binding flavors to a force-field version, face that standard on small organic semiconductor molecules.

Optimized shapes and electronic traits are compared method by method. The systematic scorecard of accuracy against cost helps chemists choose the cheapest tool that stays sound for screening new electronic materials.
arxiv-2505-10006:
Diptarka Chakraborty and co-authors merge rankings fairly with better guarantees in a 2025 paper. Rank aggregation blends many orderings into one consensus, for hiring, admissions, and search. A consensus can quietly stack the top spots against a group. Fair variants demand balanced representation near the top, but the best known algorithm only promised a factor-three closeness to optimal.

The authors first give an algorithm within a hair above factor two of optimal. A second method reaches a factor just under two point nine, whatever fairness rule is chosen, as long as a closest fair ranking can be found. Tests on real data sets backed the theory against state-of-the-art rivals. The paper sharpens a young field's core tool. Fairness in aggregation, it shows, need not cost as much accuracy as feared.
arxiv-2505-10106:
Fuel is often shot sideways into a fast air stream inside high-speed engines, and how it mixes there depends on the fuel itself. Radouan Boukharfane, in this 2025 paper, used large-eddy simulations to study sonic jets of ten fuels in air moving at Mach 2. The fuels range from hydrogen and methane to ammonia blends and a synthetic mix.

All cases were run at the same momentum flux ratio, so the fuel's own traits stood out. The study tracks shock waves, swirls, and mixing near the jet's windward side, where the first blending takes place. Weight, heat traits, and density of each fuel shape how the flow structures grow. The findings aim to guide the design of engines that can burn a wider range of fuels well.
arxiv-2505-10206:
Kendall Shepherd and co-authors published this study in 2025. It asks how stronger winds change the lives of very massive stars. Such stars, hundreds of times the Sun's mass, forge heavy elements and seed the largest black holes. Near a brightness limit, their winds may blow far harder than standard recipes say. The team put wind rules tied to that limit into a star evolution code. They modeled single stars and pairs, then checked against a real star cluster.

The stronger-wind tracks matched observed stars better. The cluster's brightest star still strains single-star origins, though mergers of pairs could explain it. In pairs, hard winds blocked mergers while stars still burned hydrogen. Leftover black holes shifted heavier in some ranges and vanished in others. Wind strength, the authors show, steers both star fates and black hole censuses.
arxiv-2505-10606:
Hector Pasten and co-authors prove two limits that hold back all Transformer models, in work from 2025. The first, isolation, says a learnable sequence must sit apart from other learnable ones, so some sets cannot be learned by one model at once. The second, continuity, says a learned sequence pulls near neighbors toward itself like a basin.

Both effects are proven for all models that use compact position codes. Careful tests show the same blocks arise at real scale, not just on paper. The authors frame the pair as basic facts about how these models store patterns, with weight for both theory and practice.
arxiv-2505-10806:
Arefin Niam and Zulkar Nine present a faster way to train graph neural networks in this 2025 paper. Such networks learn from data shaped as networks of linked nodes. Training them on huge graphs takes much memory, and when the work is split across machines, fetching data from afar eats time.

Their system, called RapidGNN, plans small training batches in advance in a fixed way. That lets it predict which data will be needed, build a smart local store, and fetch remote data early. Tests on two large data sets show much faster training and far fewer remote fetches than leading methods. Energy use also fell, by up to about a quarter in some settings.
arxiv-2505-11606:
Alfaro, Rodriguez, and Ruiz wrote in twenty twenty-five about galaxies living inside cosmic voids. Voids are vast regions with very few galaxies in them. A halo occupation count shows how many galaxies sit in each dark matter halo. In voids that count runs low, but how it changed over time was less clear. The team used a large simulated galaxy catalog to find round voids at many past times.

Void counts stayed below the overall average at every time they checked. Galaxies found in voids today had also lived below average in the past. Small void halos formed late and sit deep inside voids. Large ones formed early and sit near void edges. The results show place shapes galaxy growth over long spans.
arxiv-2505-12106:
Saleh Makkawy, Michael De Lucia, and Kenneth Barner turn Android malware into pictures and teach image networks to sort the pictures, in a 2025 paper. Android's openness feeds a flood of malware that hides through encryption and packing, dodging signature checks. Their framework, MalVis, paints bytecode using entropy and short-pattern statistics, so structural oddities stand out visually. They also release a data set of over one point three million images across nine malware families plus benign apps.

Four well-known image networks were trained on the pictures, with eight ensemble strategies and a balancing step for rare classes. The best setup reached about ninety-five percent accuracy, with strong scores across precision, recall, and agreement measures. The authors say the visual route keeps detection interpretable, since analysts can see what the model sees. The data set is offered as a shared resource for security research.
arxiv-2505-12206:
Mathanesh Vellingiri Ramasamy and Dimas Rizky Kurniasalim published a computing paper in 2025 on road segmentation for driver assistance and self-driving systems. Marking road pixels accurately helps vehicles navigate complex scenes. The team trained a modified VGG-16 network on one road dataset and a modified U-Net on another, then compared the two.

Both models reached high accuracy on their own data. Cross-dataset testing favored the VGG-16 model even though the U-Net had trained for more epochs. Scores covered F1, overlap, and precision measures. The authors discuss how architecture choice and dataset choice each shape segmentation quality in practice.
arxiv-2505-12306:
Yuwei Zhang and co-authors build a test bench for how well language models soak up fresh facts. Their 2025 paper draws facts from a famed trivia feature of an online encyclopedia, where editors pick clear, checkable items. Each fact becomes many question forms, from fill-in blanks to multi-step asks, and the set grows on its own over time.

The bench holds more than twelve thousand facts and seventy-seven thousand questions. In training trials, models that read text both ways beat the standard one-way models at holding facts, by a wide margin. To offset their small size, the team stacks groups of the two-way models as an outer fact store. That stack lifted fact accuracy further in tests.
arxiv-2505-12406:
Martin Jonas and co-authors study how to set a joint strategy for a swarm of autonomous agents in a 2025 paper. The aim is called steady state synthesis: choose behavior so that, in the long run, how often each place is visited meets given numeric targets. For a single agent, the problem can be solved fast, and simple memoryless strategies are enough to near any reachable target. Many agents change the picture.

For several agents, the authors show the problem is computationally hard, with the exact class of hardness set by the variant. Memoryless joint strategies can no longer near every reachable target. Even scoring what a given memoryless joint strategy achieves turns out to be hard. Still, the team design a fast, scalable method for a subclass of such strategies. On many random test cases, it beat a naive method based on sharing strategies by a wide margin.
arxiv-2505-12506:
Yotam Norman and Ron Meir extend invariant risk minimization, a method that learns traits that hold across settings, to data with no labels. Classic forms need labels to find traits that shrug off distribution shifts. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The new frame redefines steadiness as match of trait spreads across settings. Two methods sit inside it, a linear one that pulls steady directions under bell curve premises, and a deep generative one that splits steady from setting bound traits. Both rest on a new cause model for unlabeled data and allow made samples per setting. Tests on made data, digit sets, and face photos show the traits hold.
arxiv-2505-12606:
Shiyu Xuan and co-authors build Diff-MM, a tracker that borrows a text-to-image diffusion model to follow objects across many sensor types. Tracking improves when depth, heat, events, or words join plain video. Training data for those extra senses stays scarce.

Starting from RGB trackers wastes the priors in big generators. Their design uses the diffusion U-Net as the feature engine. Image pairs flow through a parallel extraction pipeline. A tuning module teaches the senses to complement each other. The generator's vast prior knowledge fills the data gap. One tracker then serves all modality mixes. Tests span the standard multimodal benchmarks. The approach unifies a fragmented field neatly.
arxiv-2505-13006:
Four researchers compare three ways to build a chat assistant for airport staff, in a 2025 paper. Busy airports want more automation, and staff need fast answers from flight information systems. The assistant must handle jargon, short forms, and questions that take reasoning over live data. The team built three versions, each fetching facts a different way before a language model answers.

The plain fetch version scored highest on simple accuracy in some tests but sometimes made up facts, a risk in a safety setting. A version that queries databases directly and one that searches a knowledge graph both invented far less. The graph version scored best overall and shone on questions needing reasoning steps. The authors recommend the database and graph versions for airport use, where a wrong invented answer can do real harm.
arxiv-2505-13706:
Jose and Greenstadt tested whether large language models are good at detecting propaganda in twenty twenty-five. Propaganda uses fallacies and emotional appeals to push an agenda. Spotting its techniques helps readers make informed choices, and automated detection is an active research goal.

The team compared several large models with transformer-based systems on news articles. GPT-4 scored best among the large models but still far below a RoBERTa-based baseline. All three large models beat another baseline at spotting name-calling, one of six techniques tested. Two also beat it on appeals to fear and flag-waving. The authors conclude that large models, despite their fame, lag a smaller specialized model at this task overall.
arxiv-2505-13906:
Lincoln and Maswood build an explainable deep network that stages Alzheimer's disease from brain MRI scans. Their 2025 design stacks residual blocks with several attention flavors, including grouped-query and multi-head attention, so the model can spotlight telling regions. They test it on four public datasets, sorting scans into two, three, or four disease classes.

Reported accuracy runs near the ceiling: above ninety-nine percent on most tasks, and perfect on one binary test. On a major initiative dataset, scores stayed high across the three scan planes. Four heat-map methods check that the model's focus lands on sensible anatomy, and the comparisons favor their setup. The authors pitch the network as accurate and auditable for clinical use.
arxiv-2505-14106:
Shawn Li and co-authors build a benchmark for personalized chat in this 2025 paper. Language models are judged on many skills, but sounding personal across a long talk is rarely tested as one whole. Their benchmark, PersonaConvBench, joins the two.

It holds three tasks over multi-turn chats: tagging sentences, predicting a person's impact scores, and writing text fitted to the user. The material spans ten domains drawn from Reddit. The design lets researchers see how personalization and conversation shape each other. Models that ace single replies may still lose the person over time. The set gives builders a way to measure that loss.
arxiv-2505-14506:
Heat in a solid rides on tiny vibration packets, and how far each packet travels before it scatters sets how well the solid conducts. Katharina Dudde and co-authors show in a 2025 paper that a common light-based heat probe can map those travel lengths in silicon. They change the size of the laser spot and the depth the light reaches, then read how the measured conduction shifts.

With a wide spot, the readings settle at the known bulk value for silicon. As the spot shrinks, the reading climbs several-fold, a sign that some packets fly straight across the probed zone without scattering. Matching the trend to deep theory lets the team read off the travel-length spread. A second trick, swapping the laser color to change depth, shows the same effect in steps.
arxiv-2505-14606:
Maksim Zhdanov and Vladislav Kurenkov add a physics rule into neural network models of atoms, in a 2025 paper. Such models predict energies for molecules and materials. Electric forces between atoms are a key part of those energies. Their add-on module makes each atom's internal code obey a classic equation of electrostatics.

The module can plug into any existing network of this type. It learns charges and potentials in a self-taught way from the equation itself. An energy term built from those values sharpens total energy forecasts. Extra computing cost is tiny, the authors report. Training stays light on memory and settings. Results support the broader idea that built-in physics constraints lift model performance. Code for the module is to be released publicly.
arxiv-2505-14706:
Eric Habjan, Richard Dube, James McIntyre, Mezmur Edo, and Richard Jones wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five, per its text, though the catalog names Jones alone. It uses machine learning to name the particles seen in the GlueX detector at Jefferson Lab.

The standing method sets hard cuts on track and shower traits. The team trains multi-layer perceptrons and boosted decision trees on the same rebuilt traits, from simulated GlueX data. Both learners name charged and neutral particles far more truly than the cuts. The gain comes with no new detector data, just a smarter read of what is already logged. The study makes the case for learned sorting in the GlueX pipeline.
arxiv-2505-14906:
Ye Yuan and co-authors present in 2025 a language model method that pulls structured entities from telecom texts for 6G study. Future networks lean on machine grasp of terms to run smart features. Loose text must first become clean structured records for models to use.

Their method predicts entity types and keys in a token-lean form that cuts output cost. A layered parallel decode step speeds and sharpens the extraction. A new data set holds near twenty four thousand words from more than one hundred 6G papers. Tests beat baselines on accuracy and run five to nine times faster per sample.
arxiv-2505-15006:
Phan Quoc Khanh and Le Ba Khiet give a way to compute rest points of a class of dynamical systems in a 2025 paper. The systems, named for Lur'e, can take set valued rules, which makes their rest points hard to find. Those points anchor the study of how the systems settle over time.

Their method is built for efficiency on a broad class of such systems. The same work solves a class of quasi variational inequalities, a math form with wide use. Game theory cases close the paper, where the method finds quasi equilibria of the Nash type. The authors frame the tool as a bridge between dynamics and inequality problems.
arxiv-2505-15306:
Yiwen Song and four co-authors combine weak agents into a strong one in twenty twenty-five. Training a good reinforcement learning agent is touchy work. The choice of algorithm, settings, and even random seed can swing results. Ensembles help by merging several agents, but fixed rules like majority voting do not understand the task at hand.

Their method, LLM-Ens, uses a large language model to guide the merger. The model brings task-specific semantic understanding to how agents are combined. That makes the ensemble adapt to the task instead of following a frozen rule. The authors frame the result as many weak agents beating a single strong one. Readers get a smarter way to pool agents that were each trained cheaply.
arxiv-2505-15406:
Zirui Song and co-authors build the first safety benchmark for audio language models in a 2025 paper. Models that listen and speak can be tricked into harmful output, yet no standard test measured that risk. Their benchmark, AJailBench, holds 1,495 spoken attack prompts across ten banned content classes. The prompts were converted from written jailbreaks using realistic speech synthesis.

Tested models showed no consistent resistance to the attacks. To harden the test, the team added a toolkit that warps attack audio in time, pitch, and loudness while keeping its meaning fixed. A search method tunes those warps efficiently. The benchmark gives developers a shared yardstick for audio model safety. It also exposes how fragile current spoken safeguards remain.
arxiv-2505-15506:
Debarshi Brahma, Anuska Roy, and Soma Biswas explore, in a 2025 paper, adapting vision-language models to new datasets that differ sharply from their training data. Models like CLIP generalize well with no examples at all. With only a few labeled examples, though, tuning them risks overfitting and lost flexibility.

Their method tunes the prompts fed to the model rather than the model itself. A margin regularizer keeps the tuned prompts from collapsing onto the few examples. The setting also involves distribution shift, where the new data's style differs from the old. Few-shot prompt tuning with guardrails could make giant pretrained models useful in niche fields. The paper probes exactly where naive tuning breaks down.
arxiv-2505-15606:
Marino Romero and Joshua Jeishing Wen published a 2025 paper on a family of special polynomials used in modern algebra. Wreath Macdonald polynomials blend symmetry with extra structure drawn from a wreath, a ring-like group action. Their formulas are rich but hard to compute by hand.

The pair prove a set of five-term links between operators that act on these polynomials. The links echo a known set for a plainer branch of the same family. From them, the authors draw table-like rules for key values called Pieri coefficients. Those rules turn slow expansions into quick counts over filled diagrams. Fast formulas like these help both hand work and computer algebra in the field.
arxiv-2505-15806:
Sihao Cheng, Jiaxuan Li, and Eritas Yang report a possible dwarf planet on an extreme orbit, in a paper published in 2025. The object, named 2017 OF201, now sits about ninety times farther from the Sun than Earth. Its orbit stretches to the inner Oort cloud, the shell of icy bodies at the solar system's edge.

Twenty-four sightings over twenty years fixed the orbit well. The object swings from forty-five times Earth's distance to hundreds of times farther out. If it reflects light like its kin, it spans about seven hundred kilometers, making it the second largest known in its group. Its angle breaks the clustering that had been read as evidence for a hidden Planet Nine. The authors suggest many such objects may together weigh about one percent of Earth.
arxiv-2505-15906:
Ming Zhang, Cui-Qun Chen, Dao-Xin Yao, and Fan Yang work out where superconductivity lives inside a layered nickel oxide under pressure. Their paper appeared in 2025. The material stacks double and single nickel-oxygen layers, and it superconducts up to about 64 kelvin when squeezed, with a dome-shaped response to pressure. Computer band calculations show the two layer types form nearly separate electronic worlds.

Fluctuation analysis then finds the pairing in the double layers, with the same sign-changing wave pattern as its famous cousin compound. The single layers barely pair at all; instead they act as a bridge, locking the double layers into phase through Josephson coupling. The authors say the division of labor explains the dome.
arxiv-2505-16006:
Alexei Kniazev and Simon Pustilnik took fresh spectra in 2025 of the Peekaboo dwarf galaxy, the nearest known galaxy with almost no heavy elements in its gas. Such pristine systems are living fossils of the early universe, and this one's gas holds about a fiftieth of the Sun's share of metals.

A large telescope in South Africa measured its glowing gas directly, pinning the oxygen level with far better precision than before. Two glowing regions matched closely in composition. One region's lines split into two speeds, hinting at a fast star thrown from its cluster. Archive space telescope images also turned up candidate very hot stars powering the glow. The distance stands near 6.8 million parsecs.
arxiv-2505-16106:
Xiaoshan Chen, Chen Yang, and Zhou Yang build a pricing model for data assets in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Data assets are data goods that have been processed, priced, and traded to meet demand. Most past work prices data from the seller's side, based on traits and collection cost. These authors take the buyer's side. For a buyer, data pays off by giving an edge in choices, not by earning cash at once.

Their model grows out of two robust investment and spending problems set in markets with ambiguity. The fair price falls out of an equation tied to the buyer's value functions. In effect, data is worth what it adds to the buyer's decisions. The paper speaks to economists and to firms building data markets.
arxiv-2505-16206:
Lucas Lima and colleagues studied magnetism on unusual three-dimensional lattices in 2025. They use the Hubbard model, a basic model of electrons that hop between sites and repel when they share one. Their lattices extend the Lieb design, known for flat energy bands where electrons barely move and effects grow strong.

Heavy computer sampling, backed by simpler theories, maps when magnetic order survives at real temperatures. One lattice orders with spins aligned, the other with spins opposed, and each peak ordering temperature traces a hump as repulsion grows. Flat bands build local moments fast, yet weak links between orbitals cap the ordering heat. Rich connections help the second lattice order even without flat bands.
arxiv-2505-16306:
Yizhi Zhou, Haina Zhu, and Hangting Chen present a 2025 study of what self-supervised music models learn, layer by layer. Such models train on raw music and now aid tasks like tagging and search. Yet what each layer holds, and which to use, was little studied.

The team probed two models, MusicFM and the newer MuQ. They checked the gains of self-supervised models across many tasks. They then mapped how layers specialize: early and late layers carry different kinds of information. Picking the right layer for a task changed scores in clear ways. Their analysis shows the structure inside these models and how to use them better for music tasks.
arxiv-2505-16406:
Gaofei Shen, Hosein Mohebbi, Arianna Bisazza, Afra Alishahi, and Grzegorz Chrupała test how trustworthy explanation methods are for speech classification models. Feature attribution promises to show which slices of sound drove a model's decision. Speech, though, is a continuous signal, and the usual tricks from text and images may not carry over.

The authors vary the input type, how attributions are pooled, and how long the perturbed spans are, across several tasks. Most standard methods proved unreliable for speech. The exception was perturbing whole words, which behaved well on word-level tasks. Anyone explaining speech models should heed the warning: plausible-looking heatmaps can mislead.
arxiv-2505-16506:
Włodzimierz Lewoniewski, Krzysztof Węcel, and Witold Abramowicz compare the quality of Wikipedia across 55 language editions, in a 2025 paper. Editions differ hugely in size and care. A fair score must work across languages with different grading habits.

The team built a citation index from 6.6 billion links between articles. They picked the most linked articles in each topic and language. Each article also got a synthetic quality score from 0 to 100. Combining rank and score exposed each edition's strengths and gaps by topic. The method can guide editors toward weak spots in smaller languages.
arxiv-2505-17306:
Xinpeng Wang and four co-authors show that the refusal direction in language models is universal across safety aligned languages. Refusal in English models can be mediated by a single direction in activation space. Whether that holds beyond English was unknown, yet safe behavior matters in every language a model serves.

A multilingual safety dataset is built by translating malicious and benign English prompts into 14 languages. A refusal vector extracted from English alone bypasses refusals in other languages with near perfect effect and no fine tuning. Vectors from any safety aligned language transfer to the rest. Parallel geometry of the vectors in embedding space explains the transfer and exposes a cross lingual jailbreak route.
arxiv-2505-17506:
Seokmin Ko, Ambuj Tewari, and Kihyuk Hong study how to learn a safe policy from logged data when the logs cover only part of the state space, in a 2025 paper. In offline reinforcement learning the agent cannot test actions live, so it must reason from records. Adding safety limits makes the task harder, and many past methods need full coverage or knowledge of how the data were gathered.

Their algorithm, PDOCRL, treats the policy itself as a variable in a reshaped math program and runs a back-and-forth search for the best safe point. They show the usual form of this search can settle on false answers, and they name a stronger condition that rules those out. Under that condition, with coverage of just one good policy, the method returns a near-best, near-safe policy with a stated sample bound.
arxiv-2505-17806:
Hang Yang and Dexue Zhang define a new kind of algebra and match it with a class of spaces, in this 2025 math paper. Their work extends a classic pairing, in which Boolean algebras mirror a family of compact spaces. Here the spaces carry two topologies at once, a setup used when order and approximation both matter. The algebras get a matching twist, which the authors call d-Boolean algebras.

They prove that these algebras and the matching spaces describe each other fully, as categories. The result sits beside an older pairing between a related space type and frame-like structures. The work was backed by a national science grant in China. Results of this kind let workers switch between algebra and space views, using whichever makes a proof easier.
arxiv-2505-17906:
Rounak Chatterjee and co-authors chase a subtle form of entanglement as paired photons travel, in a 2025 paper. When a crystal splits one photon into two, the pair can be entangled in position or in momentum. A stranger option links the phase of their shared wave instead, with neither position nor momentum tied. That phase-entangled state appears only as the pair propagates.

The team tracked the fading position link across distances, folded into a bench-top range by a single lens, and the data matched theory well. They then sent the phase-entangled pair through a double slit. The two-photon interference pattern differed clearly from what position-linked pairs produce, confirming the correlated phase front. Such states may serve future quantum imaging and communication schemes.
arxiv-2505-18406:
M. Kanafani and a large team measured how electrons bounce off a crystal detector in 2025. Simulation codes that track electrons through matter underpin dose estimates in medicine and detector design, but lab data at a few million electron volts are scarce for checking them. The team fired electrons across a wide energy range at a scintillator crystal and counted how many bounced back.

A near-full-angle catcher captured electrons even at steep entry angles. Compared with the Geant4 toolkit under its best physics settings, the counts agreed within a few percent. That close match raises trust in the simulations for nearby uses. New benchmark data at these energies had been a clear gap in the field.
arxiv-2505-18606:
Zhu-yao Jin and Jun Jing steer quantum systems with Hamiltonians that are not Hermitian, treating geometry as a first-class citizen. Standard control engineers the Hamiltonian and lets manifold geometry and constraints follow. Inspired by a classical principle that weighs active, constraint, and inertial forces evenly, the authors do the same here. The arena is a finite system driven in time.

Under a biorthogonal basis, the Hamiltonian can be triangularized in a constraint picture. That condition suffices to build a universal nonadiabatic passage in both halves of the state description. The target state arrives already normalized, with no artificial fix-ups. The passage resists parameter errors when its phase's real part varies fast. Perfect transfer in two levels and chiral transfer in three verify the scheme. The work extends universal control into biorthogonal quantum mechanics.
arxiv-2505-18706:
Viacheslav Sinii and co-authors show, in a 2025 paper, that a handful of steering vectors can teach a language model to reason as well as a full fine-tune. Their method trains one small vector per layer with reinforcement learning while every base weight stays frozen. On an eight billion parameter model, the added parts amount to a tiny sliver of extra size.

Across several base models and math reasoning tests, the light method matched fully tuned models. The savings are practical: less memory for the optimizer and less traffic between processors, which cuts the cost of training. A look inside the model shows the vectors amplify word directions that hang together, which sharpens the chain of thought. The authors argue that high-level reasoning needs far fewer trained numbers than assumed.
arxiv-2505-18906:
Abhijit Chakraborty, Chahana Dahal and Vivek Gupta map the young field of federated retrieval-augmented generation, in work from 2025. The approach joins federated learning, which trains across sites without pooling raw data, with retrieval that grounds language model answers in outside knowledge. Privacy-sensitive fields such as health and finance are the natural market.

Following standard mapping guidelines, the study sorts papers from 2020 to 2025 by focus, contribution and domain. Recurring designs are drawn out, along with hard spots: private retrieval, uneven clients and weak evaluation habits. The authors close with open questions meant to ground the next wave of work.
arxiv-2505-19306:
Weiming Zhi and co-authors present a way for a robot to plan safe motion from a single color photo. Most robots must first build a model of the space around them, and depth guessed from one image often has shape errors. Their framework, called VGER, takes a different route that leans on video generation models.

In their 2025 paper, a video model makes a moving-camera clip from the input photo. Frames from the clip form a multi-view set, which a 3D model turns into a dense point cloud. A multi-scale noise method then trains an implicit model of the scene, and a motion model follows that shape. Tests in indoor and outdoor settings show the method can produce collision-free paths.
arxiv-2505-19606:
Ryan Soh-Eun Shim and co-authors test whether speech encoders in the Whisper family line up languages by sound or by meaning, in a 2025 paper. Earlier work showed these models can match a spoken sentence to its translation, but matching sounds could fake that success. The team ran pronunciation-controlled experiments to strip the sound cues away.

Retrieval of translations stayed well above chance without phonetic help, in the encoders' final layers, and strongest in models also trained on translation. That points to real semantic alignment, not just echoing sounds. Cutting the encoder short, an early-exit trick, even improved speech recognition for low-resource languages the model had never seen. The authors say cross-lingual structure in speech models is deeper than sound.
arxiv-2505-19706:
Pala and four co-authors improve the models that grade each step of a language model's math reasoning. Outcome-only grading checks just the final answer, which hides where reasoning goes wrong. Their system, PathFinder-PRM, first labels the kind of error in each step, then judges the step itself.

Training used a new dataset of 400,000 steps with three kinds of step-level labels. The model reached the best score yet on a standard benchmark while using three times less data. In guided search tests it also beat the strongest rival. The authors argue that naming errors before scoring them makes step grading both sharper and cheaper.
arxiv-2505-19906:
Weijie Du and co-authors presented this 2025 method for solving many-particle quantum puzzles on a quantum computer. Classic methods for self-bound systems, like atomic nuclei, often reach only a few energy levels and give thin detail. The team built a hybrid quantum-classic approach that aims at the full set of bound states at once.

Their scheme rewrites the energy operator in a fresh input model and scans states in a set way. It also yields each state's total spin value, a key label for nuclei. As a first demo, they computed the bound states and spins of oxygen-20 with a realistic strong-force model. The same scheme may serve hadron studies in a light-front framework, widening its reach.
arxiv-2505-20006:
Raphaël Bagat, Irina Illina, and Emmanuel Vincent improved speech recognition for non-native accents in two thousand twenty-five. Systems often fail on accented speech, and data for many accents are scarce. Their method fine-tunes a model with a mixture of small adapter experts, each tuned to one accent.

The method works whether the accent is known at use time or not, with no need to retrain. Tests used the Whisper model on a corpus of second-language English speech. Word error fell clearly versus standard adapters and full fine-tuning when the accent was unknown, and fell further when it was known. The mixture also forgot less of its prior skill than rival methods.
arxiv-2505-20206:
Umut Cihan and co-authors grade large language models on the everyday job of reviewing code. Their 2025 study feeds two leading models hundreds of code blocks of mixed correctness, some machine-generated and some canonical benchmark solutions. Each model had to judge whether the code was right and fix it when it was not.

With the problem statement included, the stronger model judged correctness a little over two thirds of the time and fixed code at a similar rate. The rival model trailed on both counts. Removing the problem statement hurt both, and results shifted with the style of code. The authors conclude that model reviewers help but err often enough to be dangerous alone. They propose a human-in-the-loop review process that keeps the speed while sharing knowledge and catching faulty fixes.
arxiv-2505-20506:
Hawau Olamide Toyin and co-authors release a speech data set in 2025 for building Arabic voice synthesis. The corpus covers Modern Standard Arabic with full vowel marks in its transcripts, a rare aid since Arabic text is usually written without them. It is meant for many speaker synthesis, and it can also serve tasks like restoring vowel marks or spotting fake speech.

The set joins three parts: fresh studio recordings from six voice talents, a reshaped slice of an older Arabic corpus, and high quality synthetic speech from two commercial systems. In all it holds more than 83 hours across 11 voices, with about 10 hours of human speech from seven speakers. The team trains three speech synthesis systems and two voice conversion systems on it to show its use.
arxiv-2505-20706:
Shaohua Zhang, Yuchong Luo, and five colleagues catalog dust absorbers that live in the same homes as their quasars, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The absorbers carry the famous twenty-one seventy-five angstrom bump, a fingerprint of carbon-rich dust. Finding them at the quasar's own redshift ties them to its nucleus, host galaxy, or surroundings.

The team mined spectra and photometry for over five hundred fifty thousand quasars from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey's sixteenth data release. They identified eight hundred forty-three absorbers tied to their quasars. The bumps are weak and narrow on average, while their peak positions wander over a broad range. The average extinction curve resembles the Large Magellanic Cloud's, with a shallower rise. In quasars with broad absorption lines, the bumps shift systematically. A systematic census like this turns anecdotal dust sightings into population statistics.
arxiv-2505-21106:
Zhengyang Ji and co-authors probed social bias inside vision-language models in two thousand twenty-five. These models answer questions about images and text together. They can link neutral topics to traits like gender or race unfairly. Past work mostly measured how often bias appears. It said little about where bias starts inside the model.

The team traced how information flows through the model layers. They flagged image parts that sway answers to neutral questions. Then they ran multi-round chats to test model behavior further. Uneven use of inner information seems to drive biased replies. The method shows which parts of an image pull answers off course. Builders could use such maps to cut bias at its source.
arxiv-2505-21206:
The CMS Collaboration searches in 2025 for charge-parity violation in events with top quarks and Z bosons at the Large Hadron Collider. The catalog creator field is blank, so the byline in the text governs here. Data came from proton collisions at two energies, collected over several years.

For the first time in this channel, they use observables that are odd under the charge-parity transform. Machine learning informed by physics helps build those observables. Standard model processes predict symmetric distributions, while new effects would skew them. Results agree with the standard model within two standard deviations, and limits are set on two effective operators.
arxiv-2505-21406:
Pedro Pereira and four co-authors build a behavior based detector for malicious JavaScript in web applications. Attack methods grow more complex, so detectors need to track execution sequences rather than static code alone. Their system uses a deterministic finite automaton with weighted behaviors to capture known attack patterns.

New cases are classed as benign, partly malicious, or fully malicious by their similarity to known attacks. Partial matches matter because new threats often remix old steps. Tests on 1,058 sequences captured in a real world setting show the system finds exact matches and partial matches well. The design stays transparent in its decisions, which helps analysts audit alerts and adapt rules as threats evolve.
arxiv-2505-21706:
Gonzalo Travieso, Joao Merenda, and Odemir Bruno wrote a 2025 paper on telling networks apart by their shape. Networks model many systems, from friendships to roads to brain links. Given only the web of links, can a program guess what kind of system it came from? That task needs features that capture what makes each kind distinct.

The team proposes features drawn from random walks, where a walker hops from node to node and the path is measured. Walks reveal how tight or spread out a network is. They compared their walk-based features with leading rival methods on several data sets. The new method often won, though it lagged on some sets. The work adds a cheap, clear tool to the network analysis kit.
arxiv-2505-21806:
Brian Bue and co-authors present a 2025 computing paper on spotting greenhouse gas plumes with automated tools. Imaging spectrometers on planes and satellites can map methane leaks at fine scale. Turning that flood of data into reliable alerts still needs full automation.

The team tackles three blocks: poor data and label quality, biases in time and place, and mismatched training goals. With cleaned multi-campaign data from airborne and space instruments, their neural networks reach performance fit for operations. One multitask model finds plumes and outlines them pixel by pixel at the same time. The authors test detection across source types and regions to set deployment thresholds. They release data, models, and code, and propose shared validation standards for the field.
arxiv-2505-22206:
Enrique de Amo, David García-Fernández, and Manuel Úbeda-Flores extend a measure of directional dependence to data with any number of variables. Dependence measures usually say how strongly variables move together, but not who drives whom. Directional rho-coefficients were first defined for three variables in 2011 work by Nelsen and Úbeda-Flores. Their 2025 paper gives a general definition for any dimension and direction in the space of variables. Basic properties of the new measure are proved.

The authors also settle a conjecture from the original paper with a stronger result that holds in all dimensions. Along the way they correct a result in a later paper on a related index. Such measures serve fields from finance to climate, wherever knowing the direction of influence matters as much as its strength.
arxiv-2505-22506:
Wenjie Sun, Bingzhe Wu, Zhile Yang, and Chengke Wu study in a 2025 paper how sparse autoencoders reshape the geometry of model activations. These tools hunt single meaning features inside language model states. How sparsity itself organizes those states was the open question here.

Their SAEMA probe watches matrix rank shift as noise enters the residual stream. That watch confirms a layered structure in the learned representation. Sparse coding merges like meaning features and adds axes, sharpening gaps between features. Local and global views of the space split in their account of the effect. Tuning the global view proves a causal link from separability to reconstruction quality.
arxiv-2505-22606:
Dominic Briseno-Colunga and a team of co-authors study qubits driven by two microwave tones at once. Their twenty twenty-five paper deals with quantum bits in superconducting and semiconductor chips. Each drive that tunes a qubit also lets in low-frequency noise, which can cut its coherence time hard.

Sweet spots are drive settings where that noise bites least, and sour spots are where it bites most. With two drives of matched periods, the team maps both kinds of region using Floquet theory. They find whole manifolds of doubly sweet spots, along which settings can slide with no loss of coherence. That eases a trade-off seen with a single drive.
arxiv-2505-22706:
Fabio Rigamonti, Lorenzo Bertassi, Riccardo Buscicchio, and five colleagues re-examine a claimed pair of supermassive black holes in this two thousand twenty-five astronomy paper. Merged galaxies should often host two central black holes, among the loudest expected low-frequency gravitational wave sources. The galaxy SDSS J2320+0024 was proposed as a candidate because its light curve seemed periodic and its magnesium emission line varied. The authors reanalyzed the optical light curves in three bands with Bayesian model selection.

When periodicity competed against red noise, the g-band showed a broad posterior bump near two hundred ninety days, too broad to favor periodic models, and the other bands showed no matching peak. A periodic-only model picked a different, roughly eleven-hundred-day period but was statistically disfavored. The verdict: no significant evidence for true periodicity over ordinary red-noise variability. The binary interpretation is challenged but not ruled out.
arxiv-2505-22806:
Raluca Rufu and Robin Canup ask why so many star systems pack their planets tight, on short, close orbits. The pair argue in 2025 that such worlds start to grow while gas and grit still rain onto the disk round the young star. Past views held that growth waits till the rain stops. New sky data hint it need not wait.

In zones where rain still falls, a growing planet gains grit while gas drag pulls it in. The drag speeds up as the planet grows, so gain and loss meet at one mass. That balance yields same-size planets in a chain. The pair show such worlds can last till the gas clears. Total mass lands in a narrow band across wide settings, which fits the known tight systems.
arxiv-2505-22906:
Emmanuel Anaya González and co-authors worry that AI coding assistants make programmers passive, and they build a tool to keep humans in charge. Their system, HiLDe, lets a programmer watch and steer a language model while it writes code, rather than accepting text. The assistant highlights moments when the model makes a critical choice and offers local alternatives the user can pick, so intent guides generation at each fork.

Eighteen programmers used HiLDe and a standard assistant on security-related tasks, each trying both. Code written with the steering tool carried far fewer security flaws, and it matched the programmers' goals more closely. The authors argue the risk: in fields like software security, accepting code on autopilot can plant weaknesses that are costly to find. Their fix is not a smarter model but a better conversation with the model.
arxiv-2505-23006:
Chiwan Park and co-authors share a practical way to build production grade chat agents with workflow graphs in a 2025 paper. Large language models have lifted search, recommendation, and chatbot services. Yet real services need both flexible talk and strict rule compliance, and the random nature of such models makes those goals clash.

Their approach maps service flows as graphs, so the agent follows set paths while keeping natural talk. A case study in online shopping details the build flow and the tuning steps used. The authors frame the work as a bridge from research to real use, giving a path to agents that are scalable, controllable, and reliable at work.
arxiv-2505-23206:
Aldino Rizaldy and three co-authors fuse spectral and three dimensional point data directly in 3D space for land cover mapping. Past work crushes 3D data into flat maps, which wastes depth cues and blocks 3D forecasts. Their dual branch transformer learns shape and spectrum at once.

A cross focus step lets each mode weigh the other's traits across scales, all on raw points. On three contest sets the 3D fusion matched or beat flat methods. It also yields true 3D maps that can be flattened later, a one way gain. Code will be shared for reuse.
arxiv-2505-23406:
Binyamin Manela, Sharon Gannot, and Ethan Fetyaya present a video editor for dubbing films across languages in a 2025 paper. Dubbing needs the actor's lips to match new speech. Older tools either rebuild the whole face, which clashes with the scene, or paint over the mouth and lose details like shadows and partial coverings.

Their system, EdiDub, treats dubbing as careful editing of the original footage rather than fresh generation. A conditioning scheme keeps the edits faithful to the scene. On standard tests and on a hard set with covered lips, it preserved identity and lip sync better than leading methods. Human judges also rated its output more natural and better synced.
arxiv-2505-23506:
Sebastian Jimenez, Mira Jurgens, and Willem Waegeman argue, in a 2025 position paper, that popular methods for splitting a model's uncertainty into two kinds are fundamentally incomplete. Machine learning systems report uncertainty from data noise, called aleatoric, and from model ignorance, called epistemic. Trustworthy decisions, like medical ones, need that split to be honest.

Their first charge is bias. Unaccounted bias in the model leaks into the estimates, inflating the data noise share and shrinking the ignorance share. The system then blames the world for what is really its own error. Their second charge is partial coverage: different methods capture different slices of the variance behind epistemic uncertainty, so none measures the whole. Estimates end up hard to interpret and easy to misuse. The authors warn that safety critical use is only defensible when users fully grasp these limits.
arxiv-2505-23806:
Sihyeon Lee and co-authors present MedOrchestra in a 2025 paper on reading clinical data with language models. Cloud models are strong but seeing patient data raises privacy risks, while models run on site guard privacy yet often fail at hard reading tasks. Their hybrid design splits the work between the two.

A cloud model breaks a hard task into small steps and writes prompts for each, checked against clinical guides and made-up test cases, without ever seeing real patient data. A local model then runs those steps on site. On one hundred reports for staging pancreatic cancer, the hybrid beat local models and also beat doctors from three fields. Scores were higher still on structured reports.
arxiv-2505-23906:
Yu-Jen Chiu, Eric Weiner, and Ahmad Omar rebuild transport theory without assuming local equilibrium in a paper from 2025. The classic linear laws of transport rest on that assumption. Yet linear behavior shows up in many systems where local equilibrium is doubtful. The authors derive a mechanical theory for mixtures with several components. Their transport tensor reveals where the famous reciprocal relations break down.

The Einstein relations can fail too when equilibrium is absent. The framework is applied to passive mixtures, electrolytes in electric fields, and active matter. It also guides numerical methods for computing transport coefficients in driven systems. A worked example with nonreciprocal interactions shows the approach in action.
arxiv-2505-24006:
Agnideep Aich and seven co-authors build a spatial prediction model that respects extreme events, not just averages. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Maps of rainfall, pollution, or risk often bend toward Gaussian assumptions. Real fields can spike together in ways those assumptions miss. The team wants typical patterns and rare joint extremes in one model.

Their A2-SBNN network seeds its starting weights with a new copula, called A2. Copulas encode how values move together. Training blends a Wasserstein loss with moment matching and correlation penalties. Simulations across many dependence strengths show steady accuracy. The design manages uncertainty while mapping coordinates to continuous fields. Spatial modelers gain a route beyond Gaussian habits.
arxiv-2505-24106:
Dhruv Shah and Jorge Cortes designed controllers for neural feedback loops in a 2025 paper. Machine learning now models systems whose response to input bends in complex ways. Wrap a neural net inside a control loop and the pair form a bilinear system, whose stability is hard to vouch for.

Their frame recasts the loop with linear fractional tools and borrows from parameter-varying control. The controller comes from solving matrix inequalities offline, so it runs cheap online. Local stability of the target state is guaranteed by the math. The method gives learning-based control a safety proof it often lacks.
arxiv-2505-24306:
Kechen Li and seven co-authors build a bench that tests how well language models plan routes on a grid, alone and with classic algorithms at their side. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Models can reason about paths in words, yet most studies grade them in isolation.
