Every valid proof in the system is shown to compute, which yields a normalization result for the finitary fragment. Proofs of the right shape then denote unique functions on the natural numbers. A category model follows, where least fixpoints act as initial algebras and greatest ones as final coalgebras. The work ties a classical proof idea, descent, to modern programming semantics.
arxiv-2506-22506:
Momin Ahmad Khan, Yasra Chandio, and Fatima Muhammad Anwar wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It mounts the first study of backdoor attacks on federated prompt learning, and builds a guard against them.

In this setup many clients tune the prompts of a big vision-language model like CLIP, and no raw data moves. A rogue client can slip a faint learned noise mark into images, so the shared prompt trips on marked inputs while clean ones still score high. The guard, SABRE-FL, screens prompt updates with an anomaly detector that works in embedding space. It needs no client data or labels, and trains offline on odd data. Across five sets and four rival guards it cuts the backdoor's hit rate most while keeping clean scores.
arxiv-2506-22706:
Arun Ramamurthy and Neil Dhir work, in a 2025 paper, on cyber defense agents that stay competent when the network itself keeps changing shape. Today's automated defenders assume a fixed map, yet attackers, defenders, failures, and growth all redraw it, and agents trained on one layout overfit badly.

Their program, general autonomous cybersecurity defense, seeks policies that transfer across moving topologies and varied attacker styles, from malware to ransomware and phishing. The paper explores how to train such generalists instead of specialists. Robust defense, they argue, must treat the battlefield as fluid, not as the fixed board most training assumes.
arxiv-2506-23006:
Daniels Krimans and Hanno Kählert extend a new theory of fluid flow in plasmas in a 2025 paper. A plasma is a gas of charged particles, and when the charges bind strongly, plain fluid equations miss effects at small scales. A recent variational method adds those effects by building in how particle pairs are arranged.

The authors apply the method to a classic model plasma whose charges screen each other. They derive the motion and energy rules, check them against thermodynamics, and study small waves in the fluid. The speed of sound and the wave patterns matched computer simulations well across wide ranges, with gaps only at the strongest screening. They note the method could also serve for large, nonlinear flows.
arxiv-2506-23306:
Qi Liu, Can Li, and Wanjing Ma simulate city travel with AI agents that think in language, in a 2025 paper. Classic traffic simulators follow rigid rules and miss how varied and adaptive real travelers are. Their framework, GATSim, gives each agent a social profile, a lifestyle, and a memory that grows with experience. A layered memory stores trips with place and time tags for quick recall. Planning and quick-reaction modes let agents adapt day by day.

Agents also reflect on single trips to form general habits, in a process spanning several scales. In role-play tests the agents matched human annotators in believability. Left to run, they produced realistic city-wide traffic patterns on their own. The authors release the prototype code publicly. They pitch generative agents as a more human foundation for testing transport policy.
arxiv-2506-23406:
Tim Gerrits draws maps of uncertainty for the invisible skeletons inside tensor field data, in this 2025 paper. Engineers and materials scientists simulate stress and diffusion as tensor fields, and their topology, the surfaces where a tensor's character changes, reveals the structure that matters. Run the simulation many times with slightly different inputs and those surfaces wobble; where they might be is itself information.

Earlier work handled uncertain degenerate points and lines. Gerrits generalizes the machinery to uncertain mode surfaces of any mode value, the full family that includes neutral surfaces, with degenerate lines falling out as a special case. One framework now covers both surfaces that drift and lines that wander across an ensemble. The method is demonstrated on real simulation data sets from engineering and materials science. The point for practitioners: instead of one crisp surface that pretends certainty, they get the surface plus its halo of doubt.
arxiv-2506-23606:
Zhengkang Xiang and co-authors present SG-LDM, a 2025 diffusion model that generates LiDAR point clouds from semantic labels. Synthetic LiDAR can enrich training data where real scans are scarce or lack variety, and it lets engineers move objects around to build rare scenes. Earlier generators worked without guidance, which limits their use in real pipelines.

SG-LDM conditions generation on explicit semantic labels, so a scene layout in words and classes becomes a point cloud. It works directly in the native LiDAR space, using a latent alignment step to bind labels to geometry. The authors report state of the art fidelity for label guided generation. They also build the first diffusion based LiDAR translation framework on top of it. Translating scans across domains serves as adaptation, lifting downstream perception when a model moves to a new sensor or city.
arxiv-2506-23706:
Christoph Schnabl and three co-authors proposed in 2025 a way to run AI safety audits whose results can be verified and whose data stay secret. Standard benchmarks cannot prove a model really took the test, and both model designs and test sets are valuable property. Their audits run inside trusted execution environments, sealed hardware zones that attest to what ran inside. Neither side needs to trust the other.

Users can confirm they are dealing with a compliant model, while sensitive inputs stay hidden from outsiders. A prototype passed typical audit benchmarks against a current open model, showing the scheme works in practice. The authors aim the design at the verification demands in new AI governance frameworks.
arxiv-2506-24106:
Yanhong Li, Ming Li, Karen Livescu and Jiawei Zhou report a simple signal that predicts how well a language model will perform in 2025. Models whose internal representations spread out more widely, measured as the average cosine distance between hidden vectors, tended to achieve lower perplexity.

The link held across model families and text domains. Dispersion also proved useful without any labelled data: it ranks new examples by difficulty, flags hard slices of a new domain, and points to the layers that work best for retrieval-based methods. Adding a push-away term during training raised dispersion and improved perplexity directly. The work turns a geometric curiosity into a practical toolkit for screening and tuning models.
arxiv-2507-00006:
Models that spin one photo into many views drive 3D creation, yet scoring them fairly is tricky. Xianghui Xie, Chuhang Zou, Meher Gitika Karumuri, Jan Eric Lenssen, and Gerard Pons-Moll build a fair test in a 2025 paper. Their benchmark shuns ground-truth views, since many right answers exist.

A self-consistency score compares 3D rebuilds from split view sets instead. Twelve models face four data sets, real and fake. Robustness and real-world transfer get their own grades. Weak spots cluster on those two axes. The team's own method, built from the lessons, tops the consistency chart.
arxiv-2507-00206:
Tang, Seyam, and Yang fake full 3D brain-style scans to bulk up scant ward data in this twenty twenty-five paper. Ward scan sets are small, since access is tight and privacy rules bite hard. Flat slice fakes miss the depth links that full scans hold.

Inside, their model works in a shrunk code space learned by a first net. Guide maps mark which zone is which as the fake scan takes shape. That keeps depth form true while the math load stays low for a 3D task. Scores on a breast scan set show the fakes sit near real scans in grade. Split scores for zones in fakes near match those from real scans too.
arxiv-2507-00306:
Chao Zhang and co-authors estimate city wide travel demand from map traffic statistics instead of census or survey seeds, in work from twenty twenty-five. Planners need origin destination demand to manage traffic. Most cities lack the high grade counts and prior demand tables that classic methods demand.

Their method fits one smooth optimization problem that reproduces highway path travel times. A light analytic network model inside it needs little calibration and evaluates instantly. On Los Angeles and San Diego sensor counts, fit improved by two thirds to three quarters over a baseline. Trials in five more metro networks matched simulation benchmarks and beat the baseline on afternoon peak travel times.
arxiv-2507-00406:
Niklas Scholz and co-authors write a 2025 paper on AI feedback in programming classes. Feedback drives learning, yet teachers cannot reply to every student at once. Language models can draft replies fast, but past tools often ignored sound teaching principles such as mastery and pacing.

The team built a framework from classic feedback models plus input from local school teachers. A web app for Python lessons then gave model feedback shaped by those rules. Eight secondary school computer science teachers tested the app in a mixed study. They judged the aligned feedback helpful and at times faster and more exact than human replies. Weakness in reading live classroom context remained, so the authors pair the tool with teacher judgment.
arxiv-2507-00906:
Channyung Lee and three co-authors computed in 2025 how acceptor dopants wander inside a promising ultra-wide band gap crystal. The crystal, a gallium oxide, could anchor tougher electronics, but placing dopants well is everything. The team tested eight candidate acceptors under two regimes: fresh implantation and gentle heating.

Motion proved strongly directional, favoring two crystal axes. Each dopant's fate hinged on a race between moving and settling into place. Two candidates, calcium and magnesium, paired low movement barriers with easy settling under implantation. The rankings guide growers toward dopants that stay where they are put.
arxiv-2507-01006:
The GLM-V Team presents a family of vision-language models built for multimodal reasoning, including GLM-4.1V-Thinking and GLM-4.5V. The report shares the key lessons behind a reasoning-first training framework. It starts from a strong vision foundation model and scales reinforcement learning to sharpen reasoning. The goal is general-purpose skill across image and text tasks.

Dozens of team members contributed across data, training, and evaluation work. The models aim to handle varied multimodal problems with one system rather than narrow tools. The authors frame scalable reinforcement learning as the engine that lifts reasoning quality in vision-language models.
arxiv-2507-01106:
Yihong Du and co-authors watch sea ice age in salt water in a 2025 study. Sea ice steers Earth heat flow, and age shifts its strength and melt pace. The team grew soft, hole-filled ice in a stirred tank and tracked its slow change. Salt leaked out of the ice by spread through its pores. Pores shrank in step, a sign of age in the ice.

In time the layer turned to dense fresh ice next to well-mixed salt water. Sims of pore-free ice matched that end shape with care. The authors frame salt spread as the clock of ice age in the tank. Their rig gives labs a clean way to study a hard wild process.
arxiv-2507-01206:
Kathy Zhuang and co-authors present an augmented reality system for space robots in 2025. The catalog creator field is garbled, but the head byline names six authors. Their system, built for a NASA student challenge, targets missions like Artemis.

A headset shows the interface while voice commands run through a large language model, keeping hands free. Tracking software fixes the robot's pose in space using a stereo camera dataset built for bending robot bodies. A mission console visualizes status for the ground team. A transformer model estimates full pose from depth data in real time, even under noise and blocked views.
arxiv-2507-01406:
Vilimir Yordanov extends a classic inequality curve to several variables in this two thousand twenty-five paper. A Lorenz curve, built from a distribution, can itself be read as a new distribution. Repeating that operation gave a surprising result in his earlier work: the curves settle toward a power law.

In the multivariate version, the reshaping affects not only each variable's spread but also how the variables depend on each other. Yordanov proves that, under reasonable restrictions, each margin still converges evenly to a power law whose exponent is the golden section, and the variables become independent in the limit. The proof mixes tools from several areas. Lorenz curves are staples of economics, so the result may inform work on inequality and risk.
arxiv-2507-01506:
Kaur and Mondal build a light-front model of the pion that treats gluons as active players. In their frame, a high-energy probe strikes one gluon inside the pion. The rest of the particle acts as a spectator with an effective mass. Two equations from quantum chromodynamics set the pion's mass pattern and wave functions. One is a holographic equation used at the chiral limit. The other is the 't Hooft equation.

From those wave functions they compute how gluons are shared inside the pion. Results include several distribution types used in scattering studies. Comparisons run against global fits from data. The model stays within one momentum region and notes that limit openly.
arxiv-2507-01606:
Nick van Loo, Francesco Zatelli, and their co-authors demonstrate a single shot readout of a minimal chain that hosts Majorana modes. Their 2025 paper explains that topological qubits would store information across a pair of these modes, whose shared state is either even or odd, a property called parity. Reading that parity is the only way to use the qubit, and it demands coupling the two modes.

The chain is built from quantum dots linked by superconductors, with just two sites, the smallest version possible. The team reads parity through quantum capacitance, a measure of how the system stores charge. Their method resolves the parity in real time, seen as random switching between states. Even short chains with limited protection can now be measured cleanly.
arxiv-2507-01806:
Reza Arabpour and his two co-authors, publishing in 2025, offer a way to fine-tune language models for people who own no graphics card. The popular fine-tuning method, LoRA, trains small adapter patches instead of the whole model, but it still assumes GPU training. Their framework skips new training entirely. It learns a meta-operator that assembles a fresh adapter from a bank of ready-made ones, blended on an ordinary laptop CPU.

The test bed is a well-known open model, with a library of its adapters standing by. The assembled adapters do not match GPU-trained quality. But they consistently beat the untouched base model on downstream tasks. The authors ground the approach in theory and aim it at students, hobbyists, and labs in low-resource settings. They frame CPU assembly as the practical floor of access to model customization.
arxiv-2507-02206:
Ranyang Zhou and co-authors build a true random number generator inside computer memory and use it to hide the weights of neural networks. Random numbers underpin hardware security, but software generators can be predicted. Their design exploits RowHammer, a memory fault where rapid access to one row flips bits in nearby rows. Controlled carefully, those flips supply genuine randomness at low cost.

The team shows the flips can serve as a steady source of entropy. They then encode network weights with a mix of fixed and random flips. A key drawn from the flip behavior lets owners decode the model later. This keeps the data private and proves the model is genuine. The authors argue the approach offers strong, cheap hardware security and a fresh direction for guarding machine learning models where they run.
arxiv-2507-02306:
Ruican Zhong, David McDonald, and Gary Hsieh test in 2025 whether AI can grade app usability as well as human experts can. Expert review is a standard design check, but it costs time and pay. Their method feeds app screens to a multimodal model that writes design feedback.

Across two apps, the AI review finds 73 and 77 percent of known usability flaws. Five seasoned human reviewers find only 57 and 63 percent. The AI stays steady across tasks and shines on layout flaws. It still misses some screen parts, design norms, and flaws that span screens. Repeat runs hold stable, which supports AI as a cheap first pass before human review.
arxiv-2507-02506:
India's courts decide bail in lakhs of orders, yet language machines have almost no Indian legal data to learn from. Sneha Deshmukh and Prathmesh Kamble publish a first set in 2025: 1,200 real bail orders, each tagged on more than twenty points. The tags span the outcome, the crime kind, the law parts cited, and the court's stated reasons.

The tags were drafted by a prompt-tuned large model and then checked for agreement. Tasks the set unlocks run from outcome forecasts to summaries and fairness audits. Bail is liberty decided in a page or two, so a data set that lets machines study its patterns serves both scholars and reformers. The set is public, the authors state.
arxiv-2507-02706:
Grasser, Snellen, de Regt, and a team of co-authors wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five, the eighth in the ESO SupJup Survey. It reads the chemical prints of two young L dwarf twins in the AB Doradus Moving Group.

How planets and brown dwarfs form may be stamped in their element and isotope mixes. The team took high-resolution spectra of the pair with the CRIRES+ tool and fit them with a retrieval pipeline. Both dwarfs show firm reads of rare carbon monoxide and hydrogen fluoride. Their isotope ratios are near kin, and both sit close to chemical balance. Hints of a rare water form stay weak. Later survey papers will set the pair among kin.
arxiv-2507-03006:
Faisal Ahmed and a co-author compare two ways to pull useful traits from medical scans, in a 2025 study of eye images. One way tracks the slope of brightness at each point and sums those slopes by direction. The other way reads the global shape of an image, such as how its parts link and where holes form.

The team tested both ways on a public set of retina photos. Their tasks were to split healthy eyes from eyes with diabetic eye disease, and to grade that disease in five classes. They trained seven standard learning models and checked them with repeated splits of the data. One boosting model scored best with both trait types, near 94 percent on the two-class task.
arxiv-2507-03206:
April Tran and David Bortz improve the building blocks of a data-driven modeling method, in a 2025 paper. The method, weak form scientific machine learning, identifies systems from data without directly differentiating noisy measurements. Instead it folds the model equations together with smooth test functions, which buys robustness against noise.

Performance hinges on choosing those test functions well. The authors propose a data-driven way to build single-scale, local reference functions. Their approach estimates the integration error from the numerical scheme and picks the support size where that error is smallest, all without knowing the true parameter values. Across models, noise levels, and time resolutions, the chosen supports matched the regions of lowest estimation error. The new construction also ran faster than their earlier multi-scale global approach.
arxiv-2507-04106:
Stanisław Pawlak and co-authors study poisoning attacks on continual learning in 2025. Such systems learn task after task without keeping old examples. Poisoned data in even one task was recently shown to threaten the whole chain.

Their attack setting is stricter and more realistic: the attacker knows nothing of the model or other tasks. Only the current task's data can be touched. Plain image corruptions still badly disrupted learning, hurting both memory of old tasks and uptake of new ones. A defense frame plus a detection method based on task vectors is proposed in reply.
arxiv-2507-04806:
Zuo Ye and Gennian Ge set size limits for error-correcting codes under a rich edit measure in a 2025 maths paper. The measure counts deletions, insertions, swaps, and flips of neighbors needed to turn one string into another. Fresh interest came from DNA data storage, where such edits occur.

Past work built codes that fix a deletion plus neighbor swaps, but no size caps were known. The authors prove upper bounds for how many codewords can fit at a given length and guard level. Their bounds show a known code is near best, off by at most a fixed margin in extra symbols.
arxiv-2507-04906:
Gianmarco Tedeschi, Rune Kristian Lundedal Nielsen, and Paolo Burelli measure how loot boxes in games affect players' arousal in a 2025 paper. Loot boxes sell random rewards and have been compared with gambling, but body-level evidence is scarce. The team built a custom game so every loot box event followed the same pattern for all players.

Skin conductance sensors tracked arousal through the session, capturing both steady levels and quick spikes. Players also completed a standard scale for gaming disorder severity. The study links the two, asking whether heavier gaming problems go with stronger body responses to loot boxes. The authors frame the work as evidence for developers and policymakers weighing the risks of random reward systems in games.
arxiv-2507-05506:
Takashi Moriya and co-authors link two rare supernova kinds in 2025. Some stars in tight binaries get stripped almost bare before they explode. Those ultra stripped blasts were tied to faint fast fading events. The team shows they can also produce a rarer type marked by helium rich surroundings.

Violent silicon burning just before collapse can throw off a shell of dense matter. The explosion then slams into that shell and glows in the observed pattern. Their model uses a small pre blast ejection weeks before collapse. The result unifies two explosion families under one progenitor story.
arxiv-2507-05606:
Omar El Housni, Qing Feng, and Huseyin Topaloglu wrote this operations research paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on fairness in what an online store chooses to show. Pure revenue chasing can starve some products and crown others, which can hurt the seller over time.

The authors add a balance rule: no two offered products may differ in expected sales by more than a set factor. In the static case, where one mix is chosen once, they show the problem can be solved in polynomial time. The best mix has a clean form: a product is in exactly when its revenue and appeal clear set bars. Extra limits on the mix can be handled with an approximation oracle. In the dynamic case, with stock running down over time, their policy is near-optimal when stocks are large.
arxiv-2507-05706:
Liu and six co-authors watch a single quantum spin explore its possible states in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Ergodicity, the habit of visiting every allowed configuration, underlies equilibrium in classical physics, but quantum systems seemed barred from it by their frozen energy states.

Using a defect in diamond as the spin, the team drove it with rhythms of increasing complexity and tracked its states by full tomography. A regular beat produced no ergodic exploration, a smooth quasiperiodic drive produced partial exploration, and a Fibonacci-patterned kick sequence produced complete exploration. They tie each level to the complexity of the drive. The experiment gives the first clear evidence of this hierarchy of Hilbert space ergodicity.
arxiv-2507-06006:
Edoardo Rossi develops Bayesian tools to read galaxy histories in a 2025 project report. A galaxy star formation history tells when its stars were born. Mean age alone hides how spread out that birth was. Rossi defines a span measure from the ages by which set fractions of stars had formed.

Model libraries of composite stellar populations span varied histories, metal content, and dust. Ten spectral features, from line indexes to broad fluxes, are matched to data with Bayesian care. One task finds the finest span that spectra can truly resolve. Tests on mock galaxies then check how well spans are recovered. The tools aim at surveys that map the sky in bulk.
arxiv-2507-06306:
Neil Rathi, Dan Jurafsky, and Kaitlyn Zhou study how people across languages respond to language models that sound too sure of themselves. Their 2025 paper notes that models are known to sound overconfident in English, which leads users to lean on wrong answers. Words that mark doubt or certainty, though, work differently across languages, so the risk may vary worldwide.

The team studied five languages. Models used strength giving words often, even inside wrong answers, but the mix shifted by language: most doubt markers in Japanese, most certainty markers in German and Mandarin. Human reliance was then measured in each language. Overreliance stayed high across all of them. The study argues that global deployment needs safety checks in each language, not just English.
arxiv-2507-06506:
Russell Taylor, Benjamin Herbert, and Michael Sana translate puns from English to French with a team of AI agents, in a 2025 paper. Wordplay defeats most translation systems. A pun's sound and sense must both survive. The team entered a shared task on humor translation. Their method runs in three stages. First, top language models draft translations. Feedback comes from a new contrastive dataset built for the purpose.

Second, a guided reasoning pipeline adds sound-and-meaning embeddings. Those embeddings help find French words that echo the original's trick. Third, generator and judge agents loop together. Bad puns are scored and regenerated with comments. The aim is creativity, not literal matching. Their best runs took first and second place in the contest. Native French experts judged the entries by hand. The work links translation studies with language technology. It shows models can aim at jokes deliberately.
arxiv-2507-06606:
Qing Zhang, Guoquan Pei, and Yan Wang build a neural network that reads medical hyperspectral images by fusing what they show in space and in spectrum, in a 2025 paper. Such images, used in pathology, record a full light spectrum at every pixel, revealing tissue chemistry invisible to normal cameras. The richness is also the problem: the data are high-dimensional and spectrally redundant, so models struggle to use both dimensions well.

Their network, Omni-Fuse, mixes the dimensions repeatedly. A cross-dimensional module sharpens spatial and spectral features by letting each attend to the other. A spectral-guided step picks the spatial features most relevant to the spectrum as queries, and a two-stage decoder steers attention toward them. Despite the many attention blocks, the model stays efficient. On two microscopic hyperspectral datasets it beat state-of-the-art segmenters by over 5.73 points of Dice score. Code is public.
arxiv-2507-06706:
RSA encryption rests on the claim that nobody can compute Euler's totient of a huge number in reasonable time. Gilda Rech Bansimba, Regis Babindamana, and Beni Blaug Ibara test a statistical side door in 2025, training linear regression models to guess the totient from the modulus itself.

Their data covered RSA moduli from 64 up to 1,024 bits, each paired with its true totient. The regression learned the relation well enough to land within a small relative error on fresh samples, by their early results. The authors do not claim a break of RSA. They argue such approximations could assist certain attack classes, and they offer the work as a probe of how far learning methods reach into cryptanalysis.
arxiv-2507-07006:
Taslim Uddin Raju and co-authors present a system that both sorts and describes microscope images of tissue, in a paper from 2025. Whole slide images are huge, and many patches repeat the same area or lack a known place. Writing captions for such images is also hard.

Their system first cuts repeated patches by grouping like patches and keeping strong examples. A graph network then joins local and broad context, and the result feeds a language model that writes captions. On two data sets the system scored high on sorting accuracy and on caption quality. It beat prior methods on both tasks, which the authors say could support faster and more reliable diagnosis.
arxiv-2507-07106:
Vatsal Agarwal and co-authors test, in a 2025 paper, if a text-to-image model can serve as the eyes of a talk model. The usual eyes, CLIP, catch the broad scene but miss fine points that a query needs. Spread models, the team finds, hold rich sense marks and tight image-text ties in their guts. Text cues can aim those marks at the parts a query asks for. They then join the marks to a talk model and hit a snag: the talk model can leak the source prompt back. Causes are read, and a fix is set.

A blend of CLIP marks and cued spread marks is their end pick. Gains show most on sight-led tasks of space and build.
arxiv-2507-07606:
Quentin Le Houérou and Ludovic Patey study a family of math statements in the style of Ramsey theory, in a 2025 paper. Each statement says that any coloring of the links in an endless complete graph leaves a large sub-graph that avoids a set pattern. The authors ask how much computing power each statement needs. One class of patterns, called separable permutations, turns out to play a special role.

For those patterns, avoiding the pattern is shown to match a basic known property: the existence of an endless set that is uniform in color. For every other pattern, that match fails. The proof uses a fresh argument about what cannot be computed, even with extra help allowed. The result draws a sharp line between pattern types that look alike on the surface.
arxiv-2507-07906:
Anant Gupta, Rajarshi Bhowmik, and Geoffrey Gunow use language model agents to track what companies talk about in their earnings calls. Financial analysts follow strategic themes over time, but traditional topic models struggle as industries evolve and new topics emerge. Their agent extracts topics from call transcripts and organizes them into a hierarchical ontology.

The system links new topics to existing ones, so the ontology grows with the calls each quarter. The extracted topics then support company-level insights and trend detection over time. Evaluation measures ontology coherence, how accurately topic evolution is captured, and the ability to surface emerging financial trends. The authors present the agent as a dynamic alternative to static topic modeling for finance.
arxiv-2507-08006:
Aashish Panta and co-authors shrink vast climate data in a 2025 paper sans loss of its tale. Sky and sim reads now swell past what stores and wires can hold. Plain cuts save space but blunt the fine marks that carry the science.

Their kit stacks the data in tiers, sends it with smart picks, and lets taught models rebuild the fine grain. Costs fell by near all, from a vast sum to a small one, while the miss stayed near a degree and a half. Tests hold the marks that count for true reads. Climate teams gain a way to keep big sky lore cheap.
arxiv-2507-08106:
Yannick Gachnang and Vismay Churiwala test whether image-generation style models can predict flowing fluids, in a 2025 paper. They set out to replicate and extend DiffFluid, a study that combined diffusion models with transformers to solve fluid equations such as Navier-Stokes and Darcy flow. The question was whether the approach generalizes beyond its original setting.

Working with limited computing resources, the pair probed the method on additional simulation types, notably the Lattice Boltzmann method. Their results were mixed in a useful way: the diffusion approach bent to new problems, but cost and scaling remained hard. The paper reads as a reproducibility report, mapping where the technique shines and where engineering effort is still needed before it can serve as a general fluid solver.
arxiv-2507-08306:
Sight-and-word models can reason in words yet trip over the room in front of them. A lab team at a big tech group answers in 2025 with a model trained to do both at once. The catalog credits the group and its parent firm; the head byline names the hands, past a garbled mark. Near three hundred thousand training tales were built by a new pipe, each with its reasoning laid out step by step.

Training ran in two heats, a broad warm-up and a prize-led round, with task-tuned rewards to keep the two skills from fighting. The end model set the top mark on eight tests, in both plain and spatial reasoning. The team frame the blend, not either half, as the bar for the next round of models.
arxiv-2507-08506:
Ivanov and co-authors present an algorithm that pushes gravity readings from the surface down toward their hidden sources. Geologists use such downward continuation to locate the bodies that cause gravity anomalies. The task is unstable by nature, since small errors in the data can blow up as the field is extended downward.

The method writes the deep field as the pull of a thin, simple layer, or of its vertical change. Keeping the layer's density to one sign keeps the anomalies' signs intact, as long as the layer wraps all the sources. A non-negative least squares solver enforces that sign rule in practice. Model examples show the algorithm recovering the buried sources well. The authors frame it as a steadier route into the subsurface.
arxiv-2507-08806:
Daewon Choi and nine co-authors show, in a 2025 preprint, that trimming a reasoning model's train of thought makes it smarter. Long chains of thought help models solve hard problems. Yet the chains carry much dead weight, and attention inside them spreads thin. Wrong answers show the thinnest spread of all. The team marks each reasoning chunk with a closing instruction token. Attention paid to that token reveals which tokens actually matter. Chunks that contribute little are pruned as units, keeping the cut structured.

After pruning, the closing instruction is removed and generation resumes. No retraining is involved. Across reasoning-heavy benchmarks, accuracy climbed clearly. Gains were strongest on math contest sets, where bloated reasoning is common. The authors frame the trick as removing distraction: the model thinks the same thoughts, minus the static. Cleaner chains, they argue, are a free upgrade for reasoning models.
arxiv-2507-09106:
Kevin Bhimani and co-authors use a cyclic translation network to imitate how readout electronics shape signals in ultra-pure germanium detectors. Those detectors hunt rare events like a special nuclear decay and dark matter hits. The shape of each pulse tells analysts whether an event looks like signal or background, so simulations must reproduce electronics effects faithfully.

Classic simulation stacks correction on correction and still misses the data. Their network learns to translate between simulated and real pulse styles, carrying positional information through the process. Transfer learning adapts it across setups. Better emulation means sharper cuts and more trustworthy spectra in rare-event searches.
arxiv-2507-09506:
Junjie Wu and four colleagues benchmark whether long-context language models can say where information came from inside very long inputs. Their Ref-Long benchmark asks models to identify the indexes of documents that reference a specific key, a task needing real contextual relationships rather than simple retrieval. Three subsets range from synthetic to realistic scenarios.

Testing thirteen long-context models exposed significant shortcomings, even for advanced systems like GPT-4o. Human evaluation, format adjustments, fine-tuning experiments, and error analysis probe why. The authors position referencing as a distinct, underexplored capability that long-context marketing claims tend to hide. Data and code are released for follow-up work on attribution inside long documents.
arxiv-2507-10106:
Harshal Nandigramwar, Syed Qutub, and Kay-Ulrich Scholl build BlueGlass, an infrastructure for combining AI safety tools instead of trusting any single one. Safety checks usually each guard one flank: internals or outputs, one failure mode at a time. No isolated tool gives full assurance. BlueGlass provides the unified plumbing to compose diverse tools into one workflow.

Three demonstrations on vision-language models doing object detection show the idea at work. A distributional evaluation exposes performance trade-offs and failure modes across data shifts. A probe-based analysis of layer dynamics finds shared hierarchical learning marked by a phase transition. Sparse autoencoders surface interpretable concepts inside the model. The authors pitch the framework as foundational infrastructure. Their claim: robust AI will be assured the way bridges are, by layered, independent inspections.
arxiv-2507-10506:
Emeric Bouin and co-authors prove sharp decay rates for kinetic equations in a half-space in a 2025 paper. Kinetic models track particles that stream and collide. A wall that absorbs particles changes how fast order fades. Whole-space rates do not apply at such a boundary.

Solutions decay faster in the half-space than in open space, in two weighted norms. The rates match those of the heat equation with a fixed-zero wall. The class spans relaxation models, Fokker-Planck type equations, and a spherical velocity model of Brownian motion. The proof gives the first optimal rates for this boundary setting, closing a gap in kinetic theory.
arxiv-2507-10906:
Qunhong Zeng and co-authors test in a 2025 paper if large language models can grade commit messages in software. Commit notes explain code changes, yet many are empty or weak in practice. Auto writing of notes has leapt ahead, but grading them still leans on costly human reads.

Classic text scores assume one right note per change, which does not hold for code work. Trials with varied prompts show models that reason step by step with a few examples grade near human level. The model grader beat classic scores by a wide margin in the tests. It held fair marks for repeatability and fairness, with some swing still present. The authors frame it as a scalable stand in for human grading.
arxiv-2507-11106:
The authors present a math method in a 2025 paper for spotting outliers in data with several clusters. A classic method wraps data in the smallest balls that hold the normal points and flags the rest. Their version builds many spheres at once, one per cluster, using a strict optimization model.

A second form of the model applies the kernel trick, which lets the spheres bend around complex, curved data shapes. In computer tests, the exact method beat faster guessing methods on accuracy and steadiness. Finding outliers cleanly matters in fraud checks, medicine, and fault detection, where a missed odd case can be costly.
arxiv-2507-11406:
Henrique Ennes and Clément Maria designed compact data structures in 2025 for a classic way to describe three-dimensional spaces. Any closed space of that kind can be built by gluing two thick shapes along a shared surface, and two sets of curves on the surface capture the gluing. Storing those curves by their crossing counts against a surface mesh can take far less room than storing the whole space.

For some families the saving grows exponentially. Even so, the pair gives fast methods to compare diagrams, simplify them, spot trivial changes, and compute basic invariants of the space. Early software tests ran faster than standard tools on typical inputs, with huge gains on some.
arxiv-2507-11806:
Hendrik Kraß, Ju Huang, and Seyed Mohamad Moosavi test atom models on spongy crystals in a 2025 paper. The crystals are metal-organic frameworks, lattices with vast inner pores. They serve in carbon capture, energy storage, and speeded-up chemical work. Machine-learned atom models now promise quantum-grade accuracy at far lower cost. But porous crystals, with odd bonds and open space, barely appear in their training data.

The team built a test suite called MOFSimBench. It grades more than 20 models on shape tuning, motion steadiness, bulk traits, and guest uptake. The best broad models beat classic force fields and tuned models on every task. Training data quality mattered most, they found. Sets with wide chemistry and off-balance shapes gave the strongest models.
arxiv-2507-12206:
School maths holds a shelf of mean rules, from the plain mean chain to Jensen's rule, each oft taught as bare sums. Gourav Banerjee gives those rules a heat root in a 2025 study. He builds one wide rule from the laws of heat, in two parts.

The first part proves, in strict sums, that a set of bodies at unlike heats settles at one shared heat. The second proves that drift is the kind that heat laws favour. From the wide rule, the shelf of school rules falls out as cases. Banerjee, the sole author, adds the firm proofs that past heat takes of the rule left out. He aims the piece at students who learn best by nature's lead.
arxiv-2507-12406:
Tomoaki Okayama sharpens a numerical recipe for convolution integrals, in a 2025 paper. The Sinc convolution, proposed by Stenger, approximates integrals that blend two functions over a whole line. It is used across physics and engineering, but parts of its theory stayed unsettled, including a conjecture of Stenger himself.

Okayama first repairs the theory, settling the open issues and the conjecture. He then swaps the recipe's stretching step for a stronger double-exponential version. Analysis and computer tests show the modified formula converges faster than the original. Faster, firmer formulas for such integrals quietly speed up many fields that lean on them, from wave physics to finance.
arxiv-2507-12506:
Siyu Chen and co-authors close a gap between lab marks and math calls for a cerium hydride that conducts with no loss at high squeeze. Such hydrides draw wide hype for their high switch heat, yet plain math has trailed the lab for this one. The miss may stem from strong ties among electrons that plain tools skip. Their 2025 study pairs two math frames to hold both electrons and lattice waves.

With ties in play, more electrons sit at the key energy rim and the pair gap grows. Waves tied to hydrogen atoms also soften. Jointly, the shifts lift the called switch heat from a low mark to one near the lab mark. The near match backs the frame for kin hydrides. It also maps a path to math that can be trusted pre-lab.
arxiv-2507-12806:
Zhiwei Liu and a team of co-authors build MCPEval, a frame that makes and grades tasks for smart agents on its own. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Agents built on large models need firm tests, but past ways rest on fixed sets and hand-made data, which cap their use. MCPEval is built on a shared protocol for agent tools. It makes tasks end to end, grades them in depth, and sets the marks in a fixed form. It plugs into the agents' own tools, with no hand work to build the test path. Tests in five real fields show it can bare fine gaps in how agents do. The code is shared in the open.
arxiv-2507-12906:
Kouèssi Norbert Adédji and two co-authors chase number patterns where two named families can be built from repeated digits. Thabit and Williams numbers have fixed forms in any base. A repdigit is a number with one digit repeated, like 777. Their 2025 work asks when the named numbers equal a sum or gap of two such repeats.

For set base pairs, the team finds recipe families that yield endless many matches. For the rest, they bound the sizes so only finitely many can occur, then solve some cases in full. Such hunts blend old Diophantine tools with sharp bounds. The results sort a small corner of digit play with care. Worked cases show the method in action.
arxiv-2507-13406:
Ratul Mandal and co-authors chart the fate paths of a modified gravity cosmos with a speedy scalar field in a 2025 paper. The gravity model builds on nonmetricity, a measure of how lengths shift as they move. A DBI-essence field, born of string ideas, plays the dark energy role.

Two forms of the gravity rule, a power law and an exponential, are each turned into a flow system. Rest points of each flow map to cosmic eras, from stiff early times to late speeding expansion. Stability tests sort which eras can last. Chosen values for energy shares and slowdown match what telescopes report, keeping the models in play.
arxiv-2507-13806:
Antoine Sanner, Luca Michel, Alessandra Lingua, and David Kammer find that removing one bond can toughen a network in a 2025 paper. They simulated triangular spring networks with a crack and deleted a single bond in different positions. Intuition says damage weakens material, but the results split in two.

The energy needed to start the crack could rise or fall depending on where the missing bond sat relative to the crack tip. The energy needed to tear the whole network apart, though, never dropped and usually rose. Often the crack simply stopped at the toughest spot. When the crack detoured, bridging added even more toughness, mainly when springs break at low stretch. The work speaks to designing tough materials with deliberate defects.
arxiv-2507-13906:
Blazars are galaxies whose jets point at Earth, and their gamma ray output can flicker with near regular rhythms called quasi-periodic oscillations. Penil and co-authors study three blazars seen by the Fermi space telescope. They look for a special pattern: oscillations whose strength grows or shrinks in a straight line over time. To catch it, they cut each light curve into rising and falling stretches and analyze each stretch on its own, measuring both the period and the slow trend.

For one blazar, the flicker looks more like random noise than a true period. For the other two, the periods fit what would be expected if two supermassive black holes orbit each other and swing the jet around. The authors stress that the evidence is tentative. Longer records and more events will be needed before the binary explanation can be confirmed or ruled out.
arxiv-2507-14306:
Samarth P and colleagues turned research papers into animated explanations automatically in a 2025 paper. Their open-source system, Manimator, attacks a familiar pain: dense papers and abstract math concepts are hard to learn from text alone, while good animations take experts hours to craft by hand. The pipeline chains two language models around the Manim animation engine, a popular tool for math videos.

The first model reads a paper file or a plain prompt and writes a structured scene plan naming concepts, formulas, and visual elements. The second translates that plan into runnable Manim code that renders the animation. The authors present the tool as a way to democratize polished STEM explainer videos for teachers and students.
arxiv-2507-14506:
Yu and co-authors model a chain of nuclei with a magic neutron count in this 2025 paper. The chain holds eighty-two neutrons while protons run from fifty-one to seventy-seven. A shell model with a fresh effective interaction does the heavy lifting. The interaction was tuned by a statistical method that squeezed one hundred sixty input numbers down to thirty key ones.

Fitting to about two hundred known energy levels left errors near a hundred kilo-electronvolts. The model then matched binding energies, spectra, and magnetic moments across even and odd members. It also forecasts five proton-rich nuclei beyond today's reach, from tantalum to iridium isotopes.
arxiv-2507-14806:
Rayani Rithvik and Shantanu Desai recomputed journal impact factors for particle physics in a 2025 study. Impact factors, the average citations per paper, shape careers and library budgets, yet the official numbers come from one commercial source. Using citation data from the NASA astrophysics archive, the pair calculated fresh factors for sixteen journals in particle and nuclear physics and compared three versions of the score.

The archive-based factors showed no systematic bias against the official ones. Median-based factors differed most for two journals, and in each case a single blockbuster paper explained the gap, with one review gathering well over a thousand recent citations. The check supports the official numbers while exposing their sensitivity to outliers.
arxiv-2507-15006:
Chappelon, Ramirez Alfonsin, and Stamate present a new picture of the numerical semigroup tree, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. A numerical semigroup is a set of whole numbers closed under addition with finitely many gaps. The tree organizes all such sets by their gap count, called genus. The new picture sorts sets by a second trait called type.

Computer searches over the new picture reveal steady patterns. When type sits close to genus, counts of sets stay constant as genus grows. The team also studies how counts rise and fall and how leaves of the tree behave. Several conjectures grow out of the experiments. Each is backed by extensive computer checks, though proofs remain open.
arxiv-2507-15506:
Mi-Jung So and Mahn-Soo Choi present a general scheme for protecting quantum information from noise, in a 2025 physics paper. Quantum systems lose their stored information through contact with the environment, a process called decoherence. One defense is to hide information in a corner of the system that noise cannot touch. Earlier versions of this idea needed strong symmetry in the system, which real devices rarely have.

The authors work in Liouville space, a frame that describes open quantum systems, and use symmetry to split that space into blocks. A protected subsystem appears as one factor of those blocks, and it can survive under weaker symmetry than before. Using permutation symmetry and standard group theory tools, they build a basis that makes the noise structure easy to read.
arxiv-2507-15706:
David Peter Wallis Freeborn models how receivers learn structured messages in a paper from two thousand twenty-five, written alone. In signaling games, senders pass messages to receivers who must act on them. Standard models show receivers failing to read messages part by part, so losing one part erases the rest.

Freeborn builds simpler models where real compositional understanding can evolve. One receiver learns only from the smallest message units, while another learns from all available information. Both can treat message parts separately, so knowledge of one part survives loss of another. The paper argues these leaner models explain structured communication better than earlier, more complex ones.
arxiv-2507-15806:
Ashwin Verma and co-authors added a power cap to learning-based control in a 2025 paper. The test task is the classic linear quadratic regulator, which steers a linear system at least cost. When the system's math is unknown, policy gradient methods learn the steering by trial, using gradient steps sent over a noisy channel.

The sender faces an average power cap across a set time span. The team first solve the broad case of descent under noisy gradients. Their power plan spreads the budget across steps to cut the end error bound the most. They then carry the plan back to the control task.
arxiv-2507-15906:
Debangshu Banerjee, Kintan Saha, and Aditya Gopalan make AI alignment steadier by accounting for reward model uncertainty in a 2025 paper. Standard alignment trains a reward model on human preferences, then optimizes the AI against it. But a single reward model can be wrong, and squeezing too hard against it can make the AI worse.

The authors first show that reward models trained separately on the same data often disagree strongly. Theory then links that wobble to overfitting risk. Their fix adds a regularizer that uses the reward model's own variance, steering updates away from shaky ground. They prove this lowers the risk of ending with a worse policy, and experiments across setups confirm steadier, more robust alignment.
arxiv-2507-16006:
Fernando Aguirre and co-authors present in 2025 twin telescope designs for a proposed ultraviolet supernova mission. Type Ia blasts calibrate cosmic distance, yet the nature of the donor star stays debated. Early ultraviolet light in the first days after blast holds the key clues.

Two small telescopes watch far and near ultraviolet bands, with a third for a blue band. Delta-doped sensors and custom filters lift ultraviolet catch while blocking red leaks. The design reaches faint limits with red rejection past a hundred thousand fold. A small satellite bus keeps the mission lean and fast to fly.
arxiv-2507-16306:
Xingjian Zhang, Yizhuo Wang, and Guillaume Sartoretti build COMPASS, a team learning system for tracking moving targets. Agents must watch targets that wander under uncertainty, as in disaster response or wildlife work. The world is cast as a graph, with nodes for places and edges for closeness. Each agent acts alone but thinks through a shared attention network.

The network blends past sightings with spatial layout to guide revisits. Gaussian process models track each target and update beliefs in a principled way. Training pairs central value estimates with local policy action. Trials beat strong rivals on doubt cut, target coverage, and team coordination across shifting scenes.
arxiv-2507-16606:
Bhupal Dev and co-authors explored a rare nuclear decay in a 2025 theory paper. The decay, where two neutrons turn into two protons with no neutrinos shed, would prove that neutrinos are their own antiparticles. It has never been seen, and any rate bound guides deep theory.

The team worked inside SU(5), a grand unified theory that merges three of nature's forces. In the plain form, heavy scalar fields that could drive the decay are choked off by proton decay bounds. A discrete symmetry plus an added scalar set lifts that choke in part. The paper maps how large the scalar share of the decay can grow.
arxiv-2507-16806:
Mehul Damani and co-authors train language models to reason about their own uncertainty, in a 2025 paper. The catalog creator field adds a school name, so the head byline governs. Models trained by reinforcement with yes or no rewards get better at hard questions, but they also learn to guess with false confidence.

Their method asks the model for an answer plus a numeric confidence after reasoning. The reward joins the correctness score with a proper score for the confidence call, which rewards honest odds. The team proves such rewards yield accurate and well calibrated models. Tests across data sets show better calibration with no loss in accuracy.
arxiv-2507-16906:
Giorgio Mentasti and Carlo Contaldi give three ways of hearing gravity waves one shared language in a 2025 paper. Pulsar clocks, star position wobbles, and a shimmer in far images each sense the same faint ripples in space. Each field grew its own math, which makes pooling their data awkward.

Written in spin-weighted harmonics, each signal's pattern of agreement across the sky takes a neat closed form. The famed pulsar curve falls out as the plainest case. Wobble and shimmer get matching curves of their own. Odd wave kinds, beyond the standard two, fit the same frame. Pipelines can now blend the three data streams cleanly.
arxiv-2507-17106:
Jiazhao Wang and Wenchao Jiang present a spectrum multiplexer built from neural network filter banks, in a research paper from 2025. A multiplexer lets many narrow-band device signals share one gateway path, which lifts spectrum use. Standard methods can distort signals or run slowly, so a cleaner and faster design is wanted.

The authors treat a neural network as a filter bank by design, not by accident. Learning then tunes the bank for near-zero distortion, while hardware speeds the work. Tests reach very low distortion across signal types and settings. Speed gains reach many times over standard methods, with high packet success in field trials.
arxiv-2507-17206:
Zosiamliana and six co-authors compute, from first principles, whether a family of alkali lead oxide glasses could serve in energy devices. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The compounds swap lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, and cesium into the same lead oxide frame. Lead-based materials draw interest for turning heat or pressure into power.

Three hybrid quantum methods were compared against measured crystal sizes. One method matched best and anchored the study. All five compounds passed checks for thermal and mechanical stability. For the three with off-center crystal phases, the team computed piezoelectric response two ways. One cesium compound stood out on that measure. Heat-to-power scores landed in a promising mid range for all. The family earns a closer experimental look.
arxiv-2507-17306:
Angel Reyero-Lobo, Pierre Neuvial, and Bertrand Thirion put variable importance measures on firm ground in a 2025 paper. Scores that rank which inputs drive the output are everywhere in explainable AI, yet many are folk recipes with no guarantees. Popular ones can even crown inputs that add no information at all.

An axiomatic framework ties these scores to variable selection and to tests of conditional independence, drawing on decades of work on statistical proof. The authors propose a general recipe: define an index in theory, estimate it, and derive its guarantees. Applied across many scores, the lens shows what each really targets. Tests on simulated and real data guide practitioners to the right index.
arxiv-2507-17406:
Ayce Idil Aytekin and six co-authors tackle human pose tracking from a moving phone style camera in a 2025 paper. Most past tools assume a still camera and a flat floor. Real video breaks both rules, and tests on fake data miss how light and motion play out in the real world.

They built MoviCam, a real data set with true camera paths, scene shapes, and body motion with contact marks. Their tracker pairs a pose guesser with a camera path tool, then polishes the pose with physics rules that respect the scene. On their tests, top past tools stumbled in this hard setting, while theirs held steady for body and camera alike.
arxiv-2507-17606:
Jasper Rou explores neural network methods for pricing American put options in this 2025 paper. An American option can be exercised at any time, which makes its price obey an equation with a moving boundary. Rou prices options under two standard market models, in up to five dimensions. Two learning methods are compared: a gradient flow method and the Deep Galerkin Method.

Rou extends the gradient flow method to handle the moving boundary at the heart of the problem. A careful sampling plan during training boosts performance. Both methods reach high accuracy and outrun classic Monte Carlo pricing on speed. The gradient flow method also trains faster than its rival. The work supports neural pricing for options with many underlying assets.
arxiv-2507-18406:
Silvia Cappa and co-authors study clashing facts in Wikipedia tables across languages, in a 2025 paper. The site holds content in more than three hundred languages, but each version is written and updated on its own. The same topic can thus carry unlike facts in unlike tongues, which can mislead readers and AI systems trained on the site.

The team builds a method to gather, align, and sort tables from linked articles. They define types of clash and score how well versions line up in a sample set. The work matters for fact checking and for the design of AI that draws on Wikipedia in many languages at once.
arxiv-2507-19006:
David M Russinoff machine-checks the foundations of linear algebra. His 2025 paper is the first part of an exposition of a formalization, in the ACL2 theorem prover. It covers the elementary theory of matrices over any commutative ring, not just the real numbers.

Working over a general ring sets up later parts, where the characteristic polynomial's entries live in a polynomial ring. This installment's centerpiece is the determinant, built formally from scratch. He proves its characterization as the unique alternating multilinear function of a matrix's rows, its multiplicativity, and the correctness of cofactor expansion. The work belongs to a long program of making textbook mathematics fully proof-checked, line by line, by machine.
arxiv-2507-19106:
Smooth shear flows in a channel can stay stable even at very high speeds, proves a 2025 paper by Yaniv Almog and Bernard Helffer. The setting is a two-dimensional channel, with a laminar profile that strictly increases across the gap but whose curvature may touch zero.

A positivity condition on a certain operator, checked for every speed where the curvature vanishes, is shown to guarantee stability once the Reynolds number is large enough. Earlier results demanded stronger assumptions or excluded long waves. The new proof admits long perturbations, though still far shorter than the Reynolds number itself. The work widens the class of flows that theory can call safe at high speed.
arxiv-2507-19206:
Banks must gauge how badly loans can sour, and Davide Veronelli and co-authors bring a quantum tool to that task in work from twenty twenty-five. Quantum methods can speed up risk scores, but the circuits they need are pricey and cramped. One costly step is loading the chance curves into the quantum state.

A value-shaping trick cuts that loading cost by a wide margin. The team built the full pipeline in code and ran a test study to check it. Results backed the savings while keeping the risk scores sound. The work gives banks a more real path to quantum risk tools, though live gear limits still bind how far the method scales today.
arxiv-2507-19406:
Xinyue Wei and John Kolinski measure energy stored in stepped brittle cracks in a 2025 paper. Moving crack fronts often split into disjoint steps. A band of the stuff bridges the newly split fronts. These traits reshape stress fields and stability, yet lacked hard numbers.

The team scanned a laser sheet through brittle hydrogel samples in 3D. Tracer particles revealed how the stuff bends around steps and inside the bands. The band held strain energy in a sharp, dense way. Apparent fracture energy rose in proportion to the energy in the band. That link is the paper's central find. In-situ imaging during spread made the measuring possible. Stepped traits found in all such cracks thus carry a set energy cost. Fracture models must budget for storage in the band, the results imply. Those who design brittle parts gain a correction factor. The method extends to other clear brittle solids.
arxiv-2507-19506:
Ying-Ying Jin, Yi-Ting Wang, and Li-Hong Xie prove results in pure mathematics in a 2025 paper on gyrogroups. A gyrogroup is a set with a rule that mimics group algebra but drops one strict law. The paper studies quotient spaces, which group members into classes by a chosen sub-part.

The authors set conditions on the sub-part and then prove three linked claims. First, the quotient space has one spread property exactly when it has a nesting property. Second, it can be measured by a metric exactly when it pairs that spread property with a count rule. Third, a second count rule gives the same result when the space has the Baire property.
arxiv-2507-19606:
Maurice de Gosson wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on the geometry behind generalized coherent states. Such states are a basic tool in quantum theory, and here they are treated as Gaussian wavefunctions. The paper reviews past work, fills gaps, and pulls the results into one account.

At the heart of the work are three geometric objects: Fermi ellipsoids, quantum blobs, and microlocal pairs. De Gosson links the coherent states to each of these objects in turn. He then studies the symplectic capacities tied to them, which are numbers that measure size in a way suited to phase space. The paper serves readers who want the geometric picture of quantum states gathered in a single place, rather than spread across many sources.
arxiv-2507-19706:
Adam Muzzin and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper that lays out a large imaging survey with the James Webb Space Telescope. Past surveys mapped four deep fields with broad filters, which can hide odd sources and blur mass counts. A new treasury program adds mid-width filters for a far sharper view.

The survey spends hundreds of hours to image four known fields in eight near infrared bands and two mid infrared bands. It spans hundreds of square minutes of sky and reaches faint limits. Joined with past data, each field gains a rich filter set for a joint catalog. Aims include finding hidden sources and cutting errors in star mass counts. The team also maps star mass and birth across cosmic time.
arxiv-2507-20406:
Justin Boone, writing alone in 2025, tests whether the shape of a metabolic network predicts which genes a cell cannot lose. Standard tools simulate flows through the network to judge each gene. Those tools often miss in complex networks with many backup paths. Boone guessed that network shape alone carries a stronger signal.

He built a graph from a core model of gut bacterium metabolism. For each gene, he computed shape measures such as how central its reactions sit. A random forest model learned from those measures. Its scores were checked against a curated truth set and against the standard flow method. The shape-based model won clearly, a result with weight for drug target hunting.
arxiv-2507-20906:
Jungwon Park and co-authors present a method to inject task knowledge into a language model by picking the right attention heads, in work from 2025. One way to adapt a model is to draw a task embedding from a few examples and inject it at run time. Past versions of that idea gave uneven gains over standard tuning or in context learning.

Their method uses gradients to find which attention heads matter for a task. Injection then targets those heads. Across open ended writing, reasoning, and language understanding tasks, the method beat prior embedding methods and few shot learning. It also used far fewer trainable parameters than standard fine tuning.
arxiv-2507-21606:
Yaozong Zheng and co-authors present a tracking model that learns from unlabeled video, in a paper from 2025. Visual tracking usually needs boxes drawn by hand around targets in many frames. That labeling is costly and limits data size and variety.

Their model, called SSTrack++, trains with a weak-to-strong scheme that narrows the gap between the few labeled frames and the many unlabeled ones. Space and time consistency are taught apart: global position cues come from single frames, and motion links come from pairs. A self-prompting module tracks how the target's look changes, at both feature and decision levels. A contrast loss teaches which views show the same object. The design aims for strong tracking with almost no hand labels.
arxiv-2507-22006:
Zhou and three colleagues forecast how sharp X ray telescopes can hunt axion like particles in twenty twenty-five. These light particles may mix with photons inside magnetic plasma. The mixing stamps wavy dips on X ray spectra from bright sources. Long paths, strong fields, and rich photon counts make space X rays a keen probe.

Three source setups were simulated, from galaxy clusters to home galaxy binaries. A long look at one cluster galaxy with a current mission could beat today's best limit. Planned missions reach the same depth far faster. Field modeling and photon counts drive the reach, they find.
arxiv-2507-22306:
Sahan Sanjaya, Aruna Jayasena, and Prabhat Mishra unveil a power side-channel attack that rides on context switches, in a 2025 paper. When a system swaps programs, it saves state and flushes its pipeline, which spikes power draw. A built-in sleep call can trigger that swap on demand. The spike's height carries traces of the program that ran just before.

Unlike classic attacks, this one needs just a single spike height, not a full power trace. A power model shows how the leak can be turned into key theft. Tests on a common board recovered keys from two cipher setups. The authors warn that leftover power can betray work long after it ends.
arxiv-2507-22506:
Jirong Mao and three co-authors simulate gas falling into a black hole when gas carries little spin. Such slow-spinning inflow is thought to power some wild behavior of black hole systems, including flares. The team ran full relativity simulations including magnetic fields, in both two and three dimensions, and varied black hole spin across runs.

In all runs the flow settled into the standard calm regime known in the field. The striking result was the appearance of standing shocks: sharp fronts in the flow that form and hold their place rather than washing away. Earlier studies missed such stable structures. The authors link shock behavior to light features seen in real systems, such as flares from the black hole at our galaxy's center and rhythmic signals in X-ray binaries. They present the finding as a first for this class of simulation.
arxiv-2507-23306:
Yuhao Peng and four co-authors dissect jet particles in simulated collisions in a 2025 paper. Proton collisions at the LHC spray jets of particles. Sorting jet particles from the surrounding event soup is tricky. A classifier based on transverse activity splits events by busyness.

The team used the AMPT transport model with standard initial conditions. Pions, kaons, and protons were tracked in the jet direction and sideways regions. Subtracting the sideways yield isolates true in jet production. Spectra and particle ratios matched experimental data well in both regions. Inside jets, the baryon to meson ratio crossed over at middle momenta. That crossing depended on event activity through final state interactions. It may serve as a signature of jets interacting with their medium.
arxiv-2507-23406:
Shaykin and Kamchatnov build the theory of shock like waves in optical fibers. A strong light pulse can steepen into a dispersive shock, a rippling front rather than a clean jump. Over long fiber runs, a faint Raman effect settles the front's shape. The pair derives the slow modulation equations that govern such waves.

From those equations flow jump rules linking the states on both sides of the front. Their analytic profiles match direct computer solutions of the full pulse equation very closely. The work gives fiber engineers a pencil and paper route to predict shock shapes. It extends classic shock theory into nonlinear optics.
arxiv-2507-23606:
Andrea Loi, Roberto Mossa, and Fabio Zuddas prove a sweeping embedding result in geometry in a 2025 paper. Flag manifolds are highly symmetric spaces built from nested subspaces. The team shows every such space fits inside a single classical one while preserving both its complex structure and its metric.

From that embedding, rigid behavior follows for maps between uniform curved spaces. Certain soliton submanifolds inside mixed products must be trivial. More broadly, the three great families of uniform spaces, flat spaces, flag manifolds, and bounded domains, cannot share a common piece even in a loose local sense. The result unifies a string of earlier rigidity theorems.
arxiv-2508-00306:
Fuentealba-Bustamante and Arellano study nucleon scattering from nuclei with unequal protons and neutrons in twenty twenty-five. The effective force between nucleons inside matter may depend on that imbalance. The team builds this dependence into their model of the interaction. They base it on solutions for symmetric matter and pure neutron matter.

A folding approach turns the in medium interaction into an optical potential for scattering. The potential keeps the full nonlocal structure of the interaction. Including isospin asymmetry gave a fair match to measured cross sections at beam energies from forty to two hundred mega electron volts. For protons below about sixty-five mega electron volts, neutron matter terms improved the fit at low momentum transfer. The authors claim a real effect at those energies.
arxiv-2508-00506:
Tulsi Patel and co-authors build an unsupervised tool for labeling satellite images in a 2025 paper. Machine learning on remote sensing data needs fresh, accurate labels, but expert labeling is slow and costly. Older tools still lean on pre-labeled data, which begs the question they should answer.

Their pipeline first cuts Sentinel-2 images into uniform regions by color and space. Convolutional and graph networks then encode each region into a robust feature space. Like regions can be grouped and labeled together without any training labels. Whole landscapes can thus be charted from raw pixels alone. Land agencies gain a faster route from new imagery to usable maps.
arxiv-2508-00806:
Ping Chen and co-authors present in 2025 a framework to train large language models within tight graphics memory. Training stores vast mid-step data, and memory limits bite hard. Two past fixes each have flaws: recomputing steps wastes time, while squeezing data can hurt accuracy.

Their framework, Adacc, blends both fixes and picks per data block. Fine choices weigh block traits and live hardware limits. New squeeze methods guard accuracy by handling outlier values with care. A math-based schedule plans choices across all layers at once. The plan also updates itself as training runs. The aim is faster training with no loss in model quality.
arxiv-2508-01206:
Prathyush Kumar Reddy Lebaku and three co-authors test a cheaper way to grade roads in twenty twenty-five. Road networks cover huge areas and need frequent checks to stay in service. Manual surveys and survey vehicles are slow and labor-heavy. Satellites, meanwhile, now capture far more ground detail than before.

The team used deep learning models to judge pavement condition from satellite images. Better ground resolution means cracks and wear show up more clearly. If the method holds up, agencies could scan whole networks from orbit. Field crews could then be sent only where the images flag real damage. Readers get a test of whether space-based checks can stand in for some road-level surveys.
arxiv-2508-01706:
Aytijhya Saha and Aaditya Ramdas wrote a statistics paper in 2025 on estimating the shape of data that mixes two kinds of values. Some values vary smoothly, while others repeat at fixed points. Standard methods assume only the smooth kind, so they can fail on mixed data. The paper looks for a simple fix that keeps the old methods sound.

The key idea is plain: a value seen once likely comes from the smooth part, while repeats point to the fixed part. Wrapping old methods with this check restores sound results for a broad class of measures. The fix needs no knowledge of the fixed points or the mixing share, and it adds no cost when data are not mixed.
arxiv-2508-01806:
Ugur Abdulla, Jose Rodrigues, and Jean-Jacques Slotine worked in 2025 on steering pairs of molecules whose spins affect chemical outcomes. Such pairs may help explain how some animals sense magnetic fields. The goal was to shape an outside field so the pair reaches a desired quantum state and yields more of one product.

The model joins a quantum equation for spin with filter equations for the field. The authors prove key math traits and show the best control switches on and off. They also build a step-by-step method to find that control. Tests showed the method was steady and close to a simpler field in yield, with a gap under one percent.
arxiv-2508-02006:
Ahmad Al-Sulami, Hamza Fawzi, and Shengding Sun give exact methods for a hard optimization problem, in a 2025 paper. Each variable in the problem must be a complex root of unity, a point evenly spaced on the unit circle, and the goal is a quadratic score. Such problems arise in signal processing, signal detection in wireless systems, and ground-state searches in physics.

First, the team proves that a ladder of relaxations, the sum-of-squares hierarchy, reaches the exact answer after roughly half the levels once expected. Second, they recast the problem with half as many binary variables by using shapes called zonotopes. On test problems the new form solved up to ten times faster.
arxiv-2508-02106:
Kaiyang Ji and co-authors build a live system that cooks up believable human moves for mixed scenes in a 2025 paper. The goal is smooth play between people and avatars, human-like robots, or work machines in virtual worlds. Past tools trade speed for realism or skip safety.

The new framework plans acts and replies at once, step by step, so partners stay in sync. A trained tracker keeps feet planted and stops limbs from passing through props or people. Tests on two big motion sets beat prior tools on quality, flow, and realism. A live virtual setup for robot work shows the scheme in real use.
arxiv-2508-02206:
Luise Blank and Maximilian Urmann optimize structures made of several materials for 3D printing, in a 2025 paper. A printed part must hold its shape against gravity while it is being built, layer by layer. Overhangs can sag before the part is done. Their model treats the growing part with elasticity equations that change with build height, and it can include hardening as layers set.

The math side proves good designs exist and the cost measure behaves smoothly for a fixed number of layers. A key inequality is shown to hold with a constant that does not drift with height. The solver uses a projected gradient method enriched with curvature data and a nested scheme. Tests in two and three dimensions show steady iteration counts across resolutions and layer counts.
arxiv-2508-02406:
Jureeporn Yuennan, Allah Ditta, Thammarong Eadkhong, and Phongpichit Channuie build wormhole solutions in a modified gravity theory. Their 2025 paper works in non-minimal Einstein-Yang-Mills gravity, where a gauge field couples directly to curvature. The wormholes are static and round, with a purely magnetic field. A fixed redshift function keeps the math tractable.

For small values of the coupling, the throat and flare-out rules can be met. That allows passable wormholes with no exotic matter added by hand. Total mass grows with charge at low coupling and falls at higher coupling. Energy rules are broken only near the throat, while one rule holds throughout. Light bending stays positive, which marks an attractive field and a possible observational sign.
arxiv-2508-02606:
Stack diamond against cubic boron nitride and you get a junction between two of the widest-bandgap materials known. Cody Milne and co-authors model that interface atom by atom. Using density-functional theory, they vary how the boron nitride layer ends, how thick it grows, and how its surface is treated. Formation energies then reveal which arrangements nature would prefer.

Boron-terminated junctions are the most stable. Abrupt nitrogen-terminated ones are the least stable, though mixing carbon in rescues them. The electronic behavior flips with the ending: boron sides conduct like p-type material, nitrogen sides like n-type. Carbon-mixed junctions stay insulating. Some interfaces even host dense two-dimensional gases of electrons or holes. For high-power, high-frequency devices, the message is that the interface recipe is the device.
arxiv-2508-03306:
Kisu Yang and co-authors fix a measurement flaw in low-precision search systems in this 2025 study. Search engines rank documents by score, and running models with fewer bits per number makes ranking faster and cheaper. But coarse numbers create many tied scores, and how ties are broken can swing the final grade of a system, making tests unreliable.
