Their protocol has two parts. First, recompute the final scoring step in higher precision, which unties most near-equal documents at small cost. Second, report metrics that state the expected score, the range, and the bias caused by ties. Tests across models and data sets showed the first step sharply cut score swings. The second step recovered true expected values. Together they give low-precision search a steadier yardstick.
arxiv-2508-03406:
A delivery-route model with no valid solution is a riddle, not an answer, and Kai Li and co-authors build a diagnostician for such riddles in a 2025 paper. Users pile on conflicting demands until the feasible set is empty. Their system, MOID, pairs language-model agents with multi-objective optimization inside an automatic routing solver.

Instead of one patch, the optimizer returns a family of trade-offs between low path cost and small rule-breaking, each implying different repairs. A language-model agent then reads that family through an analysis function it writes for the case, turning numbers into plain diagnostic suggestions. Against rival language-model methods on fifty kinds of broken routing problems, MOID produced multiple actionable suggestions in a single run. The authors pitch it as decision support for restoring feasibility, not just an error message.
arxiv-2508-03506:
Phoenix Paing and Daniel James study how a single atom can squeeze a light field in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Their model is the quantum Rabi model, which couples a two-level atom to one mode of light. They go beyond the common rotating wave shortcut. Using a systematic expansion method named after Magnus, they track how the system evolves at any time.

At second order, they find a term that squeezes the field, with the squeeze set by the atom's state. They test the effect's size on a known transition in rubidium atoms. The squeezing peaks at set points in the detuning cycle. The angle of the squeeze hints at readouts that leave the atom undisturbed. The work may inform quantum sensors and light-based quantum devices.
arxiv-2508-03706:
Zhenshan Xie, Levente Baljer, M Jorge Cardoso, and Emma Robinson build a model that can simulate how a baby's brain surface grows over time. Their 2025 work responds to a real need: babies born early often follow altered paths of cortical growth, yet outcomes vary so widely that early prediction is hard.

Their graph diffusion model works on the folded surface of the cortex and can be steered to render growth for one child at a time. Trained on scans from the developing Human Connectome Project, the model kept each child's own folding pattern while aging the surface in a believable way. An age-guessing network trained apart was fooled by the output, which the team reads as a sign of sound simulation.
arxiv-2508-04106:
Shan Shen and co-authors share an open test kit for chip cell yield work that hews close to fab truth. The work dates to 2025. Yield reads for the cells drive chip gains, yet school forms skip much fab mess. Tools that shine on plain forms oft fail on true ones.

The kit has three parts. A cell build tool weaves in wire drag, cell leak ties, and edge-part swings that plain forms drop. A test stage with a plain face and stock tools makes fair races. A size-tune stage lets width picks be tried the same way by all. The kit is free for all to use.
arxiv-2508-04206:
Nazary, Tourani, Deldjoo, and Di Noia build a benchmark for recommending movies with help from language models and all of a film's media at once, in a 2025 paper. Most benchmarks use raw features or narrow fusions. Their suite aligns audio, visual, and text embeddings for thousands of films drawn from two public datasets, and uses large models to write missing synopses.

The pipeline lets researchers swap fusion strategies and recommender backbones through one configuration file. Scoring covers accuracy plus cold-start handling, coverage, novelty, diversity, and fairness. Language-model enrichment and strong text embeddings especially helped new-item recommendations. Code, embeddings, and configurations are open source.
arxiv-2508-04306:
Automatic literature reviews fail by accumulation: one wrong citation early poisons every later stage. Zhi Zhang and co-authors counter that cascade in a 2025 paper with a memory system that consolidates verified facts as the review is built. One part organizes sources in a tree that shapes the outline; another gathers evidence around hub papers and refines the text.

A third part loops back over its own history to catch errors before they spread. On public benchmarks and a new large data set, the system led on citation accuracy and content quality. The design treats memory, not just generation, as the cure for compounding mistakes.
arxiv-2508-04606:
Jasmine Bone and co-authors benchmarked in 2025 the quantum chemistry methods used to predict how carbonyl molecules absorb light too faintly to see. These dark transitions drive the sunlit breakdown of many air pollutants. A molecule's shape shifting slightly can brighten or dim them sharply, so a method must stay honest away from the resting shape.

Sixteen carbonyl compounds at rest were scored against a gold-standard calculation. The team then dragged one molecule toward its excited shape and sampled its wobbling forms to build absorption curves. Each method's curve implied a different lifetime for the molecule in sunlight. The authors say the choice of method can quietly rewrite predicted pollution fates. Their benchmark tells modelers which tools to trust.
arxiv-2508-04706:
Shalmali Bandyopadhyay and Kimsear Lor prove that certain discrete equations on unevenly spaced grids always have a solution trapped between two bounding functions. These difference equations model processes sampled at irregular times, and the boundary conditions here are mixed and non-homogeneous, which complicates the math. Earlier results covered only simpler boundary setups.

Their strategy separates the boundary effects from the equation's core structure. That split lets them apply a classic fixed point theorem inside an affine function space. The result guarantees a solution lying between a chosen lower and upper function. The work extends the upper and lower solution method to a broader class of discrete boundary value problems.
arxiv-2508-04806:
Bernard Parent and co-authors offered a new braking device for planetary entry in 2025. A capsule returning through an atmosphere can use magnetohydrodynamics, pushing against the ionized air with magnetic forces, to slow down for aerocapture. Earlier designs forced a choice: systems without electrodes acted over the whole vehicle, while systems acting at chosen spots needed electrodes in the flow. The new design aims for local action with no electrodes.

Two magnets are arranged on the shell, one with its field facing outward and one facing inward. So they close a current loop and generate a Faraday electromotive force in the plasma. In numeric models of an Earth entry capsule at very high Mach number, the device made forces several times larger than a two-electrode system using the same field strength. All results so far come from a specialized flow model code.
arxiv-2508-04906:
Abdellah Touati and Soufiane Boukhalfa propose that quark confinement is a property of spacetime geometry rather than an added force law. They study the strong interaction inside hadrons placed in curved spacetime. A new gauge potential supplies both color-electric and color-magnetic fields, including a monopole-like term and a radial Coulomb-like part.

Solving Einstein's equations for a reduced symmetry case yields a metric shaped by the Yang-Mills field. The Schwarzschild radius of the strong interaction comes out near the size of a hadron. Quark and gluon wave functions break at that surface, which reads as confinement emerging from the geometry itself. The computed energy spectra in the combined fields reproduce hadron masses with good accuracy. A residual correction term improves the match further. The authors present the model as a geometric route to a long-standing puzzle of the strong force.
arxiv-2508-05006:
Youzhi Zhang and co-authors frame molecular docking as a two-player game in work from 2025. Docking predicts how a small drug molecule fits a protein pocket, a key step in drug discovery, but joint models dock ligands worse than pockets.

In their game, a ligand module and a pocket module act as rival players that exchange predicted poses. An outer loop lets each adapt to the other, while an inner loop refines each module on its own predictions. Theory shows the training converges. On public benchmarks, accurate binding modes rose by about ten percent over prior best methods.
arxiv-2508-05306:
Mathias Bjare, Stefan Lattner, and Gerhard Widmer model musical surprise from raw audio with diffusion based models, in a paper from 2025. Surprise, or how unexpected the next sound feels, shapes how listeners hear music. A recent transformer model estimated surprise well from its own guesses about what comes next.

The authors ask whether diffusion models, which build audio by removing noise step by step, can do the same job. Their estimates fit varied data better than the transformer on a standard loss measure. Two tasks test the idea in practice: rating how surprising single notes feel, and finding segment borders in multi track songs. The diffusion models matched or beat the transformer on both. Surprise read at unlike noise levels may track features at unlike time scales.
arxiv-2508-05406:
Atsushi Ueda and co-authors upgrade a computational lens for two-dimensional quantum matter at finite temperature, in a 2025 paper. Tensor network methods compress a quantum system's state into a web of small tensors, then repeatedly coarsen the web to see the whole. Their new scheme chooses that coarsening by global optimization rather than local greed, and builds the warm, thermal state of a 2D system in a fresh way.

Together the two advances form an algorithm that reads off the universal numbers of a conformal field theory right at a thermal phase change, with high accuracy. Those numbers are fingerprints: matching them identifies which kind of transition a material undergoes. A sharper numerical route to them gives physicists an alternative to fitting critical exponents, and a tool for classifying phases in materials and model systems alike.
arxiv-2508-05506:
Shibo Wang and co-authors present MagicHOI, a method for rebuilding hands and grasped objects from short single-camera videos, in their 2025 arXiv paper. Template-free methods usually assume the whole object is visible, yet fixed viewpoints and firm grips hide large parts of it, leading to implausible shapes.

Their insight is to borrow supervision from large novel view synthesis diffusion models, which can imagine unseen sides of an object. That prior regularizes the hidden regions during reconstruction. Visible contact constraints then align hand to object. The method beat leading rivals by a clear margin, showing that generated view priors can rescue real-world hand-object capture.
arxiv-2508-05606:
Luozheng Qin and eight co-authors unify step-by-step reasoning across text and images in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Chain-of-thought reasoning helps language models by splitting tasks into steps. Vision tasks add a snag: the picture itself changes as reasoning proceeds.

Their framework, Uni-CoT, uses one model that both reads and generates images, so visual states evolve inside the reasoning. Reasoning runs at two levels: a macro level plans the task, a micro level executes each step. That split keeps computing costs in check. Structured training mixes interleaved image-text supervision with multi-task goals. On generation and editing benchmarks, Uni-CoT reached top performance with modest hardware. The authors pitch it as scalable multimodal reasoning.
arxiv-2508-05906:
Hyunseok Oh and co-authors report a diamond optomechanical device with a spin inside in this 2025 physics paper. The chip couples a vibrating diamond beam to light and to nitrogen vacancy spins, tiny defects that act as quantum sensors. The hard part is a vibration that rings long while the spin stays coherent. Their resonator's mechanical quality factor passed one million at cold temperatures. The embedded spins kept coherence for up to 270 microseconds, near bulk diamond values.

The device also handled optical power across five orders of magnitude without breaking down. Its optomechanical cooperativity ran well above one, the mark of strong light motion coupling. A high throughput membrane process plus overgrowth with nitrogen doping made the result repeatable. The authors present the platform as ready for hybrid quantum devices: sensors, networks, and computers that pass information between light, motion, and spin.
arxiv-2508-06506:
Stella Menziltsidou proposes a hybrid way to measure how fast a black hole spins, a key open problem in relativistic astrophysics. Standard methods, such as fitting the glow of hot gas or reading X-ray reflections, each carry limits in accuracy and reach.

Her approach joins theory from the Teukolsky formalism with physics-informed neural networks. The network learns under physical rules and boundary conditions, so it needs no labeled training data. In tests it settled with very small errors and beat both classic and plain machine learning methods on standard scores. She also notes it stays easier to interpret. Future work may link it to full relativity simulations and real telescope data.
arxiv-2508-06606:
Nils Niggemann and co-authors build one of the simplest possible homes for fractons, exotic excitations that can barely move. In a fracton spin liquid, the ground state comes in a huge number of versions and the rules resemble a tensor version of Gauss's law. Their model discretizes that gauge theory directly on a square lattice of spin-half particles.

The simple build exposes the state's anatomy: real-space fracton patterns, a height-field picture of the ground states, and the ripples allowed inside the fracton-free sector. Sampling the classical ground states shows the tensor law survives the strict spin length rule, so a classical Ising fracton liquid exists. Quantum nudges, though, fail to tunnel between ground states, and the state space shatters into fragments. Simulations then find either magnetic order or the classical liquid, never the quantum one. A companion paper tries larger spins as an escape.
arxiv-2508-06706:
Jaikrishna Patil and co-authors slim the rulebooks of knowledge graph completion without losing their answers. Rule-based systems explain themselves beautifully but need tens of thousands of rules, so nobody can grasp the whole machine. The team instead learns a probability distribution over cooperating rule sets, represented as a probabilistic circuit.

The payoff is drastic: seventy to ninety-six percent fewer rules reach the baseline's peak performance. At equal tiny rule counts their method beats the baseline by up to thirty-one fold, and their minimal sets keep about ninety-one percent of the full system's peak. Across eight benchmarks the small sets also waste less: fewer idle rules, fewer rules per prediction. The framework rests on Nilsson's probabilistic logic and needs no independence assumptions.
arxiv-2508-06906:
Morteza Kimiaei and co-authors survey learning-aided exact solvers in twenty twenty-five. Mixed integer optimization drives logistics, energy, and scheduling, but it is computationally hard. Machine learning might speed up exact methods such as branch-and-bound. The challenge is to gain speed without giving up guaranteed optimality.

The survey covers discrete, continuous, and mixed-integer problem forms. Applications include vehicle routing, hydropower planning, and crew scheduling. A unified branch-and-bound framework embeds learning at several points. Branching, cut selection, node ordering, and parameter control can all be learned. Supervised, imitation, and reinforcement learning each appear. The authors close with a taxonomy by solver class and learning style, plus open challenges.
arxiv-2508-07006:
Gian Mario Favero and seven co-authors build a generative model that forecasts future brain lesions in multiple sclerosis, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The disease unfolds unevenly from person to person, which makes personal forecasts valuable. Their model predicts where new or growing lesions will appear at a future scan.

The model ingests brain scans plus which treatment the patient receives. It then paints the future lesion map directly in image space. Training used thousands of trial scans from many centers and six treatments. Forecasts were accurate across all treatments. Side uses include counting future lesions, judging whether a patient will be active, and imagining the same patient's future under other treatments. The authors see causal image models as a new prognostic tool.
arxiv-2508-07206:
Konstantin Rybakov and Egor Shermatov model linear filters spectrally in two thousand twenty five. Their technique rests on the spectral form of linear systems. Input and output signals become orthogonal expansions of basis functions. Filters are described by two dimensional non stationary transfer functions.

The output signal is then modeled in continuous time. Three classic filter families test the approach in depth. Butterworth, Linkwitz-Riley, and Chebyshev filters all pass the checks. Different filter orders are covered in the tests as well. The method offers a unified way to simulate filter behavior.
arxiv-2508-07506:
Hammas Bin Tanveer, Echo Chan, Ricky Mok, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It studies who scans the IPv6 internet, the vast new address space, by setting traps that lure scanners into revealing themselves.

IPv6 is too large to scan blindly, so how scanners pick targets was a mystery. The team built the largest lure network of its kind inside a working internet provider. Over ten months it drew more than six hundred million stray packets from about nineteen hundred networks. The authors sorted the sources, tested which lure features drew the most attention, and pieced together where scanners get their target lists and how they work through them. The findings help defenders anticipate probes in an address space long assumed too big to map.
arxiv-2508-07606:
Hongtao Li and co-authors teach home robots to work in line with human values while respecting physical limits, in this 2025 paper. Language-model robots can now do many household tasks once thought out of reach. Doing the task, though, is not enough: people have preferences about how it is done, and those tastes should carry to new situations. At the same time, arms and objects obey hard physical rules that no preference can bend.

The team built a benchmark of everyday home activities judged partly by preference. Their learning method takes feedback as direct instructions and as corrections during the act. The robot must weigh both what the person wants and what physics allows. The framework aims at helpers that feel less like tools and more like considerate partners.
arxiv-2508-07706:
Philipp Huber and co-authors published a 2025 paper on the energy cost of training neural networks in parallel. Splitting training across many graphics processors lets models and datasets grow, and finishes runs sooner. What that splitting does to the electricity bill is often ignored. The team ran scaling experiments to find out.

They trained two models, an image classifier and a weather model, while varying the processor count and the batch sizes, both overall and per processor. Energy use rose roughly in line with total processor hours. The rate, though, differed a lot between the two trainings and between hardware setups. How many samples and updates each processor hour contained mattered systematically. The authors say these patterns can guide labs toward training plans that waste less energy. Their work adds hard numbers to the push for more sustainable AI research.
arxiv-2508-08306:
Dinh Triem Phan, Jérôme Bobin, Cheick Thiam, and Christophe Bobin compare methods for gamma ray spectrometry in two thousand twenty-five. The task is to name and count radionuclides from a spectrum by machine. Past methods lack shared tests, which blocks fair comparison. Their open benchmark supplies data, code, and metrics.

Three scenes test the methods: known, warped, and shifted signatures. A huge set of simulated spectra holds nine nuclides plus background. The statistical unmixing route beat learning routes on naming in all scenes. It sours when signatures are modeled wrong, though. Counting also favored the statistical route by a wide edge.
arxiv-2508-08906:
Torsten Hoefler and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 explaining the design of Ultra Ethernet, a new high-performance networking standard for artificial intelligence and supercomputing. Ethernet runs the world's ordinary networks, but the largest training clusters need faster, more reliable links than it has offered. The Ultra Ethernet 1.0 specification rebuilds the whole stack for that scale, and this paper, written by the standard's own authors, gives the reasoning.

Its centerpiece is a new transport protocol built to run largely in hardware. It promises reliable delivery at extreme scale without the stalls that plague older designs. The authors contrast their path with the last big standard in this space, set more than two decades ago. They lean on Ethernet's vast ecosystem and on huge gains in computing efficiency per bit moved. The paper frames the standard as the base for the next era of large machine clusters.
arxiv-2508-09006: Lorenzo Barca tackles a key source of error in lattice QCD, which computes particle properties on a grid, in a research paper from 2025. When researchers probe a hadron with an electric current, unwanted excited states can creep into the signal. Barca gives a general argument, backed by numbers from several hadron cases, for predicting which excited states a given current and setup will boost. The aim is cleaner, more precise measures of hadron structure.
arxiv-2508-09106:
Testing a home energy manager usually means rebuilding the test rig for every new house layout. Ninad Gaikwad and Anamika Dubey built a simulator meant to end that churn. Their tool models any number of houses, on or off the grid, as a standard learning environment. Each house can mix rooftop solar, batteries, both, or neither, and carries air-conditioning plus eight grouped circuits of loads. Real weather records and a well-known household load dataset drive the scenes.

Three starter controllers ship with the tool, two for islanded running and one for grid-tied days. Trials on single homes and a four-house community show the setup can rank control policies fairly across layouts and report the cost of computing them.
arxiv-2508-09406:
Faisal Suwayyid, Yuta Hozumi, Hongsong Feng, Mushal Zia, JunJie Wee, and Guo-Wei Wei are among the authors of this paper from two thousand twenty-five. Its text presents CAKR, a way to encode genome strings with tools from commutative algebra.

Comparing genomes across species is still hard, and algebra has rarely been used for it. The method turns short word counts of a sequence into an algebraic form that joins algebra, topology, counting, and machine learning. The team tests it on sorting genetic variants, rebuilding family trees, and sorting viruses. Across many data sets it beats five top rivals, above all on viruses, and holds its accuracy as data grows.
arxiv-2508-09606:
Alejandro Posadas-Nava, Alejandro Carrasco, and Richard Linares present an open robot control system in a 2025 paper. BEAVR lets a person run robots from inside virtual reality, using both hands at once. It works with many robot bodies, from single arms to full humanoids, using cheap store bought VR gear.

Control, recording, and learning share one system. Demonstrations are saved in a standard dataset format as they happen, ready to train robot policies. Streaming is built to add almost no delay, at or under 35 thousandths of a second. A split think and act loop lets the system scale to many robots at once.
arxiv-2508-09806:
Surfaces that minimize area, like soap films, obey an equation whose boundary values may or may not have a solution. Ari Aiolfi and co-authors give a fresh test for when a solution exists in this 2025 paper. The classic theory needs the region's boundary to curve inward in a mean sense. Many real regions fail that demand, so their cases were left open.

The new test comes from a simple one-variable equation and lets the authors build explicit walls that trap a solution. It also works for regions that stretch out without bound. In curved spaces, the test links the region's shape to the allowed boundary values in a direct way. In flat space it covers some cases where the classic method fails. The same wall trick applies to a flow that moves surfaces by their curvature.
arxiv-2508-10106:
Philipp Frey and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on simulating quantum computers built from Majorana particles, exotic states that could store information topologically and shrug off noise. Braiding these states performs computations, but braiding alone cannot do everything. Parity measurements and mixing effects complete the toolbox.

The paper gathers the theory, from the algebra of these particles to error-correcting codes, in both sparse and dense qubit layouts. It then presents a simulation method that follows the time evolution of realistic wire networks, including measurements and disorder. The result is part tutorial, part software toolbox for groups designing topological quantum hardware.
arxiv-2508-10206:
Ingham and co-authors bring group theory to scanning tunneling microscopy in a 2025 paper. The microscope maps electron states atom by atom, and hidden orders in quantum materials announce themselves through broken symmetries. Reading which symmetry broke, straight from the image, is the challenge.

Their framework sorts image components by symmetry, yielding a real-space map of local symmetry properties. Some breaking patterns, they prove, can never appear in the main zone because of extinction rules like those in crystallography. Finer sub-cell structure rescues those patterns, and the paper details how to extract them cleanly. Tests on synthetic charge-density waves and a real kagome metal demonstrate the method.
arxiv-2508-10406:
The authors extend classical potential theory into a generalized Fourier framework and give formulas to invert the potentials. Potentials built from heat and wave-like semigroups summarize how sources spread through a space, and inverting them recovers the source from its field. Working in the (k,1) transform setting, they define Bessel and Flett potentials and prove their basic properties.

A wavelet-like transform yields an explicit inversion formula for the Flett potential. A new beta-semigroup then unlocks inversion of the Riesz potential as well. Two-parameter potentials unify the Bessel and Flett cases, and the paper defines the matching function spaces for later analysis.
arxiv-2508-10506:
Two massive stars orbiting each other blow winds that crash, and the crash site speeds particles up to near light speed. Tasseroul and co-authors model the radio glow of such a system in this 2025 paper. The radio spectrum mixes warm wind glow with the crash site's non-thermal emission. At low frequencies, ionized gas soaks up radio waves, an effect called free-free absorption.

That soaking can happen in the foreground winds and inside the crash zone itself. The team used the binary WR 147 as a test case, with fresh data from a large radio array tuned for spectrum work. A simple descriptive model traced how absorption reshapes the spectrum. Lessons from one system may extend to the whole class. These binaries help stock the galaxy with fast particles.
arxiv-2508-10706:
Yasuhiro Oki settles when the Hasse norm principle holds for field extensions whose degree is the square of a prime. The principle asks whether being a norm everywhere locally forces being a norm globally, a classic fault line in number theory. For this degree family, a clean criterion was missing.

In his 2025 paper, Oki gives an equivalent condition for the principle's validity across all finite separable extensions of prime squared degree over global fields. The condition is checkable in the extension's own terms rather than by case hunting. As a check, the theorem recovers the known result of Drakokhrust and Platonov, who showed the principle holds for a broad adequate class of such extensions. Old and new results lock together.
arxiv-2508-10806:
Maria J P Peixoto and co-authors ask who actually benefits from AI explanations, and who gets left out. Explanation tools are sold as a way to make AI calls open to inspection. Most of them speak in pictures, charts, and heat maps, which shuts out users who cannot see well.

The team first reviews seventy-nine studies and finds disabled users near absent from explanation testing. They then build a four-step proof of concept for inclusive design. The steps sort AI systems, define user personas, draft prototypes, and put them before experts and users. Early signs favor plain, trimmed explanations for non-visual users over dense ones. Sound, text, and touch channels together promise fairer access. The paper calls for accessibility to join accuracy as a core design bar.
arxiv-2508-10906:
Sihan Chen, John Lalor, Yi Yang, and Ahmed Abbasi present PersonaTwin, a method for building digital twins of individual people with large language models. Their paper came out in 2025. A digital twin here is a model that answers in the style of one real person.

The method layers three kinds of information into the prompt. It uses basic facts about the person, records of past behavior, and survey measures of personality and mood. Tests used health data from more than eight thousand people. Twins built this way matched the fidelity of best-case settings. Models trained on twin answers came close to models trained on the real people, on both accuracy and fairness.
arxiv-2508-11206:
Yusuke Yamada wrote this 2025 physics paper on particle creation in the early universe's extra dimensions. Some theories give space hidden, curled-up dimensions. A gauge field living in one can drive cosmic inflation in our four dimensions, a setup called extra-natural inflation.

As the field changes with time, it builds an electric field along the hidden direction. That field can pull charged Kaluza-Klein particles out of empty space, a process named the Schwinger effect. Yamada builds the model in five-dimensional electrodynamics tied to gravity, with matter fields that create the inflation push. Even with several charged fields present, particle production goes ahead. Since their momentum is conserved, the particles are superheavy. Depending on the settings, they could serve as dark matter or even swamp the universe.
arxiv-2508-11406:
Benjamin Alt and co-authors set out in 2025 how robots can run lab tests in an open way that others can check and repeat. They picture robots that work on their own and run tests with care, the same way each time, and in full view. They give two tools to help reach that goal for robot-run science.

One tool is a semantic execution tracing framework. It logs sensor data plus notes on what the robot holds to be true. That log lets others repeat a run and check it later. The second tool is the AICOR Virtual Research Building, a cloud platform. It lets teams share robot task runs and check them at large scale. The tools join fixed step-by-step runs with semantic memory and open knowledge representation.
arxiv-2508-11606:
Ignatyuk and Samorodov study brief moments when a qubit regains coherence it had lost, in a model where sound waves in a crystal cause the loss. Their 2025 paper looks at recoherence times and the size of the regain. The qubit starts in a state set by a special unselective measurement. The sound bath can be tuned from slow to fast response regimes. Early events turn out both like and unlike the long term behavior.

At short times, the slow and middle regimes favor recoherence over the fast one, unlike at long times. The weakest recoherence sits in the same tuning range where long term loss changes from total to partial. That link ties the two time scales together. The results hint at which bath traits give the best early recoherence. Such traits matter for devices that must act before coherence fades.
arxiv-2508-11906:
Hayward boson stars are built by Sebastian S. Chicaiza-Medina and Juan Carlos Degollado in a 2025 arXiv paper. A boson star is a ball of scalar field held by its own gravity. The Hayward form adds a charged, non-linear electric frame that stays smooth at the core. The team solves the joined gravity, field, and charge sums for still, round stars.

Star families are drawn for a range of charge and core field values. One clean rule marks when such stars can live at all, set by a charge bound. When the rule fails, a horizon forms and no field ball can sit there.
arxiv-2508-12206:
Shosei Sakaguchi studies when mixing experimental and observational data sharpens what we can learn about distributional treatment effects, in a 2025 paper. In experiments, treatment is assigned at random. In observational data, people choose for themselves. Many distributional effects stay only partly known even with random assignment. The question is what the second data source adds.

He shows the combined data reveal how outcome distributions vary across hidden self-selection types. That fully characterizes the set of values the effects could take. He derives sharp bounds for broad classes of effects and gives exact conditions for when mixing the data strictly tightens the set. A linear programming approach handles extra structural limits. An empirical case shows the method at work.
arxiv-2508-12306:
Qian Cao and four co-authors add a weak-measurement trick to a gas-based sensor that reads faint magnetic fields. The sensor type is called SERF, and it is among the most sensitive tools of its kind. Weak measurement can amplify a tiny signal by a picky final filter. Here the shape of a laser beam serves as the dial that moves.

Field strength twists the polarization of the light, which is weakly tied to the beam shape. The filter then amplifies the shift of the beam to a size eyes can read. The team maps the shift curve and finds its most sensitive point, at 182.8 femtotesla units per root hertz. Since the reading rests on the own traits of the beam, not its power, power flicker hurts far less. Steadiness rose by one to two orders over the plain way.
arxiv-2508-13606:
Haoxuan Li, Wei Song, Aofan Liu, and Peiwu Qin present a system for answering questions about long documents in this 2025 paper. The task is hard when documents run long and training data is scarce, as in less common languages. Their framework, called AdaDocVQA, was built and tested on Japanese document questions.

The system works in three parts. A hybrid search step pulls the most relevant parts of a document. A data pipeline builds new practice question-and-answer pairs, with checks at several levels. The answering step adapts its setup as it runs and stops early when sure. On one Japanese benchmark, the system scored about eighty-three percent on yes-or-no questions. It scored lower on fact and number questions, and set the best reported score on a second dataset. The authors offer the design as a base for other low-resource languages.
arxiv-2508-13706:
Vinesse and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on Jupiter's auroral glow, using ultraviolet data from the Juno spacecraft. They map how two gases, methane and acetylene, absorb that glow. The maps help show the height and spread of each gas and the energy of incoming electrons.

On two close passes, both gases mostly sat where models expect, with methane reaching higher. One pass showed odd patches that traced back to a detector fault at high brightness, and a fix made them fade. Odd patches on the other pass stayed after the fix. Models suggest those come from real local shifts in gas mix or layer height. The work warns against one fixed air profile for all auroral readings.
arxiv-2508-13806:
José Eduardo Zerna Torres and co-authors built a learning system that picks network paths inside the network itself in 2025. Programmable switches can read live traffic data as packets pass. Their setup pairs that telemetry with small learning automata placed at each switch.

Each switch learns which path to favor as congestion shifts, using only local data. Tests ran on a Mininet testbed with P4-programmable switches. The learners settled on good paths and adapted when traffic patterns changed. All choices happen at line rate, with no central controller in the loop. The authors present the setup as a proof of concept for in-network learning.
arxiv-2508-13906:
Kapil Goswami, Peter Schmelcher, and Rick Mukherjee solve integer programming problems on qudits, the multilevel cousins of qubits, with a circuit built to scale. Integer programming is NP-hard and underpins finance, logistics, and engineering, yet qubit encodings waste resources by spelling each integer in binary. Qudits hold an integer natively.

Their 2025 paper extends a single-qudit scheme to many interacting qudits. A distillation step separates feasible from infeasible assignments, the cost function is written into phases and amplitudes, and phase estimation with a multi-controlled rotation picks the winner. The authors prove the optimum carries the highest measurement probability and chart the time cost. The claim is a genuine quantum speed-up with honest scaling, not a toy instance.
arxiv-2508-14006:
Mohamed Abouagour and Garyfallidis release ResPlan, a dataset of 17,000 residential floor plans in vector form. Each plan marks walls, doors and windows. It labels rooms under a 17-class scheme, from kitchens to balconies. Coordinates come in both pixels and meters. Every plan also carries a room-connectivity graph with four kinds of edges.

Older datasets are raster images only, or cover whole building floors. ResPlan instead gives complete single homes, from apartments to villas. Plans average just over eight usable rooms. The release ships with loading code, a standard split, and baselines for three tasks. Those tasks are room labeling, floor-plan generation, and plan-to-graph extraction.
arxiv-2508-14106:
Surajit Das, Gourav Roy, and Pavel Zun segment living cells in plain microscope images with a cheap, fast pipeline. Their 2025 study targets brightfield images of unstained cells, which fight back with low contrast, noise, blur from cell motion, and shapes that change over time. Many existing tools fail to handle all of that at high throughput.

Their convolutional pipeline pairs frozen pre trained encoders inside a U-Net frame, boosted with attention blocks, instance aware steps, and adaptive loss functions. Hard cases are retrained on purpose, learning rates shift during training, and an ensemble smooths the output. On a public data set of varied live cells, the system hit ninety three percent test accuracy with an average F1 score of eighty nine percent. Costs stay low enough for routine lab use.
arxiv-2508-14206:
Parisa Ebrahimian counts curves on a family of surfaces using a tropical mirror of the problem. Her 2025 paper works with Hirzebruch surfaces, a graded family of ruled surfaces, and asks how many rational curves of a fixed class pass through set points while meeting cross-ratio conditions.

Correspondence theorems say the algebraic count equals a tropical count, which can be done by combinatorics. A famous formula of Kontsevich counts plane curves this way, and versions exist for one Hirzebruch surface with point conditions alone. Ebrahimian gives a Kontsevich-style formula for every Hirzebruch surface, with several cross-ratio conditions allowed and wider freedom in how they are imposed. The count runs through tropical methods throughout.
arxiv-2508-14306:
Yuji Ikeda and co-authors train machine learning atom models that reach top tier quantum accuracy for materials held together by weak forces, in a paper from 2025. The catalog title differs from the head title, which also covers covalent networks. Gold standard quantum data barely exists for large periodic materials, which blocks direct training.

Their fix learns only the gap between a cheap baseline model and the gold standard, using small molecular pieces. Weak force pairs are added to the training set so long range pulls are captured. Errors stayed tiny on tests, and bond lengths, vibrations, and binding energies matched benchmarks. Applied to a flat carbon framework material, the model gave gold standard grade structure and gas uptake results.
arxiv-2508-14606:
Some math puzzles stay hard even when a full answer is not required. Andrei Krokhin and Danny Vagnozzi prove such a result in this 2025 paper. Their starting point is a logic puzzle called 1-in-3 SAT, where each clause needs exactly one true part. Even when a valid answer is promised to exist, finding one is hard, so the question is whether a weaker goal can be met with ease.

One weaker goal can be stated as a coloring task on a special kind of graph with ordered parts. A long-standing guess sorted goals like this into easy and hard, and this goal was a known blocker for the proof. The authors show the goal is hard, as the guess predicted. Their proof uses an algebraic method that studies the symmetries of the task.
arxiv-2508-14706:
Junying Chen and twelve co-authors present ShizhenGPT, a 2025 language model built for traditional Chinese medicine. The field's diagnosis leans on looking, listening, smelling, and pulse-taking, a rich mix that plain text models cannot reach, and good training data was scarce. The team gathered the largest such dataset yet, more than one hundred gigabytes of text and double that in mixed media.

The media span over a million images and two hundred hours of audio, plus body signals. Trained on it, the model matches or beats like-sized rivals and rivals bigger closed ones on recent national exam questions. It also leads on image tasks such as naming herbs and reading faces for diagnosis. All data, models, and code are public.
arxiv-2508-15206:
Marco Polo García-Rivera, Martha Álvarez-Ramírez, and Hildeberto Jardón-Kojakhmetov analyze a climate model of ice age cycles with slow and fast parts. Their 2025 paper studies a variant of the Saltzman-Maasch model, which tracks ice volume, ocean temperature, and carbon dioxide. The variant adds a cubic feedback in the carbon dioxide equation.

The team reduce the model to a flat surface where the slow motion lives, then map where oscillations are born or change stability. They identify two bifurcation types that govern growing cycles. A rescaled version becomes a conservative system, letting them build closed orbits exactly and test whether the orbits survive small changes. Computer continuation confirms the analysis. The work turns earlier numerical hints about glacial cycles into proven results.
arxiv-2508-15306:
Henrietta Hegyi and László Erdődi survey the security of connected cars in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Internet-connected vehicles bring smart mobility but also risks of unauthorized remote access and personal data leakage. The authors assess how well the current rulebook protects drivers. They analyzed sixteen international standards and regulations, scoring each on regulatory strength, technical specificity, supply chain risk treatment, and personal data handling.

In parallel, they surveyed users about connected vehicles. The survey asked which vehicle types people trust and prefer, and why they reject certain cars. It also gauged awareness of data risks and whether drivers feel informed about data practices. Combining the regulatory audit with public perception gives a fuller picture than either alone. The study aims at a holistic account of connected vehicle ecosystems, where technical standards and consumer trust often develop out of step.
arxiv-2508-15706:
Amir Sarfi, Benjamin Thérien, Joel Lidin, and Eugene Belilovsky built SparseLoCo in two thousand twenty-five to train language models across sites with far less data traffic. Local-update training cuts how often machines sync, but each sync still sends a full model-sized update, choking slow links. Shrinking those updates by keeping only top parts usually wrecked training quality.

SparseLoCo pairs top-part sparsification with two-bit quantization to cut the sent update by up to ninety-nine percent, yet ends with lower loss than the dense baseline. Gains held across model sizes, a mixture-of-experts model, more workers, and longer gaps between syncs. The method suits training over the open internet.
arxiv-2508-15806:
Mengjie Li and co-authors present REAL, a method for shrinking the memory that long-running language models devote to past text. That memory, the key-value cache, grows painfully as inputs lengthen, and existing eviction schemes mostly study attention heads in cases where the model reasons correctly. Failure cases, where heads show bias or distraction, were ignored.

The team builds an attention behavior matrix, modeled on the confusion matrix, to catalog head behavior in successes and failures alike. Their eviction method then strengthens the pathways tied to valid reasoning while muting the noise from biased or distracted heads. Across models and benchmarks the results were strong; on one long-context test it matched the best rival method's accuracy while using thirty-two times less space. The authors argue the field should shift from studying success only to failure-aware analysis.
arxiv-2508-15906:
Iosif Petrakis, writing alone, revisits the logic of Hilbert spaces in a 2025 mathematics paper. A Hilbert space is the standard infinite-dimensional setting for quantum theory and analysis. Standard treatments study single closed subspaces. Petrakis instead studies pairs: two closed subspaces that stand at right angles to each other, which he calls an orthocomplemented subspace.

The idea mirrors complemented subsets in constructive mathematics, where membership comes with positive information. To each such pair belongs a partial projection, an operator defined only where the pair gives enough data. Swapping the two parts acts as negation, which brings this logic closer to the classical quantum logic than an earlier one-dimensional version. Petrakis shows the setup builds quotient spaces without the usual locatedness assumption. He offers it as a new route into the constructive theory of Hilbert spaces.
arxiv-2508-16106:
Yongzhi Jin, Kazushi Okamoto, Kei Harada, Atsushi Shibata, and Koki Karube present a 2025 paper on cutting user browsing sessions at the right points. Recommenders treat a session as one run of actions, but interests can shift mid-session. Cutting at true interest changes improves the model of what a user wants.

Around each candidate cut, the method scores how similar nearby items are, using co-occurrence patterns, title and brand text, and prices. A supervised classifier learns from these scores where boundaries fall. The team hand-labeled real browsing histories to train and test it. A gradient boosting model scored best, with an F1 of 0.806. The authors argue the approach tracks drifting tastes better than fixed time gaps.
arxiv-2508-16306:
Diffusion models build images by reversing a slow noising process, and theory has lagged on how many steps that reversal truly needs. Jain and Zhang sharpen the error accounting under weak assumptions, with no smoothness demanded of the data. Their analysis splits each generation step into a clean reverse move plus a small fresh noising, which lets one kind of error be converted into another that is easier to bound.

The payoff is a step count that grows only linearly with the data's dimension and much more gently with the target accuracy than the best earlier result. The authors present the scheme as a cleaner route to guarantees for these widely used generators.
arxiv-2508-16406:
Guangyu Yang and co-authors defend chat models against jailbreak attacks with a memory of past attacks. Their 2025 paper deals with prompts crafted to make a model break its safety rules. New attack styles appear fast, and retraining a guard each time is costly.

Their system, RAD, keeps a store of known attack examples. For each fresh prompt it fetches kin cases and infers the hidden aim and trick behind it. Guards can then be updated with no training at all. A dial lets operators trade safety against how often fair prompts are refused. On a hard test set, the method cut the success of strong attacks while sparing fair queries.
arxiv-2508-16506:
Takehiko Gappo and Andreas Lietz pull apart a family of set-theoretic principles that claim the universe of sets is as rich as it could possibly be. Maximality Principles say, roughly, that anything which could become true by forcing, and stays true, already is true. Logicians slice them by formula complexity and ask how much consistency strength each slice costs.

The authors pin down the strength of the principles restricted to the two natural formula classes, and prove neither restricted version implies the other. They also calibrate a variant for extensions preserving the first uncountable cardinal, and separate another variant from a strong forcing axiom. Such fine separations chart the true price of absoluteness.
arxiv-2508-16606:
For people who cannot move or speak, typing by eye gaze may be the only channel out. Yogesh Meena and Manish Salvi built a gaze-controlled virtual keyboard in 2025 that runs on an ordinary webcam, aimed at places where costly eye trackers are out of reach. A menu of nine commands opens all fifty-six letters, cases, punctuation, and a delete key, with dwell-based and blink-based selection modes.

Twenty able-bodied users typed with a mouse, a real tracker, and the webcam for comparison. Webcam typing reached about eleven letters a minute in the faster mode, against eighteen by mouse. Users rated the webcam mode usable with low effort, backing the low-cost design.
arxiv-2508-16806:
Linear programming solves allocation problems across finance, energy trading, and logistics, but standard processors can be too slow for today's large, fast-changing cases. Xiyan Hu, Titus Parker, Connor Phillips, and Yifa Yu set out in 2025 to run a modern solver on AMD graphics processors. The solver is the primal-dual hybrid gradient method, and the work uses the open ROCm platform and PyTorch.

Their open-source implementation targets general linear programs on AMD hardware. They benchmarked it against standard test sets and established CPU solvers, using hard real-world cases — notably security-constrained economic dispatch from power grids — to tune its settings. On large problems the graphics version ran up to thirty-six times faster than the processor version. The students present the work as a course research project in industrial computing, showing how much headroom graphics hardware offers for optimization work.
arxiv-2508-17106:
Qing Liu, Juan Manfredi, and Xiaodan Zhou prove a combining rule for a nonlinear equation that models steepest-descent surfaces, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The infinity Laplace equation governs shapes set by the sharpest slope at each point. Its solutions are defined in a weak sense suited to such rough settings.

The rule says that adding two solutions, each living on its own set of variables, gives a solution on the joint domain. Workers had used this fact for special cases to ease hard proofs, but no general proof existed. The authors supply one, then extend the idea to abstract distance spaces. They also study when the same combining works for other equations of like type.
arxiv-2508-17806:
Hrant Hakobyan and Jonathan Rehmert published a research paper in 2025 on when an abstract curved surface can be reshaped, without tearing its proportions, into a flat region bounded by circles. An older theorem settled the question for surfaces sitting in the plane, under set conditions on their edges. Later work showed those conditions fail for surfaces that do not lie flat.

The pair prove that, under mild extra assumptions, one stated condition is exactly the test: a surface can be so reshaped if and only if it meets that condition. The result answers a question left open by the earlier authors. It also extends the flat case to a far wider family of surfaces.
arxiv-2508-18206:
Chaturvedi benchmarks graphics processors for training a land-cover classifier on satellite images, as a practical buying guide. The pipeline sorts Sentinel-2 imagery into land use classes with a ResNet-50 model. The whole flow, from data download to maps, runs in containers for repeatability.

Three unlike chips were timed: an Apple M3 Pro, an NVIDIA RTX 3060, and a cloud Tesla T4. The two NVIDIA cards trained up to twice as fast as the Apple baseline. Accuracy on the EuroSAT dataset stayed high across all three. The author concludes that consumer and free cloud GPUs can support scalable earth observation work.
arxiv-2508-18506:
Ajinkya Khoche and co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, a self-taught method for estimating how a 3D scene moves from laser scans. Self-driving systems need that motion sense to move safely. Hand-labeled training data is scarce and costly, which caps progress.

Their system, DoGFlow, borrows labels from a second sense: radar. Radar Doppler readings reveal motion directly, and the method turns them into teaching labels on the fly. No human ground truth is needed at any point. Older self-taught methods lag behind fully supervised ones, above all at long range and in bad weather. Borrowing a second sensor's view could close that gap. The approach turns every radar-equipped drive into training material.
arxiv-2508-18706:
Shivam Dubey and Saurabh Verma present a mathematics paper, published in 2025, introducing a new kind of fractal set. Fractals are shapes built from smaller copies of themselves, and sub-self-similar sets take only some of those copies. The authors add an extra fixed set into the construction, following an older idea for inhomogeneous fractals, and name the result inhomogeneous sub-self-similar sets.

The paper gives examples of these sets and a method to build them. It then studies their size through box dimension, which counts how many small boxes cover a set at finer scales, and asks how the Hausdorff dimension behaves under small changes. Readers get both the new definition and the first tools for measuring such sets.
arxiv-2508-19206:
Hera Brown and Jakub Konieczny ask which number systems can be fully decided by an algorithm, in a 2025 logic paper. They start from Presburger arithmetic, the arithmetic of whole numbers with addition and order, which is known to be decidable. They then add rounding of values from Hardy field functions, a class of smooth growth functions. The question is whether the richer system stays decidable.

For most such functions, the answer is no. When the added function grows polynomially faster than the identity, the extended theory is undecidable, so no algorithm can settle every statement in it. The same verdict holds for some slower but still polynomial-paced growth. The result draws a sharp line around a classic decidable theory.
arxiv-2508-19306:
Jeroen Gardeyn and Tony Wauters present a packing algorithm for cutting stock with guillotine cuts in a paper from 2025. Factories cut rectangles from larger sheets using only edge-to-edge cuts, like a paper guillotine. Bins come in varied sizes, and items may rotate. The goal is the least total sheet area.

Their heuristic works by ruin and recreate: tear a plan apart, then rebuild it toward a set goal. Goal direction keeps the rebuild from wandering. On standard benchmark sets, the method beat the best known algorithms. It won across every variant tested, with and without rotation or mixed bins. Cutting plans that waste less sheet save real money in glass, wood, and metal shops.
arxiv-2508-19706:
Ashay Burungale, Wei He, Ye Tian, and Xiangdong Ye prove a non-vanish claim for a class of number values in a 2025 paper. The values hang on a self-mirror mark over a split field with a real base. A prime of the base and a tall tower group frame the claim.

For all but a few twists of the mark, the value at one point is not zero, they show. A prime-side count of the set values is also pinned down in the work. One use wraps a past proof on a famed guess in the field.
arxiv-2508-19806:
Shenqi Wang and Guangzhi Tang propose context-aware sparse learning for event-based vision in a 2025 paper. Event cameras report change pixel by pixel, giving fast, blur-resistant sensing that suits robots. Deep models often waste that sparse signal, while spiking networks save energy but lag on hard tasks like object detection and optical flow.

Their framework, CSSL, uses context-aware thresholding to tune neuron activity to the input pattern. Sparsity then arises on its own, with no hand-tuned extra loss terms. Applied to detection and flow estimation, the method matches or beats leading systems while keeping neuron activity extremely sparse. The results point to practical, low-power event vision for devices at the network edge.
arxiv-2508-19906:
Moussa Kassem Sbeyti, Nadja Klein, Michelle Karg, Christian Wirth, and Sahin Albayrak tackle the cost of developing active learning methods for object detection, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Comparing methods normally means training many detectors, up to hundreds of GPU hours each on driving data.

Their metric, object-based set similarity, rates an active learning method without any detector training. It compares selected training sets with the target domain using object-level features, so weak methods can be discarded early. The same metric picks representative validation sets, fixing rankings that swing between evaluation splits. Tests span KITTI, BDD100K, and CODA with two detector architectures.
arxiv-2508-20206:
Elisha Dayag, Nhat Thanh Van Tran, and Jack Xin add spectral filtering to attention based forecasting in two thousand twenty-five. Transformers lead at long range time series forecasts. They lean too much on low frequencies and cost much compute. Past filter work paired filters with plain perceptrons, not transformers.

A learnable filter at the front of the model fixes the lean. It adds only about a thousand new parameters to each base. Forecast scores rose by clear margins in many tests. Filters also let the team shrink the embedding size. Smaller models thus beat their larger plain forms. Fake data tests show fuller spectrum use.
arxiv-2508-20306:
Six physicists study light from paired particles in a layered crystal in a 2025 paper. The particles, called excitons, sit in traps formed by flaws in the material. In past work those traps held them in tiny spots only a few atoms wide.

The team worked with a stack of two thin crystal sheets and tracked thin lines in the light the stack gives off. As more particles were added, the lines faded just as flow began, a sign the lines mark trapped states. Yet these states stretched for wide spans, up to ten percent of the whole sample. That reach hints the energy landscape is far less random than was thought.
arxiv-2508-20506:
A team including Sergei Tretyakov proposed a new build for surfaces that steer waves in space and time. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with metasurfaces, thin sheets packed with tiny parts. Such sheets often need in plane patterns with vast numbers of parts that change in time. That makes them hard to build. The team stacks plain sheets instead, each one smooth across its face.

Each sheet in the stack pulses at the same rate in time. But each has its own pulse shape, tuned to give a joint wave response. The parts are dense rods whose traits shift in time. Readers in wave design get a full frame to plan and tune such stacks with far less in plane fuss.
arxiv-2508-20706:
Riccardo Milocco, Fabian Jansen, and Diego Garlaschelli study how to rebuild hidden networks at several scales at once, in a paper from 2025. In finance and economics, links between banks or firms are often secret. Analysts must guess the network from totals, and the guess should stay consistent when nodes are grouped into blocks.

Standard rebuilding methods work best at one fixed scale. The authors show why those methods clash when used as embeddings across scales. They then propose versions built on scale invariance, the idea that the pattern looks the same at each grouping level. Those give consistent embeddings for rebuilding at many scales. Tests use national economic input-output data to show how the methods behave in practice.
arxiv-2508-20806:
Moriba Jah and Van Haslett introduced in 2025 a filter that tracks moving objects while admitting what it does not know. Standard estimators force doubt into single probability numbers, which breeds false confidence when sensors are sparse or hostile. Their Epistemic Support-Point Filter keeps a region of plausible states instead of one best guess. Updates use ordinal logic and compatibility weights rather than averaging.

The region grows or shrinks as evidence structure changes, with no prior calibration needed. For rival models, a Choquet integral fuses them by a shifting capacity rule instead of winner-take-all. The authors call this stance epistemic humility built into the math. They aim the tool at settings where priors are missing or misleading. The paper lays out the framework as a foundation for robust estimation under deep uncertainty.
arxiv-2508-21006:
Cody FitzGerald and co-authors walk through a case study on telling gene control models apart in a small worm, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Real data are noisy, sparse in time, and miss many states. Rival model shapes can thus fit the same data near equally well.

The team fit near fourteen thousand network models to gene data from three test settings. For each setting they found sets of models that share the traits the data support. One network sat in all three sets. It centers on three key regulators with dense, mostly boosting links. The frame can travel to other gene systems.
arxiv-2508-21306:
Aravind, Puthan, Sarkar, Merrifield, and Terrill simulate tides washing past a steep underwater mountain. Ocean mixing moves heat, nutrients, and fresh water, and tides power much of it. Flow over three-dimensional bumps sheds wakes and shear layers, not just internal waves. Seamounts may act as the ocean's stirring rods.

Their large-eddy simulation stacks a tidal oscillation on a weaker mean flow. The wake proves a mixing hotspot: attached shear layers, a hydraulic jet, and a recirculation zone all dissipate fiercely. Shed vortices churn at their edges too. Vertical shear does most of the dissipative work. Across a tidal cycle, wake dissipation runs at least four times the internal wave flux. Mixing efficiency peaks near flow reversal, at about a quarter. Purely tidal flow maximizes the normalized rates.
arxiv-2508-21606:
Nishant Chinnasami, with advisor Rasha Karakchi, builds a guard against sneaky attacks on encryption hardware in a 2025 paper. Standard encryption is mathematically sound, but on real chips attackers can pry secrets out through timing glitches or injected faults. Their monitoring system watches an encryption chip on a low cost programmable board for anomalies in real time.

Two detectors run together: a simple timing threshold and a machine learning classifier trained on corrupted blocks. Faults were simulated with delays and scrambled outputs to gather training data. The learning approach proved more accurate than fixed thresholds while staying fast enough for small devices. The design needs no changes inside the encryption itself and no special hardware counters, suiting low power systems.
arxiv-2508-21806:
Six researchers test whether genetic information can live in a crowd of fragments in a paper from 2025. Modern life copies single long molecules, which demands precise machinery. Their alternative, a virtual circular genome, spreads information across overlapping short DNA pieces. No single molecule holds the whole message. In mixtures of such pieces, mutant fragments arose but were held down.

Simulations and theory explain the suppression: mutants lose the contest for good binding partners. Healthy pieces extend off each other and multiply faster. Robust copying survives even at mutation rates expected before life began. The authors offer the scheme as a plausible prebiotic information system.
arxiv-2509-00406:
Ahmed H. Mahmoud, Rahul Goel, Jonathan Ragan-Kelley, and Justin Solomon present a GPU system in 2025 for automatic differentiation on triangle meshes. Automatic differentiation computes exact derivatives of a function defined by code, a workhorse for optimization and learning. Mesh-based computations are local and sparse, traits that general tools often waste.

Their system uses per-element forward-mode differentiation, confining work to registers and shared memory. Global gradients, sparse Jacobians, and sparse Hessians are assembled directly on the GPU, with no global computation graph or host synchronization. Users state energy terms over mesh neighborhoods, and the system manages parallel execution and derivative propagation. The design supports changing sparsity patterns as meshes deform.
arxiv-2509-00506:
Guy Avni and one co-author, Suman Sadhukhan, study bidding games played on a graph, where a token sits on a vertex and two players bid from set budgets to move it. The higher bidder moves the token and pays the bid to the other player.

Avni and Sadhukhan focus on discrete bidding, where bids must use fixed units such as cents, with mean-payoff and energy goals. Mean-payoff rewards long-run average gain, while energy requires a budget never to fall below zero. They prove threshold budgets exist, the least starting budget needed to win or hit a target, describe their structure, and show finding them lies in NP and coNP, standard complexity classes.
arxiv-2509-00806:
Reem Abdel-Salam, with two co-authors, Mary Adewunmi and Modinat A Abayomi, reports the CaresAI entry to a biomedical question answering track at BioCreative IX. The MedHopQA task requires multi-hop reasoning, chaining facts about diseases, genes, and chemicals, and rigorous evaluation matters before healthcare deployment.

They fine-tune LLaMA 3 8B on a curated dataset compiled from BioASQ, MedQuAD, and TREC, trying three setups: combined short and long answers, short only, and long only. Concept-level accuracy reaches up to a stated high value, yet Exact Match scores stay much lower, especially in testing. A two-stage inference pipeline extracts precise short answers to reduce verbosity, but strict formatting remains a challenge.
arxiv-2509-01006:
Daniela Damian, with three co-authors, introduces REConnect, a framework for requirements engineering with communities. Software shapes daily life in many communities. Requirements work must ensure systems support social sustainability. Automated elicitation risks distancing that work from lived context. AI tools have intensified this trend in recent years.

REConnect recenters the work on human connection and relationality. It was derived from twenty-six community-engaged software projects. Projects spanned rural Nepal, urban Canada, and remote Arctic Canada. Three core principles are stated. They are building trust, co-creating with stakeholders, and empowering users as agents of change. Each principle is turned into concrete actions for teams. AI use must be governed by these principles to keep human agency.
arxiv-2509-01206:
Estimating depth from a single camera view could give cheap three-dimensional vision inside the body during endoscopy. Liangjing Shao, with four co-authors, tackles the wide range of lighting and tissue scenes that make that task hard. Their framework learns without labeled depth data, a self-supervised setup.

A new block-wise mixture of dynamic low-rank experts fine-tunes a foundation model with few added parameters, choosing experts to suit each block's features. A training scheme also handles shifting brightness and reflections from wet tissue. Tests on the SCARED data set and a simulated colon data set beat prior leading methods. Shao and the team aim for depth sensing that stays reliable across diverse endoscopic scenes.
arxiv-2509-01406:
Supersymmetry pairs particles with partners, and harmonic superspace is a powerful language for writing its theories. Evgeny Ivanov and Nikita Zaigraev formulate a type of matter field, the hypermultiplet, in a four-dimensional anti-de Sitter background, a spacetime with constant negative curvature. Their start is a careful realization of the superconformal group on a special analytic subspace.

A key step embeds the AdS supergroup inside the larger superconformal group by adding a constant symmetric matrix. That matrix also fixes the cosmological constant, the value that sets the background's curvature. The team then builds an invariant mass term for the hypermultiplet by adding an extra rotation of its superfield. The construction turns into the known flat-space version when curvature is removed, linking curved and flat supersymmetry in one frame.
arxiv-2509-01606:
Transformer models place words with similar meanings near each other in an embedding space, and users often assume the reverse for sentences: near means alike. Vivi Nastase and Paola Merlo test whether that geometry holds for sentence embeddings. They compute sentence vectors three ways, by averaging word vectors, by taking a special classification token, and by taking a random token's vector.

The pair then asks whether distances between these variants predict their performance on linguistic tasks, and whether distant variants still encode the same information in the same way. Their results show the geometry of the sentence embedding space is not predictive of relative task performance. Nastase and Merlo warn that the cosine measure, the standard closeness score, need not apply as a guide to what sentence embeddings know.
arxiv-2509-01806:
Paulina R Martin-Cornejo and Denis Boyer study how fading memory shapes learning in random walks with a favored site. Their walker moves on a grid and tends to revisit past sites, a simple stand-in for animal or human movement. One special site holds the walker longer on each visit, acting like a food source. Strong memory can trap the walker near that site, which reads as spatial learning.

When memory fades slowly, the trapped state matches the perfect memory case and stays stable. Faster fading brings bursts of trapping split by spells of free wandering. Right at the boundary, learning is fastest, against the usual slowdown near transitions. Forgetting thus saves memory cost and can speed learning, echoing findings in biology.
arxiv-2509-01906:
Tam Thanh Nguyen leads six co-authors on splitting AI models adaptively between phones and edge servers over 5G. Running a full deep network on a phone drains its battery fast. Sending all work to servers risks privacy and can add delay and data load. Split computing divides the network so each side does part of the job.

Fixed split points fail when 5G channels shift over time. Their scheme estimates data throughput with AI in real time and moves the split point to match. Tests across scenarios show large gains in delay, energy, and privacy balance. The work centers on privacy focused image tasks where raw photos should stay on device. Adaptive splits keep service smooth as network quality swings.
arxiv-2509-02406:
Chris Hull and Maxim Zabzine present a 2025 theoretical physics paper reformulating gauge theories built on antisymmetric tensor fields, known as p-form fields. Such fields appear in gravity and string theory, but their interactions are awkward in standard form.

The authors work in a configuration space built from paired dual field strengths, which carries a natural symplectic structure, a geometric pairing of variables. Field equations then become the meeting point of two submanifolds, one Lagrangian and the other Lagrangian or coisotropic depending on topology. Chern-Simons interactions shape the global layout. A detailed example couples a three-form field in six dimensions to Yang-Mills theory. The approach, they argue, covers gauge systems of many kinds.
arxiv-2509-02606:
Thanh Tung Khuat and four co-authors wrote a 2025 bioprocessing paper on watching cell cultures in real time with machine learning, where data is scarce and conditions keep shifting. Raman spectroscopy, a light-scattering fingerprint, supplies the input signals.

Three strategies are compared for predicting glucose, lactate, and ammonium levels: pretrained models, just-in-time learning that rebuilds from recent similar cases, and online learning that updates continuously. Two industrial case studies show pretrained models win under some conditions, while adaptive methods win under others. Fresh offline lab measurements during a run proved vital for keeping predictions honest as cell behaviour changed. A simple mixture-of-experts blend improved accuracy and robustness across the studies.
arxiv-2509-02906:
Gautham Adamane Pallathadka and 19 co-authors built a 2025 catalog of paired white dwarfs from a large sky survey called SDSS-V. A white dwarf is the dense leftover core of a dead star. When two of them orbit each other, their light shifts in ways that reveal the pairing.

The team compared repeated snapshots of starlight for signs of motion between exposures. They found dozens of candidate pairs, most of them newly spotted, and timed rough orbits for a small subset. From those counts they estimate how common close pairs are across our galaxy. A few systems should one day send out gravitational waves, faint ripples in space that a future space antenna called LISA could hear.
arxiv-2509-03106:
Nils Erland L. Haugen and 3 co-authors simulated how silica fume forms in silicon furnaces in a 2025 study. Silica fume is a fine powder by-product that is valuable in concrete and other products. Its quality matters more as producers swap fossil furnace feed for renewable materials.

Their simulations follow nucleation, the birth of tiny particles, and condensation, the growth of those particles from gas. Brownian motion, the random jiggling of small particles, drives collisions that merge them and set the final size spread. Getting surface energy and related quantities right proved essential for believable results. Once the first particles form, released heat triggers a burst of further formation until the gas saturates. A particle-tracking approach beat a grid approach on speed and accuracy.
arxiv-2509-03306:
Paolo Bernardi and 3 co-authors addressed the security of running quantum circuits on borrowed machines in 2025. Quantum computing promises big gains in fields like drug discovery and cryptography, so the information it processes is valuable. Today's modest, noisy devices are often owned by providers a user may not fully trust.

The authors aim to identify a practical, heuristic method for checking security properties while circuits run on such hardware. The properties in view are secrecy, keeping data hidden, and integrity, keeping it unaltered. Their goal is a usable evaluation approach rather than a perfect guarantee. The setting reflects the current era of noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices. Work like this matters as sensitive workloads begin moving onto third-party quantum services.
arxiv-2509-03506:
Mathias Beiglböck and two co-authors wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on optimal transport over spaces whose points are themselves probability distributions. Transport theory asks the cheapest way to reshape one distribution into another. Their setting repeats that construction several times, building iterated Wasserstein spaces.

They prove a Brenier-type theorem there, meaning an optimal transport plan comes from a single map rather than split shipments. A specially chosen starting distribution makes that optimal map unique for every target with finite second moment. Key tools include convex potentials on a lifted space, reformulated for the multi-step structure. A main payoff is a first Brenier theorem for the adapted Wasserstein distance. That distance respects information timing, important in finance and stochastic control.
arxiv-2509-03606:
Sridhar and two co-authors' 2025 theoretical physics paper is about squeezing better performance from nanoscale heat engines built from quantum dots. The devices form an Aharonov-Bohm loop, where electrons travel two paths around a magnetic flux. Quantum interference between those paths shapes how heat and charge flow through the engine.

Using non-equilibrium Green function methods, they engineer the transmission profile, the energies at which electrons pass through. Mixing sharp Lorentzian peaks, flat boxcar shapes, and asymmetric Fano features balances efficiency against power output. Dot arrangements with four, five, and six dots in symmetric shapes are compared. A six-dot hexagonal layout reaches a very high thermoelectric figure of merit at extreme cold, while a four-dot version attains much of the ideal Carnot efficiency. Efficiency grows with dot count, while power peaks at middle sizes. Strong performance also coincides with maximal breaking of the Wiedemann-Franz law.
arxiv-2509-03706:
Seth Byard and six co-authors devote a 2025 research paper to double quantum dots made in lead telluride nanowires. A quantum dot is a tiny island that traps electrons one by one; two coupled dots form a step toward spin qubits, which store quantum information in electron spin. Here the dots are defined by electrostatic gates on semiconductor nanowires.

Transport measurements map how charge moves through the device as gate voltages change. The resulting stability diagrams show closely spaced paired triple points, signalling that the dots' charging energy is quenched, unusually small. At zero magnetic field every transport resonance shows spin degeneracy, meaning both spin states behave alike. Switching on a magnetic field splits high-bias features fourfold, lifting that degeneracy as expected. Narrow resonance patterns inside those features are catalogued, with possible origins discussed. The results move lead telluride devices one step closer to working spin qubits.
arxiv-2509-04606:
Adding a wholly new sense-like input to a large language model usually demands large amounts of paired data. Osman Batur İnce, lead author with three co-authors, propose a more sample-efficient route in a 2025 methods paper. Their method, called SEMI, uses a hypernetwork, a network that builds parts of another network.

The hypernetwork adapts a shared projector between an encoder and the language model from only a few examples of a new modality. Tests cover satellite images, astronomical images, motion measurements, and molecules. SEMI reaches useful accuracy with far fewer examples than earlier approaches need, which matters for rare data types.
arxiv-2509-04906:
Lattice fermions can carry extra conserved charges that reveal an anomaly invisible in simpler treatments. Tetsuya Onogi and one co-author study staggered fermions in three spatial dimensions plus time in a 2025 theoretical physics paper.
