UniField trains jointly on data from cars, trains, and aircraft. A shared encoder reads the shape from surface points, while a special layer adds flow details for each domain. By pooling datasets across fields, the model learns broader patterns. The authors report better generalization than models trained on a single domain alone.
arxiv-2510-24206:
Rob van Glabbeek shows that a guarded set of self referring rules has just one solution, working alone. Process algebras are math tools that describe systems step by step. In these tools, a process can refer to itself. A rule is guarded when each self call sits behind an action. That guard keeps the rules well behaved and stops loose ends.

He proves there is one solution up to a strong match of behavior. The proof holds for any such tool whose rules fit a known format. The same holds for weaker matches and for their order forms. So these match tests stay sound when guarded self calls are added. The result also gives a full, sound set of laws for the strong match in finite cases.
arxiv-2510-24506:
Tamanna Chatterjee writes alone on graded Lie algebras and sheaves. A Lie algebra is a space where a bracket rule mimics rotation twists. Grading splits the algebra into layers indexed by whole numbers. The work sits in positive characteristic, where arithmetic wraps around a prime. Chatterjee builds a theory of primitive pairs for this graded world.

Primitive pairs play the role that cuspidal pairs play in Springer theory. She fixes a symmetry subgroup and watches it act on each layer. Parity sheaves are geometric objects stacked over the algebra's points. She shows each such sheaf comes from primitive data on a subgroup. Primitivity survives the Fourier-Sato transform, a key duality tool. The results ground a graded form of the Springer correspondence.
arxiv-2510-24606:
Siheng Xiong, Joe Zou, Faramarz Fekri, and Yae Jee Cho tackle slow, costly long reads for large language models. When a model reads a very long text, its focus step grows fast and eats memory. Their fix, called DHSA, picks which parts of the text to focus on as it goes.

DHSA first ranks big chunks, then passes that rank down to single words. Tests on long search and quiz sets kept scores close to full focus while using far less of it. On one small chip setup it ran a text of 100,000 words where the full method failed.
arxiv-2510-24906:
Mikolaj Czarnecki, Michal Korniak, Oskar Skibski, and Piotr Skowron split a pool of whole, uncut goods in a fair way among players in a group game. The pool size is a whole count: seats in a house, swap slots for organs, or top traits in a model call. A fair split of such goods can not just cut a share in half.

The team names a whole good form of the known Shapley worth, a classic fair share rule. They study its traits and show it in three case works. In one case, it picks the key zones of a shot that drive a class call. The rule gives a fair way to hand out what can not be split.
arxiv-2510-25006:
Christopher R Schwarze, Anthony D Manni, David S Simon, and Alexander V Sergienko do small math tasks with weak shifts in the phase of plain light. In their rig, glass paths are set in a tweaked line form. A task is done not in a fixed state, but by a move from one state to the next.

That move taps the odd phase map of the rig, so plain linear glass can yield bent math such as splits and powers. In and out are both phase shifts off a set base point, and the out shift is read as a shift in light power. The math is near, not exact, and gets more true as the in shifts shrink. Small inputs buy more true outs.
arxiv-2510-25506:
Florian Angermeir led eight co-authors on reproducibility of language models. Maximilian Amougou, Mark Kreitz, and Andreas Bauer helped. Matthias Linhuber, Davide Fucci, and Fabiola Moyon C joined. Daniel Mendez and Tony Gorschek complete the team. Their 2025 paper studies empirical software engineering studies. Commercial language model results may not reproduce reliably.

Many publications now perform tests with language models. Reproducible results remain challenging for scholars and practitioners. They studied reproducibility across eighty-five articles total. Those articles appeared at ICSE and ASE in 2024. Eighteen supplied artifacts and used OpenAI models. The team attempted replication of those eighteen studies. Only five were sufficiently complete and executable. None of the five reproduced fully in results. Two studies seemed partially reproducible on inspection. Three studies did not seem reproducible at all. Stricter artifact testing is needed, they argue. More robust study designs would ensure publication value.
arxiv-2510-25706:
Andres N Salcedo led nine co-authors constraining cosmology with clusters. Eduardo Rozo, Hao-Yi Wu, and David H Weinberg helped. Pranav Chiploonkar, Chun-Hao To, and Shulei Cao joined. Eli S Rykoff, Nicole Marcelina Gountanis, and Conghao Zhou joined. Their 2025 paper forward-models Dark Energy Survey clusters. Run-based inference extracts cosmology from optical samples.

Abundance and weak-lensing signals of redMaPPer clusters are used. The model embeds cosmology-dependent optical choice realistically. Counts-in-cylinders method handles that choice effect. Cluster miscentering and baryonic feedback are accounted for. Lensing signals include those systematic corrections too. Assuming flat Lambda CDM cosmology, settings are obtained. Matter density and form amplitude are constrained tightly. Results agree with low-redshift form readings. Planck results differ at about two point six sigma. Run-based forward modeling proves promising for precision cosmology. Stage IV survey data will benefit from approach.
arxiv-2510-25806:
Mustafa F. Abdelwahed, Ahmed Shafee, and Joan Espasa describe a system that automates part of cyber threat hunting. Threat hunting means forming a guess about an attack and then searching a network for signs that the guess is right. Doing that by hand is slow, and the guesses can carry the bias of the analyst who made them.

Their system, APThreatHunter, uses automated planning to form hunting goals with little human input. It weighs risks from the current state of a system and checks indicators that show whether a risk is actually present. Tests with real Android malware samples showed that planning can support practical, goal based hunting.
arxiv-2510-25906:
Yiren Tong and Panagiotis Tsoutsanis present a faster way to simulate compressible flow, such as air over a wing with shock waves, on irregular grids. High order methods are accurate in smooth regions but costly and unstable near sharp jumps. Their hybrid framework switches method by region, using cheap linear reconstruction where flow is smooth and stronger non oscillatory methods only where needed.

A new detector sorts each cell in one pass as smooth, mildly rough, or discontinuous. Smooth zones keep high order accuracy, rough zones use a weighted method, and jumps fall back to a safe second order scheme. Tests in two and three dimensions, run in an open source solver, confirm the design accuracy and better stability near shocks at lower cost.
arxiv-2510-26006:
Rishika Bhagwatkar, Syrielle Montariol, Angelika Romanou, Beatriz Borges, Irina Rish, and Antoine Bosselut introduce a benchmark for spotting and explaining odd things in real images. People easily notice, reason about, and explain anomalies in a scene. Computer vision work has mostly used factory defects or synthetic fakes, which miss the range and surprise of real world anomalies.

Their benchmark, CAVE, supports three open ended tasks: describing an anomaly, explaining it, and justifying why it counts as one. Detailed annotations mark where the anomaly sits and rate its complexity, severity, and commonness, drawing on cognitive science. Top vision language models still struggle with both perception and commonsense reasoning on the tasks, even with advanced prompting.
arxiv-2510-26306:
Sophie Rosu, Luca Sciarini, Sylvia Ekstrom, and Raphael Hirschi use the slow drift of an eccentric binary orbit to probe the insides of massive stars. In a close eccentric pair, tidal interactions make the orbit orientation rotate, a motion called apsidal motion, at a rate set by a constant that reflects the star inner density profile. Standard models predict too high a value, the famous discrepancy: real stars are more centrally concentrated than models suggest.

Rosu and the team build bespoke rotating binary models with the GENEC evolution code, including tidal mixing, for the twin massive binary HD 152248. Advective diffusive mixing models match the observed constant better than magnetic ones. Large core overshooting is necessary but not sufficient, and a larger initial helium share also helps.
arxiv-2510-26606:
Kentaro Ozeki, with five co-authors, benchmarks how well large language models reason about duties and permissions. Normative reasoning deals with what ought to be done, using modals such as must and may. These models do well on many reasoning tasks, but this corner has been little tested.

Ozeki and the team build a data set of formal reasoning patterns in both the normative domain and the epistemic domain, which deals with knowledge and shares the same formal shape. Human-style cognitive factors are mixed in. Models mostly followed valid patterns, yet they slipped on specific kinds of normative steps. They also showed biases much like those seen in human reasoning studies. All data and code are public, and the authors aim the findings at making model reasoning more reliable.
arxiv-2510-26806:
Apoorva Mathur, with four co-authors, studies how molecular glues hold proteins together, water included. Molecular glues stabilise weak, fleeting protein-protein contacts, which opens drug targets once thought undruggable. Two known glues, rapamycin and WDB002, both bind the protein FKBP12 and pair it with different partners.

Mathur and the team run molecular dynamics simulations to watch what the glues change. The glues shifted how flexible each protein is, stiffening some regions. They also changed the pattern and stability of hydrogen bonds that are mediated by water molecules sitting between the proteins. The authors argue that these water-mediated bonds deserve a central place in the rational design of new glues, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2510-26906:
Kieran Loehr and Bryan K Clark improve a neural method for describing strongly correlated quantum matter. Neural Network Backflow enhances a mean-field wavefunction by letting a network adjust single-particle orbitals for each configuration. In theory it is universal for large networks, but the pair find practical gains saturate as networks grow.

Loehr and Clark instead expand the ansatz to several determinants, generated without adding variational parameters. They test a single Lanczos step and symmetry projection, benchmarked against diffusion Monte Carlo on a doped square Hubbard model near optimal doping. A Lanczos step, diffusion Monte Carlo, and symmetry projection gave similar gains at minimal cost. Optimising the projected states directly gave significantly lower energies, which they report as the lowest variational energies for that Hamiltonian on two lattice sizes.
arxiv-2510-27106:
Rajarshi Haldar and Julia Hockenmaier test whether language models give consistent grades when used as judges. Model-as-judge scoring has grown popular for rating generated text because it tracks human preference better than word-overlap metrics. The catch is reliability: the same judge may score the same answer differently across runs.

Across several generation tasks and benchmarks, the pair find low intra-rater reliability, meaning a judge often disagrees with itself. In the worst cases the ratings look almost arbitrary, which clouds any claim about how good the judgments are. The study quantifies the inconsistency and asks whether careful guidelines can still make such judges useful. For evaluation teams, it is a warning to measure judge stability before trusting judge scores.
arxiv-2510-27406:
A. S. Barabash, L. Bergé, and thirty-seven other co-authors describe a shield for a rare-event hunt in this 2025 paper. The hunt, called CROSS, sits in the Canfranc laboratory deep under Spain. It seeks neutrinoless double-beta decay, a decay that would rewrite what we know about neutrinos, ghostly light particles. The detectors are cold crystals that read heat and light together.

Cosmic muons, fast particles from space, still reach the hall and fake the signal. The shield, a muon veto, wraps the setup in panels on the sides, top, and bottom. When a muon crosses, the panels flag it so the event can be cut. Simulations matched the panel rates seen in real runs. Two trigger rules, with cuts on the heat detectors, would reject over ninety-nine percent of muon fakes.
arxiv-2510-27506:
Ke He, Thang X. Vu, and four other co-authors route data packets through a crowded satellite sky in this 2025 paper. Low Earth orbit constellations now hold thousands of fast-moving satellites. Links form and break as the fleet wheels overhead, and delays run long. Each satellite must choose paths alone, on its own clock, while guarding against bad tail outcomes.

Their framework, PRIMAL, lets each satellite act on local events rather than a shared tick. Agents learn the full spread of costs for quality goals like delay and load. A primal-dual method then keeps worst-case slips in check. In a simulated fleet of 1584 satellites, PRIMAL cut queuing delay by over seventy percent versus a recent risk-blind rival. End-to-end delay fell by nearly twelve milliseconds under load.
arxiv-2510-27606:
Yuhong Liu and eight co-authors present Spatial-SSRL in 2025, a way to teach vision-language models about space without costly labels. Such models join sight and text, yet they often judge position and depth poorly. Past training leans on hand labels, special tools, or narrow settings that limit scale.

Five auto-built tasks draw clear, checkable answers from plain color or depth photos. They ask a model to reorder shuffled patches, spot flipped patches, fill a cut patch, rank depth by region, and judge 3D position. Training on these tasks lifts scores on seven space tests for two model sizes. General sight skill stays intact, which shows self-guided drills can teach space sense.
arxiv-2511-00706:
Marcos Vinicius Cruz, Pragya Verma, and Grischa Liebel give voice to dyslexic software engineers, a group never studied in its own right. Dyslexia mainly impairs reading and writing, core acts in programming, yet early hints suggested dyslexic engineers perform on par with colleagues and may bring strengths in design. The authors run a qualitative study using socio-technical grounded theory, drawing on ten interviews, three blog posts, and one hundred fifty-three Reddit posts.

Learning to program is the hardest stage, they find, but engineers who clear it can succeed and excel at many tasks. Everyday supports such as code completion and linters are especially valuable, mitigating many difficulties. Strengths in visual thinking and creativity stand out as assets. The findings carry implications for practice and open research on what makes code easier or harder for dyslexic readers.
arxiv-2511-00806:
Guangxi Wan and co-authors present a reinforcement learning method for running large cyber physical systems, where digital choices and physical settings must be tuned together. Factories, charging stations, and traffic networks all fit that pattern, and all carry strict safety rules written in logic.

Their method, called logic informed reinforcement learning, projects each trial action onto the set of actions the logic rules allow, so every step explored is valid by construction. No penalty tuning is needed. Across factory, vehicle charging, and traffic tests, the method beat layered optimization approaches. In a robotic reducer assembly case, it cut a combined time and energy score by roughly thirty six to forty four percent, with zero rule violations.
arxiv-2511-00906:
Martino Trevisan presents DPMon, a tool for querying passive network measurements without exposing the people behind the traffic. Passive monitoring reads real traffic on a live network and supports traffic engineering, quality checks, and security work, but the data are personal by nature.

DPMon applies differential privacy, adding controlled noise to query answers so that useful patterns survive while the amount of disclosed information stays bounded. It runs on Apache Spark big data infrastructure and accepts several data formats. The paper shows that meaningful insights can still be drawn from protected results. For network operators, that balance matters: measurement programs increasingly have to justify themselves under privacy rules.
arxiv-2511-01006:
Diantong Li, Kyunghyun Cho, and Chong Liu improve Bayesian optimization for problems where each test is expensive, such as drug discovery or materials design. Bayesian optimization is efficient, but its guarantees are mostly long run results, and real budgets may allow only a handful of evaluations.

Their algorithm, ProfBO, learns from how optimization went on related earlier tasks. Those past runs are modeled as Markov decision processes. They capture procedural know how about searching well. They are then embedded into a neural network that adapts quickly to a new task through meta learning. On COVID and cancer benchmarks and on hyperparameter tuning, ProfBO found high quality solutions with far fewer evaluations than state of the art methods.
arxiv-2511-01106:
Guillaume Riviere builds a terminology for tangible user interfaces, physical objects that represent or control digital information. Earlier classifications sorted interfaces by how tangible their specimens are, but none could classify what an interface does at the level of a whole application.

His terms are blended words, each packing into itself which digital role is represented or controlled and how that role becomes physical. From the terminology he defines hallmarks of applications and four classes of tangibility at the application level, abstracting away from the shape of individual specimens. He shows the scheme on a corpus of tangible interfaces from the literature, showing the terms are descriptive and the four classes separate applications cleanly.
arxiv-2511-01406:
Abolfazl Zakeri and colleagues decide when a wireless system should bother sensing. Sensor data about the environment can guide beam selection and cut training overhead. But fresh data may be unavailable at inference because of sensing limits or sensor failures. So the sensing rate itself must be budgeted.

Their framework pairs a deep Q-network, which makes the sensing decisions, with a neural beam predictor that picks the best beam from a codebook. The age of information, how stale the latest sensor data is, enters the training of both parts, and a Lyapunov optimization reward enforces the average sensing constraint. On a real world data set, age aware training raised top one and top three beam prediction accuracy greatly under a strict sensing budget, with gains fading as the budget loosens.
arxiv-2511-01506:
Juan Perez-Navarro and D. Sierra-Porta try to see a space-weather event coming before it lands. Forbush decreases are sudden drops in cosmic ray counts, recorded by neutron monitors, that follow solar disturbances. The authors track mathematical markers of the incoming data stream, hunting for changes that show up ahead of the drop itself.

Their markers come from information theory, scaling, and geometry: several kinds of entropy, Lempel-Ziv complexity, correlation dimension, and two fractal dimensions, all computed over sliding windows of one-minute records. Tested on two events, in April 2023 and May 2024, with 28 stations each, a compact panel of markers flagged the events reliably, typically several hours early. Lead times varied a lot between stations, so the authors argue for station-by-station criteria.
arxiv-2511-01706:
Sekh Mainul Islam, Pepa Atanasova, and Isabelle Augenstein dissect how large language models write explanations. A natural language explanation can lean on two knowledge sources: the context handed to the model, and the parametric knowledge stored in its weights during training. How those sources mix, step by step, decides whether an explanation is grounded or hallucinated.

Earlier analyses forced the mixture into a one-dimensional, either-or subspace and looked at single steps. The authors build a rank-2 projection subspace that separates the two contributions more faithfully, then track them across long explanations on four question-answering datasets and three open-weight models. Supportive interactions align with the parametric direction, conflicting ones with the context direction, and hallucinated passages lean strongly parametric, while faithful ones stay balanced.
arxiv-2511-01806:
Oliver Franke, Paula Koll, Peter Silvestrov, and Piet Brouwer listen to the electrical noise of a topological edge. Their system is the helical edge state of a quantum spin Hall insulator. It is a one-way conducting channel, exchange-coupled to a magnet. The magnet's easy plane aligns with the edge's spin axis. The setup is known to leave the direct-current conductance untouched.

The authors compute the alternating-current conductance and the current noise power under a steady bias voltage. At zero frequency both take universal values, the conductance quantum and a thermal noise formula involving Boltzmann's constant and temperature. Away from zero frequency, though, both quantities are quickly suppressed, so low-frequency transport through the coupled edge is effectively noiseless, a notable quirk for a driven conductor.
arxiv-2511-01906:
Noa Izsak reports on using a language model to plan tutoring for one of the most abstract college courses in computer science: formal methods and computational models. After the pandemic, universities added extra reinforcement sessions to such courses, but the roles were often ill-defined, with little material, oversight, or connection to the teaching team.

Izsak prompted the model to think like a second-year student, surfacing conceptual bottlenecks, gaps in intuition, and likely reasoning breakdowns before each session was delivered. Those insights shaped a repeatable format mixing targeted review, collaborative examples, independent work, and guided walkthroughs. Over one semester, students reported more confidence, less anxiety, and clearer understanding, especially for the pumping lemma and comparisons of formal language power. The case suggests instructor-facing, reflective use of language models can strengthen teaching design.
arxiv-2511-02306:
Mahdi Nouraie, Houying Zhu, and Samuel Muller work on a reliability problem in the Lasso, the popular statistical method that selects a sparse set of predictors. When predictors are strongly correlated, the Lasso's choices become unstable, picking different variables from one sample to the next, and many patches have been proposed with limited success. The authors first review those existing approaches and where they fall short.

Their fix adds weights to the Lasso penalty: each predictor's weight grows with a correlation-adjusted ranking of its predictive power, so strong, trustworthy predictors are penalised less arbitrarily. Tests on simulated and real-world datasets showed more stable selection. The same weighting idea also stabilised other regularisation-based selection methods in further experiments, which the authors offer as evidence that the technique works as a general-purpose add-on.
arxiv-2511-02606:
Xiangen Hu, Jiarui Tong, and Sheng Xu build a simulation system that makes believable human behaviour for training and research in people-facing professions. Real practice is hard to arrange for trainee teachers and similar learners, and black-box neural tools give no insight into why a simulated person acts as they do. This system is instead assembled from established psychological theory: self-efficacy, mindset, and social constructivism are among its foundations.

Inside, an inner parliament of software agents, each standing for one psychological factor, deliberates and interacts to decide the simulated person's behaviour, making the reasoning inspectable rather than hidden. The authors describe the architecture and its theoretical grounding, illustrate its use in teacher training and in research, and connect the design to social learning, cognitive apprenticeship, deliberate practice, and metacognition. The pitch is openness: behaviour that can be explained in psychological terms, not just mimicked.
arxiv-2511-02806:
Ankitkumar Maisuriya, Siddhi Mali, and Sunil Mittal show a new route to quantized pumping of solitons, the self-trapped wave packets that move through a lattice in fixed steps. In linear Thouless pumping, such steps need a filled band state. Soliton pumping breaks that rule in nonlinear systems. Their 2025 paper asks what really drives the localized packets.

Working in the Aubry-Andre-Harper model, they add a synthetic nonlinearity: a cap on coupling strengths between lattice sites. The packets then pump in quantized steps. The key insight is that the packets are exactly the Wannier functions of the filled bands of the effectively nonlinear lattice, restoring agreement with linear theory. In multi-band systems, the trick merges bands and yields fractional pumping. The method could extend to other nonlinear topological systems.
arxiv-2511-03206:
Kuei-Chun Kao and four colleagues fix a weak spot of multimodal models: handling several images at once. Models often miss fine detail spread across pictures and fail to combine what they see. Prompting tricks exist, but most were built for single images or narrow tasks. Their 2025 method, QG-CoC, is a zero-shot prompting scheme that works for any number of images.

The method lets the question guide the model through a chain of captions, describing each image in the order the question demands. Tests on open and closed models, across multi-image and single-image benchmarks, showed competitive results throughout. The clearest gains came in hard multi-image cases where older prompting methods failed outright, suggesting careful caption order can substitute for retraining.
arxiv-2511-03406:
Zsolt Baja, Tamas Laszlo, and Andras Nemethi give new formulas for the delta invariant of certain curve singularities. That invariant counts how far a singular curve sits from being smooth, for curves lying as special divisors on normal surfaces whose link is a rational homology sphere. Two formulas cover that setting.

Attention then shifts to representable number semigroups tied to weighted surfaces of the same kind. Such a semigroup turns out to record values along a generic orbit curve of the surface's circle action. The delta formula yields a counting route to the semigroup's genus. A final result sorts which semigroups can arise on topological grounds alone, tying algebra, counting, and shape together.
arxiv-2511-04006:
Jonah S Gannon is the lead author among eight authors comparing observed ultra-diffuse galaxies with simulated ones from the NIHAO and HESTIA suites. For each observed galaxy with a spectroscopic dynamical mass, the team pick the simulated halo that best matches that inner mass, then compare stellar and total halo masses.

Matched simulated galaxies carry lower stellar masses than observed, and their halos fall below what the stellar mass-halo mass relation expects. Globular cluster counts instead imply observed systems live in fairly massive halos. Simulations reproduce inner dynamics but not those massive halos, a striking tension. The authors weigh observational and theoretical fixes and favour a fundamental difference in how observed systems formed.
arxiv-2511-04406:
Mohammad Amin Ghanizadeh and Mohammad Javad Dousti tackle data selection for machine translation. Fine-tuning works better when training uses the most useful examples, not just the most data. Their method pairs a learner model with a pretrained reference model to judge each example.

A learnability score rates how much each data point can help training. A batch selection step then picks groups of examples that work well together. Only relevant, high-impact examples reach the fine-tuning run. The authors present the approach as a way to cut wasted training while keeping translation quality strong, which matters when compute and clean data are both limited.
arxiv-2511-04506:
Paloma Rabaey leads seven authors modeling uncertainty inside radiology reports. Reports guide care and feed automated analysis, but they carry two kinds of doubt. Explicit doubt shows in hedging phrases whose strength depends on context.

Implicit doubt hides in what the radiologist leaves unsaid. An unmentioned finding may be absent, or just skipped for brevity. Their two-part framework quantifies the hedged findings and reasons about the silent gaps. Rule-based tools cannot grade these shades of meaning, the authors argue. Better uncertainty models could make report mining safer for clinical use.
arxiv-2511-04706:
Pelin Karadal and her co-author test whether ChatGPT answers shift with inferred political views. Language models guess user traits from conversation and may personalize without being asked. That raises bias and echo chamber concerns for everyday users.

The study builds three personas: two politically oriented and one neutral. Each persona voices views on diversity programs, abortion, gun rights, and vaccination. Their remarks are shared with ChatGPT across sessions to watch for changed answers. The authors also probe how custom instructions and memory features alter the effect, a timely check on hidden personalization.
arxiv-2511-04806:
Peter van Hintum, writing alone, derives discrete versions of classic convexity inequalities. The Brunn-Minkowski inequality governs how volumes add under set sums. Its functional upgrades include the Prékopa-Leindler and Borell-Brascamp-Lieb inequalities.

Van Hintum gives one general route from set inequalities to their functional forms. Many examples show the route at work across settings. The same heuristic then proves discrete versions for functions on integer lattices. Those rest on the discrete Brunn-Minkowski result conjectured by Ruzsa and proved recently with Keevash and Tiba. Discrete analogues matter wherever counting replaces volume. The paper gathers the examples under one unifying heuristic view.
arxiv-2511-05006:
Yang Liu proposes one Type IIA string model that aims to cover both particle physics and the cosmos. The set-up uses crossing D6-branes on a folded six-torus and yields a spectrum like the known supersymmetric model.

Within that one frame, Liu links four hard problems. Shape phases in couplings plus instanton effects give CP violation, the matter surplus comes from instanton terms with moduli-driven leptogenesis, and the mass scale gap is held by controlled breaking of supersymmetry. Anti-branes then lift the vacuum to a de Sitter state, tying collider, flavor, and cosmic signs together.
arxiv-2511-06006:
Sulaimon Oyeniyi Adebayo and Ayaz Khan clean chest X-rays with distributed deep learning while lightly hiding patient data. Denoising improves image quality, and adding Gaussian noise doubles as a cheap obfuscation for sensitive scans. The team worked with a large public chest X-ray collection.

They trained two U-Net variants under three setups: one graphics processor, a standard multi-GPU scheme, and an optimized distributed scheme with mixed precision. The larger variant gave better structural fidelity, though a perceptual score favored the smaller one at low noise. The optimized pipeline cut training time by more than sixty percent versus one GPU, with only a small accuracy cost. The authors present software tuning, not new hardware, as the practical win.
arxiv-2511-06106:
Mathew Thomas Arun, Shyam M, and Ritik Pal track how the strength of proton-decay interactions changes as energy scales shift, when new physics may enter midway. Proton lifetime limits are extremely strict, so precise low-energy predictions for the operators behind decay matter. Their focus is dimension-six four-fermion operators in a standard renormalization scheme.

New physics that conserves baryon number can appear at an intermediate scale as higher-dimensional operators. Those operators mix with the violating ones at one loop, driven mostly by top quark loops. The authors run the coefficients from the electroweak scale up through three trial intermediate scales. Mixing can drag the effective proton decay scale far down, softening the need for a vast empty desert between scales. A Python package accompanies the work.
arxiv-2511-06406:
Shuo Yang, Yinghui Xing, Shizhou Zhang, and Zhilong Niu keep infrared-visible object detectors working when one camera type fails. Pairing heat-sensing infrared with ordinary visible images serves round-the-clock surveillance and driving, but accuracy collapses when a modality goes missing, especially the dominant one. The authors study the failure through the lens of architecture compatibility.

Their Scarf Neck plugs into DETR-style detectors and adds modality-blind deformable attention, so one detector flexibly accepts either input alone or both together. A pretend-dropout training trick rehearses missing inputs in advance. The resulting detector excelled in missing-modality tests on a new benchmark and also topped standard benchmarks where both inputs are present.
arxiv-2511-06606:
S. Sakshi and colleagues give large audio-language models a sense of where sounds come from. Most such models listen through a single channel and miss direction, height, and distance, cues central to understanding a real acoustic scene. SPUR adds spatial hearing with only small changes to the host model.

An ambisonics encoder turns four-channel spatial recordings into rotation-aware features centered on the listener, fed in through a multimodal adapter. A new dataset pairs open spatial recordings with controlled simulations stressing direction, elevation, distance, and overlapping speakers. Fine-tuning on it improved spatial question answering and speaker attribution while leaving general audio understanding intact, and ablations supported each design choice.
arxiv-2511-07206:
Luiz Schirmer and seven co-authors survey geometric implicit neural representations, neural networks that encode a surface as the zero level of a signed distance function. Such networks can be trained from oriented point clouds or posed images, but plain fitting often breaks features a true distance function must have, like unit gradient everywhere. Geometric variants add differential geometry tools, normals and curvatures, as regularization terms in the loss.

The review organizes the literature around three parts: how the implicit representation is defined, how geometric loss functions are constructed. How points are sampled for training, all viewed from a differential geometry perspective. By enforcing global features during training, geometric INRs have greatly improved surface reconstruction quality. The survey gives practitioners a map of design choices and their consequences.
arxiv-2511-07406:
Sophia Tang, Yinuo Zhang, and Pranam Chatterjee want faster simulations of many interacting particles. Molecular dynamics and drug discovery need particle paths across complex energy surfaces, but full simulations are slow. Snapshot-based learning misses how interactions themselves change along a path.

Entangled Schrödinger Bridge Matching learns both the drift and the interaction structure of moving particle systems. It captures first and second order stochastic dynamics, so coupled motion is modeled directly. Tests target biomolecular systems and mixed cell populations where contacts evolve. The method aims to cut simulation cost while keeping trajectories realistic enough for screening and study.
arxiv-2511-07606:
Tianxiong Han, Tyler Slade, and Liqin Ke report hidden time-reversal breaking in a kagome metal. Kagome lattices frustrate electrons into odd states, and this compound layers vanadium kagome nets with terbium triangles that order ferromagnetically. Charge order and superconductivity nearby hint at subtle symmetry loss.

Evidence points to staggered magnetic moments inside the kagome layers breaking time-reversal symmetry. Deep in the ferromagnetic state, terbium spins should give one flat excitation, so extra structure signals the hidden order. Pinning down its source matters because similar breaking appears across kagome superconductors and may steer their exotic behavior.
arxiv-2511-07706:
Jamila Taaki, Lia Corrales, and Alfred Hero ask whether star wobble from spots can map the star itself. Astrometry tracks a star photocenter, and planets tug it measurably. Rotating starspots also shift the bright center, an effect usually dismissed as jitter noise.

A Cramér-Rao bound sets the best possible precision for recovering a surface from that jitter. A smoothness prior steadies the math where information runs singular. If spots can be mapped, the same data hunting planets also reveals stellar weather. That matters because spot patterns corrupt planet signals; turning noise into a surface map could clean exoplanet measurements.
arxiv-2511-07906:
B Kwasniewski and A Mundey develop twisted algebras for self similar groupoid actions on arbitrary directed graphs. Twists are circle valued and cover the full second cohomology of an associated product category. The work defines general, reduced, and essential algebras, plus Toeplitz versions and core subalgebras, in a broad Lp setting.

Three tools are used jointly: twisted inverse semigroups, ample groupoids, and correspondences. The authors characterize freeness, minimality, and related groupoid traits directly from the action. Generalized uniqueness theorems, simplicity tests, and rules for when the two algebras agree round out the theory.
arxiv-2511-08206:
Xiao Yang, Xuejiao Zhao, and Zhiqi Shen introduce EHRStruct, a benchmark for testing language models on structured electronic health record data. Patient records stored in relational tables guide clinical decisions, and models are increasingly asked to reason over them. Without standard tasks and scoring, claims about model skill in this setting cannot be compared fairly.

EHRStruct defines eleven tasks with twenty two hundred samples drawn from two widely used record data sets. Twenty general and medical models are evaluated, along with factors such as input format, few shot use, and fine tuning. The authors also propose EHRMaster, a code augmented method that reaches top performance on the benchmark.
arxiv-2511-08306:
Krishna Neupane and Igor Griva apply extreme gradient boosting, known as XGBoost, to detect unlawful insider trading in securities markets. Corporate insiders hold material non public information, and a few exploit it while evading legal safeguards. Transaction volumes are far too large for human reviewers to inspect one by one, so pattern finding must be automated.

XGBoost, a leading supervised classifier, is trained to flag unlawful transactions and to rank which features matter most in the decision. The reported accuracy reaches ninety seven percent in identifying unlawful trades. Feature rankings give regulators and compliance teams a starting point for understanding what insider behavior looks like in data.
arxiv-2511-09106:
Kristóf Floch and three co-authors show that two rival algorithms for real-time predictive control are secretly close relatives. Sequential quadratic programming attacks the nonlinear control problem head-on, while the linear-parameter-varying approach rewrites it around a scheduling variable; engineers have treated them as separate toolkits with separate folklore.

Using the differential form of the LPV method, the authors unify the two through a specific scheduling choice and an embedding trick from the second fundamental theorem of calculus. They then compare how fast each converges. The merger lets a zero-order version of one inherit the other's scheduling efficiency, promising cheaper robust and stochastic control. Simulation benchmarks the schemes side by side. A Gaussian-process-based controller for autonomous racing then demonstrates the unified method running in real time on real hardware.
arxiv-2511-09306:
Shao-Song Tang and Murat Abdughani explore dark matter that interacts strongly with itself through a 'super-resonance' effect. The standard cosmological model succeeds on large scales but struggles on small ones, where self-interacting dark matter may help. Resonance and Sommerfeld effects can each amplify dark matter scattering.

Combining both effects boosts the self-scattering cross section enough for candidates near one hundred gigaelectronvolts in mass. The same mechanism also enhances annihilation, which drives early kinetic decoupling and breaks the standard Boltzmann treatment. By solving coupled Boltzmann equations instead, the authors compute the relic density precisely. Their results align with observational constraints on how much dark matter the universe contains.
arxiv-2511-09406:
Alexander Korochkin, Dmitri Semikoz, and Peter Tinyakov offer one nearby source as the resolution of a cosmic-ray disagreement. Two observatories, Pierre Auger and the Telescope Array, measure ultra-high-energy cosmic ray spectra. Their results agree closely at lower energies but split apart at the top end. Something must explain the Telescope Array's excess.

The authors show a single bright nearby source, layered over an almost isotropic background, can do it. Magnetic deflections in and beyond the Galaxy spread the source's particles enough to avoid excessive clustering. The required hard spectrum and intermediate-mass composition match earlier Auger-only fits. The best-fit source position sits near M82, the brightest nearby starburst galaxy, also aligning with Telescope Array hotspots.
arxiv-2511-09706:
Muhammad Yarahmadi and Amin Salehi reconstruct the universe's expansion history with a physics-informed neural network. The setting is a Tsallis holographic dark energy model with massive neutrinos. The network's loss embeds the model's modified Friedmann equation, so reconstructions obey the physics by construction. Training data are cosmic chronometer measurements out to redshift two.

The framework jointly estimates the Hubble constant, the neutrino density, and the Tsallis non-extensivity index, with dropout simulations providing uncertainty bands. Within this model, the famous Hubble tension eases considerably, the authors report. It falls from about five sigma to between half a sigma and just over two sigma. They also bound the total neutrino mass below about a tenth of an electronvolt, matching traditional sampling analyses.
arxiv-2511-10106:
Xian-Hui Ge, writing alone, draws a basic parallel between Zeno's paradox and the black hole information loss problem. Both, Ge argues, hinge on limiting procedures that turn formally infinite constructions into finite physical answers. Building on the replica-wormhole picture, which restored unitarity to Hawking radiation, the paper moves further and defines a quantitative notion of irreversibility for evaporation.

The main result is a modular thermodynamic approach in which modular entropy, entanglement capacity, and relative entropy do the work of heat laws. Monotonicity of relative entropy supplies a generalized second law that fixes the arrow of evolution in replica space. Ge also resolves the clash with the no-cloning theorem by treating replicas as ensemble representations, not real copies, and links non-additivity in Tsallis statistics to wormhole-induced correlations.
arxiv-2511-10506:
L. H. Ford and Brian Fu study isolated laser pulses, flashes of light that exist only within a finite time interval and are strictly zero outside it. Their interest comes from quantum physics, where the shape of a measuring pulse controls how likely a measurement is to catch a very large fluctuation.

The authors compute the Fourier transform of the pulse envelope numerically and examine how fast it falls off at high frequencies. In their model of pulse creation, the transform decays like an exponential of a fractional power of frequency, with the fraction between 0.1 and 0.2 in their examples. That slow decay carries over to the probability distribution of measured operators, implying a significant chance of fluctuations far larger than the typical variance.
arxiv-2511-10706:
Zitong Zhang and Hao Sun present a method to discover the equations of motion of mechanical systems directly from data. Sparse regression techniques struggle here with rational functions and noise. The Lagrangian formalism avoids rational expressions and describes dynamics in fewer words, making it a tempting target for identification.

Their method for differentiable sparse identification adds three ingredients. First, cubic B-spline curves capture complex nonlinear shapes inside the Lagrangian. Second, a robust discovery step uses the measured data while staying within known physical limits. Third, a recursive scheme works out derivatives from the spline basis, which tames noise in second-order systems. The authors report the method beats baselines and pulls physical laws from noisy data more exactly, above all in complex mechanical systems.
arxiv-2511-10806:
Syed Mumtahin Mahmud and five co-authors present a hybrid architecture for sharpening blurred photographs. Motion and camera shake still defeat many deep learning deblurrers, especially in complex or high-resolution images, and heavy models add a computational burden of their own.

Their design runs in two domains at once. A vision transformer backbone models local and global structure in the ordinary spatial domain. An FFT-ReLU module works in the frequency domain, enforcing sparsity there to suppress blur artifacts and protect fine detail. On benchmark datasets, the combined system beat state-of-the-art models on PSNR, structural similarity, and perceptual quality. Human preference evaluations agreed, and the authors offer the dual-domain design as a practical, generalizable approach to real-world image restoration.
arxiv-2511-10906:
Zesen Huang, Marco Velli, and their colleagues report the first strong direct sign that the Sun's five-minute surface shaking reaches out into the solar wind. The work uses data from NASA's Parker Solar Probe during its three closest passes by the Sun. Those shakes, called p-modes, come from sound waves trapped inside the Sun.

Close to the Sun, the team found clear peaks in the magnetic field at the same rhythm as the surface shakes. In two cases the signal formed a large wave train that lasted about thirty-five minutes. The result shows that shaking from the whole Sun can travel outward and may help shape the wind that flows past Earth.
arxiv-2511-11506:
Lijuan Dong and four co-authors examine photon blockade, the effect where one photon passing through a nonlinear medium stops later photons from following, much as electrons block each other in Coulomb blockade. Blockade is prized as a way to make useful quantum states of light, yet adding more atoms normally fails to strengthen it.

Combining approximate analysis with full quantum simulations, the team studies a resonator holding an ensemble of emitters coupled through two-photon interactions. In that setting, both single-photon and multi-photon blockade gain a collective boost from the ensemble. The result suggests a practical route to stronger light control without demanding extreme coupling in a single emitter.
arxiv-2511-11706:
Julia Peters and six co-authors build a representation learning framework that fuses satellite data from different sensors into one feature space at fine detail in both space and time. Earth observation foundation models already turn raw imagery into ready-to-use embeddings, but most work at one fixed scale.

Ecology needs both sharp spatial detail and frequent revisits, a combination single-scale models miss. Sentinel-1 radar and Sentinel-2 optical data serve as the test case for context-aware multimodal learning. Unified, high-resolution embeddings could let researchers model ecosystem dynamics directly, without rebuilding sensor-specific preprocessing for every new question about land, water, or vegetation change.
arxiv-2511-11806:
J. K. M. Viuho and seven co-authors test an unlikely telescope material: KDP, monopotassium dihydrogen phosphate, better known from crystal optics, as a thermal blocking filter for near-infrared astronomy. Ground-based infrared work fights the sky's own glow, and thermal emission climbs steeply toward the red cutoff of modern detectors.

KDP stays transparent from the ultraviolet to about one point three microns, then turns highly opaque beyond two microns, exactly the blocking profile a shortpass filter wants. On-sky demonstrations show it working in practice. A cheap, optically clean blocker could lower instrument costs and improve filter performance for infrared cameras and spectrographs on many telescopes.
arxiv-2511-11906:
Jing-Lun Li and three co-authors derive a few-body cousin of the Lellouch-Lüscher relation, the formula that connects what experiments measure inside a finite box to scattering in open space. Their setting is ultracold atoms held in harmonic traps and optical lattices, where three-body loss rates are the observable.

The relation links those loss rates to the energies and widths of trapped few-body states. Three-body simulations confirm it holds across wide ranges of interaction strength and energy, within a single partial wave. A robust finite-volume framework lets tweezer and lattice experiments extract genuine multi-body scattering rates from trapped measurements, sharpening a precision tool for few-body physics.
arxiv-2511-12006:
Kai-Wen K. Yang and nine co-authors overturn a habit in microscopy AI. When a fluorescence model moves to a new instrument, teams retrain the whole network. That often wrecks the semantics it learned. Tests here show the opposite works better. Adapt only the earliest convolutional layers, and freeze the deeper ones.

The frame, SIT-ADDA-Auto, pairs shallow-layer adversarial alignment with predictive uncertainty. It picks the adaptation depth on its own. No labels from the new microscope are needed. Multi-metric checks, blinded expert judgment, and other validation support the claim. Predictive microscopy that survives a hardware change is what labs truly need.
arxiv-2511-12106:
Hemant Kumar Gehlot and three co-authors introduce a way to measure how social networks distort what people think others believe. Effects such as the majority illusion and echo chambers can make a local view differ sharply from the global one. Their perception gap index captures that local-to-global gap for opinions on a continuous scale.

Using spectral graph theory, they show higher connectivity makes a network harder to distort, while strong community blocks make it more prone to distortion. They also study adding links, within a fixed budget, to shrink the gap. That task has no efficient exact fix in general, but their heuristic methods get near-best results on real data.
arxiv-2511-12206:
Nishant Vasantkumar Hegde, Aditi Agarwal and Minal Moharir build an automated system to spot traffic rule breaks by motorcyclists in real time. Checking helmet use and vehicle safety by hand is slow and uneven. Their system watches for riders without helmets, missing rear-view mirrors, and reads license plates.

It uses YOLOv8 for object detection and an optical character tool for plates, trained on a custom set of labeled images widened by augmentation. Image cleanup helps plate reading in hard conditions. A web interface logs violations as they occur. Reported scores show strong precision and recall, and mirror checks are noted as a new part of such systems.
arxiv-2511-12506:
Levente Bodnár and seven co-authors confirm a conjecture about the tetrahedron in three-uniform hypergraphs, in a squared measure of density. Turán's tetrahedron problem asks how many edges a hypergraph on many vertices can have without containing a complete three-graph on four vertices. A recent result showed a balanced cyclic three-part construction is asymptotically best when edge counts are replaced by sums of squared codegrees.

The new work confirms that, in that squared setting, the same construction is the unique extremal one for large vertex counts. Key steps include a Mantel-type theorem for vertex-colored graphs that forbid certain triangles, and a new stability procedure that checks whether local changes raise the squared measure near the optimum.
arxiv-2511-12606:
Drishya Karki and four co-authors benchmark two ways of recognizing group activities: from video pixels, and from the positions and tracks of the people involved. Group activity recognition is well studied on video for surveillance and team sports, while tracking data are compact and encode spatial interaction directly, yet remain under-explored. No standard benchmark aligned both views of the same activities.

Their dataset, SoccerNet-GAR, is built from the sixty-four matches of the 2022 football World Cup. Broadcast video and player tracking are synchronized and annotated for a large set of group activities in ten categories. A unified protocol then compares strong video-based and tracking-based methods on equal footing.
arxiv-2511-12806:
Haoxi Hu computes new upper bounds for the resurgence number of a matroidal configuration, a quantity from commutative algebra that compares two ways of building powers of an ideal. Symbolic powers collect functions vanishing to given orders, while ordinary powers are plain products. The resurgence number measures the worst ratio between the two, and bounding it for configurations built from matroids has been an active problem with links to containment questions for ideals.

Hu's bound covers two cases: when the configuration's height is large, and when the height is small but the associated simplicial complex is peaked, a generalization of bipartite graphs. Examples show the remaining case cannot be improved with the same bound. The paper also gives a new proof of the known formula for star configurations using its own methods. It is a specialist contribution to the algebra of symbolic powers.
arxiv-2511-13306:
Bowen Ye, Bin Zhang, and Hang Zhao introduce DAP, a compact planner for self-driving that works in discrete tokens. Predicting only the car's own path gives weak training signal and little sense of how the scene should shape motion. DAP instead forecasts both bird's-eye scene meaning and the car's path in one autoregressive stream.

Predicted scene change can then directly guide the planned motion. A reinforcement learning stage fine-tunes the planner while keeping the safe habits learned from human driving data. With only about one hundred sixty million parameters, DAP reached top open-loop scores and competitive closed-loop results on the NAVSIM benchmark in their tests.
arxiv-2511-13506:
Ida C. Skogvoll, Benjamin A. D. Williamson, and Sverre M. Selbach use density functional theory to study twin walls in calcium manganite. In this common perovskite, the bulk forbids joined electric and magnetic order, but a ferroelastic twin wall breaks mirror symmetry locally. That break can unlock properties the bulk cannot show.

Calculations show the wall shape drives local polar distortions that couple to magnetic order through tilted oxygen octahedra. Noncollinear results find stronger out-of-plane moments on manganese atoms and a finite magnetization confined to the wall itself. Polarization, a net moment, and a magnetoelectric response thus coexist at the wall, suggesting twin walls in similar antiferromagnets may host the same effect.
arxiv-2511-13606:
Noor-Ines Boudjema and 4 co-authors gauge how well double beta decay experiments can spot a Majoron-like scalar tied to neutrinos. Searches for the neutrinoless form of the decay gather rich data on the ordinary two-neutrino form as a byproduct. A massive scalar coupled to neutrinos, and perhaps to dark sector particles, would distort the emitted electron spectrum in telling ways.

The authors map those distortions for current and future experiments and compare the reach with cosmological limits. Future setups could probe very small scalar-neutrino couplings for light scalars and stay sensitive to heavier, off-shell production above the decay energy. The study turns a side dataset of major searches into a dark sector tool.
arxiv-2511-13706:
Shih-Yu Chang builds the syntax of operator networks in the second part of the Categorical Spectral Architecture program. Coherence asks whether wired diagrams of operators always mean the same transformation, a basic demand in category theory and in Hilbert space systems alike. Without it, a network's meaning could depend on how it was drawn.

Chang introduces the Synergy Operad, a syntactic layer over the multicategory of Hilbert spaces and bounded multilinear maps. A Canonical Representation Theorem gives a structure-keeping functor from syntax to operator meaning, and a Coherence Theorem shows grammatical equivalences yield identical results. Together they expose a syntax-semantics duality for building complex operator systems with behavior that can be foreseen.
arxiv-2511-13806:
Hugo Gimbert, Corto Mascle, and Patrick Totzke solve the sequential flow problem in polynomial space with a new algebraic method. The task is to maximize flow through a graph whose edge capacities change over time, chosen step by step from a fixed finite set of labelings. Long horizons make naive search explode, so small witnesses are the key.

Their engine is a factorization theorem for finite semigroups, applied to a semigroup built from flows. That structure yields compact certificates for optimal play. The method extends to several input and output vertices and to regular constraints on the labeling sequence. The result places a temporal network problem firmly inside a clean algebraic frame.
arxiv-2511-13906:
Alejandro Anderson, Esteban A. Hernandez-Vargas, and Giulia Giordano tackle a stability question for systems that switch between modes. Such switched systems, with uncertain and nonlinear behavior in discrete time, appear in engineering and biology. The authors want a certificate that states near a chosen set are pulled toward it despite the uncertainty.

They introduce attractivity guarantee functions: if one exists for a set, robust local attraction follows. They give a way to build such functions piece by piece from contractive sets, and show a robust control contractive set guarantees the certificate exists. A case study models antimicrobial resistance as a switched system, showing the framework at work on a biological problem.
arxiv-2511-14506:
Victor Ale and four co-authors develop a hybrid method to simulate quantum electrodynamics in two space dimensions plus time. Matter fields are stored in qubits, while gauge fields live in continuous bosonic modes called qumodes. A core tension is that qumode space is non compact, yet gauge symmetry is compact. The team propose two ways to enforce that compactness.

One method squeezes qumode states onto a unit circle through a changed inner product. The other adds a penalty term to the Hamiltonian. They build the full hybrid Hamiltonian and split it into lab ready gates. In a single plaquette test the dynamics match the correct gauge invariant behavior.
arxiv-2511-14606:
Shreya Adrita Banik and three co-authors compare human and model judgments of political bias in news. Detecting bias needs reading subtle language and context cues. The team build a hand labeled data set of news articles. They then test several large language and transformer models against human labels.

Among classic transformer models, RoBERTa aligns most closely with human labels. Generative models like GPT show the strongest overall agreement with humans. Agreement, polarity, and consistency are all measured to expose divergence. Results show models and humans still perceive bias differently in key cases. The framework helps judge when automated bias detection can be trusted.
arxiv-2511-14906:
Yasser Al Eryani offers a century-scale vision essay on the future of wireless communication, written as a journey from 2025 to 2125. Rather than expecting endless new generations in the style of 6G and 7G, the essay argues that progress will turn on managing the curvature of the information landscape. A proposed organizing rule ties capacity to that curvature across physics, biology, and heat.

The essay sketches how phase-coded continuous apertures could embody the idea, with companion papers carrying the formal theory and benchmark tests. Readers should treat the piece as a speculative roadmap, not a report of built systems. Its value lies in reframing wireless design around geometry instead of generation labels.
arxiv-2511-15306:
Purvi Gupta and Rudranil Sahu settle exactly when a certain class of surfaces inside complex space can be made Lagrangian. The surfaces are compact, totally real, and immersed with a finite number of clean self-crossings, the transverse double points. A classic result says being Lagrangian for some Kahler form forces a convexity trait called rational convexity, but a counterexample showed the trait alone is not enough.

The missing condition lives at the double points. The authors prove the surface is Lagrangian for some Kahler form exactly when it is rationally convex. At each crossing, the two tangent planes must also be carried by a complex linear map to a standard diagonal form. The characterization closes a question left open by the earlier counterexample.
arxiv-2511-15506:
T. Sato, B. Petrović, and six co-authors model how the injector design of an interband cascade laser affects the point where lasing starts. These lasers build light through a stack of thin layers, and the injector feeds carriers, the electrons and holes that make light, into the active region. Lower starting current means a more efficient device.

Their model combines band structure, electric fields, and a detailed calculation of Auger loss, where carrier energy is wasted as heat. Heavy doping of the electron injector cuts the main Auger loss by lowering the hole count in key wells, matching experiments. Adding indium to the hole injector did not beat that doping strategy in their tests.
arxiv-2511-15706:
Johan Edstedt, David Nordström, and eight co-authors present RoMa v2, a model for dense feature matching between two images of a scene. Matching finds which points in one image correspond to which points in another, a core step for three-dimensional reconstruction. Dense matchers are accurate and robust, yet they still fail on hard real scenes, and the best models are often slow.

A new matching design and loss, trained on a carefully varied data mix, solve many complex cases. Training is split into a matching stage and a refinement stage, with a custom graphics kernel that cuts refinement memory. Building on a recent vision foundation model adds robustness. Extensive tests set a new state of the art.
arxiv-2511-15906:
Matthieu Kirchmeyer, Pedro O. Pinheiro, and eight co-authors introduce FuncBind, a generative framework that designs molecules atom by atom for a chosen target. Structure-based drug design tools are often built for one kind of system only, which limits their reach. FuncBind instead represents molecules as continuous atomic density fields, borrowing neural field methods from computer vision, and generates them with score-based models.

One unified model trains across diverse atomic systems, from small molecules to large ones, handling varying atom and residue counts and even nonstandard amino acids. It performs competitively in computer tests on small molecules, macrocyclic peptides, and antibody binding loops. It also produced new antibody binders verified in laboratory experiments.
arxiv-2511-16206:
Yingkang Zhang and seven co-authors report the first high-resolution radio imaging of quasars picked out because the Gaia mission recorded more than one detection for each. Such doubled sources might be quasar and star pairs, two active nuclei, or lensed quasars, and radio imaging at very fine scale can tell them apart.

The team matched the sample to radio catalogs, found 18 radio sources, and observed the three brightest with the Very Long Baseline Array at two frequencies. Each target showed one compact source at the main Gaia position and nothing at the second position. That pattern supports the pair reading and shows how radio follow-up can clean up candidate lists for dual active nuclei.
arxiv-2511-16706:
Fronefield Crawford and Haoyang Xu report a fresh search for a pulsar hiding in Supernova Remnant 1987A, reprocessing archival observations from the Parkes 64-meter telescope, some never published before. A young pulsar is expected at the remnant's heart, but none has ever been confirmed.

Both a standard periodicity search and a single-pulse search across a range of dispersion measures turned up no convincing candidates. From the silence the authors compute limits on flux density, luminosity, and single-pulse fluence. The luminosity limits are comparable to those of three famous young pulsars, the Crab, PSR B0540-69, and PSR J0537-6910, so a pulsar like those cannot yet be ruled out. The remnant's neutron star may simply beam away from Earth or shine too faintly in radio.
arxiv-2511-16806:
Led by C Kaufmann Ribeiro, with fifteen co-authors, this study reports odd magnetic behaviour in crystals of a narrow-gap material called ZrTe5. In a strong magnetic field, electrons are normally forced into set levels, and signals repeat in a steady pattern as the field rises. Here the team cooled crystals to near zero and used fields up to sixty tesla.

The measured signals did not follow the usual steady pattern and kept going far past the point where only the lowest level should remain. The authors trace the effect to a contest between two energy effects that bends the levels back, so low levels cross the key energy line again at high field. The work gives a new frame for reading such signals in this class of materials.
arxiv-2511-16906:
Hewang Zhao and Zhendong Li introduce XSF-TDA, a method for computing spin-flip excitations of open-shell molecules without the spin contamination that plagues spin-flip time-dependent density functional theory. Flipping a spin during excitation is the natural route to bond breaking states and inverted singlet-triplet gaps, but contaminated answers are hard to trust.

The method grows out of the authors' earlier spin-adapted open-shell theory for spin-conserving excitations. The paper compares strategies for suppressing contamination across unrestricted and mixed-reference variants of the spin-flip approach. Pilot calculations on prototype systems show XSF-TDA describing bond breaking and inverted gap systems more faithfully than its predecessors. It is a step toward a spin-flip method that is both simple enough for routine use and accurate enough for chemistry's hard cases.
arxiv-2511-17506:
Narjes Nourzad, Mingyu Zong, and Bhaskar Krishnamachari combine large language models with multi-agent reinforcement learning to run next-generation cellular networks. Language models reason strategically about network planning but are too slow and costly for real-time control; reinforcement learning agents adapt locally but coordinate poorly at scale. AURA splits the difference: a cloud language model sets objectives and subgoals, while base stations, modeled as learning agents, execute them autonomously.

A trust mechanism balances the agents' local learning against the external guidance, and batched communication keeps the language model's picture of the network fresh without constant chatter. In a simulated 6G scenario, AURA cut dropped handoff requests by more than half under normal and heavy traffic and reduced system failures. Agents followed the model's input in under 60 percent of decisions, evidence that the guidance augments local adaptability rather than replacing it.
arxiv-2511-17706:
Paul Tiede, William Moses, Valentin Churavy, Michael Johnson, Dominic Pesce, Lindy Blackburn, and Peter Galison present a new way to build images from very long baseline radio data. Arrays such as the Event Horizon Telescope sample only parts of an image and add strong errors, so a single best picture hides real doubt.

Their method, called HIBI, tracks doubt for the image and for the instrument at the same time. Tests on fake data, on the black hole in M87, and on another source at many radio bands recover varied shapes well. HIBI is shared freely in the Comrade software collection.
arxiv-2511-17906:
Wen-Fan Wang, Chien-Ting Lu, Jin Ping Ng, and five co-authors present AnimAgents, a system that helps creators run animation pre production. That is the stage where an idea becomes a plan covering story, script, design, and storyboards. Generative tools for each step exist, but creators must juggle them and keep continuity by hand.

AnimAgents uses a core agent plus specialist agents, with dedicated boards for each stage, to coordinate work and let creators refine single elements. In a study with professional creators it beat a strong single agent baseline on coordination, consistency, and satisfaction. A field test with working creators confirmed its value on real projects.
arxiv-2511-18106:
Hou Jian, Meng Tan, and Tian Maozai develop a regression method for data spread over space. Each predictor's effect may be one global value or may vary smoothly from place to place, and the outcome of interest is a quantile rather than an average. Their convex framework splits each effect into a global part and a spatial deviation.

A group penalty decides which predictors truly vary over space, while a graph based smoothing term keeps deviations continuous on irregular networks. They give two practical solvers and theory covering selection consistency, error bounds, and normal limits for the global effects. Simulations modeled on air pollution data recover the split accurately.
arxiv-2511-18206:
Benjamin Bakker, Ananth N. Shankar, and Jacob Tsimerman prove a bound on a class of geometric objects tied to abelian schemes. They work over a smooth curve on a finite field. Their first result says only finitely many such schemes of a fixed size exist, once objects linked by a mild map are counted as the same.

The claim then grows in two ways. Over a larger field the full space of such schemes has finite type in the same loose sense. The team also lifts the result to a broad class of Shimura spaces, for large prime settings. Such finiteness results help pin down how wild these spaces can be.
arxiv-2511-18506:
Michael Adjei Osei and Sidney Shapiro study how to evaluate hybrid quantum programs as whole workflows, not as isolated devices or algorithms. Building on a current evaluation approach, they formalize a readiness score that is aware of workflow steps. They also add a normalized speedup measure that respects quality limits, and an audit of timing and drift across a hybrid pipeline.

They also give concise Python reference code showing how to use the metrics with current classical and quantum solvers, while keeping budgets matched and results reproducible. The guidance aims to make claims about quantum utility easier to check and compare across tools.
arxiv-2511-18606:
Kensuke Nakamura and five co-authors make safety filters for robot control smoother. A safety filter watches a learned policy and steps in before a crash state. Latent filters work from camera based codes, not hand built state, so they can guard tasks whose limits are hard to model. Past filters switch hard between the task policy and the safety policy, which jars motion.

A value function from reachability theory could in principle drive a smooth filter of barrier type. The team show, in theory and in tests, that current latent learning yields value functions unfit for that role. Two clashes cause it, tied to how failure margins are coded in latent space. Their training fix targets those clashes. Smooth guarding would keep task skill while it keeps the robot safe.
arxiv-2511-18806:
Qinglei Cao, Ziyao Tang, and Xiaoqin Tang propose a better way to rebuild three-dimensional CT images from very few X-ray views. Methods borrowed from neural scene rendering can reconstruct internal structure, but they ignore what is known about the target object's anatomy, which costs precision and learning speed when views are ultra-sparse. Their framework derives a target prior from the object's own projection data and uses it to guide the reconstruction.

The prior steers which voxels get sampled and enriches the structural encoding of position, a dual strategy the authors say lifts both learning efficiency and final quality. The work addresses a practical pressure in medical imaging: fewer X-ray views mean less radiation for the patient, if the reconstruction can be trusted. Their tests target exactly that sparse-view regime.
arxiv-2511-19206:
Pedro Brito de Sa and three co-authors study boson stars in a self interacting model with one complex and one real field. Boson stars are hypothetical compact objects made of scalar fields. They compute the family of static spherical solutions across a broad range of parameters, including the strength of the complex field's self interaction.

Positive self interaction raises the stars' maximum mass and compactness, reaching masses comparable to the white dwarf limit without extremely light particles. When the real field becomes massless, solutions grow larger and stability widens. Simulated images from ray tracing show strong lensing and shadows that could mimic black holes in surveys.
arxiv-2511-19306:
Zixuan Wang, Haoran Sun, Jiaming Lu, and five co-authors improve infrared small target detection, a hard vision task where tiny targets hide in cluttered backgrounds and learned features are weak. Language guided methods using image text models help, but their text descriptions can be inaccurate and may need manual annotation.

Their end to end framework builds prompts at two levels: coarse phrases about the scene type and fine descriptions generated from the image itself, so no annotation is needed at use time. Attention mechanisms guided by that text sharpen sensitivity to likely targets in both low and high level features. Tests on three benchmarks show leading detection accuracy.
arxiv-2511-19406:
Rebecca Lee and four co-authors estimate power spectra for many biomedical time series at once. A spectrum shows which rhythms dominate a signal, such as heart rate records, and hints at the body processes behind them. Comparing many series is hard because each has its own extra variation and a different length.

Their method, HBEST, models log spectra with a cosine basis split into shared population parts and individual parts. A fully Bayesian design with shrinkage priors lets series borrow strength from each other. Simulations beat rival methods on speed and accuracy, and a heart rate variability study shows the method capturing real links in the data.
arxiv-2511-19506:
Raoul H. Kutil and three co-authors link the written descriptions of cognitive disorders to a machine-ready form for computing how alike disorders are. The DSM-5 manual defines these disorders through signs and symptoms in prose. A binary matrix form exists for similarity work, but a full matrix is impossible for the hardest cases because symptom mixes explode.

Their symptom profile generator uses a strict format of lists, sets, and numbers with small allowed variations. Complex diagnostic paths can be written compactly, read by people, and adapted with ease. Software can then generate every valid symptom combination on demand, bridging the manual's narrative and automated analysis.
arxiv-2511-19706:
Adele Myers Lantow and Nina Miolane build an image descriptor that ignores rotation while keeping everything else about the picture. Vision systems often need that invariance, but hand-crafted features describe weakly and learned ones cost speed and clarity. Their selective disk bispectrum aims at the middle ground.

The descriptor is a complex-valued vector that keeps all image information except orientation. The paper gives its inversion, its reduced cost against the full disk bispectrum, and its behavior under noise, plus a numerical approximation with accuracy guarantees. Tests confirm the invariance and robustness, offering a compact and readable alternative to learned features.
arxiv-2511-19806:
Jihan Yao and six co-authors teach vision-language models to say they cannot read something, rather than guess wrong. In scene text questions, a misread sign can be dangerous, yet models rarely know when their reading failed. Confidence scores from outputs are poorly calibrated for this job.

Their method trains light probes on the model's hidden states and attention patterns, where doubt signals hide. Three probe designs are tried, including layer-wide joins and majority votes over single layers. On four image and video benchmarks, abstention accuracy rises well above the best baselines, and the strongest signals sit in middle layers, not the last.
arxiv-2511-20106:
Li, Shi, Li, and colleagues build a speech corpus where emotions come mixed, not single. Their 2025 paper introduces EM2LDL for speech emotion recognition. Most emotion datasets use one language and one label. Real feelings blend several emotions at once. Multilingual speakers also switch languages mid-sentence often.

The corpus spans English, Mandarin, and Cantonese speech. Utterances were harvested from online platforms for realism. Code-switching within single utterances is included deliberately. Each clip carries a distribution over thirty-two emotion categories. Two hundred thirty-one unique speakers contributed recordings. Gender and age are fairly balanced across speakers. MBTI personality traits accompany a subset of voices. Baseline models used self-supervised speech encoders. HuBERT-large-EN scored best among the baselines tested. Young-to-older transfer beat the reverse direction clearly. State-of-the-art models still struggle with the fine detail. Dataset, annotations, and code are publicly released.
arxiv-2511-20206:
Markova, Larsen, von Neumann-Cosel, and a large team probe the inner statistics of indium-109. Their 2025 paper extracts nuclear level density and gamma strength. The isotope is neutron-deficient and hard to study. Data came from a cadmium-106 alpha reaction. Proton-gamma coincidences fed the Oslo method analysis.

Level density and gamma strength were obtained together. A shape method cross-checked the extraction carefully. Both quantities resemble neighboring cadmium and tin nuclei. Model predictions disagree with the data substantially though. One surprise stood out near the neutron threshold. No dipole strength bump appears in indium-109 there. Neighbors show that pygmy enhancement clearly. Theory calculations with tin isotopes framed the contrast. Capture cross sections were estimated from the new data. Proton capture matched direct measurements excellently. Neutron capture rates strayed from a standard library. Star-process simulations inherit less uncertainty now. Astrophysical p-process models gain firmer inputs.
arxiv-2511-20406:
Mishayev, Sverdlov, Amir, and Dym show a graph learning flaw strikes close to home. Their 2025 paper concerns message passing neural networks on graphs.
