They first reproduce the exact answer and the false self-trapping that plain mean field dynamics shows under strong interaction. Feeding those mean field states into that machinery then removes the trapping and matches the tunneling motion closely. Comparing ways to read averages from the correlated wave function shows agreement in some cases and sharp gaps in others. That contrast clarifies where collective versus single-particle pictures emerge and backs the method.
arxiv-2604-02006: Gao and colleagues fix a failure mode in agentic language-model reasoning with ProCeedRL, a process critic that intervenes instead of choosing. Weak actions feed noisy observations into misleading contexts, weakening later decisions and making recovery ever harder, which defeats standard exploration. ProCeedRL watches interactions through a process level critic and steers agents with reflection based demonstrations that stop errors from piling up. Learning from those demonstrations plus on policy samples, it beat the model's saturated exploration performance and lifted efficiency, with top results on deep search and embodied tasks.
arxiv-2604-02106: Nayak, Ghosh and Basu hunt data races in GPU programs by reading the host code that launches each kernel. Earlier dynamic tools miss races that never show up in testing, while static tools cry wolf over parameter values that can never occur. Their HGRD analyzer studies CPU and GPU code together, using launch time facts to rule out impossible values. It missed no true races in tests and raised no false alarms, beating dynamic rival iGUARD and static rivals GPUVerify and FaialAA on both counts.
arxiv-2604-02406: Johnson and team involve communities in defining cultural fit for AI images of artifacts. Auto checks can miss the expertise of impacted groups, so the team puts community input first, in the concept making phase, before building tests. Case studies with blind and low vision people in the UK, people in Kerala and Tamil Nadu yield defined concepts rooted in lived experience and depiction tastes. The concepts can feed auto tests via a language model judge approach, with benefits and limits discussed.
arxiv-2604-02506: Alves, Nishi and Vecchi explore Nelson-Barr models that solve the strong CP problem, the puzzle of why strong forces preserve CP symmetry. The models mix ordinary quarks with a vector-like partner of the quark doublet. An accidental symmetry delays the leading contribution to the CP-violating angle until three loops, naturally suppressing it. The models remain viable and testable, with future electric dipole moment experiments among the key probes.
arxiv-2604-02906: Kou and Chen probe proton structure with physics-guided neural networks in holographic QCD, tackling the structure function across nonperturbative and transition regimes. Their representation combines fermion-resonance and Pomeron-like AdS/QCD basis functions with a neural parametrization. The AdS eigenvalue problem and the physical proton mass constrain it. Fitted channel fractions shift continuously from Pomeron-like dominance at lower x to fermion-resonance dominance at larger x, with the crossover near one-fifth in x.
arxiv-2604-03406: Sun and colleagues present SASAV, the first fully autonomous agent for scientific data analysis and display without expert prompting or human-in-the-loop feedback. The multi-agent system profiles data on its own, retrieves context-aware knowledge, and explores display settings through reasoning. By removing reactive, data-dependent guidance, SASAV aims to scale scientific discovery and innovation.
arxiv-2604-03506: Hsu and colleagues' 2026 pipeline distills biology papers into graded question-and-answer pairs for reward-based learning. Their BioAlchemy-345K set holds over 345K scientific thinking problems in biology, aligned to the modern research topic mix. Their BioAlchemist-8B model improves over its base model by 9.12 percent on biology benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-04306: Girtsou and colleagues present HighFM, a first step toward a foundation model for fast-changing Earth observation data. Most current models use sharp satellite images that revisit rarely, a poor fit for fast events and emergency response. HighFM instead learns from high-frequency multispectral images from the Meteosat Second Generation platform, over 2 terabytes of SEVIRI imagery, adapting a masked autoencoding design with fine-grained time encodings. Fine-tuned for cloud masking and active fire detection, it beats traditional baselines and recent geospatial models on both accuracy measures.
arxiv-2604-04806: Zhang presents MIRAGE, an online simulation scheme for microservice dependencies with a language model. Static record-replay, pattern-mining, and stubs can only replay behaviour fixed at build time, scoring zero and 12 percent fidelity on error and reasoning scenes. MIRAGE instead answers each request as it arrives, reading source code, caller code, and traces while holding state across requests. On 110 scenes across three systems it reaches 99 percent fidelity for status and shape in white box mode, against 62 and 16 percent for record-replay. Each dependency costs three seconds and 0.16 to 0.82 dollars.
arxiv-2604-05306: Guo, Gu, Jin, Spanos, and Lavaei train large language models to say plainly when they are unsure, instead of answering wrongly with false confidence. One method has the model speak a confidence score at the end of its reasoning, aiming high on right answers and low on wrong ones. A second plants an uncertainty marker mid-reasoning whenever the current line of thought looks shaky. Both cut overconfident errors and improved answer quality, and both can trigger extra retrieval to repair a shaky answer.
arxiv-2604-05606: Haeupler and Paramonov keep random assignments fresh under hostile, adaptive changes with few resamples per change. They expose a time-selection attack that skews even proactive resampling and answer with a time-aggregation rule plus two new schemes. The headline use keeps graph coloring near best with sublinear mean work per change.
arxiv-2604-05806: Dąbrowski and seven colleagues manipulate antiferromagnetic domains in NiO and CoO films entirely with light. A single laser pulse thermally demagnetizes the material into random domains, while sweeping the beam drives wall motion for partial switching. Reversing the thermal gradient toggles 90-degree domains, enabling ultrafast switching without electric currents.
arxiv-2604-05906: Park and three colleagues sharpen diffusion-based image reading by pooling cross-attention maps only from the heads most tied to each idea. The method beats DAAM on mean IoU, and top heads grasp idea traits far better than low heads. Pooling just the best heads also flags cases where the model reads a prompt wrong, which helps users steer and trust the tool.
arxiv-2604-06106: Cudby and Strelchuk develop quantum optimisation for pangenome-guided sequence assembly, whose walk problem is NP-hard. They test quadratic unconstrained binary optimisation and a new higher-order binary optimisation, or HUBO. HUBO cuts variables from order N squared to order N log N. Both encodings run under nonvariational Iterative-QAOA, a fixed linear-ramp schedule with warm-start bias updates. In noiseless simulations, Iterative-QAOA finds optimal assemblies from as few as 10 to the minus 17 percent of candidates. IBM hardware closely reproduces results with CVaR-style post-selection.
arxiv-2604-06406: Luna and Summers present two approaches for task and motion planning in Graphs of Convex Sets. Task planning and movement encode as a Shortest Path Problem in an Augmented Graph of Convex Sets, but the graph grows exponentially. Both prune the graph before construction. Top-down uses a sparse Delaunay graph. The bottom-up approach orders tasks with Traveling Salesman heuristics, expanding in a window to a bounded width. Both reach optimal or near-optimal solutions faster. Bottom-up solves 1,000 tasks in about two minutes. 1-tree lower bounds quantify suboptimality.
arxiv-2604-06606: Hwang proposes an entangled-clock protocol that reads proper-time differences directly as a quantum phase. Using highly entangled multi-clock states, its uncertainty shrinks in inverse proportion to the total clock count, reaching the Heisenberg limit while staying fully immune to dynamical phase noise. The paper also weighs using this ultra-precise timing for gravitational-wave detection, pointing toward quantum-enhanced relativistic sensing and tests of fundamental physics.
arxiv-2604-06706: Csire and eight colleagues find a reversed anisotropy in the superconductor Sr2RuO4. Unconventional superconductors usually show Andreev bound states at in-plane edges while out-of-plane surfaces stay fully gapped. Here edge- and surface-sensitive spectroscopy finds strong in-gap states at out-of-plane surfaces instead, with weaker features at in-plane edges. Inter-orbital pairing of either parity explains the flip, suppressing planar edge modes while creating surface states and possibly a horizontal line node, constraining the superconducting order parameter.
arxiv-2604-07006: Cho brings Continuous Interpretive Steering for graded use-based reading in language models. Reading is graded: items enrich meaning in varied ways, and hint strength varies across items. Tests rely on prompt tweaks, but Cho treats steering strength as smooth. A dataset, GraSD, encodes graded scalar range. Tests on models show uniform steering raises readings but flattens item spread, while graded steering yields shifts aligned with range grades. Graded feel lives in mind space, found by probes.
arxiv-2604-07406: Kolář argues that the usual definition of NP clashes with Gödel's incompleteness results. For each NP language, a fast checking relation plus a size bound defines membership. He reads this as Hilbert's triple, where truth and bounded proof coincide by fiat. Gödel's own proof-checking relation is fast and fits the definition, yet incompleteness bars the trait the definition claims for it. On this reading, the semantic definition of NP cannot hold, just as Hilbert's program cannot.
arxiv-2604-07706: Samad and three colleagues reuse vine copulas for mining high-dimensional digital health record data. Old methods struggle with mixed-type data and non-linear links under simple bell-curve assumptions about varied fields. Vine copulas produce trees of pair links at varying levels, splitting a multi-way spread. The tree ranks fields by link strength and finds central fields with local links, easing mining. The use finds links between co-morbid ills, tested on different cohorts of EHR patients, providing reasons, charts, and picks for health results.
arxiv-2604-08006: Ji studies how random shocks expand contracting Lorenz maps that satisfy the summability rule of power 1. Under broad rules on maps and perturbation types, Ji proves strong random stability: steady-measure levels converge in L1 norm to the real measure density for the plain map. This beats the main result in an earlier work.
arxiv-2604-08406: Zeng and five colleagues map how often planets of each size orbit sunlike stars, using mainly Kepler's primary mission. A survival function analysis, which tracks how planet counts fall with size and distance, finds a log uniform spread for most planets except giants, plus a scarcity near twice Earth's radius. Formation scenarios reviewed in the paper aim to explain why each size band lands where it does.
arxiv-2604-08506: Raidal and three colleagues show the gravitational wave background from merging supermassive black holes carries a heavy power law tail, so its loudest signals likely come from a few strong sources. Third and higher moments diverge, limiting their use as non Gaussianity measures, but a variance averaged Gaussian approximation still describes timing residuals well. That result justifies a factored likelihood for pulsar timing inference, with a fast Python tool supplied.
arxiv-2604-08606: Sudhir and Tran-Thanh analyze recursive information markets as a fix for the buyer's inspection paradox, where inspecting information gives it away for free. They formalize whether language model buyers that can forget what they inspect would price and supply information at its true value, focusing on a new recursive version of the mechanism. The analysis connects the idea to extrapolated volition and scalable oversight in AI alignment research.
arxiv-2604-08806: Chakrabarti and three colleagues study Oppenheimer-Snyder dust collapse in metric f(R) gravity, matching a uniform dust inside to a broad Vaidya outside across a time like surface. Regular matching demands smoothness of the metric, outer bend, Ricci scalar, and its normal slope, usually ruling out Ricci flat outsides like Schwarzschild. For open outsides the edge data leave the bulk open. Limiting outside matter forces a tight linear form that sharply limits allowed outsides, leaving dust collapse open in this sector.
arxiv-2604-09306: Meuser, Weil, Lahiri, and Paraschiv propose SatQNet for entanglement routing in satellite-assisted quantum networks that can run decentralized at runtime. Quantum networks link devices, but entanglement distribution is usually short-range, and satellites extend it over long distances. Routing is hard because satellite motion creates a dynamic topology, while global information quickly goes stale. SatQNet uses an edge-centric directed line graph neural network passing messages locally on edge embeddings. Trained on random graphs, it beats heuristic and learning-based approaches and generalizes to unseen topologies without retraining.
arxiv-2604-09406: Choudhary, Saxena, and Roy propose OASIS, an online activation subspace learning algorithm for memory-efficient training. Training large language models is constrained by memory, with activations taking a substantial share. Existing methods cut memory via low-rank weights or gradient subspaces, while activation memory uses architecture changes. OASIS tracks and updates a low-dimensional activation subspace during training, projecting activations onto it without changing forward computation. That yields low-rank gradients and states kept in the subspace, with up to twice lower peak memory than full fine-tuning.
arxiv-2604-09706: Budhkar, Dhara, and Sheth expose a deployment gap in AI media detection. Near-perfect clean-lab detectors degrade sharply once images are resized, compressed, re-encoded, and changed for online platforms. Their platform-aware framework models deployment transforms, constraining perturbations to plausible meme-style bands over full-image noise. Per-image attacks slash area-under-curve scores from about 0.99 and achieve high fake-to-real misclassification despite strict visual limits. Universal perturbations exist within localized bands, revealing shared vulnerability directions. Detectors grow confidently incorrect under attack, a calibration collapse.
arxiv-2604-10206: Kartvelishvili weighs two notions of size for closed submodules of Hilbert C*-modules: essentiality and topological essentiality. For closed two-sided ideals of C*-algebras the two traits coincide, but the one-sided case is subtler. He proves they remain equal for closed right ideals of any C*-algebra. Via the link between submodules and right ideals of compact operators, he extends the result to closed submodules of Hilbert C*-modules. When things commute, he gives a shape-based account and a per-fiber test.
arxiv-2604-10306: Humes and Mohsenin present SatReg, a tuning framework for lightweight remote-sensing segmentation on edge platforms. Using a teacher, they shrink the search to two width variables, profile student models on a Jetson Orin Nano, and fit surrogate models for accuracy, latency, and power. Distillation trains the sampled students efficiently. The surrogates pick best settings for deployment targets without exhaustive search. The chosen variables affect accuracy and hardware cost differently, making reduced regression practical for hybrid CNN-Mamba segmentation in space systems.
arxiv-2604-10406: Orlando, Lamberto, Nori, and Savasta turn still quantum ripples into real light near a tipping point. Ground state links like squeezing stay sealed, since they rest on virtual stirrings no probe can catch. A swift shift of a control knob frees those stirrings as true photons, a burst called vacuum radiation. Near the critical edge, the flux and its odd quantum traits grow strong even as heat noise looms. Higher order steps matter even for small shifts, and the team folds them into one full frame.
arxiv-2604-10806: Sun and five colleagues present an open driver model for early control quality in shared-control driving, when first-seconds control after handover decides safety. Purely logic-driven models miss early shifts because driver mind states change fast. Their model grounds bounded rationality in reinforcement learning, adapting hidden mind parameters via particle tracking from driver actions. In a vehicle-in-the-loop study with 41 participants, the tuned model spots risky handovers with higher reach and longer lead times than rivals. Mind parameters line up strongly with eye-tracking metrics.
arxiv-2604-11206: Santilli, Alipour, and Moghaddam design a blueprint for digital nudging systems that treats ethics and fairness as structural guardrails, not afterthoughts. Drawing on 68 nudging strategies, 11 quality traits, and three user-profiling angles, they layer step-by-step processing with review modules that enforce regulatory compliance. Checks by 13 architects and a 15-user energy-saving trial backed feasibility and positive emotional impact.
arxiv-2604-11306: Bärmann and three colleagues give humanoid robots a memory that learns what to forget. Their H2-EMV framework builds hierarchical episodic memory from continuous perception, drops details by language-model relevance under learned natural-language rules, and revises those rules from user feedback. Tests on simulated household tasks and 20.5 hours of real recordings from ARMAR-7 cut memory size by 45 percent and query compute by 35 percent while holding question-answering accuracy, which rose 70 percent on second-round queries.
arxiv-2604-11506: Bessa and three colleagues present RedShell, a genAI tool for ethical hacking that writes malicious PowerShell code. Red teams can use genAI models to automate pentest audits, but offensive code generation lacks training and test data. RedShell combines public code samples into a ground-truth dataset for fine-tuning models in malicious PowerShell generation. Experiments show strong syntactic validity, with fewer than 10 percent of samples producing parse errors. Mean similarity scores exceed 50 percent on edit distance and 40 percent on METEOR, showing consistency with reference snippets.
arxiv-2604-11806: Stein and four colleagues present Meerkat, a tool that hunts safety violations across large sets of AI agent traces. Single-trace judges miss failures visible only across traces, while naive agentic auditing cannot scale and fixed monitors break on new behaviours. Meerkat pairs clustering with agentic search, probing promising regions without seed scenarios or exhaustive listing. It beats baseline monitors on misuse, misalignment, and task-gaming tests, exposes developer cheating on a leading agent benchmark, and finds nearly four times as many CyBench reward-hacking cases as earlier audits.
arxiv-2604-12306: Sheikh and four colleagues present the GCA framework for climate decision support in the Gulf states, pairing a curated dataset with a tool-using agent. GCA-DS holds 200,000 question-answer pairs across policies, adaptation plans, frameworks, literature, and event reporting on heatwaves, dust storms, and floods, plus remote-sensing inputs. The Gulf Climate Agent orchestrates real-time and historical signals with geospatial processing into indices and visualizations. Domain fine-tuning and tool use beat general-purpose baselines on reliability.
arxiv-2604-12406: Ramy E. Ali and Federico Penna propose LightTune, a lightweight online fine-tuning method for phones. Mobile models degrade as real conditions drift from training conditions. Standard online learning costs too much compute for constrained devices. LightTune needs no backpropagation and refines models only when performance dips below a threshold. Applied to block error rate prediction for 6G systems, it adapts to unseen channels live. Prediction error falls by up to 48.8 percent with online tuning. Throughput rises by up to 15.5 percent against table-based link adaptation.
arxiv-2604-12506: Linhao Zhang and eight colleagues fix a blind spot in audio language models. Such models reason well but miss fine acoustic detail. Speech-focused training teaches them to treat tone, emotion, and sound events as noise. Their Unified Audio Schema organizes sound into three parts: transcription, paralinguistics, and non-speech events. All three sit in one JSON format for training. The scheme lifts fine-grained perception by 10.9 percent on MMSU over same-size rivals. Reasoning skill stays robust throughout.
arxiv-2604-12606: Sucharita Barik and two colleagues build acyclic matchings on independence complexes. The work covers graphs with a simplicial vertex. It builds on matchings from specific subgraphs, step by step. For chordal graphs, the team finds homotopy types. It also covers graphs that extend comparability graphs of grid posets. The method is algorithmic, unlike earlier heavy homotopy methods. Even when the type stays unknown, the work aids homology. It gives a pre-processing step for faster homology work.
arxiv-2604-12906: John H. Dallyn and four colleagues rework the noise factor of Brillouin amplifiers. Thermal-mechanical phonon fluctuations imprint noise on the optical signal. Old work infers a factor near one plus thermal phonon occupation. A Hamiltonian coupled-mode treatment derives that factor for large gain with no phonon travel. The framework extends to forward and backward scattering, phonon travel, optical loss, and small gains. Noise can stray far from the old factor in modern devices where phonon travel reshapes dynamics.
arxiv-2604-13006: Potraghloo, Azizi, Kundu, and Pedram show that tiny wording bans make instruction-tuned language models collapse their answers. Banning a single punctuation mark or common word costs 14 to 48 percent of comprehensiveness across seven models. Blinded human judges confirm real content loss, and diagnostics trace it to planning failure: generating twice recovers 59 to 96 percent of response length. The same bans leave untuned base models largely untouched.
arxiv-2604-13106: Mahu, Sehba, and Williams give a new proof of a classical weighted sine product inequality using the log-convexity of the Gamma function and Euler's reflection formula. Two parameter choices yield two competing upper bounds for the same product, and algebraic criteria pin down exactly when each bound is sharper. Explicit results cover the general n-angle case, the 2n-angle case, and the two- and three-angle cases, with several sharp corollaries.
arxiv-2604-13206: Islam, Villarreal, Nishino, Salman, and Liu trace language-model surprises to finite floating-point rounding, tracking how rounding errors move through Transformer layers. They identify a chaotic avalanche effect in early layers, where tiny perturbations either amplify rapidly or vanish entirely. Beyond single errors, models show three scale-dependent regimes: stable, where small perturbations die out; chaotic, where rounding errors drive outputs apart; and signal-dominated, where true input variation overrides numerical noise.
arxiv-2604-13506: Zhang, Zhang, and Zhang tackle recovering an unknown drift term inside a two-dimensional heat-type equation from a final snapshot alone. They build a monotone operator whose fixed point is exactly that drift, which settles uniqueness and yields a step-by-step rebuilding procedure. Computer trials show the iteration converging steadily, and it keeps working when the final data carry noise.
arxiv-2604-13606: Gao, Lo, and Shan study equitable tree colouring. Each colour class must form a forest. Class sizes differ by at most one. Extending the Hajnal-Szemeredi theorem to this forest setting, they prove such a colouring exists for large graphs of bounded maximum degree. The colour count must clear roughly half the degree plus one. The result settles a conjecture by Wu, Zhang, and Li for even degree. For odd degree it misses by at most one colour.
arxiv-2604-13706: Sahnan and four colleagues propose Co-FactChecker, a human-AI framework for verifying claims with large reasoning models. Experts bring domain knowledge that models lack. Yet models resist calibration to natural-language feedback in multi-turn dialogue. Co-FactChecker uses the model's thinking trace as a scratchpad shared by both sides. Expert feedback becomes targeted edits to that trace, sidestepping dialogue's shortcomings. Theory favors trace editing over dialogue. Automatic tests beat autonomous and collaborative baselines, and human judges prefer its clearer reasoning and verdicts.
arxiv-2604-13806: Kim and three colleagues make post-training quantization robust at ultra-low bit widths with DASH-Q. Hessian-based methods offset quantization error via cross-channel dependencies, but noisy curvature estimates from small calibration sets degrade them at low bits. DASH-Q uses a diagonal Hessian approximation with iterative weighted least squares, discarding noise-prone dependencies while preserving salient features. It improves zero-shot accuracy by about 7 percent on average and up to about 14 percent over the strongest baselines across five language models, staying robust on tiny calibration sets.
arxiv-2604-13906: Wang and colleagues repair videos damaged in storage or transfer without knowing in advance which parts are broken. Their metadata-guided diffusion model reads motion vectors and frame types to spot corruption, predicts masks for the damaged zones, and rebuilds them while keeping intact regions untouched. A final refinement step smooths the seams between restored and original footage.
arxiv-2604-14006: Frieze and colleagues bound the maximum degree and chromatic number of powers of sparse random graphs with high probability. In the sparse regime they pin the degree's growth and sandwich the chromatic number between degree-based bounds, with equality at the top end when the power is 2. For denser graphs they give a matching order of growth for the chromatic number in terms of average degree.
arxiv-2604-14106: Gao and Elayavalli establish an exactness result, named for Toeplitz, that lifts strong convergence into the general setting of C-star correspondences. The paper offers the result as a versatile machine, built to carry convergence claims across varied cases in that setting. It points to several applications without tying the result to any single example.
arxiv-2604-14306: Causio and nineteen colleagues describe EuropeMedQA, the first full multilingual and multimodal medical exam dataset drawn from official exams in Italy, France, Spain, and Portugal. Built on FAIR rules and SPIRIT-AI guide with strict care and an automated translation flow, the dataset supports side-by-side analysis. Current multimodal models face zero-shot prompting under strict constraints to test cross-lingual transfer and visual reasoning. The test aims to resist leaks, reflect clinical complexity in Europe, and foster more general medical AI.
arxiv-2604-14606: Rong, Wang, Wang, Gao, and Lu propose UniPASE, a generative model restoring speech from varied distortions at many rates. Its DeWavLM-Omni module, distilled from WavLM on a large multi-distortion dataset, turns degraded waveforms into clean, linguistically faithful phonetic representations with minimal hallucination. An Adapter builds rich acoustics for a neural vocoder. The vocoder rebuilds high-fidelity 16-kilohertz waveforms, lifted by a PostNet to 48 kilohertz and resampled to original rates. UniPASE matches or beats state-of-the-art models and powered the first-place URGENT 2026 entry on objective scores.
arxiv-2604-14906: Ivonina and Rydzewski study how drugs bind the SARS-CoV-2 RNA pseudoknot, which steers protein making through minus-one frame shifts. The knot takes threaded and unthreaded forms, and ligand effects on folding matter for design. With spectral map, they learn collective measures from knot runs with merafloxacin and two analogs. Energy maps show weakening varies by topology: threaded forms weaken in S2, the others in S1 and S3. Landscape shifts track drug potency, while proton state shifts motion within one topology, making natural protonation critical for models.
arxiv-2604-15506: Millstone and eight colleagues measure the inner disk fraction in M17, a star-forming region of about 6,000 solar masses and about 1 million years old, from deep VLT/HAWK-I imaging. Their survey finds 10,339 sources and a disk fraction of 28 plus or minus 2 percent. It is the first X-ray-selected value in M17 to include low-mass young stars. Disk fraction shows no link to UV flux inside M17, but regions with stronger UV fields run lower, implicating external photoevaporation.
arxiv-2604-15606: Lowe and five colleagues introduce Spec2Cov, an agentic framework that closes code coverage for digital hardware designs by generating test stimulus straight from specifications. It coordinates a language model with a hardware simulator, handling compile and simulation errors, reading coverage reports, and feeding results back for refinement. Across 26 designs it reaches 100 percent coverage on simple ones and up to 49 percent on complex ones.
arxiv-2604-15706: Wang and nine colleagues pick target pretraining data with Neuron-Activated Graph Ranking, a no-training, see-through scheme. Each target gets a set of high-hit nerve cells from any LLM, drawn as a graph, and data rank by graph likeness to target cases. The scheme lifts target pretraining by 4.9 percent over random picks and tops past bests by 5.3 points on HellaSwag. Knocking out its picked cells, just 0.12 percent of all, drops scores 23.5 percent, showing a thin working spine for learning target traits.
arxiv-2604-15806: Hu and Lan study the Turán number for double stars, the largest edge count a graph on n vertices can have without containing a given double star as a subgraph. For double stars with three leaves on one side of the central edge, they determine the extremal graphs. These turn out to have richer structure than the previously solved cases with one or two leaves. The work extends earlier results for the one-leaf and two-leaf cases.
arxiv-2604-16306: Treude, Poskitt, and Hoda argue that artifact evaluation should become a first-class part of peer review in software engineering. Reviewer time is tight, while generative AI now makes polished narratives cheap to produce. Attention spent on writing or positioning buys less signal about rigour. The substance that still needs expert checking, correct methods, sound analyses, and evidence-backed claims, often lives in artifacts such as code, data, and experimental infrastructure. They frame review as an attention allocation problem.
arxiv-2604-16406: Qiu and colleagues present PHASE, a self-play system for generating believable highway traffic to test self-driving cars safely. Each simulated driver gets its own vehicle profile and context, covering cars and articulated trucks within one policy, while training stabilizes play through early stopping of hopeless states and fault-aware collision credit. Trained only on synthetic data, the system transferred without retraining to 512 unseen real high-interaction scenarios, succeeding in about 96 percent of them. Its trajectories also looked more realistic than a standard traffic model.
arxiv-2604-16606: Mohammad and Bayazıt present SafeLM, a single safety framework for shared language models. It covers privacy, security, false claims and hostile attacks at once. SafeLM trains models across sites with encrypted gradient methods for privacy. It adds attack defenses, grounded decoding against made-up claims, and robust averaging that limits rebuild quality. On factuality, toxicity and membership tests, it spots 98.0 percent of harmful content. It cuts traffic by 96.9 percent and drops inversion signal from 31.7 decibels to 15.1 decibels.
arxiv-2604-16706: Gurram audits evaluation of tool-using agents with the bench holding traces from thirteen agents across four domains. Substring judging matches human labels only near chance, while a trio is fair and a GPT-4o-mini judge is strongest. Two raters reach high agreement. Under judging, a parameter error leads to a wrong final answer about six times in ten, for proprietary and open-weight models alike. Spotting corrupted inputs and bouncing back from them are independent skills. Agents fake tool executions, and a runtime filter cuts such hallucination.
arxiv-2604-16906: Wu and three colleagues combine Nesterov momentum with quantized messages to solve distributed optimization under tight bandwidth. Momentum speeds the search by looking ahead along the descent direction, while quantization squeezes each message down. Their QANM algorithm narrows the gap to a neighborhood of the optimum at a linear rate on sensor-fusion tests, with the fastest early error drop among the methods compared.
arxiv-2604-17006: Chatzimarkou and Dimakis define a conformal limit for Nakajima quiver varieties, building on earlier Higgs-bundle work. They prove it really is the limit of a one-setting family inside one such variety, yielding a biholomorphic map between holomorphic Lagrangian submanifolds spanning two of them. The paper closes by noting the Simpson-conjecture analogue for the completeness of those surfaces.
arxiv-2604-17106: Brindise, Langbort, and Ornik track progress through multi-stage tasks for reinforcement-learning agents facing non-Markovian objectives. Given a finite linear temporal logic specification, their tracking vector updates each step, labeling each specification status true, false, or open for indeterminate cases. Applied to a formula tree, the vector encodes how a task unfolds over a trajectory, supporting new performance metrics, diverse exploration, and reward shaping.
arxiv-2604-17206: Chen presents SciDraw-6K, a curated set of 6,291 scientific illustrations made by Google Gemini image models, each paired with prompts in eleven languages. The images span eight fields — biomedical, chemistry, materials, electronics, environment, AI systems, physics, and a long other tail — and lean on schematic diagrams, mechanism figures, contents graphics, and conceptual posters. Chen describes the build pipeline, reports dataset statistics, and documents its use in a public drawing service. The set is released to support multilingual text-to-image research and prompt studies.
arxiv-2604-17306: Li and a large team review the first NTIRE 2026 contest for sharpening real phone photos, where entries had to quadruple resolution despite unknown damage to the original image. The contest drew 108 entrants, with 16 teams earning a valid final score, judged on picture quality plus speed on mobile hardware. The paper sums up the winning designs and the trends they set for fast, high-quality photo enhancement on phones.
arxiv-2604-17906: Junyoung Kim and seven colleagues frame passage retrieval as a budget-limited global search, since large language models score relevance well but cost too much to run everywhere. Their BAGEL framework spreads sparse model scores across the embedding space using one Gaussian process per query. It then picks passages to score by balancing trusted regions against uncertain ones. Across four benchmark datasets and two model backbones, BAGEL beats reranking methods under the same model budget on every dataset.
arxiv-2604-18006: Huchet and two colleagues describe QUBIC, a bolometer interferometer that watches sky polarization at millimetre waves to hunt primordial B-modes in the cosmic microwave background. Pairing bolometer power with known interferometry traits, it performs spectral imaging, getting space and spectrum data at once. That eases splitting sky parts with tricky spectra and better cleaning of foregrounds. The team builds three map methods, using frequency, component, and neural network ways, and reports that QUBIC resumed sky work in early March, including Moon work during commissioning.
arxiv-2604-18206: Lu, Jiang, Qian, and Zhou design a control system for using prompt-injected memory without retraining a model. Retrieved memory helps only when applied in the right state, so the system decides when to run a second memory-assisted pass and when to trust it. Uncertainty routing, confidence checks, and evidence-based upkeep of the memory bank govern the process. Under matched controls, arithmetic scores rise by 7 points on SVAMP and about 8 on ASDiv, with smaller gains on question-answering and agent tasks.
arxiv-2604-18506: Ferrer-Sánchez and four colleagues present a physics-guided method for boosting quantum Fisher information in many-body systems, made hard by order effects, tricky controls, and runaway growth. Their approach joins a tunable PINN with a Magnus-series treatment of ordered change, reading the slow-change gauge field and timing while keeping Euler-Lagrange form. Applied to driven spin systems up to six qubits, it beats standard Euler-Lagrange answers, with scaled QFI, good closeness, and balance. Learning the timing usually gives an edge.
arxiv-2604-19106: Ma and five colleagues ask how and when extreme-edge networks should run on AI Engines versus programmable logic. Uses demand small batches and on-chip weights under latency and throughput limits. Spatial dataflow suits small networks but fails to scale, while AI Engines offer dense compute and on-chip memory but differ from programmable logic in architecture. A latency-adjusted equivalence metric shows when AI Engines win. They add dataflow optimizations for low-latency inference and deploy networks on AI Engines that cannot fit on programmable logic with hlsml.
arxiv-2604-19206: Dong and seven colleagues propose a post-hoc flag for false negatives in defect networks. Trusting trained outputs is often unavoidable; one missed error can prove fatal. Their core idea contrasts class-specific and class-agnostic heatmaps, using their overlap gap as a score. Adversarial enhancement widens disparity. On two industrial benchmarks, it spots false negatives, reaching 100 percent recall with enhancement, at a cost to true negatives. It backs a data, model, explanation, output paradigm instead of the usual systems.
arxiv-2604-19306: Gurung and Mukhopadhyay analyze instabilities of an anti-de Sitter black hole in an Einstein-Maxwell theory from five-dimensional supergravity. A gauge Chern-Simons term drives instability, and its coupling strength hits the threshold for instability, seen near the horizon and in normal-mode analysis. Derivative terms up to fourth order bring in a mixed gauge-gravitational Chern-Simons term. With both terms, instability that varies with momentum appears below a critical temperature, giving a bell-curve phase diagram pointing to a spatially modulated solution.
arxiv-2604-19406: Li and colleagues propose HP-Edit, a human-preference post-training tool for image editing, with RealPref-50K, a dataset across eight common tasks. Common editing relies on generative diffusion models, and methods like Diffusion-DPO and Flow-GRPO have improved generation quality. Yet applying human-feedback reinforcement learning to diffusion-based editing remains largely unexplored, for lack of scalable preference datasets and tools for diverse needs. HP-Edit uses little human-preference scoring data and a pretrained visual large language model to build preference-aligned editing.
arxiv-2604-19506: Ruihong ma and Engui Fan investigate the Cauchy problem for the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a finite-genus algebro-geometric background. Initial data approach finite-genus algebro-geometric quasi-periodic solutions at both infinities. Using the Riemann-Hilbert approach combined with the Deift-Zhou nonlinear steepest descent method, they analyze the long-time asymptotic behavior of solutions. The analysis distinguishes two cases based on the genus of the background solution, tracking how the asymptotic picture changes between them.
arxiv-2604-19606: Xia and colleagues introduce AblateCell, a reproduce-then-ablate agent for virtual cell repositories. Ablations are essential for tracing gains in AI Virtual Cells. Yet they are rarely done, because cell stores are under-standard and tightly coupled to domain data and formats. Recent coding agents translate ideas into code but stop there, lacking a checker that reproduces strong benchmarks and tests which parts truly matter. It first reruns published baselines end-to-end, setting up workspaces on its own and redoing official tests with open records.
arxiv-2604-19706: Scholtens, Seri, Waalkens, and van de Weygaert develop linear perturbation theory for general Bianchi models, anisotropic yet homogeneous spacetimes that drop cosmic isotropy while keeping homogeneity. The standard cosmological model faces a growing pile of challenging findings, prompting changes to its picture. Knowing how Bianchi perturbations behave, including which wavemodes are allowed, helps reveal cosmological signatures such as CMBs and enables comparison with data and the standard model.
arxiv-2604-19806: Mollahosseini, Dupty, and Lee explore using molecular dynamics data to improve force fields for 3D molecular systems, a core challenge for AI in science. Strong data-thrifty networks now predict atomic energies and forces from single atomic configurations, but they rarely exploit the data making process itself. Such runs yield time-ordered paths of atomic positions whose energy fluctuates as they explore the potential energy surface. They do not slowly lower energy toward a minimum as geometry relaxations do.
arxiv-2604-20006: Uddin and four colleagues introduce Memora, a benchmark for long-term memory in personalized agents over weeks to months of chats. Past benchmarks mostly test fact retrieval, missing buildup over time and frequent updates. Memora covers remembering, reasoning, and recommending, with grounding checks and human review. A new metric, Forgetting-Aware Memory Accuracy, penalizes reliance on outdated memory, and tests show agents often reuse invalid memories despite small gains from memory agents.
arxiv-2604-20106: Shaikh, Patra, and Kumar prove monochromatic patterns near zero, extending a recent result of Goswami on finite colorings. Where Goswami showed the set a, b, their product, and b times a-plus-one is monochromatic for colorings of the natural numbers, the authors show the same pattern is monochromatic near zero. Near zero means working in dense subsemigroups of positive reals, with a and b chosen as small as desired. They also show the pattern x, y, their sum, and y divided by x is partition regular near zero.
arxiv-2604-20206: Tagkopoulos and three colleagues predict food taste from ingredients by treating recipes as composite materials. Hashin-Shtrikman and Reuss-Voigt bounds, borrowed from elastic moduli, cover five tastes across 70 recipes with 209 ingredient references and panel ground truth. The bounds under-predict: 77 percent of actual values exceed the upper bound, from 26 percent for bitterness to 97 percent for saltiness. Eight chemistry-proxy features cut mean absolute error by 27 to 62 percent on four tastes, using only ten interpretable features. Inverse design then recovers formulations matching target taste profiles.
arxiv-2604-20406: Barzykin and Ciceri study over the counter bond market making with quadratic stock penalty and a size weighted hit ratio target. Dualizing the hit ratio term keeps the reduced Hamilton Jacobi Bellman equation separable, yielding exact optimal controls from inverse fill chances and the Hamiltonian derivative. A quadratic Bergault style approximation gives a Riccati equation for stock curvature, keeping the exact quote map. Linearized, it splits quotes into riskless spread, stock risk correction, and hit ratio correction for multi bond and client tier cases.
arxiv-2604-20606: Ibrahim, Liu, and Wang compare six discretization schemes inside Vision Mamba, a state space model that uses zero-order hold, treating inputs as constant between samples, which weakens temporal fidelity in dynamic settings. The schemes are ZOH, FOH, BIL, POL, HOH, and RK4. Across classification, segmentation, and detection, polynomial interpolation and higher-order hold gain most accuracy at higher cost. Bilinear gives gains over zero-order hold with extra overhead, the best trade-off, and the authors recommend it as the baseline for state space vision models.
arxiv-2604-20706: Shao, Xia, and Zhao propose QuanForge, a mutation testing tool for quantum neural networks. Testing quantum neural networks remains new ground because of complex dynamics, limited clarity, and randomness in operators and measurements. QuanForge adds statistical mutation killing for a more reliable criterion. It uses nine post-training mutation operators at gate and parameter levels. A mutant generation plan yields strong mutants for robust and reliable mutation analysis. Tests show QuanForge tells test suites apart and finds weak circuit regions. The team also checks results under simulated noisy conditions.
arxiv-2604-20806: Chen, Luan, Wu, Yu, Yang, Li, Tong, Feng, Qin, and Che present OMIBench, a benchmark for Olympiad-level reasoning when the evidence is distributed over images. Its problems come from biology, chemistry, mathematics, and physics Olympiads, with annotated rationales and protocols for exact and semantic matching. Across experiments, they see clear performance gaps in existing models. Still, top large vision-language models like Gemini-3-Pro reach only about 50 percent on OMIBench. That makes OMIBench a tool for studying and improving multi-image reasoning.
arxiv-2604-21106: Kristian Schwethelm, Daniel Rueckert, and Georgios Kaissis price a single loop of a transformer block in terms of fresh parameters. Sweeping loop counts at matched depth, they fit a scaling law whose exponent lands at 0.46, halfway between a loop adding nothing and a loop matching new blocks. A four-loop 410M model thus matches a 580M plain model yet costs as much to train as a 1B one, and the exponent also exposes weak loop training and genuine gains.
arxiv-2604-21706: Muller, Ortiz, and Roberts scale a training-free method for grading dysarthria, a speech disorder. They apply it to 3,374 speakers across 12 languages and five causes, including Parkinson's disease, cerebral palsy, ALS, Down syndrome, and stroke. Degradation profiles differ by cause at group level and keep a stable shape across languages, though absolute severity still needs calibration within each corpus. All six speech backbones tested give consistent severity gradients.
arxiv-2604-21806: Li and five colleagues tackle image retrieval with several changes at once, not just one simple edit. Existing setups cover too few salient changes, causing missed entities and mismatched clauses. The team builds two instruction-rich multi-modification datasets, M-FashionIQ and M-CIRR. They also propose TEMA, a text-oriented entity mapping architecture for multi-modification queries that still handles simple ones. On four benchmarks, TEMA wins in both original and multi-modification settings while balancing accuracy and efficiency.
arxiv-2604-22106: Stryker proves the stable 2-systole stays uniformly bounded over Riemannian metrics with scalar curvature at least one, for closed spin 2-essential manifolds. In plain terms, a size measure for two-dimensional cycles cannot blow up once curvature has a positive floor. That class includes S² × S², S² × Tⁿ, and complex projective space CP^{2n+1}.
arxiv-2604-22206: Fang and Zhang study inner gradient regularity for nonlocal double phase problems, a class of equations with two growth regimes. They show the solution gradient is Hölder continuous, when the gap between two key products is small enough. The proof assumes Lipschitz continuity of the varying coefficient. Solution Lipschitz smoothness is also shown under weaker assumptions on that coefficient. Their work gives a nonlocal version of classical theory and settles a higher smoothness question raised in 2019.
arxiv-2604-22406: Baldock and three colleagues propose near-deterministic loading of optical tweezer arrays, traps that hold atoms and molecules in defect-free patterns. Array size is limited by initial loading fractions, typically 50 percent for atoms and 35 percent for molecules. Their scheme protects trapped particles with a repulsive barrier, enabling multiple loading cycles. Collision-limited lifetimes in protected tweezers exceed one second, giving filling fractions over 80 percent after four cycles. Combined with rearrangement techniques, the approach enables efficient unity filling and a scalable path to larger quantum technology platforms.
arxiv-2604-23106: Raghavan and Mallick present MOSAIC, a training-free multi-agent framework for code building without input-output test cases. Existing systems rely on run feedback and repeat improvement with test cases, which fails for science workflows lacking test cases, since creating them means solving the problem itself. Instead, MOSAIC uses student-teacher distillation grounded in examples and ordered problem breakdowns. A Consolidated Context Window keeps reasoning steady across agents, curbing hallucinations across chained tasks. SciCode tests show better accuracy, executability, and number precision over others with lightweight models.
arxiv-2604-23306: Hale and three colleagues extend optimal-node theory for summation-by-parts operators from polynomial spaces to general function spaces. Gauss-Lobatto nodes and weights are optimal for closed SBP formulations on polynomial spaces, yielding minimal-dimension operators. The same principle now holds generally: an associated Gauss-Lobatto quadrature supplies optimal nodes and weights for the SBP formulation. They give an algorithm for computing these rules, show accuracy and efficiency across function spaces, and apply them to initial boundary value problems.
arxiv-2604-23406: Zerhoudi, Roegiest, and Granitzer present IIRSim Studio, a web workbench for user simulation in information search. Existing kits are code-centric libraries needing heavy setup, limiting uptake, while the gap is infrastructure linking design, execution, and sharing. The workbench offers visual pipeline building for all users, plus component versioning and sharing through Git-backed storage. A provenance model of experiment bundles and templates clarifies replication scope, and a shared-task workflow is shown by rerunning a Sim4IA micro-task. It ships hosted and containerised.
arxiv-2604-23506: Uzner and Neufeld develop a theory of high harmonic generation in layered solids that includes hopping of electrons between layers, an effect usually ignored when the laser points within the layers. Strong enough interlayer coupling changes the emitted harmonics' angular and ellipticity patterns, they show, and the yields follow a fourth-order polynomial in the coupling. The work points to experiments that probe interlayer coupling optically.
arxiv-2604-23706: Kukučka and colleagues automate Nancy scoring of ulcerative colitis tissue slides from whole-slide images. Their method learns from case- and slide-level labels alone, using a weakly supervised multiple-instance approach. It targets neutrophilic activity and Nancy-low versus high groups across a multicentre biopsy set. Encoder choice and image detail matter greatly, and a simple ensemble rule improves full five-grade scores.
arxiv-2604-23806: De closes the training loop for thermodynamic diffusion models on an analog substrate, without routing gradients through a digital accelerator. Equilibrium propagation applied to the bilinear energy gives an unbiased estimate of the denoising score-matching gradient at zero nudge, with a sharp bias bound for finite nudging. Symmetric nudging improves the leading bias order, and end-to-end accounting projects an energy advantage of thousands of times per training step over GPUs.
arxiv-2604-23906: Sungkawichai and Trakulthongchai extend the Lonely Runner Conjecture, which claims for any speeds, some time leaves every runner at least one over k plus one from the nearest integer. They refine Rosenfeld and the second author's method with sieving and a polynomial argument. This proves it for speeds congruent to one through k modulo a prime. This needs k plus one and the prime both odd primes above k squared plus k. They give a computer-assisted proof for k equal to ten, eleven, and twelve, extending past nine.
arxiv-2604-24406: Lee, Yang, and Lizana study first-passage dynamics in a many-particle system where all particles reset to the rightmost spot. Simulations of particles drifting in a confining potential with an absorbing boundary track two arrivals: first and median group-hitting times. Resetting yields broad distributions with long plateaus spanning several orders of magnitude. Plateaus lengthen as resetting rates rise, with mean group-hitting times growing fast. First-passage dynamics grow more heterogeneous, so most probable and mean hitting times split widely, leaving no single time scale.
arxiv-2604-24506: Golkar and 30 colleagues present MIMIC, a generative model that reads many sides of a biomolecule at once. It covers DNA and protein sequence, shape, regulation, and cell context. Its split encoder-decoder can fill in missing parts of a molecular state from whatever parts are seen, and joint training beats sequence-only inputs on RNA and protein tasks. The same model also designs fixes for a faulty blood-gene splice site and new protein binders, showing one system can predict and design together.
arxiv-2604-24806: Guo and colleagues present versioned late materialization for ultra-long sequence training in recommendation systems. The Fat Row paradigm pre-materializes user histories into every training example, creating a storage and input-output wall as data redundancy grows. Their paradigm stores histories once in a fixed, locked tier and rebuilds sequences on demand via lightweight pointers. A split protocol keeps online-to-offline consistency and prevents future leakage across streaming and batch training. On production recommendation models, it cuts data system use while enabling longer sequences and gains.
arxiv-2604-25506: Sahu and five colleagues ask whether LLMs can reason well about net systems design. They find LLMs cannot: plausible plans miss constraints, hold wrong beliefs, and stick to known patterns. Checking by trial runs is often far too costly, sometimes not doable. To fill this gap, they present Kepler, joining expert rules with SMT tuning. Kepler turns needs, clashes, and trade-offs into rules, and builds designs. It works at a high level, uses rules-of-thumb, and explains calls. Kepler finds links missed by LLMs and backs orderly search.
arxiv-2604-25606: Hu and two colleagues propose C-PINN, a physics-informed neural network frame built on the Cordès condition for linear and fully nonlinear equations in non-divergence form. Building the operator structure into the loss function improves training stability and solution accuracy. The frame extends to Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman and Monge-Ampère equations for optimal transport. Tests show the method is effective and robust, including on high-dimensional problems. Its broad scope offers wide interest.
arxiv-2604-25906: Alvarez and Zhai study how to make any document collection navigable, like the Web, without hand-built hyperlinks. Hyperlinks enable flexible movement between pages, but manual links miss a corpus's implicit semantic structure. The authors formalize the problem as building a Hypergraph of Text, then propose several construction methods. They also introduce effort ratio, a metric for judging the structural quality of a built hypergraph. Experiments show even simple TF-IDF baselines can match language-model methods on effort ratio.
arxiv-2604-26006: Gurian and six colleagues build an analytical Population III star formation model from the cosmological background to protostellar disk fragmentation. The approach joins models across scales: environment to halo, halo to cloud, cloud to fragmenting disk. Alone and jointly, the models match leading simulations while staying cheap and clear. Varying Lyman-Werner flux shifts halo-scale efficiency across more than two orders of magnitude, from about 10^-3 to about one half. At cloud scale, efficiency stays at or above one fifth, so unstable clouds convert well into Population III stars.
arxiv-2604-26206: Cacioli follows a pilot finding: a prompted model sandbags through position collapse, not answer dodging. The follow-up tests fixed order against a position policy, shuffling option order across thousands of items and tens of thousands of trials. The planned same-letter diagnostic did not confirm fixed place tracking. Checks revealed a soft spread attractor: under sandbagging, response positions stayed stable under content turns. Accuracy spiked at the top position and fell elsewhere; a second model was a non-compliant null control.
arxiv-2604-26506: Xin and seven colleagues built SafeReview, a shield for LLM-based peer review against hidden prompts planted in papers. Attackers plant instructions to sway verdicts, threatening scholarly honesty as language models join review. SafeReview trains an attacker maker and a defender side by side. The maker crafts ever sharper injections, while the defender learns from preference data to keep verdicts steady between clean and attacked papers. Tests showed tougher defense, better-kept rankings, and carry-over across attacker designs.
arxiv-2604-26606: Martínez-Sebastián and four colleagues measured nitrogen abundances in 117 Galactic O-type stars to separate binary-interaction products from effectively single stars. For helium-normal stars, nitrogen peaks slightly above birth values and extends to 8.4 dex, matching single-star models with efficient mixing and modest rotation. Helium-rich stars split into two peaks, none matching single-star predictions, pointing to binary origins. Helium-normal giants of luminosity class III, however, show less nitrogen than mixing models predict, so rotation alone cannot explain the pattern.
arxiv-2604-26706: Banerjee bounds the leakage of confidence sets after black-box selection, where the reported object is chosen by a preliminary search rather than fixed in advance. Classical selective inference works best when the search forms an explicit selection event, but many searches are opaque. The note shows selected-target noncoverage stays within nominal noncoverage plus a distance measure comparing the data's marginal law with its law given the selected object. At once, a mutual-information bound follows, and sample splitting emerges as the zero-leakage case.
arxiv-2604-27306: Zerhoudi, Granitzer, and Mitrovic propose NuggetIndex, a governed atomic search system for maintainable retrieval-augmented generation. Standard search-aided systems are judged by fact-based metrics yet retrieve passages or static claims. That unit mismatch hinders maintenance as corpora evolve and misses old facts or source disputes. NuggetIndex stores atomic information units, called nuggets, as managed records linked to evidence with a time span and a life state. Filtering invalid or retired nuggets before ranking prevents outdated information from entering results.
arxiv-2604-27606: Bin Habib and three colleagues present ZAYAN, a self-supervised contrastive framework for tabular remote sensing data. ZAYAN learns at the feature level rather than the sample level, needing no explicit anchors and no class labels, while building a disentangled, redundancy-minimized embedding space. It pairs a pretraining module, ZAYAN-CL, with a Transformer, ZAYAN-T, for downstream classification. Across eight data sets, ZAYAN beats tabular deep learning baselines, holding up under label scarcity and distribution shift.
arxiv-2604-28106: Méndez and Semino ask why zinc-imidazolate frameworks end up as one crystal form rather than another. Their self-assembly simulations, sorted by neural nets, show early clusters and later glassy middles already vary with the final form. Choice of form thus seems set at the early cluster stage, well before final crystals form.
arxiv-2605-00006:
Mrinal Kanti Roychowdhury gives an explicit study of optimal quantization on a sphere, the problem of placing a limited set of points so they best represent the whole surface. Working with geodesic distance on the unit sphere, he analyzes three highly symmetric discrete models in full analytic detail. The aim is benchmark cases where the optimal answer can be written in closed form rather than only computed.

The models place points evenly on the equator, on two small circles at matched latitudes north and south, and on a single small circle. For each, he derives the optimal quantizers and mean-square errors, proving that optimal cells form unbroken arcs with midpoint representatives. Curvature is shown to reduce distortion on a single circle while keeping the standard decay rate. The results clarify how curvature changes quantization on curved spaces.
arxiv-2605-00406:
Huw Price proposes a deflationary reading of the famous Bell correlations in quantum physics. Experiments inspired by John Stewart Bell's work show linked particles behaving in ways widely taken to prove the world is nonlocal. That reading sits in tension with relativity, unless realism about an independent world is abandoned. Price points to a familiar statistical effect instead: selection bias.

How a sample is selected from a larger population can create correlations between unrelated variables, or hide real ones, and preselection through preparation of the starting state is a known source. Price argues that the selection in standard two-particle Bell experiments is exactly such a preselection, and that it has been overlooked in this setting. On his account, the correlations are selection artefacts, and neither relativity nor realism needs to fall.
arxiv-2605-00506:
Tom Utting, Mario Giulianelli, and Arabella Sinclair model how speakers choose what to say in dialogue as a cost-sensitive choice among alternatives. Some alternatives serve the speaker's fixed goal, while others are merely plausible in context. By separating the two sets, the authors can read the same cost measure as speaker-oriented or listener-oriented, and ask which cost speakers actually seem to minimize.

They generate both kinds of alternative sets with language models, then test production choices in open-ended dialogue under strict and probabilistic versions of cost minimization. Minimizing surprisal, roughly how unexpected an utterance is, relative to the goal-directed alternatives gave the strongest account of what people said. Rival costs based on even information spread or on length predicted more weakly and less consistently. The study offers alternative-conditioned optimization as a principled frame for studying the pressures that shape natural speech.
arxiv-2605-00606:
Surendra Kumar Gour and Malay K. Nandy propose a route to the universe's matter-antimatter imbalance that needs no supersymmetry. Their engine is a complex scalar field whose own coupling terms plainly break a global symmetry. Three sample forms are studied, each making tangled source terms in the field's rules of motion.

Starting from a fully even start, those source terms build a real charge density: the asymmetry is created by the motion, not inserted. At late times the density falls in just the way needed to leave a constant baryon-to-photon ratio, a freeze-in by motion. One family of potentials works across a wide range of scalar masses. Another needs masses too light to be believed. A third gives an asymmetry that does not depend on the mass at all. If the charge passes well to plain matter, the route can match what is observed.
arxiv-2605-01206:
Ryoi Ohashi, Hiroki Isobe, Ryota Nakai, and Kentaro Nomura study tunneling duality in fractional quantum Hall states, focusing on the Read-Rezayi state. Point-contact geometries allow either quasi-particles or electrons to tunnel, and the two descriptions should be dual. Treating non-Abelian edge operators requires new tools, so the authors introduce a phase-shift instanton that incorporates phase factors from primary fields into the instanton gas framework.

Using that method, they reformulate the Moore-Read duality and obtain an explicit dual description for the three-level Read-Rezayi state. Quasi-particle tunneling phase shifts map strong quasi-particle tunneling to weak electron tunneling. In the strong-coupling regime, nonlinear conductance is evaluated analytically and universally follows a quartic voltage scaling for both states, reflecting a topological constraint on the tunneling particle.
arxiv-2605-01306:
Mohamed Sy's doctoral dissertation joins laser spectroscopy, a method that reads gases from the light they absorb, with machine learning to spot many gas species at once in harsh settings. Standard tools fail when spectra overlap, noise is high, or some species in the mix are unknown.

Sy tests five linked tools. A denoising network cleans shock-tube signals from fast fuel breakdown tests. One framework flags unknown species without full calibration, and a blind method rebuilds both amounts and spectra from mixed data alone, checked on blends of up to eight gases. A derivative-based step pulls out weak species hidden under broad ones. A final tool gives certified labels for organic vapors. Each method is checked in real experiments, pointing toward fast, sturdy gas sensing for engines, air monitoring, and plant safety.
arxiv-2605-01406:
Ayaka Murakami and Kouichi Takemura find closed-form special solutions of the q-Heun equation, a difference equation that plays the role for q-series that Heun's equation plays for ordinary differential equations. Exact solutions of such equations are rare and prized, since they anchor both theory and computation.

The pair start from solutions of polynomial type, answers that end after finitely many terms. Applying q-integral transformations, operations that act like integration in the q-world, they turn those seeds into new solutions of the same equation. Each new answer is written as a finite sum of q-hypergeometric functions, the q-versions of the classic special functions. The construction adds to the short list of cases where the q-Heun equation can be solved in named functions, a step toward a fuller map of its solution space.
arxiv-2605-01506:
Detao Bai and six co-authors build one encoder that takes in sight and sound together, the way people do. Current omni-modal models use separate encoders and a lopsided diet. Video is sampled at a frame or two per second against audio many times denser, so motion detail and cross-sense timing are lost.

Their OmniEncoder runs a single Transformer backbone that embeds both streams at a matched 25 frames per second in one shared space. Three devices make it work: a token template that tags what is what, a position scheme tuned for mixed streams, and a shifting time window that keeps cost sane. Against a strong split-encoder baseline on the same token budget, the unified model gains a lot on smooth visual tasks. Those tasks include sign language and fine sports actions, and the model holds its own on audio-visual tests.
arxiv-2605-01706:
Ghazal Danaee and four co-authors make active learning for brain scans fair as well as cheap. Labeling medical images costs expert hours, so active learning picks the most useful scans to label next; standard picks chase raw uncertainty and can quietly leave one demographic group badly segmented.

Their weighted entropy strategy bends the uncertainty score by each group's current performance on the labeled set, so weak groups get labeled first. A masked, scaled entropy, confined to the target region, keeps organ size differences from faking uncertainty. On synthetic brain images with a planted bias in one structure, a 3D U-Net is trained under several strategies. The fairness-aware picks cut group disparity sharply against both random and standard sampling, from balanced and lopsided starts alike. The authors count the study among the first on fair active learning for segmentation.
arxiv-2605-02106:
Terry Dorsey and Kevin Huggins argue that AI should be built around memory, not just model weights. Current systems do well through large models, retrieval, and static training sets. Yet they struggle to keep a lasting record of past work. They also struggle to place that record in time, track its source, or explain it.

Their Dynamic Gist-Based Memory Model treats past experience as a clear, lasting structure. A user can inspect that structure and read it in new ways over time. Memory becomes a core base for reasoning, not a side store. The paper lays out that shift and describes how gist-based records change as new interactions arrive.
arxiv-2605-02306:
Chang Liu and colleagues revisit Gaussian filtering for state estimation, using information geometry as the lens. Exact Bayesian filtering works only for linear Gaussian systems. Nonlinear cases rely on approximations, such as extended and unscented Kalman filters. The tutorial frames prediction and update as inference over state distributions.

Their new filter refines the mean and covariance step by step. It uses natural gradient descent on the manifold of Gaussian laws. That respects the family's own geometry and keeps the covariance positive definite. The paper serves as a tutorial as well as a method paper. It highlights basic questions about Gaussian filtering that the geometric view makes clear.
arxiv-2605-02406:
Benjamin Kraus and colleagues build an ultra-stable, transportable ultraviolet laser for an aluminium quantum logic clock. Optical clocks need such a laser to probe a narrow clock transition precisely. Their system reaches a fractional frequency instability near two parts in ten thousand trillion, using an ultra-stable cavity with crystalline mirror coatings and a frequency quadrupling chain of two single-pass doubling stages.

Acceleration sensitivity, measured on all three axes, is among the lowest recorded for transportable systems. A further trick partly cancels photo-thermal noise against photo-birefringence noise. That cancellation mitigates noise from optical power fluctuations inside the cavity at lower Fourier frequencies, a key limit for portable clock lasers that must leave the lab.
arxiv-2605-03006:
Valentin O. Deliyski, Galin N. Gyulchev, Daniela D. Doneva, Petya G. Nedkova, and Stoytcho S. Yazadjiev model direct images of thin disks around rotating black holes with added scalar hair. A massive scalar field changes the paths of light near the horizon, so it should also change the pattern of polarized light from the disk.

Their main finding is a shift in the twist of the polarization vector, which was largest for the least scalarized cases they studied. That result points to local path effects, not total field strength. With vertical fields at steep viewing angles, the twist direction can also flip.
arxiv-2605-03306:
John M. Hitchcock shows that languages needing exponential-size circuits are typical inside symmetric exponential time, in the resource-bounded category sense. Category here measures largeness through a game, extending classic results that placed the same circuit class as small inside a larger space class.

Hitchcock defines smallness against single-valued strategies for the symmetric class and turns a known range avoidance algorithm into a winning game strategy. That makes the exponential circuit class meager there, so its complement, languages that truly need huge circuits, is comeager and thus typical. The note ties circuit lower bounds to descriptive largeness.
arxiv-2605-03406:
Dae Woong Ham, Stefanus Jasin, and Xuejun Zhao ask how researchers should decide when a sequential hypothesis test has seen enough evidence to reject. Group sequential tests check the same hypotheses at several stages as data arrive, spending a type-1 error budget across checks. Classical spending rules are valid, but which is fastest was unclear.

The authors optimize the rejection criterion directly, under the same error controls, using sample average approximation combined with mixed-integer linear programming. Their optimal approach dominates classical Lan-DeMets, Pocock, and O'Brien-Fleming procedures in their comparisons. A striking pattern emerges: optimal solutions usually spend the error budget aggressively early. They also apply the method to a recent empirical study.
arxiv-2605-04206:
Katja Froehlich and five co-authors present a way to find dryland sites where native plants might regrow and survive without long-term watering. Their case study is Saudi Arabia, where many past planting efforts have relied on costly irrigation in a water-scarce land.

Using climate records, satellite data, and expert-chosen reference sites, they build a climate score and map it across the country. Sites where the climate looks good but plants are still sparse are flagged. The screening then narrows the search to thirteen priority places. Nearby healthy ecosystems serve as targets for what regrowth could reach.
arxiv-2605-04306:
Fritz Lekschas and Nezar Abdennur present a tool for exploring high-dimensional data by touring through two-dimensional views of it. Any single flat view loses information, so tours animate a path through many views, but older tools limit how freely a user can steer that path.

Their interface mixes preview images, smooth scrubbing along paths between views, direct manual control, and a wandering automatic tour in one place. It renders millions of points with graphics hardware, runs in a web browser, and works with Python and JavaScript. They show it on text, image, and single-cell data.
arxiv-2605-04406:
Tushar Das and three co-authors propose a learnable geometry for the symmetric positive definite matrices that appear throughout machine learning, from covariance data to medical imaging. Networks using these matrices have relied on fixed geometric rules, much like hand-crafted features, which limits what they can express.

Their metric is built from a spline-based transformation that is constrained to stay monotone, avoiding the folding and gradient failures of looser designs. Two versions, acting on spectra or on a matrix factorisation, can approximate any suitable transformation and contain earlier pullback metrics as special cases. The result is a geometry that adapts to data instead of being chosen in advance.
arxiv-2605-04606:
Yichen Li, Qiankun Liu, and Ying Fu propose an unsupervised object detector that knows what categories it is finding, without using any hand-labelled training data. One-shot detectors need labelled examples, while general unsupervised methods propose boxes but cannot say what kind of object each box contains.

Their method uses unlabelled reference images. A similarity score between a predicted object and the references guides learning. It pushes the model toward features tied to each class, through a loss designed for that purpose. The same framework can also run in a category-blind mode when no references are available. Number-based and visual tests on both modes show the approach works. It narrows the gap between label-free detection and labelled-data accuracy.
arxiv-2605-05106:
Lakshita Jindal and Kavita Jain study how defects correlate with each other when a quantum system is driven across a phase transition in finite time. The Kibble-Zurek mechanism predicts average defect counts from the slowing dynamics near the critical point. Correlations between defects, described here as kink-kink correlations, need more than that basic picture.

Working with the one-dimensional transverse-field Ising model under an algebraic quench, the pair examine the correlation at the end of the drive. For faster-than-linear quenches the correlator depends only on the Kibble-Zurek length, while slower quenches bring in an extra length scale from phase differences between low-energy modes. The work tests which features of earlier linear-quench results are universal.
arxiv-2605-05206:
Xiaoyu Wu and five co-authors study outlier tokens in diffusion transformers used for image generation, a few tokens with unusually large values that attract heavy attention while carrying little local information. The phenomenon was known in vision transformers but not in generative models. The authors find it in both the encoder and the denoising transformer of modern pipelines.

Simply masking the large tokens does not help, suggesting the real problem is corrupted local patch meaning rather than extreme values alone. Their Dual-Stage Registers add register tokens at both stages, trained where possible and created at test time otherwise. Across image benchmarks the intervention reduced outlier artefacts and improved generation quality.
arxiv-2605-05606:
Many real systems are only glimpsed through sparse, noisy measurements. Yu Wang and Arnab Ganguly infer the hidden paths and parameters of stochastic differential equations from such data. Classical smoothing methods suffer from path degeneracy and scale poorly, so the authors take a variational route.

They describe the posterior equation through a backward score, a gradient field defined by a Kolmogorov equation, and learn it with neural networks. A likelihood objective then tunes the model parameters in an EM-style loop. On nonlinear test systems, the method stayed accurate with very few observations and scaled better than Markov chain Monte Carlo.
arxiv-2605-05806:
Retrieval-augmented generation bolts a search engine onto a language model, and the seam between them causes mismatches. Elad Hoffer and six co-authors ask whether an attention-based model can retrieve from its own representations instead. Their framework, INTRA, lets decoder attention score pre-encoded evidence chunks and reuse them directly as context.

Retrieval and generation become one mechanism, and context encoding is amortized across queries. On question-answering benchmarks, INTRA beat strong engineered retrieval pipelines on evidence recall and final answer quality. The work suggests the retriever was inside the model all along.
arxiv-2605-05906:
Axion-like particles could be the dark matter, and if they decay into photons, the sky should faintly glow at radio frequencies. Wen-Qing Guo proposes hunting that glow by cross-correlating radio intensity maps with the galaxy distribution from the 2MASS Redshift Survey. Ambient radiation, from the cosmic microwave background and an extragalactic radio backdrop, stimulates the decay and boosts the signal.

The survey covers the local universe, within redshift a tenth. Guo builds the theoretical framework for the cross-correlation, including those stimulation effects. A detection, or its absence, would probe micro-electronvolt-scale axion-like dark matter in a new way.
arxiv-2605-06106:
Mathis Degryse and three co-authors close a gap in the theory of learning augmented online bidding. In online bidding, an algorithm raises bids step by step for tasks such as resource allocation and clustering.
