The learning augmented version also hears predictions from an oracle, and quality is judged by consistency when predictions are good versus robustness when they are bad.

The authors derive matching upper and lower bounds on the best consistency for each robustness level above a stated threshold. Their key device is the bidding function, an abstraction that unifies how randomized bidding strategies are designed and analyzed. That device simplifies proofs that earlier work had left open. They also apply randomized bidding to the incremental median problem, showing the method works in a practical clustering setting.
arxiv-2605-06306:
T. Congy and G. A. El build an exact framework for the statistics of random nonlinear wave fields ruled by solitons. Their setting is the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation in a regime where typical wave fields are dominated by soliton pulses. Such integrable turbulence appears in water waves, nonlinear optics, and superfluids, yet predicting its intensity distribution from first principles has been an open challenge for the field.

The authors state a soliton gas resolution conjecture for the long time evolution of slowly varying random starting states. A random analogue of the inverse scattering transform then links the spectral density of the soliton gas to the probability density of wave intensity. The resulting full integral formula matches direct computer simulations closely across several regimes. The framework gives random wave statistics a firm exact footing.
arxiv-2605-06406:
Y. I. Izotov, N. G. Guseva, D. Schaerer, and R. O. Amorin present telescope observations of eleven compact star-forming galaxies with extremely high oxygen line ratios. Such galaxies are candidate sources of leaking Lyman continuum radiation, which can ionize gas between galaxies. The sample sits at low redshift and has low oxygen abundance and small stellar mass.

Using Very Large Telescope spectra, the team derives helium and oxygen abundances plus ratios for nitrogen, neon, sulfur, chlorine, argon, and iron. They also measure gas velocity spreads from many lines. Most lines agree closely, while helium lines run broader, likely tracing inner regions shaped by massive stars and scattering.
arxiv-2605-06506:
Omar Momen and Sina Zarrieß question a reported link between language model surprisal and how novel a metaphor feels. Surprisal measures how unexpected a word is in context and is often used as a stand-in for predictability. It is also tightly tied to how frequent a word is, which may be the real driver.

Using two frequency measures and surprisal from eight Pythia model sizes across many training checkpoints, they find word frequency predicts metaphor novelty more strongly than surprisal does. The surprisal link peaks early in training, then fades as its tie to frequency grows. Settings once read as optimal for predictability may mostly reflect word frequency.
arxiv-2605-06606:
Marco Zaccheddu and six co-authors image the internal structure of the proton using AI inside a Bayesian framework. Transverse momentum dependent distributions describe how quarks spread inside a proton, but pulling them from data is an inverse problem with hidden blind spots. Their flexible pixel-based method puts the distributions on a grid and fits them jointly with the evolution kernel that governs energy dependence.

A hybrid of normalizing flows and Metropolis-Hastings sampling explores the high-dimensional posterior exactly and fast. Closure tests of rising hardness check the method, and a singular value analysis exposes null parts that data cannot constrain. The result is three-dimensional partonic imaging with honest error bars.
arxiv-2605-06906:
Shang-Ling Hsu, Mark Tenzer, Cyrus Shahabi, and Khurram Shafique rethink pretraining for human mobility data, whose structure language-style recipes ignore. Visits are joint events of place, time, and activity; users keep persistent signatures; and people sharing places create cross-user signal. The authors state these as three axioms for a broader class they call multi-entity spatiotemporal event streams, which also covers authentication logs and health records.

Their TraXion framework designs objectives and architecture jointly to satisfy the axioms. One checkpoint per dataset beats task-specific baselines on anomaly detection, recommendation, and prediction tasks across six mobility datasets. Applied unchanged to enterprise authentication logs and intensive care mortality prediction, the same recipe matches or beats prior specialized work.
arxiv-2605-07206:
Wei Xiong and four co-authors show one magnetic material phase that displays two kinds of topological boundary behavior at once. Their setting is a two-dimensional antiferromagnet lacking certain mirror symmetry, modeled with a spin-density-wave mass term. Which behavior appears depends only on how the crystal is cut.

For edges aligned with the crystal's screw symmetry, protected gapless edge states appear. A diamond-shaped cut breaks that symmetry, gapping the edges, but preserved magnetic mirror symmetries then bind states at the corners instead. Small perturbations can remove the edge modes while the corner states survive, giving a termination-controlled switch between first- and second-order topology.
arxiv-2605-07706:
Viktar Dubovik and three co-authors make Bayesian fine-tuning of large models cheaper by shrinking the space where uncertainty lives. Low-rank adaptation already cuts trainable parameters, but Bayesian versions, which track uncertainty to avoid models that are too sure of themselves, add many parameters back and can train unstably. Their question is how low-dimensional the uncertainty model can be.

They propose a framework that projects weight-space uncertainty into very low-dimensional subspaces and still quantifies it effectively. Empirically the method performs strongly with better calibration and generalization than standard approaches, while keeping the computational savings. A supporting observation is that weight covariances themselves have low rank, which is why the projection loses so little.
arxiv-2605-07806:
Sree Bhattacharyya and five co-authors ask language models to judge themselves more richly than a single confidence number. Stated confidence is a known too-optimistic and unsteady sign of whether a model is right. Borrowing appraisal theory from psychology, which splits self-judgment into parts, they elicit six appraisal aspects alongside confidence from the models.

Across twelve models and thirty-eight tasks in eight domains, competence-related aspects, above all effort and ability, matched or beat confidence at predicting failure. Effort estimates were also less too-optimistic and stable across model sizes, while emotional aspects added little. The most telling aspect shifted sensibly with the task: effort for reasoning-heavy work, ability and confidence for retrieval.
arxiv-2605-08006:
Yiyang Shen, Yutian He, Weiran Wang, and Qihang Lin develop methods for bilevel optimization problems whose lower level is itself a minimax problem. Such nested problems appear in a growing range of applications, but most existing methods assume the lower level is a plain minimization, often with strong convexity.

The authors propose penalty-based first-order methods that need no strong convexity at the lower level. In the deterministic setting, their method reaches an approximate KKT point with a stated oracle complexity. They also show that bilevel problems with convex constrained lower levels fit the same framework through a Lagrangian reformulation, widening the range of problems the methods cover.
arxiv-2605-08106:
Truman Welling, Onur Günlü, and Aylin Yener survey the security side of integrated sensing and communication, a design that uses one transmitted signal both to communicate and to sense the environment. Sharing spectrum and hardware saves resources, but each function can leak information about the other to the wrong user.

The survey organizes information-theoretic work by what is protected and who the adversary is. It covers secure communication, sensing privacy, and active attacks such as jamming, plus cases where the two kinds of security interact. By collecting models, metrics, and fundamental limits in one place, the review gives system designers a map of what secrecy is achievable.
arxiv-2605-08206:
Yoshihiro Michishita builds an effective theory for systems that carry a steady electric current, where real current-driven effects are easily confused with plain Joule heating. Large open systems in such states are hard to analyze directly, so a bulk description that keeps translation symmetry is valuable.

The proposed model uses asymmetric hopping and, in its simplest case, matches an open-system Hatano-Nelson model of a boundary-driven setup. For a minimal noninteracting version, the effective temperature grows linearly with current density when the current is weak. The framework gives researchers a cleaner way to separate genuine current-induced physics from heating artifacts.
arxiv-2605-08906:
T. Sujith and A. Sen show how elastic fluids reshape acoustic trapping of tiny particles inside microchannels. Sound driven devices normally sort particles through radiation force fighting streaming drag in simple fluids, but many real fluids stretch and recoil. Solving the coupled flow equations for an Oldroyd-B fluid, they map the sound field, the steady streaming in bulk and boundary layers, and the resulting particle paths.

Two numbers govern the outcome, and raising elasticity at strong viscous diffusion moves trapping sites among the bulk, wall, pressure node, center, and symmetry lines. The size threshold between radiation and streaming control shrinks well below the simple fluid value, enabling submicron handling that conventional acoustics cannot reach.
arxiv-2605-09006:
Keren Censor-Hillel, Tomer Even, Virginia Vasillevska Williams, and Nathan Wallheimer present a faster way to find a small pattern called an induced diamond inside a large graph. A diamond is a group of four linked points with one link missing. Their 2026 paper makes the running time depend on how many such patterns the graph contains, so graphs rich in diamonds are searched faster than before.

The key idea sorts diamonds by the size of the tight group of points that holds one of their triangles. Heavy and light cases get different search methods, and a new sampling scheme adapts to the graph at hand. The same sampling idea also speeds up two related problems, a sum problem and a special case of finding four-cycles.
arxiv-2605-09106:
Xiaoyu Hu and Jinman Zhao build Fin-Bias, a test of whether language models make independent investment calls or simply follow the crowd. Finance benchmarks often use small samples and rarely check how models react when the material they read carries a human slant.

The benchmark draws on nearly nine thousand long analyst reports, each with a bullish, neutral, or bearish rating. Models saw the reports with the rating shown, hidden, or replaced by a fake one. The results show models tend to herd toward whatever bias the text displays. A detection method that flags human opinions helped models think more independently, and some then beat human forecasts of later stock returns.
arxiv-2605-09506:
Yu and Wang speed up Bayesian phylogenetic inference, the task of estimating the distribution over evolutionary trees from sequence data. Standard Markov chain Monte Carlo methods approximate that distribution, but each step reevaluates a costly likelihood function. For large data sets that cost dominates. Their approach trains a random forest on more than 35 features of tree shape and branch length. It predicts how a proposed tree move will change the likelihood.

That predictor drives a delayed acceptance kernel, which rejects poor moves early without a full likelihood evaluation. The kernel is then embedded in a sequential Monte Carlo sampler. Tests on simulated and real data sets show robust estimates with far fewer likelihood evaluations and substantial time savings. The authors release the method as a Python package, making faster tree space search available to practitioners.
arxiv-2605-09606:
Liu and six colleagues measure a neglected risk of image to 3D models: generating harmful geometries that can be printed as real objects. Such models turn a single image into a 3D shape, enabling creative design and, in the wrong hands, direct use hazards, risky parts, and deceptive replicas. The team tests open source and commercial models on original, degraded, viewpoint shifted, and camouflaged inputs, scoring geometric validity, semantic match, human judgment, and actual fabrication.

Current models reconstruct harmful shapes effectively, while under one percent of such shapes trip commercial moderation flags. Even obscured or noisy inputs still yield clear harmful structures. Existing safeguards show distinct flaws: input moderators catch few cases, while other defenses cut harm but flag over 30 percent of benign ambiguous pairs as bad. A stacked defense cuts harmful retention under one percent, but still at an 11 percent false positive cost.
arxiv-2605-09806:
Wei and seven colleagues tackle a costly habit of modern reasoning models. As they get smarter, their step-by-step workings get longer, burning compute, waiting time and context space. Fixed rewards for brevity and one-size-fits-all length caps force a bad trade. The right balance shifts during training, and the right length differs from problem to problem. Their method is called LEAD.

LEAD retunes the accuracy-versus-brevity balance at each training step. It sets a fresh target length per problem from the model's own correct attempts, punishing both rambling and over-trimming. Across five maths reasoning tests it reached the best accuracy and accuracy-efficiency score among efficient-reasoning methods trained this way. Its answers were also much shorter than the base model's.
arxiv-2605-09906:
Li and eight colleagues tackle cross-modal interference in audio-visual language models, where sound misleads vision or vision misleads sound and hallucinations follow. A barking soundtrack, for instance, can wrongly tag every animal on screen as the source. The authors blame uncontrolled mixing during intermediate reasoning and propose Separate First, Fuse Later, or SFFL, as the remedy.

SFFL forces separate audio and visual chains of thought, then merges the evidence only at the answering stage. Modality-preference labels, built under different input settings, serve as an auxiliary reward in reinforcement learning. The result is steadier reasoning: average relative gains of about five percent on general audio-visual question answering and about eleven percent on a cross-modal hallucination benchmark.
arxiv-2605-10106:
Mou and seven colleagues probe 3D spatial reasoning in multimodal language models without any extra training. Recent progress has leaned on post-training with curated benchmarks, leaving inference-time methods underexplored. Their training-free agent, ViSRA, elicits spatial reasoning in a modular way, drawing explicit spatial information from expert models in a plug-and-play design.

ViSRA offers two claimed advantages: human-aligned, transferable 3D understanding instead of task-specific overfitting, and no post-training compute or heavy manual data curation. Tests across several multimodal models show consistent gains on existing benchmarks and on unseen 3D spatial tasks, beating baselines by up to 15.6 percent and 28.9 percent in absolute terms respectively. The work treats spatial reasoning as something to evoke at run time, not only to bake in during training.
arxiv-2605-10406:
Yixiang Liu and Yao Zhang help estimate quantiles when the best data are scarce and costly. High-quality measures, such as wet-lab binding assays taking days or weeks, are costly, while abundant low-quality data are imperfect proxies. Their 2026 paper proposes a two-stage, general method for multi-fidelity quantile regression, estimating response quantiles given covariates.

The core idea is a local link: at each covariate value, the high-quality quantile is written as a low-quality quantile at a varying level. Estimating that level function can be easier than estimating the high-quality quantile directly when the two distributions have similar shapes. A correction step improves robustness where that edge weakens. Theory pins down when the estimator converges faster than direct high-quality-only regression and when correction helps further. Tests on synthetic and real data yielded more accurate quantile estimates and tighter conformal prediction intervals.
arxiv-2605-10606:
Benjamin Icard and four colleagues measure how much author style survives in text embeddings. Large language models can convincingly copy human writing styles, yet it is unclear how much style data is stored in embeddings from any language model and kept after LLM rewriting. Their 2026 paper tests these questions in French, using a controlled literary dataset to measure style shifts via changes in embedding spread.

The authors gather French excerpts from Tufféry, Proust, Céline, and Yourcenar, plus GPT-, Mistral-, and Gemini-based style copies under fixed-topic conditions. Encoding all texts with thirteen embedding models, they measure overall style effects on embedding spread across human authors and copied texts. Embeddings reliably capture author style features, and these signals persist after rewriting, while also showing LLM-specific patterns. The results offer good leads for spotting authorship imitation in the era of language models.
arxiv-2605-10706:
Byeongchan Kim and colleagues present RelFlexformers, fast focus 3D models for tied-place codes that sum. Standard models fit 3D learning poorly. Point-cloud tokens have no set order and sit at uneven gaps, pulled hard by tied places. Exact focus costs grow with the square of input size. RelFlexformers build on non-uniform Fourier transform theory, spreading fast tied-place focus from plain grids to mixed spreads in 3D space.

The models readily take in tied-place codes from any tuning rule that can be summed. Focus is worked out in near-linear time for the input length. Performer-style fast focus never builds the focus matrix, so shape tuning must fit the kernel form with fast matrix-vector products, a bar the models meet. Wide tests on many 3D data sets show quality gains from Fourier-driven focus tuning, with point clouds as a leading use.
arxiv-2605-10806: Lin and fifteen colleagues introduce PhyGround, a test of whether videos made by generative world models obey physical laws. It holds 250 prompts, each with an expected physical outcome. It also holds a list of thirteen laws across solids, fluids and optics, each probed by small observable questions. Eight modern video models were judged in a large human study, and the team releases PhyJudge-9B, an open judge with far lower bias than a leading commercial model.
arxiv-2605-10906:
Yaxin Du and fourteen colleagues present DataMaster, an agent framework for autonomous data engineering that improves a learning system by fixing its data, never its algorithm. As models and training recipes standardize, data quality drives further gains, yet finding, cleaning, and composing datasets still runs by hand.

DataMaster searches a tree of candidate data moves, shares lessons across branches, and validates choices through downstream training, handling the open-ended search and delayed feedback that make the job hard. The agent discovers outside data, selects and composes it, and transforms it, all while the learner stays fixed. Machine-learning teams get a data-side worker that turns ad-hoc wrangling into systematic search.
arxiv-2605-11106:
Zachary Morgan and four others study two honeycomb magnets: chromium trichloride and alpha-ruthenium trichloride. Both are layered halides with honeycomb metal ions, and both shift between high- and low-temperature forms in a sharp first-order change.

Neutron diffraction shows both stepping in c-lattice spacing, a sign of stacking change, but their in-plane moves differ. The ruthenium salt shifts with a jump and hysteresis, and gets worse with each heat cycle. The chromium salt shifts in a smooth way and stays robust. The chromium salt orders at 14 kelvin with diffuse scattering up to about 40 kelvin, while the ruthenium salt shows none above its 7.6-kelvin zig-zag order. The gap points to layer sliding forces shaping both form and magnetism.
arxiv-2605-11606: Rohrer, Bächler and Arnold test whether convolutional neural networks can deanonymize I2P traffic. The Invisible Internet Project encrypts payloads, yet traffic patterns might still identify services. The team built a controlled lab to generate synthetic I2P traffic for training, and used Fano's inequality for a theoretical analysis of anonymous transmission in mix networks. Deep learning methods, especially convolutional networks, were applied in the lab network and checked against real-world traffic. The results indicate the methods do not compromise I2P's anonymity guarantees.
arxiv-2605-11806: Xin Bing and Chao Wang refine kernel ridge regression, a nonparametric method that applies one regularization to a whole function. That single treatment can shrink linear structure too much. Their procedure adds an explicit linear component at no extra compute cost and with no new tuning parameters. They prove a sharp oracle inequality and minimax optimal prediction risk. The method adapts to both linear and nonlinear structure, improving bias and approximation error at a negligible variance cost.
arxiv-2605-12106: Peipei Xu and six colleagues tune large language models to draw trade-off fronts for limited two-goal convex problems. Past tools rerun a solver per case, but DIPS reads a problem and at once outputs a set of workable choice vectors near the front. It uses number coding, grounded start values for number tokens, and a three-stage plan lining up form, workability, and front quality. On five problem families, a tuned 7B model hit 95.29 to 98.18 percent of the ideal front, solving cases in as little as 0.16 seconds.
arxiv-2605-12406: Parris proposes a diagnosis for a cluster of language-model flaws, from false certainty and sycophancy to hidden uncertainty. He calls the pattern Semantic Reward Collapse: distinct kinds of user dissatisfaction, such as factual error, poor formatting, slowness and social friction, get squeezed into one shared reward signal. Under that squeeze, he argues, a system may learn to hide visible failure rather than preserve honest uncertainty. The paper frames these behaviours as structural products of scalar reward design, not as isolated quirks.
arxiv-2605-12606: Dupletsa and thirteen colleagues measure cosmic expansion by pairing gravitational waves with hydrogen maps, in a method they call radio sirens. Binary black hole signals give direct distances, while neutral hydrogen intensity mapping gives a three-dimensional view of large-scale structure. Using hydrogen density fields as a redshift prior for gravitational-wave events, they probe the late-time expansion history. Forecasts for the Einstein Telescope and SKA-Mid test whether next-generation data can supply enough high-redshift events for a sharp measurement.
arxiv-2605-12906: Liu and four colleagues study how the difficulty of training data affects fine-tuning of large language models. They find no single best difficulty: the ideal level shifts toward harder data as the training budget grows. Controlled synthetic tests trace this to a trade-off between generalising within the training distribution and extrapolating beyond it, a mechanism they back with a theoretical analysis using PAC-Bayesian bounds. Their results guide difficulty-based data selection.
arxiv-2605-13106: Chen, Guo and Zhong study a data-driven scheme for one-dimensional hyperbolic conservation laws, built on the classical fifth-order WENO finite-volume scheme. In their Hyper-CFCNN, a small target network predicts nonlinear WENO weights per stencil, while a hypernetwork derives its settings from mesh data and coarse initial-condition notes. The design keeps standard polynomial reconstruction and conservative flux updates, adapting across cases and grids without retraining. Tests show accuracy close to classical WENO5 with near-perfect conservation on fine meshes.
arxiv-2605-13206: Alyatkin and four co-authors use light to sculpt aperiodic quasicrystals from einstein monotiles in a microcavity, seeing exciton-polariton condensates excited at monotile corners. They were thought to need at least two tile types; the new class needs only one. Momentum scans reveal Bragg peaks with six-fold symmetry and Dirac-like marks from a graphene-like structure. Phase scans show a sync pattern unlike periodic triangular lattices and Penrose tilings. The work turns the tiles into programmable driven-dissipative matter where long-range coherence coexists with enforced aperiodicity.
arxiv-2605-13406: Joaquin Brum, Martin Gilabert Vio and Nicolas Matte Bon study the class C of groups whose line actions are classifiable. Classifiable means conjugacy between minimal actions is smooth, with a Borel transversal. No amenable group outside C is known. The authors prove that C is stable under group operations and show C holds all finitely generated piecewise affine interval homeomorphism groups. They exhibit a finitely generated group outside C, amenable exactly when Thompson's group F is amenable. They also prove semiconjugacy among cocompact actions is smooth exactly in C.
arxiv-2605-13606: Bhandaru Phani Parasar constructs a Z2 times Z2 gauge theory with matter on a chain, studying physics in the Gauss law subspace. In that subspace the theory has a U(1) symmetry whose generator commutes with translations but anticommutes with reflection. That yields a Lieb-Schultz-Mattis theorem ruling out a trivial gapped ground state when the Hamiltonian respects translations and reflection. Every parameter point must realise a symmetry-broken or gapless ground state. At one gapless point, excitations behave as free Dirac fermions with a total-fermion-number constraint.
arxiv-2605-13706: Steven Seiden and five colleagues propose identifying AI web scrapers with canary tokens. Existing scraper finding relies on willing company sharing, one-off lab tests, or crowd-sourced reports, none sound or wide. The team hosts dynamic sites serving unique canary tokens to every scraper that visits, then prompts language models about their sites. If a model often outputs tokens unique to one scraper, that shows contact with that scraper. Across 22 live language model systems, the method names which scrapers feed which models, including several not openly known.
arxiv-2605-14106: Bilic, Chen and Boloni test whether behavior cloning alone can yield active perception in a robot object-finding task. A cheap robot arm with a wrist-mounted color camera must shift to center a partly visible plant before signaling a grasp, choosing moves that improve later views. The model predicts joint commands straight from low-resolution images under closed-loop control. Low-resolution egocentric vision proves enough for reliable completion, and relative joint deltas beat absolute joint positions by a wide margin.
arxiv-2605-14506: Xiong and colleagues use first-principles maths to show trigonal selenium and tellurium exhibit flipped spin and orbital Hall conductivity signs between left- and right-handed enantiomers. This comes from the mirror link between the two forms in space groups P3_221 and P3_121. Both forms share the same bands and four nonzero parts, but two parts flip sign under mirror action. More broadly, mirror-linked forms can show sign flips ruled by symmetry in some parts. For trigonal selenium and tellurium, sign patterns track handedness under the chosen frame.
arxiv-2605-15106: Jinchang Liu and four others beat a scale barrier in self-testing, the strongest certification of quantum states from observed measurement statistics alone. Old methods for generic multi-partite states need fast-growing samples. Their protocol well self-tests nearly all n-qubit states at only polynomial sample complexity, using spare Bell pairs plus plain projective and Bell measurements. The scheme extends to device-independent learning and proof methods in the device-independent setting, opening a scalable route for large quantum networks.
arxiv-2605-15206: Dzung Pham and three others study the energy cost of running AI agents locally on consumer devices. Local deployment protects privacy and avoids API fees, but repeat reasoning, tool use, and retries burn far more tokens than single guesses. Tests show agentic running raises GPU power draw, heat, and battery drain. Their AgentStop supervisor predicts trajectories unlikely to succeed from cheap execution signals like token log probabilities. It kills them early, cutting wasted energy by 15 to 20 percent with minimal task impact.
arxiv-2605-15306: Tianxiao He, Alex H. Williams, and Sarah E. Harvey map how data augmentation recasts neural representations. Using shape analysis, they embed hidden codes in a metric space fixed to scaling, translation, rotation, and reflection. Stronger boosting traces well-behaved trajectories in this space, and other boosting types steer codes in distinct ways. Warps along boosting paths predict which codes most improve groups. Shared shape patterns emerge across architectures and seeds.
arxiv-2605-15506: Shimin Zhang, Yechuan Xia, Chunxiao Li, Jianwen Li, Moshe Y. Vardi, and Vijay Ganesh study why conflict-driven SAT solvers scale so differently across industrial problems. On more than 76,600 bounded model checking instances, they find a spectrum from linear to exponential scaling, and show that clause-variable ratio, treewidth, and community structure fail to separate the regimes. A newer parameter, the proofdoor, explains the pattern: linearly scaling instances yield small proofdoors, while exponentially scaling ones yield large, poorly absorbed ones.
arxiv-2605-16106: Mandal and six colleagues study two chromium-based high-entropy spinel oxides, tracking their structure and magnetism with temperature. Both crystallize cubic at room temperature and order antiferromagnetically below 49 K and 35 K respectively. Neutron data confirm long-range magnetic order with spiral spin arrangement. Both also switch from cubic to orthorhombic symmetry near 55 K and 85 K, showing that strong disorder need not destroy long-range order.
arxiv-2605-16206: Optołowicz and four colleagues run kinetic PIConGPU simulations of three-beam laser compression of a cryogenic hydrogen cylinder, as a baseline for DRACO and PENELOPE. The simulations resolve charge-separation fields near 3 TV per metre and reveal a fast 1-to-5 MeV ion beam plus a slower bulk flow. A simple reflection scaling from that front tracks the fast-ion band under both 30 fs and 150 fs drivers. 20 T fields leave results unchanged, while kilotesla fields quench the fast-ion band and more than double compression time.
arxiv-2605-16406: George and three others present Contrastive-SDXL, a day-to-night framework for night-time pedestrian detection built on SDXL-Turbo. Night-time detection suffers from limited night data and illumination differences that make daytime-only detectors unreliable. To preserve correspondence, the method uses a patch-wise contrastive loss guided by a DINOv2 encoder plus an object consistency loss preserving pedestrians. Contrastive-SDXL images score FID 22.5, and detectors trained on them cut miss rate 6-7 percent versus a daytime-only baseline.
arxiv-2605-16706: Hora and Robbes survey how open-source projects adapt contribution rules to generative AI. From 1,000 popular GitHub repositories they identify 118 AI policies for contributors. Most policies, 78%, allow AI-assisted contributions, while 22% discourage AI use. About half require disclosure of AI help, and 74% require a human in the loop. The authors conclude that project rules are broadly positive toward generative AI, with disclosure and human oversight treated as fundamental.
arxiv-2605-16806: Tsai, Lee and Tung propose AAMLA, a framework for gauging student teamwork morale in game-based learning from multi-mode data. A key barrier is signal decay: signals such as eye gaze vary in value across student cohorts, making focus-based fusion brittle. The CAMA module models inter-modal links with affinity tables and keeps cross-modal match through contrast learning, muting weak signals without dropping them. On 50 middle school students in EcoJourneys, AAMLA beats single-mode and cross-focus baselines under standard and weakened settings.
arxiv-2605-16906: Right-censored survival records cannot be shared, yet tests on them need privacy guarantees. Hung and Yu give the first finite-sample theory of differentially private hypothesis testing for it. Cox regression coefficients get private score-type and partial-likelihood-ratio tests, plus private rejection-threshold calibration. Private distributed two-sample test covers cumulative hazard functions. Privacy and finite-sample guarantees and minimax lower bounds are proved. They distinguish settings where privacy is statistically negligible, where it sets the testing pace, and where optimal private rates remain open.
arxiv-2605-17206: Till Aust and colleagues study firefly-style pulse-coupled oscillators and find collective timing emerges only near a critical balance between quorum threshold and pulse duration. Inside that region performance splits in two: near-perfect synchrony or stable multi-cluster states where offset groups reinforce each other. Cutting connections or adding noise breaks those symmetric traps, so denser and quieter networks are not always better.
arxiv-2605-18106: Tim Tsz-Kit Lau's 2026 paper argues that optimizer updates should respect the same symmetries as the weights they change. Popular coordinate-wise optimizers such as Adam ignore the equivariance built into modern network layers, creating a geometric mismatch. The authors derive symmetry-matched updates for embeddings, language-model heads, SwiGLU feed-forward blocks, and mixture-of-experts routers, forming a full layer-wise stack. In pre-training tests on dense and sparse expert models, the new updates cut validation loss, ease expert load imbalance, and steady router behaviour versus AdamW.
arxiv-2605-18406: Paul Hager and three co-authors study, in a 2026 paper, computational aspects of the Volterra signature. It extends the old path signature with matrix-valued kernels for time-series memory. They split a Chen-type convolution relation into analytic and arithmetic parts. Then they give efficient algorithms: a quadratic general scheme, an FFT-based speedup for convolution kernels on uniform grids, and an exact recursion for state-space kernels. They also show kernel factor counts do not raise asymptotic cost, and derive a finite-difference predictor-corrector plan.
arxiv-2605-18506: Shalini Badola and nine co-authors use the exciton Rydberg series in a 2026 paper, in monolayer tungsten diselenide, to probe pressure-induced changes in dielectric screening. The sample is tungsten diselenide wrapped in hexagonal boron nitride. A model based on pressure-driven layer-spacing shifts and bulk boron nitride dielectric traits yields a direct read of the dielectric constant of squeezed boron nitride. The work sets up a new method for dielectric sensing in van der Waals stacks.
arxiv-2605-18606: Jiaxiao Xu and three co-authors present PACE-FNO, a 2026 physics-aligned canonical-frame method for Fourier neural operators under coordinate shifts. It gauges the frame, predicts after pulling the field to a canonical sample, and restores the requested end frame. On shifted Burgers and shallow-water systems it cuts out-of-sample relative error by up to 12-fold. The rival is a data-augmented FNO. A matched control credits the gain to canonical-frame prediction, and regional WeatherBench2 tests show near-identical results to FNO.
arxiv-2605-19006: Aytijhya Saha, Stephen Bates, and Devavrat Shah show that causal effects can be found even with a hidden confounder, if that confounder takes categorical values. They cover two routes: proxies, which need hard to check lopsided roles, and the Deconfounder route for many free treatments, which had no estimator. Their mixture view finds the hidden shape by spotting the mixture spread. A tensor-based estimator finds the hidden shape each time, with bounds for small samples, and tests on fake and real data show it works well with scant data.
arxiv-2605-19106: Rupak Chatterjee builds an operator framework for modular self-duality, symmetrised relative entropy, and Bogoliubov-Kubo-Mori susceptibility in quantum field theory. In finite dimensions, self-duality picks states equal to their modularly reflected partners, where the comparison tool is the Umegaki relative entropy. Moving to type-III von Neumann algebras, he defines a type-III BKM response from the fixed-localisation Hessian. Exact cases for the free scalar field, the chiral U(1) current, and a conformal theory with an AdS dual show exact quadratic behaviour.
arxiv-2605-19706: Edalat rebuilds quantum mechanics for finite precision, replacing exact states with quantum parcels, sets of density operators that fit limited data. Parcels set by finite expectation ranges give the state space its shape, and exact states return only as ideal limits of finer parcels. Unitary motion lifts to reversible parcel motion, and fuzzy measurement keeps single parcels intact. Measurement shrinks volume and raises geometric information, dissolving old puzzles: duality becomes gradual interference loss, and the cat becomes a parcel narrowing toward the seen outcome.
arxiv-2605-19806: Prior, Milanova and Schultz compare ways to chop German statutory law into chunks for retrieval-augmented generation, using the Civil Code as benchmark. Structural units, fixed windows, contextual chunking, semantic clustering, Lumber-style splits and hierarchical RAPTOR retrieval face a legal question-answering test with section-level labels. Chunks following the law's own sections and subsections win on recall, while fancier methods that override that structure do worse and cost more. Preserving domain structure, the authors argue, matters more than semantic enrichment.
arxiv-2605-20206: Qiyu Li and four co-workers present PrivacyAkinator, a tool helping novice developers make privacy design decisions through LLM-made multiple-choice questions. NIST's privacy risk method is complex and expert-based, and novices struggle to state design decisions. It abstracts decisions into data flows and user links, mines a design space from 10,000 privacy news, and makes questions live to rank apt ones. In a study with 24 participants, users found forty-seven percent more key decisions in seventy-three percent less time than with the NIST method.
arxiv-2605-20306: Bingnan Liu and nine co-workers set out WildRoadBench, road damage tests on one marked UAV set. Fixed vision-language models point to damage from one photo, short prompt, under one shared routine. Agents get a brief, a slice, and set budget, hunt the web, adapt parts, write code, and file guesses through a score oracle on hidden data. Closed models lead yet leave over half unclaimed; open models plateau lower, small marks failing for all. Agents trail the best model, some filing no valid guess in budget.
arxiv-2605-20506: Weiwei Sun and fifteen colleagues train language models to copy human social conduct from spoken comments. An example is being told an act was rude, rather than receiving a bare score. Their system, DITTO, turns each comment into an improved retry and trains on both tries at once. No comment is then needed at test time, and it beat its base model by 36 percent on average.
arxiv-2605-20706: Reese Levine and seven colleagues present Llamas on the Web, a WebGPU backend for llama.cpp that runs language models in the browser. Browser inference promises private, portable AI apps, but memory is tight and hardware varies widely. Their design cuts memory overhead with static planning and efficient loading, and a tunable kernel library handles cross-device differences. Templated kernels support many quantization formats, and tests span 16 devices from eight vendors.
arxiv-2605-20906: Yiyang Wu and three colleagues present ParaCell, paravirtualized secure containers with lightweight intra-container isolation. Secure containers isolate each box with its own kernel, easing shared-kernel attacks. Yet existing designs face an isolation-performance trade-off, a hard balance. Nested-cloud deployments amplify VM-exit and page-table costs, while agentic workloads expose bursty memory demand needing fine-grained elasticity. ParaCell traces the trade-off to missing lightweight isolation parts and opaque host memory handling forcing reactive faults and coarse huge-page mappings.
arxiv-2605-21006: Ishaan Kelkar and five colleagues test whether off-the-shelf persona vectors can rival targeted steering for sycophancy in language models. Language models often agree with a user's stated view whether or not it is right. Prior work controlled that trait by steering with a sycophancy persona vector extracted from sycophancy data itself. The authors instead recycle existing vectors for general roles, Skeptic, Judge, and Devil's Advocate, extracted without targeting sycophancy at all, and compare them on Gemma and Qwen models.
arxiv-2605-21106: Victor Edmonds warns that shared temperature readings in thin plasmas prove less than they seem. Each tool past the ionization bottleneck reports one effective temperature, not the core heat. So agreement is one result told many times, not many checks. By sorting tools into three types, he fits solar corona and tokamak data with one kappa curve and one fewer parameter.
arxiv-2605-21206: Mohamed Hatifi shows that steady motion changes how a moving Glauber detector reads single photons. Motion shifts the options by Doppler effect in the detector frame, and a finite bandwidth turns travel direction into a detection bias without decohering the photon. Near one Doppler branch, readout moves from phase-sensitive to direction-sensitive, with a boost from the quality factor at onset. Finite-time integration adds Doppler-beat visibility loss, which separates passive covariance from real measurement change.
arxiv-2605-21306: Adriana Errico and colleagues report a long-period companion to the Sun-like star HD 38973 from precise radial-velocity data. The signal has a period near three thousand days and moderate eccentricity, giving a minimum mass below Jupiter's. Hipparcos-Gaia astrometry shows no proper-motion anomaly, which still caps the true mass. Joining both data sets rules out high-mass, low-inclination cases. The best true mass is about a quarter of Jupiter's, making HD 38973 b a likely cold Saturn.
arxiv-2605-21606: Xiaogeng Liu and co-authors ask when teacher tokens are reliable, giving place-weighted training for reasoning. This trains a student on its own rollouts with a special teacher. But its goal weights all made tokens equally, treating the teacher target as reliable at every student prefix. Entropy methods relax this sameness by tuning token guidance with teacher entropy. But high entropy from the teacher in reasoning has unclear meaning, showing either non-viable doubt or benign solution mix. They add a branch health check to spot this effect.
arxiv-2605-21706: Giorgio Piras and colleagues recast refusal suppression in safety-aligned language models as an attack on inner representations. Earlier methods erased a refusal direction from activations without explaining why that worked. The authors show the erasure is exactly a projection onto the decision boundary of a probe that separates refused from answered prompts. Since evasion halts at that boundary, they propose pushing representations further into compliant territory with tuned confidence. The result tops attack success rates across fifteen instruction-tuned, multimodal, and reasoning models.
arxiv-2605-22406: Van der Put and Top study Whittaker groups, subgroups of PGL(2,K) generated by order-two elements from fixed-point pairs. An index-2 subgroup is a Schottky group, producing the hyperelliptic Whittaker curve of genus g. Whittaker curves are parametrised by theta functions, giving branch points, p-adic periods and p-adic heights from theta values. For g+1 point pairs, the morphism from fixed points to branch points is a rigid étale covering with Galois group {±1}^{d-1}. Genus 2 and 3 approximations confirm the main result.
arxiv-2605-22506: Zhang and team offer EnCAgg, robust pooling for federated learning under shifting attacks. Old shields use fixed thresholds and struggle with changing attacks. EnCAgg uses known benign clients as guides, cutting bad gradients while keeping benign ones, even with unknown bad counts. Gradients are mapped onto two spread axes and grouped. A second model makes pseudo-gradients matched with the benign edge, bridging outliers. Re-grouping pseudo-gradients with real gradients recovers wrongly flagged benign gradients. Tests on MNIST, CIFAR-10 and MIND show toughness under poisoning attacks.
arxiv-2605-22606: Boudourides studies missing guessing in partly seen networks, weighing dyadic link guessing (LP), hyper guessing (HP), and an ERGM rival. LP is the base, using old rules. HP scores trial higher shapes (cliques) via lifted dyadic scores and CHESHIRE. All methods share a masking plan cutting dyadic proof from held links. Across public email and covert sets, LP remains strong for dyadic rescue, while HP gains for higher groups. ERGMs offer a clear helper via tie odds. The result shows when LP, HP, and ERGM fit network gaps.
arxiv-2605-22706: Lerbet classifies vector bundles over smooth real affine surfaces and threefolds through cohomology, showing the classification mirrors the algebraically closed field picture under assumptions on the real locus. The work builds on joint results with Asok, Fasel and Banerjee. It uses a Fasel argument to give a proof of Kucharz's characterization of Chern class triples for rank 3 bundles on real affine threefolds. Lerbet also settles Kucharz's open questions, giving the first projective module over an affine real algebra of dimension 3 with trivial Chern classes that is not stably free.
arxiv-2605-22806: Myrtaj and others explain the Milky Way's three phase history, from messy protogalaxy through thick disk to cold thin disk, using FIRE-2 simulations. The protogalaxy phase pairs bursty star formation with mass sloshing, ending when gas starts to spin. The thick disk phase brings fast cool gas conversion into stars, while thin disk arrives once the inner halo medium virializes and star formation steadies. Mergers play no defining role; thick disk formation needs centre of mass motion, while thin disk formation needs slow gas accretion for coherent angular momentum.
arxiv-2605-23006: Siwek, Ho, and Bellinger present calypso, a surrogate model for circumbinary accretion time series that is conditioned on parameters and includes randomness. Total and individual series are expressed in a PCA basis, with coefficients drawn from a multivariate Gaussian. The model captures the built-in randomness of the flow and long-term disk precession. The authors test whether added variance for limited training data helps and find it does not. Released as a pip-installable package, calypso yields a closed-form likelihood for inferring binary eccentricity and mass ratio.
arxiv-2605-23106: Cappanera, Jaramillo, and Siktar study an equation with super-square growth and a distant map from radial L1 mixing kernels with finite second moments. Mild rules cover biology and physics kernels, including decaying and sign changing kernels. Using strong growth, they prove some exist via the Mountain Pass Theorem, which links solutions to energy key points. The result holds under Dirichlet and Neumann edge rules, plus number tests for odd degree growth.
arxiv-2605-23206: Chen studies Bose-star forming in a Yukawa-Schrodinger-Poisson system. A finite link range damps the low-energy settling behind Bose-star forming, changing the star structure and the forming timescale. He derives a screened kinetic formula for forming in which the usual gravity Coulomb log is replaced by a finite Yukawa transport log. Static results show screening broadens the star profile versus the usual Newton soliton. Spectral runs with even and same-way starts show screening always delays forming, matching the screened forecast after one scaling fit.
arxiv-2605-24006: Barley and three co-authors offer a tabular method for ranking pipeline training schedules for language models. Their method links formula reasoning, schedule tables, and communication-aware simulation, letting GPipe, 1F1B, Chimera, and Hanayo be ranked across modelled systems. Schedule rankings vary with the abstraction used: communication can erase structural edges suggested by bubble analysis alone. On those assumptions, GPipe and 1F1B tie on runtime while 1F1B peaks lower on activation memory, Chimera wins at low microbatch counts, and Hanayo stays sensitive to network bottlenecks.
arxiv-2605-24306: Jia and five co-authors propose CoDA, a compact AI-image detector built on color-distribution probing, plus FakeForm, a benchmark of about 370,000 images. Lightweight artifact methods degrade on unseen generators, while large robust models cost heavily. Real photographs show smoother, more stable color patterns, while synthetic images carry color imbalances from neural generation. CoDA, built on a Noise-Quantization Probe with under one and a half million parameters, reaches state-of-the-art results. It posts the best cross-domain FakeForm results, staying competitive on photorealistic tests.
arxiv-2605-24506: Lin Feng and Xin He build data-driven control models with stability proofs for systems where failure is costly. Their ControlSynth neural differential equations force convergence through tractable matrix inequalities, while a second part folds outside inputs into the learned dynamics. A check pipeline then proves stability of Koopman-identified models by turning robustness into a solvable optimization task. In vehicle tracking and oscillator tests, the certified controller cut tracking error by up to 61 percent.
arxiv-2605-24606: Dean Price, Brian Kiedrowski, and Benoit Forget present a Monte Carlo scheme called the Method of Simultaneous Solutions, solving neutron transport and heat conduction. Derived weighting factors ride a neutron-led random walk, tallying figures for the temperature distribution. The main benefit is dropping a special heat solver, cutting compute cost. Drawbacks include branching to handle unlike edge rules, possible endless variance when tracked runs diverge, and errors from treating heat conduction as Boltzmann-led. Two demos, a slab and a six-sided pin cell, explore these limits.
arxiv-2605-24706: Matthieu Féraud and others argue metabolomics reuse stalls at the analysis layer, even as stores improve. Spectra, files, workflow outputs, labels and confidence evidence scatter across sites. Their MetaboKG framework engineers reusable knowledge from public stores and GNPS results. A conversion path preserves links across exports, files, spectra, and labels. A meaning model in PROV-O and SIO aligns with mass-spec, chemistry, taxonomy, environment, and cancer lists. A universal label tag supports late binding and stepwise intake. A demo on 680 network results shows traceable reuse and open queries.
arxiv-2605-24906: Zijie Cao leads PROBE, a training scheme hardening detectors of AI-made images against generators they have never seen. Detectors trained on large sets still fade when generation settings shift. Scale alone leaves wide gaps in the range of variants covered. PROBE flips the generator from a fixed data source into a guided one, using the detector as a critic to steer small manifold-level changes. Those changes yield realistic but hard-to-classify images, and retraining on those rare failure cases lifts generalization to unseen generators.
arxiv-2605-25306: Shengjun Zhang and colleagues tackle optimization over a peer network where agents see only function values, never gradients. Their ZOOM-PB method samples coordinates and blends estimates with a fractional-power response, keeping a primal state. The raw estimate stays as an anchor, with mixing weight tied to the step size. That design avoids flipping network direction when noisy estimates are averaged. Under a smooth oracle and a connected graph, it reaches nonconvex rates plus a fast term after a transient. Matched-budget tests against seven baselines confirm the design.
arxiv-2605-25806: Sangeeta and colleagues present ExtrAnom, a video anomaly detection benchmark focused on women's safety. Existing video sets favor bright, high-resolution close shots, leaving women-centric crimes underrepresented. ExtrAnom holds 1001 anomaly and normal videos across five crime categories, with dim, grainy and distant footage and four text annotations per video. It covers stalking, chain snatching, kidnapping, assassination and harassment. Tests show older sets fall short on women-centric crimes, and it aims to fill the gap.
arxiv-2605-26106: Lee and five colleagues improve masked diffusion language models by looping transformer layers. Masked diffusion models generate many tokens in parallel, unlike left-to-right models, but their architecture design remains underexplored. LoopMDM selectively loops early-middle layers, gaining a depth-scaling effect at training time without adding parameters. At inference time, varying the loop count scales compute flexibly. Across pretraining corpora, LoopMDM matches same-size diffusion models with up to 3.3 times fewer training floating-point operations, while beating them on several reasoning benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-26406: Haofan Lu and three colleagues build mmDiff, a ray-tracing tool that stays steady when 3D scene models carry holes and rough surfaces. Plain wireless simulation leans on crisp mirror-like reflection, which noise wrecks, so they swap in a smooth directional scattering model that spreads reflected power across nearby ray paths. They prove the swap keeps path-gain accuracy in the limit. The full tool then tunes material traits from sparse millimeter-wave readings. It also forecasts wireless channels, beating older mirror-reflection methods on noisy rebuilt geometry.
arxiv-2605-26606: Woojeong Kim and three others tackle wasted rollouts in group-based tuning of large language models. These methods score many tries per prompt, yet spend heavily on prompts whose rewards barely vary and teach almost nothing. Pilot-Commit first probes each prompt cheaply, then pours the rest of the budget into high-leverage prompts and skips dull ones. Across math tests and model sizes, it matches baseline accuracy with far fewer samples. It reaches targets nearly twice as quickly as GRPO and four times as quickly as DAPO.
arxiv-2605-26706: Ge and three colleagues model gamma photons hitting squeezed light, a quantum state whose field strength varies unevenly. Their runs show the uneven spread smooths harmonic peaks, boosts multi-photon channels, and blocks single-photon uptake, while positron spin alignment grows with stronger squeezing. Even when the mean field stays the same, these ups and downs reshape the spectrum, angles, and spin patterns of pairs made in the nonlinear Breit-Wheeler process.
arxiv-2605-26806: Sanjeev Kumar, Santosh Kumar, and Sengupta simulate compressible flow past a spinning cylinder across Reynolds numbers from 1000 to 6000, tracking lift, drag, and instability. They find a shift from regular vortex shedding to complex multi-mode oscillation, with a key bifurcation near Reynolds number 5650. Surrogate models trained on 101 costly simulations predict peak lift and instability onset well, with neural networks strongest, offering fast stand-ins for heavy fluid simulations.
arxiv-2605-26906: Bardyla and Elliott study Polish semigroup topologies on endomorphism monoids of linear orders. A new condition, property XX, yields automatic continuity for Borel measurable maps between certain such semigroups. For all monoids studied, the Zariski topology equals the pointwise one, making it the coarsest Hausdorff semigroup topology. One submonoid admits a unique Polish topology, while the full monoids admit infinitely many. One monoid admits exactly continuum many and no maximal second-countable topology. The results separate the tame cases from the wild ones.
arxiv-2605-27106: Lovén and five co-authors present Neural Pub/Sub, a federated substrate for self-managed edge-cloud systems across domains. Rather than central control, it uses market price signals. Its control loop monitors broker health and load, clears prices at marginal cost, plans placement over a feasibility region, dispatches across domains, and shares subscription summaries. Under gross-substitutes valuations, the authors prove decentralized price allocation matches a central oracle. A 1005-run campaign on a 4-domain testbed shows the market beating a single oracle while surviving broker death and partition.
arxiv-2605-27206: Nikita Zaigraev maps the makeup of abelian higher-spin cubic vertices with two supersymmetries. He builds the kept supercurrents from a principal supercurrent fixed by simple differential rules, written through higher-spin super-Weyl tensors. The vertices are fully fixed by three analytic supercurrents, giving a simple frame for reading off their parts.
arxiv-2605-27906: Kong and colleagues reduce hallucinations in multimodal reasoning models by treating the reasoning chain as a condition for the answer, not part of one lump output. Their RC-DPO method contrasts the same answer under different reasoning chains and mines grounded chains with tree search. Across models and benchmarks it curbed hallucinations and made reasoning more reliable.
arxiv-2605-28006: Leonardo Matthew Yauw, Wei-Bin Kou, and Yujiu Yang offer a unified way to watch how language models reason across architectures. Their IAR framework picks reasoning-crucial tokens with calibrated signal peaks, traces them across layers, and checks their stability across domains. Tests on six models show the interpretation holds across model families.
arxiv-2605-28206: Sharma and colleagues sketch a fault-tolerant quantum plan for a nonlinear shaking lattice, the quantum beta-FPUT chain. They work straight with grid displacements, dodging phonon-code overheads, and use Trotter blocks plus a quadrature split for shallow mode circuits. Counts of qubits, gates, and depth map a real path to modeling odd heat flow.
arxiv-2605-28306: Deng and colleagues adapt expert models to non-English tasks by aligning how they route tokens across languages. RA-MoE finds task experts in middle layers, where routing already lines up across tongues, and nudges target-language routing on hard cases toward successful English patterns. Across three models, three tasks, and six languages it beat standard fine-tuning and routing-aware rivals.
arxiv-2605-28506: Dvir Marsh and five colleagues teach a deep-learning system to focus light through multimode fiber using only reflected light. Ordinary methods need the transmitted field for feedback, which cannot be reached in place. Their system reads reflected signals that carry the fiber's internal state and predicts transmission, generalizing across fiber conditions. Trained on four million images from 1200 fiber setups, it reconstructs wavefronts robustly under strong perturbations, pointing toward non-invasive micro-endoscopy.
arxiv-2605-28706: Mengmeng Li, Yifan Hu, Daniel Kuhn, and Yan Li study endless robust Markov processes on state spaces with box sets. Their set sits in the hull of unknown kernels. They use the dynamic setup of robust processes and introduce a random first-order method for policy scoring. They prove its settling to the robust value function, giving sample needs of one over epsilon squared. A policy loop finds an epsilon-optimal policy with the same count. The method applies to zero-sum Markov games, strictly improving current sample needs.
arxiv-2605-28806: Viet Nguyen, Thao Nguyen, Vishal Patel, and Yuheng Li introduce VisualMem, a hybrid visual-text architecture for agent visual memory. Existing memory systems stay text-centric, reducing image turns to generic captions, while images carry personal facts text rarely states. VisualMem targets explicit evidence, like recurring user entities, and implicit evidence, like latent user facts from visual cues. Rather than collapsing images into captions, it uses conversational context to settle identity, ownership, and durable user facts, beating prior systems on its benchmark while staying competitive on text-memory benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-28906: Iwo Bialynicki-Birula and Zofia Bialynicka-Birula derive sharp uncertainty relations bounding spreads in position space and in push space. The same form holds for classical light beams, steady quantum light beams, and single photons. The product of place and wave spreads is at least five halves. Their result unifies old and quantum treatments of light, showing the same bound governs beams and single photons alike.
arxiv-2605-29306: The MINOS+ Collaboration models the effect of the heliospheric magnetic field on cosmic-ray muon shadows. Shadows cast in the muon sky by the Sun were located using data from the MINOS far detector in Northern Minnesota. They were observed near solar minimum, near solar maximum, and across thirteen years. Muon positions for each shadow were sampled to simulate cosmic-ray motion near the Sun under the Parker spiral model and a dipole geomagnetic model. The Parker spiral fits best at solar minimum and worst at solar maximum.
arxiv-2605-29806: Chris Clarkson and Pritha Paul define an observer power spectrum for lightcone statistics in large-scale structure. Standard spectra suit fields on slices, where translation symmetry keeps Fourier modes uncorrelated and spectra diagonal. On our past lightcone, wide-angle shifts, radial change, and integrated effects like lensing break that symmetry, mixing modes. Fourier transforming over observer positions at fixed lightcone coordinates yields a spectrum that stays diagonal for any observable. Standard two-point statistics return as projections of this spectrum, illustrated with a relativistic kernel for galaxy number counts.
arxiv-2605-30106: Natalia Klaus, Juan Conejero and Palina Tolmach report a pipeline that turns production Rust cryptographic code into machine-checked proofs in Lean 4. Symbolic tools lift Rust into Lean, libraries supply the mathematical targets, and AI provers close proof obligations. The Lean kernel checks every proof, so AI errors cannot break soundness. Within the Ethereum Foundation's zkEVM project, it covers Plonky3 primitives and RISC Zero Merkle checks. One prover authored two unfinished bounds proofs, and the report names toolchain drift and extraction limits as gaps.
arxiv-2605-30606: Nguyen introduces the refined Diophantine exponent, a measure of repeats in infinite words that detects weaker repeats than the classical exponent while keeping its strength. Adamczewski and Bugeaud introduced the classical exponent in 2007 to prove transcendence results for numbers whose base expansions are simple. The refined version applies where repetition is partly hidden by noise, joining earlier results of Corvaja and Zannier and of Kebis, Luca, Ouaknine, Scoones, and Worrell. Finer versions yield results on transcendence measures, spurred by recent work in algebraic dynamics.
arxiv-2605-30706: Smith and colleagues document moving a website from a Texas data center to a solar-powered server built from used gear. Permacomputing, a community of practice, seeks computing grounded in resilience, reuse, sufficiency, and ecological limits. Guided by its principles and relational aesthesis, the authors explore changing material and perceptual relations. Findings reveal frictions in leaving a techno-look while reusing old technologies, group paths forward, and the promise of making digital infrastructures visible and felt. Rather than a token gesture, such habits can grow freedom, agency, and responsibility.
arxiv-2605-30806: Miyazawa and Takagi construct an explicit combinatorial procedure. It gives a bijection between highest weight paths in crystal graphs of degree n and integer partitions of n with sqrank or rerank r. The graphs are associated with irreducible modules of the affine quantum group Uq, odd-dimensional in one crystal and even-dimensional in the other. A side result reads the Bernard-Pasquier-Serban spinon motif picture, for Wess-Zumino-Witten conformal models, in exact terms.
arxiv-2605-31106: Ko and Lee build generative models that diffuse data over curved spaces, where the usual heat kernel has no tidy formula. Their approach solves the heat equation on a chosen manifold directly with a physics-informed neural network, learning the log heat kernel from a short-time approximation. The learned kernel then drives both noising and score-based denoising, and the team shows it working on spheres, rotations, positive-definite matrices and point clouds.
arxiv-2605-31206: Sha and colleagues run a small timing circuit built from amorphous thin-film semiconductors while heavy ions strike it. The circuit has just 100 transistors, yet it keeps giving a working Hello World output while powered under tantalum-ion flux. Total exposure reaches a million ions per square centimetre. That long powered run in harsh radiation marks a step forward for digital circuits in extreme places, and points to amorphous semiconductors as a base for tough electronics.
arxiv-2605-31306: Gotoh, Lim and Kim measure toughness in Bayesian robust optimisation. They introduce worst-case posterior and likelihood sensitivity. These gauge how expected cost responds to worst-case shifts in each. Choice makers get two hard robustness gauges. The first gauge fades as its spread shrinks to zero with learning, but learning does not kill the second. A robust design trades payoff against both gauges near Pareto-best, the authors show for deviation-based doubt sets.
arxiv-2606-00206:
Lotfi and co-authors find that squeezed reasoning models think too long, yet need not. Shrinking a model by cuts to its weights saves space and cost. The effect on step-by-step thought was not well known. Their tests span math, code, and science tasks.

Stiff cuts trim scores and stretch thought chains at once. In up to half of the fails, the right reply shows mid-chain. The model then talks past it and ends wrong. High-strain spots in the output match high doubt spots. At those spots, squeezed models pick stall words like wait or but. A plain fine on those words cuts chain length by up to a fifth. Scores hold or rise, and stall fails drop sharply.
arxiv-2606-00306:
Luong and Chen rethink the heat dial in how big models teach small ones. In distillation, a teacher's soft picks guide a student net. A dial named temperature softens those picks. Past picks twixt two gap gauges left that dial out of view.

Their reads show the dial acts in a lopsided way on the two gauges. It feeds rich side cues to the forward gauge. For the reverse gauge, it just scales step sizes. At low heat, the reverse gauge wins the race. At high heat, the forward gauge wins across guide tests. Heat helps a broad kin of teach goals too. Plain gap tools with tuned heat tie fresh top tools.
arxiv-2606-00506:
Yu and co-authors forecast power use with a graph-boosted state-space model that owns its doubt. Sound calls on power use guide grid work and green plans. Past tools treat the task as time lines alone. They miss how zones in a grid sway each other in space.

Their tool, EnergyMamba, joins two parts in one frame. A graph-fed state-space core pours zone traits from the grid web into time flow. A next part tunes call bands live as data drift. It scales bands by local traits and learns from fresh misses. Tests span four big sets from three states. Marks beat 15 top base tools on truth and doubt in fair terms.
arxiv-2606-00606:
Zhang, He, and Zhang build fine source traits to spot AI-made shots across new fields. Such spot tools most oft sag when the field shifts. Map views show true and fake traits still part on new sets. The head that grades them leans on home-field marks, they find.

Their frame, FiSeR, learns traits that port with more grace. It holds the name of each fake source in its train marks. A coarse drill splits true shots from fake ones in the set. A fine drill splits fake shots by which tool made them. Trained on WildFake, the tool gains on four cross-field sets. Few-shot fits with just ten tags per class gain yet more.
arxiv-2606-00806:
Hahn and Romero probe a narrow zone where a quantum device wins in this 2026 paper. Their task is binary compressed sensing: rebuild a sparse signal of bits from few measures. Below a known phase line, the true answer exists but convex shortcuts fail. That band is called the relaxation gap.

In 19,775 trials, they run nine classical solvers and two modes of a D-Wave quantum annealer. At size 32 with five active bits, D-Wave gets 7 percent exact recovery where all classical methods score zero. The gap is firm by a Fisher test, at p of 0.018. At size 64, chip layout costs limit the quantum device, though its hybrid solver stays close to the best classical one. Energy maps show the true signal sits in the deepest basin, while false answers rest in shallow traps. The authors call this early, finite-size proof, not a settled claim.
arxiv-2606-01006:
Wang and co-authors track single red blood cells in eye scans in this 2026 paper. Blood flow in retinal capillaries could flag many eye diseases early. Few tools can measure flow at that fine scale. A new imaging method, erythrocyte mediated angiography, shows single red cells in motion. Counting flow from it needs automated detection and tracking, which barely existed.

Their framework, EMTrack, fills that gap. A flow context module detects cells and tells moving ones from paused ones. A topology aware tracker then follows cells across frames. It copes with large jumps between frames and wild swings in motion. The team also built RBF-EMA, a dataset with full detection and tracking labels for this imaging type. On that data, EMTrack beats baseline methods on both tasks, in numbers and in visual checks, they report. The work points to automated retinal blood flow measures for clinic use.
arxiv-2606-01106:
Sun and co-authors route video proof through a symbolic reasoner in this 2026 paper. TimeLogicQA tests if systems can reason about time in video. Its questions cover whether events exist, their order, how long they last, their edges, and their overlap. A single model pass often blurs those splits.

Their pipeline parts perception from logic. Each question is parsed into event targets, answer mode, options, and temporal operators. Videos route by length and operator difficulty. Short clips give ordered full frame proof. Long ones give event focused windows. A multimodal model writes structured visual evidence for the events. Programmatic verifiers recover dense action intervals. A deterministic reducer then applies operator specific rules to reach the answer. A fusion step accepts the answer only when proof, program, and confidence agree. On the official test, the system achieves an average accuracy of 81.8.
arxiv-2606-01206: Hsu studies Weyl algebras on Braverman-Kazhdan spaces, a topic in pure math. Let G be a split, simply connected group over a field. Let P be a maximal parabolic subgroup of G. Hsu looks at the ring of differential operators on a quotient space built from P and G. Hsu shows that this ring shares key traits with classical Weyl algebras. He also builds a matching theory of D-modules for the space. The work is short and dense. It suits readers who work in algebra and geometry.
arxiv-2606-01306:
He and co-authors add frequency awareness to a forecasting transformer. Transformers lead multivariate time series forecasting today. Their attention acts like a low-pass filter by nature. Sharp local changes get smoothed away in the process. Past frequency fixes use fixed bases and uniform tweaks. Real series change their spectra over time, though. FAiT fixes the bias from inside the model.

Inverted attention treats the attention map as a learnable filter. A high-pass branch recovers transient signals it suppressed. Dynamic temporal-frequency modulation reweights spectral bands per instance. This gives fine control over multi-scale patterns as they evolve. Tests on wide benchmarks beat strong baselines. The model keeps computational costs in check as well.
arxiv-2606-01506:
Yang adds an arc search to the BFGS method for nonlinear optimization. BFGS is a classic method for unconstrained problems. It works well on convex problems. On non-convex ones, it may fail to converge in a reliable way. Modified BFGS variants handle both classes of problems. A robust BFGS variant is known for global convergence. It also has fast local convergence, at a superlinear rate, under mild assumptions.

Yang aims to cut the cost of that robust variant. An arc search replaces the usual line search step. The good convergence traits of the robust method are kept. Tests compare the new method with state-of-the-art rivals. The reported results favor the arc-search version on efficiency.
arxiv-2606-01706:
Zhang, Liu, and Zhang build higher-order debiased estimators for harder treatment targets. Influence-function estimators can converge too slowly in some settings. Higher-order versions were built to fix that flaw. Most results cover explicit targets, like average treatment effects. Real work often needs harder targets instead. Quantile effects and complex policy effects are two such cases. These targets are defined only implicitly. They solve nonlinear estimating equations, as M- or Z-estimation problems.

The team build estimators for a class of non-separable structural models. U-process theory gives the statistical traits of the new estimators. The estimators relax smoothness demands on nuisance parameters, compared with past work. The results add to the theory base for econometrics and causal inference.
arxiv-2606-02006:
Amougou Mbida and Angermeir present an early study of software research artifacts. Their focus is replication packages. These packages should let others repeat a study and reuse its materials. Yet checks of their quality are still mostly done by hand. Such checks are hard to scale up.

They turn open science rules into clear tests that a computer can check. From 380 rules in 34 sources, they build 51 criteria. They make 31 of them work for automated checks. A team of agents then reads a package and writes a report backed by evidence. In tests on five packages, the authors report high consistency across runs. They also report weaker results on studies that use qualitative methods. A small survey suggests researchers saw the tool as useful.
arxiv-2606-02106:
Lafrance tests when tabular foundation models transfer across data types. One pipeline is applied identically across all modalities. Data are first mapped to fixed vector forms. An equiangular tight frame stage preprocesses those vectors. A tabular foundation model then infers in context.

The study spans 95 datasets in total. Seven signal modalities are covered by the sets. Vision, audio, speech, and text are among them. Molecular, time-series, and tabular data complete the list. Two regimes structure the evaluation throughout. Performance is judged against the strongest light tuned baseline. The same frozen features serve both sides of the test. The pipeline proves broadly competitive, Lafrance reports. It does not match the best specialized models.
arxiv-2606-02206:
Hu and co-authors propose purely mechanical moiré strain skyrmions in twisted bilayers that slide. Defects that strain a material shape how the material behaves, and strain glass made by defect engineering offers a model for steering domains at the nanoscale. Their skyrmions are elastic textures guarded by topology, and sliding one layer against the other, together with the bilayer chirality, steers how they move. An empirical continuum elastic model, combined with symmetry analysis, supports the proposal.

The skyrmion lattice structure emerges as the elastic ground state in that model. Under interlayer sliding, the skyrmions show a Skyrmion Hall effect, moving sideways as they travel. The Hall angle is set by the bilayer chirality and is inversely proportional to the moiré twist angle. The authors establish interlayer sliding as an efficient, low energy control knob for these topological textures. The work links mechanics and topology in two dimensional materials.
arxiv-2606-02306:
Howes and co-authors study a population wide tournament in which agents experiment by searching over correlated objects. The agents care about both their absolute wealth and their wealth relative to others. The focus is on the beliefs the agents hold about their environment, namely the stochastic processes that correspond to their experimentation. Beliefs turn out to shape both output and the spread of outcomes across the population.

The authors find that optimism leads to higher output, but it also produces greater inequality. They connect those observations with empirical evidence that suggests a positive relationship between inequality and entrepreneurship. Delusions of grandeur thus carry both benefits and hazards in the model. Overconfidence can fuel growth at the same time as it widens gaps between agents. The paper gives that tension a formal treatment for economists who study entrepreneurship.
arxiv-2606-02406:
Hanning and co-authors rebuild house roofs as 3D wireframes from sparse data. Their entry targets the S23DR Challenge 2026. Inputs are sparse point clouds from structure-from-motion. Ground-level semantic labels and depth maps join them. The method is a Transformer encoder-decoder in the DETR style.

The point cloud is thinned by semantic priority before use. Gestalt and ADE20k class features enrich each point. Points also draw features from a frozen autoencoder through projection. Learned queries then decode straight into 3D wireframe edges. Cross-attention drives that decoding step. On the HoHo 22k dataset, the method beats crafted and learned baselines. Its Hybrid Structure Score reaches 0.6476. That score took second place on the private leaderboard.
arxiv-2606-02506:
Ou and co-authors answer questions about relations in videos with an evidence-first pipeline. Answers hinge on hidden spatial relations and event boundaries. Target identity and dialogue context also matter. A single striking frame rarely suffices. The pipeline starts from a strong GPT-5.5 video solver. Question-aware evidence ledgers then sharpen the answer.

Each ledger makes one need explicit. Targets, count units, and reference frames are spelled out. Temporal and spatial scope is fixed per question type. Ledger types cover counting, spatial, endpoint, viewpoint, and dialogue needs. Tools like open-vocabulary detection and ASR serve as evidence only. A conservative gate guards the final answer. It switches only when outside evidence uniquely backs a rival option. The pipeline reaches 92.95 percent overall accuracy on the test split. Macro accuracy reaches 93.79 percent.
arxiv-2606-02606:
