Their database paper appeared in Frontiers in Psychology in 2014. Pictures of food can trigger craving and sway choice, yet labs used inconsistent image sets with unknown traits.

The database holds five hundred sixty-eight food images and three hundred fifteen non-food images, each with detailed data. Nearly two thousand people from German-speaking countries and North America rated the images for liking, arousal, tastiness, desire to eat, recognisability, and visual complexity. Entries also list nutrients, energy density, and physical traits such as brightness and contrast. Shared standards should make findings across labs easier to compare.
europmc-pmc4076506:
Yoshiki Vázquez-Baeza, Meg Pirrung, Antonio Gonzalez, and Rob Knight introduced EMPeror, a tool for viewing high-throughput microbial community data in three dimensions. Their paper appeared in GigaScience in 2013. Sequencing let ecologists profile microbes in ever more samples, and projects like the Earth Microbiome Project raised the need to explore such data with rich background details.

EMPeror runs in a web browser and plots communities as spheres on principal coordinate axes. Users can colour, resize, hide, or relabel points by any sample metadata, rescale axes, show individual microbe types, and view resampled data to judge how solid a cluster is. Parallel coordinate views are also offered. The open-source tool is tailored to microbial ecologists exploring large sample sets.
europmc-pmc4086106:
Xavier Robert and Patrice Gouet built ENDscript 2, a web tool that pulls the key traits out of a protein shape file and shows them in clear form. Their paper came out in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014. The new build was made from scratch to be fast, right, and easy to use.

From one file, the tool makes neat charts. One chart lines up kin proteins and shades each spot by how much it has stayed the same. A second part shows the shape parts found by test. A third part adds a long list of traits of the stuff of the protein. All of this is also mapped onto views in 3D that the user can move. Users from new hands to experts can tune the tool to their needs.
europmc-pmc4112806:
Nicole Wilkinson and Kostas Pantopoulos reviewed the IRP/IRE system, the body's iron-sensing switch, as revealed by mouse models. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Pharmacology in 2014. Two iron regulatory proteins bind marks on certain messenger RNAs, raising or lowering production of proteins for iron, oxygen, and energy handling.

Cell studies had set out the basics. Mouse work showed wider duties. One protein governs red blood cell production and gut iron absorption by controlling a hypoxia factor's message. The other dominates iron uptake and haem building in young red cells. Mice lacking the first develop excess red cells and lung hypertension; the second's loss gives a different pattern. The review shows how a local iron switch also runs whole-body iron balance.
europmc-pmc4148706:
Christopher J. Oliphant, Andrew N. J. McKenzie, and colleagues showed that two immune cell types talk to each other to expel parasitic worms. Their study appeared in Immunity in 2014. Group 2 innate lymphoid cells release a signal, IL-13, that protects against worms but harms in allergy and asthma.

Using mouse models that remove these cells, the team found helper T cell responses falter without them. The innate cells carry the display molecule MHCII and converse with antigen-specific T cells: T cell IL-2 feeds the innate cells' growth and IL-13 output. Innate cells lacking MHCII could not drive efficient expulsion of the worm Nippostrongylus brasiliensis. The dialogue, the authors argue, boosts the handover to adaptive immunity and shapes type 2 responses.
europmc-pmc4241506:
Dimple Chakravarty and a team of eleven co-authors found a long non-coding RNA driving prostate cancer in Nature Communications in 2014. Prostate cancer growth is usually steered by the androgen receptor, but the oestrogen receptor alpha also sits in these tumours with an unclear role. Long non-coding RNAs, which regulate genes without making proteins, offered a place to look.

Combining binding maps with RNA sequencing, the team listed the non-coding transcripts the oestrogen receptor controls. One, NEAT1, stood out as the most overexpressed in prostate cancer, and two large patient cohorts tied high NEAT1 to worse progression. Cancer cells rich in NEAT1 shrugged off androgen-blocking drugs. NEAT1 reshapes the chemical marks on target gene promoters to favour their activity. The authors name it a driver of aggressive, treatment-resistant disease.
europmc-pmc4253006:
Maria Tsompana and Michael J. Buck reviewed ways to map open chromatin in Epigenetics and Chromatin in 2014. Genes switch on where the DNA packaging loosens, letting control proteins reach promoters and enhancers. Those open sites can be found genome-wide by cutting or tagging DNA where it is exposed, then sequencing what comes out.

The review compares the main assays, enzyme-based and chemical, for what each actually isolates and where each misleads. Open sites mark the control elements active in a given cell type, so the maps reveal which genes a cell is prepared to use and how that changes in development and disease. Practical cautions on sample handling and data analysis run through the paper, which closes with what the field needs next: gentler methods and finer resolution.
europmc-pmc4265206:
Maria Thom wrote a solo review of hippocampal sclerosis in epilepsy in Neuropathology and Applied Neurobiology in 2014. Hippocampal sclerosis, a scarring pattern of neuron loss in the hippocampus, is the most common finding in the most common focal epilepsy, mesial temporal lobe epilepsy. A 2013 international classification gave pathologists shared ground, and Thom takes stock.

Certain traits, granule cell spread and mossy fibre sprouting, mark the epilepsy-linked form and help separate it from sclerosis of other causes. What starts the scarring stays unsettled: fever seizures in childhood, genes, inflammation, and early development all have evidence and gaps. Thom argues post-mortem studies add what surgical samples cannot, the whole network's changes and the marks of decades of seizures. Several subtypes likely hide under one name.
europmc-pmc4282306:
Nita Gandhi Forouhi and Nicholas J. Wareham give an overview of diabetes as a world health problem. Their article appeared in Medicine in 2014. Numbers with diabetes stood at hundreds of millions in 2013 and were set to climb steeply by 2035, driven by rising obesity and unhealthy ways of life.

The article separates type 1 from type 2 diabetes, with type 2 making up the great bulk of cases. It covers the harm diabetes does across the body, from eyes, kidneys, and nerves to heart and blood vessels, and the early deaths and costs that follow. The piece gives clinicians a compact account of causes, spread, and burden.
europmc-pmc4299606:
Georg Zeller and eleven co-authors tested whether the microbes in stool can flag colorectal cancer early. Their study appeared in Molecular Systems Biology in 2014. Certain bacteria had been tied to this cancer, but no one had shown whether stool microbe patterns could screen for it as well as the standard blood in stool test.

Stool DNA from a study group of just over one hundred and fifty people yielded microbe markers that separated patients from controls about as well as the standard test. Using both together raised detection of cancers by more than forty five percent while keeping false alarms level. The markers worked in early stage disease and held up in groups from other countries.
europmc-pmc4373506:
Mariya Petrova, Elke Lievens, Shweta Malik, Nicole Imholz, and Sarah Lebeer reviewed vaginal Lactobacillus bacteria as signs and agents of health, in Frontiers in Physiology in 2015. In about 70 percent of women, these bacteria dominate the vaginal community, and in any one woman a single species can make up nearly all of it. Four species turn up most often. Their waste products in vaginal fluid can block bacterial and viral invaders at a key entry point.

A Lactobacillus-led community thus serves as a marker of a healthy vaginal ecosystem, the review argues. That balance shifts fast with menstruation, sex, pregnancy, and infection, and its loss, with rising diversity, marks bacterial vaginosis. The authors caution that lacking such dominance does not by itself mean disease. They also survey how fluid tests and molecular counts read the community.
europmc-pmc4520006:
Gudrun Winter and four co-authors review what the amino acid arginine does in plants, in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2015. Nitrogen limits plant growth in most soils, since plants need large amounts to build DNA and proteins. Among amino acids, arginine packs the most nitrogen per carbon, which makes it a handy store of spare nitrogen.

Plants build arginine in chloroplasts from ornithine, and the rate is tightly tuned to the plant's food state, though some steps stay poorly mapped. The review covers how arginine moves within and between cells, and what it feeds into. Products include proline, nitric oxide, and polyamines, each with its own debated route. Transport and breakdown, the authors argue, matter as much as synthesis for plant health.
europmc-pmc4541706:
Wiep Scheper and Jeroen J. M. Hoozemans review the cell's protein-folding alarm in brain diseases, in Acta Neuropathologica in 2015. When misfolded proteins pile up in the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell's folding workshop, three sensors named PERK, IRE1, and ATF6 launch the unfolded protein response. Clumped proteins are also the hallmark of Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and related diseases, so a link was suspected.

A decade of work has tested that link in patient brain tissue and in cell and mouse models. Findings clash between models, often for method reasons. The authors argue that human brain material is the key reference for judging the response's real role, and they weigh the evidence disease by disease.
europmc-pmc4574606:
Stephane E. Castel and four co-authors set standards for measuring which gene copy a cell uses, in Genome Biology in 2015. Each person carries two copies of most genes, and allelic expression analysis checks whether one copy works harder than the other. The approach feeds studies of gene regulation and RNA decay, but its read counts are riddled with technical traps.

Low-quality or double-counted reads, genotyping slips, mapping bias toward the reference copy, sample handling effects, and uneven sequencing depth can all fake an imbalance. The paper tests each error source and gives correction guidelines. With their quality controls, detection of true allelic differences improves. Tools for producing clean allelic data at scale are included.
europmc-pmc4584306:
Marta Alenquer and Maria João Amorim review how viruses exploit exosomes, in Viruses in 2015. Exosomes are tiny vesicles cells release when internal bubble compartments fuse with the cell surface. They carry sorted proteins, lipids, and RNAs between cells, shaping health and disease. How cargo is chosen and whether compartments are destroyed or released remain open questions.

Viruses are natural hijackers of such systems, and the young field of exosomes in infection is still debating basics. The review first lays out what exosomes contain and how they form, then the control points that steer them. It closes on viral infection, where exosomes can in principle smuggle any factor with the right sorting signal, a vulnerability viruses appear to use.
europmc-pmc4611506:
Corinne F. Maurice and colleagues' 2015 survey centres on gut microbes in wild wood mice across two years. Most mouse microbiome work uses lab animals, whose lives differ sharply from wild ones. The team sampled mice in two nearby woodlands and sequenced a bacterial marker gene. The work appeared in The ISME Journal.

Ten bacterial phyla colonized the mice, with Lactobacillus the most common genus, and likely pathogens were widespread. Season drove the biggest shifts in both years. As diets moved from insects toward seeds, Lactobacillus fell while Alistipes and Helicobacter rose. Place, sex, breeding status, and gut worms mattered less. The study shows that environment and season, not just the host, shape natural gut communities.
europmc-pmc4651906:
A 2015 study from Mario dos Reis and colleagues centres on the limits of dating animal origins with molecular clocks. Fossils place definite two-sided animals in the Cambrian, yet DNA studies often push their split far earlier. Earlier clock studies used little data and glossed over fossil uncertainty. The team used an unprecedented molecular dataset with four fossil calibration strategies. The work appeared in Current Biology.

Their estimates place the crown animal group in the Cryogenian period, with most two-sided animal phyla diversifying in the Ediacaran. But the error bars stay wide no matter the strategy. Ancient fossil ambiguity and clock irregularities cap how precise such dates can be. Pinpointing divergences tightly enough to test links with geological events is not yet possible, the authors conclude.
europmc-pmc4655306:
In 2015, Michael T. White and colleagues published an analysis on antibody responses to the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine and what they mean for how long protection lasts. The vaccine targets a surface protein of the malaria parasite. The analysis reused data from a phase 3 trial run between 2009 and 2014. It appeared in The Lancet Infectious Diseases.

Data covered 8,922 children and 6,537 infants in Africa. Older children made stronger antibody responses than young infants. Antibodies faded in two phases: a fast component with a half-life of about forty-five days and a slow one near five hundred ninety-one days. A booster raised the long-lived share of the response from twelve to thirty percent. Linking antibody levels to malaria cases let the authors model how vaccine protection wanes.
europmc-pmc4688306:
Toshirou Nishida, Jean-Yves Blay, Seiichi Hirota, Yuko Kitagawa, and Yoon-Koo Kang summarized care for gastrointestinal stromal tumors in Gastric Cancer in 2016. These tumors, called GISTs, are rare cancers but the most common sarcoma of the gut. Targeted drugs such as imatinib changed their treatment, while surgery stays central for a cure. The five authors compare the current guidelines from American, European, and Japanese bodies.

Most advice matches across the guidelines. GISTs split into subtypes by gene faults, in genes such as KIT and PDGFRA, and the subtype shapes care. Small differences remain, for example in imatinib dose for one mutation type. Shared aims run through all versions: sharper diagnosis, better survival, and control of costs. The review gives clinicians one clear map of standard diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up.
europmc-pmc4718806:
Xiao-chen Bai, Eeson Rajendra, Guanghui Yang, Yigong Shi, and Sjors H. W. Scheres sampled the shapes of gamma-secretase in eLife in 2015. Gamma-secretase is a membrane protease that snips many proteins; its mishandling of one target feeds Alzheimer's disease, and of another, cancer. Earlier freezing-based imaging by this group produced a structure whose cutting subunit, presenilin, looked partly disordered. The new work sorts the old images more finely to reveal the molecule's moving states.

Three distinct conformations emerged. In one, an extra helix appears that belongs to none of the known parts. Binding of a blocking drug, or of that extra helix, froze two of presenilin's helices that otherwise swing freely. From the pattern the authors build a model of how a substrate slides into the cutting zone. The study turns one blurred snapshot into a small movie of the machine's working poses.
europmc-pmc4736106:
Xiangzhao Ai, Chris Jun Hui Ho, Junxin Aw, and a large team built nanoparticles that gather inside tumors by chemical reaction, in Nature Communications in 2016. Getting nanomedicines to pile up in tumors is a standing problem. The team's particles carry a disguise: peptides that a tumor-associated enzyme snips off. Snipping exposes a reactive group that bonds covalently to a partner group on neighboring particles, cross-linking them into clusters too big to wash away.

The clustered particles glow more brightly under laser light, thanks to their rare-earth crystals, which sharpens tumor imaging. The same light boosts production of a cell-killing oxygen form by attached sensitizers. In mice, the system slowed tumors whether injected into the tumor or into a vein with a targeting ligand added. The authors offer the enzyme-triggered clumping as a general trick for placing nanomedicines exactly where disease chemistry is active.
europmc-pmc4754406:
Susana Romero-Garcia and three colleagues review lactate in Frontiers in Immunology in 2016. Lactate is the sour by-product tumors make in bulk when they burn sugar fast, even with oxygen present. Long treated as waste, it now looks like an active force inside tumor tissue.

The review traces lactate from its making to its effects. Tumor cells and support cells both release it, and it re-tunes the cells around them. It also dulls immune cells that should attack the tumor, which helps cancers hide. The authors weigh drug plans that block lactate handling and note its use as a warning sign for how a case may go. The piece frames lactate as a target worth testing in care.
europmc-pmc4756306:
Mausita Karmakar and three co-authors study neutrophils in Nature Communications in 2016. Neutrophils are the most common white blood cells at infection sites. ATP, a molecule cells spill when stressed, gathers at those same sites. Whether ATP switches on the neutrophil alarm system was the open question.

Human and mouse neutrophils both carried working P2X7 receptors, the ATP sensors at issue. ATP opened the sensor, drained key ions, and woke the NLRP3 inflammasome, the alarm complex that releases the fever signal IL-1β. Strength of response varied by a person's gene variant. In infected mouse eyes, neutrophils were the main sensor carriers, and mice without the sensor cleared the germs poorly. The findings place this pathway at the heart of early infection defense.
europmc-pmc4906406:
Jacob J. Chabon and co-authors read tumor DNA from blood in Nature Communications in 2016 to map how lung cancers resist EGFR-blocking drugs. Blood-borne tumor DNA allows repeat sampling without new biopsies. The team profiled 43 patients on rociletinib, a third-generation EGFR blocker for non-small cell lung cancer.

Nearly half the patients, 46 percent, carried several resistance routes at once after earlier blockers, a sign of deep tumor variety within one person. Rociletinib resistance repeatedly involved MET, EGFR, PIK3CA, ERBB2, KRAS, and RB1 changes, plus one new EGFR fault, L798I. A blood draw can thus watch resistance evolve and hint at the next drug pairing.
europmc-pmc4987906:
Enis Afgan leads the Galaxy team reporting the 2016 update of their biomedical analysis platform. Their paper appeared in Nucleic Acids Research in 2016. Next generation sequencing floods labs with data that need heavy computation. Many biologists lack informatics training, so analysis, not data, became the bottleneck. Since 2005 Galaxy has offered a web environment where advanced tools run through menus and forms, with every step tracked automatically for later inspection or reuse.

The update highlights features for large scale work: bigger datasets, richer workflows, and easier sharing of exact analysis histories. Transparency is the design core, since a tracked history lets others reproduce a result or audit it. The authors describe Galaxy as shared infrastructure for a field in a computation crisis. New features aim to keep the platform usable as data volumes keep climbing.
europmc-pmc4990706:
Kun-Hsing Yu and six co-authors teach a computer to predict lung cancer survival from microscope images alone. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2016. Pathologists read tumor slides by eye to diagnose non-small cell lung cancer, but their calls predict survival poorly. The team gathered more than two thousand whole slide images from a cancer atlas, plus a Stanford tissue array set. Software extracted nearly ten thousand quantitative features describing cell shapes, textures, and tissue patterns.

Machine learning picked the features that split shorter term from longer term survivors in stage I disease. The split held for both adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, the two main types. It also validated on the independent Stanford set. The authors argue automated image features can feed precision oncology, adding an objective prognosis layer to the standard slide reading. The method, they note, transfers to other organs.
europmc-pmc5081106:
The NCD Risk Factor Collaboration tracks world diabetes since 1980 in The Lancet in 2016. A global target aims to halt the rise in adult diabetes prevalence at its 2010 level by 2025. To judge progress, the collaboration pooled 751 population studies with biomarker measurements from 4.4 million adults and modelled trends for 200 countries from 1980 to 2014.

Age-standardised prevalence rose from 4.3 percent to 9.0 percent in men and from 5.0 percent to 7.9 percent in women. The number of adults with diabetes nearly quadrupled, from 108 million to 422 million, driven by rising prevalence together with population growth and ageing. Prevalence in 2014 was lowest in northwestern Europe and highest in Polynesia and Micronesia, at nearly 25 percent. Growth was faster in low- and middle-income countries. On post-2000 trends, the authors imply, few countries stand placed to meet the 2025 target.
europmc-pmc5082806:
Georg Goergen and four co-authors report the fall armyworm's arrival in Africa in PLoS ONE in 2016. This moth caterpillar is a prime pest of maize across the Americas, long kept out of other continents despite occasional interceptions in Europe. In early 2016, outbreaks hit maize in southwestern and northern Nigeria, Benin, and Togo, and on São Tomé, where the government appealed to the FAO for help.

At first the damage was blamed on local armyworm species. Morphology and DNA barcoding settled the question: the specimens matched fall armyworm references exactly. Specimens from Nigeria and from São Tomé fell into two separate clusters, differing slightly from each other. That pattern points to two independent introductions, not one spreading invasion. The authors warn briefly of what a established American maize pest could mean for tropical African harvests, where maize is a staple and defenses are untested.
europmc-pmc5124306:
Ola Brynildsrud, Jon Bohlin, Lonneke Scheffer, and Vegard Eldholm introduced a software tool called Scoary in Genome Biology in 2016. Genome-wide association studies link gene variants to traits in humans, but bacteria have barely been studied this way, partly because their genomes shuffle and cluster in ways human methods do not handle.

Scoary scores every gene in a bacterial pangenome, the full gene set of a species, for links to a trait such as drug resistance, while correcting for family relatedness among strains. It runs fast, asks little of the user, and makes few assumptions about evolution. The tool is written in Python and released under an open license, aiming to make bacterial association studies a routine part of microbiology.
europmc-pmc5127806:
Michael J. Crosse, Giovanni M. Di Liberto, Adam Bednar, and Edmund C. Lalor introduced a free MATLAB toolbox in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience in 2016. The toolbox links brain signals to natural, ongoing stimuli such as speech, a harder problem than the brief flashes and beeps of classic brain response studies.

Their method fits a filter, called a temporal response function, that maps features of a stimulus onto the brain's electrical or magnetic response, or the reverse. The paper reviews the history of such approaches and explains the regularized regression at the toolbox's core, including how to tune it for each data set. Worked examples show the outputs researchers can expect, and the authors close with the tool's limits and room to grow.
europmc-pmc517706:
Robert C. Edgar described the MUSCLE alignment program in BMC Bioinformatics in 2004, writing solo. Aligning many protein sequences at once underpins family trees, structure prediction, and spotting key residues, but growing databases were outrunning existing programs in both speed and memory.

MUSCLE, first introduced in a shorter paper, is detailed here with several new accuracy and efficiency techniques, plus a MUSCLE-fast option for high-throughput work. On four standard benchmarks it matched or beat rival programs, including CLUSTALW and MAFFT. The fast variant aligned 1,000 sequences of average length 282 in 21 seconds on a desktop. That is typically two to three orders of magnitude faster than CLUSTALW, at similar accuracy. The program is free to download.
europmc-pmc5206706:
Po-Yuan Tung, John D. Blischak, Chiaowen Joyce Hsiao, David A. Knowles, Jonathan E. Burnett, Jonathan K. Pritchard, and Yoav Gilad published a methods study in Scientific Reports in 2017 on noise in single-cell RNA sequencing. The work asks where the unwanted variation in these experiments comes from and how study design can limit it.

Working on the Fluidigm C1 platform, the group ran three replicates from three human stem cell lines and added molecular tags meant to correct for copying bias. Genotype drove most of the real differences, yet repeat runs of the same material still varied a lot. Counts from the molecular tags also shifted with both biology and technique, so they are not a clean measure of gene activity. The paper closes with a practical design framework for future single-cell studies.
europmc-pmc5260006:
Shihai Zhang, Xiangfang Zeng, Man Ren, Xiangbing Mao, and Shiyan Qiao reviewed new functions of branched chain amino acids in the Journal of Animal Science and Biotechnology in 2017. The three branched chain amino acids, leucine, isoleucine, and valine, are essential nutrients best known as muscle building blocks and as triggers of the mTOR growth pathway. Recent work keeps finding them at work far beyond protein building.

Both too little and too much of them in the diet can push fat breakdown. Isoleucine stands out for raising glucose uptake in gut and muscle. Leucine added to feed improves meat quality in finishing pigs. The group also supports mammary health, milk quality, embryo growth, gut development, and both arms of the immune system. On the warning side, high blood levels of these amino acids, a sign the body is clearing them poorly, mark early obesity and diabetes.
europmc-pmc5313206:
Tomislav Hengl led a large team in building a world soil map in PLoS ONE in 2017. Soil data used to come only in coarse maps with weak accuracy. Farmers, climate models, and land planners all need finer detail. The SoilGrids system aims to fill that gap with computer models trained on real soil samples from around the world.

The new maps split the world into squares of two hundred and fifty meters. They predict carbon, density, acidity, sand and clay shares, and more, at seven depths down to two meters. The models learned from about one hundred and fifty thousand soil profiles and a stack of satellite and climate layers. Cross checks showed the models explained a good share of the spread in each trait. The maps are far sharper and more accurate than the older one kilometer version.
europmc-pmc5324806:
Leighann Sherry and co-authors tested film growth in a drug-proof yeast in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2017. The yeast, Candida auris, first showed up in a 2009 ear case in Japan. It resists key drug classes and is hard to name with standard lab tests. It has caused grave blood and wound infections and hospital outbreaks on several continents.

The team asked if the yeast can build biofilms, the slimy films that shield microbes on surfaces. In lab tests, it stuck to plastic surfaces and built films that shrugged off drugs that kill free-floating cells. One drug class was mostly powerless against the films. The common disinfectant chlorhexidine still worked on them. Film growth may help explain how the yeast lingers in hospital rooms and spreads between patients.
europmc-pmc5337506:
Simón Guendelman, Sebastián Medeiros, and Hagen Rampes reviewed mindfulness and feeling control in Frontiers in Psychology in 2017. Mindfulness training has shown gains across many states of poor feeling control. Brain scans tie practice to change in zones for focus, feeling, and self-thought. The team asked how those changes link to the ways people steer their feelings.

They sort the work by four study models: trait mindfulness in daily life, brief guided practice, full training courses, and expert meditators. Feeling control comes in two broad styles: top-down, driven by thought, and bottom-up, driven by body and sense input. Mindfulness seems to work through both, and the authors split its tactics the same way. They close with a body-based frame that joins brain, mind, and clinic views, and a call for sharper terms in the field.
europmc-pmc5390006:
Tong Guo, Wendy Noble, and Diane P. Hanger review the tau protein in health and disease in a 2017 paper in Acta Neuropathologica. Tau normally helps hold the inner frame of nerve cells steady. In a group of brain diseases that includes Alzheimer's disease, tau instead clumps into tangles, and nerve cells fail and die. The review covers tau's normal jobs in and beyond nerve cells.

Tau helps pass signals, shapes how nerve links change with use, and guards the cell's DNA store. Chemical tweaks after the protein is made steer where it sits and what it does. Changed or clumped tau can spread its bad form to healthy tau. The authors trace the chain of harm that follows and mark the steps where drugs might break it.
europmc-pmc546406:
Sveistrup reviews virtual reality as a tool for helping patients regain movement after injury or stroke. Her review appeared in the Journal of NeuroEngineering and Rehabilitation. Good rehab starts early. It uses real tasks and much repetition. Virtual reality can supply all three. It places therapy inside settings that feel like daily life. Patients grasp objects and move through virtual space. The tasks feel close to real-world ones. Therapists can grade the difficulty with care.

The systems build interactive scenes on screens. Displays range from desktop monitors to head-mounted units. Touch devices add a sense of contact. Sensors track the body in real time. Treatment can fit each patient while staying standard across clinics. The review compares virtual practice with real-world practice where data exist. Early evidence supports the promise of the medium. Safe, challenging practice is its core strength, the author concludes.
europmc-pmc5467206:
Rees and co-authors sharpen a gene editing method that rewrites single DNA letters without cutting both strands. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. The method is called base editing. It swaps one base pair for another directly. Two limits held it back. The editor sometimes changed the wrong sites. It also relied on delivering DNA into cells. The team tackled both problems at once.

First, they added mutations to their third-generation editor. The new version, HF-BE3, kept its aim far better. Off-target edits fell sharply. Next, they delivered the editor as a protein-RNA complex instead of DNA. That made the editing DNA-free. Protein delivery of the standard editor beat even plasmid delivery of the careful one on accuracy. On-target editing stayed just as strong. They proved the approach in living animals. Zebrafish embryos and the inner ear of mice were edited cleanly.
europmc-pmc5491406:
Roth and co-authors report a Global Burden of Disease study in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology. It estimates the burden of cardiovascular diseases for 10 causes, from 1990 to 2015. Many regions lacked clear, current figures. The study joins death records, surveys, cohorts, and registries into one set of estimates. A social and economic index helps explain the patterns.

In 2015, about 422.7 million people lived with cardiovascular disease, they estimate. Such diseases caused about 17.9 million deaths that year. Age-adjusted death rates fell in all high-income countries. Ischemic heart disease caused the most health loss worldwide, with stroke second. Poorer regions saw slow gains or none.
europmc-pmc549606:
Pao and co-authors report a cancer study in PLoS Medicine on drug resistance in lung tumors. Some lung adenocarcinomas shrink on the drugs gefitinib or erlotinib. Those tumors carry activating faults in the EGFR gene. Yet patients who respond at first later relapse. The cause of that acquired resistance was unknown.

Tumor samples from six relapsed patients were checked for new EGFR faults. Three tumors held a second mutation, called T790M, the authors report. It sits in the drug's target region of the protein. Lab tests showed this change makes EGFR resist both drugs. No relapsed tumor held a KRAS mutation. The finding pointed drug makers toward new designs.
europmc-pmc5502906:
Lakens presents a practical primer in Social Psychological and Personality Science on equivalence testing. Standard significance tests cannot prove that an effect is absent. A flat result may just mean the study was too small. Researchers often make that error anyway, he notes. Equivalence tests offer a sound way to support a null claim.

The method sets upper and lower bounds for the smallest effect worth caring about. Two one-sided tests then check whether the effect sits inside those bounds. If both pass, the effect counts as practically zero. The primer ships with a spreadsheet and an R package. It also advises setting the bounds before data collection.
europmc-pmc5520106:
Teichert and co-authors report a vascular biology study in Nature Communications on the Tie2 receptor. Tie2 signaling guides new blood vessel growth and settling. Textbooks assign this receptor to endothelial cells only. Pericytes, the support cells hugging vessel walls, also carry it at low levels. What it does there was unknown.

Pericyte Tie2 works and restrains sprouting, they report. Silencing it made pericytes more eager to migrate. Deleting it in mouse pericytes briefly slowed retinal vessel growth. The same deletion later boosted tumor growth strongly. Signaling runs through calpain, Akt, and FOXO3A proteins. Vessel control is a two-way talk between both cell types.
europmc-pmc5535906:
Eckschlager and co-authors review a class of cancer drugs called histone deacetylase inhibitors, or HDAC inhibitors. Their article appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Cancer grows through gene changes, but also through shifts that switch genes on or off. HDAC enzymes help control that switching.

These drugs can halt the cancer cell cycle, force cell death, cut new blood vessel growth, and aid immune attack, the authors report. Three such drugs were cleared for some T-cell lymphomas, and one for multiple myeloma. Many more are in trials for blood and solid cancers. Effects vary by drug, dose, and cancer type. The authors see the most promise in pairing these drugs with other drugs or with radiation.
europmc-pmc5541706:
Rice and co-authors present a research article in Oncogenesis. Their subject is pancreatic cancer, a cancer known for stiff, scar-like tissue. The team asks whether that stiffness changes cancer cells themselves. They test cells grown at stiffness levels like those in real tumors.

The authors report that stiff settings pushed cells toward a mesenchymal state. Marker proteins shifted, and cell shape changed as well. Stiffness also made cells resist the drug paclitaxel. It did not have that effect for gemcitabine. Mouse models and several cell lines support the findings. Readers see how the tissue around a tumor can help it survive treatment.
europmc-pmc5544206:
Matar Boumosleh, Jaalouk, and co-authors present a cross-sectional study in PLoS ONE. They surveyed 688 undergraduates at a Lebanese university. The questions covered phone habits, sleep, mood, and daily life. Short scales screened for depression and anxiety symptoms.

Signs of phone addiction were common in the sample. About 36 percent felt tired in the day after late-night phone use. A like share said they sometimes slept under four hours due to phone use. After other factors were held in check, depression and anxiety still predicted higher addiction scores. Type A personality and heavy weekday use also linked to higher scores. Readers get a clear snapshot of phone habits and mental health in young adults.
europmc-pmc5544706:
Tang and co-authors present a research article in Nature Communications. Their subject is the NLRP3 inflammasome, an immune complex inside cells. When it switches on, it drives release of inflammatory signals. The signals matter in diseases such as gout and type 2 diabetes.

The team traces a chain of events before that switch. Potassium leaves the cell, mitochondria are harmed, and reactive oxygen builds up. Chloride channel proteins then move to the cell surface. Chloride flows out, which helps the complex assemble and act. Blocking that step stops the response. Readers get a clearer order for events that were once hard to place.
europmc-pmc5594206:
Xin Yang and co-authors map a chemical mark on messenger RNA in Cell Research. The mark is 5-methylcytosine, or m5C. It was long known on transfer and ribosomal RNA. Its job on messenger RNA stayed unclear.

The team charted m5C across human cells and mouse tissues. Marks cluster in CG-rich stretches, just past the start of protein-coding regions. Patterns are shared across mammals, yet shift by tissue and time. An enzyme called NSUN2 writes most of the marks. A shuttle protein, ALYREF, reads them. ALYREF binds marked RNA and helps export it from the nucleus. Removing NSUN2 broke that export. Adding back the working enzyme fixed it. A dead version could not. Readers get a writer-reader pair that governs RNA traffic.
europmc-pmc5642006:
Burgess, Small, and Thompson present a methods review in Statistical Methods in Medical Research. It compares estimators used in Mendelian randomization. That approach uses genetic variants as instrumental variables. A valid instrument links to the exposure but not to confounders. It also must reach the outcome only through the exposure. Under those rules, causal effects can be drawn from observational data.

Four families of methods get compared. They are ratio, two-stage, likelihood-based, and semi-parametric methods. The authors weigh bias, coverage, and efficiency for each. Weak instruments get special attention, since they distort estimates. A score-based approach helps when many weak instruments are used. Practical advice guides readers on choosing a method.
europmc-pmc5718706:
Racle and co-authors present a method to count cell types inside tumours. Their research article appeared in eLife. Bulk tumour gene data mix many cell types. Immune cells in that mix shape outcomes. Their algorithm estimates each cell fraction. It covers cancer and immune cells at once.

The method uses fresh expression profiles. Each major non-cancer cell type has one. It corrects for cell-specific mRNA content. Unknown cell types can be included too. The team validated the method three ways. Flow cytometry was one check. Tissue staining and single-cell data were others. Human melanoma samples were tested. Colorectal tumours were tested as well. The tool is public online.
europmc-pmc5753206:
Zerbino and co-authors present Ensembl 2018, the latest state of the Ensembl genome project. Ensembl gathers, processes, and shares genomic data in the open. Its browser is the main window onto a large hidden infrastructure. Release 90 holds exactly 100 genome assemblies.

The project covers gene annotation, comparative genomics, genetics, and epigenomics. Whole genome alignments and gene trees span many species. This update centers on handling more assemblies at once. It also backs work on reading genome meaning for medicine. Browser gains round out the changes described. Its services range from quick browsing to genome-wide analysis.
europmc-pmc5758806:
Baud and co-authors find that seizure risk in epilepsy follows multi-day rhythms. Seizures seem random, which makes them hard to foresee. The team used data from implanted brain devices in 37 people. The devices tracked seizures and odd discharges between them for years.

Those discharges swung with daily cycles and with personal multi-day cycles. The multi-day cycles most often ran 20 to 30 days. They stayed stable for up to 10 years in men and women. Seizures clustered on the rising phase of the multi-day wave. Joining both cycle phases gave a strong marker of relative seizure risk.
europmc-pmc5788906:
Schetters and co-authors review how microglia and T cells interact in the inflamed brain. Old views of brain immunity have shifted fast. Lymphatic drainage from the brain was found, and microglia proved more varied than thought. T cells now look key to brain immune balance and to degeneration.

The review joins these threads into one account. Microglia present antigens inside the brain during chronic degeneration. They and CD4 T cells build up together and shape each other. Shared gene patterns appear across diseases. Current trial treatments shift this microglia T cell balance, they note.
europmc-pmc5837306:
Munafò and co-authors warn that who joins a study can quietly bend its results. Their paper appeared in the International Journal of Epidemiology. Big cohorts power modern genetics and health research. Volunteers, though, rarely mirror the wider public.

The twist is a bias named for colliders. When two traits both sway participation, studying only participants links them falsely. Dropout over time can do the same damage. Simulations show even mild selection can warp gene and trait links. The fix starts with honesty about whom a sample truly represents. Known selection factors can then enter the analysis.
europmc-pmc5860606:
Kulmanov and co-authors present DeepGO, a tool that predicts protein functions. Their article appeared in Bioinformatics. New sequencing yields protein sequences far faster than labs can test them. DeepGO uses deep learning to guess what a protein does. It learns from the amino acid sequence itself. It also uses a network of protein interactions across species.

Predictions follow the structure of the Gene Ontology. That system holds over 40,000 function classes with set links. The model uses those links as background knowledge. Tests used the standards of a community assessment exercise. The authors report clear gains over BLAST baselines. Gains were strongest for cell location predictions. A web server and source code are both provided.
europmc-pmc5877606:
Jun and co-authors review electrospun fibrous scaffolds for tissue engineering. Their article appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Electrospinning draws fine fibres with electric force. The mats it makes mimic the matrix around natural cells. Their tiny fibres and linked pores suit cell growth. Such scaffolds aim to rebuild damaged tissues and organs. The review covers the basic principles of the process.

It then surveys ways to build complex fibre geometries. Three-dimensional stacks with layered order get close attention. Design must match the target tissue's structure and job. Settings such as voltage, flow, and distance shape the result. The authors present routes toward working artificial tissues.
europmc-pmc5931106:
Brown and co-authors estimate the share of UK cancer tied to changeable risk factors in 2015. Their article appeared in the British Journal of Cancer. They used national surveys and cancer records for that year. Attributable fractions were built by age, sex, and exposure. Results cover each UK nation apart and together. Only links with strong causal proof were counted.

Nearly four in ten cancers were attributable, they report. The share was 37.7 percent across the UK. Scotland had the highest share, England the lowest. Smoking was by far the largest single cause. Overweight and obesity ranked second among factors. For ten cancer types, over 70 percent were attributable.
europmc-pmc5994406:
Pierpont, Limper, and Richards review the past, present, and future of rituximab, the first oncology monoclonal antibody. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Oncology. Rituximab binds the CD20 protein on B cells. Approved in 1997, it improved outcomes across B-cell cancers. It was the top-selling oncology drug for nearly a decade. How it works in real patients is still partly unclear. Most mechanism data come from cell studies, they note.

No biomarker predicts who will respond, beyond CD20 itself. Two newer anti-CD20 antibodies now offer distinct actions. Biosimilars are arriving as the patent expires. Wider access and better prediction may reshape its use.
europmc-pmc6033006:
Shakibazadeh and co-authors define respectful care during childbirth in health facilities. Their evidence synthesis appeared in BJOG. Reports of disrespect and mistreatment keep many women from facility care. Yet the term respectful maternity care lacked a shared working definition.

The team combined 67 qualitative studies from 32 countries. They grouped the findings into twelve domains. These cover freedom from harm, privacy, dignity, and informed consent. They also cover family support, fair treatment, and skilled staff. Women's views proved much alike across countries. Readers get an evidence-based typology for maternal care programs. It frames respect as far more than the absence of abuse.
europmc-pmc6035906:
Glumac and LeBeau review the role of CD133 in cancer. Their concise review appeared in Clinical and Translational Medicine. CD133 is a protein found on cell surfaces. It has been proposed as a marker of cancer stem cells. Such cells may drive growth and treatment resistance.

The marker's accuracy is hotly debated, though. Culture conditions and weak assays cloud the picture. Some antibodies also miss altered forms of the protein. High CD133 levels in tumors do predict worse progress. The review sums up the evidence on both sides. It also compiles immune therapies aimed at CD133 cells. Readers get a balanced guide to a contested marker. Its prognostic value may outlast the stem cell dispute.
europmc-pmc6078906:
Stephens and co-authors map the hurdles facing cultured meat on its way to market. Their article appeared in Trends in Food Science and Technology. Cultured meat grows muscle cells without raising livestock. It belongs to the wider field of cellular agriculture. The team drew on lab work and over seventy expert interviews.

Technical problems come first. Cell sources, growth media, and scale-up all need work. The social debate often shrinks to ethics and shoppers. The authors push it wider, toward politics and industry shape. Rules for approval remain unsettled and fuzzy. United Kingdom policy supplies the detailed case. Readers get a full agenda for a young food industry.
europmc-pmc6227606:
The GBD 2017 Causes of Death Collaborators measured deaths by cause worldwide. Country progress goals need solid cause data. This study updates earlier Global Burden of Disease work. It appeared in The Lancet. It covers 282 causes from 1980 to 2017.

The database mixes death registers and verbal autopsy data. Cancer registries, surveys, and police data also feed it. Vague or implausible codes were reassigned to true causes. Models then estimated deaths by age, sex, and place. Coverage spans 195 countries and territories. Subnational estimates grew to more countries. The authors track falls in child deaths and infection deaths. They also track rises in deaths from chronic disease.
europmc-pmc6277706:
Bain and Schridde review the macrophages that guard the gut wall. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. The gut meets more foreign material than any other organ. Its macrophages keep peace with food and normal microbes. They also stand ready against true invaders. When that balance breaks, bowel inflammation can become chronic.

Gut macrophages come in varied forms along the gut wall. Their birth source and local setting shape what each form does. Signals from the gut itself stamp their identity. Infection and inflammation rewrite that identity. The authors trace how the cell mix changes in disease. Those changes make the cells a tempting drug target. Open questions close the review. Answering them may yield new bowel disease therapies.
europmc-pmc6299006:
Piehl and co-authors give the first count of plastic debris on a farm field. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports. The field sits in southeast Germany. It had never had plastic-rich fertilizer or farm plastic use. The team still expected some contamination from normal farm work.

They used infrared analysis to sort and count the debris. Macroplastic pieces came to 206 per hectare. Microplastic particles averaged 0.34 per kilogram of dry soil. Polyethylene was the most common plastic type. Films and fragments made up most finds. The authors warn that fields using mulch or sludge likely carry far more plastic.
europmc-pmc6307306:
Maleki Vareki argues that two tumor labels must be read together to predict drug response. The article appeared in the Journal for ImmunoTherapy of Cancer. Some tumors are called hot because immune cells crowd inside them. Others are cold, with few immune cells present. A second label counts total mutations in the tumor. High counts can create more targets for immune attack.

Neither label alone explains who benefits from checkpoint drugs. Melanoma and lung tumors are often hot and responsive. Prostate and pancreatic tumors are cold and rarely respond. Some cases break the simple pattern, though. The author urges judging tumors by both traits. That pairing should better pick patients for immunotherapy.
europmc-pmc6382806:
Asadi and co-authors report a study in Scientific Reports on particles from speech. Coughs and sneezes are known to spray droplets. Normal speech also releases many tiny particles, too small to see, that can carry germs.

The team measured particle output while people spoke at set loudness levels. Louder speech released far more particles, from about one to fifty per second. The pattern held across English, Spanish, Mandarin, and Arabic speech. A few people were superemitters, releasing far more than others. The findings matter for judging infection risk in rooms where people talk.
europmc-pmc6401206:
McCutcheon and co-authors review dopamine and schizophrenia in Trends in Neurosciences. For decades, the standard account blamed dopamine paths to the limbic brain for psychotic symptoms. New imaging work has shifted that picture.

Dopamine faults now look strongest in the dorsal striatum, a region for habit and action. The review joins this finding with new knowledge of striatum structure. It asks how striatal faults could produce delusions and other symptoms. Treatment ideas follow from that revised map. The authors argue the old mesolimbic story needs to be replaced, not just patched.
europmc-pmc6441206:
Mou and co-authors review ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death first named in 2012, and its prospects as a cancer treatment lever. Unlike apoptosis, ferroptosis kills through runaway lipid peroxidation: mitochondria shrink, their membranes condense and rupture, and the cell's own iron feeds the damage.

Non-coding RNAs feature heavily in the newest regulation findings, and the death pathway cross-talks with autophagy, which can supply free iron by digesting ferritin. Abnormal ferroptosis shows up across many cancer types, and several familiar drugs and natural compounds turn out to trigger it. Open questions about control and safety still separate the concept from routine clinical use.
europmc-pmc6470706:
Benmebarek and co-authors explain how CAR T cells kill, tracing the engineered receptor from target binding to tumor cell death. A single-chain antibody fragment gives the T cell its aim, free of the usual MHC restriction, and docking creates a non-classical immune synapse. What happens next decides whether the therapy works.

Killing runs mainly through perforin and granzyme release and through the Fas death pathway, while secreted cytokines sensitize the surrounding tumor stroma. Persistence and output hinge on the receptor's parts, its spacer and costimulatory domains, working together. Successes in blood cancers and failures in solid tumors frame the closing assessment of design choices.
europmc-pmc6492006:
Adl and co-authors issue the updated classification of all eukaryotes, revising their 2012 scheme in light of a flood of environmental DNA. Sequencing soils, deep marine water, and other neglected habitats has massively expanded the known tree, revealing novel clades and whole genera found only as sequences until they could be placed.

The revision confirms eukaryotes form at least two great domains, dissolves the old Excavata as a natural group, and firms up Haptista and Cryptista. Protists keep the emphasis, since they hold most of the diversity. Practical additions include primer sets tuned per clade for environmental sampling, a guide to feeding guilds, and a standardized taxonomy for East Asian users.
europmc-pmc6506906:
Smeland and co-authors report survival in the EURAMOS-1 osteosarcoma cohort. Their report appeared in the European Journal of Cancer. EURAMOS-1 joined four study groups across Europe and America. It enrolled patients aged 40 or younger with high-grade bone osteosarcoma. Standard treatment used methotrexate, doxorubicin and cisplatin, plus surgery.

Between 2005 and 2011, the study registered 2,260 patients. At a median follow-up of 54 months, five-year event-free survival was 54%. Five-year overall survival was 71%. Spread to the lungs at diagnosis was the strongest adverse sign. Axial tumour site and spread beyond the lungs also worsened outlook. Poor response to pre-surgery chemotherapy predicted worse results after surgery.
europmc-pmc6510306:
Chung and co-authors present wireless skin-like monitors for newborn intensive care. Their report appeared in Science. Standard NICU monitors need wires and stiff sensors stuck to fragile skin. Those systems can injure skin and block parent contact.

The team built two soft, ultrathin devices that work as a pair. One sits on the chest and records the electrocardiogram. The other rests on the foot and records blood flow signals. Both run without batteries and stream data in sync. Together they yield heart rate, breathing rate, oxygen level, and temperature. They also track pulse arrival time as a stand-in for blood pressure. Tests on infants from 28 weeks to full term matched clinical systems.
europmc-pmc6523806:
Laxa and co-authors review the plant antioxidant system in drought tolerance. Their review appeared in Antioxidants. Water shortage cuts plant growth and crop yield. Survival is not the whole story. Speed of recovery after drought also drives performance.

Drought disturbs metabolism and raises reactive oxygen and nitrogen species. Those species can harm cells, yet they also carry stress signals. The authors compile data on superoxide, hydrogen peroxide and nitric oxide. A meta-analysis compares transcript, protein and activity changes. Tolerance seems tied most to stronger ascorbate-based antioxidant action. Resurrection plants fit that view. They hold strong antioxidant systems for severe dry spells.
europmc-pmc6524306:
Sharma, Misba and Khan review the fight between antibiotics and bacterial biofilms. Their review appeared in Antimicrobial Resistance and Infection Control. A biofilm is a group of cells stuck to a surface. The cells sit in a self-made matrix of DNA, proteins and sugars. That matrix gives strong protection from drugs.

Biofilms drive lasting infections, notably on medical devices in hospitals. Quorum sensing helps control their growth. The authors survey ways to block biofilm growth. Two newer ideas get special focus. One is CRISPR-Cas gene editing. The other is photodynamic therapy. Both are proposed against infections from hard-to-treat resistant bacteria.
europmc-pmc6542806:
Egidi and co-authors map the fungi that rule the world's soils, writing in Nature Communications. Soil fungi drive nutrient cycles and plant health, yet their global leaders were unknown. The team sampled 235 soils across six continents and nine biomes, and read the fungal DNA in each.

Just 83 fungal types — under 0.1% of all types found — dominate soils worldwide, making up about a fifth of all fungal reads. Most are wind-spread generalists of the Ascomycota group. Their genomes carry extra genes for stress tolerance and resource uptake, which may explain their reach. The authors map where each leader thrives and what drives it, a base for guarding soil function.
europmc-pmc6562906:
Harrell and co-authors review the mesenchymal stem cell secretome — the cocktail the cells release rather than the cells themselves — writing in Cells. The secretome bundles soluble proteins, nucleic acids, lipids and extracellular vesicles. Study after study finds it heals much like transplanted stem cells do, while skipping their risks, such as stray differentiation after engraftment.

That profile suits emergencies. Unlike cells, which need weeks of culture, secretome stocks can be made in bulk from commercial lines and used for crises like liver failure, stroke or heart attack. The review traces how its growth and immune-calming factors switch on anti-death, pro-survival pathways in injured tissue across the liver, lungs, joints, gut, heart and nervous system.
europmc-pmc6667406:
Monteagudo-Mera and co-authors review how probiotics and prebiotics stick to host surfaces. Their mini review appears in Applied Microbiology and Biotechnology. Sticking is a classic pick rule for probiotic strains. It allows brief settling in the gut. That contact supports immune tuning and barrier strength. Probiotics also block pathogens from binding sites. They secrete germ-killing compounds as well. Prebiotics can act as decoy receptors for pathogens. That blocks pathogen binding to gut cells.

Most evidence comes from gut cell line studies. Reading those results onto living guts stays uncertain. The authors call for richer models with resident microbes. Synbiotic products may extend probiotic residence time.
europmc-pmc6756106:
Marquand and co-authors explain normative modeling for mental disorders. These statistical models work like children's growth charts. They map how a biological measure should vary across people, given age or other factors. A patient can then be scored by how far they deviate from the norm. That gives answers for one person, not just group averages.

Psychiatric disorders vary hugely in biology from person to person. Group averages blur that out. Normative models have parsed this variation well in brain imaging studies. The review offers a shared framework linking the many methods proposed. It surveys uses on imaging biomarkers in psychiatry. The goal is a common language for a fast-growing field.
europmc-pmc6800406:
Dent and co-authors present international clinical practice guidelines for identifying and managing physical frailty in older adults. An expert task force from the International Conference of Frailty and Sarcopenia Research wrote them. They used the GRADE method to rate evidence strength behind each recommendation. Where evidence was thin, consensus-based recommendations filled the gap.

All older adults should be screened for frailty with a validated tool suited to the setting, a strong recommendation. Positive screens should trigger a fuller clinical assessment. Care plans must address polypharmacy and other drivers. Multi-component exercise, mixing resistance, aerobic, and balance training, improved strength, balance, disability, and falls in frail elders. The guidelines stress person-centered care throughout.
europmc-pmc6802306:
Haas and co-authors benchmarked methods for detecting fusion transcripts in RNA sequencing data. Gene fusions drive many cancers. BCR-ABL1 appears in about 95% of chronic myelogenous leukemia, and TMPRSS2-ERG in about half of prostate cancers. Tools to find fusions split into two families: read-mapping methods and de novo assembly methods. The team tested 23 of them, including two of their own.

Simulated and real cancer data were used. STAR-Fusion, Arriba, and STAR-SEQR proved most accurate and fastest overall. The top three all build on the STAR aligner. Assembly-based methods were less accurate at detection. They still earn their place by reconstructing fusion variants and tumor viruses, both important in cancer research.
europmc-pmc6871006:
Roux and co-authors set reporting standards for virus genomes, in Nature Biotechnology. Virus particles vastly outnumber living cells in most habitats, yet only a tiny fraction of viruses have been grown in a lab. Sequencing of whole environments now recovers genomes of viruses never isolated. The paper notes that more than 750,000 such genomes were reported in the past 2 years covered.

Without standards, those records vary wildly in quality and description. The authors define minimum information for an uncultivated virus genome, called MIUViG. It covers how the genome was assembled, how complete it is judged to be, and what context must accompany it. High-quality drafts are defined by completeness against the expected genome length.
europmc-pmc6906306:
Giobbe and co-authors report a study in Nature Communications on a natural gel for growing organoids. Organoids are mini-organs grown from stem cells, with wide promise in medicine. Their growth usually needs a gel drawn from mouse tumours, which no regulator accepts for clinical use. Synthetic gels are clean but carry no biological instructions. The team sought a middle path.

They stripped pig small intestine of its cells, leaving the natural matrix behind, and turned it into a hydrogel. The gel kept the tissue's biochemical signature. Human organoids of the gut family, including stomach-type tissue, formed and grew in it. The authors argue such decellularised gels could carry organoid culture toward clinical-grade production.
europmc-pmc6929606:
Peng and co-authors review type H blood vessels in bone. Their review appeared in Theranostics. Bone growth and vessel growth are tightly linked. Type H vessels were identified only recently. They express high levels of Endomucin and CD31. They can also induce new bone formation.

The authors summarise the signals that regulate these vessels. Key factors include PDGF-BB and SLIT3. HIF-1 alpha, Notch, and VEGF also play roles. The review explains how type H vessels shape osteogenesis. It then weighs therapies that target them. Aims include faster fracture healing and less bone loss. Osteonecrosis, osteoarthritis, and bone metastases are also discussed.
europmc-pmc7031906:
Guo and co-authors review Clostridium bacteria as possible probiotics in the Journal of Animal Science and Biotechnology. These bacteria form a large share of the normal gut community. They help keep the gut stable and calm. Some strains ease inflammation and allergic disease in studies.

The review explains how the bacteria help. Their products, such as butyrate, feed gut lining cells and strengthen the barrier. They also interact with the immune system. Diet and body state shape which species thrive. The authors then weigh the risks. A few Clostridium species release harmful toxins. Safety checks are vital before use, they stress. The goal is new probiotics for people and farm animals.
europmc-pmc7101506:
Guo and co-authors studied how existing heart disease and heart muscle injury affect death risk in COVID-19, in JAMA Cardiology. Some patients deteriorate fast, and early reports showed acute heart injury in a share of cases. Their case series examined whether these heart factors predicted fatal outcomes.

Patients with underlying cardiovascular disease who developed myocardial injury during hospital care faced greater risk and worse outcomes, the study reports. Troponin levels, a blood marker of heart damage, separated the groups. The findings pushed heart monitoring into COVID-19 care early in the pandemic, and raised questions about common heart drugs such as ACE inhibitors in these patients.
europmc-pmc7110906:
Xu and co-authors review the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling pathway in neurodegenerative diseases and tumours, in Cell & Bioscience. The pathway helps control cell growth, death, metabolism, and blood vessel growth. Its parts are many, and its wiring is complex. When it fails, disease can follow.

The review lays out the pathway's structure, and how it switches on and off. It then traces its role in ischemic brain injury, degenerative brain diseases, and cancers. Drugs that block the pathway are also surveyed. Some have done well in early studies, and a few reached clinical tests in blood cancers and solid tumours. Readers get a compact guide to a major drug target, and to why it remains hard to control.
europmc-pmc7182206:
Minh and co-authors introduce IQ-TREE 2, software for building evolutionary trees from DNA data. Their article appeared in Molecular Biology and Evolution. The program uses maximum likelihood, a statistical method for picking the best-fitting tree. Version 1 appeared in 2014 and saw wide use. Genome-scale data since then demanded faster methods and richer models.

The new version adds many models of sequence evolution. It also speeds up standard tests of tree shape. On one dataset, a support test dropped from hours to about 1.5 minutes. That is a speedup of more than a thousandfold. Fast topology tests run in parallel as well. The authors present the tool as ready for the genomic era. Biologists comparing species or viruses gain a quicker, flexible option.
europmc-pmc7190606:
Brunello and co-authors review how harmful tau protein leaves cells and spreads. Their article appeared in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences. Tau tangles build up in the brain in Alzheimer's disease and related disorders. These clumps can pass from cell to cell. Each new cell may then form its own clumps. This prion-like spread may drive disease progress. The review focuses on how tau gets out of cells.

The authors describe several release routes for tau. Some tau crosses the cell membrane directly. Other tau leaves inside small vesicles such as exosomes. Cells may shed tau to cut their own toxic load. Tau can also be released in normal cell activity. Neighboring brain cells then take the protein up. The authors weigh what is known and what stays unclear. Readers get a map of a key step in tau disease spread.
europmc-pmc7221106:
Kolla and co-authors chart how the mouse inner ear's hearing epithelium develops, cell by cell. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Hearing depends on the organ of Corti, a strip of specialized cells in the cochlea. Its cell types are few and packed tightly together. That made their development hard to study one type at a time.

The team profiled about 30,000 cochlear cells at four developmental stages. They identified both known and previously unknown cell types. Outer hair cells, the sound amplifiers, passed through four phases of gene activity. Fate mapping checked how precursor cells choose their paths. Signals such as the TGF-beta pathway were examined along the way. The atlas gives hearing research a detailed developmental reference.
europmc-pmc7298606:
Suleyman and co-authors describe the first COVID-19 patients treated across a five-hospital system in metropolitan Detroit. Their case series appeared in JAMA Network Open. The series covers 463 consecutive confirmed patients seen during the early phase of the outbreak in southeast Michigan. Most, 72.1%, were African American, and 94.0% had at least one other health condition.

Of the 355 patients admitted to hospital, 39.7% needed intensive care. Among intensive care patients, 80.8% were put on invasive mechanical ventilation, and 40.4% died within 30 days. The authors present the series as a record of how hard the early surge hit this community, and as a baseline for judging later improvements in treatment and outcomes.
europmc-pmc7318306:
Colunga Biancatelli and co-authors propose pairing quercetin, a plant flavonoid, with vitamin C as an experimental therapy against COVID-19. Their paper appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Vitamin C supports immune function and has shown promise in the critically ill. Quercetin has antiviral properties studied in many settings, and vitamin C recycles it in the body, extending its action.

Given together, the two may exert a stronger combined antiviral and immune-calming effect than either alone. The authors present the evidence for using the pair to protect high-risk groups and as an add-on for patients alongside drugs such as remdesivir or convalescent plasma. Their argument is for priority testing: both substances are safe and cheap, with a sound biological rationale, in a pandemic short on proven treatments.
europmc-pmc7325106:
Hemminki and co-authors review oncolytic viruses for cancer treatment in the Journal of Hematology and Oncology. These are viruses shaped to infect and kill cancer cells while also waking up the immune system. Adenoviruses get the closest look, as a model for the wider field.

Reports going back over a hundred years, plus modern trials, suggest such viruses can be safe and can shrink some tumors. The authors describe ways to make them stronger, such as adding genes that boost immune attack at the tumor. They also weigh pairing the viruses with radiation, chemotherapy, and checkpoint drugs. Cold tumors that the immune system ignores may become visible after infection, they argue.
europmc-pmc7338506:
GeurtsvanKessel and co-authors compare COVID-19 antibody tests in Nature Communications. Reliable serology, testing blood for antibodies, was in growing demand for both diagnosis and population surveys. The team ran a detailed head-to-head evaluation of the available assays.

Performance varied widely between tests, and a test's value depended on the stage and severity of disease. One total-antibody ELISA, from Wantai, performed best overall at detecting working antibodies, including the kind that neutralize the virus. Its cutoff could even hint at protective antibodies. The authors stress that any assay needs proper validation before wide deployment. Readers get a practical guide to choosing a test for a given job.
europmc-pmc7352706:
Ammar and co-authors present an international survey report in Nutrients. It studies eating and activity during COVID-19 home confinement. The online survey ran in April 2020 in seven languages. This report covers the first thousand or so replies.

The survey drew 1,047 replies from Asia, Africa, Europe, and elsewhere. The authors report drops in all levels of physical activity. Daily sitting time rose from about five hours to eight. Food habits also worsened, with more snacks and less control over eating. Binge drinking was the one habit that fell. The authors warn that steps to stop the virus also harmed daily health habits. Readers get an early cross-country snapshot of lockdown life.
europmc-pmc7470306:
Morgantini and co-authors survey burnout among healthcare professionals during the COVID-19 pandemic. Front-line staff faced heavy workloads and stress. Knowing burnout risk helps leaders support staff and guard care quality.

A total of 2,707 professionals from 60 countries took the survey. Fifty-one percent reported burnout, well above earlier rates. Burnout rose when work spilled into home life and when staff felt pushed beyond their training. Contact with COVID-19 patients and making life-priority choices also raised risk. Enough protective equipment lowered the risk. Burnout ran higher in high-income countries than in poorer ones. The authors urge training, family support, protective gear, and mental health resources. Institutions and governments share the task.
europmc-pmc7527506:
Rao and co-authors build hybrid cell membrane nanovesicles to fight cancer return. Cancer cells use CD47 as a do not eat me signal. That signal stops macrophages from eating them.

The vesicles carry a variant of SIRPα with stronger binding. They also carry signals that shift macrophages toward attack mode. Both tricks disable key defenses at once. In melanoma models, treatment cut local return and distant spread. Loaded with a STING agonist, vesicles also slowed triple negative breast cancer. The authors report the vesicles were safe and stable. They can also carry drugs and be edited.
europmc-pmc7575906:
Duan and co-authors review the SARS-CoV-2 spike glycoprotein and what it means for vaccine design. Spike proteins stud the surface of mature virus particles. They drive attachment, fusion and entry into host cells.

Surface position makes spike a direct immune target. It is the main target of neutralizing antibodies. Most vaccine plans therefore center on the spike protein. The review covers how spike is made in cells. It also covers spike structure, function and antigenicity. Recent progress in each area is summed up. Insights aim to guide spike-based vaccine immunogens. Therapeutic design based on spike is also discussed for future work.
europmc-pmc7616806:
Romanello and co-authors deliver the 2022 Lancet Countdown assessment, framed around fossil fuel dependence. Concurrent shocks shaped the backdrop for this edition. War in Ukraine and energy prices strained health systems.

Extreme weather hit every continent during 2021 and 2022. Floods and wildfires killed and displaced many people. Heat records fell in many countries that year. Vulnerable groups faced 3.7 billion more heatwave days in 2021. That compares with annual levels in 1986–2005. Heat deaths rose by 68% between the compared periods. Climate shifts also aid spread of infectious disease. Coastal waters suit Vibrio spread better than before. Malaria season length grew in highland areas of the Americas.
europmc-pmc7641006:
Koonin and co-authors track telehealth use in the United States during the early COVID-19 pandemic. CDC had urged virtual care to support distancing. Data came from four large national telehealth providers.

Visits in the first quarter rose by 50% versus the prior year. In week 13 the rise reached 154% year on year. Most visits were for problems other than COVID-19. The COVID-19 share still grew fast in late March. It rose from 5.5% to 16.2% in three weeks. The shift changed how care was delivered at speed. Policy waivers may keep access gains after the pandemic. Both acute and long-term care could benefit, the authors note. Data covered age, sex and place of residence for visits.
europmc-pmc7674206:
Patel and co-authors review a class of stubborn pollutants and ways to clean them up. The pollutants are polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, or PAHs. They come mostly from human activity, persist in soil and water, and resist breakdown. They can cause cancer and harm immune function.

The review covers where PAHs arise, how people are exposed, and their toxic effects. It sums up chemical and physical cleanup methods, from filtration to heat. Its main focus is green biological cleanup with bacteria, fungi, algae, and plants. The authors also cover mixed methods and the chance to gain useful products during cleanup.
europmc-pmc7707106:
Whittington and co-authors propose one model for both space memory and relation memory. The brain's hippocampal system handles both kinds of tasks. The model is named the Tolman-Eichenbaum Machine, after two pioneers of memory research. It splits the work between two cell groups with distinct jobs.

In the model, entorhinal cells encode the structure of a task. Hippocampal cells bind that structure to what the senses report. After learning, its fake cells mimic real ones, from grid cells to place cells. It also fits data from non-spatial tasks. The model predicts that brain maps keep their structure when scenes change, which the authors confirm in rat data.
europmc-pmc7719906:
Bull and co-authors present the World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity. An expert group weighed proof on activity, sitting, and health for all ages. The new rules update the global guidance last set in 2010.

Adults should get 150 to 300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity each week, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous work. Children and teens should average 60 minutes a day of moderate to strong activity. Muscle work is urged for all age groups. For the first time, the rules cover pregnancy, chronic illness, and disability. Sitting less is urged for all, though no firm cap could be set.
europmc-pmc7734206:
Piedra-Quintero and co-authors review CD38, a molecule that tunes immune cell behavior. CD38 can act as an enzyme that drains NAD, as a signal sender, or as a sticky receptor. It sits on many immune cells, at the surface and inside the cell. Its levels vary by cell type and species.

In immune cells, CD38 shapes growth, cell movement, cytokine release, and NAD supply. In autoimmune disease it can drive harm in one setting and calm it in another. The effect depends on the disease, the cell, and the model used. The authors sort the disputes and point to new tools that may resolve them.
europmc-pmc7750006:
Ladds and co-authors record the lived experience of people with long Covid. About 10% of COVID-19 patients have symptoms past 3 to 4 weeks. The team held 55 interviews and 8 focus groups. In all, 114 patients took part, many of them health professionals themselves.

Patients described a baffling illness with many shifting symptoms and no clear outlook. Many felt loss and stigma. Care was hard to reach, hard to navigate, and split into silos. Some felt well supported; others felt brushed off. From these tales the authors draft quality principles for long Covid services: easy access, shared burden, continuity, and clear clinical ownership.
europmc-pmc7764106:
Breijyeh and Karaman give a broad review of Alzheimer disease, its causes and its care. The disease erodes brain cells and is the main cause of dementia. Thinking fades and daily independence is lost. Two classic theories blame a broken chemical signal or amyloid buildup. Age, genes, head injury, and vessel disease add risk.

Only two drug classes are approved today. They ease symptoms but do not stop the disease. New work targets tau, amyloid, inflammation, and free radical damage. The authors survey disease-modifying drugs, helper proteins called chaperones, and natural compounds. Their aim is a map from current limits to the next wave of therapy.
europmc-pmc7779006:
Davis and co-authors give the 2021 update of the Comparative Toxicogenomics Database, known as CTD. CTD links chemicals, genes, traits, diseases, and exposures. Its goal is to clarify how the environment affects human health. Curators read the literature by hand and code the links they find.

Curated content rose by 20% in this update. CTD now holds 45 million toxicogenomic relationships. These span over 16 300 chemicals and 51 300 genes. They also cover 5,500 phenotypes, 7,200 diseases, and 163 000 exposure events from 600 species. New anatomy pages let users view chemical and trait links by body site. Chemical pages gained more synonyms and 1,600 amino acid compounds. The authors present CTD as a tool for building testable ideas about disease causes.
europmc-pmc7840906:
