Borcherding and co-authors map the immune setting of clear cell kidney cancer one cell at a time. This cancer answers immunotherapy at a high rate. Oddly, it carries few mutations. The team sequenced single immune cells from tumors and blood. Samples came from three patients.

The team profiled 25,688 immune cells from the patients. Another 11,367 cells from four other people served as comparison. Tumors held more CD8+ T cells and macrophages than normal kidney tissue. Tumor T cells split into distinct states. One fast-growing subgroup, marked by MKI67, may drive progression. Cell subgroup patterns predicted patient outcomes better than broad measures. The authors flag subgroups worth targeting in therapy.
europmc-pmc7857406:
Buss and co-authors estimate that three-quarters of Manaus, Brazil, caught SARS-CoV-2 in its first wave. The city peaked in May 2020. Hospitals broke under the load and cemeteries filled. Control steps there were light. The team read blood donor samples over time.

Antibody rates climbed fast month by month. Corrections for fading antibodies lifted the estimate. The final attack rate came to about three in four residents. That level nears herd immunity claims. Spread since then tests that idea hard. The authors warn that even such high rates may not stop new waves. Their count is a warning for unmitigated spread anywhere.
europmc-pmc7885606:
Harrison and co-authors report a study that built a quality appraisal tool for mixed-methods research. Systematic reviews in health services often include studies of many designs. Judging the quality of such mixed sets is hard with tools made for one design alone. The team set out to fix an earlier tool.

The authors reviewed all papers that had cited their earlier QATSDD tool, 197 in all. They also surveyed first authors of those papers for hands-on feedback. The feedback pointed to unclear scope and hard-to-use criteria. The revised tool, called QuADS, was then tested for agreement between raters. It reached a reliability score of k=0.66, with good face and content validity. The study gives reviewers a tested way to judge diverse studies.
europmc-pmc8010506:
Alzubaidi and co-authors give a broad survey of deep learning, from basic concepts to future directions. Deep learning has become the leading approach in machine learning. It matches or beats human performance on some hard tasks. Earlier reviews each covered only one slice of the field. This one aims at the whole picture, as a starting point for new researchers.

The survey sets out the main types of deep networks and how they learn. It then traces convolutional neural networks in depth, from AlexNet to the High-Resolution network. The authors list open challenges and proposed fixes. They cover uses from cybersecurity to medical imaging. Hardware tools, benchmark datasets, and an evolution matrix round out the tour.
europmc-pmc8129206:
Grieshaber-Bouyer and co-authors argue that neutrophils form one developmental continuum, not a set of discrete subsets. These front-line immune cells vary bewilderingly in look and behavior. The team sequenced single neutrophils from healthy and inflamed mouse tissues. Standard clustering split them into shifting, unstable groups. Diffusion mapping and RNA velocity told a simpler story. The cells line up along one timed spectrum.

They name that spectrum neutrotime for its clock-like order. It runs from immature pre-neutrophils in the bone marrow. Mature cells in blood and spleen mark its far end. The steepest changes hit at two handover points. Human neutrophils trace the same transcriptomic arc. Cells entering inflamed lung, belly, or joint keep the mature signature. Each site then layers its own extra program on top. One spectrum, many local costumes, is the model. Targeting harmful stages without wiping the line is the hope.
europmc-pmc8481206:
Terwee and co-authors clear up the concept of minimal important change for health questionnaires. This value marks the smallest change over time that patients feel matters. Confusion with the smallest detectable change has clouded many published values.

The authors define the concept and show how to use it well. They give practical steps for estimating sound values. A systematic review then gathered such values for PROMIS measures. Fifty studies were found, though 19 used weak methods. Values from the sounder studies spread widely. The authors recommend the predictive modeling method for future work. They suggest a value of 2 to 6 points as a working guide.
europmc-pmc8515906:
Canton and co-authors review reactive oxygen species in macrophages, their sources and targets. Macrophages use these molecules to kill invading germs. But ROS also guide signaling, cell development, and gene activity. The outcome turns on where they form and how long they last.

Too much ROS has long been known to harm cells. Broad antioxidant drugs have failed in many diseases, though. That failure hints at the finer signaling roles now in view. NADPH oxidase was the first known ROS source in macrophages. Mitochondria now stand out as a second key source. The review maps these sources to guide sharper therapies.
europmc-pmc8617206:
Hu and co-authors review the JAK/STAT signaling pathway from basic science to clinic. This pathway sends signals fast from the cell surface to the nucleus. It was found more than twenty-five years ago. It controls key steps in cell growth, cancer, and inflammation.

The review covers the parts of the pathway and how it switches on and off. It then traces what goes wrong in cancer and autoimmune disease. Drugs that block this pathway now treat several of these diseases. The authors weigh the gains and limits of those drugs. Readers get a full tour of a pathway at the heart of many treatments.
europmc-pmc8988306:
Cao and co-authors hunt rubber-derived quinones in city water, air, and soil. Tire antioxidants called PPDs have spread through the environment for decades. What they turn into was largely unknown. One product recently proved deadly to coho salmon. The team built a mass spectrometry platform with home-made standards. Five quinones turned up everywhere they looked. Urban runoff, roadside soil, and air particles all held them. Every source traced back to human activity.

The team then measured levels of quinones and parent compounds. Patterns differed by material in striking ways. Intake estimates for Hong Kong followed. Children took in up to 7.30 nanograms per kilogram daily. Adults took in from 1.08 upward. Quinone exposure topped that of the parent antioxidants. The authors call for toxicology work. Rubber's hidden products may carry real risk.
europmc-pmc9060606:
WHO Solidarity Trial Consortium investigators report final results for four repurposed drugs in hospital patients with COVID-19. The trial enrolled 14,221 patients at 454 hospitals in 35 countries. Three drugs, lopinavir, hydroxychloroquine, and interferon, had already stopped early for futility. Remdesivir continued, and deaths were close between its group and controls: 602 of 4,146 patients died on remdesivir versus 643 of 4,129 on standard care.

Meta-analyses pooling all trials of these drugs point the same way. None of the four showed a clear effect on hospital deaths. The authors present the findings as a firm guide for treatment choices.
europmc-pmc9135406:
Rutz and co-authors describe the LOTUS initiative for open knowledge management in natural products research. The field relies on scattered, non-standard databases that are hard to combine. The core data unit is a referenced pair linking a molecular structure to its source organism. Sharing such pairs openly could transform the field.

LOTUS has harmonized and validated more than 750,000 referenced structure-organism pairs. Its data sit on Wikidata and are mirrored on a public site. That home widens access and lets the community help curate records. Links into the wider Wikidata graph may yield new chemical and biological insights. The authors present LOTUS as a step toward a shared, open knowledge base for the field.
europmc-pmc9192206:
Hussain and co-authors review modern diagnostic imaging, its applications, and its risk factors. Imaging makes pictures of tissues and organs to check normal and abnormal function. Methods include X-ray, CT, PET, MRI, SPECT, mammography, and ultrasound. Combined tools like PET/CT and PET/MRI push resolution and safety further.

The review lists uses across heart disease, cancers, brain disorders, and complex fractures. Each method carries benefits as well as risks, notably radiation exposure for some. Steps to cut that exposure are described in the text. The authors expect steady advances to make imaging a routine measure for many diseases. Readers get a broad survey of a field central to modern diagnosis.
europmc-pmc9278006:
Yin and co-authors benchmark AlphaFold for modeling protein complexes from sequence. They test several versions and settings on 152 diverse pairs of interacting proteins. Success means a near-native model ranked at the top. They also compare against classic docking methods that use unbound structures.

AlphaFold produced near-native top models in 43% of cases. Docking managed only 9%. Antibody-antigen pairs, though, failed almost completely. A multimer version did little better on those, at 11%. T cell receptor pairs were also modeled poorly. The authors map which sequence and structure traits predict failure. Deep learning, they conclude, already beats docking for many transient complexes.
europmc-pmc9448806:
Feng and co-authors show that lactate can raise the stemness of CD8 T cells and boost anti-tumor immunity. Lactate is a fuel made from glucose breakdown. Its effect inside tumors is mixed and hard to split from acid effects. The team tested lactate apart from that acid load.

Sodium lactate given to mice with MC38 tumors slowed tumor growth. The effect needed CD8 T cells to work. Single-cell profiling found more stem-like TCF-1 bearing T cells inside tumors. Lactate blocked histone deacetylase enzymes in the cells. That raised acetylation at the Tcf7 gene locus and lifted its output. T cells pre-treated with lactate fought tumors well after transfer. The work points to a new lever for cancer immune therapy.
europmc-pmc9617606:
Liu and co-authors build IsoNet, a deep learning package for isotropic reconstruction in electron tomography. Cryo electron tomography shows cell structures in their native place. A missing wedge of data blurs views along one axis. That blur has long blocked clear reading of tomograms.

IsoNet learns from the raw tomograms themselves in loops. Each round rebuilds part of the missing wedge data. The rounds also lift the signal over the noise. No sub-tomogram averaging is needed for the gain. The team tested the tool on three data types. It resolved lattice faults in immature HIV particles. It set out the layout of a flagellar rod in fine detail. It also spotted heptagon bearing clathrin cages in a synapse. The authors say the tool frees cell tomograms for direct study.
europmc-pmc9671806:
Gogishvili and co-authors report the EMPOWER-Lung 3 phase 3 trial of cemiplimab plus chemotherapy in lung cancer. Cemiplimab alone had already beaten chemotherapy in high PD-L1 cases. This trial tested the pair as first treatment for advanced disease. It took patients no matter their PD-L1 level or tumor type.

The double-blind trial randomized 466 patients in a two to one split. The drug arm had 312 patients and the placebo arm had 154. All got platinum-doublet chemotherapy with their assigned drug. Median overall survival was 21.9 months on the pair. It was 13.0 months on chemotherapy with placebo. The trial stopped early once preset survival marks were met. Severe adverse events came more often in the drug arm. The authors say the pair works for both squamous and non-squamous disease.
europmc-pmc9825606:
Martin and co-authors report Ensembl 2023, the genome annotation platform after two decades of growth. Ensembl builds gene maps for vertebrates and model species. Its tools and services evolve with the public genome flood. Biodiversity projects now pour out reference genomes fast.

This update follows the field's shift toward pangenomes. Many breeds and strains now carry their own assemblies. Human haplotypes from the first pangenome graphs were annotated. Ninety-four assemblies from 47 people anchor that work. The variant effect predictor gained fresh updates. Protein structure views from the AlphaFold database were woven in. A beta build of the new website went live. Fast draft annotation now serves species without RNA data. Repeat libraries grew into an extensive collection. The goal is quality maps across the tree of life. Free access stays the platform's standing rule.
europmc-pmc9836206:
Muik and co-authors test whether vaccine sera can neutralize the Omicron variant of SARS-CoV-2. Omicron carries an unseen load of spike mutations. Those changes threatened to blunt antibody recognition badly. The team used sera from people given the BNT162b2 vaccine.

Sera came from 51 participants after two or three doses. They faced Wuhan, Beta, Delta, and Omicron pseudoviruses in tests. After two doses, Omicron blocking fell more than 22-fold. Wuhan blocking titers stood far higher in the same sera. One month after a third dose, the picture flipped. Omicron titers rose 23-fold from the two dose level. They matched Wuhan titers seen after two doses. Live virus tests on a subset confirmed the pattern. The authors say three doses may protect against Omicron disease.
europmc-pmc9841506:
Li and co-authors review CRISPR and Cas9 therapeutics, weighing progress made and prospects ahead. The editing system can fix harmful base changes for good. It can also shut off disease causing genes outright. That promise makes it a hoped for tool of future medicine.

Many Cas9 variants and offshoots now serve different jobs. Base editors and RNA editors widen the reach further. The hard part is delivery to sick cells inside the body. Nonviral carriers with targeting skills draw the field's focus. Disease traits themselves may flag where carriers should go. The review sorts the field by editing type first. Delivery vectors get their own long survey next. Disease traits that guide targeting complete the frame. Trial successes so far are gathered and judged. Open safety and precision problems are stated plainly.
ford-fifth-queen-1906:
The Fifth Queen, published in 1906, opens Ford's trilogy on Katharine Howard, fifth wife of Henry VIII. Katharine comes to a court eaten by faction, a young Howard girl carrying her family's hopes after the Cleves marriage fails.

Ford builds the Tudor court as impressionist theater: whispers, ceremonies, spies, and the slow gears of policy turning behind tapestries. Cromwell watches the new queen rise as his own power thins. The novel prizes atmosphere over pageant, truth of feeling over chronicle. It began Ford's most sustained historical achievement, completed in two further volumes of high quality. Historians praise its feel for the period.
frus-1861-d106:
Lord Lyons wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 11 October 1861. The letter is document 106 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The file places this Lyons note after later papers, a quirk of the printed order. Its October date ties it to the busy autumn exchange on claims and sea rights. Lyons writes as the voice of the British cabinet in Washington, firm and correct in every line. The printed order of the volume groups by post, so dates must guide the reader here. Dates, in this volume, are the thread that ties the posts into one story.
frus-1861-d206:
Writing on 6 May 1861, William H. Seward sent Bradford Wood a second letter in five days. The letter is document 206 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

A second letter to Copenhagen in five days rounds out Seward's first orders to Denmark. Small posts got short letters, but they got them on time. The note closes the slice at the far edge of the Secretary's wide spring sweep. On time letters to small posts kept the whole service in step that spring. In step service, from the greatest post to the least, was Seward's spring design.
frus-1861-d306:
One more voice from abroad reached Washington on 17 August 1861: Mr. Bigler writing to Seward. It was printed as Document 306 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d106:
News and judgment from Charles Francis Adams reached Seward's desk in a letter dated 18 July 1862. It was printed as Document 106 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d206:
Earl Russell wrote from London to Lord Lyons in Washington on 23 January 1862. And the instruction stands as Document 206 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Russell ran British foreign policy; Lyons carried it out in the American capital.

Instructions like this crossed the ocean by steamer and governed Lyons's talks for weeks after they were written. January's letters from Russell came as London settled its view of the war for 1862: watch, trade carefully, and avoid a break with the Union. The printed copy lets Americans of the day, and readers now, see that guidance whole. Lyons also reported home on each note, so most of these papers exist in two archives.
frus-1862-d306:
Document 306 is the second Seward dispatch to William L. Dayton dated 23 August 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Secretary of State William H. Seward sent the set to Paris together.

Splitting one mail into three letters let each subject stand alone for filing and reply. It also let the Secretary vary his register: instruction in one, information in another. This middle letter of the set belongs to the week before Bull Run, when Washington still hoped the Virginia campaign might end the summer well. French public opinion ran warmer for the Union after the emancipation news arrived.
frus-1862-d406:
On 2 August 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Horace J. Perry, who was minding American business in Madrid. It is Document 406 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Washington's Madrid file ran heavy in 1862 because Spain touched the war at several points: Cuba, the Gulf trade, and the joint expedition in Mexico. Perry, as secretary of legation, often served as the acting head of the post. Seward's instructions guided his words with Spanish ministers. The letter is one link in a chain that kept Spain formally neutral through the war's most doubtful months.
frus-1862-d506:
On the eve of the Seven Days battles in Virginia, 21 June 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to James Shepherd Pike. The instruction is Document 506 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Neither writer nor reader of this letter could know that Richmond was about to be relieved and the Union's spring confidence broken. Seward's orders at midsummer still spoke the language of imminent success, which his ministers repeated at their courts. When the news turned, those same ministers had to explain the reversal. The dispatch thus catches the Hague correspondence at the last moment of the old story, before the hardest summer of the war rewrote it.
frus-1862-d606:
After a gap in the printed Mexican instructions, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Thomas Corwin in Mexico City on 23 August 1862. The letter is Document 606 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

By August the French were deep in Mexico and the Union was reeling from a summer of defeats. Seward's instruction still held the year's line: sympathy for the Juárez republic, protest against the European enterprise, and no second war. Corwin's value in Mexico City was presence itself, an American minister standing with the republic while his own country could send nothing else. The dispatch reopens the file at the moment both crises, Mexico's and America's, were at their worst.
frus-1862-d706:
On 9 October 1862, William H. Seward wrote to Charles N. Riotte, the American minister in Costa Rica, for the second time in three days. The letter is document 706 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. It closes the Riotte run in the volume.

Paired letters like these are the grain of the printed record: brief, plain, and tied to the small points of a post's work. Seward's note, read with the one before it, shows how Washington broke its orders into parts an envoy could act on. The Costa Rica file is short, but it rounds out the map of American posts kept up during the war.
frus-1863p1-d106:
William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 2 March 1863, the tenth of twelve letters to him dated that day in this file. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 106 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Ten sheets in, the day's work nears its end. Seward's batch writing let each point in the British file stand alone, so Adams could press them in any order as talks allowed. This letter is the tenth of the set. Read in line, the dozen form the fullest single-day statement of the Union's London brief in the volume. This letter is one of its closing parts.
frus-1863p1-d206: Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 21 May 1863. It is document 206 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the London correspondence on Britain and the Civil War. Letters on this route carried Adams's reading of British policy while Washington worked to keep Britain from backing the Confederacy.
frus-1863p1-d306:
On 6 October 1863, orders left Washington for London: Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The paper is document 306 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

For readers today, these instructions reveal the thinking inside the State Department as clearly as any memoir. They show choices being made in real time, with poor information and high stakes. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d406:
One entry in the running Washington exchange, this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, is dated 2 March 1863. It stands as document 406 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Washington believed Confederate agents used British ports, ships, and soil too freely. Seward pressed Lyons to have his government tighten its watch. It dates from the spring when British debate over aiding the South was still live, and every note counted. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d506:
A 9 May 1863 dispatch from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington reached William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d606:
Document 606, dated 10 August 1863, records a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1917-72PubDipv06:
This retrospective volume covers public diplomacy from 1961 to 1963. It belongs to the 1917-1972 subseries of the Foreign Relations set. Documents run from December 1960 to November 1963. They record how America presented itself abroad. Information programs and cultural efforts fill the files. The Kennedy years supply the whole span.

A mid-volume paper shows the era's harder edge. Rusk writes on defoliant work in South Vietnam. His November note weighs holding a zone near Saigon. Such memos sit inside the diplomacy record. Public words and secret war planning shared one government. The volume prints both without comment. Readers can judge the gap themselves. It is a source book on Cold War persuasion.
frus-1919Parisv06:
Volume VI closes the Council of Four's minutes. They run from May 24 to June 28, 1919. The last date is the signing at Versailles. Meetings multiply as the deadline nears. Two sessions a day become routine in June. A mid-volume report fixes Hungary's fate by telegram. The Allies declare frontiers that shall permanently divide Hungary. Czechoslovakia and Roumania gain their lines in that wire. Hungary's forces must accept the stated borders.

The report answers a letter received June 17. Such paper moved armies that summer. The volume joins decision to ceremony. Its minutes end where the treaty signs. Readers watch the peace harden into text. June's pressure fills every page.
frus-1941v06:
The neutrality committee opens the 1941 republics volume. Uruguay's old proposal wins American support next. An American state at war with outsiders should not count as belligerent. Chile drafts a plea to humanize war. Republics are asked to beg Spain's neutrality. Then December's declarations ripple south in files. Each republic's answer is filed by country. Rio's foreign ministers meet in January 1942. Their preliminaries close the general section. Lend-Lease ground rules for the hemisphere follow. Strategic exports are licensed with new care.

A mid-volume file shares aviation fuel secrets. Phillips Petroleum opens its iso-octane work to visitors. Bartlesville and Borger host the studying technicians. Such transfers armed the hemisphere's air arms. The volume is solidarity under sudden war. Its files turn neighbors into allies.
frus-1942v06:
Chile's slow courtship fills the 1942 sixth volume's front. Defense teamwork is sought in a long file. Copper and other strategic goods follow. American exports to Chile are licensed with care. Oil use must shrink while tankers run short. Money controls need Santiago's joining too. Colombia then signs on in earnest. Its military mission pact dates from May. Naval advisers stay by renewal of old terms. Rubber Reserve buys Colombia's whole surplus. Lend-Lease signs in March that year. Two Italian tankers pass to American hands.

Debt talks and a health program close Colombia's list. A mid-volume report dissects Ecuador's money office. Italian accounts suffered whether loyal or not, it notes. Only the president could fix the machinery, it judges. The volume is resources diplomacy at war.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d106: Chiang Kai-shek wrote to Roosevelt on November 9, 1943, and the letter is Document 106 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Chiang was preparing to travel to Cairo, a journey that would take him out of China in wartime for the summit. His letters to Washington that month carried both requests and assurances. The record gives the date and the names. The text in the Foreign Relations series holds the particulars.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d206:
Prime Minister Churchill telegraphed President Roosevelt on 10 November 1943 with a complaint about France. Changes in the French National Committee had left Charles de Gaulle as its sole president, and Churchill says he is not at all content with that outcome.

The body the Allies recognized, he points out, rested on a co-presidency shared by de Gaulle and General Giraud, a body of a totally different character. Churchill suggests that Britain and America keep an attitude of complete reserve toward the new arrangement until he and Roosevelt can discuss the position together. They would soon do so in person at Cairo.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d306:
The entry under this title contains no draft text at all, only the editors' note about one. The document it names is an American draft of the Cairo communiqué, dated 24 November 1943, carrying amendments in President Roosevelt's own handwriting, and preserved in the Roosevelt Papers.

From the note, Harry Hopkins dictated the typed draft to Warrant Officer Cornelius in the solarium of the President's villa. It was the afternoon of 24 November. By Cornelius's later account, Hopkins worked without any prepared notes or papers before him. Roosevelt's handwritten changes on this draft were then worked into the revised version of 25 November, which is printed later in the volume. Readers should note the mismatch: the catalog title promises the draft itself, but only its history is given here.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d406: Harry Hopkins and President Roosevelt exchanged two short handwritten notes at Tehran on 1 December 1943, near the end of that day's luncheon meeting. The scrap, preserved in the Hopkins Papers and printed in facsimile in Sherwood's book, concerns the evening's dinner. Hopkins asks what the President thinks of letting the Russians give dinner that night, calling it his last chance at Russian food. Roosevelt scrawls back his answer underneath: OK, but I have to leave early, as the party sleeps at the camp. The brief exchange is the whole document.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d506:
The United States Chiefs of Staff produced another memorandum on December 7, 1943, the day after the Second Cairo Conference ended, and the State Department printed it in the Cairo-Tehran volume. The American chiefs were still with the traveling party as the conference broke up.

Memoranda written just after a summit often fix a side's reading of what was agreed, before memory can soften it. The American chiefs used such papers to protect the decisions they had won and to frame the orders that followed. For the reader, this text shows the work of consolidation: a great conference being converted, within a day, into positions and instructions.
frus-1943v06:
Continuing the American Republics coverage, Volume VI of the 1943 Diplomatic Papers works through the region country by country. Colombia opens the volume, with its move into belligerency against Germany and its pledge to the United Nations Declaration. Naval mission accords and sales of strategic materials follow.

Joint steps to curb Axis money deals in Colombia fill later papers. Like its companion volume, the book mixes treaties, trade talks, and embassy reports from across Latin America. Wartime needs drove most contacts, from raw materials to port and base rights. The record shows close ties and sharp friction in the same pages.
frus-1944-quebec-d106:
A September 5, 1944 letter carried Hull's advice to President Roosevelt. The State Department printed the letter in its Quebec 1944 volume. It came one week before the conference opened in Canada. Hull's letters that month carried the department's final advice.

Last-week letters before a summit tend to be practical. They confirm positions, flag disputes, and suggest answers. Roosevelt left for Quebec City days after receiving this one. Churchill was then crossing the Atlantic to join him. For readers, the message shows preparation nearing its end. The written record was about to give way to spoken argument.
frus-1944-quebec-d206: An editors' note marks another dinner meeting at Quebec for which nothing of the discussion survives. No record has been found of the substance of the conversation. The time of the dinner and the names of those present are taken from the President's Log. The note preserves the meeting's place in the conference schedule while honestly recording that its content is lost.
frus-1944v06:
China alone fills Volume VI of the 1944 Diplomatic Papers. General war ties lead, with China's weak front and American aid at the center. Vice President Wallace's June visit and his talks with Chiang Kai-shek follow in detail.

The Hurley and Nelson missions as the President's personal envoys come next. A long run tracks Kuomintang-Communist talks and the Army observer team sent to Communist ground. Sino-Soviet friction over Sinkiang also appears. The papers show an ally near collapse and a civil conflict held back only by war. Money and supply fights run through the later papers.
frus-1945-50-intel-d106:
National Intelligence Directive No. 4, dated 2 April 1946, came from the National Intelligence Authority, the board of secretaries above the Central Intelligence Group. The numbering alone shows the new system at work. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Directives from the authority bound all the departments' intelligence arms at once, which no single department could do. By the fourth directive, the machinery of January was producing a steady stream of common rules. Readers should note how fast the paper system grew: an authority, a director, a group, and numbered orders within ten weeks. Whatever its limits, the arrangement of 1946 proved that central direction could run, and its papers taught the lessons the 1947 law would use.
frus-1945-50-intel-d206:
The Deputy Director of Central Intelligence (Wright) addressed a letter to the President’s Administrative Assistant (Murphy) on 27 January 1947. It is document 206 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The war had just ended, and the United States was keeping a central spy service in peace for the first time.

The text is one side of an exchange, set out in full under the writer's own name and title. Its worth now is the voice: a chief stating his case as he wished it to be read. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d306:
The Assistant Director for Policy Coordination (Wisner) addressed a memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 29 October 1948. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 306 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. It was a season of stock-taking: the CIA was a year old, and its friends and critics were both writing things down.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d406:
W. Park Armstrong, the State Department's intelligence chief, drafted a memo to Under Secretary of State James Webb on 23 December 1949. The draft is document 406 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

A draft shows thought before it hardens into a fixed stand. Armstrong led the department's analysts, and Webb was the Secretary's chief deputy for running the department. The paper lets readers watch a senior aide frame an issue for the man just below the Secretary himself. Webb soon left to run the space agency's parent body, but in 1949 he was State's strong second in command.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d106:
“Relations Between UNRRA and the Soviet Government” is the heading of this briefing book paper of 18 January 1945. Prepared for the President's trip, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It sets out why relief in Eastern Europe needed Moscow's full cooperation, and why that cooperation had lagged.

The paper lists the delays. Governor Lehman's June request to visit Moscow went unanswered for months. Visas for UNRRA staff bound through Soviet territory for Poland and Czechoslovakia were slow. So were plans to move supplies. Then, on 18 January, Soviet officials said two Black Sea ports could take relief goods, and transit would be allowed. The paper wonders if Moscow's stance has truly turned.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d206:
Stalin closed the French question for the moment on 10 December 1944. His short message to Roosevelt, received in translation, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It reports the outcome of de Gaulle's Moscow visit.

Together with the general, Stalin writes, they reached a decision on the pact. A Franco-Soviet pact of mutual assistance would serve both Franco-Soviet relations and European security in general. The pact was signed that very day. As for France's postwar border, the question stands postponed, as he had already written. The brief note ends a three-cornered exchange in which Washington and London had both blessed the pact in advance.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d306:
Britain's delegation at Malta set out its demands on the Allied Control Commissions in Bulgaria and Hungary in a memorandum dated February 1, 1945. London insisted its officers in those countries get fair freedom to move and to send messages home. It also objected to choices made in Britain's name without British agreement.

For Hungary, London noted, agreed rules for the commission already met the first point. The paper asks that the same rules be adopted for Bulgaria, and that British and American officers be consulted before decisions during the first period. It captures early friction over Soviet-run commissions in Eastern Europe.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d406:
Poland dominated Hiss's notes at the foreign ministers' meeting of February 9, 1945. Stettinius opened with the home front. America faced a hard fight over joining the world organization, he said. Settling the Polish matter in a way the world would accept mattered greatly at that moment, for reasons of morale.

His notes then track the bargain's shape. The President's commission idea was dropped. All three sides agreed the Polish government should hold three elements: the Lublin Poles, plus democrats in Poland and abroad. A commission in Moscow would consult first with Lublin and with Polish leaders at home and outside. The shorthand shows the formula being born.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d506:
Three more unproductive hours: Ambassador Harriman's cable of March 5, 1945, reports the Poland commission stuck in Moscow. Every argument he and Clark Kerr advanced was brushed aside. He had told Molotov that the President would be shocked to learn of Molotov's obstruction. The commission could not even call representative Polish democratic leaders to Moscow for consultation.

Stalin, Harriman reminded him, had agreed at Yalta to inviting men like Sapieha and Witos. Why did Molotov now go back on that position? Molotov answered that the communiqué was the anchor for the commission's work, and no other conversations counted. The cable shows the Yalta formula dissolving within a month.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d106:
Ambassador Harriman asked to be included in the Berlin trip in a telegram to the Secretary of State on June 27, 1945. The message is document 106 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It reached the State Department only on July 4, a week after it was sent from Moscow.

Harriman assumes the President and the Secretary would want him at the meeting. That rests on his knowledge of many matters on the table, above all those touching the Far East. He asks to be told, so he can make his plans. He also suggests being ordered to take Vyshinsky to Berlin for a day before the meeting. Vyshinsky ran the Soviet arrangements. He could settle on the spot questions that might stall at the military level. The cable shows the ambassador working to stay central to the summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d206:
Edwin Pauley made sure Moscow was formally told reparations would be raised, in a letter to Ambassador Harriman dated July 11, 1945. The letter and its enclosure form document 206 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The enclosure is Pauley's note to Ivan Maisky, his Soviet counterpart on the reparations commission.

As the President's personal representative, Pauley writes Maisky. He advises the Soviet government on one point. The general subject of reparations will be one of the topics the President may wish to raise. He may raise it at the meeting of the three heads of government. The talk may cover points from his letter of July 3, where the Moscow commission had deadlocked. He asks Harriman to forward a copy through Molotov, so there can be no question the Soviet government was properly notified.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d306:
King Michael of Rumania confided his doubts to Melbourne in Bucharest, and Melbourne reported them on July 8, 1945. Stalin had just awarded the King the Soviet Order of Victory. The Russians had also given him two airplanes. Michael said he was bewildered by these sudden gifts.

Past experience, the King said, taught him that Moscow acted from hard motives. He distrusted the new warmth. He also denied rumors of a secret Rumanian-Soviet military pact, and he hoped Potsdam would read the Yalta declaration fairly and win Rumania a government that truly spoke for its people.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d406: Winant's telegram from London of July 4, 1945, reports a single step. It was sent under the code address Comea 318. That day the European Advisory Commission approved, in substance, a draft agreement on the French zone in Germany. The texts were to be checked the next day by an experts' subcommittee. That check came before signature. The message went to the Department. It was repeated to Paris, for Ambassador Caffery and for Murphy.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d506:
Liquidation of the London Polish ministries is reported in Winant's cable from London of July 6, 1945. Hankey, he was told by the Foreign Office official directly concerned with Polish affairs, will leave for Warsaw on July 10. An Interim Treasury Committee for Polish Questions will be appointed to liquidate the Polish civilian ministries in London.

The committee will consist of one Pole for each ministry to be liquidated, acting under British supervision. The final list of Poles contains alterations made at the request of Mikołajczyk's supporters. The official stressed, though, that these Poles have no official representative status. They act merely as advisers to the British on the liquidation, whose work includes payment of pensions.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d606:
State Department staff wrote a briefing paper on winning Soviet backing for the Cairo Declaration, June 29, 1945. It is document 606 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The Cairo statement had been issued on December 1, 1943, without Stalin as a party.

The paper first restates what Cairo promised. Manchuria, Formosa, and the Pescadores would go back to China. Korea would in due course become free and independent. Japan would lose all Pacific islands seized since 1914 and all lands taken by force and greed. Soviet support, the paper argues, would strengthen U.S. policy in the Far East. It would also bar Moscow from making land claims in Manchuria itself. The brief was written to arm Truman for his first meeting with Stalin as President.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d706:
Ambassador Winant reported a London talk between Turkey's foreign minister and Eden on July 12, 1945. His secret wire is document 706 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The Foreign Office showed Winant's staff its record of the meeting.

Minister Saka called the recent Soviet approaches to Turkey sinister in character. He believed the fourth, unnamed matter Molotov had raised was the most serious of all. It was, he judged, a Soviet wish to draw Turkey into the Russian orbit, in economics and politics alike. Eden's side counseled a cooler reading of Soviet method. For bargaining, they noted, Moscow often states its requests in extreme terms. Saka was also reminded that Britain had entered a formal caveat in Moscow after the June 7 talks. He asked if the Straits would be discussed at the Big Three meeting and was told that was the plan.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1006:
The Navy Department cabled Admiral Harold Stark, commander of American naval forces in Europe, on July 18, 1945. British Admiralty messages had revealed a gap. No American seat exists on the Capcraft Commission, the body handling captured enemy small craft. Nothing guards the American interest in sending such craft, tugs included, for prompt use in the Pacific.

The need there is urgent: seagoing tugs are wanted for approved Pacific operations. Stark is told to seek equal American representation on the commission, or set up a counter body. One idea is to swap captured German tugs for American tugs now serving in Europe. The shipping and war agencies in Washington back the move.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1106:
An internal note of the United States team at Potsdam, this memorandum is dated 31 July 1945. The summit had two days left to run. Notes of this kind recorded choices, summed up meetings, or fixed the American stand for the record as the talks wound down.

While this note was written, staff were drafting the final protocol, the signed list of all the summit's choices. An internal memorandum is not a speech or a press line. It is the team talking to itself on paper. That makes it useful evidence of what the Americans thought they had won, lost, or still hoped to settle.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1206:
The War Department wrote to the American team at Potsdam on 25 July 1945. Notes from the Pentagon to the summit carried military guidance and news from home. The line kept the envoys tied to the department that ran the army holding Germany.

The department's stake in the talks was direct. Its forces would enforce whatever the leaders signed, from borders to the rule of the zones. Word from Washington could shift what the team asked for or accepted. This cable is the home brass checking in with its envoys, mid-summit. It shows the peace being drafted with one hand and prepared for with the other.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1306:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to Secretary of War Stimson on 18 July 1945. The letter joined two men who shared a rare burden. Britain had backed the atomic project from its early days, and Churchill knew its state nearly as well as the Americans.

A note from the prime minister to the war secretary, two days after the first test, sits inside the atomic thread of the summit. Churchill and Stimson had dealt with each other through the war's hardest choices. This message is that tie at work in Potsdam's first week. It shows the bomb's secret binding the alliance's top men in a channel of its own.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1406:
On 6 August 1945 Caffery addressed a cable to Secretary Byrnes himself, rather than to the acting secretary. The volume prints a run of Caffery cables to the secretary from that day. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Byrnes had come home from Potsdam to a department full of unsettled files, France among them. A cable aimed at the secretary personally asks for his eye above the staff's. Caffery, who had just spent days in close work with Bidault, had much to lay before him. Readers should note the channel: when the stakes rose, the ambassador wrote to the top, and the volume lets us follow the paper upward.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-106:
On July 25, 1945, the United States delegation at Potsdam put this memorandum into its working files. Memoranda bound the delegation together. They spread news of side talks, briefed officers, and fixed agreed lines before the next session. The paper survived in the conference archive and was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Because it was written for insiders, the memo speaks in direct terms. It shows the American team sharing one picture of where things stood. Readers can pair it with the formal minutes of the same day. The two forms together show both the talks and the machine that ran them.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d806:
Melbourne reported from Rumania on July 22, 1945, in document 806. The acting representative in Bucharest wrote to the Acting Secretary of State. His letters form a near-weekly spine for the volume's Rumania file. This one entered the second Potsdam volume as the conference turned into its second week.

Steady reporting from a hard post has cumulative force. Melbourne's facts built a case Washington could use. Readers watch a mission documenting its own squeeze. The document shows the alliance's eastern posts still functioning as its eyes. Their reports are why the summit's Balkan record can be read with ground truth attached.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d906:
Britain's delegation set out its view of restitution and replacement in the paper of July 21, 1945. Sir Walter Monckton presented it in the Economic Sub-Committee. Like the Soviet draft, it confines restitution to identifiable property taken from invaded lands, however the taking happened.

The paper draws a hard line on replacement. Goods that cannot be traced, or were destroyed, may be replaced only in the case of works of art. Even then, a swap must not harm learning by moving art from its proper home. All other claims for lost loot lose special priority. They join the general pool of reparation claims.
frus-1945v06:
The British Commonwealth and the Far East share Volume VI of the 1945 Diplomatic Papers. Britain leads, with postwar credit talks, the Lend-Lease settlement, and a revised oil pact. Air rights and base support fill many cables between London and Washington.

Canada and Australia follow with accords on industry, transport, and joint boards. India takes a long section, on its politics, surplus property, and trade treaty talks. Far East papers on Japan's surrender terms close the volume. The mix shows an empire's partners settling war accounts and planning an uneasy peace.
frus-1946v06:
Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union fill Volume VI for 1946. Bulgaria, Hungary, Poland, and Rumania each get long runs. In each, Washington pushed for broad governments and free votes, with mixed results.

Czechoslovakia's aid and trade deals and Finland's bank credit sit apart from that pattern. Soviet reports and stalled Lend-Lease settlement talks follow. Yugoslavia closes the volume, with shot-down American planes among the incidents. Embassy cables show influence shifting east. Each capital's story turns on how much room Moscow left it. Recognition choices show how little leverage remained in most capitals by then.
frus-1947v06:
The Far East fills Volume VI for 1947, from Burma's new ties with Washington to Japan's slow path toward a peace treaty. Occupation control and reparations claims take long Japanese sections. Korea's case went to the United Nations that year.

Indochina and the East Indies show nationalist revolts against French and Dutch return. The Indonesian case reached the Security Council. The Philippines, now a republic, works out its ties with its former ruler. Consular reports catch Asia in transition. Old rule was ending at a different pace in each land. Trade files with the new republics run through the volume's second half.
frus-1948v06:
The Far East and Australasia fill Volume VI for 1948. Indonesia takes the longest run, as its revolt against Dutch rule reached the Security Council. Indochina's fight against French return follows in a shorter block.

Japan's occupation, reparations, and recovery plans fill the northeast sections. Korea draws hundreds of papers, on its politics and its appeal to the General Assembly. The Philippines and Pacific island claims round out the volume. Reports from consulates show colonial rule ending in war in some lands and by pact in others. Island sovereignty claims add a Pacific thread.
frus-1949v06:
The Near East, South Asia, and Africa fill the largest 1949 volume, Volume VI. Security interests and oil open the regional record. Greece's civil war ends in these pages, with its UN debate beside it.

Israel takes the longest run, on armistice deals and failed peace bids. Iran, Saudi Arabia, and Syria follow in shorter blocks. Kashmir and Prime Minister Nehru's visit lead South Asia. A Tangier meeting of consuls opens the Africa pages. The volume shows three regions pulling American power in at once. Consular and legation upgrades mark the growing American presence.
frus-1950v06:
East Asia and the Pacific fill Volume VI for 1950, a year the Korean War remade. Regional aid and pact talk open the record. The China area follows, with consulates closing on the mainland and the Formosa question sharpened by war.

Trade bans and frozen assets mark the break with Peiping. Indochina draws growing aid for French Union forces. Japan's peace treaty drive and the Philippines' troubles fill later runs. The papers catch a policy built for one Asia being rebuilt for another, under fire, in a matter of months. Korea's war pulls the volume's later country files into its orbit.
frus-1955-57v06:
Volume VI of the 1955–1957 set covers the American Republics at the regional level, plus Mexico and the Caribbean. General policy leads, with hemisphere defense and arms aid in long runs. Aid and trade policy toward the region follow.

The Panama meeting of American presidents in July 1956 takes its own block. Mexico and the Caribbean states then fill the country files. The papers show a patron taking stock of its own backyard. Aid was the main tool, and each grant came with a defense or trade string that the files name plainly.
frus-1961-63v06:
Volume VI of the 1961–1963 set holds the Kennedy-Khrushchev exchanges alone, Documents 1–120. Letters and messages between the two leaders run the full three years. Vienna's aftermath, Berlin, and Cuba all pass through this channel.

The editors note that eight volumes carry the core Soviet record. This one keeps the direct line in a single place. Test ban talk fills the mid-sample. Tone swings from stiff notes to near warmth. The letters show how two men with vast arms bargained in prose, each line weighed by staffs before it crossed.
frus-1961-63v11-d106:
A memorandum of conversation records Secretary Rusk's talk with the British Ambassador on October 28, 1962, at 6:15 p.m., as the missile crisis broke. Rusk stresses that no cozy deals were made. Khrushchev gains only a pledge of no invasion while the weapons leave under checks.

Ormsby Gore asks what forum should carry the gain forward, NATO talks or Berlin. Rusk warns against crowing over the West's stronger place. The crisis is not yet closed, he notes. Allied backing, he adds, had shown Khrushchev the price of his course. The talk turns from relief to the next moves.
frus-1969-76v06:
Vietnam from January 1969 to July 1970 is the field of Volume VI in the 1969-1976 Foreign Relations series. Its 348 documents run in one sequence. They open with the new Nixon team's first choices on the war. They cover troop withdrawals, the secret talks in Paris, and the move into Cambodia in 1970. Bombing of the North, halted in 1968, is debated in the background.

The records include phone talks between Nixon and Kissinger and cables from Saigon. They show secret contacts with Hanoi's envoys alongside public deadlock. Policy at home, above all protest and Congress, shapes each step. The volume ends with the Cambodia operation still fresh.
frus-1969-76ve06:
Africa from 1973 to 1976 is documented in Volume E-6 of the 1969-1976 series. A regional section opens the volume. Country sections follow for Burundi, Guinea-Bissau, Kenya, Nigeria, Sudan, Uganda, and Zaire. The Horn of Africa takes the largest share. Its chapters track Ethiopia's revolution and the shift in ties with Somalia. Zaire's section covers the Angola war's spillover and ties with Kinshasa.

The records mix cables on aid, bases, and arms. Uganda's section deals with the Amin regime and its shocks. Sudan's covers the wake of its civil war. The volume shows Africa rising on the U.S. agenda as the decade turned.
frus-1981-88v06:
The Soviet Union from October 1986 to January 1989 fills Volume VI of the 1981-1988 Foreign Relations series. Its 183 documents run in one sequence. They open in Reykjavik's wake and follow the road to the INF Treaty of 1987. Talk records show Shultz and Gorbachev reviewing arms cuts topic by topic. A reduction to 6,000 warheads is among the points of agreement carried forward. Summits in Washington and Moscow anchor the middle of the volume.

The papers also cover Afghanistan's wind-down and human rights cases. By the close, the tone is one of working partnership. The volume ends the series' Soviet arc on a high note.
galsworthy-man-of-property-1906:
John Galsworthy published The Man of Property in 1906, the novel that opened the Forsyte Saga. Galsworthy came from a wealthy family much like the one he describes. He wrote the Forsytes as a portrait of upper-middle-class England and its worship of ownership.

Soames Forsyte, a solicitor, treats everything as property, including his beautiful wife, Irene. He builds a grand house at Robin Hill and hires an architect, who falls in love with Irene. Jealousy, scandal, and a shocking crime follow. Galsworthy makes Soames both villain and victim of his own creed. The novel launched one of the great family sagas in English fiction.
gao-gaoreports-b-296206:
Research Analysis and Maintenance protested a sole-source Army award in GAO decision B-296206, dated July 12, 2005. The winner was Computer Sciences Corporation. The work was to run and keep up foreign threat systems. The firm held the old deal for the same work. It said the Army wrongly shut it out.

GAO denied the protest. The Army judged the firm's past work on its live deal as not fit. The firm had not fixed that poor work well. That doubt made the sole-source pick sound. An incumbent with poor marks has no right to a fresh shot. The case turns on a weak record in hand.
gao-gaoreports-b-299806:
AHNTECH protested an Air Force review of its proposal for base operations support. The work serves Manas Air Base in Kyrgyzstan. Services span dining and other base needs. GAO decided B-299806 on August 15, 2007.

The agency found flaws under one technical subfactor. On that base, it cut the bid from the contest. The terms said bids could be cut on just that ground. So no hidden test was at play. The firm also claimed uneven treatment. GAO found the marks tracked the stated tests for each bid. A flaw called a weakness in a stronger bid can still sink a weak one. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299906:
Bighorn Lumber Company protested a Forest Service timber sale award in Colorado. The Two Elks sale sat in the Medicine Bow-Routt National Forest. The award went to Trapper Peak Timber Company. GAO decided B-299906 on September 25, 2007.

The case turned on a claimed bid error. The sale asked for one weighted average bid rate. A fix for an error needs a clear test. The true bid sum must show on the face of the bid. Or clear proof must back the claimed sum. Here, neither test was met. The claimed true bid could not be pinned down. An agency may not fix a bid on a guess. GAO sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-400106:
Masai Technologies Corporation saw its protest thrown out — GAO decision B-400106, dated May 27, 2008. The Army sought tech aid from schedule firms for a health research shop. The firm had filed a plea with the agency on one point. It then came to GAO with a new point on set-asides. That point came once the quote clock had run out. A mail note to a small-firm desk was pled as a past plea.

GAO dismissed the protest as too late. The GAO point was not the point pled at the shop. A mail tip to a desk is no plea at all. Terms of a call must be fought before the clock runs out.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-806:
College textbook prices are examined in GAO-05-806, a report dated July 29, 2005. Nearly half of undergraduates get federal aid. So book costs shape the total cost of college. GAO measured how prices have moved. It asked what drives the change. And it asked why the same U.S. book can sell abroad at a different price.

GAO found prices nearly tripled from December 1986 to December 2004. They rose at an average of 6 percent a year. That is twice the pace of inflation. Added extras best explain the recent rise, GAO said. CD-ROMs and other study aids now come bundled with books. Publishers cite teacher demand. Sellers worry that extras and fast new editions push costs up needlessly.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-906:
Wind power and wildlife is the subject of GAO-05-906, a report issued September 16, 2005. Wind farms have grown fast in the United States. Some sites have killed migratory birds and bats. Biologists worry about which species are hit and what the toll means for whole populations. GAO reviewed studies and expert views. It sampled six states with wind development. It also mapped who regulates the farms and who guards wildlife.

GAO found impacts vary by region and species. Farms in northern California killed large numbers of raptors. Farms in Pennsylvania and West Virginia killed large numbers of bats. Other areas show lower tolls, though most farms killed some birds. Many farms have never been studied, so no firm national verdict exists. Few studies test ways to cut deaths. Regulation rests mainly with state and local bodies, GAO found.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-106:
Exchange visitor oversight is faulted in GAO-06-106, a report dated October 14, 2005. Over 280,000 foreign visitors come each year on exchange programs. Two categories draw scrutiny here: summer work travel and trainees. Past reviews found visitors in unauthorized activities. GAO examined how the State Department manages the two programs. It named the risks they carry and the data at hand to judge them.

GAO found oversight too weak to guard against abuse. The department checks sponsors mainly by reading documents. It rarely visits sponsors or host employers. Sanctions in the rules are hard to enforce, officials say. The department has been slow to fix known flaws and update the rules. A new monitoring unit was planned, but its funding was not secured. Risks include visitors overstaying and the trainee track serving as a plain jobs channel.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-206:
Conflict-of-interest controls at a homeland security research office are faulted in GAO-06-206, dated December 22, 2005. The Science and Technology Directorate hires experts from national laboratories under a personnel act. These borrowed experts lead research portfolios. Some of the office's research money flows back to those same laboratories. That overlap raised hard questions. GAO checked the controls meant to guard against conflicts. It also traced the role the borrowed managers play in steering projects and funds.

The office is improving its controls, GAO found, but gaps persist. Its process for placing projects and funds was never made final. No records show how placement choices were made. Waivers for managers were only now being sought. Borrowed staff also miss ethics training shaped to their odd dual status. Five of the portfolio managers came from the national labs. Without clear rules and records, no one can prove the funding choices were clean.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-306:
The FBI's Trilogy technology project and its loose controls draw fire in GAO-06-306, published February 28, 2006. Trilogy, begun in 2001, was the bureau's largest technology upgrade to date. It refreshed the bureau's basic systems but failed to lift its case applications. Missed deadlines and rising costs pushed the total to nearly $537 million. Congress asked whether controls could catch improper payments to contractors. It asked whether payments rested on sound proof. It asked whether the bureau could account for gear the money bought.

Controls were weak, GAO found. Questionable contractor costs were paid, and assets went missing. GAO issued 27 recommendations in reply. They target invoice review at the bureau and its contracting partner. They also demand a full grip on Trilogy assets and future buys. The report is a case study in paying first and checking later. Its lessons carried into the bureau's next big system, Sentinel.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-706:
Errors in stamping documents secret are the subject of GAO-06-706, a GAO report dated June 30, 2006. Misclassification blocks needed sharing of facts, can hand foes useful information, and wastes millions on needless handling. GAO examined the Defense Department's information security program. GAO asked whether the program was run in a way that keeps classification errors low across the vast department.

GAO found a lack of oversight and uneven execution of the program. The program ran in a decentralized way, down at the component level. The office in charge had limited involvement in the components' work. It did little monitoring or review of their classification activity. GAO said the department could cut the risk of errors with tighter central checks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-906:
Spending plans for a federal electronic records archive are reviewed in GAO report GAO-06-906, dated August 18, 2006. Since 2001 the National Archives and Records Administration has built the Electronic Records Archives system. It aims to fix hard problems in making and keeping federal electronic records.

Law required the agency's fiscal year 2006 plan to go to Congress. The plan sought release of about $22 million to build the system. GAO checked the plan against the terms set in law. It found the agency had fully met three of five past GAO points, and part-met two. GAO urged a firmer process for outside review findings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1006:
Passports and visas, and the fight against fake travel papers, are examined in GAO report GAO-07-1006, dated July 31, 2007. Fake travel papers are often used to try to enter the United States. Trust in real papers rests on strong design, plus sound issue and check steps.

GAO studied the traits of U.S. passports and visas, and how word on those traits spreads. It tested the soundness of how papers are issued. It watched how papers are checked at ports of entry. Field work took in seven passport offices, nine ports, and two consulates in Mexico. Design and issue had grown stronger, GAO found, but more must be done.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-106:
New energy tech, and the hard road to market, is surveyed in GAO report GAO-07-106, dated December 20, 2006. The United States leans more on crude oil and natural gas than it did almost 30 years ago. Imports will grow without sharp change, GAO notes, and carbon gases add a climate risk.

The Department of Energy funds research on renewable, fossil, and nuclear tech. GAO traced funding trends and plans for that work. It named the chief blocks to building and fielding new tech. It studied what states and six other lands do on the same front. Key hurdles remain, the title states, for tech that must meet future needs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-206:
Immigration cases need lawyers, and the homeland security legal offices say they are short of them. GAO reviewed their staffing planning in GAO-07-206, issued April 17, 2007. The report covers the legal offices of three components. They handle enforcement, inspections, and immigration services. GAO asked how each office counts its needs and places its lawyers. It also asked how they cope with shortfalls.

None of the three offices had fully written down its planning methods, GAO found. Two of them lacked solid data on attorney workloads. One office set staffing by a rough ratio to immigration judges. Rising caseloads make the gaps more costly, GAO warned. Without records, staffing choices cannot be checked or repeated. GAO gave the department's general counsel five steps to take. They center on documenting methods and building real workload data systems. The aim is a staffing case that can stand up before Congress.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-106:
In GAO-08-106, dated November 16, 2007, GAO investigated housing contracts let after Hurricane Katrina in Mississippi. The storm destroyed or damaged 134,000 homes and 10,000 rental units in that state alone. The Federal Emergency Management Agency housed displaced people in mobile homes and trailers. In 2006, it let 15 contracts to maintain the units and sites.

GAO estimates that weak oversight led to about $30 million in wasteful or improper payments from June 2006 through January 2007. Poor task orders wasted as much as $16 million. Faulty invoice review passed an estimated $16 million more. GAO set out six actions, starting with checks for contractor overpayments.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-206:
Budget methods for long-term debts are weighed in GAO report GAO-08-206 (December 20, 2007). The federal budget has swung from surplus to deficit since 2000. Long-term fiscal exposures have more than doubled in that span. Cash-based budgets often hide those future costs until bills come due. A Senate panel asked GAO to update its study of other nations' practice.

Six nations first reviewed in 2000 still use accrual budgeting in part. Others have widened or rejected the method since. GAO finds accrual figures useful in select areas. They cannot carry the full long-term picture, though. It urges Congress to require more data on future costs of today's choices.
gibbs-scientific-papers-vol-1-1906:
J. Willard Gibbs published his core papers during his life, and his Scientific Papers gathered them in 1906. Volume one holds the thermodynamics work, centering on his long paper On the Equilibrium of Heterogeneous Substances. Gibbs taught at Yale and worked in near quiet. His math reshaped how scientists treat heat, energy, and chemical change.

The volume presents the phase rule, which predicts how substances in balance behave. It also sets out chemical potential, a key tool for judging reactions. His geometric methods picture these relations in clear shapes. Together the papers founded much of physical chemistry. Few single volumes carry such weight.
gibbs-scientific-papers-vol-2-1906:
Volume two of the Scientific Papers of J. Willard Gibbs, issued in 1906, ranges past thermodynamics. Gibbs wrote on dynamics, the study of motion under forces. He also reshaped vector analysis, the math of quantities with direction. The notation he built for it is the one physics still uses today.

Alongside those works stand his papers on the electromagnetic theory of light. Unpublished fragments close the volume and show his mind still at work. The set pairs with volume one to give his whole output. Readers find a style of rare compression and calm. Almost every page started lines of later research.
gorky-mother-1906:
Mother, Maxim Gorky's novel of 1906, was first published in English the same year in an unsigned translation. Pelageya Vlasova, a beaten factory widow, watches her son Pavel join the socialist movement. After his arrest she takes up his work, carrying leaflets and learning to speak for the cause herself.

Her growth from fear to courage forms the spine of the novel. Factory scenes, trials, and secret meetings show Russia stirring before revolution. Gorky based Pavel on a real young worker he had known. The book later became the model for Socialist Realist fiction in the Soviet Union. Read plainly, it remains a moving tale of a mother's awakening.
guida-alla-chimica-che-suo-mezzo-conduce:
Carlo Lancillotti, a physician and chemist of Modena, wrote this Guide to Chemistry in Italian, here in an enlarged Venetian edition of 1706, with new additions and figures. Its title promises to lead lovers of the art through operations on every mixed body, whether animal, mineral, or vegetable. It declares how their salts, oils, essences, magisteries, and mercuries are drawn out, and how colors, cosmetics, and other rare secrets are made.

Lancillotti calls the work most useful to doctors, apothecaries, alchemists, painters, goldsmiths, and other curious persons. The book belongs to the age when chemistry and alchemy still shared one workshop. Recipes crowd its pages, in the practical manner of the secrets tradition. For a modern reader it is a thick sample of Italian chymistry at the turn of the 1700s, hard in its old print yet rich in period craft.
guns-of-the-gods-a-story-of-yasmini-s-yo:
Guns of the Gods, a story of Yasmini's youth by Talbot Mundy, is an adventure novel set in British ruled India. Mundy builds each chapter around a spoken motto, many of them credited to Yasmini herself, a princess whose wit drives the intrigue. The contents promise gold hunting, duty bound officers, elephants, camels, and a plot closing in on a ruler named Gungadhura.

Chapter sayings sketch the whole campaign in advance. A soldier insists that duty is what he is paid to do. A warning says the toils, meaning the nets, are closing around the Maharajah. Another voice claims the princess as its own cause. British officials, Indian princes, and Yasmini's private network of agents circle each other through eighteen chapters. Treasure, loyalty, and disguise supply the motion, and the girl at the center out talks nearly everyone.
haddon-magic-and-fetishism-1906:
Alfred Cort Haddon led the Cambridge expedition to the Torres Straits in 1898, a landmark of modern fieldwork. This short 1906 book draws on that work to explain magic and fetishism for general readers, in plain terms.

Haddon defines magic as the attempt to control events by rites and spells, and the fetish as an object believed to hold power. He illustrates both from the islanders he knew, and from reports worldwide. His aim is sympathy as much as theory: to show the logic inside practices Europeans mocked. The book is a compact doorway into early anthropology's central questions.
harold-the-last-of-the-saxon-kings-volum:
Book Six of Harold is titled Ambition. It opens with great rejoicing in England. King Edward has been induced to send the prelate Alred to the German Emperor's court. His errand is to fetch Edward Atheling, the King's kinsman and the great Ironside's son. In childhood that prince and his brother Edmund had been given by Canute to the King of Sweden. It was said, without good authority, that the Swedish king was meant to make away with them.

The Swedish king instead sent the boys to Hungary, where they were honorably reared. Edmund died young; Edward married a daughter of the Emperor. The Atheling's return raises the great question of the succession to a childless king. Every party in the book feels the pull of that empty throne. Lytton slows the tale here to weigh claims and ambitions, before the storm years begin.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum:
Thomas Carlyle's sixth volume holds Book Six of his Friedrich history: the double-marriage project and the Crown Prince going adrift under storm-winds, 1727 to 1730. An English marriage for Friedrich and an English bridegroom for his sister Wilhelmine have become a European intrigue. Carlyle fishes traces of the prince from what he calls a disastrous beggarly element.

The Kaiser's spectre-hunt after influence, the treaties of Seville and Vienna piecing political nature together again, and horror-struck courts fill the diplomatic chapters. At home, Friedrich plans escape from his father's tyranny, befriends Katte, and drifts toward the catastrophe of 1730. Carlyle's sympathy for the prince and contempt for the diplomacy grow on every page.
holinshed-s-chronicles-vol-2-of-6-slice-:
Raphael Holinshed's chronicles open their second volume in this slice. The hosted set is the London edition of 1807, reprinted in 1965. The original third volume began at Duke William the Conqueror. Holinshed compiled it to 1577, and others continued it to 1586.

This slice treats William the First's England and its church order. Rules for councils and for consecrating archbishops fill some pages. Canterbury and York dispute who must travel to whom. The chronicle mixes high politics with such dry, vital points of rule. Readers start the Norman line in the great Elizabethan compilation, modernized only in print.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-06:
One hard winter gives Volume 6, from 1897, its lasting fame. The book covers Quebec in 1633 and 1634 under Thwaites's editorship of the series. Le Jeune chose to spend the cold months with the Montagnais in the woods.

He shared their hunger, their fires, and their cramped tents for months. Frost, smoke, and scarce game mark his daily notes from camp. Two whole ways of seeing the world meet around one fire. Le Jeune writes with humor, grit, and rare respect for his hosts. The result ranks among the most vivid and human pages in all the Relations.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-zorogon-1: Aaron Zorogon was a Turco-Jewish scholar who flourished about the middle of the seventeenth century. He wrote "Bet Aharon," a book of sixty homilies set in the order of the sections of the Pentateuch. It also holds some comments on the "'En Ya'aḳob," the haggadic collection of Jacob Ḥabib. The book came out after his death. His son Elihu published it in Constantinople in 1678-79.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abdimus-ben-r-j: Abdimus ben R. Jose is one form of the popular name of R. Menahem ben R. Jose. The entry lists the other forms as Abirodimus, Avradimus, Vradimas, and Vradimus. For the root of the name it sends the reader to Jastrow's Dictionary, volume one, page 375. Six passages are cited in its short bibliography, from the Jerusalem Talmud, Sifra, Shabbat, and Nedarim. No life or teaching of the man is set out here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abimi-a-contrac:
Abimi is a name borne by several amoraim, all strong in the Halakah, and the entry sets out the chief two. The first was a Babylonian halakist of the third century, quoted with no added surname. Most of his teaching came down through Rab Ḥisda. He held a tradition that the old Tabernacle, with all its boards and fittings, was hidden in chambers under the Temple when the First Temple was done.

The second Abimi was a Babylonian amora of the fourth century, a disciple of Rabbah bar Naḥmani. He and his brother 'Efa were hailed as the sharp scholars of Pumbedita. The two brothers, the entry adds, tried to set aside for Babylon the Bible law on fruit from young trees. That law stands in Leviticus, chapter 19, verse 23, and their bid is noted in Kiddushin.
