Yizhak bar Redifa was a scholar of Palestine in the fourth century. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He passed on the tale lore of Rabbi Ammi to men. His name stands at the head of such tales in three books.

He once asked the scholar Jeremiah to rule on a point. He got a vague reply and no firm rule then. His own work treats the tales of Samson at length. One note of his treats a verse in Isaiah on dress. He says pert girls put scent in their shoes in those days. They stamped their feet to wake base lust in young men. He likened that lust to the bite of a snake in heat. More notes treat the tribe of Benjamin and its fate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zechariah-ben-s:
Zechariah ben Solomon Ashkenazi was a German Talmud man of the 1500s. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He served as rabbi of the north rite Jews at Jerusalem. He died in that town at the end of his life.

He was the father-in-law of Joseph Caro, the great codifier. Caro speaks of him as a man deep in the law books. His name stands with that of David ben Zimra on a writ. In 1565 a case of the rite of halizah split the town. A man had wed the widow of his dead brother then. That act broke the north rite rule of that land. Zechariah and his peers cast that man out at once. David ben Zimra held that the ban had no right base.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zutra-mar-i-153:
Mar Zutra the First was exilarch, the head of Babylon's Jews, from 401 to 409. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He followed Mar Kahana in the office and lived in the days of R. Ashi. Though his rank was higher, he had to follow Ashi's enactments.

Zutra left Nehardea and made his home at Sura. There he held a yearly reception at the opening of the harvest season. Delegates from all the Babylonian communities came to it, and the gatherings were called rigli. Other delegations also visited him at Sura. The entry admits that nothing further is known about his career.
jonson-volpone-1606:
Ben Jonson wrote Volpone in 1606, and many call it his masterpiece. Jonson set the comedy in Venice and named his characters after animals: Volpone is the fox, his servant Mosca the fly. The play mixes sharp satire with a plot built like a trap.

Volpone, a rich old magnifico, pretends to be dying so that hopeful legacy hunters shower him with gifts. Mosca helps each visitor believe he will inherit everything. The game grows crueler until Volpone tries one trick too many. Jonson ends with unusually harsh punishments for a comedy. The play remains a fierce, funny study of greed eating itself.
journal-of-discourses-vol-06:
Volume Six, from 1859, finds the Saints home again in their valley. A federal army camps in their midst, a daily test of patience. Young turns the discourses toward the hard work of consolidation.

Building the kingdom's farms, shops, and institutions fills the sermons' plans. Speakers urge self-reliance in food, cloth, and tools of every kind. Faith becomes statecraft, preached in the Tabernacle week by week here. The tone cools from war heat toward patient, daily construction. Readers watch a refuge turn into a lasting commonwealth in Utah's valleys. Patience, in these talks, counts as a form of warfare by other means.
kenelm-chillingly-volume-06:
Volume six of Kenelm Chillingly opens Book Six with Sir Peter leaving for London. News that Kenelm has left town without a word appalls him. The journey's real purpose is a resettlement: twenty thousand pounds for Chillingly Gordon, his cousin's son. That business done, Sir Peter breakfasts with his cousin Mivers.

Mivers, a bachelor, delivers a set speech at the omelette against marriage. Bachelorhood, he insists, is the only safe protection of a man's positive happiness. His statistics on marriage's dangers amuse and irritate the widowed baronet in equal parts. This volume turns the novel's marriage debate onto the older generation. Sir Peter must weigh family duty against Kenelm's stubborn freedom.
kipling-puck-of-pooks-hill-1906:
Rudyard Kipling wrote Puck of Pook's Hill in 1906 for children, including his own. Kipling had settled in Sussex, in the south of England, and set the stories in the fields near his house. Two children, Dan and Una, perform a bit of Shakespeare in a meadow on Midsummer's Eve.

Their play summons Puck himself, the last of the old People of the Hills. Puck brings figures out of England's past to tell their stories: a Roman soldier on Hadrian's Wall, Norman knights, and others. Each tale ties the land to the people who held it. Kipling turned history into living memory for young readers.
kore-kosmou-mead-1906:
The Kore Kosmou, the Virgin of the World, is the longest Hermetic piece that survives, kept by the anthologist Stobaeus. In it the goddess Isis teaches her son Horus how the world and mankind were made. G. R. S. Mead turned it into English in 1906, within his study Thrice-Greatest Hermes, and the piece is given here on its own.

Isis tells of the souls sent down into bodies, their forgetting, and their long road back to the stars. The tale mixes Egyptian myth with Greek thought on fate and the elements. Mead, a theosophist, read Hermes as a sage of a single ancient wisdom. His version made the Kore Kosmou a favorite of English readers of the Hermetic books.
kropotkin-conquest-bread-1906:
Peter Kropotkin published The Conquest of Bread in 1906, in its English form, as the classic program of anarchist communism. Kropotkin wrote for workers who made everything and owned little. He argued that food, housing, and goods already produced could meet everyone's needs if shared by free agreement.

Chapters plan how a free society would take over bakeries, farms, and workshops and run them without wages or bosses. Kropotkin attacked the wage system as the root of poverty amid plenty. He answered fears of laziness with examples of willing work. The book shaped anarchist movements worldwide and still serves as their clearest statement of the world they want.
lagerlof-wonderful-adventures-nils-1906:
Selma Lagerlof published The Wonderful Adventures of Nils in 1906, a children's book written to teach Swedish geography. Nils is a lazy boy who torments animals on his farm. A magic spell shrinks him to tiny size. He flies off on the back of a goose, joining a flock of wild geese.

The flock travels the length of Sweden, from south to far north. Nils learns kindness, courage, and the ways of animals on the way. Folk tales and natural facts fill each stop. Swedish schools used the book for years. It remains a beloved classic, read far beyond Sweden for its charm and wonder.
lea-inquisition-spain-vol-1-1906:
In 1906 Henry Charles Lea turned from the medieval Inquisition to its most famous child: the Spanish Inquisition. This first volume of his History of the Inquisition of Spain tells how Ferdinand and Isabella founded the Holy Office in 1478. Lea wrote from the Spanish archives with his usual cold precision.

The converso crisis drives the tale: Jews who had taken baptism, watched by neighbors and hunted by the new tribunal. Lea lays out the founding, the first inquisitors, the burnings at Seville, and the expulsion of the Jews in 1492. He shows how crown and church built the machine together. The volume opens the standard history of the Spanish tribunal.
lea-inquisition-spain-vol-2-1906:
The second volume of Henry Charles Lea's History of the Inquisition of Spain, from 1906, opens the machine and shows its gears. Jurisprudence and procedure are the subjects: how a case began, how it was tried, and how it ended at the auto de fe. Lea draws the picture from the tribunal's own papers.

Secret denunciations, endless prison waits, torture within set rules, and sentences read in public theater fill his chapters. He explains the edicts of faith, the familiars, and the censors of books. The auto de fe, part sermon and part spectacle, gets its full anatomy. Lea's dry account of legal horror is the standard one in English.
lockyer-stonehenge-astronomically-consid:
Astronomer Norman Lockyer argued that Stonehenge was built as a star and sun temple. His 1906 book extends that claim to stone sites across Britain. Lockyer founded a famed science journal and led solar studies.

He measures the alignment of stones against solstice sunrise lines. Temple avenues, he says, point to key stars and seasons. His method helped birth the field now called archaeoastronomy. Critics dispute many of his dates and links. Yet his core claim, that builders watched the sky, won wide support. The book is a bold thesis, fully worked out.
london-white-fang-1906:
Jack London published White Fang in 1906, a wolfdog's passage from the Yukon wild to domestication. The companion mirror of The Call of the Wild reverses Buck's road: tame blood calls this hero toward the fire. London answered critics who charged him with faking nature by building the tale on careful Klondike observation.

White Fang, three parts wolf, learns the wild's law from his mother Kiche and the famine winters of the Mackenzie country. Gray Beaver, Beauty Smith, and a San Francisco dog pit teach him man's cruelty. Weedon Scott, a mining engineer, tames him with patience and kindness, a method no hand had tried on the fighting wolf. In California White Fang saves Judge Scott from a convict and earns his rest at Sierra Vista. The book's study of heredity and environment made it a school classic.
lowell-mars-and-its-canals-1906:
Percival Lowell set out his canal scheme in full grown form in this book of 1906. It rests on eleven more years of watch at his Flagstaff lens since his first Mars book. The lines on Mars had grown in his maps to a vast web of works.

Lowell gives charts, plates, and counts to show the canals are too straight to be a trick of nature. He reads them as the last great work of a race on a world that dries year by year. The book is the high case for a lived in Mars, made by its chief voice.
lucretia-volume-06:
Volume 6 of Lucretia pauses for a retrospect on its heroine's lost years. The narrator looks back between the death of Dalibard and her return. Lucretia arrives unannounced at William Mainwaring's house, dressed in widow's weeds. Susan welcomes her with tender warmth and quick forgiveness.

Mainwaring has risen as the active partner in a bank. His house is prosperous, and Lucretia seems gentle, frank, and changed. Yet the reader knows her training in darkness too well. Lytton asks whether such a nature can truly be reformed. The volume sets fair seeming against a poisoned past. It prepares the final acts of the tragedy.
machen-house-of-souls-1906:
Machen's tales of awe and dread stand gathered in The House of Souls of 1906. Its crown is The White People, a girl's diary of rites learned in the Welsh hills. Lovecraft took that tale as his model for the folk horror story.

A Fragment of Life tells of a clerk who wakes to wonder in a dull London life. The Red Hand hunts a killer by signs cut in stone and chalk. Hill, street, and suburb all hide old gods in Machen's world. The book is his gift at its peak, in one strong volume.
mandeville-fable-bees-1806:
Bernard Mandeville, a Dutch doctor settled in London, published The Fable of the Bees under the motto Private Vices, Publick Benefits. The edition of 1806 given here holds the poem, the complete Remarks, and the second part. His scandalous claim was simple: the greed, vanity, and luxury that preachers damned were the very springs of trade and wealth.

A hive of bees thrives while its members cheat and spend, then falls poor when all turn honest. Mandeville pressed that paradox until churchmen and moralists cried out. Hutcheson, Berkeley, and Adam Smith all felt bound to answer him. The Fable remains the great provocation of early economics, cheeky, shrewd, and impossible to ignore.
margery-gred-a-tale-of-old-nuremberg-vol:
Volume six of Margery tells how the hunted Herdegen was found. Ann and Margery seek him in the Lorenzer Wald, the city forest. He hides in a simple beekeeper's hut where no horseman can pass. Even in peasant's weeds, Margery finds her brother a goodly man.

Herdegen clasps his sweetheart Ann as ardently as on his homecoming. Then he sees Margery in mourning dress and takes her to his heart. One dear to him has died while he was hidden away. His eye is steadier now, and his voice graver and calmer. Ebers mixes flight, love, and grief in these forest scenes.
mark-twain-s-letters-volume-5-1901-1906:
Volume five of Mark Twain's Letters covers 1901 to 1906. Many letters go to Twichell, his pastor and oldest friend. Paine heads the year 'Mark Twain as a Reformer.' A Louisville paper marveled at the humorist's transformation.

The genial joker had become a knight errant with a lance. He broke it against Church or State when they blocked mankind's road. Summers at Saranac and the McKinley assassination mark these pages. Protest letters against empire and cruelty pour from his pen. Grief for his wife shadows the public honors. The sage writes on, witty, wrathful, and tender.
mctaggart-dogmas-religion-1906:
Some Dogmas of Religion, published in 1906, is McTaggart's fearless examination of what religious belief can survive reason. He takes up dogmas one by one, God, freedom, survival, and the soul, and weighs each from an idealist standpoint.

His results startled readers: he argues against a personal, all-powerful God while defending survival after death and the primacy of love. McTaggart was an atheist who thought religion's emotions truer than its creeds. The book's candor and calm made it notorious in Edwardian Cambridge. It remains one of the most honest works of its kind in English.
mead-thrice-greatest-hermes-vol-2-1906:
G. R. S. Mead, a scholar close to the Theosophical movement, published Thrice-Greatest Hermes in 1906. Volume two translates the surviving sermons and fragments of the Hermetic literature. The Corpus Hermeticum tracts and the Perfect Sermon appear here.

Mead renders Hermes as a living teacher rather than a museum piece. Flowing commentary surrounds the translations and explains their spiritual teaching. Generations of seekers met Hermes through Mead before any other writer. His warm style contrasts with Walter Scott's drier academic edition. For the occult revival of the early twentieth century, Mead's Hermes was the standard doorway.
mead-thrice-greatest-hermes-vol1-1906:
G. R. S. Mead opens his great English Hermetica in Thrice-Greatest Hermes, Volume One, from 1906. Prolegomena come first: the history and meaning of the Hermetic writings. Mead, a Theosophical scholar, traces Hermes Trismegistus through Greek, Egyptian, and early Christian worlds with patient and loving erudition.

He asks who wrote the sermons and why they mattered so long. Pagan wisdom and church doctrine meet in his wide survey here. The edition brought Hermes to the modern English reader in full. This first volume is the doorway: a map and a history that prepare the reader for the sacred texts themselves in the volumes after.
mead-thrice-greatest-hermes-vol2-1906:
Sermons and fragments fill the second volume of Mead's Thrice-Greatest Hermes, from 1906. The divine Pymander and kindred wisdom discourses speak in Mead's clear English. Hermes instructs his son Tat and other seekers on God, mind, fate, and the soul's long road through the spheres to its home.

These mystical dialogues fed Renaissance magic for two centuries and more. Modern Theosophy drew on them just as eagerly in Mead's day. His notes guide the reader through hard symbols with care. The volume forms the heart of his edition, the Hermetic scriptures themselves, texts that shaped occult thought from Ficino to the present.
mead-thrice-greatest-hermes-vol3-1906:
Outlying pieces complete Mead's Thrice-Greatest Hermes in this third volume, from 1906. Excerpts, fragments, and testimonia gather around the core sermons here. Mead adds his full survey of Hermetic literature, mapping all that lies around and beyond the central texts of the tradition in Greek, Latin, and Arabic.

Scholars use the volume as a reference shelf for the whole Hermetic world. Lost books leave traces in these rescued scraps and citations. Mead's labor spared later students years of hunting through rare tomes. The full set remains the standard English gateway to Hermes Trismegistus, and this closing book is its index, attic, and treasure room in one.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-06: Sixth in Gutenberg's Napoleon series comes this volume by Bourrienne. Its file is etext number 3556, posted first in April 2001. The memoir's own pages never start within the sample. Contents, therefore, cannot be stated from the evidence held for this entry.
moyle-institutes-justinian-1906:
Emperor Justinian ordered the Institutes in 533 as a first textbook for law students in the Roman Empire. J. B. Moyle's English translation, in the 1906 edition used here, made the short work a staple for students of Roman law. Justinian's compilers built it on older teaching books, chiefly the one by Gaius.

Four books lay out the law in order: persons and their status, property and wills, promises and wrongs, and how suits are brought. The style is brisk and plain, since new students had to grasp the whole map at once. Civil law systems across Europe and beyond grew from this frame, so the book still earns study.
mr-justice-raffles-pg9806:
E. W. Hornung's 1909 novel brings back Raffles, the gentleman thief, and his friend Bunny. The contents list nineteen chapters with names like Camilla Belsize and Corpus Delicti. Cricket, crime, and court all appear in the titles. Bunny narrates, as in the earlier Raffles books.

Raffles moves through London society as a sports hero. In secret he plans burglaries against the rich who host him. Bunny helps, doubts, and records each risk. The chapters mix matches, thefts, and narrow escapes. This Project Gutenberg text gives the full chapter list up front, so readers can see the shape of the plot at once.
my-novel-volume-06:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton's sixth book opens with Mr. Caxton at his most abstract. Life, he says, comes whole or in fractions. A man's whole life is what he holds alone in his study. His shared life is sliced up by all who need him.

Captain Roland growls that he grasps not a word. Caxton explains with a locked door and a round sum of cash. Each friend dips a finger in the bag, he says. Some take much, some little, and some none at all. The chapter turns a family joke into a small philosophy of self, fame, and use.
ocean-of-story-kathasaritsagara-tawney-1:
Volume six of The Ocean of Story, in the Penzer edition from 1924, presses Tawney's Kathasaritsagara past its midpoint. Somadeva's design now shows plainly: a prince's rise carried on a flood of other men's fortunes. Kings in the tales lose thrones to gamblers, regain them by wit, and lose them again to love.

Penzer's comparative notes follow single motifs, like the life-token, through dozens of literatures. His learning can startle, yet the tales themselves stay brisk and bright in Tawney's English. The Sanskrit original ranks among the longest poems of India, and its scale is the point. An ocean is not read; it is sailed, story by story. Volume six keeps a fair wind for that voyage.
openalex-w1502501606:
Juan Pérez-Jaramillo, Rodrigo Mendes, and Jos Raaijmakers wrote this review. It appeared in Plant Molecular Biology, online in June 2015. The subject is the rhizosphere, the soil around plant roots. Microbes there defend plants and help them take nutrients. Plants can recruit helpful microbes from the soil.

Domestication cut the genetic diversity of modern crops sharply. That loss may have weakened helpful microbe partnerships, they argue. Farming moves, root secretions, and litter changes also matter. The authors propose a back-to-the-roots research framework. Wild relatives and native soils may reveal lost traits. Restoring those partnerships could help future crops grow well.
openalex-w2063890406:

Stool samples came from hunter-gatherers and farm villagers. Urban Americans provided a comparison group. Microbe types differed between city and traditional groups. Hunter-gatherers formed a distinct subgroup of their own. A microbe group called Treponema marked traditional guts. Rebuilt genomes showed these microbes were not disease types. Diet and daily life seem to shape the gut deeply.
openalex-w2113355006:

Climate-smart farming pursues three goals together. It aims to raise farm productivity and incomes. It aims to build resilience to climate shocks. It also aims to cut farming's climate footprint. The authors group research needs into three themes. Farm systems, landscapes and assessment all feature. Knowledge gaps are listed within each theme. Science-based action is urged throughout.
openalex-w2147990606:

They pooled score changes on the standard obsessive-compulsive severity scale, measured before and after stimulation. Their analysis aimed to settle how well the treatment works overall and how safe it is. They also hunted for patient traits that predict a good response, to guide future candidate selection.
openalex-w2292484606:

Twenty-five teams reported observations through rapid circulars, and the paper summarizes their coverage, timing, and depth. As a black hole merger, the event promised little light to find. openalex-w2742337206:

Its detailed lessons therefore cannot be stated from the evidence kept here.

The survey found the disease to be very common in livestock. In about half the countries, more than twenty percent of herds and flocks were infected. Most countries required the disease to be reported, yet only twenty-two had formal control programs. Those programs sat mostly in wealthier countries with advanced veterinary services, while many free-living wild species were also infected.
openalex-w4210717506:

The authors recognise fifty-seven provinces, grouped into three subregions and two transition zones. Provinces rest on species found nowhere else, while their borders follow ecoregions shaped by climate, geology, and life. The paper supplies the map as a digital shapefile and raster file. Other researchers can now reuse the same borders in their own studies.
openalex-w4213099706:
Marc Desquesnes, Marisa Gonzatti, Alireza Sazmand, and colleagues review how to diagnose animal trypanosomoses, in Parasites and Vectors in 2022. The review covers the main parasites, including those behind sleeping sickness in people and Nagana, Surra, and Chagas disease. It then compares three families of tests: finding the parasite itself, detecting its DNA, and detecting antibodies. Each method's sensitivity and accuracy are weighed. The authors aim to give vets and labs one integrated guide to a confusing test landscape.
openalex-w4310708706:
Patrick Munk, Christian Brinch, Frederik Møller, and colleagues read the genes in sewage from one hundred one countries to map antimicrobial resistance. Sequencing the samples produced tens of billions of DNA fragments. The team searched them for known resistance genes and for marker genes of all life. A small share of reads carried resistance genes, varying by place. The result is a global landscape of resistance, useful for spotting hotspots and tracking whether control efforts work.

Combined with microwave background data, the results stay close to that model. Some combinations mildly prefer dark energy that changes with time, a hint the team reports with care.
openalex-w4410112906:

The team recreated those lung fluid levels in a hollow-fibre infection model. The model simulates drug exposure and bacterial growth under controlled conditions. At those levels, the drug killed the pneumonia bacterium. It killed both normal strains and strains resistant to levofloxacin. The results confirm that the high lung levels drive the drug's killing power.
openalex-w7204997306:
Joelma Silvestre dos Santos Silva led a Portuguese-language interview study, in Brazil in 2026, on rabies perception among residents of Chã Grande, a municipality in Pernambuco. Most interviewees recognized rabies as a grave, fatal disease. Frequent interactions with wild mammals were found, including hunting and repeated sightings, notably of armadillos and foxes, the fox belonging to the terrestrial wild rabies cycle. openalex-w7207808606:
Elizangela David Nonato, Suely de Freitas Pimenta, and Robson Costa Pessoa review the Manchester Triage System as used with older patients in emergency care. The system sorts arriving patients by clinical priority, and an aging population now fills emergency rooms with people carrying several diseases, frailty, and symptoms that do not present in textbook ways. The authors gathered national and international studies on how well the protocol fits this group.

Manchester triage helps organize patient flow and rank urgency, the review finds, but used alone it can misjudge older patients, whose risk does not always match the standard flowcharts. The authors pair the tool with qualified clinical judgment, repeat checks, broader geriatric assessment, teamwork, and humane communication. Their verdict: keep the system, but never let it replace trained attention to the specific needs of old age.
openalex-w7212111906:

In the Ciranda, children make and remake their own cultures through play. They mix with each other and with adults in ways that teach all sides. Mothers and carers do far more than feed and guard. They help shape the teaching life of the space. The author calls the Ciranda a fresh model for early years care. It guards the rights of both the children and their student mothers.
openalex-w7212135306:

Memory thus does more than rebuild what was. It shapes what workers think is just, and what they dare to claim. The past, in this view, is one more field of the class war.

The study asks how officers adapt to the cameras and what changes in daily service. It concludes that camera use in police incidents supports legitimacy and transparency. Recorded action, the authors argue, can bring police and society closer. Training and proper use remain central to that promise. The work adds a state-level case to wider Brazilian debate on policing technology and public trust.

Readers get an overview of how the field has grown, which approaches appear most often, and where study is still thin. openalex-w7214617306:
Monaliza de Mello e Silva Scansetti Corrêa led a 2026 literature review on ceramic laminate veneers, the thin shells dentists bond to teeth for aesthetic restoration. The review weighs preparation designs against mechanical resistance, marginal adaptation, and clinical longevity, the traits that decide whether a minimally invasive restoration survives daily use. Veneers attract interest because they combine function and appearance while removing little tooth structure. By gathering the recent literature in one place, the authors give clinicians a basis for choosing a preparation style with open eyes about the trade-offs each design carries.

Using national hospital information system data, they counted several hundred admissions among city residents and a small number of in-hospital deaths. Admissions climbed steadily across the period, reaching their highest level in the first ten months of 2025. Men accounted for slightly more than half. Young teenagers formed the largest five-year age band among admissions, a striking finding, while people aged sixty and over concentrated most deaths. The authors conclude that persistent growth, with real weight among the young and greater severity among the old, demands local surveillance and continuous care in primary services.

Chemical fungicides are the usual control, but they risk resistant strains and environmental harm. The team exposed seeds infected in the lab to two microwave frequencies for thirty, forty-five, or sixty seconds and tracked both fungus and seed germination.

Longer exposure at the higher frequency cut infection to very low levels but killed the seeds outright, destroying germination. A shorter treatment at the lower one struck the better balance, cutting fungal incidence while keeping germination high. Microwave treatment can strongly suppress the fungus, the authors conclude. But parameters must be tuned with care so disinfection does not cost the seed its life, the condition for any practical use by growers.
original-short-stories-volume-06:
Fifteen tales crowd volume six of Maupassant's Original Short Stories, from That Costly Ride and Useless Beauty to The Rondoli Sisters, in the English translation shared across the set. Maupassant returns here to a favorite ground: respectable people quietly crushed by money, rank, and their own illusions.

That Costly Ride opens on the household of Hector de Gribelin, a clerk in the Ministry of Marine at sixty pounds a year. His noble family had lived on a meager income in strict economy; with two children, economy has curdled into concealed, shamefaced misery that still keeps up appearances. Educated by an old priest and unprepared for life's rude struggles, Hector is exactly the man Maupassant's Paris devours. The volume's pathos and irony grow from such households.
paul-clifford-volume-06:
Volume 6 of Paul Clifford opens at chapter twenty-eight with the gang around a small fire. Pepper teases MacGrawler, the Scottish cook to the robbers, and Tomlinson and Long Ned trade insults about Scotland. MacGrawler's patriotism stings at every joke.

The comedy sits beside the danger, since these are highwaymen between expeditions. Lytton keeps the talk sharp and the thieves oddly likeable. Through the banter the book's question persists: whether men like these are villains by nature or by the making of the world that raised and now hunts them.
pelham-volume-06:
Volume 6 of Pelham turns from drawing rooms to a murder hunt. The country is in confusion, and the officers of justice search everywhere for the killers. Thornton and Dawson are examined at length and discharged, since no evidence touches them. A glove found in a shed seems to confirm their story.

Suspicion falls instead on a muffled horseman seen near Newmarket, whom witnesses describe as tall, short, and everything between. Pelham, whose own evidence pointed to that horseman, leaves Chester Park for London with a heavy heart. Reginald Glanville, his friend, stands at the centre of the mystery closing in.
plaw-109-162-2006:
Violence against women and the Justice Department are reauthorized together in Public Law 109-162, signed January 5, 2006, though named the act of 2005. Its stated purpose is to authorize money for the Department of Justice for fiscal years 2006 through 2009, alongside the women's programs.

Title I strengthens court and police tools: STOP grants, grants to encourage arrests and enforce protection orders, and legal help for victims. It adds training, full faith and credit for protection orders across state lines, and privacy protections for victims of domestic, dating, and sexual violence and stalking. Other sections cover sex offender management, a stalker database, federal victim assistants, and training grants for law enforcement.
plaw-109-163-2006:
The yearly defense policy bill for fiscal 2006 is Public Law 109-163, the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2006, approved January 6, 2006. It authorizes money for military activities, military construction, and defense work in the Department of Energy, and it sets how many people each service may have that year.

Three divisions organize the long act. Division A holds Department of Defense authorizations, starting with procurement for the Army, Navy and Marine Corps, and Air Force. Division B covers military construction authorizations. Division C covers Department of Energy national security programs and other authorizations. Committees named in the act are the congressional defense committees, reflecting Congress's yearly control over defense plans.
plaw-109-164-2006:
Human trafficking, at home and abroad, is the target of Public Law 109-164, the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2005, approved January 10, 2006. It authorizes money for fiscal years 2006 and 2007 under the Trafficking Victims Protection Act of 2000 and adds new duties.

Title I fights trafficking in other countries, including prevention work tied to post-conflict and emergency aid, protection of victims, and stronger prosecutions. It also adds work on forced labor and child labor. Title II turns to trafficking inside the United States: prevention, a grant program for help to victims, protection for young victims, support for state and local efforts, and a report to Congress.
plaw-109-165-2006:
Treatment for people who survived torture is funded again by Public Law 109-165, the Torture Victims Relief Reauthorization Act of 2005, approved January 10, 2006. It amends the 1998 act of the same name to authorize money for treatment programs and centers in the United States and abroad.

United States policy, as stated here, favors centers in emerging democracies and post-conflict places abroad, near refugees where safe, and at home in regions with many immigrants or refugees. For domestic centers, the sample authorizes twenty-five million dollars for each of fiscal years 2006 and 2007, drawn from Health and Human Services amounts. A following section authorizes money for foreign treatment centers.
plaw-109-166-2006:
Student art for conservation is the small program renewed by Public Law 109-166, the Junior Duck Stamp Reauthorization Amendments Act of 2005, approved January 10, 2006. It reauthorizes and amends the Junior Duck Stamp Conservation and Design Program Act of 1994, under which students submit duck stamp designs in competitions. 

The sample rewrites how money from licensing and marketing the stamps may be spent. Proceeds stay available until used. They may pay only for awards, prizes, and scholarships for winning or superior designs. They may also pay awards for schools, students, and teachers, award ceremonies, and winners' travel to those ceremonies. The costs of licensing and marketing itself are covered too.
plaw-109-167-2006:
Passport fees could rise under Public Law 109-167, the Passport Services Enhancement Act of 2005, approved January 10, 2006. It lets the Secretary of State set and collect, by regulation, a surcharge on each passport application. The stated reason is the higher demand for passports caused by steps taken to meet section 7209(b) of the Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004. 

The surcharge comes on top of normal fees, and the money is kept as an offsetting collection for the State Department to pay those added costs. The power to collect it ends after September 30, 2010.
plaw-109-168-2006:
Public Law 109-168 makes only technical corrections to the Energy Policy Act of 2005, and it says so in its own title. Approved January 10, 2006, it fixes wording in the Solid Waste Disposal Act. One phrase changes from or a regulated to of a regulated. A new subsection on government-owned tanks is redesignated. Years in one section move from 2005 through 2009 to 2006 through 2011. Each change is small. 

In the energy act's Title XVII, references to the clean coal power initiative are corrected, including naming the Department of Energy's Clean Coal Power Initiative for Fischer-Tropsch work.
plaw-109-169-2006:
A trade deal with Bahrain enters United States law through Public Law 109-169, the United States-Bahrain Free Trade Agreement Implementation Act, approved January 11, 2006. Implementing acts like this one approve an agreement already negotiated and change domestic law where the deal requires it.

Title I approves the agreement and covers its entry into force, its relation to federal and state law, early implementing actions, consultation before proclaimed actions, and dispute settlement. Title II handles customs: tariff changes, rules of origin for deciding where goods come from, customs user fees, and enforcement for textile and apparel trade. Title III, beginning in the sample, deals with relief from imports that harm domestic producers.
plaw-109-170-2006: Another few weeks for expiring PATRIOT Act powers is all Public Law 109-170 provides. Approved February 3, 2006, the very day the prior sunset fell, it amends section 224(a) of the USA PATRIOT Act by striking February 3, 2006 and inserting March 10, 2006. Nothing else in the law changes. It was the second short extension in this sequence, following the December 2005 act in this slice. It kept certain provisions of the 2001 antiterrorism law in force. Congress was still finishing work on a longer renewal.
plaw-109-171-2006:
Budget savings across many federal programs are packaged in Public Law 109-171, the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005, approved February 8, 2006. It was written as a reconciliation bill, the fast-track budget process Congress used under its fiscal 2006 budget resolution to change spending and revenue law together.

Its ten titles show the reach. Agriculture and housing come first, followed by the digital television transition and public safety, transportation, Medicare, and Medicaid with the State Children's Health Insurance Program. Later titles cover human resources, education and pension benefits, home heating help under LIHEAP, and judiciary matters. Each title carries the detailed cuts or changes for its area.
plaw-109-172-2006:

Seed grants of up to one million dollars go to each state that has not yet created a qualified high risk pool, to pay for creating and first running one. Grants for operating losses go to states whose pools cap premiums at no more than twice standard risk rates. The pools must offer at least two coverage choices. They must also have a way to keep funding losses after federal grants end.
plaw-109-173-2006:
Public Law 109-173 exists to line up other laws with a banking reform passed just before it. It is named the Federal Deposit Insurance Reform Conforming Amendments Act of 2005. Approved February 15, 2006, it enacts the technical and conforming amendments needed. Those amendments implement the Federal Deposit Insurance Reform Act of 2005. 

The sample's first fix concerns government deposits: a government depositor counts as a separate depositor from any other federal or public unit officer, employee, or agent when insured deposit amounts are figured. The rest of the act proceeds in the same housekeeping style across deposit insurance law.
plaw-109-174-2006:
Disaster lending after the 2005 hurricanes receives fresh money in Public Law 109-174, a short supplemental spending act approved February 18, 2006. For fiscal year 2006 it adds seven hundred twelve million dollars to the Small Business Administration's Disaster Loans Program Account. The money covers the cost of direct loans under section 7(b) of the Small Business Act. The money stays available until spent. 

It is drawn by transfer from Disaster Relief money in Public Law 109-62 and is labeled an emergency requirement under the fiscal 2006 budget resolution. Loan costs are defined by the Congressional Budget Act of 1974.
plaw-109-175-2006:
Cranston, Rhode Island, has a post office named for Holly A. Charette under Public Law 109-175, approved February 27, 2006. The Postal Service facility at 57 Rolfe Square is known and designated as the Holly A. Charette Post Office. The designation follows the standard form used for such honors.

The sample states only the naming and the standard reference rule; it gives no biography of Charette and changes no postal operations, staffing, or funding.
plaw-109-176-2006:
Unemployed storm victims keep help longer under Public Law 109-176, the Katrina Emergency Assistance Act of 2006, approved March 6, 2006. The act's full title is the Katrina Emergency Assistance Act of 2006. 

The rule covers a person eligible because of a disaster declaration for Hurricane Katrina or Hurricane Rita. The declaration must date from on or after August 29, 2005. For such a person, the President must make that assistance available for 39 weeks after the declaration date. The act changes the length of help, not who qualifies for it.
plaw-109-177-2006:
Long-running arguments over antiterrorism powers came to a head in Public Law 109-177, the USA PATRIOT Improvement and Reauthorization Act of 2005, approved March 9, 2006. It extends and modifies authorities Congress said were needed to combat terrorism, after the short extensions in this same slice kept them alive week by week.

The table of contents shows the main fights. Sections cover sunset dates, the lone wolf rule for individual terrorists, how long surveillance of non-Americans may last, and access to business records under section 215, with an audit of that access. Other parts add oversight of emergency disclosures, multipoint electronic surveillance, attacks on railroads and transit systems, forfeiture, and material support rules.
plaw-109-178-2006:
Signed the same day as the main PATRIOT Act renewal, Public Law 109-178 adds civil-liberty clarifications to it. Its full name is the USA PATRIOT Act Additional Reauthorizing Amendments Act of 2006, and it was approved March 9, 2006.

The act states three points plainly. People who receive FISA orders can challenge the secrecy rules attached to them. People who receive national security letters need not reveal their lawyer's name. Libraries are not wire or electronic communication service providers unless they provide specific services. Section 3 then writes judicial review into FISA section 501, allowing a recipient to petition against a production order and, after at least one year, against its nondisclosure order.
plaw-109-179-2006: Public Law 109-179, approved March 13, 2006, makes a technical amendment to the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act about who may receive Settlement Common Stock. Its stated aim is to help shareholders consider proposals to open that stock to missed enrollees, eligible elders, and eligible people born after December 18, 1971. The change itself is wording. Section 36(d)(3) is renumbered. Its references to a resolution are widened to include an amendment to articles of incorporation under section 7(g)(1)(B). Both routes for such a proposal are covered.
plaw-109-180-2006: Scio, New York, gains a memorial name for its post office in Public Law 109-180, approved March 14, 2006. The Postal Service facility at 4422 West Sciota Street is designated the Corporal Jason L. Dunham Post Office. Under the second section, federal laws, maps, regulations, and records that mention that facility are read as naming the Corporal Jason L. Dunham Post Office instead. Naming acts of this kind honor a person through a hometown building; the text contains no life story and makes no other change to postal business.
plaw-109-181-2006:
Fake brand goods drew criminal penalties in Public Law 109-181, approved March 16, 2006, whose first section is the Stop Counterfeiting in Manufactured Goods Act. Congress found the economy losing tax money and tens of thousands of jobs to counterfeit goods, with one customs estimate putting the yearly cost at two hundred billion dollars.

The findings name counterfeit auto parts, including brake pads, plus medicines, tools, toys, clothing, and appliances among the invaded industries. Lawmakers also cited links between counterfeiting and terrorist groups raising and laundering money, and a broad threat to public health and safety. The act then amends the federal trafficking law in title 18 to provide the criminal penalties its title promises, aiming also at stronger anti-counterfeiting terms abroad.
plaw-109-182-2006: How much the federal government may borrow was raised by Public Law 109-182, a one-sentence joint resolution approved March 20, 2006. It amends section 3101(b) of title 31 by removing the old dollar limit on the public debt and replacing it with eight trillion nine hundred sixty-five billion dollars. Debt limit resolutions like this one do not spend money or set taxes; they lift the legal ceiling so the Treasury can keep paying obligations Congress has already approved. The vote came in March 2006 after House passage the previous April.
plaw-109-183-2006: Endangered fish in two western river basins keep their recovery programs under Public Law 109-183, approved March 20, 2006, and named the act of 2005. It reauthorizes the Upper Colorado and San Juan River Basin recovery implementation programs by amending Public Law 106-392. Several funding figures rise: one amount goes from forty-six million to sixty-one million dollars, and a larger one from one hundred million to one hundred twenty-six million dollars. Deadlines move from 2008 to 2010. The Elkhead Reservoir enlargement is also added beside Wolford Mountain Reservoir.
plaw-109-184-2006: In Flora, Illinois, the post office at 312 East North Avenue becomes the Robert T. Ferguson Post Office Building by Public Law 109-184, approved March 20, 2006. The statute is two sections long. Section 1 gives the facility its new designation, and section 2 provides that references to it in any United States law, map, regulation, document, or other record mean the Robert T. Ferguson Post Office Building. The sample offers no account of Ferguson's life or work; it records only the honor and the rule for future references.
plaw-109-185-2006: Joliet, Illinois, is the setting for Public Law 109-185, approved March 20, 2006, which names the Postal Service facility at 2000 McDonough Street the John F. Whiteside Joliet Post Office Building. From approval onward, that is the building's official designation. Any mention of the facility in federal records, maps, or regulations is deemed to refer to it by the Whiteside name. Congress passed many such naming laws in this period, each handled town by town; this one is confined to the Joliet facility and changes nothing about mail service there.
plaw-109-186-2006: Public Law 109-186, approved March 20, 2006, honors John J. Hainkel, Jr. by attaching his name to a Louisiana post office. The facility at 105 NW Railroad Avenue in Hammond is designated the John J. Hainkel, Jr. Post Office Building. Its references section follows the standard pattern for this kind of law. Mentions of the Hammond facility in laws, maps, regulations, papers, or other federal records count as references to the building under the Hainkel name. The enrolled text is short and contains no biographical findings about its honoree.
plaw-109-187-2006: A Texas facility receives the name Lillian McKay Post Office Building under Public Law 109-187, approved March 20, 2006. The building in question stands at 1202 1st Street in Humble, Texas. Section 1 makes the designation. Section 2 directs that references to that facility in any law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record count as references to the Lillian McKay Post Office Building. As with its companion naming acts that day, the measure is honorary and leaves postal operations unchanged.
plaw-109-188-2006: Springfield, Illinois, already called its postal facility at 1927 Sangamon Avenue the Northeast Annex; Public Law 109-188, approved March 20, 2006, redesignates it the J.M. Dietrich Northeast Annex, keeping the old geographic label inside the new name. Because the act is a redesignation rather than a first naming, its first section says so expressly. The second section applies the usual rule that references in federal laws, maps, regulations, and records to that facility mean the J.M. Dietrich Northeast Annex. Nothing alters the annex's services beyond its name.
plaw-109-189-2006: Kentucky's Hodgenville, the town tied to Lincoln's early life, is honored in the name chosen by Public Law 109-189, approved March 20, 2006. The Postal Service facility at 102 South Walters Avenue is designated the Abraham Lincoln Birthplace Post Office Building. References to the facility in United States laws, maps, regulations, documents, or other records are then read as references to the building by that Lincoln name. The act states the designation only; the connection it celebrates is carried by the name itself.
plaw-109-190-2006: Pittsburgh appears twice in this run of naming laws, first in Public Law 109-190, approved March 20, 2006. It designates the Postal Service facility at 3038 West Liberty Avenue as the Congressman James Grove Fulton Memorial Post Office Building. That memorial form of name is one the other Pittsburgh entry in this batch does not use. References in federal laws, maps, regulations, or records to that facility are deemed references to the Fulton memorial building. The text gives the address and designation, with the standard reference rule, and nothing further.
plaw-109-191-2006: Local veterans are the honorees of Public Law 109-191, approved March 20, 2006, which names a Michigan post office for them as a group rather than for one person. The facility at 6483 Lincoln Street in Gagetown becomes the Gagetown Veterans Memorial Post Office. After the designation, the standard rule applies. A mention in a law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record of the United States is treated as a reference to the Gagetown Veterans Memorial Post Office. The measure is a naming act only.
plaw-109-192-2006: Smithfield, North Carolina, is home to the facility renamed by Public Law 109-192, approved March 20, 2006, as the Ava Gardner Post Office. The building stands at 201 North 3rd Street. Under the act, it is known and designated by the Gardner name. References to it in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, or other records count as references to the Ava Gardner Post Office. The enrolled text supplies no biography and no findings; the honor rests in placing a famous name, associated with Smithfield, on its hometown post office.
plaw-109-193-2006: On Franklin Avenue in Pearl River, New York, stands the Postal Service facility that Public Law 109-193, approved March 20, 2006, designates as the Heinz Ahlmeyer, Jr. Post Office Building. Unlike most naming acts in this batch, the sample gives no street number, only the avenue and town. The references section then provides that mentions of that facility in United States laws, maps, regulations, papers, or other records are references to the Heinz Ahlmeyer, Jr. Post Office Building. The act is honorary in full, with no operating provisions.
plaw-109-194-2006: A staff sergeant's name goes on a Florida post office building through Public Law 109-194, approved March 20, 2006. The facility at 8501 Philatelic Drive in Spring Hill is designated the Staff Sergeant Michael Schafer Post Office Building, rank included in the official name. Any reference in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record to that facility is deemed a reference to the building under the Schafer name. The two-section text states the honor plainly and adds no findings about Schafer's service.
plaw-109-195-2006: Knox, Indiana, receives its naming act as Public Law 109-195, approved March 20, 2006, designating the Postal Service facility at 205 West Washington Street the Grant W. Green Post Office Building. The second section carries the customary direction: references to the facility in laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records of the United States are references to the Grant W. Green Post Office Building. Readers looking for Green's story will not find it in this text, which is limited to the designation and that reference rule.
plaw-109-196-2006: Pittsburgh's second naming law in this batch is Public Law 109-196, approved March 20, 2006, for the facility at 770 Trumbull Drive. That building is designated the Clayton J. Smith Memorial Post Office Building. The word Memorial sets its form apart from a plain post office building name. Under section 2, references in federal laws, maps, regulations, or other records to the Trumbull Drive facility are deemed references to the Clayton J. Smith Memorial Post Office Building. The act does not explain who Smith was.
plaw-109-197-2006: Public Law 109-197, approved March 20, 2006, gives Punta Gorda, Florida, a post office building named U.S. Cleveland, a name in a different style from the personal names around it in this run. The facility at 130 East Marion Avenue is known and designated as the U.S. Cleveland Post Office Building. References to it in United States laws, maps, regulations, documents, or other records are then treated as references to the U.S. Cleveland Post Office Building. The sample contains the designation and reference sections only.
plaw-109-198-2006: Dennison, Minnesota, appears in Public Law 109-198, approved March 20, 2006, which designates the Postal Service facility at 37598 Goodhue Avenue as the Albert H. Quie Post Office. The long rural-style address helps set this entry apart from the city facilities in the same day's naming laws. Section 2 provides that any reference to the facility in a federal law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record is a reference to the Albert H. Quie Post Office. The enrolled text states no facts about Quie beyond the honor itself.
plaw-109-199-2006: Closing this long run of March 20, 2006 naming acts, Public Law 109-199 designates the facility at 545 North Rimsdale Avenue in Covina, California, as the Lillian Kinkella Keil Post Office. The designation takes the facility's official name from Keil, in the plain post office form rather than a memorial building form. References to the Covina facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, or other records are deemed references to the Lillian Kinkella Keil Post Office. The act is two sections long and purely honorary in content.
plaw-109-200-2006: Baltimore's facility at 1826 Pennsylvania Avenue is named, by Public Law 109-200, approved March 20, 2006, for a state lawmaker: the Maryland State Delegate Lena K. Lee Post Office Building. The title Delegate is part of the official name, which sets this entry apart in the day's long list. References to the facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, or other records are deemed references to the building by that full name. The text is the standard two sections, designation and references.
plaw-109-201-2006: In Clinton, Massachusetts, the post office at 320 High Street becomes the Raymond J. Salmon Post Office under Public Law 109-201, approved March 20, 2006. The act uses the plain post office form, without Building at the end. Its references section deems any mention of that facility in a United States law, map, regulation, document, or other record to be a reference to the Raymond J. Salmon Post Office. No findings explain the choice of name, and no postal service provisions are changed.
plaw-109-202-2006: Two names share one memorial in Riverton, Utah, under Public Law 109-202, approved March 20, 2006. The building at 12760 South Park Avenue is designated the Mont and Mark Stephensen Veterans Memorial Post Office Building. The double name and the veterans memorial form set it apart from single-person naming acts nearby. Federal references to the Riverton building in laws, maps, regulations, or records count as references to the building under that full Stephensen name. The act contains the designation and reference sections only.
plaw-109-203-2006: Honolulu's entry in the March 20, 2006 naming batch is Public Law 109-203, for the facility at 1271 North King Street on Oahu, Hawaii. It is designated the Hiram L. Fong Post Office Building. This act packages its two rules as subsections of a single section headed with the Fong name, instead of using separate designation and references sections. References in federal laws, maps, regulations, papers, or other records to the facility are deemed references to the Hiram L. Fong Post Office Building.
plaw-109-204-2006: Heating help money was moved a year earlier by Public Law 109-204, approved March 20, 2006. It amends the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program section of the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005. Amounts that read two hundred fifty million and seven hundred fifty million dollars for fiscal year 2007, as a one-time obligation, become five hundred million dollars each for fiscal year 2006. A new limit bars using the funds for planning and administering, and the end date moves from September 30, 2007 to September 30, 2006.
plaw-109-205-2006:
Normal trade relations with Ukraine are authorized by Public Law 109-205, approved March 23, 2006, ending the need for yearly reviews tied to emigration rules. Congress found Ukraine lets its citizens emigrate freely, has had normal trade treatment since 1992, and has met the Trade Act's emigration requirements since 1997.

Further findings praise Ukraine's progress since independence in 1991 toward democratic institutions and a free market, its record on religion and minority rights, and its security steps. Those include ratifying START I and the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, handing over its last Soviet-era nuclear warheads in 1996, and refusing help for an Iranian reactor program in 1998. Ukraine's NATO Partnership for Peace role since 1994 is also noted.
plaw-109-206-2006: Not every naming act in this batch concerns a post office. Public Law 109-206, approved March 23, 2006, designates the Department of Veterans Affairs outpatient clinic in Appleton, Wisconsin, as the John H. Bradley Department of Veterans Affairs Outpatient Clinic. The name takes effect from enactment, and the clinic keeps it in law from then on. References in any United States law, regulation, map, document, record, or other paper to that clinic are deemed references to it under the Bradley name. Care at the clinic is not addressed.
plaw-109-207-2006: A nickname is written into federal law by Public Law 109-207, approved March 23, 2006. The Postal Service facility at 122 South Bill Street in Francesville, Indiana, is designated the Malcolm Melville Mac Lawrence Post Office, with Mac set off as his familiar name. The act folds designation and references into one headed section, with references in laws, maps, regulations, papers, or other records deemed to name the Lawrence post office. The sample gives no account of Lawrence himself.
plaw-109-208-2006: Flood insurance claims after the 2005 hurricanes drive Public Law 109-208, the National Flood Insurance Program Enhanced Borrowing Authority Act of 2006, approved March 23, 2006. It temporarily raises how much the Federal Emergency Management Agency may borrow to run the National Flood Insurance Program. In section 1309 of the 1968 act, the figure eighteen billion five hundred million dollars is replaced by twenty billion seven hundred seventy-five million dollars. The increase is designated as emergency spending under the fiscal 2006 budget resolution.
plaw-109-209-2006: Permit applicants who pay to speed up Army review keep that option through 2006 under Public Law 109-209, approved March 24, 2006. It extends the authority of the Secretary of the Army to accept and spend funds contributed by non-federal public entities to expedite processing of permits. The legal change is one date in section 214(c) of the Water Resources Development Act of 2000: March 31, 2006 is struck and December 31, 2006 inserted. Without the act, the funding authority would have ended that spring.
plaw-109-210-2006: Families traveling to a service member's grave or funeral get passport fee relief from Public Law 109-210, approved March 24, 2006. It amends the Passport Act of June 4, 1920, which already waived fees for some relatives of a deceased member of the Armed Forces traveling abroad to visit the grave. The new wording adds widower beside widow, adds grandparent to the list of relatives, and covers travel to attend a funeral or memorial service as well as a grave visit. The waiver follows that purpose.
plaw-109-211-2006: States with extra freedom over federal school funds keep it under Public Law 109-211, approved March 24, 2006. It extends the flexibility program in section 4 of the Education Flexibility Partnership Act of 1999, often called Ed-Flex. The extension runs until Congress renews part A of title I of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act. It covers any state that was an Ed-Flex Partnership State on September 30, 2004. A state's designation continues only if the Secretary of Education finds its performance under its waivers justifies the extension.
plaw-109-212-2006: Public Law 109-212, the Higher Education Extension Act of 2006, approved April 1, 2006, is another short bridge for college programs, following the December 2005 extension in this slice. It amends that earlier act by striking March 31, 2006 and inserting June 30, 2006 as the extension date for programs under the Higher Education Act of 1965. A rule of construction protects the funding terms set by the Higher Education Reconciliation Act of 2005, part of the Deficit Reduction Act. This extension may not limit or alter those authorizations and durations.
plaw-109-213-2006:
The Tuskegee Airmen receive a congressional gold medal, awarded to them as a group, under Public Law 109-213, approved April 11, 2006. Congress said the medal honors their unique military record, which inspired deep reform in the Armed Forces.

The findings tell how the unit began. In 1941 President Franklin Roosevelt overruled his top generals and ordered an all-Black flight training program, a day after the NAACP sued for Howard University student Yancy Williams and others. Because of segregation, Black pilots trained at a separate field near Tuskegee, Alabama. Army studies had claimed Black men were unfit for leadership and flying, yet the Airmen excelled, and about 992 Black pilots graduated from the Tuskegee program.
plaw-109-214-2006: A small triangle of federal land near the Capitol changes hands in Public Law 109-214, approved April 11, 2006, the Supreme Court Grounds Transfer Act of 2005. Jurisdiction over the parcel passes, without payment, from the Architect of the Capitol to the Supreme Court. The parcel lies in Reservation Number 204 in Washington, bounded by Constitution Avenue on the north, Maryland Avenue branches on the west and south, and 2nd Street on the east. The parcel then counts as part of the Supreme Court grounds, not the Capitol grounds.
plaw-109-215-2006: Milk pricing rules are tightened by Public Law 109-215, the Milk Regulatory Equity Act of 2005, approved April 11, 2006. Its purpose is fair treatment among dairy farmers and handlers for packaged fluid milk sold in federal marketing areas, and in some non-federal areas supplied from them. New language makes covered handlers follow all minimum and uniform price rules. The rules are those of the federal milk marketing order for the county where their plant sits. They apply when handlers sell packaged fluid milk in a state requiring minimum prices for raw milk.
plaw-109-216-2006: A seat on the Smithsonian Institution's governing board is filled by Public Law 109-216, a joint resolution approved April 13, 2006. It appoints Phillip Frost of Florida as a citizen regent of the Board of Regents, in the class of members who are not in Congress. Frost fills the vacancy left when the term of Manuel L. Ibanez of Texas expires on May 4, 2006. The appointment runs six years, starting on the later of May 5, 2006 or the date the resolution was enacted.
plaw-109-217-2006: The same board keeps a sitting member under Public Law 109-217, approved April 13, 2006, a companion to the Frost appointment in this batch. Alan G. Spoon of Massachusetts is reappointed as a citizen regent of the Board of Regents of the Smithsonian Institution. His existing term was due to expire May 4, 2006, and the vacancy that would have followed is filled by reappointing the incumbent. The new term runs six years and takes effect May 5, 2006, under the same Revised Statutes provision cited in both resolutions.
plaw-109-218-2006: Disaster cleanup contracts should favor local firms, and Public Law 109-218, the Local Community Recovery Act of 2006, approved April 20, 2006, clarifies that preference. It amends section 307 of the Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act. A contract or agreement under that section may be set aside for award based on a specific geographic area. A sense of Congress adds that the Corps of Engineers should promptly carry out a Government Accountability Office decision of March 20, 2006 on a named solicitation.
plaw-109-219-2006: Irrigation contracts in Wyoming and Nebraska are extended by Public Law 109-219, approved May 5, 2006, and called the Glendo Unit contract act of 2005. It amends the Irrigation Project Contract Extension Act of 1998. The contracts are between the Bureau of Reclamation and certain irrigation water contractors. They are tied to the Glendo Unit of the Missouri River Basin Project. Three dates move the same way: December 31, 2005 becomes December 31, 2007, covering the contract period, limits on going beyond it, and action required before it.
plaw-109-220-2006: Where a presidential memorial may stand in Washington is settled by Public Law 109-220, a joint resolution approved May 5, 2006. Federal law requires Congress to approve a commemorative work placed in Area I of the District of Columbia within a set time after notice. The Eisenhower Memorial Commission was already authorized to build a memorial to Dwight D. Eisenhower on federal land, and the Secretary of the Interior had judged that it should sit in Area I. The resolution approves that location.
plaw-109-221-2006:
Many small fixes to Indian law are gathered in Public Law 109-221, the Native American Technical Corrections Act of 2006, approved May 12, 2006. Despite the word technical in its name, its table of contents reaches settlements, land leasing, gaming, and lending.

Title I makes technical amendments, including two to the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, transportation reimbursement for the Mississippi Band of Choctaw, and a Fallon Paiute Shoshone settlement. Title II covers Indian land leasing, with a Prairie Island land conveyance, authorization of 99-year leases, and certification of rental proceeds. Later titles amend National Indian Gaming Commission funding, the Indian Financing Act, and Native American probate reform.
plaw-109-222-2006:
Tax cuts are extended and other tax rules adjusted in Public Law 109-222, the Tax Increase Prevention and Reconciliation Act of 2005, approved May 17, 2006. Like the Deficit Reduction Act in this slice, it was a reconciliation bill under the fiscal 2006 budget resolution, this time amending the Internal Revenue Code.

Title I extends and modifies existing provisions, including increased expensing for small business, the capital gains and dividend rates, and rules for controlled foreign corporations. Title II holds narrower items: taxation of certain settlement funds, the active business definition, veterans' mortgage bonds, and capital gains treatment for self-created musical works. A vessel tonnage limit, an arbitrage rule, and music copyright cost rules also appear in the contents.
plaw-109-223-2006:
Chief Justice William H. Rehnquist is memorialized by Public Law 109-223, a joint resolution approved May 18, 2006, after his death in office. Its findings trace his service: nominated by President Nixon in 1971, he sat as an associate justice from January 1972 to September 1986, then as the sixteenth Chief Justice until September 2005. Those 19 years made him the fourth longest serving Chief Justice. 

Congress praised his intellect, fairness, and humor, and noted that, despite thyroid cancer, he gave President George W. Bush the oath at his second inauguration in January 2005. The resolution is a congressional memorial, not a program or funding law.
plaw-109-224-2006:
Land for the Puyallup Indian tribe in Washington must be taken into trust under Public Law 109-224, approved May 18, 2006, under the heading Puyallup Indian Tribe Land Claims Settlement. The Secretary of the Interior is required to accept the conveyance of the parcels described in the act and hold them in trust for the tribe. 

The parcels lie within the Puyallup Reservation in the city of Fife, Pierce County. They are identified by boundary line and short plat records held by the Pierce County Auditor, including lots beside State Route 5. The act itself fixes which parcels are covered.
plaw-109-225-2006:
A Hawaiian refuge for endangered waterbirds grows under Public Law 109-225, the James Campbell National Wildlife Refuge Expansion Act of 2005, approved May 25, 2006. The refuge sits in Honolulu County, on the Kahuku Coast.

Congress found the Fish and Wildlife Service manages the refuge to help four species of endangered Hawaiian waterbirds recover. The service leased about 240 acres of ponds, marshes, springs, and nearby land from the estate of James Campbell and had contracted to buy that land in full ownership. It had also identified about 800 more acres of valuable habitat next to the refuge, in the same estate. The estate's coast holds dunes, wetlands, and strand that support threatened and endangered species.
plaw-109-226-2006:
Coastal barrier maps are the focus of Public Law 109-226, the Coastal Barrier Resources Reauthorization Act of 2005, approved May 25, 2006. It reauthorizes the Coastal Barrier Resources Act, which limits federal support for building on fragile coastal barriers. The sample first defines terms such as system unit and otherwise protected area. 

It then orders the Secretary of the Interior to report within two years to two congressional committees. The report covers the digital maps of system units and protected areas made under a mapping pilot project. The Secretary must consult the governors of states where those areas lie.
plaw-109-227-2006:
Troops in combat zones gain a retirement savings right from Public Law 109-227, the Heroes Earned Retirement Opportunities Act, approved May 29, 2006. Combat pay is normally excluded from gross income, which could block a service member from counting it toward individual retirement plan contributions. The act amends the tax code so that, for contribution limits and deductibility, compensation is figured without regard to that exclusion. 

It applies to tax years beginning after December 31, 2003, with a window after enactment for catch-up contributions for earlier years covered by the rule. The exclusion itself stays in place; only the retirement math changes.
plaw-109-228-2006:
Protests at military funerals are restricted by Public Law 109-228, the Respect for America's Fallen Heroes Act, approved May 29, 2006. It amends titles 38 and 18 to bar certain protests at cemeteries run by the National Cemetery Administration and at Arlington National Cemetery.

Under the new section, no one may hold a protest on such cemetery property unless the superintendent or director approves. A separate ban covers the hour before and after a funeral, memorial service, or ceremony. Within 150 feet of a route into or out of the cemetery, no one may willfully make noise or a diversion that disturbs the event. The law was Congress's answer to disruptive picketing at fallen soldiers' funerals.
plaw-109-229-2006:
Court employees join a disaster leave-sharing system under Public Law 109-229, approved May 31, 2006. Federal law already ran an emergency leave transfer program, in which employees could receive donated leave during disasters and emergencies. This act amends section 6391 of title 5 to add the judicial branch. 

The Office of Personnel Management must provide for judicial branch employees to take part as well. They may join any emergency leave transfer program under that section. The office acts after consulting the Administrative Office of the United States Courts. The change is a single new subsection, inserted and renumbered into place.
plaw-109-230-2006:
San Francisco's Old Mint, nicknamed the Granite Lady, is honored with a coin by Public Law 109-230, approved June 15, 2006. It directs the Treasury to mint commemorative coins for the Old Mint, the first commemorative coin ever to honor a United States mint, according to Congress.

The findings give the building its due. The mint was created in 1852 to turn California gold rush gold into coins. Architect A. B. Mullett designed the Old Mint Building. Its solid build let it survive the 1906 earthquake and fire, leaving it the only financial institution able to open at once as the city's disaster relief treasury. Its coins carry the S mint mark, including rarities like the 1870-S three dollar piece.
plaw-109-231-2006: Muskogee, Oklahoma, has its veterans hospital renamed by Public Law 109-231, approved June 15, 2006. The Department of Veterans Affairs medical center there is designated the Jack C. Montgomery Department of Veterans Affairs Medical Center, taking effect from enactment. The act uses a headed single section. It pairs the designation with a references rule. Any mention of the center in a federal law, regulation, map, document, record, or other paper counts as a reference to the Montgomery medical center. No biography of Montgomery appears in the text.
plaw-109-232-2006:
Money from a commemorative coin is redirected by Public Law 109-232, the Lewis and Clark Commemorative Coin Correction Act, approved June 15, 2006. It amends the act that issued coins for the Lewis and Clark Expedition bicentennial, clarifying where the proceeds go. Half goes to the National Council of the Lewis and Clark Bicentennial and half to the Missouri Historical Society. 

Any of that money still unspent by June 30, 2007 must be transferred to the Lewis and Clark Trail Heritage Foundation. The money funds a trust for stewardship of the Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail.
plaw-109-233-2006:
Veterans' housing and jobs are joined in Public Law 109-233, the Veterans' Housing Opportunity and Benefits Improvement Act of 2006, approved June 15, 2006. It amends the veterans laws in title 38 and labor-run job programs.

Title I covers housing: adapted housing help for disabled veterans living for a time in a family member's home. It also covers home loans whose rates can change. It makes permanent the authority for direct housing loans to Native American veterans. A spouse of a Native American veteran may qualify too. Title II covers jobs. It raises employer awareness of veterans' skills. It changes the veterans employment advisory committee. It renews funding for homeless veterans reintegration programs.
plaw-109-234-2006:
War and storm costs are paid in one emergency bill, Public Law 109-234. It is the Emergency Supplemental Appropriations Act for Defense, the Global War on Terror, and Hurricane Recovery, 2006, approved June 15, 2006. Supplemental bills add money mid-year, outside the regular budget, for needs Congress treats as urgent; this one covers the fiscal year ending September 30, 2006.

Title I is headed Global War on Terror Supplemental Appropriations. Its first chapter, oddly, is Agriculture. It gives three hundred fifty million dollars for Public Law 480 Title II food aid grants. The grants pay for goods supplied abroad. They go, as far as possible, to already approved fiscal 2006 programs. The amount is labeled an emergency requirement under the budget resolution, a label repeated through such bills.
plaw-109-235-2006: Broadcasters face much higher fines for dirty broadcasts under Public Law 109-235, the Broadcast Decency Enforcement Act of 2005, approved June 15, 2006. It raises penalties for television and radio violations of the bans on obscene, indecent, and profane language. A new subparagraph in the Communications Act caps a forfeiture for a broadcast licensee, permit holder, or applicant. The cap is three hundred twenty-five thousand dollars. It applies for each violation or each day of a continuing one. A continuing violation from a single act is capped at three million dollars in total.
plaw-109-236-2006:
Mine disasters earlier in 2006 stand behind Public Law 109-236, the Mine Improvement and New Emergency Response Act of 2006, called the MINER Act, approved June 15, 2006. It amends the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act of 1977 to improve safety in mines.

Section 2 turns to emergency response. Each underground coal mine operator must run a continuing program to improve accident preparedness and response at each mine. Within 60 days of enactment, the operator must write and adopt an accident response plan for each mine. The operator must update it as operations and technology change. It must be shared with miners and their representatives. Plans must provide for evacuating everyone endangered by an emergency.
plaw-109-237-2006: Arriba, Colorado, a small town on the eastern plains, gets its naming act as Public Law 109-237, approved June 23, 2006. The Postal Service facility at 520 Colorado Avenue is known and designated as the William H. Emery Post Office. The act gives the designation and references together in one headed section named for Emery. References in federal laws, maps, regulations, papers, or other records to that facility are deemed references to the William H. Emery Post Office. The sample states nothing about Emery's life.
plaw-109-238-2006: Public Law 109-238, the Second Higher Education Extension Act of 2006, approved June 30, 2006, continues the chain of short college program extensions in this slice. It moves the date in the Higher Education Extension Act of 2005 from June 30, 2006 to September 30, 2006, keeping programs under the Higher Education Act of 1965 temporarily extended. Its rule of construction matches the April 2006 extension: nothing here limits the funding or durations set by the Higher Education Reconciliation Act of 2005 in the Deficit Reduction Act.
plaw-109-239-2006:
Foster children waiting for homes across state lines are the concern of Public Law 109-239, the Safe and Timely Interstate Placement of Foster Children Act of 2006, approved July 3, 2006. Its aim is better protection for children and state accountability for safe, prompt placements.

Congress urges states to adopt the revised Interstate Compact for the Placement of Children. It also urges them to meet the act's deadlines for completing and approving home studies. That way children move faster into safe, permanent homes. The act then amends the Social Security Act's state plan rules to require an orderly, timely process for interstate placements. Placements meant mainly for mental health treatment in licensed residential facilities are carved out of the stated policy.
plaw-109-240-2006: Small rural hospitals keep a financing break under Public Law 109-240, the Rural Health Care Capital Access Act of 2006, approved July 10, 2006. It amends section 242 of the National Housing Act, which governs the Federal Housing Administration program of mortgage insurance for hospitals. The change extends an exemption for critical access hospitals, the small rural facilities that serve areas far from larger hospitals. In plain terms, a single date moves: July 31, 2006 becomes July 31, 2011, giving the exemption five more years.
plaw-109-241-2006:
The Coast Guard's yearly authorization is Public Law 109-241, the Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Act of 2006, approved July 11, 2006. It authorizes money for the Coast Guard for fiscal year 2006 and makes technical corrections to laws the service administers.

Title I authorizes appropriations, sets military strength and training levels, adds a supplemental authorization, and calls for a web-based risk management data system. Title II ranges widely: vessel anchorage and movement authority, international training, officer promotion, the Coast Guard band director, one-step turnkey design-build contracts, and reserve recall authority.
