Barcoding sorted the catch into thirty-one genetic clusters, most of them new to the global barcode library, proof of how much diversity sits undocumented on one island. Clock estimates place the main lineages' origins in the Miocene, before the island itself took shape, so the beetles are heirs of mainland forests later stranded by rising seas. For conservation, Cat Ba is not a depauperate offshoot but an archive, and its beetles deserve the archive's protection.
plos-pone-0352206:
Lismaryin Muñoz-Requene, Pedro Sánchez-Zamora, and Rosa Gallardo-Cobos measured how exposed Nicaragua's North Caribbean Coast is to tropical cyclones, town by town. The region is among the country's most storm-hit and poorest, and climate change is loading the dice further. They built a vulnerability index from twelve indicators covering exposure, the fragility of people and housing, and each municipality's capacity to adapt.

The map that emerged is uneven. Bonanza combined high exposure and fragility with weak adaptive capacity, while Waslala showed sturdier structure. Three clusters of towns shared similar risk profiles. A single regional plan would fit none of them well. For disaster agencies, the index names where shelters, drainage, and income support buy the most safety before the next storm season, not after the damage is photographed.
plos-pone-0352506:
Isabel von Känel-Cordoba and seven colleagues gather everything known about the half-distance Ironman triathlon, in this 2026 PLOS ONE systematic review. The event — a swim, a long bike ride, and a half marathon — has boomed worldwide, yet research has trailed the full-distance race. Searching five databases, the team assembled eighty-six studies covering training, nutrition, body measures, weather, and medical issues.

Cycling emerged as the strongest single predictor of finish time. Professional men peaked around age twenty-eight, women around thirty-two, and participation is growing fastest among women and older athletes. Racing temporarily dents immunity and muscles, then recovers. The authors note the field's blind spots: small samples and too few women studied.
plos-pone-0352906:
Rafael Flores and co-authors designed a family of lipoic-acid-derived molecules aimed at a brain receptor tied to neurodegeneration. The sigma-1 receptor is implicated in Alzheimer's disease and related disorders, and diverse, easy-to-make activators are wanted. Their 2026 design follows a three-part recipe: a sulphur-bearing hydrophobic head, a flexible amide linker, and a greasy tail.

Twenty-one molecules were designed, docked in the computer, synthesised, and tested for binding at both sigma receptor types. Three stood out for selective sigma-1 binding in the nanomolar range, though a standard comparison ligand bound far tighter still. Flores and colleagues keep the three as starting leads for a follow-up round of structure tuning.
plos-pone-0353106:
Yinchun Wang and four co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One language study of Chinese scholars speaking academic English. Their focus is hedging, the words speakers use to soften claims. Hedging is a known stumbling block at conferences and defenses. The team built a large corpus of Chinese scholars' spoken English. They compared it with an American academic speech corpus. Verb-based hedges were the focus.

Chinese scholars used far fewer personal stance markers like 'I think.' They used far more shared markers like 'we see.' The authors read this as a strategy that favors group harmony and shared duty. The study does not stop at diagnosis. It builds a classroom module with worksheets to train these forms. The aim is fewer communication failures in high-stakes settings.
plos-pone-0353206:
Limin Tang and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One experiment on licorice stem and leaf silage as cattle feed, tested in laboratory rumen fluid rather than live animals. The team prepared silage at four dry matter levels and followed fermentation over seventy-two hours, measuring gas output, acidity, nutrient breakdown, and the microbes involved. A licorice feed additive was included in the silage.

The batch at fifty-five percent dry matter performed best overall, producing the most gas and microbial protein, breaking down nutrients fastest, and supporting the richest microbial community. Helpful fermentation products also peaked earlier in that batch. Statistical rankings placed it first among the four, and the authors recommend that moisture level for turning licorice stems and leaves into useful dairy feed.
plos-pone-0353306:
Wieland and colleagues compared two advanced methods for fitting random epidemic models in a 2026 study. Epidemic models that include chance events help forecast outbreaks, but working out their settings from data is mathematically hard. The team tested both methods on three standard disease models of rising complexity.

Each method had to recover known settings from data produced by the models themselves. Their strengths differed by model and data richness, giving modelers a practical guide on which to pick. Fast, reliable fitting matters during real outbreaks, when officials need quick forecasts that honestly reflect uncertainty. The comparison saves future teams from choosing a fitting tool blind.
plos-pone-0353506:
Sabah and Alaa presented a self-tuning method for grouping texts by topic in a 2026 study. Modern language models turn text into rich numeric codes, but each model shines in different fields. Older blending methods fix how much each model counts ahead of time, wasting their complementary strengths.

Their framework lets a search algorithm adjust the blend weights as grouping proceeds, with no labels needed. Better blends should give cleaner clusters for tasks like news sorting and routing technical questions. The work targets a quiet but costly step in text systems, where poor grouping early on degrades every later answer. Dynamic weighting offers a path to clusters that fit each collection's own character.
plos-pone-0353606:
Hattan Abutarboush and colleagues report in 2026 on a thin microwave absorber built from printed rings. Their design uses two nested rings on a common circuit board material, with four small stubs placed evenly around the outer ring and a solid metal backing. Keeping the build to one layer was the central aim.

Tests of a made sample matched computer models and showed strong uptake in six separate frequency bands, each above nine tenths of the incoming energy. Lower bands linked mainly to magnetic responses, while higher bands mixed electric effects as well. A simple flat design that handles several bands at once could help with shielding, sensing, and reducing unwanted radar reflections.
plos-pone-0353706:
Natthapon Inta, Annmarie Grealish, and Mary Leamy explore what recovery from mental illness means in Thailand, in this 2026 PLOS ONE interview study. Recovery is a guiding idea in modern mental health care, but its meaning shifts between cultures. They spoke with service users, family carers, and health professionals in primary and community services, then tested the themes in feedback workshops.

Participants described recovery as moving from symptom relief toward hope, meaning, and social connection. Family backing, community acceptance, and trusting relationships with staff were central, while obstacles appeared at personal, family, service, and community levels. From this, the authors propose a recovery support model fitted to Thai culture.
plos-pone-0353906:
Niu and colleagues, in a 2026 study, ask whether immune system genes raise the risk of clogged heart arteries in people from Northeast China. The HLA genes help the immune system tell self from invader, and they vary a lot between people. The team compared two HLA genes in about two hundred people, split between those prone to artery clogging and controls.

Dozens of gene variants were counted. Two single variants appeared more often in the disease-prone group, but neither survived strict correction for the many tests run. A paired combination of the two variants, inherited together, was more than twice as common in the disease-prone group. That signal also faded under the strictest correction, though its size was too large, the authors argue, to dismiss as pure noise. They label the pair a candidate risk marker and call for much larger studies to confirm or refute it.
plos-pone-0354206:
Lyu and colleagues, in a 2026 review, work out how much exercise helps depression among middle-aged and older people with Parkinson's disease, and which kinds help most. Earlier trials tested exercise one dose at a time, which hid the shape of the benefit. The team pooled twenty-five trials and modeled dose on a continuous scale, counting weekly energy spent.

Benefit followed a curve, not a straight climb. Gains held across a broad middle band of weekly dose and peaked near its center; at the highest doses the effect turned unstable. Two kinds of exercise stood out: exercise paired with mental training, and mind-body exercise such as tai chi styles, both peaking at the same middle dose. Walking helped only at higher doses, and several other types showed no dependable range. The authors say dose and kind must be prescribed together, like a drug and its amount.
plos-pone-0354606:
Nnaemeka Iriemenam and co-authors tested front-line health staff at seven Nigerian sites for coronavirus antibodies late in the pandemic. Health staff faced the worst exposure, and counts of past infection guide safety plans. Their 2026 study enrolled more than twelve hundred nurses, lab staff, doctors, and pharmacists for blood tests and a habits survey.

Antibodies were near universal: about ninety-eight in one hundred staff tested as past-exposed. Most hits bore the mark of the virus's inner protein, a sign of true past infection, not shots alone. Nurses were three times as apt to test as past-exposed as lab staff. Half the staff still lacked shots at the time. The team urges stronger shots and ward safety for front-line staff.
plos-pone-0354706:
Fei Chen and co-authors propose in 2026 a better way to estimate the health of lithium ion batteries from electrical response tests. Single response measures miss how ageing parts of a battery interact, giving weak predictions. Their method picks several response features that track capacity loss, then feeds them to a neural network tuned by three search methods borrowed from nature.

Across test conditions with plenty of data and with noisy, scarce data, tuned networks kept errors low and stable. Two of the tuning methods stood out in the hardest cases. Reliable health estimates matter for safe use of batteries in vehicles and portable devices.
plos-pone-0355106:
Issiaka Sare and co-authors tested a locally isolated fungus as a malaria mosquito killer and traced its effects across generations. Fungi offer an eco-friendlier alternative to chemical insecticides, but their full life-history costs to mosquitoes were unclear. Their 2026 study exposed a major malaria vector to two strains of the fungus at larval and adult stages.

Larvae were reared in spore-dosed water, and survivors were followed for lifespan, wing size, egg laying, and blood feeding. Separately, sprayed adult females were followed through their offspring's survival. Survival analysis used standard hazard models, with other traits compared across treatments. Sare and colleagues frame the results for biocontrol planners weighing fungal sprays against resistance-prone chemicals.
plos-pone-0355406:
Amit Hasan and co-authors report in 2026 the first known case in Bangladesh of a fungus causing leaf spot on quinoa, a nutritious grain like crop with growing local promise. Sick plants at a university farm in Dhaka yielded one fungus again and again from spotted leaves. Shape study, gene sequencing, and family tree analysis named the culprit, and infection tests on healthy plants reproduced the spots.

The fungus was reisolated from the newly sick plants, completing the classic proof of cause. Colonies grew grey to black with curved, thick walled spores. The authors warn growers to watch for this emerging threat and urge resistance screening and joined up disease control.
plos-pone-0355506:
Benedicto Mgala and colleagues explore in 2026 daily life for patients in Tanzania who must take warfarin for life after receiving an artificial heart valve. The drug prevents dangerous clots but needs tight dose control, a strict diet, and regular blood checks. Twelve patients at the national heart institute gave in depth interviews about their routines.

Many felt better after surgery, yet diet limits, side effects, low mood, and lost work weighed heavily. Keeping blood levels in range was hard amid money strain, uneven drug use, mixed advice, and scarce testing away from the centre. The authors call for a clearer, joined up path of care.
plos-pone-0355606:
Qiuhong Deng leads a 2026 PLOS ONE study of why cervical cancer resists immunotherapy, treatment that frees the immune system to attack tumors. A protein called IGF2BP1 reads a chemical tag on gene messages, named m6A, and was suspected of helping tumors dodge immune attack. Its control was unknown.

Across datasets and four cancer cell lines, IGF2BP1 ran high and tracked with poor survival. Silencing it slowed growth and made tumors respond better to a checkpoint drug, with more killer T cells entering and firing. Another protein, HDAC2, normally keeps IGF2BP1 repressed by cleaning tags off its gene switch. Losing HDAC2 frees it. Targeting the axis partly restored drug effect.
plos-pone-0356006:
Vicente Lopez-Chavarrias, Irene Aldea, and Jovita Fernández-Pinero published a 2026 software paper in PLOS ONE introducing PePApipe, a tool that automates genome analysis for African swine fever virus. The virus devastates pig farming and triggers trade bans, and tracing outbreaks needs full genomes, yet the analysis steps were scattered across separate programs. The pipeline chains thirteen tools into one workflow, from raw sequencing reads through quality checks, genome assembly, and variant listing.

PePApipe was built for laboratory professionals with little computing background, needing only basic command-line skills, and it can run on a single machine or a computing cluster for batches. Outputs arrive in structured folders: a consensus genome plus a file of differences from a chosen reference, with intermediate files kept and steps switchable. The authors say one automated path cuts user error and makes results reproducible, easing the step from sequencer to outbreak report.
plos-pone-0356206:
Daisuke Sudo and Daisuke Toyoda ran a pilot trial testing whether eye exercise training adds anything to leg strengthening for thirty community-dwelling older adults. The bid was to cut falls by sharpening vision. Their 2026 randomized study trained both groups' legs for eight weeks. Half also drilled six visual skills on a dedicated training system. The skills ran from eye-hand coordination to peripheral perception.

No clear advantage appeared. Adjusted comparisons showed no confirmed differences in visual or physical outcomes. Several estimates leaned toward the vision group on exactly the skills practiced, though with wide uncertainty. The authors are candid: thirty people cannot settle the question. The pilot's real product is a blueprint for a properly powered trial with fairer controls and meaningful endpoints.
plos-pone-0356806:
Irina Elena Ionescu and colleagues compared two standard recipes for growing dendritic cells, the immune system's teaching cells, from mouse bone marrow, because the recipe quietly changes what the cells become. Their 2026 laboratory study grew cells with one growth factor alone or with a second added, then compared surface markers, cytokine output, and the ability to coach naive T cells.

Cells grown with the single factor looked mature yet still answered bacterial stimuli with cytokines and primed T cells in an antigen-specific way. Adding the second factor kept cells less mature but introduced nonspecific T cell signaling that could muddy experiments. The message for immunologists is to choose, and re-check, the recipe against the exact question being asked.
plos-pone-0356906:
Guillaume Bouguéon and colleagues test how long prepared bags of idarubicin, a workhorse drug against blood cancers, stay safe to use. Hospital pharmacies would like to prepare doses ahead, but shelf life in modern plastic bags lacked solid data. The team filled bags at two strengths in two common fluids. Some bags were stored cold. Others sat at room temperature. Samples were assayed across a full month, alongside checks for particles, acidity, and salt balance.

Drug levels stayed above ninety-five percent of the starting strength through day thirty in every condition, with no breakdown products detected. Bags showed no color change or precipitate, particle counts stayed within limits, and acidity and salt balance did not drift. Bouguéon and colleagues say pharmacies can safely prepare a month ahead under either storage style.
plos-pone-0357006:
Nayana Gunathilaka, Deshaka Jayakody, and Iranga Dilshan mapped fifteen years of rickettsioses in Sri Lanka. These are tick- and mite-borne fevers that are often missed. Their 2026 analysis used weekly national case reports from all twenty-five districts between 2009 and 2023. Satellite weather data was paired with the reports. The aim was to find where and when the diseases strike, and which climate conditions travel with them.

More than eighteen thousand cases were reported. They were heavily concentrated in Jaffna in the north, with the central highlands next. The modeling linked incidence patterns to local climate and geography. Knowing the hotspots and seasons lets health officials aim fever testing, public warnings, and vector control. They can target the districts and months where these under-recognized illnesses actually cluster.
plos-pone-0357106:
Julia Ruß and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article in veterinary medicine. It measures serum reverse triiodothyronine, a thyroid-related hormone in blood, in three groups of dogs: those with hypothyroidism, those whose illness is not thyroidal, and healthy dogs. Thyroid tests in dogs are notoriously muddied by other illnesses.

Nonthyroidal illness can make a healthy thyroid look underactive, leading to wrong treatment. Comparing this hormone across the three groups tests whether it separates true thyroid failure from the shadow of other disease. Veterinarians diagnosing sluggish, gaining dogs are the readers who need cleaner thyroid markers.
plos-pone-0357206:
Ruy Felipe Melo Viegas led a team of eight authors who compared blood and saliva tests in heart failure patients, in a PLOS ONE study from 2026. Checking a failing heart now means drawing blood to measure stress and injury markers. The team asked whether saliva could carry the same signals in useful amounts.

Viegas and his co-authors measured three markers in both fluids: one linked to heart strain, one to heart muscle injury, and one to inflammation. Setting the saliva values beside the blood values shows how close a spit test could come to the standard. A simple saliva check would make repeat testing easier for patients who need close tracking.
plos-pone-0357406:
Huawei Wang led a team of five authors improving crane scheduling in railway freight yards, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Rail-mounted gantry cranes move containers between trains and trucks, and poor scheduling jams the whole yard. The team built a flexible scheduling method that balances several goals at once.

Wang's model weighs speed against energy use and fairness across jobs, instead of chasing one target. Yards must make that trade-off daily as trains arrive off schedule. A model that bends without breaking helps dispatchers keep freight moving. Faster, steadier yards lower the cost of rail freight, which matters for shifting goods off roads and cutting transport emissions at the same time.
plos-pone-0357706:
Aysegul Erinc and colleagues ask whether a simple blood score predicts survival in people with scarring lung disease who do not have diabetes. The score combines fasting sugar and blood fat values and is often read as a sign of insulin resistance. Records covered well over a hundred patients on anti-scarring therapy, followed for close to three years on median, with lung tests and survival tracked.

The abstract reports the cohort's profile and the study design in detail, linking the score with lung function and death from any cause. Because patients here stayed within the non-diabetic range, the work tests whether small shifts in the score still carry meaning. Erinc and colleagues frame the score as a cheap add-on to scans and lung tests when judging outlook.
plos-pone-0357806:
Katie L Kowalski led a team of eight authors measuring rehabilitation science across Canada, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. They asked who produces rehabilitation research, how much they publish, and what impact it has. Their data mixed public records with a survey of faculty across the country.

Kowalski's faculty-wide picture shows where the field is strong, where it is thin, and who shapes its future. Universities and funders can use that picture to spot gaps, such as regions or topics with few active researchers. Rehabilitation serves an aging population with growing needs, so the health of its research base matters beyond academia. The study offers a baseline for judging future growth.
plos-pone-0357906:
J. Richard T. Korecki and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for project FIERCE, a trial testing a meditation program built for stressed doctors. Most healthcare providers report burnout, poor sleep, and low mood from workplace strain, and mindfulness courses help but rarely target positive emotion. Their six-week program, BEST, delivered online, adapts the Buddhist Four Immeasurables practice to cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity.

Ninety full-time doctors will be randomized to the program or a waitlist, completing surveys and giving blood samples at the start, middle, and end. Perceived stress is the main outcome, with burnout, depression, well-being, and sleep also tracked, with blood inflammation markers adding a hard-data layer. The design also tests what carries any benefit, measuring compassion, positive affect, equanimity, and mindfulness as candidate carriers. A positive-emotion focus, they hope, proves stronger medicine than attention training alone.
plos-pone-0359206:
Kathryn Date and eight colleagues published this study protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. It describes the CONIFAS2 study, a feasibility test of a nature-based intervention for children with ADHD. The intervention was co-produced, designed together with the people who would use it.

A feasibility study asks whether a bigger trial can work at all: will families join, stay, and accept the activities? Nature-based activities are a low-drug option many families welcome, but they still need proper testing. Researchers planning the full trial, and clinicians who advise families with ADHD, are the readers for this groundwork.
plos-pone-0359306:
Monique Bussmann, Marieke Groot, Chris Kuiper, and Mieke Cardol published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is an ethnographic multi-case study of musical encounters in healthcare, moments when music is brought to patients. The authors call these encounters precarious, valuable yet fragile, and explore why.

Perspectives come from both care professionals and the musicians themselves, whose views of the same visit can differ sharply. Ethnographic observation across several cases shows how setting, timing, and expectations make or break a musical visit. Arts-in-health organizers and hospital staff hosting musicians are the readers for this account.
pmc-10654506:
Dmitry Molotkov and co-authors mapped how eye signals land in the mouse brain in a 2023 study. The map, called retinotopy, keeps the layout of the visual field as signals pass from the eye to a midbrain hub. The team watched single cells and fiber ends live with a light based method that tracks cell activity.

Fiber ends from the eye tiled the hub in near perfect order, with tiny placement errors. Local hub cells kept the layout with less sharpness, and models traced that gap to few inputs per cell. The map thus seems built by the incoming fibers themselves, not rebuilt by local wiring.
pmc-10656006:
Agnese Benzonelli, Ian Freestone, and Marcos Martinon-Torres investigate in 2023 how alloy choice shapes the prized patinas on Japanese sword fittings. Since the fifteenth century, craftspeople have colored copper alloys like shakudo with hot baths, reaching deep blues and blacks. The team varied tin, gold, and silver in test alloys and compared results with historic pieces. Analyses covered both looks and chemistry.

Gold and the absence of tin kept the oxide layer thin, giving a smooth, fine finish. A first color study on historic fittings confirmed each metal's pull on final color. Thin patinas proved key to the desired effect. The work explains craft choices that tradition passed down without written reasons.
pmc-10656306:
Joseph Spear, Jesse M Ehrenfeld, and Brian J Miller wrote a 2023 viewpoint arguing that artificial intelligence can cut the waste in American health care delivery. Care now eats nearly a fifth of the national economy, and past reforms have mostly added paperwork for patients and doctors alike. The authors cast AI as a thresher that can strip that burden away.

They map three zones of opportunity: automating administrative work, augmenting clinical practice, and a third zone of system-level gains. In each, they argue, AI can lower cost, improve care, and give time back to both sides of the clinic door. The piece is a policy argument, not a trial report.
pmc-10656406:
Jie Hao and co-authors explain a recent discovery of how plants warn neighbors about aphids, and how viruses sabotage the alarm. Their 2023 commentary unpacks work identifying the airborne signal methyl salicylate, released when aphids attack. A gene module controls emission; a partner protein lets receivers convert the signal into their own defense cue.

The viruses that aphids carry fight back with elegance: a conserved piece of their proteins drags the emission switch out of the nucleus for destruction. Silencing the alarm raises aphid success and virus spread together. The commentary places this tug-of-war in the longer story of plant communication, whose molecular basis long stayed murky. Practical stakes follow: breeding or editing crops to protect the alarm pathway could defend whole fields, since the signal is communal. Few defense traits protect the neighbors as well as the plant itself.
pmc-10656506:
Aline Seger and co-authors split in a 2023 study patients with lone REM sleep behavior disorder into clinical subtypes. Acting out dreams is the sharpest early sign of coming Parkinson's disease. Whether subtypes already exist at this prodrome stage was little charted.

Sixty six patients with sleep lab proof of the disorder got full motor and non motor workups. A two step cluster pass sorted them by smell, brain wave pace, and dream sleep tone. Mood, disease span, and motor scores also fed the sorting features. One cluster pairs late onset with heavier non motor load yet shorter disease span. The other pairs early onset with a milder course, and brain scans back the split.
pmc-10657406:
Fengjing Liu and co-authors report a way to build tiny layered wires in this 2023 study. Each wire has a core of one material and a shell of another, a design used in light sensors. Growing clean shells is hard because the crystal grids of the two materials rarely line up, which causes defects at the join.

The team used traits of the shell material itself to sidestep the mismatch. They built many core-shell pairs with smooth surfaces and shells of controlled thickness. One pair sensed light in both directions and helped detect infrared light. Another gave more than a hundredfold boost in response over the plain wire. The method may aid future tiny light devices.
pmc-10661906:
Vladimir Koblizek and co-authors analyze deaths in chronic lung disease in a 2023 study. The earlier POPE study sorted COPD patients in Central and Eastern Europe into four clinical types but did not track who died. This follow-up, RETRO-POPE, asked which patient traits predict death from any cause. Better prediction could flag high-risk patients earlier.

The two largest national groups, from the Czech Republic and Serbia, supplied 801 patients with full data. Patients were grouped both by clinical type and by a five-cluster scheme based on other illnesses, lung function, age, weight, and breathlessness. After about seven years, just over half were still alive. The analysis compares survival across both grouping systems to see which sorts risk better.
pmc-10671806:
Fatima Alam and co-authors review how sex and gender shape e-cigarette use and its health effects. E-cigarettes deliver nicotine, flavorings, and other substances, and studies link them to lung harm, worse respiratory disease, and behavioral effects. Much of that research ignores sex as a variable. The review gathers studies from 2018 to 2023 that did report sex differences.

The search finds 115 relevant studies. Reported differences cover reasons for starting, smoking history, device and flavor choices, and use of other substances. They also cover body responses to nicotine and toxicants in e-liquids, flare-ups of lung disease, and behavior such as anxiety, depression, sexuality, and bullying. The authors conclude that sex and gender influence susceptibility to the harms of vaping. They urge future studies to build these variables into their designs from the start.
pmc-10675206:
Normanda Souza-Melo and co-authors study tail anchor proteins in a parasite in 2023. Trypanosoma cruzi causes Chagas disease and reshapes itself at each life stage. A zone that glues its tail to the body steers growth and inner layout. Two proteins of that zone were little known in this species.

The team used gene editing to tag and delete the proteins in the insect stage of the parasite. They then tracked shape, growth, and inner movement of parts. Lessons from kin species did not fully transfer, which makes the direct test valuable. Knowing the glue zone may expose weak points in a hardy parasite.
pmc-10675406:
Othmane Atanane and colleagues built a tiny learning system in 2023 to catch water leaks. Cities face rising water stress and shortages. Leaks in building pipes waste large amounts silently. Sensors plus on-device learning can spot leaks locally. Local decisions cut delay and central system costs. The team used an existing sound dataset for plastic pipes. Sound clips became image-like patterns for analysis. Five image network designs were adapted through transfer learning. The best model was then shrunk for a small board.

All networks learned to detect leak sounds well. One efficient design scored highest on every measure. Its test accuracy came close to ninety-eight percent. After compression, it ran on an Arduino-class edge device. Inference took about two seconds per check. Memory and storage needs stayed very small. The authors present a near hands-off leak watcher. Real buildings could host such devices widely, they argue.
pmc-10688506:
Kinga Dora Kovacs and a large team of co-authors describe a new way to deliver tiny parcels into single living cells, in a 2023 technical report. Cells trade small bubbles called extracellular vesicles, which carry signals and cargo. Watching what one bubble does inside one cell is hard, so the team built a robotic microscope that can inject bubbles straight into a chosen cell.

The robot uses a fine hollow needle guided by force sensing. It placed glowing bubbles into four kinds of cells, from heart muscle cells to cancer cells, with high precision. The bubbles first sat in a tight spot inside the cell, then drifted outward toward the edge. The authors present the method as a tool for studying how single cells handle these parcels one at a time.
pmc-10690806:
Anna-Stiina Wallinheimo, Simon Evans, and Elena Davitti study a new language trade skill in a 2023 paper. Interlingual respeaking makes live subtitles in another language: a human repeats speech while software transcribes and translates it. The craft leans on working memory and fast task switching. Their five week training course let them test whether practice in the skill itself trains those mental muscles.

Very little was known about how this human AI teamwork shapes cognition. Trainees were measured around the course for complex memory and switching skill. Gains would argue that the new workflow builds transferable strength, not just technique. The results speak to training design across the language industry as AI reshapes its jobs.
pmc-10691006:
Hao Yang, Shifeng Yang, Jixing He and colleagues linked a glucose transporter to a chemical tagging process that helps gastric cancer spread in 2023. GLUT3 feeds sugar into cancer cells, and the study asked whether it also drives lactylation, a modification of histones fuelled by lactate.

Single-cell data showed GLUT3 enriched in primary and metastatic tumours, tracking with the lactate-making enzyme LDHA. Knocking GLUT3 down in cancer cells cut their ability to migrate and invade, and lactylation marks fell with it. Restoring LDHA reversed the effect, and animal tests agreed. The team proposes GLUT3 as a possible diagnostic marker and drug target for gastric cancer.
pmc-10693106:
Qian Wu and co-authors heat blood-derived fibrin membranes to tune their strength and lifespan in a 2023 study. Horizontal platelet rich fibrin helps dental and surgical healing, but flimsy membranes tear and vanish too fast. Heat promises a no-additive way to firm them up.

Membranes were baked across a ladder of temperatures and tested under the microscope, in stretch rigs, and against enzymes. Hard heating past a threshold stretched survival to three or four weeks and raised breaking strength. Cell viability inside the membranes and bone cell growth fed by their extracts were checked too. A sweet spot for the oven is the practical prize.
pmc-10693206:
Anais Vannutelli, Aida Ouangraoua, and Jean-Pierre Perreault published a study in 2023 on the evolution of G-quadruplexes across the three kingdoms of life. These folded DNA and RNA structures affect gene activity and disease, yet their history is murky because their sequences align poorly. The team sidestepped direct alignment by grouping matching genes across species and tracing the folded structures inside gene trees.

Few such structures are shared across all kingdoms. Vertebrates keep a modest set, plants fewer, and microbes almost none in common. Prediction by kinship raised the shared counts somewhat. Partner proteins that bind RNA seemed to nudge the structures' evolution only slightly. The authors supply a method for tracing these elusive structures.
pmc-10693606:
Bo Cao and co-authors solve a boundary puzzle at a giant open pit coal mine in a 2023 paper. At the Zhundong mine in Xinjiang, raised inner rows between two mining areas forced crews to strip the same ground twice. That wasted stripping adds cost with no coal to show for it.

The team fitted a curve to the main coal seam, sliced the end wall of the second area into sections, and computed a stripping ratio for each slice. The ratios pointed to a best boundary spot, shifted about fifty-five meters west of the old line. Slope stability checks at that spot, run with a strength reduction method, passed safety needs. The new boundary also skips roughly sixty-six million cubic meters of needless stripping. The method offers other mines a worked example of math-led boundary setting.
pmc-10693706:
Jiahong Shi and co-authors report a 2023 study of a new gum surgery method for deep defects in the bone around teeth. The method uses a small scope to clean the root and place bone graft material, all without a cut in the gum.

They compared 21 patients treated with the new method against 21 who had scope-aided cleaning alone, checking both groups after one year. Both groups improved, but the graft group gained more tooth attachment and lost more pocket depth. Bone defect depth shrank by a similar amount in both groups. The authors suggest the no-cut method can aid healing with less trauma and less gum loss.
pmc-10694906:
Wang and ten co-authors build tiny particles that attack breast tumors two ways at once. Their 2023 paper pairs heat therapy with flooding the cell's power units with calcium. Past calcium carriers could not hold the dose high enough for long. The new carrier packs a plant drug and a dye inside chalk-like shells.

Once inside tumor cells, the shells break down in acid and free calcium. The flood drops the cells' energy output. Near-infrared light heats the cells and speeds the breakdown. Cell and animal tests showed the paired attack slowed tumors. The team frames the work as a step toward combined nano-therapy.
pmc-10695906:
Geyse Ribeiro and a large team wrote a 2023 materials paper on nanowires of manganese oxide doped with zinc for supercapacitors. Such oxides are cheap, safe and hold much charge, but ions move slowly in them. The team grew defect-rich wires in one pot, with zinc content tuned across several levels. Wire width shrank as zinc rose.

Charge storage did not rise in a straight line with zinc, though. It peaked at a middle loading, a volcano pattern. That best material held a very high charge per gram in tests. It also improved hybrid device results. The method avoided stray crystal phases during growth.
pmc-10696706:
Han Zhang and six co-authors pool evidence on whether human herpesvirus infection raises cervical cancer risk, in a systematic review from twenty twenty-three. Human papillomavirus is the established cause of cervical cancer. What other viruses add remains unclear. The team searched major databases and appraised study quality with a standard tool.

Sixty-seven studies that fit, covering seven herpesviruses, entered the meta-analysis. Overall, herpesvirus infection was linked to higher odds of cervical cancer and of lesions that come before cancer. Herpes simplex virus type 2 and Epstein-Barr virus each showed positive correlations with both outcomes. Herpes simplex type 1 and cytomegalovirus showed no such link. The roles of three rarer herpesviruses stayed unclear in the data. The review suggests some herpesviruses may act as cofactors alongside papillomavirus.
pmc-10696806:
Janvier Karuhije and seven co-authors survey what Rwandans know and believe about Ebola and how ready the country feels, in a study from 2023. Rwanda borders regions with repeated Ebola outbreaks, so public preparedness matters. A mixed survey design measured facts, attitudes, and habits together.

Over a thousand people in five districts answered questionnaires, and ninety-eight joined interviews or group talks. Nearly everyone had heard of Ebola, and over ninety percent would accept vaccination. Yet only about half knew the disease is viral, and fewer knew it starts in wild animals. Ninety percent saw Rwanda itself at risk, shaped by closeness to Congo.
pmc-10698906:
Nomonde Ngoma and seven co-authors test whether farm growth promoters can trigger toxin-carrying phages from Escherichia coli O157:H7, in a study from 2023. Four approved promoters used in South African food animals were tested, with ultraviolet light as a comparison, on 47 bacterial isolates. Released phages were checked for toxin genes and structure by several lab methods.

Phages were induced from most isolates, with rates that varied by method. The freed phages were diverse in form and gene content, and most carried shiga toxin subtype genes. The authors warn that promoter use in animals could free such phages inside animal or human hosts, and they back tighter limits on these compounds.
pmc-10699206:
André Lino and co-authors compare two ways of paying hospitals for appendix surgery in a 2023 review. Brazil's private system traditionally pays fee-for-service, a charge for every item and act, while bundled payment gives one fixed sum for the whole episode under diagnosis-related groups. The team systematically gathered studies comparing the two for appendectomy, the commonest emergency operation.

From more than seven hundred papers, six studies qualified for pooling. Patients under bundled payment left hospital sooner than those under fee-for-service. The review also weighed complications and total costs between the models. Payment design is invisible to patients, yet it steers how long they stay and what care is worth doing. Evidence from a routine operation helps policymakers judge whether bundling saves money without harming recovery.
pmc-10699306:
Malcolm Lim and seven colleagues deliver chemotherapy to breast cancer that has spread to the brain using antibody-guided nanoparticles. Brain metastases resist standard chemotherapy because effective doses are toxic and little drug crosses into the brain. Their hyperbranched polymer carrier targets the HER3 receptor, common on these metastases, and releases doxorubicin faster in acidic compartments inside cells.

In cell tests the targeted carrier killed breast cancer cells selectively. In a mouse model it slowed tumor growth, shrank tumors, and extended survival, with fourteen times more carrier reaching the brain than an untargeted version. Heart and ovary toxicity were lower than with free drug. The authors see a path to treating brain metastases more safely.
pmc-10702506:
Jinyu Gao and co-authors speed up the cleanup of chlorate in water eighteen-fold by adding vanadium to a standard catalyst, in this 2023 study. Chlorate is a toxic leftover from industry, farming, and water disinfection. Palladium catalysts can reduce it to harmless chloride, but slowly. Vanadium is cheap and earth-abundant, making it an attractive booster if the chemistry cooperates.

Spectroscopy and electrical tests show the trick. Palladium splits hydrogen, which turns dissolved vanadium into a lower state. That state cycles back and forth, attacking chlorate in the water rather than sitting on the support. Tuning the water's acidity keeps the cycle spinning at its best rate. A working redox loop like this could make chlorate treatment practical at real plants instead of a laboratory curiosity.
pmc-10703906:
Doubling a laser's frequency on a chip would put a versatile tool inside compact photonics, but it usually demands bulky crystals and careful alignment. Marco Clementi and co-authors built such a source on a silicon nitride chip. A semiconductor laser locks itself to a tiny ring resonator on the chip, narrowing its line to as little as 41 hertz. The intense circulating light then writes its own periodic pattern into the material through a light-driven effect, enabling the doubling.

The device runs on milliwatts of pump power and emits over 2 milliwatts of doubled light, an efficiency of 280 percent per watt under electrical drive. The pattern can be rewritten to cover the main telecom bands, with no electrodes needed. The authors argue standalone, coherent, efficient doublers like this can join the integrated photonics toolbox.
pmc-10704106:
Sprengholz, Henkel, Böhm, and Betsch warn in twenty twenty-three that distorted memories of the pandemic could hamper preparation for the next crisis. Studies in Germany asked people in twenty twenty and again in late twenty twenty-two about their past risk views, behaviour, and trust in science and government. Recalled answers were then checked against what people had actually said earlier.

Recall bent systematically with vaccination status. Vaccinated people overrated their past caution and trust, while unvaccinated people underrated theirs, above all when vaccination was core to identity. Paying for correct recall shrank the bias, so it was not mere forgetting. Stronger bias tracked harsher judgments of past policy. The authors fear rival stories of the crisis will deepen division.
pmc-10704406:
A European food safety panel gives in a 2023 opinion a safe upper level for manganese intake. The panel was asked by the European Commission to judge harm from excess manganese in food. Reviews of human and animal studies were run to weigh the proof.

Brain harm stands as the critical effect of too much manganese in the proof. Yet the data can not pin a clean dose response curve or a firm reference point. In place of a true upper limit, high end natural food intakes serve as the guide. A safe level of 8 mg per day was set for adults, including pregnancy. The opinion explains why that level carries reasonable confidence of no harm.
pmc-10704706:
Emma Douglass, Clare Johnson, Geraldine Lucas, and Sally Dowling ask mothers with intellectual disabilities what feeding guides they actually want in a 2023 study. More such women are becoming mothers, fewer breastfeed, and health leaflets are rarely checked with them.

Four women reviewed videos, easy read sheets, and varied feeding images in a focus group, using photos to spark talk. Two themes emerged: a hunger for real choice in images and tastes, and doubts about how easy the easy read material truly is. The women ask services to work with them, not just for them.
pmc-10704806:
Stephen Morris and co-authors compare care costs for people with ataxia across three European countries. Their 2023 survey asks whether attending a specialist ataxia centre changes how much health care patients use and what it costs. Little was known about the price of treating this group of movement disorders.

Patients in the United Kingdom, Italy, and Germany reported their service use over twelve months. Replies came from one hundred eighty-one British, ninety-six Italian, and forty-three German patients. For most kinds of contact, use differed little between centre attenders and those who never attended. Costs per patient were tallied by group and country. The authors frame the survey as a base for judging whether specialist care pays for itself in this rare-disease field.
pmc-10705506:
Shan Xu, Rezarta Frakulli, and Yilan Lin compared four radiation styles for newly found glioblastoma in a 2023 network analysis. The brain tumor is fierce, and clinics can aim radiation by older shaping, by modulated beams, by sweeping arcs, or by protons. Head-to-head trials are few, so the team wove direct and indirect evidence into one network.

Six trials and comparative studies held 816 patients in all. Proton therapy came out ahead on overall survival against every other style. It also led on the time before the tumor grew again. The authors suggest protons as a standard choice for selected patients. They frame the result with care, since the network leans on few studies and some indirect links.
pmc-10707006:
Adriana Pane and co-authors present a case report from 2023 on tube feeding for an adult with phenylketonuria, a rare inherited condition often shortened to PKU. People with the condition cannot handle a part of normal protein, so their diet has to stay very low in that part for life.

The report explains why standard tube feeds do not fit such a diet, since no ready made formula covers full energy and protein needs without the harmful part. The team describes how they built a feed for one adult patient and what had to be checked each day. Their account fills a clear gap, as the first adults treated from birth now face care needs that past guidance barely covered.
pmc-10707106:
Sergey Gorbin and co-authors synthesize new phosphorus-bearing glycoluril compounds. Their twenty twenty-three paper uses the Birum-Oleksyszyn reaction, joining an aldehyde, the glycoluril core, and triphenyl phosphite in one pot. Benzaldehyde and two ring variants supplied the aryl part.

Yields ran from fair to good as catalysts and conditions varied. The reaction makes twin forms of each product; liquid separation split them cleanly. Nuclear magnetic resonance on three nuclei, plus a crystal structure and quantum calculations, pinned each form shape. Glycolurils host guests and build molecular cages; adding a phosphonate arm opens new binding tricks for that toolbox.
pmc-10707206:
Valentina Gardini, Chiara Ruini, Eliana Tossani and colleagues set out a trial protocol for a virtual reality programme aimed at unhealthy habits in 2023. Instead of targeting one disorder, the HOME intervention tackles three shared drivers: poor emotion regulation, experiential avoidance and low psychological flexibility.

Groups at risk for nicotine dependence, alcohol abuse and eating problems will receive the VR programme or wait, with checks before, after and at three and six months. The team expects gains in behaviour, the three shared factors and stress. If it works, one transdiagnostic tool could serve several prevention programmes at once, which the authors argue would be cost-effective for general population health.
pmc-10707406:
Tianlong Ding and six co-authors test if the cell shear ADAM17 marks fate and immune mix in liver cancer. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-three. This cancer is the most death-dealt tumor kind, and ADAM17 had been tied to tumor birth. Gene use in big cancer banks, life-span curves, cell runs, and mouse runs were all brought to bear.

High ADAM17 use tied to short life, late stage, and high blood marks. Paths lit near it span shape shift, flare, and growth chains. Its use also tracked immune cell mix and brake marks in tumors. Cell and mouse work showed it drives growth and spread. The team read it as a fate mark.
pmc-10708306:
Yi Pan and co-authors reviewed in 2023 branched polymers, with a focus on use in the Chinese oil industry. Flooding fields with polymers helps push out more crude oil. The common linear polymer used for this loses strength in heat and salt because of its shape.

Branched forms, including tree-like and highly branched types, may hold up better. The review covers how each type is made and where it is used in practice. It weighs the gains and drawbacks of each method. The authors say large-scale use still needs more field tests. Cost and speed of making the material are among the concerns to settle first.
pmc-10708606:
Bartosz Musznicki and co-authors model city sensor networks from open data, in a 2023 paper from Poland. Wireless sensors need well planned links to move data well. Real maps of devices can give truer models than made up layouts.

The team wrote a set of methods that turn device location data into graph models of links. They built both snapshots and time spanning models for four large Polish cities. Tests then probed how the modeled networks behave and where they are weak. The authors close with paths for more work. City staff and network designers can use the approach to plan sensor rollouts on real streets.
pmc-10708806:
Madiha Khan and co-authors report a new material for sensing ethanol gas, in a 2023 study. Good gas sensors must be stable, picky, and quick, and finding materials that do all three is hard. The team combined two metal oxides, zirconium oxide and cobalt oxide, into tiny hybrid structures. They tested the mix as the active layer of a sensor at 200 degrees Celsius.

The sensor picked out ethanol clearly at low levels and answered a test pulse in under a minute. Its slow recovery, about six minutes, is a drawback the authors note. They credit the porous shape, which lets gas reach active sites, and an inner electric field where the two oxides meet. The results mark the pairing as a strong candidate for ethanol detection.
pmc-10709906:
False teeth collect slime films that threaten the mouth beneath, and the plastic they are made from decides how much film sticks. Salma Fathy and co-authors compare two denture plastics in a 2023 study, each made by hand packing and by computer milling. Discs of each kind were soaked in a bath carrying tiny particles of a common antiseptic.

The milled acetal discs came out roughest, before the soak and after. Every group grew far less film once coated, and the effect held for nineteen days as the antiseptic leaked out slowly. Before coating, roughness predicted film; after coating, it stopped mattering.
pmc-10710606:
Kenichi Sato and co-authors report, in a 2023 conference abstract, results for a combined salvage therapy in brain tumors that came back. The therapy, called AVAgamma, pairs a focused radiation method, gamma knife, with a drug that starves tumors of blood supply. Sixty-four patients with recurrent glioblastoma were treated after their first-line care failed. Results were set against thirty past patients who got radiation alone at relapse.

Time without growth after the combined therapy ran a median of six months, and median survival ten months. Survival from first treatment reached twenty-five months, ahead of twenty-one for radiation alone, though the gap fell short of firm statistical proof. Five-year survival also ran higher with the combo, above all in patients who were still in good shape at relapse. The authors credit the drug with better local control.
pmc-10711006:
Moving DNA or RNA into cells is a daily lab task, but the fatty carriers used often kill many of the cells. Tatsushi Yoshida, Kenta Yamasaki, and Kenjiro Tadagaki show in a 2023 study that the deaths follow the cell's own suicide program, called apoptosis. When they added a drug that blocks the enzymes driving that program, far more cells survived the procedure.

The drug also raised the share of cells that took up the new genetic material. The authors propose the blocker as a simple add-on that makes this common lab method gentler and more reliable, with possible uses in gene therapy and vaccines.
pmc-10711406:
Cynthia Miller and Brittany Zwischenberger describe small cut heart bypass surgery with a focus on women, in a paper from 2023. The method joins a key chest artery to the main front heart artery through a small cut, often with robot help and no heart lung machine.

Women tend to fare worse than men after standard bypass with a split breastbone. The small cut route may ease that gap. The authors walk through how the robot aided form is done, step by step. They stress tweaks in craft that can lift results for women who need the surgery.
pmc-10711906:
A standard heart tracing hides patterns no human eye can summarize, and deep learning might read heart failure severity straight off the waveform. Sanshiro Togo and co-authors trained a residual neural network in 2023 on twelve-lead ECGs from patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a thickened-heart condition. Severity grades came from symptom class and a blood marker, with pretraining on a large public ECG archive to offset the small local sample.

The model sorted mild-to-moderate from severe cases with solid scores, and explanation maps showed it staring at the QRS complex in milder cases. The authors suggest ECG-based deep learning could flag failing patients during routine screening of this population.
pmc-10712106:
Xia Zhang and co-authors compare drug free therapies for chemo nerve damage in 2023. Nerve harm from chemotherapy is its most common side effect. No proven treatment yet prevents or cures it. Drug free options such as exercise and other physical methods show promise, but which works best was unknown.

The team searched four databases for randomized trials of such therapies. They ran both direct and network wide comparisons across trials. Outcomes covered pain, nerve symptoms, daily life quality, and sense and movement signs. The ranking can help clinics pick the best supported option for patients in pain.
pmc-10712906:
Bacteria learn to shrug off the viruses that hunt them, which is why phage therapy sometimes fails mid-treatment. Mianzhi Wang and co-authors train the virus first. They isolated a phage that lyses a major lung pathogen, then let it coevolve with resistant bacteria. The trained descendant regained its killing power. A single amino acid change in its tail fiber explained the comeback: the fiber could grip the resistant cells again.

Using the trained phage together with its ancestor delayed resistance longer than either alone. Tests in dishes and in infected mouse lungs showed better outcomes. The strategy borrows evolution itself as a drug development tool: let the predator rehearse on tomorrow's prey before the patient ever meets it.
pmc-10714106:
Chelsea Modlin and co-authors draw lessons on fair partnership from running adaptive platform trials in poorer countries. Their 2023 paper reflects on trial designs that test many treatments at once and adapt as results arrive, which spread fast during the pandemic. Such trials in low- and middle-income countries run through partnerships between local teams and groups in rich countries.

Those partnerships can entrench the very imbalances they should fight, in money, credit, and control. Drawing on literature and a meeting of trial leaders, the authors map the dimensions along which equity must be checked. The aim is practical: partnerships designed so that local researchers gain ground, not just data.
pmc-10714506:
Noriyuki Kimura and co-authors built models to predict brain amyloid from wearable sensors and lifestyle data in a 2023 paper. A cheap screen for high amyloid could cut costs and patient burden in Alzheimer trials and care. Their study followed older adults in a Japanese city who had mild memory problems or memory complaints but no dementia. Participants wore sensors, answered surveys, took thinking tests, and had brain scans.

Records from more than one hundred twenty people, with follow ups in later years, fed the learning models. Three model types were trained to call whether a scan showed high amyloid, set by a standard cut off. The models were built to stay readable, so users can see why a call was made. Scores were averaged over many rounds of cross checking. The work tests whether daily life data can flag who most needs a costly brain scan.
pmc-10716106:
Zhou and coauthors review tiny implanted sensors that track body signals in animals. Live tracking alerts vets to illness in animals early. It also helps probe how human illness works. Implanted chemical sensors meet that need with little harm.

Such sensors work without blood draws and cause little pain. They can track glucose, ions, and other body marks nonstop. The review traces how the field grew over years. It sums up sensor designs, coatings, and power needs. It also maps uses in farm and lab animals. Gaps hold long-term stability and safe removal.
pmc-10716406:
Rebecka Steffen Johansson and three co-authors checked whether heart attacks with clean arteries leave a flow flaw years later, in a study published in 2023. Such attacks have many roots; one is small vessel disease, which early scans can miss. A quarter of cases receive no diagnosis from the first scan. Their group held 15 such patients with clean first scans, plus 15 matched peers.

Five years on, a stress scan read blood flow through the heart wall. The former patients ran lower flow than the peers, with no gap in other scan marks or risk facts. Pill use split the groups on one drug type. The authors read the low flow as small vessel disease at work, late if not at first. They urge flow readings in the follow-up of such cases.
pmc-10717106:
Cleaners that keep food plants safe can, over time, train bacteria to resist them, and sometimes antibiotics too. Ricardo Wu-Chen and co-authors exposed twenty-seven Salmonella strains in 2023 to slowly rising doses of five food-grade disinfectants. The strains varied in drug resistance and family type, letting the team see which backgrounds adapt most.

After exposure, twenty-two of one hundred thirty-five evolved lines had gained resistance to some of fourteen important antibiotics. A common disinfectant called BAC produced the most cross-resistance, while peroxide most often lowered resistance. Gene scans found mutations behind the shifts. The authors warn that unregulated disinfectant use in food settings can feed the wider antibiotic resistance problem.
pmc-10717706:
Jihao Ma and co-authors study brain activation during food anticipation in mice in work from 2023. Mice fed one meal a day at a fixed time become active before feeding, a behavior tied to the insular cortex and lateral hypothalamus.

The team tracked a marker of neuron activity in both regions over fifteen days of restricted feeding. Active neurons, including orexin neurons, grew in number day by day. The two regions peaked at different points in the schedule. The pattern suggests the regions play distinct roles in building the anticipation network.
pmc-10720806:
Dongyao Xu, Youbao Huang, and Wei Wang published a letter in 2023 commenting on a trial of pain control after keyhole gallbladder surgery. The trial found that adding surgical pain techniques to drugs beat drugs alone, for pain at rest, pain on coughing, and sleep on the first night. The letter writers praise the work, then raise points they see as gaps.

One concern is that the trial did not state which gallbladder diseases its patients had. People with long-standing gallbladder inflammation hurt more after surgery than those with simple polyps, so the mix matters for reading the results. The letter goes on with further comments in the same spirit. Such exchanges help readers weigh how far a trial's findings can travel.
pmc-10721206:
Zhiyong Yin and co-authors mapped how sperm forms in the honeybee testis, cell by cell. Male bees are haploid and make sperm through an unusual meiosis whose second division can be lopsided, yielding one normal and one small spermatid. Nobody knew the molecular script of that split. The team sequenced RNA from single testis cells of drones three and fourteen days after emergence.

Young testes were busy making sperm; older ones held only late stages. The roadmap forks after meiosis into two paths, toward full spermatids and toward the small ones. The small cells carry the fewest active genes and the least RNA of any type. Oddly, they switch on many young genes found only in bees' insect order, and carry a high mutation load. The authors link this strange biology to the odd division itself.
pmc-10729006:
Steven Lynn and co-authors report a 2023 study of a scale for ego loss. Ego loss, a fading sense of self, is a hallmark of psychedelic drug use. The team built a ten-item scale to rate it in daily life. Here they check the scale again in a fresh group. Student volunteers, 527 in all, filled in the scale and related measures online.

The check found the same two-part shape as before. One part covers ego loss and one covers unity with others and the world. Scores held steady and linked well with traits such as mindfulness and dissociation. Sleep and mood measures also fit the expected pattern. Drug researchers get a tested tool for a state that is hard to pin down. A sound scale lets studies compare ego loss across drugs, doses, and settings. The sample is students, not patients, so clinic use needs its own checks.
pmc-10729106:
Nothando Ngwenya, Chido Dziva Chikwari, Janet Seeley, and Rashida Abbas Ferrand present a debate on whether adolescence means the same thing in Africa as in the Global North, in a 2023 article. The debate was held in 2018 at a symposium in Mwanza, Tanzania. How adolescence is defined shapes health programs and global policy for young people.

Supporters of the standard view argued that puberty and brain growth form a distinct phase everywhere. They noted that rites, laws, and customs mark it across cultures, so no regional split is needed. Opponents argued that the idea is shaped by local beliefs and values. In their view, the northern concept clashes with African life because it prizes the individual over the community and imports set gender and social roles. The article leaves the question open, as a live issue for policy design.
pmc-10730406:
Cancer cells hunger for the amino acid serine, and most import it rather than build it, yet the importers were unknown. Papalazarou and co-authors screened the whole solute carrier family in colorectal cancer cells, watching nutrient use and growth. Two carriers stood out: SLC6A14 pulls serine across the outer membrane, and SLC25A15 moves it inside mitochondria. A third, SLC12A4, also helps with uptake.

Blocking SLC6A14 together with either partner shrank serine intake and slowed tumor growth in dishes and in animals. The effect hit hardest in cells whose own serine production was weak. The carriers emerge as candidate drug targets.
pmc-10734006:
Linlin Wu and Chunfang Gao review sugar coating on the tiny vesicles that cells shed, with a focus on cancer, in this 2023 paper. Cells release membrane bubbles loaded with proteins and other cargo. The sugars on those vesicles shape how they form and where they land.

The review covers lab methods for isolating and reading vesicle sugars. It tracks how coating changes uptake by target cells. Roles in spread, cell talk, and immune therapy are surveyed. Protein changes inside cells, driven by vesicle sugars, also come under review. Blood tests might one day read these sugar signatures for cancer. The field is young, and the authors chart its open questions.
pmc-10734206:
Petrova and colleagues test how long stays in a new tongue land reshape sound picks in this twenty twenty-three study. Tongues weigh pitch and length in unlike ways when speech sounds are sorted. Grown learners may or may not pick up the new weights with time abroad.

Inside, Mandarin-born folks with long UK stays weighed length more like UK-born folks in speech tests. Newer guests still leaned on pitch far more in those same speech tests. In music beat tests, both guest groups leaned on pitch more than UK-born folks did. Both guest groups also fought to shut out pitch when a task asked for loud-based picks. Time abroad retunes speech picks in set spots, the team says, not all at once.
pmc-10734306:
The inner ear's balance organs are tested by moving the head along precise axes, and that usually means strapping the head still. Barbara La Scaleia and co-authors remove the strap in a 2023 methods paper. They present algorithms that deliver motion aligned with the head's own axes while the head stays free.

The system tracks the moving head and steers a six-axis motion platform so the stimulus keeps its intended direction relative to the skull. It was validated in two settings, with the head resting and with the person actively tracking a target. Testing balance in natural, unrestrained conditions matters for older patients and those who cannot tolerate helmets. The authors frame the work as a step toward vestibular testing that resembles real life, standing and looking around.
pmc-10735606:
Catherine Garcia and Lauren Brown examine in 2023 how social position and biology together shape thinking skills in older Hispanic and Latino adults. This group is the fastest-growing share of older Americans and faces high risk of cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease.

Research has covered many social and cultural factors, the authors note, but the pathways that produce unequal rates of dementia are still poorly mapped. They call for work that follows people across the life course and at several levels at once, from neighborhoods to bodies. Their piece lays out a framework for research that takes both identity and biology seriously.
pmc-10735806:
Self-neglect is the allegation Adult Protective Services hears most, and a 2023 study by Samantha Tuft, Farida Ejaz, and Courtney Reynolds asks what makes case managers confirm it. The team worked with Oklahoma's agency during the pandemic.

Phone interviews captured 188 community-dwelling clients reported for self-neglect. A statistical model weighed age, gender, income, race, schooling, thinking status, daily-living difficulty, depression, and recent care events. The model explained about a quarter of the variation and sorted cases correctly about eighty-two percent of the time. A past short nursing home stay and a history of falls raised the odds of validation, while a past hospitalization lowered them. The predictors hint at what evidence persuades investigators.
pmc-10735906:
Jennifer Saucedo and co-authors test whether family-work friction carries depression into retirement in a 2023 study. Older workers juggle job demands against home demands, and spillover runs both ways. The retirement decision may ride on that spillover.

Health and Retirement Study data followed 1,031 workers aged fifty-one and up from 2008 to 2018. All had moved to partial or full retirement by the end. More depressive symptoms meant more friction in both directions and a higher chance of retiring. Family-to-work friction, though, lowered the retirement chance, and it carried a real indirect effect. Work-to-family friction showed no such carry. The split suggests home strain delays exit even as mood pushes toward it.
pmc-10736306:
Robert Graham, Isha Karmacharya, Traci Wilson, and Molly French report on how Area Agencies on Aging have moved into housing work. These local agencies mainly serve older adults under a federal aging law, and housing was not a core task. Need has grown, though, as affordable and accessible homes get scarce. Their 2023 report draws on national surveys of the agencies from 2019 and 2022.

By 2022, eighty-one percent of agencies ran at least one housing or homelessness program. Interest in training on the topic jumped from thirty to forty-six percent over the same span. Programs range from home repairs to owning senior housing. The authors stress that partnerships with local groups carry much of the work, and that the shift is still growing.
pmc-10736406:
Jourdyn Lawrence and Ichiro Kawachi ask whether racial discrimination in institutional settings harms cognitive function. Black adults in the United States face the lasting legacy of structural racism plus everyday social stress, and gaps in cognitive aging persist. Inflammation has been proposed as one path by which discrimination gets under the skin. The team drew on the CARDIA study, which follows Black and white adults over time.

To guard against measurement error and hidden confounding, the authors used an instrumental variable analysis. That design aims at an unbiased, causal estimate rather than a simple correlation. They linked reports of discrimination in settings like work and housing to a battery of standard thinking tests. More reported discrimination went with worse cognitive function. The authors argue that the results point to institutions and policy as places where action could protect brain health, rather than placing the burden on individuals alone.
pmc-10736606:
Salom Teshale gives a 2023 talk summary on how states can carry out the 2022 National Strategy to Support Family Caregivers. The national plan lists steps that states and other non federal groups can take on their own. States can widen access to services, join work across agencies, and track caregiver data to check that help meets real needs.

Several states lead on tools that assess what each caregiver needs. Teshale sets out frames states can use to track whether their steps are done and whether they work. The summary draws on a national center that helps states share what they learn, and names state efforts that match the plan's steps.
pmc-10736706:
Debra Dobbs and co-authors test a teaching program for dementia end of life care in a 2023 study. Assisted living staff often lack confidence to plan care with residents who have dementia and their families. A prior trial of the program lifted written advance care plans in treated homes from low to majority levels.

The follow up pilot asks whether staff self efficacy is the gear behind that lift. Staff rated their faith in caring for dying persons, with and without dementia, before and one month after teaching. Treated staff showed the larger rise in full agreement on both items. The check sets up a fuller mediation test.
pmc-10736806:
Poor sleep and chronic pain feed each other, and both corrode mental health. Christina Mu and Soomi Lee ask whether holding a job, and which job, changes those links. They use a long-running national study of midlife adults, measured twice about a decade apart. Sleep quality, sleep length, pain sites, and pain interference were all tracked. Depressive and anxiety symptoms formed the outcomes.

As sleep worsened and pain grew, mental health symptoms rose in every group. The links ran stronger among non-workers than workers. Among healthcare workers, pain and sleep tied more tightly to depression, though not clearly to anxiety. Combined poor sleep and heavy pain sharpened anxiety for all. The study suggests support should be tailored: the same bad night lands differently depending on a person's work life.
pmc-10737006:
Yong Kyung Choi and Shih-Yin Lin test whether ChatGPT can help spot delirium in older adults in a 2023 study. Delirium is a sudden confused state, common and serious in older people with thinking problems. Family caregivers often report its signs, but many lack confidence in judging them, which can delay care.

The team trained the model with prompts built around a seven item caregiver scale for delirium. It then scored five tested case stories, each run three times for steadiness. Some scale items were scored right in all cases, while others gave mixed results when set against human experts. The authors treat the work as an early check on aid for caregivers.
pmc-10737106:
Shelley Condon, Brian Cox, and Patricia Parmelee test a gratitude practice in 2023 among older adults with chronic knee or hip pain. Thankfulness exercises have shown promise for easing pain's toll, yet few studies focus on older people, who bear much chronic pain. Their trial asks thirty-eight adults, average age about sixty-eight, to write down three things they feel grateful for each day.

Half journaled for two weeks and half did not, while all took nightly phone calls and interviews before and after. Gratitude levels, both as a trait and as a daily state, tracked well-being closely. Well-being rose over time in both groups, though, and income also predicted well-being, which shows pain's uneven burden.
pmc-10737206:
Meishan Ai and co-authors mapped how aging reshapes brain wiring in adults at high risk of Alzheimer's disease, in a 2023 study. All 153 volunteers were healthy in mind but had a close relative with the disease. The team built wiring maps from brain scans and gave tests of speed, switching, and word memory.

Older age went with more divided, sparser wiring networks and hubs of greater traffic. Older adults also took longer on the switching test and recalled fewer words. Schooling and test scores were weighed beside the wiring traits. The work adds detail on how the brain's white matter ages before symptoms in those at high risk.
pmc-10737306:
Marguerite DeLiema and Kathleen Wilber published a 2023 symposium summary on making research partnerships work in the study of adult maltreatment. Protecting abused or neglected adults takes many professions at once: health care, social services, police, and courts. Researchers who build screening tools or test interventions must team up with the agencies that do that protection work.

The piece collects lessons from early career researchers who have done so. One team describes joint projects with a large Texas health system and protection agencies in Oklahoma, including how they adapted when the pandemic disrupted data collection. Another analyzed interviews with state agencies in Montana for themes about collaboration. The lead author adds guidance on administrative barriers, such as contracts and legal agreements between sectors. The aim is practical: help the next studies start with trust and shared systems already in place.
pmc-10737406:
Matthias Hoben, Emily Dymchuk, Stephanie Chamberlain, and Anna Beeber study care team ties with family caregivers in a 2023 paper. Family and friend caregivers are key to life in nursing and assisted homes. COVID-19 rules changed how they could join resident care. Most past work heard only the family side of that shift.

The team ran focus groups and interviews with 37 care staff. Staff came from six congregate care settings in total. Talks showed pressure and conflict from some families. They also showed real support flowing both ways. Joint choices with families proved vital in hard times. The authors urge lessons from good cases for future crises.
pmc-10737706:
Mohammad Rababa, a solo author, studies how feeling close to family relates to agitation in older adults with dementia, in a 2023 Jordanian study. Most people with dementia would rather stay home than move to a nursing home, a preference reinforced by local culture and faith. Yet work outside the home leaves many alone for long hours.

The study compared 51 adults with dementia living at home and 51 in nursing homes. It measured emotional closeness, social network size, and positive and negative feelings, then set them against agitation levels. Neglect at home can harm body and mind, so the balance of ties matters. Findings can guide family support that keeps home living safe rather than merely preferred.
pmc-10737806:
Phyllis Cummins, Runcie Chidebe, Rita Karam, and Jenna Kramer report, in a 2023 study, what health care employers want from community college graduates. These colleges train many of the aides and nurses who care for an aging population. The team asked which basic skills, reading, number work, and problem solving, matter most on the job.

They interviewed college leaders, teachers, and ten employers from home care, nursing homes, and hospitals. Employers said they work closely with the colleges, hosting clinical rounds and advising on courses. Number skills such as measuring drug doses, clear speaking with patients and families, and calm problem solving ranked high. New nurses sometimes lacked leadership skills, a gap both sides are trying to close.
pmc-10737906:
What older adults eat may shape how sharp their minds stay, and that link may not run the same in every group. Isabella Arellanes, Eileen Crimmins, Jennifer Ailshire, and Jung Ki Kim test the link in a 2023 study. They use a national survey of 6,845 older adults, with diet scored on a standard healthy eating index.

Only 11 percent ate what counts as a good diet. Hispanic adults scored best on diet quality, ahead of both Black and White adults. Yet better diet tied to better thinking scores only among White and Black adults. The link did not hold for Hispanic adults. The authors say diet programs may need group-specific design.
pmc-10738106:
Dakota Witzel and Kelly Cichy introduce a symposium on how daily relationship strains move emotions in a 2023 overview. Across mid and later life, everyday ties shape health, and feelings are one channel through which that shaping runs.

Four talks use dense daily tracking designs. One links felt control to same day and next day emotional hits from social stress. Another ties stress reactions to later sleep. A third weighs marriage and memory loss in daily loneliness. The last follows caregiver stress and felt isolation. Together they map feelings as the daily hinge between ties and health.
pmc-10738206:
Rafael de Cabo and Mustapha Bouhrara review new scanning methods for aging research in a paper from 2023. The methods use magnetic resonance, the same base idea as hospital MRI scans. New versions can probe tissue structure and chemistry without cutting or harming the sample. The review centers on lab animals used as models of human aging.
