The authors explain how water in tissue reacts to magnetic fields in ways that reveal density, acidity, and fine structure. They survey tools such as diffusion imaging and chemical exchange methods. These scans could track aging over time and test treatments in the same animal. The pair urge wider use of the methods in aging trials.
pmc-10738306:
Heba AlDossary and co-authors review in a 2023 study a front-line tool to make clinic care kinder to older adults. The tool is a short form that patients fill in while they wait, covering eight questions tied to four care aims. It was sent to more than eleven hundred retail clinic sites.

A survey of the nurse staff who used it drew one hundred replies. Staff rated the form easy, welcome, and useful, and their trust in doing and charting the four aims rose after its use. Visit time fell as well. A small form, it seems, can shift daily care for older patients.
pmc-10738506:
Timothy Ly, Rebecca Allen, Jeanne Cundiff, and Jason DeCaro study how daily discrimination relates to everyday memory judgments in a 2023 paper. Metamemory means how well people judge their own memory, and slips in it can be counted as subjective cognitive complaints. Stress may erode that accuracy, so the team asked whether days marked by discrimination show more complaints.

They used daily diary data from close to eight hundred adults aged twenty to seventy-five in a national midlife study. On days when a person faced more discrimination than usual, their metamemory accuracy dipped. Daily mood balance also mattered, and race and ethnicity shaped the patterns between people. Past lifetime discrimination sharpened the daily effect. The authors argue that daily social stress can cloud the mind's self-monitoring.
pmc-10738706:
Doyle and co-authors hunt the marks of superagers, elders whose memory matches people twenty years younger, in two Hispanic cohorts. Superaging was defined strictly: eighty or older, recall at least at the level of 55-to-64-year-olds, and no impairment at any wave. Of 640 Puerto Rican study participants, 45 qualified; of 180 in a national retirement study, 31.

In both samples the same traits predicted membership: more education, fewer limits on daily activities, and fewer depressive symptoms. Chronic disease counts, self-rated health, and body mass did not. The pattern, the authors argue, reflects resilience, bouncing back, rather than resistance to illness, and names levers for population programs.
pmc-10738806:
Alba Iaconi and co-authors study how nursing home staff view their work setting in western Canada in 2023. Work context is tied to care quality and resident life quality. The team used a standard tool with ten parts, from leadership to free time and space. Near five thousand staff from ninety one homes took part.

Managers gave the highest scores on context. Nurses came next. Practical nurses and care aides gave the lowest scores. Care aides scored lowest on physical health. Practical nurses scored lowest on mental health and on most context parts. The authors call for more staff and time. They urge focus on the groups that give most direct care.
pmc-10739106:
Moyosoreoluwa Jacobs, Peter Lichtenberg, and Wassim Tarraf (2023) compare subjective cognitive decline across racial and ethnic groups in the United States. The condition, a person's sense that their memory or thinking is slipping, can be a sign of Alzheimer's disease and dementias. Those diseases are expected to double in prevalence by 2060, with group differences. The authors use 2015 survey data on 142,657 adults aged forty-five, comparing non-Hispanic White, non-Hispanic Black, and Hispanic respondents.

Beyond who reports decline, they examine five consequences it can bring, such as limits on activities and trouble communicating with providers. Models test how much of the gap three factor kinds explain: predisposing ones like age, enabling ones like insurance, and health needs like chronic disease. Black respondents reported decline slightly more often, at 13.5 percent, despite White respondents being older on average. The analysis aims to show where intervention could narrow the gaps.
pmc-10739206:
Andrea Sillner and co-authors study how fading memory changes what older adults want from health care communication. Their 2023 study samples adults over fifty living in the community, who rated how their memory and thinking had shifted over five years. Talking with doctors and nurses now happens in person, by video, and through web portals, and each channel makes its own demands.

When memory slips, following a portal message or a fast phone call gets harder, and satisfaction can fall. The team links self-rated cognitive change to channel preference and satisfaction. The findings aim to help clinics match how they reach patients to what those patients can comfortably use.
pmc-10740406:
Jiseok Yi and co-authors studied how drug-resistant Salmonella germs react to stresses found in food plants, in work published in 2023. The germ, Salmonella Typhimurium, can spoil food safety when it survives cleaning and storage. The team exposed the germs to a common drug, lactic acid, and salt, alone and in pairs. They then measured how the germs changed and whether they grew harder to kill.

Germs that met the drug first kept strong resistance to it, even after later acid or salt stress. Mixed stresses raised the share of injured cells and, for the drug-plus-salt group, left behind hardy persister cells. Some groups also gained resistance to other drugs, while acid or salt alone left germs easier to kill with several drugs. The results warn that plant stresses can shape tougher germs.
pmc-10740806:
König and co-authors model how much heart risk stays behind after cholesterol lowering, and how age shapes it. Strong evidence backs the view that LDL cholesterol drives cardiovascular disease. Patients still need clear numbers on what a given drop buys them. Even at best cholesterol levels, a real residue of risk remains. The team built math models from trial data for relative and total risk cuts.

Age stood out as a clear driver of starting risk. Its odds ratio was 1.02 per year in their checks. Data from the Whickham cohort matched that pattern. The models help doctors explain both the gain from treatment and the risk that persists.
pmc-10741206:
Aleksandra Dajnowska and co-authors map, in a 2023 study, where a hormone-like peptide called spexin shows up in the cow gut. Spexin influences feeding and metabolism in small animals, but large farm mammals were a blank. The team sampled three gut segments from Holstein-Friesian cattle, the true stomach, the small intestine's middle stretch, and the colon, and stained them for the peptide and its receptor's gene.

The receptor gene spoke loudest in the small intestine segment. Staining patterns differed by region in a telling way. In stomach and small intestine, the peptide sat mostly in the lower nerve web of the gut wall. In the colon it concentrated in the deeper nerve web that drives movement. The authors read this geography as a clue to segment-specific jobs, from secretion to motility, and offer the map as a first reference for ruminant gut regulation.
pmc-10741906:
Feilong Wang and co-authors present, in a 2023 paper, a whole body teleoperation system that lets a human operator steer a dual arm robot by moving their own arms. Humanoid arms have many joints, so copying a human arm faithfully is hard. A single sensor also loses the arm when body parts block its view.

Their strategy fuses several sensors. Finger posture is captured as bending angles for each finger. A depth camera tracks the arm's movement in space. Together the feeds drive an arm movement tracking system that mirrors the operator onto the robot. Experiments checked robustness and real time performance. The system kept control stable and recognition accurate even in occlusion heavy situations. Better mirroring opens teleoperation to delicate tasks, from remote handling to assistive care, where a clumsy robot is not an option.
pmc-10742006:
Hui Liu and co-authors report the full genome of sweet tea, a tree valued for its leaves, in a study published in 2023. Sweet tea belongs to a large genus of the beech family that had no reference genome until now. The team assembled the genome at the scale of whole chromosomes. Their assembly spans about nine hundred fifty million base pairs with a high completeness score.

The map predicts about thirty-seven thousand protein-coding genes, and repeated sequences make up nearly two-thirds of the genome. The lineage shows no fresh whole-genome doubling beyond an ancient event shared with kin. Family tree analysis places the split between sweet tea and the oak genus at about fifty-nine million years ago. The authors say the resource will support work on sweet tea and its relatives in the beech family.
pmc-10742806:
Mamiko Sato and co-authors studied drinking among Japanese women in fertility treatment in a 2023 paper. The study sits inside a wider project on work and mental health during assisted reproduction. Alcohol use during treatment can affect outcomes, so the team asked which social factors track with continued drinking.

Participants answered surveys on habits, work, and mental state after starting treatment. The analysis weighed factors such as job strain and distress against drinking risk. Knowing which women are most likely to keep drinking lets clinics offer support where it counts, without blanket lectures. The findings feed counseling that respects the heavy emotional load of fertility care.
pmc-10743006:
Wu and co-authors build a phone-linked sensor that detects a potent food toxin at the point of need, in a research paper from 2023. The toxin, aflatoxin B1, contaminates crops like peanuts and corn and harms health at tiny doses. Lab tests are accurate but slow and place-bound.

Their sensor stands its capture probes on tiny DNA pyramids, which space the probes evenly and keep them upright. That order boosts binding and speeds electron flow, sharpening the signal. Paired with a phone app and a pocket workstation, the sensor found the toxin down to 3 picograms per milliliter. Tests in peanut, soybean, corn, and lake water gave sound recoveries. Results matched a gold-standard lab method.
pmc-10743306:
Eddy Wang and co-authors build lab models of inflamed human skin from real skin samples in a 2023 paper. Animal models and rebuilt epidermis miss much of real skin's complexity, including its barrier fats and immune mix. The team instead takes living human skin kept outside the body and triggers it in different ways to mimic disease states.

One setup drives new blood vessel growth, one mimics harsh irritation, and one sustains immune cell attack. They track tissue damage, invading cells, signal proteins, and the skin's fat profile under each trigger. The irritant and chronic models showed deep disruption and strong immune influx, while the vessel model changed less. Such human-based models could test new skin drugs more faithfully than animal work.
pmc-10743606:
Bogdan Cylwik and co-authors test whether two blood-based scores can stand in for liver biopsy in primary sclerosing cholangitis, a disease that scars the bile ducts and liver. The scores, Hepascore and FibroTest, are patented formulas built from routine blood markers. The study covered seventy-four patients with the disease and thirty-eight healthy people, and every patient also had a biopsy to grade the scarring.

Both scores rose in step with the biopsy stages. Hepascore separated patients with serious scarring from those without it almost perfectly, reaching full specificity and near-total sensitivity at its cut-offs, with perfect overall accuracy scores. FibroTest performed well but less sharply, missing more cases at its thresholds. The authors conclude that both scores can serve as a first screening step and greatly cut the need for biopsies, with Hepascore the stronger of the two.
pmc-10743706:
Tanveer Alam Khan and co-authors review how a plant hormone family helps crops bear harsh conditions, in work from 2023. Drought, heat, and salt may cut food yields by a quarter by 2050 if left unchecked. The hormones, called brassinosteroids, steer seed sprouting, vein growth, and breeding in plants.

Their signal chain lets plants answer stress through tuned gene work and harm cleanup. Two decades of study still leave gaps in how the chain acts under each stress. The review sums up that proof and argues that tuning the chain, its making, or its sensing could breed tougher crops for a warming world.
pmc-10743806:
Yibing Liu and co-authors ask whether freezing oyster larvae leaves lasting marks on their gene-control system. Their 2023 study is the first to check epigenetic effects in offspring of the Pacific oyster after larval freezing. High death rates after thawing have long limited the use of freezing in breeding and hatchery work.

Right after thawing, DNA methylation levels and several regulator genes shifted clearly, and two histone marks changed as well. Yet by day eight after fertilization, methylation had returned to normal, and the gene shifts faded at the earliest larval stages. The pattern matched survival data, suggesting that the harm from this freezing method is brief rather than lasting.
pmc-10744206:
Sappington and Spencer review how adult western corn rootworms move, and what that means for pest control. Movement shapes the beetle's spread, its gene flow, and how fast it beats control tools. Past data conflict: some show short trips, others imply long-range spread.

That clash echoes two known puzzles, Reid's paradox and Slatkin's paradox. The authors propose that the species is partly migratory, with two behavior types. Some beetles stay local as residents, while others migrate over long distances. That split model could improve forecasts of range growth and resistance spread in cornfields.
pmc-10744306:
Andreea Rotundu and co-authors review whether technology can strengthen home exercise therapy for people with peripheral artery disease of the legs. The disease narrows leg arteries, causing pain on walking, and supervised exercise helps, but clinic programs are hard to attend. Remote rehabilitation using digital devices offers an alternative.

Searching two major databases yielded nearly two and a half thousand studies, of which twenty-five met the review's criteria. The authors compared technology-assisted home programs with conventional rehabilitation or usual care. Outcomes ranged from walking capacity and quality of life to motivation, acceptance of the devices, and inflammation markers. They conclude home exercise guided by devices can be folded into care successfully, provided programs fit each patient's clinical profile and emotional state.
pmc-10744806:
Bo Men and co-authors study how fast-melting modified asphalt grips stone in this 2023 paper. Road life depends on asphalt sticking firmly to aggregate rock. A fast-melting SBS modifier promises stronger bonds with easier handling.

The team used surface free energy theory to grade the bond. Droplet angles with three test liquids fed the energy math. Cohesion, adhesion work, and stripping resistance were computed for several doses. Higher modifier doses raised cohesion and adhesion while cutting stripping work. The fast-melting version beat classic SBS asphalt at equal dose. Its energy ratio also topped the standard mix. Results support the new modifier for longer-lasting pavements.
pmc-10745906:
Constanze Gummelt and six co-authors published a microbiology study in twenty twenty-three on how an anthrax-like bacterium manages to form spores despite a genetic oddity. Bacillus cereus biovar anthracis causes fatal disease in African rainforest wildlife. Every strain carries a large insertion inside sigK, a gene spores cannot form without.

During sporulation the insertion is cut out, restoring the gene, and the team asked whether that extra step slows or blocks the process. Gene expression tracking and electron microscopy showed it did neither. Two mutant strains did fail, but because of damage in other regulator genes. The work explains how this unusual pathogen keeps a life stage it needs to spread.
pmc-10746006:
Huiting Xu, Xinxin Xiang, Weizhe Ding, Wei Dong, and Yihong Hu review ways to make human B cells live and divide forever in the lab, in work from 2023. B cells make antibodies, and immortal lines keep making the same antibody endlessly. Such lines speed drug antibody work and diagnostic products.

Routes include infection with a herpes virus, infection with a monkey virus, direct gene edits, and switching on a surface signal. The review weighs how each route works and what it yields. Human antibodies from these lines dodge the rejection that animal antibodies can trigger. Over one hundred antibody drugs are now approved. The authors close with open problems and next steps.
pmc-10747106:
Steven Gameiro and five co-authors map variants of human papillomavirus type sixteen in North American head and neck cancers, in a two thousand twenty-three virology paper. In cervical cancer, these intratypic variants clearly differ in risk and outcome; in head and neck cancer they were barely charted.

Combining a Southwestern Ontario cohort with Cancer Genome Atlas cases gave one hundred forty-nine HPV16-positive tumors. Nearly all belonged to lineage A, and about half carried the T350G change in the E6 gene. That variant tracked with differences in tumor staging and disease-free survival in simple analyses, though not after adjustment. Immune response measures also differed, hinting the variant may carry prognostic value.
pmc-10747306:
Yingshan Zhu and co-authors test a copper-grabbing drug in 2023 for Wilson's disease, where a broken copper carrier lets the metal pile up in liver and brain. The standard drug works but can trigger severe, sometimes lasting, nerve damage, partly because it grabs other metals too. Their candidate was built to take copper and only copper.

In toxic milk mice, the standard model of the disease, oral doses lowered liver copper and raised copper in droppings, dose by dose. Both effects beat the standard drug head to head. The team nominates the compound as a drug candidate worth advancing toward patients.
pmc-10747506:
Norphanphoun and Hyde report new fungus species on mangrove trees in Thailand. The fungus genus holds major plant pathogens worldwide. Four species were detailed from mangrove ecosystems in the study. Two species proved new to science in Thailand.

A known species was found on a new host there. A fourth species from Taiwan mangroves set a host record too. Gene analysis plus form traits backed each identification. The host tree was a common mangrove type in both sites. New data expand the known diversity of the genus. Mangrove links of these fungi are now clearer.
pmc-10748306:
Natasha Samsunder and colleagues reviewed how well COVID tests performed in South African studies during the first years of the pandemic. Their scoping review, published in twenty twenty-three, gathered peer-reviewed work from March twenty twenty to August twenty twenty-two. Some studies tested gene or antigen detection, which finds the virus itself, while more studies tested antibody detection, which finds the body response after infection. The team compared sensitivity, meaning how often each test correctly flagged an infected person.

Sensitivity ranged widely for both test families, from poor to perfect depending on the study. Timing explained much of the spread. Gene and antigen tests worked best when samples came early in infection, while antibody tests worked better later, once the response had developed. The authors conclude that no single assay was both sensitive and specific enough on its own, so timing and test choice must be matched carefully.
pmc-10748406:
Wook Nam and co-authors look for signs that predict when BCG therapy will fail in early bladder cancer. BCG, a vaccine strain put into the bladder, is a standard treatment, but failure can force major surgery. One suspect is the HER2 protein, tied to a genetic class of these tumors.

The team reviewed 160 patients treated at one Korean hospital, 67 of whom got BCG. Tumors positive for HER2 came with worse signs, and their owners answered BCG less well. Immune cells in those tumors looked worn out. Sorting patients by HER2 and by a standard risk score, the authors argue, can flag who needs a different plan early.
pmc-10748506:
Amir Elalouf, Hadas Elalouf, and Ariel Rosenfeld review how the immune system and fungal infections interact in people who receive organ transplants. Transplant surgery gives hope to patients with failing organs, and drugs that calm the immune system have raised survival. Those same drugs leave recipients open to fungal infections, which often cause vague symptoms and are hard to spot. The review seeks a balance between keeping the new organ safe and fighting infection.

The authors cover the basic immune response to fungi, new findings on how that response changes, and ways to adjust treatment. They stress early diagnosis and note that a stronger innate immune response might let doctors lower the calming drugs safely. The review also points to gene effects on immune and fungal interaction, and to single-cell tools paired with machine learning as a route to new markers. It closes with open questions and research directions.
pmc-10748806:
Pimwan Sookplung and co-authors work out the right dose of a brain guard drug for neck artery surgery in a 2023 study. During the operation, called carotid endarterectomy, a drug named thiopental can shield the brain while blood flow is clamped. The dose that brings on a burst suppression pattern on brain wave monitors was not known.

Records from a Thai institute covered 57 patients treated from 2009 to 2019 without a shunt tube. About 42 percent reached the target brain wave pattern, at an average dose near 26 milligrams per kilogram per hour. Events around surgery did not differ by group, and no deaths followed in a month. The team offers that dose as the target.
pmc-10749206:
Chengyao Peng, Ali May, and Thomas Abeel hunt for gut microbes that flag methane output from cows in a 2023 paper. Cow burps carry methane made by rumen microbes fermenting fiber, a real share of farm greenhouse gas. If key microbes could be named, feed could be tuned against them. The team borrowed machine learning tools proven in human gut studies and set them on two large public data sets from Holstein cows.

Random forest regression predicted emissions best. Permutation tests then ranked which inputs mattered, surfacing several native rumen microbes as markers, among them a fungus genus and two bacterial groups. Herd location and feed details, such as fat and fiber intake, also helped predict output. The authors offer the markers as targets for precision feeding trials.
pmc-10749306:
Daniel Runco and seven colleagues published a pilot study in two thousand twenty-three on a stress protein in children with cancer. The protein, GDF15, drives nausea and appetite loss in adults with cancer. Nothing was known about its levels in children just diagnosed.

Thirty children with new cancer and twenty-seven matched healthy children took part. Blood levels of the protein were about twice as high in the cancer group at diagnosis. The children also gave body measures and answered quality of life surveys, repeated three months later. Early follow-up data showed no clear change in levels over that span. The authors frame the protein as a possible target against cancer-related malnutrition in children.
pmc-10749806:
Hitoshi Ichikawa and co-authors report a throat lymphoma found during a routine stomach scope exam. Their twenty twenty-three case report follows a fifty-five-year-old man who had lost weight. The exam was a screening esophagogastroduodenoscopy, not a search for cancer.

The scope showed swollen, pale, glossy lumps in the tonsils at the palate and tongue base. A scan showed strong sugar uptake in both tonsils, a sign of active tumor. Small biopsies could not settle the type, so the tonsil was removed for study. Cell tests proved a peripheral T-cell lymphoma at the earliest stage. The case shows the value of a close look at the throat during scope work.
pmc-10751906:
Jun Wang and co-authors print custom radiation shields for women's reconstructed chests, shaped to each body by 3D printing, in a 2023 study. After mastectomy and reconstruction, radiotherapy needs a bolus, a layer that pulls the dose up to the skin. Flat sheets gap and fold on rebuilt contours, scattering the dose. Thirty patients treated between 2019 and 2021 wore printed, individualised boluses instead.

Dose coverage of the target volume stayed strong and even, with a good homogeneity index, and the printed shells hugged the chest wall, dosing organs at risk within limits. Skin toxicity was graded by a standard scale. The authors conclude the custom bolus delivers precise treatment where one-size sheets fail. The work is part of radiotherapy's wider turn toward printing the interface between machine and patient.
pmc-10753706:
The authors review nano-scale drug targeting for breast cancer in a 2023 paper. Breast cancer is the second most common cancer in women after skin cancer. Case counts are projected to climb sharply by 2040. Conventional hormone and chemo formulations suffer weak targeting and poor drug behavior.

Nanomedicines include liposomes, particles, micelles, and hybrid carriers. Small carriers in a favored size range penetrate tissue better. They also linger in tumors through enhanced retention effects. Active targeting further sharpens delivery to cancer cells. Theranostic carriers merge therapy with imaging in one platform. Gene delivery via hybrid carriers is also explored. Carrier size, shape, charge, and surface traits govern stability and uptake. Clinical progress and remaining hurdles are surveyed in turn. The authors frame nanomedicine as a route to safer, sharper breast cancer care.
pmc-10753906:
Michele Valsecchi, Amparo Galindo, and George Jackson present a 2023 modeling study of plastics. Polyethylene is a half-crystal plastic used in films and pipes. Hydrocarbon fluids soak into it, and that uptake matters for packaging and plant safety. The team joins a fluid model with a structure model of the half-crystal form. Chains that tie crystals together are counted by the structure model.

Each sample gets one parameter set fitted to past lab data. With that single set, the model predicts uptake curves for many pure fluids. The match shows that fluid forces and sample structure split cleanly. Engineers can then predict uptake for new fluids from one calibration. Plastic makers get a tool that cuts soak testing. The split also clarifies which traits belong to the polymer grade and which belong to the fluid, a distinction that guides material choice.
pmc-10754506:
Yuzhu Guo, Yang Li, Hua-Liang Wei, and Yifan Zhao open a 2023 research collection on new theories, models, and AI methods for brain dynamics, decoding, and stimulation. The brain links many regions across scales in constant flux, so its study spans medicine, biology, and engineering. How stimulation changes brain activity needs firmer grasp to tune care.

Brain signals pack rich detail in time, space, waves, and links between zones. New deep models can read such signals end to end, yet meaning must still be drawn with care. The collection pairs top down and bottom up methods toward that aim. Decoding thought and guiding stimulation are its two poles.
pmc-10755606:
Frederick Dun-Dery and co-authors tracked long COVID in children across Canada in a 2023 study. Kids were tested for the virus at fourteen pediatric emergency departments. Families were followed at ninety days, six months, and twelve months. The goal was a firm count of lasting post-COVID conditions.

Children under eighteen who tested positive were compared with those who tested negative. Data were gathered from 2020 to early 2022. Symptoms and daily limits defined the condition at each visit. A clear rate helps schools and clinics plan support. It also calms or confirms parent worries with real numbers.
pmc-10759906:
Andrew Stewart, John Gensel, Linda Jones, and Karim Fouad wrote this 2023 review on why spinal cord repair therapies stall before reaching patients. Regrowing the injured cord is a huge task, and gains in animal studies have rarely turned into gains for people. The authors walk through the hurdles that explain that gap.

First comes the model problem: animal injuries differ from human ones in size and place, and that difference alone can doom a therapy. Next comes design: real repair will likely need combined treatments plus rehab training, which are hard to test cleanly. Reporting habits add a quieter flaw, since null or messy results often go unpublished. The paper gives trial designers a checklist of traps that reach beyond cord research into all of regenerative medicine.
pmc-10765606:
Kai Hu and a team of co-authors teach computers to name human actions from skeleton data alone. Working from body joints strips away background and lighting noise that confuse normal video. Graph networks suit the skeleton's shape, but older ones underuse the body's known structure and how limbs coordinate.

Their network stacks three ideas. A topology module reads the body plan from coarse to fine while weighing channel importance. A coordination module models how opposite and same-side limbs move together. A global module then catches patterns across space and time at several scales. On the two big NTU benchmarks, accuracy reached the low-to-mid nineties across the standard splits.
pmc-10772406:
Yan Li and co-authors map proteins in bowel cancer tumors to sort who replies to chemoradiation and targeted drugs, in a study from 2023. Why some tumors resist care was only partly known.

Protein maps of more than two hundred fifty tumors split the cancer into four types with split traits and care replies. Immune control stood out as a driver of drug reply. One heat guard protein fed radiation resistance, while a second protein level tracked poor reply to a targeted drug. The team built score models that called care reply with high truth.
pmc-10793606:
Danielly Yani Fausto and co-authors study how menopausal symptoms relate to sexual function and activity in women in menopause. Published in 2023, the cross-sectional study enrolled 96 women aged 40 to 59 who scored positive on a menopause rating scale and met a hormone level cutoff. Women on hormone replacement therapy were left out.

Women who stayed sexually active had lower scores for body and mood symptoms and a lower total symptom score. They also scored better on four parts of sexual function, including excitement and comfort, and on the total index. Not being active added over five points to the symptom score, whatever the type of menopause. The authors link staying active with fewer symptoms.
pmc-10796206:
Jae Lee and co-authors review in 2023 what is known about tibolone, a synthetic steroid for menopause care, and breast cancer risk. The drug acts like estrogen in brain, vagina, and bone, yet stays quiet in womb and breast tissue. That split profile raises a fair question about breast safety.

Past studies split on whether use lifts breast cancer risk at all. The review weighs recent work with a focus on Asian groups, where data were thinner. Tissue-selective action forms the base case for low breast effect. Readers get a current map of proof for clinic talks with patients.
pmc-10801106:
Eti Muharremi and Gentian Vyshka look at the health of the three leaders who met at Yalta in nineteen forty-five. Their twenty twenty-three article covers Franklin Roosevelt, Joseph Stalin, and Winston Churchill, who all suffered strokes after the conference. Their failing health played out behind a veil of secrecy.

The authors review each leader's state during and after Yalta, the role of high blood pressure, and other risk factors that could have been changed. Roosevelt died before the war ended, which forced a leadership handover at a key moment. The deaths of Churchill and Stalin shaped the early Cold War. The piece argues that hidden illness in top leaders is a world-shaping force.
pmc-10801906:
Lin Wang and three colleagues published a combined analysis in two thousand twenty-three on a gut-related chemical and stroke. The chemical, TMAO, is made when gut microbes process certain foods. Whether its blood level predicts brain infarction and recovery was disputed.

Fifteen studies with over forty thousand patients, all from China or Germany, were pooled. Higher TMAO linked to worse disability scores three months after stroke. It also linked to first strokes, to repeat strokes, and to greater severity at onset. No clear link with death after stroke appeared. The authors rate TMAO as a marker of risk and outcome rather than a proven cause. They note all data came from just two countries.
pmc-10806106:
David Hou and co-authors show that trained B cells can rally a special kind of killer T cell against glioblastoma, a hard-to-treat brain tumor, in this 2023 study. Tumors of this type shut down immune attack, and the B cells found inside them normally suppress T cells. The team instead activated B cells with three signals to turn them into strong antigen-presenting cells, which they named B Vax.

In lab tests, these B cells woke up T cells better than untreated B cells and pushed them to multiply. The T cells they produced looked stem-like, with high TCF-1 and low PD-1, a profile linked to lasting responses. When such T cells were placed into tumor-bearing mouse brains, the approach showed promise against the cancer.
pmc-10808806:
Alison Pearson writes a call to action for parents of disabled children in a paper whose head dates it to 2023. The plea centers on mothers, while it names fathers too. COVID-19 cut support and raised stress for these families in the United Kingdom. Lockdown left many cut off with no break. Work life for parent-carers took a long hit as well.

Pearson calls the mix a perfect storm. Yet the group stays missed by policy and by research both. The call runs to state, to bosses, and to the research world. She asks for care plans that count carer strain, work rules that bend, and studies that ask carers what they need. The piece is a stance paper, not a data study, and it writes from the UK scene.
pmc-10822906:
Haijun Han and co-authors test a probiotic against allergic rhinitis in adults, in a study published in 2023. The strain, a Lactobacillus plantarum called GUANKE, was known to balance immune replies. Adults with a past of the allergy took the probiotic for four weeks. Scores for nose and other symptoms were logged before and after, as were blood marks.

Symptom scores fell a great deal, and control scores rose in step. Sub-scores for runny nose, itch, sneeze, and tears each improved. Blood levels of the allergy antibody IgE dropped in a marked way. Twenty immune signal proteins shifted, six up and fourteen down. Those proteins cluster in cytokine and chemokine paths, which fits the balance claim.
pmc-10826606:
Hongmei Deng and ten co-authors study how COVID-19 vaccination fared in over a thousand pregnant women infected with the Omicron variant in Shanghai, in this 2023 study. Large pregnancy samples had not been reported from China. Seven hundred and seven women had received one to three doses of an inactivated vaccine, and 317 unvaccinated women served as comparison.

Women with three doses left hospital sooner than unvaccinated women, about nine days against eleven. Antibody rates rose with vaccination, and antibody positive patients also recovered faster. Mild side effects, mostly fatigue, appeared in about twelve percent of vaccinated women. Delivery choices and newborn health scores were unaffected, and all 120 newborns tested negative for the virus and its antibodies. The authors judge the vaccine safe and helpful in pregnancy.
pmc-10832806:
Fernanda Saavedra and co-authors ask how people in Peru and Chile see the sea and plastic waste in a paper whose head dates it to 2023. Sea plastic is a world ill, and care starts with how folk frame the sea. The team held long talks with 44 people, 24 in Peru and 20 in Chile. Theme checks of the talks found shared frames.

Both groups saw the sea in warm terms, tied to a felt bond with it. The sea serves fun and work: swims and views, fish and trade. Those uses link to the roots of plastic waste. Worry ran most to harm for people, less to harm for sea life. Fix ideas leaned on lone acts, since trust in state acts ran low. Chilean talks gave the state a bigger role. The authors urge plans that join lone acts with firm public acts.
pmc-10834706:
Ana João Santos, Irina Kislaya, Carlos Matias-Dias, and Ausenda Machado examine why people in Portugal do or do not take flu and COVID-19 vaccines. Their study's journal record is dated 2023. The team surveyed 1,050 adults by phone or online and read their answers through the Health Belief Model. That frame weighs how at risk people feel, how bad the illness seems, and what blocks action.

Only about three in ten people had taken the flu vaccine. Feeling unlikely to catch flu was the main reason for skipping it, followed by blocks such as supply shortages and fear of side effects. COVID-19 vaccine uptake was far higher, above eight in ten, helped by a strong sense of how severe that disease could be. People who took the flu shot also rated the COVID-19 vaccine as more useful, a link the authors discuss for future campaigns.
pmc-10835806:
Ting Zhu, Yaoyao Feng, Xiaoxuan Dong, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It streamlines the official variety test for wintersweet, a beloved Chinese flower with a tangle of named varieties, using machine vision and a genetic algorithm to pick the traits that matter.

Variety certification checks distinctness, uniformity, and stability, normally by hand. The team measured forty-two flower traits automatically with pattern recognition, including fourteen new ones. Eight classifiers competed; random forest won, and the outer petals alone carried the strongest signal. A genetic search then trimmed the list to twenty-two core traits, lifting accuracy to just over ninety-nine percent. Clustering on those traits drew a family tree of twenty-three varieties. The authors say the trimmed test is faster and sharper for breeders registering new wintersweets.
pmc-10864506:
Mwaba Sifanu and co-authors analyze, in a study whose journal version is dated 2023, dust exposure records from a Zambian copper mine. Breathing fine mine dust can scar lungs for good, so mines must measure and control it. The team reviewed measurements taken from 2017 to 2022 across two shafts and a processing plant, and judged the mine's own monitoring plan as well.

The file held 253 measurements. About six percent ran above the South African limit used for comparison. Plant areas such as screening and crushing rooms showed the highest peaks, up to eighteen units in one tipping area. Average levels stayed modest. The bigger finding was method: the mine sampled too few spots each year to support firm judgments. The authors urge a standard sampling plan, such as the European EN689, across Zambia.
pmc-10881706:
Mortazavi and co-authors warn that a Mars mission's smallest passengers may decide its fate. Astronauts carry trillions of microbes, and spacecraft grow their own microbial life. Space radiation does not just threaten human cells; it trains microbes too. The paper, published in 2023 though the catalog lists 2024, argues this contest deserves planning before launch.

Radiation-toughened microbes can gain resistance not only to radiation but to ultraviolet light, heat, drying, and antibiotics. If microbes adapt faster than their hosts, infections could turn lethal far from any hospital. The authors call for measuring how much change to expect, then building safeguards into mission design. Studying microbes in space, they add, could also pay off in health checks and new radiation treatments back on Earth.
pmc-10896906:
Heimann, Weiss, and Muller study brain stimulation and language in aging, in work dated twenty twenty-three. Language skill and its brain side balance decline with age. Word fluency also drops and can signal early dementia related change.

Their study gave mild direct current stimulation over a left frontal language area, paired with word fluency training. Ultrasound Doppler measured blood flow shifts that show language lateralization during tasks. Groups held younger healthy elders, older healthy elders, and patients with mild cognitive impairment. The test asks whether stimulation can soften age related language change, a low cost idea worth careful proof.
pmc-10903306:
Hande Bakirhan and Serap Irgat link diet patterns to heart risk in a 2023 study from Turkey. What people eat shapes cardiovascular health over years. Three lenses are used at once: a heart-healthy diet score, Mediterranean diet adherence, and the phytochemical richness of meals. Over fourteen hundred healthy volunteers took part.

Two standard risk engines scored each person ten-year and lifetime risk. Worse heart-diet scores tracked higher risk on both engines. Mediterranean traits tracked lower risk in score categories. Plant chemical content is weighed in the same frame. The study supports diet quality screening as a cheap first step in heart prevention for adults.
pmc-10909106:
Siwaporn Thanasan and co-authors present a 2023 journal article testing whether a cheap stain test alone can certify HER2-positive breast cancer. Full guidelines pair the stain test with a gene probe test, but the stain is cheaper and easier where budgets are thin. The Bangkok team ran both on 510 tumors, then judged the stain against gene amplification for borderline and strong-positive cases.

Agreement proved strong: sensitivity near eighty-eight percent, specificity near ninety-four, and accuracy near ninety percent. Strong-positive stains almost always meant true amplification. The authors suggest a firm 3+ stain could stand alone to start anti-HER2 treatment without waiting for the gene test.
pmc-11037506:
Ashish Subedi and co-authors published this summary article in 2023 on the British Thoracic Society's updated guidance for pleural disease. The pleura is the lining around the lungs, and its diseases include fluid build-up, infection, and collapsed lung. The society's 2023 guideline replaced a 2010 version and covers how to investigate and manage these conditions, backed by a companion statement on procedures.

The article walks through the main changes. For a collapsed lung, care now follows symptoms: quiet cases can be watched or managed outside hospital, while risky cases still need drainage. It explains needle aspiration versus chest drains, and notes that graded talc remains the agent of choice for sealing the pleural space. Procedure details cover chest tubes, long-term catheters, biopsy, and thoracoscopy, along with handling complications. Mesothelioma and rare pleural diseases sit outside this guideline's scope.
pmc-11198306: Lorna Swan and co-authors issue a society statement on sexual health for adults living with congenital heart disease, published in 2023. As survival improves, care for this group has shifted toward quality of life and well-being, yet sexual health remains a neglected corner. A healthy sexual life carries physical and emotional benefits, but heart conditions, surgeries, and anxieties can all interfere. The statement, from an international adult congenital heart society, catalogs the barriers patients face. It also maps the advice, allyship, and advocacy that clinics should offer in response.
pmc-11525906:
Deb Nag and five co-authors update the account of what causes obstructive sleep apnea, in a 2024 review. Apnea, where breathing repeatedly stalls in sleep, is tied to obesity and lifestyle and carries wide effects across body systems. Anatomy, function, and habits have long been studied as causes. The review focuses on newer evidence that inflammation and immune mechanisms help drive the disease itself, not just suffer from it.

Understanding causes precisely is the path to prevention rather than lifelong machines. The authors gather the validating studies for immune pathways and discuss what they open up: targeted drugs and preventive steps for people at risk. The piece serves clinicians who manage apnea and researchers hunting its roots.
pmc-11531906:
Rumana Hossain and Veena Sahajwalla review new ways to pull valuable metals out of electronic waste, in a 2024 paper. Demand for electronics keeps rising, and so does the pile of discarded devices. Those devices hold precious metals and rare earth elements. Much of the waste still goes to landfill or burning, which wastes resources and leaks toxins.

The review surveys both standard and emerging recovery methods. Several can reclaim metal alloys and rare elements with good efficiency. Turning waste into a feedstock could feed factory supply chains and cut the need for fresh mining. The authors stress the gains for both the economy and the environment. They frame e-waste recycling as a core part of a circular economy for metals, where materials loop back into use instead of ending as trash.
pmc-11532506:
Guoou Xie, Tiezheng Qi, Yiyan Yao, Dongcai Feng, and Weimin Zhou report a 2024 study on a gene that may sort bladder cancer patients by likely course and best care. Bladder cancer is the tenth most common cancer round the world, and its mixed nature blunts current tests and drugs. The tissue around a tumour shapes its growth, so genes that track that setting could guide care.

The team focused on one such gene and first read its immune profile across cancers. In bladder cancer alone, high gene levels linked to a friendly set of traits: better outlook, a calmer subtype, and low immune cell entry. Low levels linked to poor outlook, a harsher subtype, and high immune entry, but also to more gain from radiation and immune drugs. The gene may help split patients for the right treatment.
pmc-11533406:
Zhao Bi and co-authors ask how long breast cancer surgery should wait after a COVID-19 infection in a 2024 study. Operating too soon after infection may raise complication risk, but delays carry their own costs in cancer care. The team compared patients operated on during a wave in China with a pre-pandemic control group.

Infected patients had about double the complication rate of controls. Timing mattered: surgery within two weeks of infection carried the highest complication rate, near a fifth of patients. Waiting at least two weeks brought the rate down near the control range. All complications resolved during ten months of follow-up without deaths or delays to further cancer treatment. The authors advise caution inside the two-week window.
pmc-11533606:
Ling-Chu Chang and co-authors review a form of cell death called paraptosis in 2024, and ask whether doctors could use it against cancer. Paraptosis differs from the better known cell death paths. Cells that die this way fill with fluid pockets, their inner parts swell, and the process does not rely on the enzymes that drive the usual death path.

The review gathers recent work on what triggers paraptosis and on the signal paths inside the cell that carry it out. Many natural products, lab-made compounds, and new tiny drug carriers can start this death program in cancer cells. The authors argue that aiming drugs at paraptosis could give a fresh option for tumors, since it works through a route that differs from standard treatments.
pmc-11538206:
Haque and co-authors train an AI model to outline rare hormone tumors on whole-body scans, in a research paper from 2024. The tumors, pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas, can spread and grow hard to count by hand. A tracer-based PET and CT scan is the standard way to picture them.

The team trained a 3D nnUNet model on scans from patients with spread, inoperable disease. On held-out scans, the model matched expert outlines well for the main tumor group. It also worked, less strongly, on two other tumor cohorts used as extra tests. Small, faint lesions were the ones most often missed, and the liver caused most false calls due to its high background signal. The authors say the tool could speed tumor burden checks during care.
pmc-11539606:
Emelia Danquah and Nestor Asiamah present a 2024 study on sitting at work in Accra, Ghana. Long sitting is a known health risk, and many jobs keep staff seated for hours. The authors asked 1,000 workers in public and private firms about their sitting time. They split sitting into parts, such as lunch, desk work, and meetings.

Workers in service firms sat longer at lunch than staff in factories did. The key find was a link with how much support workers felt their firm gave for health. Staff who felt more support sat less in total and in most parts of the day. Desk sitting was the one part with no clear link. The authors back firm health support.
pmc-11545106:
A gene test for skin melanoma claims to sort patients by risk more finely than stage alone, and Ryan Durgham and co-authors pooled its track record in work from twenty twenty-four. Their review drew thirteen studies with near fifteen thousand patients. Survival was split by the test's risk classes.

Five-year survival tied to the cancer ran near full in the lowest class, high in the middle band, and markedly lower in the top class. Freedom from return and from spread split the same way. The pooled proof backs the test as a risk tool, the authors conclude. They still urge care: the spread of study results stays wide at the top class.
pmc-11545606:
Jan Patrick Chu and Jagjit Singh Gilhotra present a rare case of herpes eye disease in both eyes. Their 2024 case report concerns a woman aged 42 from Kenya with two years of painful red eyes and blurred sight. Her immune system was sound, and the attacks began after childbirth.

Tests found herpes simplex signs in her blood, while other causes were ruled out. Eye scans showed swelling at the back of both eyes. Steroid shots and drops, plus an antiviral drug, calmed the flare. Her sight improved to near normal and the swelling cleared. The authors note that the low immunity of pregnancy may have let the virus take both eyes.
pmc-11546606:
Ioannis Liampas and co-authors review blood markers for frontotemporal dementia. Their 2024 review sorts which tests help and which do not. This dementia attacks behavior and language, and can mimic mental illness. Blood tests would be cheaper and kinder than scans or spinal taps.

One marker, neurofilament light chain, stands out. It helps separate the disease from psychiatric look-alikes and tracks decline. Its heavy-chain cousin may flag the turn into full dementia. A marker called progranulin can spot carriers of one gene fault. Total tau disappoints, though its altered form may help against Alzheimer's confusion. A protein named TDP-43 looks promising for diagnosis. The review maps a fast-moving test menu.
pmc-11548506:
Meng Li and co-authors forecast how climate change will move the homelands of two magnolia subspecies in East Asia. The tree, Magnolia sieboldii, is a prized ornamental whose wild stands are already struggling. Using a habitat model fed with sightings and climate data, the team mapped where each subspecies can live now and under future climate paths.

Warm-season rain shaped both ranges most, but the two parted ways on other factors: one answers mainly to temperature swings and yearly warmth, the other to altitude and dry-season warmth. The first subspecies, now spread wide across northeast China, Korea, and Japan, should push north and grow. The second, scattered in Japan and southern Chinese mountains, should shrink southward. The authors urge priority protection for the shrinking one, mixing wild protection, cultivation, and cross-breeding.
pmc-11563306:
Md Chowdhury and co-authors image lung airflow with a boosted propane gas on a standard scanner, in work from 2024. Lung ventilation scans usually need special gases and scanners tuned to rare nuclei. A proton-based gas could run on the scanners hospitals already own.

The team polarized propane gas with parahydrogen to boost its signal hugely. The signal strength rivals that of water in tissue, despite lasting only seconds. That window proved long enough for a breath and a scan. A low-field clinical scanner imaged an excised rabbit lung in two seconds. The demo opens a path to cheap, fast lung airflow scans in regular hospitals.
pmc-11565706:
Moritz Krebs and Ferdi Schüth made nitrite and nitrate directly from liquid ammonia with electrochemical craft, in a study published in 2024. The two salts feed farms and chemical plants, and a small local production could cut truck and plant load. Earlier electrochemical methods worked in water with weak ammonia. Theirs works in the pure liquid, a first.

Oxygen, activated at the negative pole, does the oxidation. The pair of salts came out with a joint charge yield past forty in a hundred. That rate makes the route worth a scale-up look. The authors frame it as green power put to work: when wind and sun spill surplus, store it as salt. Cold liquid handling is the price of the craft.
pmc-11568606:
Yimin Xue and co-authors profile gut microbes and their chemistry in mice with acute viral heart inflammation. Their 2024 study infects mice with coxsackievirus B3, which enters through the gut and can inflame the heart muscle. The gut-heart link is suspected in this disease, but the microbial side was little mapped.

Infected mice lost gut microbe richness and variety, with clear shifts in major bacterial groups. Nearly two hundred chemical products in the colon changed, most of them lipids. Several fatty acids stood out in the lipid pathway and tracked tightly with specific gut genera. The authors argue these shifts may help drive the heart disease and deserve deeper study.
pmc-11570406:
Shenghao Xue and co-authors review how cells eat their own worn parts, and what that means for skin disease, in a 2024 paper. The process, autophagy, keeps cells in balance. It comes in three forms that clear waste by different routes.

When the process slips, skin diseases can worsen. The review covers six of them: psoriasis, lupus of the skin and body, vitiligo, eczema of the atopic type, patchy hair loss, and systemic sclerosis. For each, the authors sort what is known about the three waste routes. They map where the process is overactive or stalled. The aim is to guide new studies and, in time, drugs that tune the process for skin patients.
pmc-11571206:
Grace Freeman-Gallant and co-authors study how sunlight driven chemistry ages a fatty acid found on air particles, in work from 2024. Organic particles in the lower atmosphere can hold light absorbing compounds. Those compounds trigger oxidation at the particle surface, yet that surface aging is poorly understood.

The team used weight and vibration measures on thin films of nonanoic acid, a model fatty acid. Four light sensitizers were compared, from a marine organic mix to simple molecular stand ins. The work tracks how each sensitizer drives photooxidation of the film. Results help explain how aerosol surfaces change in sunlight, which affects air quality and climate.
pmc-11574006:
Jessica Z Zhao, Jing Xia, and Clifford P Brangwynne watch cell core drops bend as cells squeeze through gaps in a 2024 study of cell moves. Spread cells must warp their cores to pass tight gaps in flesh on the way. How that warp hits the rich drops in the core was dim till now in the field.

Cells on the move squash their web, and the drops in it bend and merge, they find in the runs. Front and back halves of the core act in split ways in the squeeze at hand. Back-half slack lets fresh drops form in that zone of the core.
pmc-11575006:
A liver cancer protein called DDX20 helps tumor cells move, unless DAPK restrains it. Yan Ye and co-authors trace how DAPK protects DDX20 from destruction. The cell tags DDX20 for the proteasome with ubiquitin. The tagger is an enzyme named TRIM25, which binds the protein's first 244 building blocks. DAPK interacts with that same segment. By sitting there, DAPK blocks the tagging and steadies DDX20 levels.

The three proteins form a joint complex in cells. Removing TRIM25 weakens the DAPK-DDX20 pair, so TRIM25 also acts as a bridge. Silencing TRIM25 slowed liver cancer cell migration and invasion. The authors cast TRIM25 as the cancer-promoting partner in the trio.
pmc-11576606:
Shim and co-authors set out a protocol, published in 2024, for a study hunting inflammation signals that can be measured without needles. Long-lasting body-wide inflammation drives many chronic diseases. Tracking it today means blood draws, which burden patients and clinics. The team proposes combining several noninvasive sources: signals from skin, breath, saliva, and wearables. Their cross-sectional study will compare each against blood markers, the gold standard.

If some combination tracks blood levels well, daily home monitoring becomes plausible. That could catch flares early and cut clinic visits. The protocol details who will be recruited and how the streams will be fused. It is published ahead of results so the plan is on record. The study's name, NOVA, signals the intended novelty of the approach.
pmc-11577906:
Shahrul and five co-authors surveyed young adults in Malaysia in twenty twenty-four about braces fitted by non-dentists. Cheap, easily reached treatment from unlicensed providers is growing and can harm patients. The team asked what young people know and think about this practice.

An online survey drew four hundred twenty-six replies, with an average age near twenty-three. About seventy-six percent knew non-dentists fit braces, mostly learning of it through social media. Low cost was the top reason for choosing them, followed by no waiting list. Most respondents knew the practice is illegal and can cause harm. Legal enforcement was the favored fix. Job type, more than gender or schooling, shaped legal awareness in the results.
pmc-11578206:
Whisper Grayson and four co-authors measure the price of converting a failed hip repair into a replacement too soon. Their 2024 study follows ninety-one patients whose broken hip or socket had first been fixed with hardware, then later converted to a total hip replacement. Such conversions already carry more risk than first-time replacements, and the team asked whether timing matters: early means within six months of the first surgery.

Twenty-two patients converted early, and their complication rate ran about double the late group's, though the gap did not reach statistical significance. Deep infection, further surgery, and replacement of the new joint all clustered in the early group. One difference was firm: early patients needed blood transfusions far more often. The authors counsel that patients be warned plainly about the high risks of early conversion, so the timing choice is made with open eyes.
pmc-11579906:
Yasunori Yokochi and co-authors reported a rare neck vessel case in 2024. A woman had a congenital abnormal link between the carotid artery and jugular vein in her neck, found ten years earlier as a pulsing lump and left alone. Such links rarely cause pain.

Over the decade the outflow veins swelled and twisted. Turning her head then squeezed the jugular vein, pushing blood back toward the brain and causing severe headache and neck pain. Imaging confirmed the mechanism. Blocking the shunt with coils and glue ended the pulsing, headache, and pain at once. The authors warn that quiet congenital shunts can worsen slowly and deserve follow-up.
pmc-11580006:
Ipek Cicekli and Raika Durusoy wrote a 2024 paper on whether parents who smoke raise a child's risk of type 1 diabetes. In this disease the immune system destroys the cells that make insulin, usually in childhood. Genes explain part of the risk, but smoke in the home has been raised as a possible trigger.

The team compared two hundred forty-eight children aged four to fourteen. One group had the disease and the other was healthy, and parents answered a survey face to face about smoking at home and during pregnancy. Mothers' smoking in pregnancy did not differ between groups. Parents of children with the disease did smoke more cigarettes per day at home. Studies of this kind cannot prove cause, but they mark where deeper work should look.
pmc-11580306:
Eyaya Habtie Dagnaw and colleagues measured late abortion care in Ethiopia in 2024. Five hospitals in the South Gondar district took part. Women of reproductive age seeking induced abortion were interviewed. Just under four hundred women joined through systematic sampling. Late presentation meant arriving after the early safe window. Interviews at the clinic captured personal and pregnancy factors. Models tested which factors tracked with late arrival.

About one woman in five presented late. Living in a rural area raised the odds. Irregular menstrual cycles raised them far more strongly. Slow decisions about ending the pregnancy raised them most. Pregnancies from incest also linked to late arrival. Past contraceptive use lowered the odds of lateness. The authors urge awareness drives in rural communities. Teaching should cover late-care risks and complications. Faster decisions could cut illness and death, they argue.
pmc-11584506:
Helia Azkia and co-authors report ten years of a home-grown tissue bank in a 2024 orthopedics paper. Ligament, meniscus, and cartilage grafts usually come from commercial banks at high prices; their hospital instead attached a small non-commercial bank to its organ donor program in 2014.

Thirty-one donations yielded over eleven hundred grafts, stored deep-frozen after disease and bacteria screening, with only a small fraction discarded for positive cultures. More than five hundred recipients have been treated, with no transplant-related complications recorded. The local grafts cost a tenth to a seventh of commercial prices. The authors present the model as reproducible for other centers.
pmc-11584706:
Ludovico Lami and Bartosz Regula solve exactly how much entanglement can be distilled under a broad family of forbidden operations. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-four. The distillation rate for noisy quantum states is among quantum information's oldest open questions.

Their operation class, dually non-entangling channels, preserves both separable states and separable measurements. Under it, the distillable entanglement equals a tweaked version of the regularised relative entropy, measured separably. Only one such exact formula existed before, for a narrower class. A bonus falls out: under these rules, every entangled state yields some distillable entanglement. Their upper bound also settles a question posed by Li and Winter about entropy variants. Dilution costs match the wider theory, proving a strong irreversibility.
pmc-11585106:
Huilin Tang and co-authors compare drug mixes for a weak heart that pumps too little blood, in a 2024 study. They pool results from forty-nine trials with more than ninety thousand patients. Their method lets each mix be ranked against the others, even when trials did not test every pair head to head.

One four-drug mix stood out for cutting deaths from any cause and for cutting hospital stays for heart failure. That mix joins a drug that opens blood vessels with a heart-rate drug, a hormone-blocking drug, and a newer sugar-lowering drug. A like mix with a fifth kind of drug ranked best for deaths from heart causes. The authors say newer drugs add real gains on top of standard care, and they give doctors a ranked guide for choosing a mix.
pmc-11585206:
Yi-Feng Ren and co-authors read single cells from hazy lung growths to trace how their immune setting shifts as cancer spreads, in a 2024 study. Such growths, seen on scans as ground-glass spots, can stay quiet or turn invasive, and scans alone cannot tell which path they will take. The team sampled tumors at several stages and types.

Two kinds of immune cleaner cells changed most across stages. One kind teamed with killer T cells in early, hazy tumors and seemed to hold the line. The other kind grew dominant in solid, spreading tumors and helped them advance. The contrast may point to stage-specific ways to aid the immune fight.
pmc-11585606:
Ruiying Shao and co-authors solve wave equations for ferroelectric thin films in a 2024 study. Such films carry solitary polarization waves and serve modern electronics. Their governing equation is nonlinear and hard to solve exactly. Three fresh methods are brought to bear.

A Paul-Painlevé approach is applied to this equation for the first time. Expansion techniques then extract the wave dynamics in closed forms. Bright and periodic solutions emerge from a variational scheme as well. Graphs display each solution family. Cross-checks between methods vouch for the results. Engineers modeling film devices gain dependable formulas for how polarization waves travel and hold shape.
pmc-11586106:
Bats carry many viruses without falling sick, a talent no other land mammal matches. Rui Li, Wenliang Zhao, Apeng Chen, Zhiqiang Wu, and Gejing De explore that talent in a 2024 study that pairs evolution analysis with a map of the research field. They ask which immune traits set bats apart, and what past virus contacts left behind.

The team hunted fossil viruses in the genomes of nine bat species and seven other mammals, finding heavy deposits from three retrovirus groups in bats. Across 28 mammal genomes, bat gene families had grown in telling places: one interferon type, a heat-shock protein, and a receptor family tied to inflammation. Other families shrank. The literature scan then charted which bat immunity topics draw the most current work.
pmc-11586406:
Thottempudi Pardhu and co-authors classify human motion through walls using radar and a new deep network tuned by a wolf-inspired optimizer. Motion checks matter for health care and security work. Cameras raise privacy worries that radar avoids.

Ultra-wideband radar pulses pass through walls to catch movement. The signals are gridded, then mined for key features. Their network fuses a Kronecker design with a classic LeNet. A fuzzy twist adjusts the network's inner layers. A spotted grey wolf algorithm tunes the settings. The system sorts motions without filming anyone directly. Through-wall sensing suits elder care and rescue work. Accuracy gains are reported against rival models in tests.
pmc-11587106:
Fumiko Yamamoto, Takeshi Yokoyama, Yan Su, and Masataka Suzuki test how sex differences arise in the silkworm in this 2024 study. Classic theory says insect sex is set inside each cell, with no sex hormones involved. Yet some traits seem shaped by outside signals, so the team checked which force dominates in one tissue.

They studied the fat body of mixed-sex silkworm larvae, where male and female cells sit side by side. Comparing gene activity between normal males and females found over two hundred sex-linked genes. A math model predicted each gene's activity from the mix of cells present. For most genes, the predictions matched the real readings closely. The result supports cell-by-cell control for this tissue.
pmc-11587606:
Huan-Yu Zhao and co-authors show, in a 2024 study, how one membrane protein wrecks the top bottom organization of breast lining cells, an early step toward cancer. Healthy epithelial cells are polarized: their top and bottom faces differ, and that order holds tissue architecture together. Losing polarity is a hallmark of early ductal tumors.

The protein, RHBDF1, sits in the cell's internal membranes. When overproduced, it drives a polarity kinase into the nucleus. Stranded there, the kinase cannot join the polarity complex it normally anchors at the cell's boundary, so the complex fails to form. Junction proteins that seal cells together also fade, and the cells grow more mobile. The mechanism is a theft: the polarity machinery is not destroyed, just deported to the wrong compartment. Blocking that deportation is a conceivable way to keep early lesions orderly and contained.
pmc-11587806:
Yixin Chen and co-authors review how organophosphate pesticides harm the nervous system in a 2024 paper. These compounds are used worldwide in farming and pest control. Exposure can cause nausea, tremors, and convulsions, and severe cases can end in breathing failure or death. The review sums up the toxic mechanisms and how they interlock.

The compounds block a key enzyme and also act through receptors and other targets beyond that enzyme. The authors outline links between poisoning and later disorders such as dementia, developmental conditions, and Parkinson's disease. They also explore treatment ideas that might soften the damage. Readers get a broad map of harm pathways and their ties to chronic brain disease.
pmc-11590206:
Julianna Coleman and eight co-authors grade TikTok videos about contraception as a source of health advice, in a research paper from 2024. Many people now learn about birth control from social media, not just from people they know. The team wanted to know if popular videos were clear and correct.

They scored one hundred seventy-four teaching videos with standard tools. Most videos were easy to understand and stayed on topic, but few told viewers what steps to take. Videos made by health workers scored higher on accuracy and trust than videos by others. Health workers' videos also drew most of the views, which the authors see as a reason to post more.
pmc-11590406:
Gaku Yamamichi and colleagues fish prostate cancer's secretions for a blood signal that bone spread has begun, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Bone metastasis is castration-resistant prostate cancer's fatal turn, and PSA watches it poorly. Screening the broth of four cancer cell lines found twenty-seven hundred proteins; the team pursued the GDF15 propeptide, a precursor fragment also secreted by bone cells.

The fragment proved an accomplice: it sped cancer cell growth, invasion, and migration, and in mice worsened bone metastasis. It also stoked both bone-building and bone-eating cells, remodelling the neighborhood tumors exploit. In four hundred sixteen patients it diagnosed bone spread far better than PSA, and its ups and downs tracked bone scan changes during treatment while PSA wandered. The authors propose it as an early-warning biomarker for intervention.
pmc-11590806:
Some babies are born with a gut that lacks nerve cells in its last stretch, so food can not pass and the bowel blocks. Alan Burns and Allan Goldstein review that ill, Hirschsprung disease, in 2024. They trace how the gut's own nerve net forms in the womb and where that growth can fail.

Nerve stem cells must breed, trek the full length of the gut, and mature into nerve and glue cells. A slip at any step leaves a stretch bare, and surgery must cut that stretch out. Yet many patients keep bowel woes for life, and fresh finds show the harm runs past the bare cells. The review hunts for roots of those wide harms and for fresh care paths.
pmc-11592206:
Flapping wings can lift tiny aircraft, but the motion is unsteady and hard to control. Zhang and co-authors design and build a tailless micro air vehicle with two pairs of wings in an X layout, each pair driven on its own. Independent drive lets the craft fly fast, turn sharply, or hover, and gives it extra strength against faults.

Simulations show a clap-and-peel wing action that boosts lift, and bench tests with a six-axis sensor map how wing settings change thrust and turning force. With tuned settings, the prototype took off and flew under control from the ground, a step toward practical insect-like flight.
pmc-11592306:
Christopher Berlin and co-authors compare, in 2024, long-term outcomes for bowel cancer that has spread to both liver and lungs. Surgery to remove both sets of spread tumors is debated, since proof of lasting benefit is thin. The team reviewed one hundred ninety-two patients treated at a large academic center.

One hundred patients had both tumor sets removed, while the rest had non-surgical care. Even after matching the groups for baseline differences, the surgery group lived much longer, with median survival more than double. The authors argue for an aggressive surgical approach in carefully chosen patients. Selection remains key, since not every patient can bear such surgery.
pmc-11592606:
Valentina La Rosa and co-authors review how soft touch shapes the growth of babies born too soon, in a paper from 2024. A kind of touch that soothes, run through fine skin fibers, bonds the baby to its carer and calms stress. Two hands on cares, skin to skin time and the kangaroo hold, put that touch to work in wards for frail newborns.

Both cares steady heart rate, breath, and body heat in the reviewed work. They also lift mood rule and thought growth as the child ages. The team urges wards to fold soft touch into daily care as a norm. Open asks stay: how touch marks genes, and how to tune each care to each child.
pmc-11594106:
Savelyev and co-authors build a soft material that can carry electric signals and suit use in tissue repair. Healing nerve or heart tissue needs scaffolds that pass the body's own signals. Their gel mixes bovine serum albumin, gelatin, a light-sensitive dye, and carbon nanotubes. A laser shaped the gel into fine structures through two-photon polymerization. The team reports a strong light response, with a cross section of 580 GM.

The mix was thick enough to hold shape across the full pattern area. Light bending inside the gel helped the shaping process along. Tests confirmed the finished structures conduct electricity. The authors see uses in neural interfaces and in scaffolds for tissues that rely on signals.
pmc-11594406:
Nikola Lenar and colleagues published a sensor study in 2024. They compared two conducting plastics used in chemical sensors. The sensors measure potassium and similar ions in solution. A thin transducer layer sits inside each electrode. Its material affects stability, lifetime, and signal quality. One plastic is known as POT. The other is a PEDOT blend. The team compared both materials directly.

First they checked structure, wetting, heat, and electrical traits. Then they built potassium sensors with each plastic. The POT layer repelled water very strongly. That trait pointed to a longer sensor lifetime. The PEDOT blend gave higher electrical capacitance instead. Higher capacitance steadied the sensor signal over time. Both materials performed well in tests. Designers can choose based on which strength matters most.
pmc-11597106:
Gerard Pérez-Pi and co-authors built a free-standing carbon nanofiber film studded with cobalt phosphide particles to make hydrogen in a microbe-assisted cell, in this 2024 study. The films come off a scalable spinning process plus a heat treatment. They are porous, with surface area up to about five hundred square meters per gram.

As catalysts for splitting hydrogen out of water, the films needed under 140 millivolts of extra push at working current. Wired directly as the cathode of a microbial electrolysis cell, the film ran at just 0.75 volts. Hydrogen came out at under thirty kilowatt-hours per kilogram, a strong efficiency mark. The authors pitch the film as a cheap, sturdy electrode.
pmc-11597406:
David Whiteside, Sofía Chambi-Trowell, and Michael Benton defend their claim that a small Triassic fossil is an early lizard kin. The fossil, Cryptovaranoides microlanius, came from latest Triassic rock in England. In 2022 the team named it a crown squamate, which pushed the group's age back by thirty-five million years. A 2023 paper instead cast it as an archosauromorph, kin to crocodiles and dinosaurs.

In this 2024 reply, the team rechecks the fossils in the rock and in CT scans. They list errors of sight and reading in the rival work and fix the trait scores. With those fixes, each tree test places the fossil with lizards, not with archosauromorphs. The early date for crown lizards stands.
pmc-11597606:
Joseph Blondeau and co-authors compare antibiotics against two swine lung bacteria in a 2024 study. One drug, a newer fluoroquinolone, was recently approved for swine respiratory disease. Hard lab data on its strength against field isolates remained scarce.

The team measured two thresholds for the new drug and seven rivals. The first threshold stops bacterial growth, and the second blocks resistant mutants. Farm isolates of both bacterial species went through the tests. The new drug posted the lowest values on nearly every measure. For one species, half the strains stopped at the smallest tested dose. Such lab rankings help veterinarians pick drugs that work now and resist failure later.
pmc-11598906:
Annika Bartel and co-authors tested a stain for a mutated cancer protein in dog carcinomas in two thousand twenty-four. Changes in the BRAF gene are part of cancer profiling in both humans and dogs. The team asked if two commercial antibodies could reliably detect the dog form of the mutation in tissue samples.

They tested two hundred twenty-seven tumors from eleven body sites and confirmed results with a sensitive DNA test. Mutated cases appeared in prostate, bladder, and mouth cancers, while other types tested negative. Both antibodies gave consistent cell staining and matched the DNA results. The authors say biopsy staining could help guide targeted drug treatment for those three cancer types in dogs.
pmc-11599506:
Zhuo Zhang, Hetian Du, Weijie Gao, and Donghui Zhang review engineered immune cells for heart repair in a 2024 article. Macrophages are immune cells that rush to heart injury, clear dead cells, and guide repair. Their behavior shifts over time, from driving inflammation early to calming it later.

The review covers the roles of both resident and recruited macrophages in heart disease. It then turns to engineering: cells can be tuned or loaded to home to injured heart tissue, cut inflammation, limit scarring, and support regrowth. Recent studies of such engineered cells are summed up. The authors see them as a promising living therapy, though much testing remains before routine use.
pmc-11599706:
Biao Yin, Liping Mo, Wei Min, Shan Li, and Cunwei Yu published an algorithms study in twenty twenty-four improving the beetle antennae search method and applying it to wireless sensor coverage. The original algorithm, modeled on how beetles sniff toward food, converges imprecisely and gets stuck in local optima. Three fixes were combined into a new version.

A dynamic step size sharpened accuracy, a golden sine update diversified the search, and a criss-cross disturbance helped escape traps. On twelve benchmark functions the new method beat the original and several rivals. Applied to networks of thirty and fifty sensor nodes, it achieved better coverage than seven competing algorithms.
pmc-11599906:
Jakub Smoleń and co-authors develop, in 2024, a light building material that turns waste into part of green design. They made porous ceramic granules from waste and used them as filler in an epoxy-based concrete. Two granule sizes were tested, and soaking them in resin first proved useful, since resin in the pores grips better.

Concrete made with only the finer granules was strongest, reaching high values in both crushing and bending tests. The material let heat pass about half as fast as standard concrete and absorbed very little water, which suggests good frost resistance.
