The authors present it as a candidate for sustainable building parts.
pmc-11600906:
Šimun Naletilić and Ema Gagović lead a team dissecting wild carnivores across Croatia for heartworm, a mosquito-borne parasite of dogs that also threatens people. Their study appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Golden jackals are expanding across Europe, raising reservoir questions. Foxes and badgers share the same landscapes.

Hearts from hundreds of animals collected in rabies surveillance were examined. A small share of jackals carried the worms, confirmed by shape and gene tests. Loads ran from a couple of worms to several per animal. No fox and no badger carried the parasite. Infected jackals were all adults, some hosting a breeding pair. The authors identify jackals as a wildlife reservoir worth watching. Dog protection in jackal country gains an argument. Continued surveillance can track whether prevalence climbs.
pmc-11601206:
Liu and eleven co-authors shape a jellyfish bot whose body is its own fuel tank in this twenty twenty-four study. Sea bots most haul a stiff pack that just feeds their gear and brains. A soft tank could spread that weight and shrink the bot's drag in the sea.

Inside, two flow-cell builds were cast in the soft bell shape of a jellyfish. Each build runs on zinc pairs, one built to charge back and one mixed type. The bot swam on flow cells alone, with most of its weight as fuel broth. Charge per bulk and per face both beat stiff pack norms by wide shares. Swim time on one fill ran past an hour in the team's tests.
pmc-11602806:
Vikram Patil and Prakashan Chellattan Veettil studied rice farmers in eastern India in 2024, asking how a farmer's attitude to risk shapes the choice of new farm methods. Farming is risky, and new practices can help farmers cope. The team used survey data to test which farmers took up which tools and what that did for their harvests.

Farmers who liked risk were more likely to take up machines. Farmers who avoided risk leaned toward rice types that cope with stress, which cost little to adopt. Both choices raised yields. The authors urge support such as shared machine hire and better seed supply so more farmers can gain.
pmc-11603806:
Wenqiang Yan and a large team report a rare and fatal case that followed CAR-T cell therapy, in this 2024 case report. The treatment uses a patient's own immune cells, retrained to attack myeloma, a cancer of the blood. It has helped many people whose cancer came back, but it can also trigger severe side effects.

In this case, the treated cells grew in two waves instead of one. The first wave, on day seven, brought a strong fever syndrome. The second, on day 28, brought low blood counts, a severe immune overreaction, and infections with several germs at once. Stem cell infusions helped the blood counts a little, but a virus spread to the brain and the patient died. Detailed immune tests across both waves show how the cell mix changed, and the case warns teams to watch for late second waves.
pmc-11603906:
Jinkyeong Lee and five colleagues compare the genes of Vibrio vulnificus bacteria from patients and from nature in South Korea. People catch this germ from raw seafood or seawater. It can cause blood poisoning and wound infections. The team studied fifteen strains from patients and eleven from the environment.

They found twenty sequence types, and eight were new. Both groups often carried a gene linked to drug resistance. Worryingly, both groups also failed to respond to third-generation cephalosporins, drugs used to treat the infection. Patient strains resisted more drugs overall. Yet counts of harm-causing genes, and traits like sticking to cells and swimming, were much the same in both groups. The authors say strains from nature are just as risky, and drug resistance checks must go on.
pmc-11604706:
Noura El-Naggar, Ragaa Hamouda, and Naglaa Elshafey use artificial intelligence to boost production of a cancer drug enzyme in a 2024 study. The enzyme, L-asparaginase, is a cornerstone of treatment for childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The catch is that many bacterial versions also carry a sister activity that causes side effects. A soil microbe they isolated makes the enzyme without that sister activity.

The microbe, a Streptomyces strain, grows on solid beds of mixed soybean and wheat bran. The team varied four inputs, the bran mix, sugar, the enzyme's raw material, and a nitrogen salt, under a designed experiment plan. A neural network then learned the response surface, predicted the best mix, and was checked against real runs. Smarter tuning of a cheap fermentation could widen the supply of a front-line drug.
pmc-11605006:
Irepan Salvador-Martinez and co-authors read evolution in human immune cells where they live, cell type by cell type, in a 2024 study. Immune genes adapt under pathogen pressure, but most studies ignore which cells express them. Human Cell Atlas data let the team rate adaptation across the immune landscape at cellular resolution.

Barrier tissues and developing progenitors carried the strongest adaptation signals. Lung T and killer cells facing the air showed confirmed tuning. Lab-grown macrophages revealed adaptation in the earliest response genes. The pattern favors stopping invaders at the gates, the authors say, and it maps the bodys old battlegrounds.
pmc-11606106:
Yitagesu Eshetu and Tigist Getachew mapped where mothers die in Ethiopia and what factors raise that risk, in work published in 2024. Data came from a national health survey from 2016, covering more than ten thousand women. Their model joins standard risk factors with smooth map effects.

Place of delivery, number of prenatal visits, marital status, wealth, mother age, and birth order each shaped the risk. Four regions showed higher rates of maternal death than the rest. The special model fit the data better than simpler ones. The authors say maternal death in Ethiopia is shaped by social, personal, and geographic factors together.
pmc-11607306:
Rukhsar Sabir and Tahir Mehmood race three neural networks at spotting melanoma in skin images in a 2024 paper. Melanoma is the deadliest skin cancer, and early catches save lives. The team trained a plain convolutional network, a ResNet-18, and an EfficientNet-B0 on the same image set. Their pipeline normalized and augmented images, then segmented, extracted features, and classified.

EfficientNet-B0 won clearly, at ninety-seven percent accuracy. The runner-up reached eighty-seven, and the basic model eighty. The winner also led on sensitivity, specificity, and the other reported scores, with a three percent error rate. The authors say the result shows compact modern networks can classify skin lesions with near-expert polish in this setup. They present the comparison as guidance for groups building screening tools, while the task's stakes demand care.
pmc-11607806:
Jasper Zhao Zhen Wu, Olga Zayts-Spence, and Zoë Fortune published this conceptual paper in 2024 on mental health stigma at work. Research on how stigma operates through language in organizations is thin, and models are lacking. Building on classic ideas about stigma as a language of relationships, the authors propose a model of how workplaces produce and reinforce it. The model draws on in-depth interviews with 23 professional services employees in Hong Kong.

In their model, the workplace is a discursive space where stigma moves across three layers: face-to-face encounters, organizational practices, and wider social beliefs. Everyday talk, including how employees manage what others know about them, carries stigma between those layers. The authors say the model shows how stigma can quietly govern relationships and even career prospects. They offer it as a tool for analyzing stigma in other organizations.
pmc-11607906:
Yuhan Yan and eleven co-authors test a drug pairing for a blood cancer that has come back, in a research paper from 2024. The cancer is multiple myeloma. One part of the treatment trains a patient's own T cells to attack the cancer. Those cells work well at first, but the disease often returns within months.

Patients who then took a daily drug called pomalidomide stayed in remission longer than those who did not. Every patient responded to the cell therapy, and most who took the drug reached a deep response. Side effects stayed manageable over a long follow-up. Lab tests show the drug helps the trained cells kill cancer and survive longer.
pmc-11608306:
Priscilla Gomes da Silva and co-authors sample outdoor air in a Spanish city for traces of the COVID virus, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Most air studies had focused indoors, leaving open-air spread unclear. Air was drawn at nine spots in Valladolid's center during winter two thousand twenty-one, in both crowded and empty settings.

Six of twenty samples tested positive for viral RNA. Every positive came from a crowded spot, none from empty ones. Amounts were small next to indoor finds. The authors tie presence to crowd size and relaxed safety habits. Outdoor air can carry the virus, they conclude, mainly where people pack in.
pmc-11609306:
Yanni Lin and co-authors show how a chemical tag controls a cancer-promoting protein in a 2024 cell biology study. The protein SIX1 helps switch cancer cells to aerobic glycolysis, the sugar-burning style tumors favor, but how growth signals steer it was unclear.

Growth factors trigger a kinase that tags SIX1 at one serine spot, and that tag both activates its glycolysis program and shields it from destruction. A second enzyme removes the tag. Oddly, a lysine substitution mimicked the tag's effects while the usual look-alike substitutions did not. In human liver tumors the tag ran high and tracked with worse behavior.
pmc-11611106:
Mega Hasanul Huda and a large team combine past trials to judge whether technology helps tuberculosis patients finish treatment, in a 2024 paper. TB care takes months of daily medicine, and many patients stop early, which breeds drug resistance. Phone reminders, video checks, and other digital tools have been proposed to keep patients on track. The team searched six databases for randomized trials published from 2018 to early 2023.

Two reviewers checked each trial's quality with a standard bias tool. Results were pooled with a random-effects model, and the team also checked for publication bias. The analysis weighs adherence, treatment completion, and overall success together. Its findings can help health programs choose which digital support is worth paying for.
pmc-11611206:
Heather Deel and co-authors build a DNA-based score for soil health, in a study from 2024. Good soil rests on a rich crowd of microbes, but most farm tests skip gene facts and lean on bulk traits. The team asked if microbe gene roles could call how a soil is farmed.

They took 536 soil samples from 26 states, across 52 crops and grass lands. Gene reads plus a guess tool gave each soil a profile of microbe jobs. A learning model then picked the enzymes that best tracked soil health marks. That set forms the new score, called MISH. The score tracked plain health marks and farm habits well. The DNA test is cheap and works across climates, which could put gene facts in the hands of more farms.
pmc-11611706:
Tianxiao Feng and co-authors pool trials of a neck manipulation for pinched nerves in a 2024 review. Cervical radiculopathy sends pain and weakness down the arm from a squeezed neck root. Rotation-traction manipulation is a signature hands-on method in Chinese orthopedics for this pain.

Eight databases were searched for randomized trials of the method. Pain scales led the outcomes, joined by disability, function, neck motion, and curve measures. Harm reports were gathered as a safety check on the technique. Pooling many small trials can firm up a verdict on benefit. Patients choosing hands-on care deserve that firmer ground.
pmc-11611906:
Ara Monadjem and co-authors published this data paper in 2024, the African bat database. Where each species lives is the bedrock of conservation, yet bat ranges are poorly mapped, above all in Africa. Museum specimens sit mostly overseas, and new species keep splitting from old ones. The team gathered 17,285 checked locality records for all 266 bat species of sub-Saharan Africa.

Each record is backed by a specimen or gene proof and matched to current names. From the points they built range models and computed the standard area measures used on the Red List of threatened species. An online viewer makes the data open to all. The authors offer the set as a base for ecology and for guarding bats, a group that pollinates, hunts pests, and seeds forests.
pmc-11612106:
Debora Stefanova and co-authors found that a class of cancer drugs can block many kinds of viruses, for an unexpected reason. The drugs were made to block a growth signal receptor on cells. Their 2024 study tested them on cells infected with both DNA and RNA viruses.

The drugs stopped infection early, after viruses reached the cell but before they got going. Surprisingly, the effect did not come from the named target. Gene and drug tests pointed instead to a family of cell enzymes, above all one called Lyn. Blocking that enzyme did most of the work. The finding names a fresh target for broad virus drugs, the team say.
pmc-11612206:
Yuanchao Luo and co-authors present a 2024 study on whether high blood sugar on arrival predicts pneumonia after hip fracture surgery. Hip fractures strike older adults, and pneumonia is a feared complication of the repair operation. The team mined records for 1,267 older patients admitted with hip fractures.

Patients were split by admission glucose into normal and high groups. Matching methods paired similar patients across the groups to strip out other differences. The analysis then estimated the pneumonia odds tied to high sugar alone. It also traced how risk climbs as glucose rises, dose by dose. Separate checks compared patients with and without diabetes. The work aims to flag a cheap, early warning sign that wards can act on.
pmc-11612506:
Rencheng Li and co-authors ask what fire does to the carbon locked inside plant silica. Phytoliths, microscopic glass bodies formed in plant tissues, carry carbon into soils where it can rest for ages. Fire is known to alter their nutrient and metal loads, but its effect on their carbon had been skipped.

The team compared phytoliths from six grasses and their ashes, plus soil phytoliths along a pine forest gradient from unburned to burned. Burned material shifted: carbon content and dissolving behavior varied by species in the grasses. In forest topsoil, phytoliths from burned ground held more carbon and dissolved less, favoring preservation. Fire, the authors conclude, rewrites this quiet carbon store.
pmc-11613406:
Vladimir Resanovic, Aleksandar Resanovic, and Zlatibor Loncar published a case report in 2024 on a rare hernia that traps bowel in elderly patients. An obturator hernia pushes tissue through a small canal in the pelvis. It strikes mainly frail older women, hides from routine examination, and kills when diagnosis comes late.

Their patient was an eighty-three-year-old woman with cramping pain, vomiting, and constipation in the right lower belly. A CT scan revealed the trapped hernia, and emergency surgery confirmed a loop of small bowel caught in the canal. Because of her asthma the surgeons chose an open operation. The authors weigh open against keyhole repair and argue the choice should fit each patient, with early scanning and fast surgery as the constants.
pmc-11613906:
Jiaqi Tan and co-authors map the CPP gene family in Moso bamboo, a plant famed for shooting up at record speed. CPP proteins steer plant growth from sprouting to maturity and help with stress. No one had charted them in this bamboo before.

The genome holds 17 family members, falling into three subfamilies with shared structures and motifs. Their kinship runs closer to rice than to the model plant Arabidopsis. Shape modeling confirmed the classic DNA-gripping domain. Gene activity varied by tissue and answered to two growth hormones. The map gives breeders and biologists targets for the bamboo's rapid-growth trick.
pmc-11614406:
Alida Naude, Lisa Brown, and Amisha Kanji show how teamwork spared a dizzy man an unneeded brain operation. The 56-year-old carried a small cavernous hemangioma, a tangled blood vessel knot, plus balance symptoms. The knot alone seemed to call for neurosurgery. Their 2024 case instead routes him through audiology, ear-nose-throat, and physiotherapy testing. Three vestibular tests form the core: head impulse, caloric, and evoked potential checks.

The tests blamed the inner ear, not the brain lesion. A right-side peripheral vestibular fault explained the symptoms. Care switched to a nonsurgical plan aimed at the ear. The team frames the case as a decision template: test the balance organs fully before cutting near them.
pmc-11614606:
Qi Xie and colleagues build a bone scaffold that also fights germs, in this materials study from twenty twenty-four. Bone defects need a filler that invites new bone and resists infection after surgery. Their scaffold starts from collagen, the protein of bone's frame, spiked with graphene oxide sheets loaded with curcumin, the active part of turmeric.

The mix was freeze-dried and cross-linked into a sponge. The team measured its pores, water handling, breakdown rate, and how slowly it let curcumin seep out. One recipe, with a low share of the loaded sheets, hit the sweet spot: friendly to cells and steady in release. In dish tests, cells stuck, lived, and multiplied better on it than on plainer scaffolds, bone-forming activity rose, and bacteria fared worse. The authors say the bone-friendly, germ-hostile mix is a sound base for smarter bone repair materials.
pmc-11615106:
Štefan Tóth and co-authors study gut lining change in germ-free piglets in a 2024 paper. The piglets start life with no gut germs at all, a clean base for tests. One group then had its gut seeded with a common gut germ on the fifth day of life.

The team tracked how fast lining cells renew and die in two gut spans. Seeded piglets grew lining cells faster in the small gut, a sign that span feels the germ most. Death marks and stress marks shifted in the deep layer of the gut wall as well. The work shows how a first germ wakes the gut lining.
pmc-11615206:
Guanting Duan and co-authors test play-based therapy for empathy in children with intellectual disabilities in a 2024 study. Empathy development lags in this population without support. Sports games offer a natural social practice ground. Cognitive-behavioral techniques were woven into the games.

Thirty-one children aged seven to eight joined the trial. They attended mainstream schools with their diagnoses. Random allocation formed experimental and control groups. Both groups kept regular physical activity throughout. The experimental group added eighteen weeks of the special program. A standard empathy questionnaire measured outcomes before and after. Groups started statistically identical on every score. The program group then gained notably on total and factor scores. Its post-test scores also beat the control group's clearly. The authors conclude the intervention works as designed. Inclusive classrooms gain an evidence-backed activity model.
pmc-11615306:
Ridhwan Lye and co-authors test whether a computer model can judge sex from skull scans better than a person. Forensic experts often judge sex by eye from bones, but eye judgments can carry bias. They can also lose accuracy when used on groups far from the ones they were built on. The team trained deep learning models on two hundred head scans of Indonesian people.

The best model learned sex and skull traits at the same time. It reached ninety-seven percent accuracy, well above the human judge at eighty-two percent. Maps of the model's focus showed it used both known skull traits and overall size and shape. The authors see such tools as aids that can cut bias in forensic work.
pmc-11616306:
Yu Xiong and co-authors survey a decade of growth in radiopharmaceuticals, drugs labeled with radioisotopes for imaging or therapy. Their 2024 letter focuses on radionuclide drug conjugates, precision drugs that carry a radioactive payload to a target. Two approved products showed the approach can work well in patients.

The authors counted trials of such conjugates over ten years using an industry database. A few hundred trials were found, yet barely half remain active, and most finished trials sit in early phases. The letter frames this as steady, incremental progress rather than a breakthrough wave. It argues the field's promise is real but young, with many candidates still proving safety and benefit. The survey gives clinicians and investors a grounded map of where the area stands.
pmc-11616506:
Fei Chen and co-authors review stubborn babesiosis in a 2024 paper. The tick-borne parasite disease has grown into a wider public health threat. Most cases clear, yet some linger or return with parasite counts too low for standard tests to catch.

Lingering cases occur with and without weak immune defenses, and they strain both diagnosis and drug care. The review maps where such cases arise, how labs now hunt the parasite, and why relapse takes hold. Care advice stresses repeat, long watch until the parasite is truly gone. The authors call for fast, sharp, cheap bedside tests and for new drug mixes built for low-count disease.
pmc-11616706:
Yo Fukushima and co-authors chart how a major earthquake redrew the Noto Peninsula coast in Japan. Their 2024 study covers the magnitude 7.5 quake that struck on New Year's Day, driven by a thrust fault with slips near ten meters across a long zone. Satellite data and field checks rebuild the ground shift.

The north coast rose up to 4.4 meters, pushing the shore seaward along its whole length. Mountain slopes slid in a pattern that matches bend faults, and side faults inland woke in step. Land shapes carved by past quakes line up well with this event's shift. The case shows, in one sharp day, how quakes build landscapes over ages.
pmc-11617306:
Mathieson and fourteen colleagues test whether EEG monitoring is feasible for newborns with encephalopathy in Uganda, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Birth-related brain injury is a leading cause of childhood death and disability. Continuous EEG is the gold standard for neonatal brain monitoring, but low-income country data are lacking. The cohort was recruited at a Kampala referral hospital.

Diagnostic-quality EEGs were recorded for fifty of fifty-one recruited babies, showing feasibility. Background activity was graded over the first three days, and seizures were annotated remotely by experts. Clinical presentation was tracked with standard scoring systems. Of thirty-nine children followed to eighteen to twenty-four months, thirteen had died and seven had neurodevelopmental impairment. The study links EEG patterns to early childhood outcomes in a low-resource setting.
pmc-11617406:
Kristen Prentice and co-authors set out a fresh definition of health equity for the United States in this 2024 paper. The COVID-19 pandemic laid bare wide gaps in health between groups. The authors draw on public health, social science, money studies, and human rights work to frame what fair health should mean now.

They trace the roots of the idea and weigh proof on why gaps persist. Their claim is that fair health is not just a matter of justice. It is also a smart, practical goal that lifts the health of the whole nation. The paper closes with steps for policy, clinic practice, and research to close the gaps.
pmc-11618406:
Ayah Zaidalkilani and co-authors test how salt water shifts the growth of three table beet types. The study appeared in 2024. Salt blocks plants from taking up key food and can poison them at high load. Yet salt-tough beets could open new ground for the crop.

Pots were grown for two seasons with tap water or four salt loads. One type, a dark red sort, did best of the three. The lowest salt load raised growth traits by up to about a fifth. The next load gave the top gains in some food and mineral traits. Salt changed sugars, color parts, and stress marks in the leaves as well.
pmc-11618506:
Joao Canning-Clode and co-authors hang growth plates in the dim sea zone to watch which foul life lands there, in a study from 2024. The dim zone, twixt bright top and dark deep, is one of the least read sea worlds. A crewed sub set plates of two stuffs at three depths for two years.

Plates stood straight and flat at each depth past a set of sites by one isle chain. Depth, plate pose, and plate stuff all bent which crowd grew. Depth and pose bent it most. The run gives the first long tale of dim zone foul crowds at this isle chain. Mend work in dim seas can build on these laws.
pmc-11619306:
Bianca Albers and co-authors debate how strictly health interventions must be delivered as designed, using two trial cases. Their 2024 paper deals with fidelity: whether core parts of an intervention and its rollout plan were delivered as intended. Without fidelity data, complex trial results cannot be read with confidence. Yet strictness is now questioned, as local conditions may demand adaptation. The authors call modern fidelity a balancing act.

Three tensions structure the debate. First, core components are often poorly known, so fidelity rules involve judgment calls that should be made transparent. Second, fidelity is context bound and must be rethought in each study. Third, fidelity focuses on single actors, though systems shape delivery too. The two cases come from hybrid trials that test effects and rollout together. The authors argue for firm cores with flexible edges.
pmc-11619406:
Kristen Morin and co-authors set out a 2024 protocol to evaluate a transitional housing program in Sudbury, Ontario. The program serves people who use substances, face homelessness, and live with a mental health condition. Northern Ontario carries sharp versions of all three challenges. The evaluation will judge effects on patient outcomes, health care use, and how clients themselves see the program.

The design runs several studies in parallel: records analysis, before and after interviews, and in depth qualitative interviews. People who use substances, frontline staff, and decision makers help run the evaluation as partners. A wide set of statistical tools will handle survival, repeated measures, and group outcomes. The team aims for evidence on whether such housing steadies lives, raises social capital, and narrows health gaps for this group.
pmc-11619706:
Maryann Mason and co-authors describe a door-to-door overdose prevention pilot in Illinois, in a 2024 case study. Many people who use drugs never reach the vans or centers where harm reduction supplies are usually handed out. The Block-by-Block program, running since 2022 at five sites in four counties, brings naloxone training and test strips to homes and neutral neighborhood spots.

Local partners host the visits, reaching users plus their friends, family, and neighbors in areas hit hardest by fatal overdoses. The paper reports how the model was put into practice and how feasible and acceptable it proved, as a template for reaching hidden populations.
pmc-11620806:
Latifa Taoufiq and five co-authors track groundwater quality on the Angads Plain near Oujda, Morocco, in a 2024 study. Farm and town growth press on the aquifer under the plain, and managers need a clear map of its health. The team used mapping software to compare two snapshot years.

They tested five markers of pollution and salt at sampling points in 2014 and 2020. One nitrogen marker rose at most points, while two others fell. Salt markers held steady. Overall, more points slid into the middling quality class by 2020, a trend the maps make plain for local water planners.
pmc-11622206:
Ming Han and nine co-authors search for blood signs of a dangerous clot in the liver's portal vein among patients with advanced cirrhosis, in this 2024 study. The clot lacks a sensitive early marker. The team focused on webs of DNA that white blood cells cast out, called NETs, and on the enzyme that chews them up.

Blood from 145 patients in one study and 33 in a second was checked for the web markers and enzyme activity. Patients with clots showed more web debris and weaker enzyme activity, with or without liver cancer. One debris marker alone sorted patients well, and combining all three measures sorted better. The authors propose the imbalance as a diagnostic lead for a complication that now hides until late.
pmc-11622506:
Harald Brüssow traces how deadly bird flu reached North America and spread through farms, in a 2024 review. The H5N1 virus first appeared in China in 1996 and swept Eurasia, killing birds and sometimes people. North America stayed free of it until 2014, a puzzle the review unpacks with genome evidence. Two separate arrivals carried the virus across the oceans.

Migratory birds first brought it from Siberia along the Pacific route, sparking a costly 2015 poultry outbreak in the Midwest that faded after containment. A second wave crossed the Atlantic in 2021 and spread down the East Coast, this time spilling into many mammals. In 2024 it erupted in dairy cows across fourteen states, moved by milking gear and animal transport. The review closes on the naming tangle the virus's family tree creates for public communication.
pmc-11622606:
Shinya Tanaka and colleagues compare hip fracture care in older Japanese patients before and after the COVID-19 pandemic began. Their 2024 retrospective multicentre study spans three hospitals.

Nearly nineteen hundred patients aged sixty-five and older who had hip fracture surgery were grouped by injury year, from twenty nineteen through twenty twenty-one. Patient numbers fell by roughly seven percent in both pandemic groups. Waiting time for surgery, hospital stay, and in-hospital death or complication rates did not change significantly. Infection did increase in the early pandemic group. The study shows how major societal disruption affected fracture numbers more than perioperative management.
pmc-11623106:
Lili Wu and six co-authors predict maize seed germination without destroying the seeds, in a 2024 study. Standard germination tests take long experiments and ruin the seed. The team instead fused several kinds of information about each seed of one variety: camera images of the seed and its inner cracks, plus electrical readings converted to voltage.

Color, shape, texture, crack count, and voltage features fed five different prediction algorithms. The random forest won clearly. It trained in about five seconds, hit 92.88 percent accuracy, and posted the lowest errors of the group. Neural networks, support vector machines, and two other methods trailed behind. The authors conclude that fusing image and electrical data with a random forest gives seed producers a fast, nondestructive way to forecast germination rates.
pmc-11623806:
Mahfuzur Rahman and co-authors ask whether the pandemic changed how many children Indian women wanted, and had, using the country's giant family health survey. The 2019-21 round happened to straddle the lockdowns, splitting thirteen states and territories into pre- and post-lockdown samples. That accident of timing makes a natural experiment.

Descriptive comparisons and multilevel models track fertility behavior and desire across the divide, accounting for the complex survey design. Economically poorer states showed distinctive patterns in the results. Knowing whether crisis suppresses births, delays them, or shifts intentions helps planners read the demographic aftershocks still moving through the world's most populous country.
pmc-11624006:
Natsuki Ishida and co-authors sort gullet growths by where they sit round the tube, not just down it. Length place is the stock sort; the round place was thin-read. Their 2024 study reads just under two hundred growths took by a scope cut craft. Counts per round wall and per length span form the grid. The front wall set stands out: its growths run least by mid size.

Front growths also hold the most slim, skin-deep share. Wall-wise counts can steer how scope teams hunt and how deep they cut. A growth's round home may mark its age in the tube.
pmc-11624206:
An interview from 2024 profiles Rachael Dangarembizi, a brain scholar at the University of Cape Town in South Africa. She built the first lab in Africa that studies how fungus harms the brain. Her work joins bench science with ward insight to lift care for such brain ills.

In the talk she tells how top-grade work can grow where funds and gear run thin. She has won many prizes and leads groups that build brain science skill across Africa. Her aim is home-grown craft and kit that can drive real finds. Young scholars in lean posts gain a worked case of reach built from rigor.
pmc-11624606:
Chen Ranran and co-authors present a 2024 study on forecasting a full day of eye pressure swings from daytime readings alone. Pressure inside the eye rises and falls over 24 hours, and big swings worsen glaucoma. Round-the-clock monitoring is cumbersome, so the team trained machine learning models to infer the swing class from routine measures.

Records from monitored patients supplied 22 features. Statistical screens sorted them into four subsets of rising strictness. Five classification algorithms were trained and compared on accuracy, sensitivity, and curve scores. The winning model was unpacked with an explanation method that ranks each feature's push on the prediction. A reliable forecast could spare patients overnight stays in pressure labs. It could also flag hidden swingers for closer care.
pmc-11625506:
Yuanhang Wang and co-authors report a fast response in a man with a rare, aggressive chest tumor tied to a missing gene called SMARCA4. Their 2024 case report and literature review describe a fifty-five-year-old whose cancer had spread to lymph nodes, the chest lining, and bones. Tests showed the tumor lacked a marker that often predicts benefit from immune drugs.

A first drug pair failed, and scans showed growth after one cycle. The team switched to a three-way mix of chemotherapy, an immune drug called penpulimab, and a vessel-blocking pill. The tumor then shrank quickly. The authors weigh this rescue path for a cancer that still has no standard effective treatment.
pmc-11625706:
Yang and seven colleagues use polarized light to grade healing of the Achilles tendon in twenty twenty-four. The tendon at the heel is often torn, and doctors lack a clean way to score how well it heals. Their method shines light that vibrates in set planes and reads how tissue bends it. No dyes or labels are needed.

Hurt tendons bent light less and in a more jumbled way than healed ones. Computer models of the tissue tied those shifts to thicker fibers, straighter fiber lay, and more collagen. The team built a single score from the light data. It draws a map that shows injury and grades how well each treatment worked.
pmc-11626206:
Awatif Alrasheeday and nine colleagues present a 2024 survey on why patients with type 2 diabetes struggle to live healthily. Over five hundred patients at primary care centers in Hail City, Saudi Arabia, rated the barriers they face to good eating and exercise. About thirty-five percent felt blocked on eating and twenty-eight percent on activity.

Lack of motivation topped both lists, followed for eating by poor information about healthy diets. Workplaces that discourage activity were the leading social barrier. Younger, better-educated, recently diagnosed, and insulin-using patients reported more eating barriers, while women, married patients, and poorer patients reported more activity barriers. The authors argue self-care programs must attack motivation and information gaps group by group.
pmc-11627506:
Juliana Amaral Prata and co-authors examine how nurse-midwives cared for women in labor during the COVID-19 pandemic, through the lens of Jean Watson's theory of human caring. Pandemic rules pushed care toward cold, procedural routines. The team interviewed forty nurse-midwives in 2021 and sorted their accounts against the ten elements of Watson's Clinical Caritas process.

The care they described touched all ten elements, grouped into five dimensions. A creative dimension showed in the workarounds staff invented to keep care human under restrictions. Humanistic and cultural dimensions shaped the manner of care itself. Those in turn fed an educational dimension and a spiritual one. The authors conclude that the midwives managed a transpersonal quality of care, keeping person-to-person connection alive in spite of rules that nearly always pushed the other way.
pmc-11628206:
Manon Marquet and co-authors report a 2024 study of unborn boys with both slow growth and a birth flaw of the penis. In this flaw, the urinary opening sits on the underside rather than the tip. When slow growth joins the flaw, doctors worry about gene or hormone causes that may shape the child's path.

The team gathered all such cases from five Paris scan sites from 2013 to 2021. They logged gene and hormone checks, birth results, and later surgery and function. Readers learn how often deep flaws turned up, and how the children fared after birth and repair.
pmc-11629206:
One-time gene therapy promises to free people with hemophilia from endless factor infusions. Saarang Deshpande and co-authors pool the trial evidence in this 2024 review, covering twenty trials and nearly four hundred men with severe forms of hemophilia A or B.

Both therapies cut yearly bleeding and infusion counts sharply. Factor levels for type B held near their peak after two years, while type A levels faded to about half, showing weaker staying power. About one patient in five had a serious side effect, but no clots or immune blockers appeared. The authors weigh lasting benefit against durability as the field's open question.
pmc-11629506:
Susanne Frennert and co-authors ask why care tech has come to feel like home gear in Swedish old-age care. Tech aids spread through town care and melt into day rounds, yet what staff take them to mean was thin-read. Their 2024 study draws on just under two hundred photo-text pairs from sixty-one staff in four towns. Theme craft sorts the pairs by tech kind and the sense staff lend each.

One word keeps up: ease of use, and at times its lack. Care tech earns its home place when it trims work, not when it adds steps. High aims from town halls land or die at that plain bar. The read can steer buys: pick the tool staff will call handy by week two.
pmc-11630606:
Hasibul Hassain Emon and colleagues published a public health study in twenty twenty-four on overweight and obesity among university students in Bangladesh. The team wanted to know how common excess weight is and how it connects with grades and self-esteem. Data came from a structured questionnaire given to six hundred students at Jahangirnagar University.

Nearly four in ten students were overweight or obese, with rates higher among males. Obese students showed the lowest academic performance across disciplines. Body mass index correlated negatively with self-esteem, and physical activity measures were also recorded. The findings link heavier weight with both weaker grades and poorer psychological well-being in this student group.
pmc-11630706:
Guillermo Ceniza-Bordallo and co-authors review low back pain during and after spaceflight, in a review paper from 2024. Spaceflight changes the spine and can trigger acute or lasting pain in astronauts. Animal studies add data, yet no full synthesis covered spine changes and pain rates together across humans and animals.

The review follows standard reporting rules and a registered protocol. Eleven studies passed screening from more than one hundred abstracts. Evidence shows astronauts lose muscle and face spine changes in flight. Pain rates during and after flight are reported across studies. Quality and evidence strength are graded. The synthesis guides countermeasures for crew spine health.
pmc-11631406:
Laura Kemppainen and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four register study of death rates among older migrants in Finland. Migrants often outlive native-born peers, a pattern called the mortality advantage. Whether it holds into old age, by cause of death, was unproven there.

All deaths over nearly two decades were analyzed for people aged seventy and over. Standardized rates compared migrants with Finnish-born residents. Breakdowns by cause and region of origin followed. Regression adjusted for age, sex, income, and residence. Evidence of a migrant advantage appeared across various causes, adding old-age data to a debated field.
pmc-11631606:
Changqin Luo, Qingmin He, and Xiaocui Yang present a 2024 case report on gallbladder stones that were not truly stones. A 54-year-old woman had belly pain and swelling for a month, yet her first ultrasound was clear. After she took the antibiotic ceftriaxone for a chest infection, she felt pain under her right ribs.

A CT scan then showed what looked like gallbladder stones. Six weeks after she stopped the drug, a follow-up exam showed the stones were gone. That vanishing act confirmed drug-induced pseudolithiasis, a sludge that mimics stones. The authors also review how the drug causes this effect, how it shows up, and how to spot it. Their summary helps doctors avoid needless surgery.
pmc-11631706:
Xin Liu and co-authors build a machine learning warning system for blood clots after colon cancer surgery, in a 2024 study. Deep vein thrombosis in the legs strikes up to forty percent of these patients after surgery and can travel to the lungs. The team gathered records for over four hundred patients treated from 2021 to 2024, covering blood tests, body measures, other diseases, tumor stage, and surgical details.

Because clots were the minority outcome, they balanced the data synthetically, then let three feature-picking methods nominate the strongest predictors before training rival models. The best model sorts patients by risk so staff can give blood thinners, stockings, or closer watching to those who need them most. A validated risk score turns a feared complication into a managed one.
pmc-11632106:
Fengjiao Du and co-authors profiled the immune receptor sets in pleural TB in 2024. This form of tuberculosis gathers fluid around the lung and is China's most common TB outside the lungs. Immune cells pool in that fluid, so its receptor mix may mirror the fight at the site.

Ten patients gave blood and pleural fluid cells. Deep sequencing read the T-cell and B-cell receptor chains in each sample. The sets in fluid and blood were not the same, though some clones were shared. Fluid and blood also answered the germ's proteins in their own ways. A grouping tool flagged receptor clusters tied to the germ. The map may help build immune-based tests.
pmc-11632406:
Birce Sena Tömekçe and co-authors explored what a ring-shaped molecule does on a silver surface, in a 2024 study. The molecule, a borazine ring carrying bromine atoms and an oxygen group, is a possible building block for thin carbon sheets dotted with boron and nitrogen. Such sheets could have tunable electric traits, but the reaction steps on a surface were not well known.

Using a fine scanning probe and X-ray tools at low temperature, the team watched the molecules as heat drove step-by-step changes. The molecules first formed ordered patterns, including a woven lattice with a distinct electric signature. In the end they linked into a random covalent net holding boron, nitrogen, and oxygen atoms. The findings guide the design of future building blocks for sheet materials.
pmc-11633006:
Andreas Ekholm and four co-authors published an imaging study in twenty twenty-four on predicting breast cancer growth-rate scores from microscope slides instead of gene tests. Proliferation signatures help personalize treatment, but sequencing is not always available. The team trained deep learning models on whole slide images paired with RNA data from eight hundred nineteen patients.

Two convolutional networks learned to estimate an eleven-gene proliferation score and the MKI67 marker gene. On unseen internal cases the predictions correlated strongly with the true values, and moderately on a fully independent external set of nearly a thousand tumors. Survival modeling confirmed the image-based scores still carried prognostic weight. Slides, in short, leak molecular information a network can read.
pmc-11633206:
Haipeng Chen and six co-authors read how a sea berry breed meets drought in growth and gene use. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. The shrub is a prime tree for dry lands, prized for world and purse worth. Year-old plants sat in three water grades for one hundred twenty days, and root gene and protein reads were run.

Drought cut height, stem width, root mass, and a shield rate, while main roots grew long. Thousands of genes and hundreds of proteins split by grade. Plant call paths lit in both dry grades, and fat shield cells joined in the hard grade. The shrub shifts shield spends as dry deepens.
pmc-11633306:
Hasta Handayani Idrus writes a letter in 2024 on a study of a gene flaw in a Chinese family with a stiff-heart disease. The study, by Dong and colleagues, used whole-exome sequencing to find a missense change in the FLNC gene. Idrus praises the hunt and adds notes for readers.

The letter backs FLNC screening when this disease is suspected in a family. It notes that sequencing can guide not just diagnosis but forecasts and care picks. One caution is raised: heart drugs the patient took can ease signs and sway how results read. Gene load and type-to-sign maps should follow, Idrus urges. Early finds let teams act before the disease turns grave.
pmc-11634406:
Jehad Aldali and co-authors estimate how common gastroparesis is among diabetic patients in Riyadh in a 2024 study. Gastroparesis, slow stomach emptying, varies widely in reported rates. The team also asked whether metformin, a common diabetes drug, links to its symptoms.

An online survey reached several hundred clinic patients, most with type 2 diabetes of long standing. A standard symptom index scored stomach complaints, and blood sugar control was often poor in the sample. Rates and drug links are reported with care for the survey design. Local clinics gain a baseline for a complication that is easy to miss.
pmc-11634606:
Mingyi Xu and co-authors build, in a 2024 study, a scoring model to warn which children with Mycoplasma pneumonia might develop a collapsed lung segment despite standard treatment. This pneumonia is common in childhood, and the collapse complication is serious. The team reviewed five hundred seventy-two children treated at their center, of whom forty suffered the complication. Admission-day records, lab values, and scans were compared between the two groups.

Six factors entered the final chart: fever length, a white cell ratio, platelet count, two liver and tissue enzymes, and age. The model's sorting accuracy was solid in testing. Children flagged early could get closer watching and stronger care before the lung segment fails. The authors call the model a preliminary aid that needs outside testing before wider use in clinics.
pmc-11635206:
Meng Chen and colleagues review whether exercise helps people recover after pulmonary embolism. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in twenty twenty-four. Survivors often keep shortness of breath and a lower quality of life. Exercise helps in heart disease and chronic lung disease, but its value after embolism was unclear.

The team searched seven databases for trials in these patients. Only two studies with a few hundred participants qualified. Pooled results showed no clear gain in walking test scores. Quality of life scores also showed no clear gain. The authors present a thin evidence base, so readers should treat exercise advice for these patients as still unsettled.
pmc-11635306:
An EFSA expert panel weighs the safety of a food enzyme in a 2024 opinion. The enzyme breaks down a plant fiber and comes from a fungus strain. Makers want it used in four food production processes. The panel reviewed exposure, gene harm tests, and a rat feeding study.

Exposure in European diets stayed far below the rat no harm dose. Gene harm tests raised no concern for the panel. The enzyme's protein shape matched no known allergen in database checks. Allergy risk from foods made with farm inputs could not be fully excluded, though.
pmc-11635506:
Chen and co-authors report a 2024 route to solar cells made from a layered perovskite, a crystal that can turn light into power. Cells of this kind often work worse than full three dimensional forms because their flat layers lie the wrong way on the base. The work was done in a glove box with fairly high moisture in the air.

By using mixed dip solvents, the team made the layers stand more upright, which helps charge move through the cell. The best cell reached higher power output than a cell made with a single solvent. A changed charge transport layer raised output still more, and the cells lasted about one month in open air.
pmc-11635606:
Kathrin Demmler and Ann Tutwiler review the links between diet, nutrition, and climate, past and present, in work from 2024. Global work on nutrition, much of it led by one alliance, has made gains against malnutrition. Yet lack of key nutrients persists, above all in parts of Africa and South Asia.

The authors urge that nutrition be woven into climate plans and that food systems be made more resilient. They cite a global movement, a food systems dashboard, and local public private partnerships. Stronger policy must align nutrition, climate, and equity goals. More funding, better data, and new technology are also needed, they argue.
pmc-11638006:
Mona Gouran and Siobhan Brady review how each cell type in a plant root reads its surroundings and adjusts its growth, in a 2024 review. Roots thread through soil where water, salt, microbes, and nutrients shift meter by meter. Each cell type answers in its own anatomical and molecular dialect, and together the answers set the root system's shape. Much of the cell-level map comes from the model plant Arabidopsis, read gene by gene.

The review connects stress signals to the timing of development itself: cues can speed, stall, or reroute a cell's program, changing its identity and job. New single-cell and spatial gene-reading methods promise the same map for crops and wild species, and for combined stresses, not just single ones. The authors aim the synthesis at breeding roots that hold up under harsher fields.
pmc-11638206:
Dayuan Liu and seven co-authors report a rare cell growth inside a child's brain in a 2024 paper. The growth comes from Rosai-Dorfman disease, a mild disorder where immune scavenger cells pile up. It most often swells neck glands. Inside the brain's fluid spaces it is very rare and hard to spot, since scans mimic other tumors.

A five year old boy had repeat headaches and seizures from such a mass. Surgery took it out, and lab checks showed the disease's hallmark cells and marks. Ten years on he stays free of seizures and regrowth. The team also found six like cases in the record, all with good ends after surgery, which fits the disease's calm nature.
pmc-11639006:
Kathy Liu and seven co-authors published a 2024 population study of health care use and cost during COVID-19 in Alberta, Canada. Covering 255,037 adults with confirmed infection from March 2020 to December 2021, the team tracked community and hospital care across the first four waves. Hospital care dwarfed other costs, at a marginal cost near 21,700 Canadian dollars per hospitalized patient.

Emergency department costs peaked in wave 2, while outpatient costs fell after wave 1. ICU care in wave 2 cost notably less than in wave 1, a drop of about 24,000 dollars per admission. The authors stress that severe infections drive spending. They call for studies of the social factors behind shifting use, to plan better for the next pandemic.
pmc-11639906:
Fluid drawn from a cow's rumen seeds lab tests of feed digestion, but no two draws are alike, and that noise clouds results. Marica Simoni and co-authors probed the variation in 2024, sampling four hay-fed Holstein cows by esophageal tube across three weeks, before feeding and at two points after. They profiled microbes, fermentation acids, and enzyme activity.

Which cow donated, and which week it was, reshaped the microbe mix, while time since feeding mattered less. Digestion of fiber in the lab stayed steady across cows, though some enzyme activities wandered by week and hour. The authors reinforce a simple fix: pool fluid from several cows and run more replicates.
pmc-11640106:
A sharp lemon-scent oil from an Asian tree could lift foods and scents, if its mixes held. The head of this report is dated 2024 (the catalog says 2025). Naiwen Xing and five co-authors steadied the mixes by tying fish-skin gelatin to a starch sugar through dry heat. Four sugar sizes were tried. A mid-large one lifted the steadiness score by more than one and a half times over plain gelatin.

The tied films wrapped oil drops at near half the old size. Their surfaces turned more water-shy, and their charge neared the mark for a stable mix. The tied gelatin also fought rust-like decay harder in two bench tests. The team pitch the dressed gelatin as a green emulsifier for food use.
pmc-11640406:
Turker Tuncer and six co-authors coined a word-like language for heart trace readings, in a paper published in 2024. Heart traces sort hearts well, but their decisions are hard to explain. Their language, Cardioish, turns each trace lead into marks and builds a phrase from the lead transitions. A four-step framework pulls features, picks the best, classifies, then speaks the phrase as the reason.

On two public sets, one for mental illness and one for heart attacks, the framework topped 99 in a hundred on classification accuracy. The phrases let a reader see which lead transitions drove the decision. The authors tie the phrases to heart map theory as well. They present the language as a bridge: strong scores that a doctor can read.
pmc-11640506:
Shi and co-authors build a season-aware model to assess Japanese sardine stocks in the Northwest Pacific. Stock checks often miss how fish move with seasons and place. Their model folds migration patterns into seasonal abundance indexes for assessment.

Results show sardine numbers rising steadily over the study window. The stock's center of gravity shifted clearly toward the northeast. The stock looked sustainable, with a 94.8 to 99 percent recovery chance. The authors still urge careful management, given the species' wild swings in the past. They frame the method as a tool for distant-water fishery science.
pmc-11640906:
Zhao and co-authors test a natural antibiotic, azalomycin F, against eczema-like skin disease in mice. The compound also fights fungi and tumors and calms inflammation. Mice with chemically induced skin lesions got the drug on their backs for 12 days. Doses ran from 10 to 30 mg per kg. The team scored lesions, counted scratching, and read skin tissue. Blood levels of IgE and several alarm cytokines were measured too.

Mid doses cut lesion scores and scratching the most. Skin thickening and mast cell entry also fell. Blood IgE and four inflammatory signals dropped with treatment. Gene reads probed the pathways behind the gains.
pmc-11641006:
Roberts and co-authors show that plants can build cellulose fibers by a side route that skips the standard maker enzymes, in a 2024 paper. A kin group of enzymes, the CSLD family, was known to matter for tip growth and cell splits. Whether they form skin complexes or spin true fibers stayed open.

The team bred moss mutants that lack the standard makers yet live. Under fine scopes, the mutants still spun fibers that matched those of leafy plants grain for grain. Freeze-crack views showed the same rose-shaped skin clusters that house the standard makers. The authors credit the kin enzymes for the fibers and tie their special roles to when and where they switch on.
pmc-11641106:
Zhen-Bing Dai and co-authors built a surface whose light matter waves can be switched and steered at very small scales, in work published in 2024. Such waves in thin materials promise tight control of light. Man made patterns suffer from loss and weak confinement, which has slowed progress.

Their surface forms naturally in a twisted carbon sheet stack, where local strain creates a pattern of soliton lines. Changing strain direction flips and tunes how the waves interact with those lines. The team also reshaped the waves' path, phase, and direction within tiny footprints, and switched directional waves electrically. The authors see a route to nanoscale light control in stacked materials.
pmc-11641206:
Xiuyue Xu and six co-authors map a family of genes in blueberry plants that help the plant cope with stress. They search the full blueberry genome, group the genes by shared traits, and then test how active each gene is in roots, stems, and leaves under salt, cold, and a stress signal.

They found more than twenty genes in the family, most more active in stems and leaves than in roots. Most genes changed activity under stress, and their control regions held many stress linked switches. The map gives breeders targets for hardier blueberry crops.
pmc-11641306:
Zorana Mutavski and her team pack elderberry waste extracts with pressed carbon dioxide. Their study from twenty twenty-four gives worth to a juice trade scrap. The scrap is rich in rutin, a plant compound that guards cells. A packed shell should hold its strength for use in foods or health pills.

Five extraction paths gave the first extracts for the work. Plain paths and paths with ultrasound, microwave, and boosted steps were set side by side. A gas-based PGSS step then formed the shells. Two food-grade carriers went in at a set ratio. Yield, catch rate, and grain traits told of success. The waste stream turns into a source of food stuff this way. Waste-to-worth work gains one more case in point here.
pmc-11641606:
Katarzyna Potyka and Józefa Dąbek track an inflammation signal across the stages of coronary artery disease. The signal is tumor necrosis factor alpha, a protein that helps drive vessel damage. The team measured how actively its gene and its two receptor genes were read in blood cells from 240 people: healthy controls and patients with early, stable, and acute disease.

As the disease stage worsened, the main gene's activity rose significantly, while the receptor genes' activity fell. Neither the number of blocked arteries nor the heart's pumping fraction changed that pattern. The authors read the opposing drift as a fingerprint of the disease's advance. They suggest it could serve as a marker for early, noninvasive diagnosis, catching artery disease before it declares itself in a crisis.
pmc-11641706:
Lazarros Chavalala, Rachel Tsakani Lebese, and Lufuno Makhado interview nurses about why men in a South African province avoid health care, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Men's reluctance to seek care tracks with worse outcomes and shorter lives, and norms of masculinity are suspected drivers. Fourteen professional nurses spoke in semi-structured interviews.

Nurses pointed to self-medication, distrust of Western medicine, and reliance on traditional healers. Men, they said, tend to seek care only when illness turns severe, feel uncomfortable with female nurses, and prize respectful treatment. Cultural norms remain a barrier, especially around intimate examinations by female clinicians. The authors call for services that take those norms seriously.
pmc-11641906:
Danilo Di Giorgio and co-workers review ten years of neck management in early mouth cancer at one Italian center, in a 2024 paper. In early-stage oral cancer with no sign of neck spread, about a third of patients still hide metastases in the neck. Whether to operate on the neck at once is debated.

Records covered one hundred twenty-one patients treated over a decade. The tongue was the most common site. Neck care split between planned dissection, watchful follow-up, and sentinel node biopsy. Survival was tied to the true node stage found later. Outcomes favored planned dissection and sentinel biopsy over watching alone. The authors share their center's experience to inform the debate.
pmc-11642006:
Tomasz Gasior reviews new tools for finding and grading heart muscle disease, in an update from two thousand twenty-four. These diseases change the shape and work of the heart for reasons other than blocked heart arteries. Gasior covers scans of the heart and gene tests, and how the two fit together.

Heart scans can show wall size, scars, and weak spots, while gene tests can show risk passed through families. Used together, they help doctors judge the risk of sudden death and choose who needs a shock device. New tools such as smart software and strain scans may sharpen care further.
pmc-11642206:
Yuqi Hong and colleagues published a 2024 review of ribosomal proteins in reproduction. Ribosomes build all cell proteins. Their component proteins do more than that. Evidence ties them to egg and embryo development. Several stress pathways run through them.

The review covers cell stress, oxidation, growth, and recycling pathways. Each pathway links these proteins to fertility. Diagnostic marker potential is discussed. Drug targeting possibilities are also raised. Mechanisms remain partly unclear, the authors admit. Reproductive medicine could gain new tools from this biology. The paper maps a fast-growing research front.
pmc-11642306:
Natalia Wronska and co-authors test films made from chitosan that fight fungi, as a way to keep food fresh for longer. Their 2024 study checks plain chitosan and types mixed with zinc oxide or graphene, for use on fungi that spoil food.

The team put the films to Aspergillus flavus and Penicillium expansum. The zinc oxide mix stopped spores from sprouting in both strains, and time on the films cut how many spores stayed alive. The films also changed how well fungal cell walls let things pass, most of all in Aspergillus flavus. Tests on human skin cells found no harm to genes in fibroblasts. But keratinocytes did show DNA harm with the zinc oxide mix. The team says such films could cut the use of man-made fungicides.
pmc-11642406:
Brain blood flow routes in a harsh aorta surgery are compared by the authors in work dated 2024. The surgery fixes a torn main artery, an event that can end in death or brain harm. Flow can be fed to the brain from one side or both sides while the chest is open. The team looked back at 147 urgent cases from 2018 to 2023.

Cases split by flow route showed no gaps in base traits or in most outcomes. Lasting brain harm stood apart. It hit near eighteen percent of one-side cases and near five percent of both-side cases. The team backs both-side flow as the safer pick.
pmc-11642606:
Sayeh Nikpay, John Bruno, and Colleen Carey analyze a court ruling's effect on a federal drug discount program in a 2024 paper. The 340B program lets some hospitals and clinics buy outpatient drugs at deep discounts and use the profit to fund care. Profit size depends on which patients count as eligible.

A recent court case challenged the agency's long-standing definition of a patient. The new definition could expand the program greatly and add administrative complexity. It could also create conflicts when an insured patient's prescription counts for more than one provider, a problem the authors work through.
pmc-11642706:
Daniel Aguilar-Nunez and co-authors test whether a radiofrequency treatment changes the elasticity of the heel tissue band, in a 2024 trial. The band, the plantar fascia, can cause heel pain when stiff or damaged. Healthy active adults got six sessions of a set radiofrequency treatment over two weeks, and their tissue was scanned at six time points up to three months later.

Changes in elasticity lasted up to a month after treatment, at points near where the band meets the heel bone. Other points along the band showed no change. Controls are used for comparison in the open trial design. The authors call the result a first step toward knowing how long such effects last in tissue. Similar effects have been reported in tendons elsewhere in the body, they note.
pmc-11643206:
Rozenn Langlet and colleagues worked on seed coatings that leave out microplastics, in a study published in twenty twenty-four. Film coatings protect seeds during treatment and planting, but many contain plastic that rules now push growers to replace. The team tested several stand-ins, including starch-based syrups, plant gums, cellulose, and other polymers, with and without a thickener. Using a light scattering method, they watched how particles settled, how clear liquid formed on top, and how well settled particles could be mixed back in.

Each stand-in changed settling behavior, generally slowing how fast particles sank while making remixing harder. The thickener helped some mixes and hurt others, depending on the polymer. One gum-based mix remixed especially well. The authors offer remixing ability as a practical test when judging plastic-free coating recipes.
pmc-11643306:
Marcin Małysza and co-authors test a printed mold insert for metal casting in a 2024 study. High pressure casting molds run hot and crack under repeat cycles. A printed insert can carry cooling channels that hug the part shape. The team compared its heat stress against a standard steel mold.

Heat treatment of the printed steel mattered more than print settings. Treated samples reached high strength with modest stretch before breaking. Shaped cooling raised stress slopes inside the insert, they found. Toughness at high heat remains the key demand for such inserts.
pmc-11643706:
Yaohui Xu, Yang Zhou, Yuting Li, Maziar Ashuri, and Zhao Ding reviewed ways in 2024 to improve a leading hydrogen storage material. The compound holds an exceptional amount of hydrogen by weight, but it releases it only at very high heat, reacts slowly, and cycles poorly. Three fix strategies dominate the field.

Catalysts speed reactions and improve cycling through interface and electronic effects. Shaping the material at the nanoscale controls its structure and softens its heat and speed limits. Pairing it with a second hydride destabilises it while keeping capacity high. The review weighs progress in each line and warns that holding the engineered structures through cycles, and suppressing stubborn intermediate phases, remain open problems.
pmc-11644206:
Guangshuo Feng and co-authors drop weights on sandwich panels to learn which core takes a hit best. The panels pair stiff glass-fiber skins with either polystyrene foam or cork wood at the center, a swap builders eye for greener materials. A drop tower struck samples at several energies, and computer models mirrored the tests blow for blow.

The wood-core panels met the striker with higher peak force than the foam-core ones. In both designs, damage began at the struck face, the core crushed and deformed, and the back skin failed last. Simulations matched the experiments well enough to trust for design play. The authors offer their data to engineers choosing cores for impact duty, with cork wood a credible stand-in.
pmc-11644306:
Wu and colleagues coat cotton fabric in twenty twenty-four with silver particles that conduct electricity and kill bacteria, using plant compounds as helpers. The plant compounds, drawn from natural sources, drive a classic silver mirror reaction that lays the particles down evenly. The result is a durable hybrid coating with two useful traits at once.

The team compared plant compounds of different sizes. Smaller ones gave a tighter, denser coating, while a well-known plant acid gave the most stable coating, keeping strong conductivity after repeated washing. Electric tests confirmed the plant compounds shield the silver from dissolving. The coated fabrics also showed clear germ-killing power. The route offers a greener swap for synthetic chemicals.
pmc-11644406:
Joaquín Marzano-Felisatti, Rafael Martínez-Gallego, José Pino-Ortega, and six colleagues track young beach volleyball players in this two thousand twenty-four study. Young players often split time between indoor and beach volleyball, and their physical demands were unknown. Thirty-two young male players, grouped by age, under fifteen or under nineteen, and by specialization, were tracked across forty matches with wearable electronic performance systems recording distances, set duration, and acceleration profiles.

Older players and beach-focused players covered more distance per set, about seven hundred nineteen meters against roughly six hundred, and hit higher maximum accelerations and decelerations. Indoor players, oddly, performed more total acceleration and deceleration actions per set. Set outcome, winning or losing, showed no clear physical differences. The authors conclude age and focus, more than match result, shape the physical profile of youth beach volleyball, informing age-matched training loads.
pmc-11644506:
Spinelli and co-authors test epoxy blends filled with carbon tubes and graphene flakes. Blends with two fillers can beat blends with just one filler type. The team used two load levels, 0.1 and 0.5 weight percent of mixed filler. Those loads sit below and above the point where charge starts to flow. The tube-to-flake mix changed from run to run by plan. Hardness, depth of press, and stiffness came from fine press tests.

A planned test grid showed how each filler share moved the scores. A curved fit then linked filler shares to the traits they sought. Shape scans backed up the press test scores. The best and worst blends went to full sim runs for a closer look. Matched sim scores gave more clues on how the blends bend and bear load.
pmc-11644806:
Rice plants with brittle stems are useful for studying what gives the plant its strength, but most known brittle mutants sit on different genetic backgrounds, which makes them hard to compare. The authors created forty-five brittle mutant lines from the IR64 variety using sodium azide, and sorted the lines with a finger-bending test and texture measurements. They measured the cell wall makeup of each line to see which parts track with brittleness.

Cellulose content showed the strongest link: lines with less cellulose in their walls were more brittle, with a correlation of minus 0.78. Hemicellulose, lignin, and silica played smaller roles. The team computed hydrolysis and feeding indexes, which point to uses for the straw beyond the field. Brittle lines with varied wall makeup could serve as animal feed or as feedstock for bioenergy, so the collection has value for basic research and farm use.
pmc-11644906:
Saud Sattar and co-authors watch battery fluid change color during use as a sign of wear, in this 2024 study. Lithium-ion cells lose capacity as their electrolyte breaks down, faster at high temperature. State of health checks usually need the cell opened or rested. This team placed optical sensors on working cells to track the fluid's color in real time.

Cells cycled at high temperature showed clear color shifts as they aged. Those shifts tracked the fade in capacity across the tests. Heat sped both the color change and the degradation. The authors frame color as a live, visible marker of electrolyte breakdown. They aim to turn this qualitative link into a measured health gauge in later work.
pmc-11645006:
Madaín Pérez-Patricio and seven co-authors detect plant stress in 2024 from a single color photo. Checking crops for stress usually needs trained eyes on site or cutting leaves for lab work. Both routes are slow or harmful at farm scale.

Their method rebuilds the plant in 3D from one photo, segments the crop, and separates its leaves. A deep network then judges stress from the reconstruction. In real-world tests the pipeline beat a plain 2D classifier by over twenty percent on precision, recall, and combined score. The authors pitch it as a low-cost scouting tool for growers.
pmc-11645306:
Wolfgang Bomicke and co-workers follow enamel wear from zirconia dental bridges over five years, in a 2024 clinical study. The bridges are resin-bonded and made from a strong white ceramic with polished biting surfaces. The question was how much they wear down the natural teeth that bite against them.

Six patients wore either inlay-retained or wing-retained bridges, and yearly molds tracked wear on both sides of the mouth. After five years, teeth biting against ceramic had worn more than control teeth. No wear showed on the ceramic itself. The authors say the wear stayed within the range seen for other common dental materials.
pmc-11645906:
Qing Zhao Ruan and co-authors review what happened when Botox-style shots for chronic migraine were forced off schedule during the COVID-19 years, in a 2024 paper. Clinics worldwide cut elective care, and the shots were postponed against patients' will. The team gathered the published record through early 2024.

Nine papers met the bar. They told one story: long delays, worse migraine force and frequency, and falling patient satisfaction. Follow-up care also frayed. Clinics leaned on remote visits and on a newer drug class, CGRP antibodies, to bridge the gap. The authors urge standing plans so a future crisis does not halt needed migraine care again.
pmc-11646406:
Lu and co-authors describe pneumonia caused by a germ caught from birds, a cause doctors often miss. The germ spreads from parrots and poultry, and standard tests rarely catch it. Their 2024 study reviews 52 cases found by gene sequencing at one Chinese hospital between 2022 and 2024, and sets out the pattern of illness.

Every patient had fever, and most had cough and fatigue. Only eighteen reported clear contact with birds or poultry. Scans most often showed a solid patch in the lung, and many blood markers of inflammation ran high. Once sequencing named the germ, all patients got targeted drugs and recovered fully, with stays near nine days on average. The authors urge early testing when bird contact is possible.
pmc-11646806: Saurav Jha and co-authors report in 2024 a case of a rare swelling in a grown woman: a hydrocele of the canal of Nuck. That canal is a small passage in the groin, present in female development, which normally closes. When it stays open and fills with fluid, it forms a pocket that can be mistaken for more common groin problems. The authors stress that fast diagnosis and surgery are the keys here. Careful examination, right imaging, and clean technique, they say, bring good long-term results.
pmc-11647406:
Feeding vinegar to dairy cows sounds like folklore, yet organic acids can shift rumen fermentation, so the idea merits a fair trial. Seongjin Oh, Tomohiro Mitani, Masahito Kawai, and Koichiro Ueda fed grain vinegar to nineteen lactating Holsteins in 2024 in a crossover design.

Milk yield, fat-corrected yield, silage intake, rumen measures, and blood markers all stayed put; the vinegar neither helped nor hurt production. One signal moved: three branched-chain fatty acids in milk, compounds tied to rumen stress, dropped substantially on vinegar. Newly made milk fat held steady. The authors conclude the additive is safe at the tested dose, with a subtle fingerprint in milk chemistry worth a second look.
pmc-11649406:
Yitong Jiang and co-authors test a mix of immune proteins to guard piglets against African swine fever in 2024. The viral disease is deadly and threatens pig farms round the world. No vaccine is on sale for it. The team fused three swine immune proteins with an antibody part. The fusions were made in lab cells.

Tests showed the fusions fought a test virus in two cell systems. They switched on a set of defense genes in pig cells. Piglets given the mix before infection had lower virus loads. Death came later, and tissue harm was less than in untreated piglets. The authors see the mix as a path to prevent and treat the disease.
pmc-11649706:
Kou and Deng test whether tumor DNA floating in the blood can forecast how metastatic bowel cancer will respond to treatment. They reviewed 134 patients treated at their center in 2020 and 2021, splitting them by whether circulating tumor DNA was detectable in plasma. The groups started out similar on standard measures. Their treatment responses, survival, and side effects were then compared.

Patients with no detectable tumor DNA did better on every front. Their tumors shrank more often, their disease stayed controlled longer, and they lived longer, with a one-year survival of about 74 percent against 55 percent. They also suffered fewer adverse events. Tumor DNA status tracked with standard tumor markers as well. The authors present the blood test as a promising, noninvasive guide for personalizing therapy. As a single-center retrospective study, it invites confirmation in larger, prospective cohorts before clinics lean on it.
pmc-11649906:
Baddouri and Hannig weigh probiotics as an add-on cure for periodontitis in a 2024 clinical perspective. The gum disease is common, and many types of microbes play a part in it. Probiotics might help standard care by bringing oral microbes back into balance, but hope for them may run ahead of the proof.

The review looks at forty clinical studies. The results were mixed, since the studies used distinct designs, types of probiotic, and outcome measures. Gains looked stronger in severe cases. With longer follow-up, gains varied and in some cases faded. The authors urge care, and call the case so far promising but not yet settled, let alone proven.
pmc-11650606:
Dolendra Karki and co-authors build a fiber-optic sensor for alternating magnetic fields in a 2024 paper. Power grid operators need live measures of current and its magnetic field. A magnetic nano-fluid can sense fields, but its slow response had limited it to steady fields.

The team used the fluid as the cladding on a light guide built for a special self-imaging response. With the structure and fluid tuned, response time fell under one millisecond. The sensor tracked fields up to 15 kilohertz, far into the alternating range. Tests at the 60-hertz line frequency of grids showed it could meter current in real conditions.
pmc-11651606:
Dung Nguyen, Yu Wei, Erin Belval and colleagues built an optimisation model that decides where to clear fuel breaks across a landscape in 2024. The mixed integer programming model uses large sets of simulated wildfires to pick the treatments that protect the most land and the most homes at the wildland urban interface.

Test cases for Southern California showed how the best layouts shift with fire behaviour and management goals. Compared with a rule-based simulation approach, the optimiser found clearly better treatment plans within reasonable solving times. The team presents the model as a flexible planning aid that managers can adapt to other regions and to more complex fuel break problems.
pmc-11652206:
Youtian Zhang and three co-authors review in 2024 how a common group of chemicals in plastics may cause a birth defect of the penis in males. In hypospadias, the urinary opening forms in the wrong place. Exposure of a mother to these chemicals, called phthalates, during pregnancy is a known risk, and rodent studies let teams trace how the harm unfolds.

From 326 papers, twenty-two fit the review.
