Their findings fell into five paths, led by disruption of sex hormone signals, with cell change, self-eating, cell death, and blood vessel growth also in play. A stress agent in cells linked the paths. The authors see hormone disruption as the likely first step.
pmc-11652506:
When an artery inside the skull tears, doctors must choose between two blood-thinning strategies, and Seong-Joon Lee and co-authors compare them in real hospital data. The study covers 311 patients with symptomatic but unruptured tears treated between 2010 and 2021. One group received anticoagulant drugs and the other received antiplatelet drugs.

The anticoagulant group arrived sicker, with more strokes and more narrowed arteries, so the team matched patients to level the comparison. After matching, early worsening, repeat stroke, and three-month death rates did not differ between the strategies. Many patients switched from anticoagulants to antiplatelets during care, and that switch group showed more early artery changes. The findings suggest either approach can serve when the tear has not burst.
pmc-11652906:
Forhad and co-authors describe a live water quality monitoring system for treatment plants, in a 2024 study. Plant staff must watch water traits closely to keep treated water safe. Their system links sensors through the internet of things, a network of connected devices. It tracks acidity, dissolved oxygen, total dissolved solids, and temperature around the clock.

Sensor data flow to a central platform with cloud storage and analysis tools. A programmable controller lets staff adjust the setup and add new measures with ease. The system runs on low power and reports values with a very small error margin. Live alerts, stored history, and remote viewing support faster upkeep choices. Plants can spot problems early rather than after harm is done.
pmc-11653106:
Hongshuang Qin and co-authors test a light-activated porphyrin against drug-resistant staph bacteria. Their twenty twenty-four paper uses blue light therapy, which suits skin infections since blue light stays shallow. Reactive oxygen made on the spot kills germs that shrug off antibiotics.

Five porphyrin variants were compared as light drugs for this role. The bromo form in the title led the set. Such light drugs are few for blue light, so each new candidate counts. The team read how well the compound wakes under blue light and wipes out resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Light therapy with a strong local drug could treat skin infections while sparing deep tissue.
pmc-11653606:
Splitting water and alcohol with light to release hydrogen needs catalysts that catch photons well. Asier Agrelo-Lestón and co-authors build hybrid catalysts that pair gold compounds with titanium dioxide. A coumarin-based part acts as the light catcher, thanks to its strong color.

The team compared gold complexes and gold particles at two loading levels under ultraviolet and visible light. Adding gold boosted hydrogen output up to 2.7 times over a standard gold reference. Detailed imaging and spectroscopy showed tiny gold particles forming in the best samples. One sample partly converted during use, and that change explained its top production rate. The authors credit the mix of light-catching dye, gold helpers, and light-amplifying particles for the gains.
pmc-11653706:
Face reading in autism may split into an early step that works well and a late step that works less well. Darko Sarovic and co-authors tested that split with brain wave scans in work from twenty twenty-four. Men with autism and matched peers watched real faces, face-like objects, and plain objects during the scans.

Early brain waves split face-like inputs from plain objects in both groups, which hints that face spotting stays intact. Late waves split real faces from the rest in both groups too. Yet peers showed a stronger late split of faces from objects than the autism group did. The team reads the late stage as where rich social facts are pulled from a face.
pmc-11653806:
Yuta Katsumi and co-authors ask whether brain shrinkage seen on a first scan can forecast how fast a rare dementia will worsen, in work from 2024. The illness harms the back of the brain first, so sight and space skills fade early. How fast it moves varies a lot from person to person.

The team studied thirty-four patients and twenty-four healthy adults of like age. Patients showed the most shrinkage in back brain areas, above all in the sight network. Shrinkage in a network that guides focused looking best forecast faster decline in daily function. The authors say such a scan measure could help doctors plan care for each patient. They note the finding needs to be checked in new groups.
pmc-11653906:
Xia Yu and six co-authors build a warning system for dangerous night-time low blood sugar in type 1 diabetes. Night lows can strike without waking the patient, so early warning has real stakes. Older methods miss key signals hidden in mixed, multi-source data. Their 2024 framework uses deep learning with a new attention design.

Features are drawn at several scales and from several dimensions of patient data. A guidance step feeds medical prior knowledge into the attention weights, sharpening what the network learns and making its focus readable. On a public clinical data set, the system warned of 94.91 percent of night lows. Its F1 score reached 96.35 percent. Comparisons put it ahead of existing approaches in both accuracy and practicality.
pmc-11654006:
Gabriele Soares Maydana and co-authors report a 2024 study of how dentists read X-rays of filled back teeth. Decay under a filling is hard to spot, and joining scan reads with clinic facts may catch more of it. The team had a specialist panel read more than two hundred bitewing images in two rounds.

In the first round the panel saw images alone. In the second, after a gap, they saw the same images with a clinic score and signs of lesion activity. Choices on whether to restore shifted between the rounds, and score agreement was weighed, which shows what the added facts change.
pmc-11654206:
Anthony Cnudde and a large team of co-authors build a pocket scale for judging when a herbal product might clash with a patient's medicines, in this 2024 paper. Herbal products feel safe to many users, yet active plant compounds can interact with drugs, sometimes with serious consequences. Clinicians had almost no quick tool for sizing up a given herb-drug pair.

Their scale, BABINE, grew out of six rounds of expert discussion over case reports and clinical studies. The experts distilled the criteria they kept returning to when judging risk, and the team turned them into a transparent scoring method. The scale knowingly simplifies the pharmacology. Its promise is speed and consistency: a clinician can grade an interaction's risk in the room, from published evidence, instead of improvising. The authors offer it as a practical guardrail for everyday practice.
pmc-11655306:
Zhiyong Wang and colleagues build a gene score to forecast how liver cancer will behave, in this study from twenty twenty-four. The genes all involve lysosomes, the cell's recycling sacs, which tumors can bend to their growth and spread. The team mined large public cancer databases for gene and outcome data on liver tumors.

From many candidates, machine learning picked four lysosome genes that, combined, form their index. Patients with high scores fared worse and had more immune cells crowding their tumors. The score also tracked with how tumors might answer drug and immune therapy, tested in the data. To check the biology, the team silenced one gene, CTSV, in liver cancer cells, and the cells grew and moved less. The authors offer the index as a tool to sort patients by risk and to guide treatment choices, pending checks in the clinic.
pmc-11655906:
Keerthana Ravichandran and co-authors find the least part of a cell protein that killer T cells need to pull in a granule mark. The study appeared in 2024. The protein helps cells take back spent kill sacks at the kill face. That pull-back lets the cells kill more than once.

Fine scans showed the protein moves to the kill face when spurred. Forms from mouse, man, and fly were tried in cells that lack the protein. The first stretch of near one hundred links was the least part that fixed the pull-in. Two spots in that stretch proved key, one a dock tag and one a lone link.
pmc-11656006:
Giovanni Sergio Utrilla, Irene Roman Degano, and Riccardo D'Ambrosi review whether platelet-rich plasma helps knees heal after meniscus repair surgery, in this 2024 systematic review. The plasma, drawn from the patient's own blood, is injected in the hope of speeding tissue repair. The authors gathered randomized trials that compared the treatment against placebo.

Only three trials qualified, covering one hundred thirty-nine patients in all. Scans alone showed no clear gain for the plasma group in any trial. When scan and scope checks were combined, the repair failure rate did favor the plasma group, and one scope-only study also found a gain. Pain and knee-function scores pointed in mixed directions across the trials. No study reported complications from the treatment. The reviewers conclude the evidence is too thin to settle the question and call for larger trials.
pmc-11656206:
Ozgen and coauthors check a fast lab test for a joint compound in creams. The compound belongs to a family used in skin and joint goods. Past tests were slow and needed long prep steps. The new test aims for plain, quick checks in routine labs.

The method pulls the compound straight from gel or cream. Samples then go right into the test device for reading. Checks proved the test is straight, exact, and stable. Global guide rules set the bars those checks had to meet. Both gel and cream forms passed with high scores. Labs can now assay such goods with far less prep.
pmc-11656406:
Xin Dan and co-authors gathered the best proof on food care during chemotherapy in 2024. Good nutrition can help patients endure treatment, yet guidance is scattered. The team searched global databases for guidelines, reviews, and expert views. They rated the quality of each source with standard tools before drawing lessons.

Their summary pulls the strongest advice into one place for clinical use. It also flags gaps in the proof, with a focus on stomach cancer care. Studies of both forward and backward looking types were weighed. Nurses and doctors gain a clear base for feeding plans that support patients through hard treatment cycles.
pmc-11656506:
Mohammed and co-authors compare two ways to treat an abscess that forms around the appendix. Antibiotics alone are one option; adding a drain placed through the skin is the other. No agreement exists on which works best, and some surgeons favor removing the appendix.

The team searched PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus, and trial registers for matching studies. Duplicates were removed and papers were screened for fit. Pooled results compared hospital stay length and treatment success between the two groups. Mean differences came with 95 percent confidence ranges. The findings aim to guide care for this common surgical emergency.
pmc-11656606:
Yuxin Nong and co-authors tested a citrus compound on blood vessels in two thousand twenty-four. Sepsis damages the vessel lining, causing leaks. A bacterial toxin drives that damage in lab models. The compound, a sweetener relative from citrus, may protect. Its antioxidant action is the proposed mechanism. Mice and cultured vessel cells were both studied.

Dye tests measured vessel leakage in the mice. Cell assays tracked survival and programmed death. Barrier strength was tested with labeled tracers. Sticky vessel surfaces were probed with immune cells. The compound preserved barrier function under toxin attack. Stress markers inside cells fell toward normal. Inflammatory releases from the lining also dropped. The results nominate it for sepsis support research.
pmc-11656706:
Florian Schunck and co-authors report a 2024 study that ties gene activity data into a model of chemical harm in zebrafish embryos. Risk testing for the chemical industry needs sound predictions with less animal testing. Gene data gathered over time may link cell events after exposure to effects on the whole animal.

The team built a model around nrf2, a gene that acts as a stress regulator in cells. Its activity level stands in for damage, which then drives detox steps and death in the model. Fitting the model to rich data sets took tools from molecular biology, dynamic modeling, and Bayesian statistics. The test case asked whether nrf2 activity can predict death in zebrafish embryos. The authors present the method as a template for using molecular markers in survival forecasts.
pmc-11657106:
Alan Barnicle and a large team of co-authors analyze in 2024 genomic instability in more than two thousand ovarian cancer patients across six trials of the drug olaparib. Drugs of this class changed ovarian cancer care. The team asked what patterns of DNA repair failure appear across tumor samples from those trials.

Repair deficiency was tested in 2,147 tumors. About half carried BRCA mutations, and those tumors scored far higher for genomic instability. Tumors with other repair gene mutations showed mixed scores. The analysis maps how instability scores vary by mutation type, aiding patient selection for this drug class.
pmc-11657206:
Nura Yousef and eleven colleagues published a 2024 nationwide survey on awareness of consanguinity and genetic disease in Saudi Arabia. Consanguinity means marriage between close relatives. More than half of marriages in Saudi Arabia are between first cousins, which raises the prevalence of inherited diseases and the cost of long-term care.

Earlier studies found limited awareness of this link, even among educated Arabs. The national study gauged public understanding of how cousin marriage relates to genetic disease in children. It also explored the challenges of raising awareness without offending cultural norms. The authors discuss potential solutions to reduce the national healthcare burden, such as premarital screening and genetic counseling services.
pmc-11657306:
Nick Lan and co-authors link diabetic foot ulcers to heart, kidney, and metabolic disease in this 2024 review. Foot ulceration is a serious but preventable complication of diabetes. It leads worldwide causes of hospital stays, amputations, and disability in the disease.

Patients with ulcers carry more heart risk factors, heart failure, and kidney disease than other patients with diabetes. Their risk of cardiovascular death runs over twice as high. The authors propose one connected system with shared mechanisms. Inflammation and infection from the ulcer are cast as key mediators. The review urges treating the foot as a window on the whole body.
pmc-11657606:
Anika Ruisch and co-authors review what it costs to give children preventive malaria medicine in the rainy season, in a 2024 paper. The program, used in 17 countries, gives monthly antimalarial doses where the disease peaks seasonally. Planners need firm cost data to budget and to judge value for money.

The team searched five databases for studies from 2012 to 2023 that used clear costing methods. Six studies across nine countries made the cut. Financial cost per child for a full course ran from 1.71 to 12.46 dollars, with economic costs in a higher band. Costs shifted with delivery stage, from pilot to full scale-up. The review gives funders a grounded range for planning seasonal campaigns.
pmc-11657706:
Zhaojun Wang, Xin Su, Donglei Shi, and Li Wei mine US drug harm reports for kidney damage tied to a bone drug in 2024. The drug treats bone spread of cancer and weak bones. It is also known to strain the kidneys. The team pulled two decades of reports where it was the prime suspect. Several math methods cross checked the signals.

Twenty five kidney and urinary harms stood out. Death of kidney tubules was the most reported. Top harms shifted by the illness being treated. One rare water balance harm led in lung cancer cases. Most events came after long use, then within the first month. The authors urge kidney checks tuned to each use case.
pmc-11658106:
Wenchen Wang and five co-authors report a 2024 cohort study on lifestyle, genes, and colorectal cancer risk in people with prediabetes. The team asked if a healthy way of life can offset a high genetic risk for this cancer in that group, and how the two forces add up.

Data came from more than twenty thousand UK Biobank members with prediabetes and no cancer at the start. Each person got a lifestyle score and a polygenic risk score, each split into grades. High genetic risk more than doubled cancer risk in the data. Models then test how the two scores act on each other.
pmc-11658306:
Chuanfan Zhong and co-authors linked a DNA repair pathway's activity to how advanced prostate cancer answers hormone-blocking drugs, in a 2024 study. These cancers often respond at first, then resist. Using a per-sample enrichment method, the team found the repair pathway running higher in poor responders.

They built a gene score from the pathway that split patients into risk groups; the high group answered the drugs worse. Mutation maps and pathway analyses fleshed out the groups' differences. Lab and animal tests then checked the pathway's effect on drug sensitivity and DNA repair directly. The authors propose the score as both a forecast tool and a target lead.
pmc-11659106:
Tsukasa Shimamura and Takaki Miyata film living brain tissue in mouse embryos to measure how cell nuclei move before each cell divides. In the sheet that forms the front of the brain, parent cells pull their nuclei to the top surface in the last phase before division. That move had never been measured at large scale in three dimensions.

Films from days eleven to thirteen of growth showed the upward move slowing, with more pauses, as the sheet grew crowded. Tests that forced extra cell growth confirmed crowding itself slows the move. The team also found that past division sites were spread at random, not in clusters or neat rows.
pmc-11659606:
Alexandra DeLone and four co-authors trace how childhood hardship shapes young adults with chronic illness in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Early adversity is known to blunt emotion control and worsen mental health. Their group carried an extra load: long-term medical conditions. The authors tested a chain of links between the past and present adjustment. Illness-related thoughts sat in the middle of the chain.

Five hundred fifty-seven college students with chronic conditions answered surveys. Worry about the illness and feeling intruded upon by it carried the effect forward, joined by poor emotion regulation. Each link suggests a support target. Counselors might ease illness worry before tackling mood. Psychologists of chronic illness are the readers.
pmc-11662206:
Shoghik Ghazaryan and co-authors summed up in 2024 what is known about ladybird beetles in Armenia and nearby lands south of the Caucasus. Surveys there go back to the first half of the nineteenth century. The team combined past reports with their own recent field work.

Eighty-four species are firmly known from Armenia. Two of them were found in the new field samples but had never been reported in print, so they count as new country records. Fourteen more were reported only for the wider region. Armenia list is a bit shorter than those of its neighbors. It holds more species found only in the Caucasus and fewer foreign species than either neighbor.
pmc-11662906:
Robinson and seven co-authors discuss ethics in psychedelic pain research, in work from twenty twenty-four. Psychedelics have a long history of cultural and medical use. Interest has surged again, most of all in psychiatry, with early promise for hard to treat depression.

Chronic pain is a major burden with few non opioid options, so psychedelics are being explored there too. National funding has resumed after decades of little support. The authors warn that pain patients with limited autonomy are vulnerable. Consent, risk, benefit, and complex drug rules all need careful handling before trials expand.
pmc-11663706:
Anne Marmagne, Fabien Chardon, and Celine Masclaux-Daubresse present a study whose head gives the year as 2024. The catalog lists it under 2025. Autophagy is a cell recycling system that moves nitrogen from aging leaves to seeds. Arabidopsis mutants without autophagy age early, stay small, and yield few seeds. Their seeds also carry skewed nitrogen and carbon levels. The open question is where the fault lies: in the leaves that send, or the seeds that receive.

The team restored one key autophagy gene in only one tissue at a time. A leaf-aged promoter drove the rescue in source leaves. A seed promoter drove it in seeds alone. Comparing the two rescues splits local roles cleanly. Plant scientists get a tissue-level answer to a whole-plant puzzle. Seed quality in crops may one day be tuned by guarding recycling in the right tissue only.
pmc-11664006:
Bjornar Asebo and co-authors present a system and method in a 2024 paper on night light from the air. Balloons and drones now gather sharp images of artificial light at night, but shaking in flight blurs the take. Better in flight steadiness and faster picking of good frames are both needed.

A design for a steady high resolution camera rig for balloons and drones is set out first. A fast algorithm, FAHRIS, then sorts, groups, and stitches the images. Three flights over Italy tested it: a balloon that rose very high over Florence, and drone flights at lower heights. The method held up across all three datasets.
pmc-11664506:
Electrochemists who design catalysts face a maze of settings, flow, concentration, and voltage, where the system flips between good and bad operating regimes. Zone diagrams map those regimes, but drawing them has been limited to toy systems. Plumeré and Johnson recast the map in geometric terms.

Their method computes the current output across a grid of parameters and reads the result as a landscape. In this picture the geometry carries the whole diagram: curved regions of the surface mark the boundaries between kinetic zones, and flat regions mark the limiting zones themselves. Software can then chart the full parameter space of a complex system automatically, something neither hand analysis nor brute simulation manages well. The authors aim the tool at rational design of energy conversion devices.
pmc-11665606:
Peilin Xu and co-authors survey hard childhood events and adult mental health across China in a 2024 study. The data come from a national survey of more than twenty eight thousand adults held in the mid twenty tens.

In the deep interview group, just over a quarter reported at least one hard event in childhood, and many of those reported several. Neglect led the list, with hitting next. Four patterns of events emerged, from low risk to loss of a parent. Each pattern tied to later mood, worry, and drug illness in distinct ways. The authors weigh how much adult illness could trace back to those early harms.
pmc-11666306:
Jean-Claude Tardif and Simon Kouz put a large heart-attack trial in perspective, in a 2024 article. After a heart attack, two drug ideas compete for a place in routine care. One is low-dose colchicine, an old anti-inflammatory that cut repeat events in earlier trials. The other is spironolactone, which blocks the hormone aldosterone and helps failing hearts, though its routine use after every major heart attack was unproven.

The trial they discuss enrolled patients whose heart attacks were treated with stents. It asked whether colchicine reduces repeat artery events and whether spironolactone reduces heart failure plus artery events. The authors walk through the evidence before the trial, including the odd fact that one colchicine study ran during the pandemic, and frame what the new results should change in practice.
pmc-11666906:
Wangzhao Tian, Wenwen Yang, Xiaorui Wang, and Yanjiang Yang present a 2024 study of how food choices may affect a common bowel condition. The condition forms small pouches in the wall of the colon. Diet is thought to play a role, but cause and effect are hard to prove from surveys alone.

The team used gene variants as natural experiments to test twenty diet factors. Case data came from a Finnish biobank with more than thirty thousand patients, and diet data came from the UK Biobank. Pork intake and two kinds of fish intake linked to higher risk in the checks. Dried fruit intake linked to lower risk.
pmc-11667006:
Sunghoon Choi and co-authors build a harm model in a 2024 study to call where thin walls will tear. Cars, ships, and planes rest on thin shells that must fail in a safe way in a crash. Past models miss the tear point as strain paths swing from squeeze to stretch.

Their model is tuned for shell parts from shear, pull, and flat-pull tests. It calls the tear shift under shear half again as well as a camera-grade read. Neck-to-tear spans from pull tests set the break curve for thick shells across the strain span. Crash teams gain a model built for the parts they bend most.
pmc-11667606:
Chanbeom Kwak and co-authors train hearing testers in virtual reality in a 2024 paper. A VR hearing test can be cheap, real like, and run at will by the trainee. Whether pros would take to it in a course was not known.

Thirty one testers, split between pros and students, used a VR tone test on a headset. A digital twin made the room feel true to life. Surveys based on a tech uptake model scored both VR and bench tests. Ratings for the two were much the same in the tests. VR may join hearing courses sans push back from staff.
pmc-11667706:
Alexandra Balola, Sofia Ferreira, and Isabel Rocha published a review in two thousand twenty-four on turning plastic waste into bacterial feedstock. PET plastic can be enzymatically broken down, yielding ethylene glycol, a two-carbon molecule mostly discarded today. Escherichia coli might eat it and make valuable chemicals instead.

The review surveys natural and engineered pathways that let this workhorse bacterium grow on ethylene glycol. Protein and metabolic engineering strategies for converting it into target products are assessed. Closing the loop from waste plastic to biochemicals is the prize. Hurdles include slow growth on the substrate and pathway balance. The authors offer routes to make the approach industrially real.
pmc-11668806:
Jinsong Yang and eight co-authors test whether a fused strain of helpful bacteria makes better silage from king grass. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. Silage is fermented fodder, and its quality hinges on which bacteria drive the ferment.

The team compared three mixes: two parent strains on their own blend, and a hybrid strain made by fusing parent cells. The hybrid batch had the lowest propionic acid yet more total organic acids. Some batches held less crude fiber and more soluble sugars than others. Over time the hybrid batch changed in a steady way, and gene reads showed Lactobacillus taking over as the lead strain. The work suggests hybrid strains can lift feed quality for livestock farmers.
pmc-11669006:
Emma Bassan and seven co-authors use text mining to survey the whole literature on assistance dogs. Their overview was published in twenty twenty-four. Trained dogs help people with many physical and mental conditions, and the research pile grows fast and wide.

A keyword search on one database yielded four hundred and fifty articles. The team charted them by year, place, and outlet. Automated mining then picked out the most telling words. A topic model split the set into themes. The exercise showed the shape of the field across all its angles at once. The authors argue that such machine reading can support scholars facing topics too large to review by hand in reasonable time.
pmc-11669606:
Petar Stamov, Aleksandar Zlatarov, and Stefan Mihaylov describe the surgical care of a fourteen-year-old girl with Rapunzel syndrome in a 2024 case report. The syndrome is rare. Hair that a person swallows cannot be digested, so it mats with food and mucus into a solid ball in the stomach. In this syndrome, the mass also trails through the stomach outlet into the gut beyond.

Small hair masses can grow for years with few signs, and they are often tied to mental health problems. Left alone, they can block the gut or wear holes in it. Surgery is the standard cure, by scope, by keyhole surgery, or by an open operation. The authors say an open operation remains the first choice, and they stress that full care joins surgeons, child doctors, and mental health staff.
pmc-11669706:
Rachel M Wise and co-authors open a journal collection on how poisons and aging shape each other. Their 2024 editorial frames the theme as a coin with two sides. On one side, age changes how the body handles toxic chemicals. On the other, toxic exposures can speed up aging itself and make its burdens worse.

The editors note that longer lives mean more older people worldwide, so the stakes keep rising. Aging already stands as the top risk factor for diseases such as Parkinson's and Alzheimer's. The collection gathers studies on how toxic effects shift across life stages, and how exposures wear down the body's balance over time. The editorial sets out why the two fields belong in one conversation.
pmc-11669806:
Katie Harron and eleven colleagues published a policy paper in two thousand twenty-four on research into England's health visiting service. Health visitors support every family with children under five. Yet evidence on what the service achieves is thin, and stakeholders disagree on what to study first.

The team consulted parents, policymakers, and service leads, and reviewed the literature. Parents wanted research on care that feels responsive and easy to reach. Officials wanted clear descriptions and ratings of current and ideal services. The authors warn that studies using routine data alone will likely miss real effects. They call for planned prospective and experimental studies on outcomes from bonding to school readiness.
pmc-11671506:
Min Li and co-authors assemble in 2024 a self-selected microbe mix that boosts wheat seedlings in salty alkali soil. Salt lands shrink yields and waste farm ground worldwide. Helpful root bacteria can anchor plant partnerships that resist salt stress.

Seedlings pick their own partner mix from root-zone soil across rounds. A four-strain blend in a set ratio emerges from that selection. Gene reads of the root zone track how the mix forms. Treated seedlings grow far better under salt stress than untreated ones. Salt ground thus gains a living tool rather than a chemical one.
pmc-11672506:
Dora Onely Roblero-Mejia and co-authors report a new bacteria-made compound with germ-killing power, in this 2024 paper. The source is a soil bacterium that lives inside a medicinal plant. Genome mining flagged a gene cluster for a peptide of a known class, here named embleporicin.

The team copied the core genes and built the compound in a cell-free system. The product killed a test bacterium used in such assays. The report is the first of its kind for this bacterial genus, and the first time a compound of this class from this family was made by cell-free means. The authors back genome mining of plant-dwelling microbes.
pmc-11672606:
Zsolt Biró and co-authors ask whether returning wolves stress red deer in Hungary in a 2024 study. Wolves vanished from much of Europe but have spread again in recent decades, reappearing in Hungary since the 1990s. Red deer are a main prey in the region.

Game managers mapped a growing wolf range in the northern mountains since 2014. Deer stress hormone levels differed little between wolf and wolf-free zones in hunted samples. Body condition, judged by fat stores, also matched across zones. The authors conclude the young wolf population has not yet pressed deer hard, against hunter expectations of intense effects.
pmc-11672706:
Coch Tanguy Floyde Tanga and nine co-authors published a review in twenty twenty-four on antimicrobial resistance in African great apes. Resistant bacteria are a global health threat, driven mainly by antibiotic overuse in people, livestock, and farming. Because apes share many pathogens with humans, they may reveal how resistance spreads into wild environments.

The review covered sixteen studies, most on wild apes living near people to different degrees. A few compared wild and captive animals or tested captive apes alone. The authors map what is known about resistant genes in apes and point out the gaps. Apes, they argue, can serve as sentinels for human-driven resistance.
pmc-11672806:
Few drinks are studied as much as coffee, and few findings clash as often: it may shield arteries or burden them. Mabel Buelna-Chontal reviews the evidence in 2024, weighing coffee's many compounds against atherosclerosis, the slow clogging of artery walls. Some compounds fight oxidation and inflammation; others, found in unfiltered brews, raise cholesterol.

Studies in cells, animals, and people suggest moderate filtered coffee leans protective, while heavy intake can tip the balance. Coffee also seems to enrich gut microbes, which may help against weight gain. The author stresses that brew style and dose decide which side wins. Clearer trials are needed before firm advice can rest on the evidence.
pmc-11673106:
Martin Kovařík and co-authors studied how electron beam exposure changes nanotube devices in two thousand twenty-four. Making nanoscale devices often involves electron beams, and a standard transistor setup is used to measure new materials. The team watched tungsten disulfide nanotubes while the beam hit them inside a microscope.

Exposure changed each nanotube's resistance by a factor of two to fourteen, and the change did not reverse over hours to days. Surface potential scans pointed to charging of the supporting oxide as the main cause, not damage to the tube itself. The authors warn that care is needed when measuring nanostructures on insulating oxides that face electron exposure during or after fabrication.
pmc-11673606:
The authors test whether belly fat, more than weight itself, tracks with weaker lungs in women. Their 2024 study splits fat into the layer under the skin and the visceral layer around the organs. The visceral kind is already tied to insulin trouble, low-grade inflammation, and reduced lung function.

Body makeup was read by an eight-electrode impedance device in three groups: normal weight, overweight, and grade I obesity, roughly twenty to thirty women each. The visceral-fat link to lung measures showed only in the obesity group, where several breathing scores fell as visceral fat rose. The overweight group showed no such pattern. The authors argue that where fat sits matters as much as how much there is.
pmc-11673806:
Yongcheng Li and co-authors run computer simulations of a swimming foil near the ground in a 2024 study. The foil mimics a fish fin, bending in a traveling wave to push itself forward. Such designs inform small underwater robots. The team asked how a nearby floor or wall changes the foil's speed, thrust, and efficiency. They tested both flat and full three dimensional models at several wall distances.

The wall helped in every measure. Flow near the wall raised forward speed and cut wasted energy. The best cases gained about thirteen percent in speed and about ten percent in efficiency. The team also traced how the flow patterns behind the foil changed near the wall. They say the findings give useful guidance for designing bio inspired underwater vehicles that work near surfaces.
pmc-11674006:
Miriam Kaňuchová, Veronika Brindza Lachová, Kateřina Bogdanová, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It tests a wound-healing pair: an extract of agrimony, a plant long used on wounds, and a lab-made antibacterial compound, given together.

Agrimony extract is rich in polyphenols and fights oxidation. The partner compound kills bacteria in dishes while sparing the skin cells that rebuild tissue. The team checked the pair against staphylococcus, a common wound germ. They watched skin cells turn into the contractile cells that close wounds, lay down matrix, and multiply. They also tracked two growth signals in skin and vessel cells, and followed healing in rats day by day. The aim is a treatment that closes wounds faster without losing its germ-fighting edge, bridging herbal medicine and synthetic chemistry.
pmc-11674106:
Katarzyna Osipowicz and co-authors test how well a fluorescence test diagnoses a mouth disease, in a 2024 study from one Polish centre. The disease, oral lichen planus, can look like related lesions, so tissue tests are used to confirm it. The team compare a direct fluorescence test and a blood antibody test with the standard tissue examination.

Among sixty-six patients with mouth changes that suggested the disease, only half were confirmed by tissue tests. A fully typical fluorescence profile still matched tissue results in only a bit over half of cases. One deposit type, fibrinogen, gave the best accuracy of the markers studied, at about sixty-one percent. The authors conclude the two methods complement each other. Neither should be used alone when the diagnosis is in doubt, they say.
pmc-11674206:
Cindy Cheng and co-authors build a wearable device to spot low oxygen in body tissue in a 2024 study. Low tissue oxygen, called hypoxia, can damage organs if missed. Current checks rely on symptoms or on single measures that miss early onset. Sweat lactate, a chemical that rises when cells lack oxygen, has been flagged as an early marker for pressure sores. Neither signal alone is enough, so the team combined both in one patch.

The device pairs a gel sensor that changes color with sweat lactate and a near infrared sensor that reads tissue oxygen. Tests on lab tissue models and on human sweat after exercise went well. Worn on the body, it tracked lactate spikes and oxygen dips together during a low oxygen protocol, and the two signals moved in step. The authors suggest uses from surgery recovery to sports and sepsis watch.
pmc-11674406:
Huakun Jia and co-authors built a cactus-spined chip that counts cancer exosomes down to a single particle, in a 2024 study. Prostate cancer sheds tiny vesicles into blood; catching them early could spare biopsies. The chip's floor is a two-layer forest of plastic microspheres, cactus-like at the nanoscale, that amplifies Raman light scattering. Two aptamer probes sandwich each target vesicle, one on the chip and one on a glowing nanoparticle tag.

The response stayed linear across five orders of magnitude of concentration, with a floor of one particle per microliter. The target was a prostate cancer cell line's exosomes. The authors pitch the sensor for early diagnosis and treatment steering.
pmc-11674506:
Pauline Holmer and co-authors survey fertility worries in childhood cancer survivors in a 2024 Canadian study. Treatment can lower fertility, and that risk weighs on survivors for years. The team measured how common such concerns are and what traits travel with them.

Survivors treated at an Alberta clinic answered a long-term survivor questionnaire over several years. All had been diagnosed before adulthood and were at least two years past therapy. More than three hundred survivors took part, with a smaller group tracked across three rounds. Knowing who worries most helps clinics offer timely counsel and fertility checks. Survivorship care, the study shows, must plan for family life, not only for cure.
pmc-11674706:
Cigarán-Mendez and a large team (2024) tested whether pain thresholds and questionnaires can sort women with migraine from those without. Migraine diagnosis rests on symptoms, so an objective measure would help. The team measured pressure and dynamic pain thresholds at head, neck, and distant sites in 100 women with migraine from specialist centers, half episodic and half chronic, and 50 women without headaches. They also recorded headache features, burden, and anxiety and depression scores.

Women with migraine were more sensitive to pressure everywhere, and the chronic group was more sensitive at the temple muscle than the episodic group. Yet no single measure, clinical, psychological, or physical, reached acceptable accuracy for telling the groups apart. The authors conclude that widespread pressure sensitivity is real in migraine but cannot serve as a diagnostic test, and they call for work on what the sensitivity means clinically.
pmc-11674806:
Tassilo Dege and co-authors report a rare sweat gland cancer on a finger that was first taken for a wart, in work from 2024. The cancer grows slowly, mostly on hands and toes, and mostly in men. Telling it from benign sweat gland tumors is hard on sight alone.

Their patient was a man aged fifty-two with a growing finger tumor. Under the microscope, the growth showed the tube and spike forms of this cancer, with a telling stain pattern. Tests found the virus type HPV-42, which is strongly tied to this cancer, and ruled out a common mutation. The authors say these checks help sort look-alike tumors and guide care, since the cancer can return or spread.
pmc-11674906:
Christopher Sennett and colleagues studied a protein best known from Parkinson disease for its role in blood platelets. Platelets release stored granules when they clump to stop bleeding, and that release depends on a molecular clasp that fuses granules with the cell surface. The protein, alpha-synuclein, helps assemble similar clasps in other cells, but its platelet role was unclear. Writing in twenty twenty-four, the team studied mice that lack the protein and examined platelets in the lab and bleeding in living animals.

Mice without the protein showed weaker platelet clumping, secretion, and sticking, and they bled longer. When platelets switch on, the protein gains a phosphate tag and moves to the cell membrane, where it partners more with clasp parts. That tagging depends on calcium and a known signaling pair, and a natural platelet brake blocks it. The authors conclude the protein helps build the fusion clasp.
pmc-11675006:
Meera Elmasri and colleagues review why a bladder cancer treatment often causes urinary symptoms, in a twenty twenty-four article. The treatment, called BCG, places a weakened germ into the bladder to wake the immune system against the tumor. It works well, yet many patients get urgency, frequent urination, and pelvic pain. Some quit treatment because of these effects, which can hurt their cancer outcome.

The review argues the symptoms grow from swelling, a leakier bladder lining, and changed signaling in the bladder wall. These shifts likely disturb both the nerves that sense fullness and the muscle that squeezes. The authors draw on proof from other bladder disorders and from trials in cancer patients. They call for more work to pin down the exact chain of events.
pmc-11675106:
Ariella Levisohn and co-authors surveyed Black mothers in Boston about care after birth in a 2024 paper. Black birthing people attend postpartum visits at lower rates, a gap tied to worse outcomes. The team surveyed 121 people who had delivered within two years, using validated stress and empowerment scales plus demographic questions.

One third never attended their postpartum appointment. Public insurance, less than a college degree, and working outside the home each predicted missing the visit. Those who attended reported lower stress and higher empowerment scores. The commonest barriers were no time off work, COVID concerns, and no childcare. The authors call for institutional and policy support built around those concrete obstacles.
pmc-11675306:
Mary Fox and co-authors report what state asthma programs need from health information, in a 2024 paper. Asthma is the most common chronic disease of childhood in the United States, affecting about five million children. Control takes work at personal, household, and community levels, and state programs support that work.

The team surveyed the websites of state programs, funded and unfunded by the CDC, then interviewed program managers. Goals and activities looked similar across programs, though funded ones engaged more. Most programs draw teaching materials from federal agencies or national groups. Their top complaints were reading levels set too high and too few translations for diverse families. Managers also asked for more research support, including help for young adults and incarcerated people.
pmc-11675406:
Emel Unal Turhan and Esabil Emrah Koca tested ways to kill germ films on plastic food surfaces. The germ was Escherichia coli, which can grow as a sticky film that resists plain washing. Their method pairs sound-based shaking in warm liquid with mild food acids. Cups of plastic held the films while the team varied acid type, heat, and time across set runs.

Warmth, time, and acid choice each shifted the kill rate in clear ways. The best run used an organic acid at 50 degrees for five minutes and cut live cells by a wide margin. Two ways of counting the film, live cells and cloudiness, agreed well with each other. The team fit a math model that predicts the kill rate from the run settings, for use in food plant checks.
pmc-11675606:
María Elena Soto and five co-authors reported three cases of a heart valve infection marked by oxidative stress, in twenty twenty-four. In this illness, infective endocarditis, germs infect the heart valves and the body's redox balance is lost. The team took valve tissue from three patients who had valve replacement surgery and whose course was tangled by the infection, and set it against tissue from patients without the infection.

The infected tissue showed raised activity of several defense enzymes that fight oxidative damage. At the same time, a key protective compound fell, while two damage markers rose. The authors say the infection tips the valves into oxidative stress, and that the stress feeds on itself in a loop. That loop harms the heart further and may help drive the fatal course the illness can take.
pmc-11675906:
Dmitry Vishnevetskii, Elizaveta Polyakova, Yana Andrianova, and seven colleagues create light-responsive gels in this two thousand twenty-four materials paper. Their system combines a cysteine-silver sol with iodate anions. In darkness, weak, snot-like gels form, but only within a narrow iodate range. The team probed self-assembly with many techniques, from thickness and light measures to electron microscopy and X-ray methods.

Visible light raised gel thickness sharply and changed their color in a striking way. Microscopy showed the network transform: many round and oval particles appeared and the gel fibers thickened. Analysis revealed a redox reaction producing silver iodide and silver oxide particles in and on the sol particles. The base sol responded only to iodate over many other common ions. The authors present a new low-weight gel maker with light-sensitive traits, of possible use for sensing.
pmc-11676106:
Da Hyeon An and co-authors test an alder tree extract and its compound oregonin against muscle loss in lab cells. Muscle loss with age raises death risk and other illness in older adults. Plant compounds that protect muscle could offer gentle new options.

The team used mouse skeletal muscle cells stressed in two ways. Hydrogen peroxide caused oxidative stress, and a steroid drug caused wasting. They then added the hot water extract or oregonin alone. Tests tracked cell survival, cell death signals, and muscle protein balance. They also tracked growth and breakdown pathways inside the cells. The study reports how each treatment shifted those markers. It supports more work on this tree extract for muscle health.
pmc-11676206:
Xianheng Ouyang, Jiangling Pan, Hui Rao, and Qiaoyun Sun model where a eucalyptus-munching wasp could invade next, in a study from 2024. Leptocybe invasa, a tiny gall wasp, has cost eucalyptus growers dearly since escaping its native range on the coattails of global planting. The team fed sightings and climate data into a tuned MaxEnt model.

Temperature, rainfall, and human influence drove the forecast. Comparing niches, the wasp has clearly expanded into conditions it never used at home. Future suitable ground concentrates in East and Southeast Asia, Western Europe, and southern Oceania, and grows under climate scenarios. The authors offer the niche framework as an early-warning template for other invaders.
pmc-11676406:
Anastasia Kornienko and co-authors make tiny particles to boost X ray based cancer therapy in a 2024 study. The therapy uses X rays to trigger light driven chemistry that kills tumor cells. Their particles pair a cerium fluoride core, which glows under X rays, with a vitamin related molecule that helps pass energy into harmful oxygen forms.

The round particles were about 100 nanometers wide and glowed with high yield. Under X rays they made reactive oxygen in a way that depended on acidity. The particles did little harm to normal cells but hurt tumor cells more. With X rays they cut tumor cell survival sharply, raising sensitivity about twofold, while acting as protectors for normal cells.
pmc-11676506:
Nobutake Tamai and colleagues published a biophysics study in 2024. They studied how sugars affect model cell membranes. The membrane lipid is called DMPC for short. Four single sugars were tested in water solutions. Two were common sugars, glucose and fructose. Two were rare sugars, allose and psicose. Heat scanning measured membrane phase changes precisely. Some samples had equal sugar inside and outside vesicles. Others deliberately had unequal sugar concentrations.

Sugar amount barely changed transition temperatures overall. Transition heat also stayed largely stable across sugars. Unequal sugar split the main transition peak clearly. That splitting happened for every sugar tested. Most sugar likely stays outside the membrane interior. Such results inform food and cell preservation science. Rare sugars behaved much like common ones here.
pmc-11676706:
Nikolay Kalitin and co-authors test a compound against brain cancer in 2024. Glioblastoma is a fast, deadly brain tumor with few good drug options. The compound builds on a ring scaffold used for several anti-tumor agents, with a sugar-like group attached.

In dishes, the compound killed diverse tumor cell lines and patient-derived cultures. It beat the standard drug on growth blocking in those tests. Treated cells stalled at a late growth phase in a dose-linked way. In mice, it strongly curbed graft tumor growth, and computer work pointed to a cell-cycle enzyme as a likely target.
pmc-11676906:
Abumayyaleh and co-authors track how age shapes outcomes when a heart enzyme rises but arteries show no blocking culprit. Such troponin rises have many causes and blur into heart attacks with open arteries. Screening over 24,000 records from 2010 to 2021, the team assembled 373 such patients and sorted them into four age bands.

In-hospital trouble climbed steeply with age: major adverse events hit 15 percent of the youngest band and 47 percent of those over seventy. One rhythm glitch peaked instead in the fifties group. Eleven years on, cardiovascular death ran higher in older patients, while other-cause death did not differ. Age, the authors conclude, is a strong risk marker in this murky diagnosis.
pmc-11677006:
Clara Lopes and co-authors present a 2024 review of how the physical environment rewrites the chemistry of brown algae, the large seaweeds that structure many coasts. These algae answer stress with a rich brew of compounds that defend them and interest industry, from medicines to cosmetics and food. What a batch contains depends heavily on where and when it grew.

The review covers studies from 2014 to 2024 on six drivers: water motion, temperature, light, nutrients, season, and saltiness. For each, the authors weigh how the compound profile shifts and what that means for the ecosystem. The synthesis doubles as a prospecting guide for harvesting bioactive compounds reliably.
pmc-11677206:
Asimina Ganotopoulou and co-authors test whether a blood enzyme linked to artery disease also tracks a stiffening of the heart in people with type 2 diabetes, in a 2024 paper. The enzyme, ADAMTS-7, helps remodel tissues and blood vessels and is known to play a part in atherosclerosis, the clogging of arteries. Its tie to heart function was barely studied. The team measured the enzyme in patients' blood and examined their hearts with ultrasound.

The heart problem in view is diastolic dysfunction, where the heart relaxes poorly between beats. That problem rose strongly with age but showed no clear link to enzyme levels. Looking at single ultrasound measures, the enzyme leaned positive only with one timing measure, deceleration time, while age explained most of the rest. The authors say the enzyme's role in this heart problem, and in heart failure among diabetics, needs more study before any verdict.
pmc-11677306:
Gianna Dipalma and nine co-authors review surgery for sleep apnea in children in a 2024 paper. The disorder blocks the airway in sleep and is the most common breathing ill of its kind. For children, cutting out the tonsils and adenoids is the standard fix, but softer options now crowd the field, and the team weighed each against the rest.

Their search swept three databases and found more than twenty thousand papers, of which fifteen fit the review. Full removal beat watchful waiting on behavior and quality of life. Partial tonsil cuts and a throat widening craft gave kind results with less pain after surgery and fewer snags. The authors still call for large trials to settle which child should get which cut.
pmc-11677606:
Dalin Wang and seven co-authors tune a peptide gel to drip-feed a bone-growing protein over three weeks. Their 2024 study works in the dish with a lab-made version of a protein used to fuse spines and heal fractures. Its clinical problem is the burst: too much at once causes side effects. Three gel recipes, differing in how much peptide they contain, were loaded with the same dose and sampled for twenty-one days.

The loosest gel, at half peptide, released the protein steadily across the whole run. The two denser gels released far less after the first week, effectively hoarding the dose. The reason showed in the gel's structure: the loose recipe was more porous, swelled less, and was less stiff. The authors conclude the recipe dial controls the release clock, and that the loose version's profile is the one worth testing in animals.
pmc-11677706:
Tiny robots that swim through fluids could sniff out disease markers far faster than still sensors. Selva Sharma and co-authors review micro- and nanorobots built for color and fluorescence based biosensing. They cover how the robots are made, from carved top-down fabrication to chemistry-driven assembly, and how they move, pushed by magnets, electric fields, light, or living cells.

Motion stirs the sample, so color changes and glow signals develop faster and read more sharply, lifting both sensitivity and selectivity. The authors weigh the field's open problems: keeping the robots stable, making them body-safe, and plugging them into existing test gear. They close with an outlook for chemical and biological sensing.
pmc-11677806:
Daniel Ricardo Delgado and four co-authors published a pharmaceutical chemistry study in twenty twenty-four measuring how the antibiotic sulfamethazine dissolves in mixtures of two solvents across nine temperatures. Solubility decides whether a drug can be formulated, and blending solvents is a standard trick to raise it. The shaking-flask method produced the data.

Solubility was lowest in pure propanol at the coldest temperature and highest in pure acetonitrile at the warmest, rising in a smooth logarithmic pattern between. The effect tracked the mixture's acid-base character rather than its solubility parameter. Dissolving absorbed heat and was driven forward by entropy, with strong compensation between the two. Such maps help formulators pick solvent blends rationally instead of by trial.
pmc-11678106:
Hao Wen and colleagues catalog a master gene family across the sugarcane genome, in this study from twenty twenty-four. GRAS transcription factors steer plant growth, development, and stress response. The hybrid cultivar ZZ1, a commercial Saccharum, had never been surveyed. The haul was enormous: seven hundred forty-seven complete GRAS genes, sorted into eleven subfamilies.

The family proved structurally diverse yet motif-conserved, with promoters crowded by signal-responsive elements, hinting at complex environmental control. Predicted protein structures showed conserved cores with flexible disordered tails. Network analysis tied one member, ShGRAS21A, to the response against smut, a major cane disease. The authors deliver the census as groundwork: breeders and engineers now have addresses for the genes that may govern cane stature, stress tolerance, and disease resistance.
pmc-11678206:
Ahmadi and co-authors test whether fish oil and whey protein, taken around a muscle damaging workout, speed recovery in female futsal players. Fifteen players took part in a blinded crossover study, trying each plan in turn. Their 2024 paper compares doses taken before the workout, after it, or a placebo.

The workout used 200 jumps while wearing weighted vests. Two days later, the before dose group jumped higher and showed stronger leg force than the other groups. Soreness was lower for both dose groups in the first hours after the workout. Some measures, such as swelling and flexibility, did not differ. The authors say timing matters, with the before dose working best.
pmc-11678306:
Elena Kuvaeva and co-authors reconstruct how a fruit fly gene lost pieces of its ancestral toolkit, and what that loss means across evolution. Their 2024 study concerns the d4 gene family, whose proteins help steer development and cell fate in many animals. Mammals carry three family members with a full three-part domain structure; the fly carries two relatives, each missing parts.

One fly protein keeps only the first domain. Tracing gene copies across insect and vertebrate lineages, the authors found duplications in flies and repeated, independent specialization elsewhere. Mammals even make a shortened splice form resembling the fly's stripped protein. They propose that producing such partial proteins is a recurring evolutionary move, not a defect. The fly gene, toothrin, may act like that mammalian short form. The study turns an oddity of fly genetics into a general lesson: evolution edits proteins by subtraction as readily as by addition.
pmc-11678406:
Di Kong and co-authors test a known pattern in ecology on scraps of city woodland in Qingdao, China. On true islands, the count of species grows with area, but on very small islands that growth slows or stops, a break called the small-island effect.

The team surveyed seventeen remnant patches and found 331 plants. The break in the pattern showed for woody plants only, with area bounds that split trees from shrubs. For shrubs, patch shape and sealed ground mattered. For trees, the gap to a source of new species and night light were among the drivers the authors name.
pmc-11678606:
Zhengying Zhang and co-authors study a gene in a small alga that helps switch on growth through a key cell pathway, in a 2024 paper. The pathway, known by the short name TOR, helps cells balance growth with food and energy supply. In this alga, the gene makes a protein with a repeated shape seen in related proteins.

The team raised the gene's activity in the alga and saw stronger growth through photosynthesis, the process that turns light into food. Gene activity scans showed shifts in transport proteins and in a signaling path that moves sugars and other goods across cell walls. The authors argue the gene helps tie light capture, sugar use, and energy signals together through the TOR pathway.
pmc-11678706:
Andreea Herascu and co-authors wrote this 2024 review on insulin resistance in people with type 1 diabetes. Insulin resistance is best known as the core fault in type 2 diabetes, yet it can also develop in type 1. When it does, blood sugar targets grow harder to reach and the outlook worsens.

The review explains how the resistance arises and what it travels with, such as excess weight and a sedentary life. It also covers the harm that follows, above all a higher risk to the heart and blood vessels. Since these patients already take insulin, resistance must be gauged by stand-in measures like an estimated glucose disposal rate. The authors survey the main fixes, from diet and exercise to drugs such as metformin.
pmc-11678806:
Jessica Patricia Wiseman and Divya Maitreyi Chari wrote a lab study in two thousand twenty-four on materials that might help heal brain injury. For deep wounds in the brain, no therapy now helps tissue regrow. Bridges made of biomaterials are one hopeful route, and materials already approved for surgery could reach patients faster.

Testing such materials needs models that mimic real injury without heavy cost or animal use. The authors used thin slices of living brain tissue, kept alive in the lab, with a simulated injury. Into that setting they placed a surgical-grade biomaterial. Then they watched how nerve cells reacted to and grew with the material.
pmc-11678906:
Céline Damiani and a team of co-authors test new malaria drug parts in the lab, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. The compounds are arylamino alcohols, kin to the partner drug mefloquine. The team checked how well each one blocks the forming of beta-hematin, a stand-in for the waste crystals malaria germs make.

They compared three pairs of mirror-image forms against two strains of the malaria germ. Chloroquine, mefloquine, and enpiroline served as reference drugs. Some new forms killed germs well, blocked crystal growth strongly, and harmed liver cells little. The results help explain how this drug family works and which forms merit more study.
pmc-11679706:
Jerome Dinga, Victor Titanji, and nine co-authors linked malaria and body nutrient levels in young children in Cameroon, in work from twenty twenty-four. In Buea Health District, malaria and poor diet both hit children under five hard. Germs can also drain the very nutrients a child needs. The team drew blood from eighty children in early twenty twenty-four and measured a panel of nutrient markers.

Levels shifted between sick and well children. Ferritin, a marker tied to iron stores, ran higher in children with malaria. The team reads such shifts with care, since illness itself can move these markers. Still, the data help clinics judge when low nutrients and malaria feed each other.
pmc-11679906:
Xiaozhou Ye and co-authors review machine learning for reading human activity from sensors in work from 2024. Such systems use data from worn or placed sensors to tell what a person is doing.

The review focuses on a key problem: sensor data vary a lot between people, devices, and settings, while many studies assume the data are uniform. The authors sort the kinds of variation, match each kind with fitting learning methods, and list datasets in use. Fixing this gap could raise accuracy, cut computing cost, and help build personal models with less labeled data.
pmc-11680006:
Wenxiang Zeng and co-authors show that microplastic feeding worsens joint inflammation in lupus-prone mice, in a 2024 study. Microplastics enter bodies through air and food, and their health effects are only beginning to be mapped. Lupus frequently inflames joints, yet no work had asked what the particles do to lupus arthritis. Female mice of a lupus-like strain received oral microplastics at two doses from eight weeks of age.

Exposed mice showed more synovial damage, worse knee structure and function, and higher oxidative stress and cell death. Two signaling pathways were activated in the joint tissue, as the title names. For an autoimmune disease with joint pain as a daily burden, a common pollutant acting as an aggravator deserves attention.
pmc-11680106:
Edward Mocarski, writing alone in two thousand twenty-four, reviews cytomegalovirus biology through the lens of cell death suppression. These betaherpesviruses persist for life in their hosts by outmaneuvering the immune system.

Programmed cell death is a host defense that can kill infected cells before the virus finishes replicating. Over two decades, studies of virus-encoded death suppressors have mapped how cytomegaloviruses block apoptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, and a newer mitochondrial protease pathway. Those inhibitors also calm inflammation, helping the virus balance persistence against clearance. Mocarski argues the suppression machinery explains both the virus's success and its danger when host immunity fails.
pmc-11680206:
An eight-year-old beagle kept swallowing pieces of his cotton toys, and months later he arrived at the clinic off his food, vomiting, with a sore belly and dark stools. Andrada Negoescu and co-authors report what surgeons found: a tumor growing in the wall of his small intestine. The removed mass proved to be an osteosarcoma, a bone cancer growing far from any bone, with cotton fibers embedded inside it.

The tumor cells carried the markers pathologists expected for that diagnosis. Seven months later, nodules appeared in the dog's liver. He died ten months after the surgery. The authors present the case as the first documented one of its kind, possibly seeded by the swallowed fibers.
pmc-11680306:
Jia Li and eleven co-authors test how well rabies vaccine production removes leftover DNA from host cells. The Vero cell rabies vaccine is the most widely used human rabies vaccine. Leftover host DNA raises safety concerns, and world rules cap both cell passage counts and final DNA levels.

The team tracks each key production step for antigen recovery and DNA removal. Sensitive lab tests measure DNA amount and fragment size, and an assay measures viral antigen content. Rates are computed step by step and checked across several commercial batches for stability. The analysis shows which steps do the heavy lifting for DNA removal and supports the scientific basis of the current process.
pmc-11680406:
Polina Iarema and co-authors study a virus that infects gut bacteria, pulled from a drug mix sold to treat infections. The virus, named Sxt1, was grown on a common lab strain and turns out to be a close kin of a classic virus called T3, yet with a wider range of hosts.

The team set out the genes and traits of the new virus and tested which strains of the host it could infect. Some inner parts differ from its kin, and its tail fibers are longer, with changes in the zones that pick a host. Those changes may explain why Sxt1 can infect more strains than T3 can.
pmc-11681606:
Alham Alonaizan and co-authors review blood fat levels in Saudi patients with lupus, in a 2024 paper. Lupus raises heart risk, and abnormal lipids are part of that story. The team examined 138 patients at a Riyadh hospital clinic, most of them women with an average age near thirty-seven, and set their lipid panels against disease activity and drug use.

Average cholesterol and fat values sat in moderate ranges. Use of hydroxychloroquine came with slightly higher lipid levels, though not significantly, and steroids showed no clear effect. Patients whose lupus had hit the kidneys carried higher triglycerides and related fats than those without kidney involvement. The authors call for lipid watching as part of routine lupus care in this population.
pmc-11683506:
Yanan Zhao and co-authors surveyed, in a 2024 study, how caring for a child with autism reshapes parents' work in China. Care loads fall unevenly on mothers and fathers, but hard numbers were scarce. The team ran a national online survey of families.

Parents of 5,018 children and teens with autism, aged two to seventeen, took part. Only 37.3 percent of mothers held jobs, against 96.7 percent of fathers. Over half of mothers had quit work to give care, against 2.8 percent of fathers. Mothers stayed employed more often when single, less schooled, or backed by grandparents. Grandparent help also kept fathers employed. The gap frames care policy as a gender equity issue.
pmc-11683606:
Abdullah Alshememry and co-workers develop antibiotic nanoparticles for eye drops, in a 2024 paper. The drug delafloxacin kills a wide range of bacteria that infect the eye. Loading it into tiny polymer particles could help it stay and act longer on the eye surface.

The team made particles by a standard emulsion method and checked their size, charge, and drug content. The best batch trapped most of the drug and released it slowly over four days. Tests showed no unwanted reaction between drug and polymer. Lab tests found strong activity against several bacteria, including a drug-resistant staph strain. The work is presented as a step toward topical eye treatment.
pmc-11684006:
Julia Kinsolving and co-authors issue a caution in 2024 about a supposed cancer drug lead. A computer screen had flagged a compound as blocking a receptor that drives gut cancers, based on a glow-based test. Such tests can mislead when the compound blocks the glow itself rather than the target.

On retesting, the compound proved to be a strong blocker of the glow enzyme at the same dose reported for the cancer effect. Two glow-free methods, a receptor sensor and a gene readout, showed no effect on the receptor or its target gene. The team underlines why screening hits need counter-screens that check the detection tool itself.
pmc-11686706:
Reem Hamdy Mohammed and co-authors compare imaging for early rheumatoid arthritis in a 2024 study. Ultrasound of muscles and joints can spot inflammation that plain X-rays miss. The question is how each method lines up with disease activity and daily function scores.

Adults with disease under two years and active symptoms had both scans across many joints on both sides. Activity was scored with DAS28 and function with a health questionnaire. Forty patients, mostly women in early middle age, took part. If ultrasound tracks activity better, clinics can adjust drugs sooner. The study gives rheumatology teams local proof for a tool many already own.
pmc-11688206:
Jiayan Huang and co-authors test whether large language models can sort small liver nodules under a standard ultrasound scheme, published in 2024. The scheme, CEUS LI-RADS, is used for patients at risk of liver cancer. The question was whether chat models could apply its rules to small lesions well enough to help in diagnosis.

The study used records of high-risk patients with untreated small lesions over many years. Four chat models were given structured imaging traits from the reports. Two of the models agreed with themselves strongly across repeats, and beat the other two. One model also found more true cancer cases than its close peer, at similar rates on other measures. The authors frame this as a feasibility test, not yet a clinical tool.
pmc-11688306:
Rui Lv, Daochun Li, Shiwei Zhao and colleagues simulated how exercise intensity interacts with coronary stent design in 2024. Their computer model couples a balloon, stent, plaque and artery with the blood flow through them, and it follows the stent as it expands and settles.

The shape of the stent's connectors changed the stress on plaque and artery wall. Risky flow zones, with low wall shear stress and long particle residence time, clustered near the stent ends. Moderate exercise shrank those zones a lot, but maximal exercise added little further benefit. The findings offer design guidance for connectors and suggest moderate activity may be the sweet spot for patients after stenting.
pmc-11688806:
Gretchen Tucker and co-authors examine unmet needs of non-spousal dementia care partners in a 2024 study. Research on these helpers outside marriage is thin. Needs may differ by race and gender in patterned ways. A structured care needs assessment supplied the measures.

Data covered over four hundred care partners from two community studies. Partners were mostly women and mostly Black in the sample. Gender alone showed no link to overall unmet need share. A race-by-sex interaction emerged strongly instead. Black male partners carried the highest unmet need rates. White female partners carried the lowest rates. Behavior management needs differed sharply by race. Substitute decision-making needs differed even more sharply. Documentation needs also ran higher for Black partners. The authors urge tailored support for non-spousal helpers. One-size programs will miss the worst-served groups.
pmc-11688906:
Raquael Joiner and co-authors tracked how relationships change as people step into caring for an ageing family member, in a 2024 study. Family caregivers supply most elder care, often at a cost to their own well-being, yet outcomes vary widely. Good relationships are thought to buffer the strain, but it was unclear whether gaps in relationship quality appear only after caregiving starts.

Using eight waves of a national ageing study covering three hundred and sixty-six caregivers, the team modeled relationship quality before, during, and after the shift into care. On average, relationship quality did not shift significantly across the transition. But people differed: those who began with stronger relationships declined less before care started, then dipped more sharply at the onset. The findings suggest earlier relationship strength shapes how the caregiving years unfold.
pmc-11689006:
Deborah Paone, Jeanne Schuller, and Sarah Szanton describe in 2024 an add-on to a proven home program for older adults, this time aimed at their care partners too. CAPABLE helps elders age safely at home through nursing, therapy, and home repairs; the new version formally includes the family helpers who make it work.

Built over three years with partners, elders, clinicians, and managers shaping the design, the prototype was piloted in 2023 at three American sites with at least a year of CAPABLE experience. Follow-up surveys and interviews judged how the partner support landed. The work treats caregivers as part of the care team, not furniture.
pmc-11689106:
Sarah Canham and three colleagues compare how older and younger people experiencing homelessness get around, in a 2024 study. The team re-analyzed interviews with 18 shelter residents in Salt Lake County, Utah, sorting answers by age group. Both groups relied on public transit, a homeless-services shuttle, and walking.

Older participants also used taxis when they could afford or share them, and they rode transit mainly to reach health care, while younger ones rode to jobs. Costs pinched both groups. Older riders asked for benches to rest on, more public bathrooms, and safer crosswalks. The authors say the age split points to practical fixes for transport equity.
pmc-11689306:
Rui Kang and Jia-jia Zhou ask what makes older migrants in China want to settle where they moved. The study surveys 598 migrants aged fifty and up in Shenzhen and Guangzhou. Settlement intent and willingness to transfer household registration are the outcomes. Adaptation, hometown attachment, and neighborhood factors are weighed together. Multinomial models sort who leans toward staying, leaving, or undecided.

Settling in psychologically and joining community life raise the odds of staying and transferring registration. Volunteering and welfare access cut reluctance. Hometown ties pull the other way: close friends back home and living parents there resist settling. Oddly, rating the local physical setting highly raised indecision. Policy, the pair suggest, should feed belonging, not just services.
pmc-11689406:
Basia Belza presents, in a 2024 symposium paper, a session on scoping reviews as a method for mapping research on healthy aging. A scoping review sorts the literature in a field by its nature, features, and volume. It suits young or sprawling fields, where the first need is a map rather than a verdict.

The session teaches how to run such a review, then shows recent examples. One builds on a World Health Organization report to sort ways of reaching health equity for older adults. A second takes up social frailty, the risk that comes from lacking social resources. A third sorts evidence on mealtime interventions for people with dementia in care homes, using a person, setting, and activity model. Later talks cover music based interventions and community activity programs for dementia. Together they show the method's range.
pmc-11689506:
William Chopik wrote this 2024 paper on life satisfaction and how sharply people react to daily stress as they age. Past work ties well-being to health, but most studies track stress over short spans only. Chopik used three waves of a national daily-life study, run from about 1996 to 2017, with 1,500 adults, to track change over two decades.

Stress reactivity fell with age, which matched earlier work. People high in life satisfaction reacted less overall, and the link held on both calm and heavy stress days. A second model hinted the arrow may also run the other way: calmer stress responses may lift later life satisfaction. Chopik frames daily stress as one path by which well-being builds up over a life.
pmc-11689706:
Dana Ketcher and seven co-authors share lessons, in twenty twenty-four, from an Indigenous dementia project. Their work is community-based, meaning the community helps guide the study. Yet at the data analysis stage, community voices are often left out. That gap matters most for groups that have faced bias and loss. The team built a way to include community members in reading and coding talks and texts.

Their frame brings in community researchers and advisors, even those new to such work. It aims to check scholar bias and center local values and world views. The paper walks through their step-by-step method, built by trial over many rounds.
pmc-11689806:
Pamela Elfenbein describes a campus program that brings caregivers of all ages into one monthly circle. Most caregivers of older adults are over 45, yet a 2020 national study found that 11 percent are also in school, full or part time. Her 2024 presentation shares the plan of a group run by Adult Children of Aging Parents in Hall County. Students, staff, faculty, and community caregivers meet side by side.

Each meeting offers information, resources, and peer support, aiming at a better life for caregivers and the older adults they serve. Learning flows both ways: young and old trade skills and views. The plan rests on a named principle for age-friendly universities, the fourth such principle, which promotes shared learning across ages. Elfenbein gives the steps in full so other campuses can build a similar program.
pmc-11689906:
Kina White and Paulita Edwards-Childs tell how the health department in Mississippi built an age-friendly public health system. The state is not known for public health spending. While the state's total population falls, its population aged 65 and older grew a lot from 2010 to 2021. The health of older residents called for a planned reply.

With national aging and health groups as partners, the department took up a six-part frame for age-friendly public health systems. It earned exemplar status. It formed an advisory committee from many sectors and a statewide action plan. It made a healthy aging data report and county profiles with over 120 indicators.
