Staff gave them by hand to mayors in all 82 counties. With partners, it also built a champion program of older volunteers.
pmc-11690006:
Kina White and Paulita Edwards-Childs describe, in twenty twenty-four, Mississippi's public health plan for dementia. The state has the highest death rate from Alzheimer's disease and related illness in the nation. Risk is higher in rural areas, and all of the state's counties lack enough doctors. Black residents and tribal groups bear a large share of the burden.

The plan, part of a national BOLD effort, stresses joint work across groups. Steps include town teaching, aid for caregivers, early checks, and dementia-friendly services. It also works with tribal nations and weaves in their healing ways. Churches and towns that welcome people with dementia are early examples.
pmc-11690106:
Sean Halpin sums up a 2024 meeting session on cancer care for older adults, from first diagnosis through life after treatment. Age adds strain to an already hard path, with more health needs and more stress at each step. Four talks in the session look at that path from four angles.

One talk studies how nurses teach patients with a blood cancer before a stem cell procedure. A second follows immigrant Latina patients through their care. A third looks at peer support for older Nigerian women with breast cancer that has spread. The last uses survey data on symptom load and life quality in older survivors. Together the talks show why care must fit age and culture, not just the tumor.
pmc-11690406:
Katherine McGilton, Karen Spilsbury, and Carl Thompson lead a symposium, in twenty twenty-four, on fixing long-term care world-wide. Years of study have not moved many care home rules, they note. Staff face poor terms and shaky jobs. Homes struggle to hire and keep good staff, and to give care that fits each resident. The session brings work from several countries to one stage.

Talks cover how to draw and keep staff, and the right mix of skills on a team. One talk shares a nurse-led change to breakfast time in care homes. Others review steps taken by states in Europe, both before and during COVID-19.
pmc-11690606:
Joseph Gaugler and co-authors test, in a 2024 study, a coaching program for one of caregiving's hardest transitions: moving a relative with dementia into residential care. The Residential Care Transition Module offers six telehealth sessions of psychosocial support and education. Two hundred forty family caregivers were randomized to the program or usual care and surveyed over twelve months on stress, depressive symptoms, competence, and confidence.

On the headline measures, the program group did no better than the control group. Two subgroups told a different story. Caregivers whose relatives had moved within the prior three months showed falling depressive symptoms early on. Employed caregivers in the program grew in self-efficacy across the year. The authors read the mixed result as a lesson in heterogeneity: dementia caregiving is not one situation, and support lands where timing and circumstance fit. Measuring what caregivers themselves value may show benefits the standard scales missed.
pmc-11690706:
Ginger Williams and six co-authors describe how Colorado State Extension adapted a healthy aging course. Their twenty twenty-four report covers the Aging Mastery Program, a ten-session course in English and Spanish. The team took it to Native American, Spanish-speaking immigrant, and East African refugee groups in Colorado. These groups face high rates of poor health and isolation, in part due to language gaps.

Staff used state data to pick sites, then held listening sessions to build trust. They trained and paid local champions to teach the course. Champions later helped write grants and plan new sessions. Work is now set to grow to eight more towns.
pmc-11690806:
Laura Sands and co-authors track in 2024 how often older adults who need help with daily tasks go without it, and how that state changes over time. An unmet need means a person cannot finish a task, such as moving around or washing, because no one is there to help. Past work had not asked whether that state comes and goes or stays fixed.

The team used a national study of aging from 2011 to 2014 and looked at three pairs of yearly talks in a row. Most older adults who needed help with movement or self care had no unmet need at any point. A small share had unmet needs again and again. The study also sorts who tends to gain help and who tends to lose it. Care plans can use that to catch people before a gap in help becomes a crisis.
pmc-11691206:
Jennifer Crook and co-authors studied extreme heat and food insecurity among low-income older adults in a 2024 paper. Heat strains health, and older people with little money already struggle to eat well. The team interviewed 45 adults in Central Florida communities and measured food security with a standard federal questionnaire.

Thirteen participants were food insecure and 32 were secure. The insecure group reported stronger heat effects on their health, daily activities, and sleep than the secure group. No clear difference appeared for food access or hydration itself. The authors argue that heat and hunger compound each other in this group, so aid programs should plan for both at once.
pmc-11691306:
Gretchen Tanbonliong presents a bill of rights for people living with obesity, in a 2024 symposium summary. Obesity is now classed as a chronic condition, and age adds its own hurdles on top. Weight bias and age bias together block fair care, leaving many patients blamed rather than treated. The bill was drafted to reset that stance, promising respect and full, unbiased care for every patient.

The symposium gathers the voices that shaped the bill, from patients to providers. It shows how clinics can put the bill's rules to work in daily care. It also lays out how doctors and patients can team up around its research-backed principles. Tanbonliong frames the bill as both a shield for patients and a guide for systems that want equity in weight care.
pmc-11691406:
Kimberly Delgado and Donna Roberson wrote a 2024 study on how nursing home staff spot urinary infections in residents. Wrong antibiotic use is common in these homes and can harm or kill frail residents. Urinary infection is the top stated reason for those drugs. Doctors are often off-site, so nurses lead the early call.

The team interviewed nursing staff about cases they suspected. Three themes came out of the talks. A resident acting far from their norm was the key early sign. Staff took ownership of the response, at times bending set protocols to put the resident first. The authors urge that nurses join future studies.
pmc-11691506:
Yi-Hsiu Lin and Tsuann Kuo published a study in 2024 on a life review program in Taiwan, seen from the perspective of the leaders who run it. In life review groups, older adults meet weekly to reflect on their life events, guided by set themes. The program has been implemented in Taiwan for more than ten years.

More than eighty program leaders participated in a survey and interviews. Most were women, and most held at least a college degree. Leaders reported that the groups helped older adults communicate with family members and strengthened family bonding. The groups also gave participants the courage to face difficult past events. Participants integrated their past into a coherent whole and looked to the future with more hope. The findings link the program to less depression, less loneliness, and greater self-confidence among older adults.
pmc-11691606:
Pui Yin Cheung, David Curtis, and Ming Wen study how neighborhood street layout and food access link to mortality among older adults, in a 2024 paper. Disadvantage across several dimensions has drawn growing attention. The authors ask whether education and gender together reveal new neighborhood effects.

Walkable street connectivity and living in a low-food-access area are the two traits examined. Both matter for older adults with limited function. Data come from two waves of a national study, covering those aged sixty-five and over with 12,141 person-years over fifteen years. Models control for personal and area traits such as income and education mix.
pmc-11691706:
Gerald Liao, Jackson Wezeman, and Warren Ladiges gave a symposium talk in two thousand twenty-four proposing the house cricket as a model for aging research. Aging studies use many animal models, each with trade-offs in lifespan, cost, and access to organs. No model captures all of human aging, so fresh candidates are worth testing.

The domestic cricket offers a short life, simple but well-defined organs, cheap upkeep, and new nerve growth in a brain region like the hippocampus. In a pilot, adult crickets fed chow mixed with flax oil lived significantly longer than controls. The authors stress how fast and cheap such dietary tests can run.
pmc-11691806:
Lindsey Anderson and co-authors probe body chemistry in blood and muscle of men with cancer who face wasting, in a study from 2024. Cancer wasting eats muscle and cuts daily function, and no approved drug care exists in the United States or Europe.

Seventy five men set for belly surgery gave blood and muscle samples. The team tied chemical patterns to grip strength, stair climb power, muscle size, and past weight loss. Fat chemistry was off in muscle and blood where muscle was low or weight had fallen. Paths tied to worse stair power faded once strict checks were applied.
pmc-11691906:
Loneliness in nursing homes deepened during pandemic lockdowns, and one project asked whether a self-driving robot could help fill the gap. Zeynep Abul, Sakeena Raza, and Lynn McNicoll report early findings in this 2024 paper from a quality improvement project. The robot, called Temi, moves on its own and carries a screen for face-to-face contact.

The team interviewed fifty-four long-term residents and asked a playful question: with a magic wand, what would you do with the robot? Two thirds asked for activities with it. Games led the list, with chess, cards, bingo, and word games named most. Others wanted walks outside, singing, drawing, exercise, or plain talk. Fifteen residents wanted nothing to do with the robot. The team plans to shape the robot's program around these wishes.
pmc-11692006:
Lenora Smith and Charles O'Brien present a 2024 paper on Neurospective, a phone app platform built to catch cognitive decline early. No cure exists for Alzheimer disease, so spotting decline early matters: lifestyle steps may slow the slide from mild impairment. The app aims to make screening cheap, engaging, and available anywhere.

Its tests are mini-games modelled on standard clinic screens, probing language, memory, reasoning, and problem solving. The platform also gathers broader user data and plans machine learning on top, to sharpen the screening over time. The authors present the design as a route to dementia checks that reach people long before a clinic visit would.
pmc-11692106:
Kathy Lee, Jessica Cassidy, and Soeun Jang interview community groups serving elders with dementia in a 2024 study. Home and community organizations are the front door for many families, yet how they reach people and what they actually deliver varies widely and is rarely documented.

Providers from nine organizations described their playbooks in depth. Three themes emerged: shaping outreach and services to each culture, coaxing isolated elders and caregivers to engage, and collaborating across organizations. Groups serving diverse communities leaned on inventive routes, from faith-based outreach to edutainment with stories and drama. The study hands funders and planners a field view of what creative care looks like.
pmc-11692206:
Lillian Hung and five co-authors published a study in 2024 on families using telepresence robots with relatives who live in long-term care homes. A telepresence robot lets family members visit by screen. When a loved one moves into care, family caregivers shift from being the main caregiver to being visitors, a transition many find difficult. The COVID-19 pandemic made it harder, with strict protocols and long periods apart.

The study ran from May 2021 to August 2023 in five urban care homes in British Columbia, Canada. Twenty family care partners used the robots and shared their experiences in interviews. Four themes stood out. The robots reduced the burden on care partners and helped them work with staff. They also gave care partners more control over their own role and expanded what visits could accomplish. The authors say more research is needed on how sustainable such use is over time.
pmc-11692306:
Thinh Huynh and co-authors report early results, in a 2024 conference paper, on how a single bout of exercise shifts brain-support factors and stress hormone levels in middle-aged and older adults. Such shifts may explain part of how regular activity guards the brain. The team asked whether long exercise history or current daily activity better predicts the response.

Fifty-four healthy adults took a fitness test, wore activity trackers for a week, then exercised once for blood checks. Long-term history did not predict either response. People who moved more day to day showed a stronger brain-factor rise and a smaller stress hormone rise. The brain-factor link faded with age, which hints that timing of activity matters.
pmc-11692406:
Makenna Green, Jamie Mayer, Laura White, and Gail Kouame review service learning as a pipeline into dementia care jobs, in a 2024 paper. Dementia cases climb as the population ages, and the care workforce gap widens with education cited as a barrier. Service learning puts students to work with patients while they study.

The review searched seven databases and kept thirty-two studies of health majors whose courses included community work with adults with dementia. Clinical rotations were excluded to isolate the teaching model. Most programs leaned on preparatory training plus direct contact and reflection. The authors extract student traits, program parts, and outcomes across the set. Their aim is a recipe for courses that both teach and recruit the next dementia workforce.
pmc-11692506:
Katherine Luci and co-authors pilot a video-group program for veterans living with mild cognitive impairment, in a 2024 study. The nine-session program, MiND-MCI, mixes peer support with lessons on memory, coping, and healthy habits. Sixteen veterans aged 61 to 79, all testing in the impaired range, joined from home. Attendance and retention were tracked, along with usability and acceptability questionnaires.

Eighty-eight percent stayed the course, attending seven of nine sessions on average. Eleven veterans joined at least three quarters of the sessions. Satisfaction scores ran high across three separate measures. Facilitators flagged tech troubles and wide variation in impairment as the main hurdles, and prized the peer support. The authors judge the format feasible and worth a fuller trial.
pmc-11692706:
Angela Perone and three co-authors set out a framework that puts power at the heart of fair aging, in a report published in 2024. Loneliness and social isolation in old age are well-recorded harms, but most work is set in the United States and skips power. Their framework joins power theory with the social and political drivers of health. It maps five kinds of power and how they shape who receives what care.

Three cases show the framework at work. One reads loneliness among rural Indigenous elders in Taiwan. One reads isolation among city elders in mainland China. One reads both among nursing home residents in Spain. Each case maps how power shapes the drivers and where fair action can step in. The authors aim the framework at researchers, government staff, and hands-on workers alike.
pmc-11692806:
Yunhwan Lee and co-authors study gaps in healthy aging in South Korea in this 2024 paper. Healthy life span there reached 73 years in 2021, among the highest in the world. The team built a healthy aging index from body, mind, and social measures, and tracked it across four national surveys from 2011 to 2020.

Each survey held about 10,000 people aged 65 or over. Healthy aging rose overall across the decade, but the gap between the most and least schooled groups widened. One birth group, born from 1935 to 1944, scored notably lower, which the authors link to hardship in early life. The index also fell steeply with age.
pmc-11692906:
Jay Kayser and Kimson Johnson present a 2024 study of social isolation and thinking in older US adults. Past work assumed that gaining and losing isolation mirror each other. They use eight years of national aging data to test that idea, tracking changes within the same people.

Rising isolation raised the odds of possible or probable dementia. Falling isolation did not lower those odds. The same one-way pattern held for word recall: harm from rising isolation, no gain from falling isolation. Sense of direction broke the pattern, improving and worsening both ways. Work speed and planning showed no link. The authors argue that stopping isolation early beats trying to reverse its harm.
pmc-11693006:
Limei Chen, Mengzhao Yan, and Philip Rozario ask whether taking part in community life still helps older adults after the strain of COVID-19. Group activity and social ties are thought to lift health and mood in later life. The pandemic's curbs put that claim to a hard test. Their 2024 study links two waves of a national survey on social life, health, and aging.

Volunteering and going to meetings tied strongly to better partner relationships, even under pandemic stress. Faith activities also helped, most when stress ran high. Social support boosted the gains, though it could shrink the solo gain from volunteering. Group life also shielded body and mind health from stress. The authors call community life a buffer worth guarding.
pmc-11693306:
Matthew Brault asked whether vision loss at first measure predicts a move into residential care for older adults, in a 2024 study. Nursing homes and assisted living are common in later life and costly, so early risk signs matter. The study drew on a national aging survey from 2021 and 2022.

Vision was tested on a tablet tool in over 2,700 participants, covering near sight, distance sight, and contrast sensitivity. About two percent lived in residential care a year later. Near and distance sight loss showed no firm link with that move. Contrast sensitivity loss did: it more than doubled the odds. Walking speed and repeated falls explained part of that link. Brault suggests contrast loss may flag risk on its own, and that eye care could delay placement for some adults.
pmc-11694706:
Samuel Carbunaru and co-authors build a machine learning model to predict survival after bladder surgery, and check it for fairness, published in 2024. Models of this kind are now common in health care. Yet a model can work unevenly across sex or racial groups, which is a real concern in bladder cancer care.

The team trained several model types on a national cancer data base to predict five-year survival after the bladder is removed. They scored both accuracy and fairness across groups. A boosted tree model scored best at first pass. They then tried three methods meant to cut unfair gaps between groups, and compared how much each method helped while keeping the model useful.
pmc-11696406:
Song Lv and co-authors described a 2024 solar system that tries to use the full range of sunlight. Solar cells waste light outside their working band as heat, which lowers their output. The team's design splits the light by color: bands the cell can use go to the cell, and the rest go to a heat-based generator. A passive cooling layer that sheds heat to the sky widens the gap the generator works across.

Outdoor tests checked the design against a computer model, and cell surface heat fell by a small margin. The team then used the model to test how wind, damp air, and air heat change output. Their study suggests pairing light splitting with sky cooling can raise how much of each sunbeam becomes useful power.
pmc-11700606:
Livestock farming has long reacted to problems after animals fall sick or fall behind. Caleb Grohmann and Jared Decker argue in a 2025 overview that sensors and artificial intelligence flip that order, letting managers act before trouble lands.

Cameras, wearables, and production records now stream in automatically around the clock. Learning models fold those streams into daily forecasts of health, well-being, and output for each animal or herd. Managers can plan interventions from those forecasts instead of from yesterday's losses. The new measurements also give breeders better traits to select for, targeting the real drivers of sustainable production rather than rough stand-ins. The authors frame the shift as farm-wide, not a single gadget.
pmc-11706606:
Jiwon Jeong and co-authors found a brain signal in fruit flies that stores early social experience, in a study published in 2024. Flies form social clusters, but the rules behind their spacing were murky. The team measured how far apart individual flies keep in a group across 175 bred strains. Strains that huddled close tended to grow slowly and eat less, yet group living made up for those costs.

Flies raised alone lost the benefits of group life and could not adjust their spacing under stress. Gene scans showed isolation reprogrammed a small set of pathways, above all a brain chemical called Drosulfakinin. Three pairs of brain cells make that signal, and in males it acts through one receptor to keep social spacing flexible. Tweaking those cells mimicked the effects of isolation or company. The authors propose a dedicated memory circuit for early social life.
pmc-11709506:
Hao Hu, Jason Ulrich, and David Holtzman ask whether tau itself drives T cell responses in a mouse model, in work from 2025. Alzheimer's disease involves clumps of amyloid and tau proteins in the brain. Past work found strong T cell activity where tau builds up, and removing T cells blocked tau driven damage.

The team predicts which tau fragments could be shown to T cells by immune markers. Early tests found several tau peptides that trigger strong T cell responses in the model mice. Tau pieces found outside cells and new shapes formed in tangles may act as triggers. The group also built T cell lines to test direct effects. Results support tau as a self antigen in this setting.
pmc-11709606:
Manchumad Manjavong and a large team of co-authors test a short questionnaire spotting thinking problems through everyday function. The full tool asks how well people manage daily tasks; the short form keeps twelve items. The team drew data from a major Alzheimer's study with about sixteen hundred participants, split by diagnosis from healthy to dementia. They checked how well the short form separates groups, whether answers come from the person or a study partner, and how scoring style matters.

Partner answers separated healthy people from impaired ones better than self-reports. Adding a memory-concern question lifted self-report accuracy to match. The short form separated mild impairment from healthy aging and from dementia, though telling mild impairment from dementia by self-report was weak. Partner scores did better at every step. The authors offer cut-off values for clinics needing a fast screen.
pmc-11709806:
Changyi Ji and four co-authors study in 2025 how brain cells behave early in a mouse model of tau disease, a class of illness tied to tangled tau protein and memory loss. Earlier work with light-based imaging had already shown odd cell activity in awake mice at later disease stages.

Here the team records calcium signals from single cells and looks at how whole networks act together at an early stage. They ask what drives the drop in cell activity and the breakdown of network patterns. Understanding these early changes could point to when treatment might help most, before clear symptoms appear.
pmc-11709906:
Robin Hilsabeck and co-authors test three quick cognitive screens for sorting referrals to a dementia clinic in this 2025 paper. Specialists in dementia are scarce, and wait lists for full evaluation are long. Clinics need a fair way to decide who most needs the deep workup.

Staff gave brief screens during intake interviews with older adults. The study asks how well each screen sorts patients by level of impairment. Good sorting sends urgent or unclear cases to full testing first. It can also spare clearly mild cases a long, costly wait. The results give clinic managers evidence for triage rules. Fair triage matters as demand for memory care keeps rising.
pmc-11710006:
Hsiao-Tien Chien Hagar and Min-Hao Kuo studied how abnormal tau protein harms brain cells, in work published in twenty twenty-five on Alzheimer disease. Tau that carries too many phosphate groups is a hallmark of the disease, but how it kills cells is still unclear. The team made this altered tau in the lab and applied it to a human nerve-like cell line. They tracked cell shape and survival, and used mass spectrometry to see which proteins changed within hours of treatment.

The altered tau caused strong shape changes and cell death within about a day. One protein, heme oxygenase one, dropped more sharply than any other early on. The authors then tested whether restoring that protein protects cells, and whether the two proteins bind directly. Their results point to a harmful tug of war between altered tau and a normally protective enzyme.
pmc-11710106:
Learning you carry two copies of a gene variant that sharply raises Alzheimer's risk is heavy news, and most studies of that moment have enrolled few minorities. Daniela Diaz Caro and co-authors study the disclosure inside a Latino community program in a 2025 paper. Eleven participants aged 41 to 64 received their results in counseling sessions over video, in Spanish or English.

Counselors walked through genetics, the result, and prevention options, quoting a risk estimate of about 55 percent by age 85 drawn from a local aging study. Session recordings were transcribed and analyzed for content. Six participants had a family history of the disease. The paper reports the immediate reactions and questions, groundwork for support that fits the community receiving the news.
pmc-11710206:
Lara Huyghe and co-authors test a memory skill in early Alzheimer disease in a 2025 paper. Holding linked features of an object in mind, such as shape plus color, rests on a deep brain region hit early by tau buildup. Whether that skill slips before symptoms, and tracks tau there, was not settled.

Three groups took a short-term memory test with shape-only and shape-plus-color rounds. People with amyloid buildup, with or without mild problems, scored lower than amyloid-free peers in most rounds. Tau load in the deep region tracked total scores across all comers and among the healthy group alone. The link ran stronger for the binding rounds. The authors propose the test as an early marker.
pmc-11710306:
Lara De Deyn and fifteen co-authors map in 2025 how the Alzheimer's risk gene ABCA7 is expressed across brain cell types, and what breaks when it fails. The gene's transporter moves lipids and helps cells eat debris, but its many message variants and cell-specific patterns have tangled its story. Single-nucleus sequencing of frontal brain tissue supplied the atlas.

Samples came from mutation carriers, patients without the mutation, and healthy controls. Cell-by-cell expression and gene activity shifts were compared by genotype and disease state. The atlas shows where the gene works hardest and which pathways sag when it is lost. Such maps guide the search for drug targets in a gene whose risk effect rivals better-known Alzheimer's players.
pmc-11710406:
Emma Rhodes and a large consortium team link rising resting heart rate to empathy loss in families carrying frontotemporal degeneration genes, in a 2025 paper. Body signal control and social feeling are tied in this disease, but pre-symptomatic carriers were little studied. The team followed hundreds of carriers and non-carrier relatives for up to seven years.

In symptom-free participants, a climbing resting heart rate came with steeper decline in both emotional and cognitive empathy, carrier or not. Among carriers, the emotional empathy link held across disease stages. The work repeats an earlier smaller finding in a much bigger sample. The authors suggest heart rate drift may flag early social decline in at-risk families.
pmc-11710506:
Benjamin Chapin and co-authors present a 2025 study on sight based focus before surgery. Older adults can face delirium after an operation, a state of confusion that raises harm. The team asked if simple focus tests done before surgery could flag who was at risk.

They studied adults aged sixty five and older who had planned bone surgery. Each person did line and cue tasks that test how focus shifts. After surgery, most had no delirium, while a small share had mild or full signs. Two focus scores tracked with later delirium scores, while age and a broad test did not. The authors urge more work on these cheap tests.
pmc-11710606:
Gregory Cary and co-authors use machine learning to pick which gene variants to combine in future mouse models of late-onset Alzheimer's disease. More than 75 risk spots in the genome feed into the disease, and dozens of mouse strains already carry single modeled variants. Their 2025 paper argues that stacking the right variants together should yield mice that mirror the human disease more closely.

The team measured how each variant, and some lab stressors, shifted gene activity in existing strains. Those shifts became inputs for models fit to gene-activity changes seen in human Alzheimer's cohorts. Several model types, from regularized linear fits to random forests and neural networks, ranked which variants mattered most. The rankings point breeders toward the combinations most likely to reproduce disease features, saving years of trial and error in model building.
pmc-11710706:
Daichi Shigemizu and co-authors ask whether a gene-based risk score can pick out people most likely to gain from dementia prevention work. The score adds up many small gene variants to gauge a person's built-in risk. Their 2025 study first builds a score for the Japanese population from a large gene scan. It then applies the score inside a trial of diet, exercise, and brain training for people with mild memory loss.

The score split trial members into high and low risk groups. Among high-risk members under seventy-five, the program lifted thinking scores in a clear way. Older members showed no such gain in either group. The authors say the score could screen for who gains most, while noting their data set is small.
pmc-11710906:
Chayanee Sae-lim and co-authors describe breast cancers carrying a PALB2 mutation in Korean patients, in a 2024 study. PALB2 faults raise breast cancer risk, but Korean clinical data were thin. At Severance Hospital, 1,463 patients without BRCA1 or BRCA2 faults had broad gene testing between 2016 and 2019; seventeen, about one percent, carried PALB2 changes.

Their median age at diagnosis was forty-six, tumors were mid-sized, and all were grade two or three, with about a quarter triple-negative. Against the non-carrier group, though, no trait differed clearly. The authors add the first Korean numbers to counseling for a mutation whose carriers need tailored screening and family advice.
pmc-11711806:
Pietro Ameri and Susan Dent wrote in 2024 about the neglected half of cardio-oncology: how heart disease shapes cancer. Cancer and its treatment harming the heart is the classic story. The flip side is newer: heart disease shares roots with cancer, may feed tumor growth, and can block the best cancer care.

Their piece discusses a large Israeli cohort study in the same journal issue, tracking adults free of both diseases at entry. The findings add weight to prevention and early cancer checks for heart patients. The authors urge clinics to screen in both directions, not one.
pmc-11711906:
Lauren Pollack and co-authors examine what paramedics know when they reach a critically ill patient with dementia. Most patients and families prefer comfort-focused care near the end of life, yet breathing tubes and ventilators are used ever more often in this group, with no matching gain in survival. Their 2025 study reads ambulance narratives for eighty-one such patients treated in one health system.

The patients averaged eighty years old, about half lived in nursing homes, and most showed signs of advanced dementia. Breathing trouble, confusion, and suspected sepsis were the top reasons for the call. Crews noted the dementia history in only about a third of cases, a substitute decision-maker in a fifth, and any advance directive in about a fifth. The authors say crews often lack the facts needed to match care to the patient's wishes.
pmc-11712106:
Feyikemi Mary Akinyelure and co-authors set out a proposed training project for carers in Lagos, Nigeria, in a 2025 plan. Older people in Nigeria often face neglect or abuse, with the poor hit hardest, the authors write. Their project trains carers in cognitive therapy: guided table activities, memory exercises, and problem solving games.

The plan is to train one hundred twenty health care assistants each year. Training covers dementia knowledge in theory and dementia screening in practice. Results will be judged with a standard mental state exam and a clock drawing test. The team hopes trained carers will extend life and cut the impact of dementia. The plan also tests whether such training can run well in Lagos.
pmc-11712206:
Ríona Mc Ardle and co-authors pilot a home activity tracking plan for older couples in a 2025 study. Walking supports healthy ageing, but researchers need honest records of how partners and neighborhoods shape it. Twenty-one couples took part for seven days.

Each person wore a motion sensor on the lower back, carried a phone with a GPS app when out, and kept a nightly activity diary. Nearly all wore the sensor for the full week and all finished their diaries. The GPS app captured about three quarters of the days, with most gaps blamed on tech faults. Couples found the kit acceptable overall. The authors say the plan is ready for larger studies of walking and ageing.
pmc-11712306:
Paola Ruiz Puentes, Nestor González, Daniel Crovo, Beatriz Grimaldi, and Ram Mukunda used AI to untangle schooling, wealth, and cognitive decline in 2025. High education is widely seen to shield the aging brain. Yet schooling is tangled with culture and income, and studies clash.

Data came from a Mexican aging study of adults over fifty, with detailed thinking tests in two waves. A random forest and a transformer model were trained to predict screening scores from life history, health, and care use. Living conditions, not schooling alone, may carry much of the effect, the authors suggest. The models aim to sort which factors flag risk, toward fairer prevention in settings where schooling is scarce.
pmc-11712406:
Hong Zhao and co-authors probe a strange health pattern in 2025: cancer survivors develop Alzheimer's disease less often. Large studies covering nine million people put the drop at about a third, and careful checks suggest cancer itself, not its treatments, may protect the brain. The team tests the idea in mice.

They inject a few breast cancer cells into young Alzheimer's-model mice and watch brain plaque growth. Plaques shrink versus cancer-free controls. Fluid packets from tumor-bearing mice also stir immune signals in the brain. Using spatial gene mapping near plaques, the authors hunt for the protective factors and for existing drugs that mimic them.
pmc-11712506:
Ann-Kathrin Schalkamp and co-authors test whether wrist-worn motion data can flag future dementia. Their 2025 study uses a large British health bank with more than thirty-three thousand adults, two hundred one of whom later got a dementia diagnosis. Models built on motion data faced off against models built on genes, habits, blood tests, and early symptoms.

Motion models beat gene and habit models at picking out future cases, and matched blood and symptom models. A merged model did best of all. Top signals were age, a gene risk score, light activity levels, and the longest unbroken sleep stretch. The authors say motion data alone does not top the rest, and richer motion traits need study for screening use.
pmc-11712706:
Byron Creese and co-authors lay out a study protocol in a 2025 paper on dementia care. About half of people with dementia show distress linked behavior that goes unmanaged. A young firm sells sensor socks that track body state around the clock and flag early distress signs. The planned study asks whether care home research can use the socks well.

The team will judge uptake and workability: will residents wear them, and will the data flow hold up? Both questions come before any claim that the socks improve care. Sensor tools often fail at this plain stage, so testing it head on saves later waste. A workable sock could give staff an early warning that a resident is growing upset.
pmc-11712806:
Ismael Luis Calandri and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on running a dementia prevention trial across twelve Latin American countries. The trial, LatAm-FINGERS, tests lifestyle change rather than drugs, the first of its kind on that scale in the region. Its people share a language yet differ widely in wealth, culture, and care access.

The team describes how each site helped design the work, so plans fit local life. Shared training and local champions kept sign-up and follow-through on track. The paper also notes a second goal: teaching the public that dementia can often be held off. Their playbook may guide prevention trials in other mixed regions.
pmc-11712906:
Yu Mi Choi, Hyun-Ju Seo, and Seong Min Kim present a 2025 methods paper that checks whether a short quality-of-life tool works well for family caregivers of people with dementia. The tool, called HINT-8, has eight items. It had not been tested in this group in Korea before.

The team gave the tool, along with two longer standard tools, to 340 caregivers reached through dementia centres and home nursing services. Their plan compares scores across the tools and repeats the tool to test stability over time. A short tool that proves sound would help services spot caregiver needs quickly and plan support.
pmc-11713006:
Lasya Sreepada and co-authors link biological age to unusual Alzheimer's patterns in this 2025 paper. Most Alzheimer's disease eats first at memory regions, but atypical cases hit the outer cortex harder and often start young. The team asked whether a biological age measure, read from DNA marks in blood, tracks that atypicality better than calendar age.

From a national study pool, 646 people with DNA and brain scan data were classed as biologically younger, neutral, or older than their years. Cortical thickness was measured across regions and compared with controls. The study tests whether accelerated biological ageing lines up with the cortical pattern, which would refine how onset age is understood.
pmc-11713106:
Tavia E Evans and co-authors present a 2025 study of genes, sex, and shrinkage of the hippocampus, a brain area central to memory. The team asked whether a person's inherited risk for Alzheimer's disease speeds up that shrinkage, and whether the effect differs between women and men and across disease stages.

They followed 1,051 people in the ADNI cohort with gene data and repeat scans over up to eight years. Risk scores were built with and without the APOE gene region, which is known to raise risk. The study tests how much of the gene effect on brain change runs through that one region alone.
pmc-11713306:
Nicole Lemon and five co-authors tested in 2025 whether blocking a mitochondrial enzyme can protect brain blood vessels in Alzheimer's models. Amyloid buildup kills vessel-lining cells and leaks the blood-brain barrier. Past lab work showed broad blockers of this enzyme family prevent that death. The team focused on the two mitochondrial forms, one of which rises in amyloid models.

A selective blocker stopped amyloid-driven cell death and vessel activation in human brain vessel cells. Knocking out one form gave the same protection and kept the barrier tight. In Alzheimer's model mice treated for ten months, the blocker prevented cognitive decline and cut amyloid and tau buildup. The authors target these enzymes for vascular protection in dementia.
pmc-11713406:
Ravinder Singh and Aditya Sunkaria study genes for proteins that cells release, using a lab model of Alzheimer's disease, in this 2025 paper. Released proteins can show up in blood or spinal fluid, so they may serve as early signs of the disease. The team hunted for such genes in brain cells.

They filtered a human protein atlas for released proteins, then matched those against brain cell proteins and known disease genes. Twenty-four candidate genes stood out. The team then treated nerve cells in dishes with forms of amyloid to mimic early disease. They measured which candidate genes changed their activity, a step toward new early markers.
pmc-11713606:
Francisco López-González and co-authors examine chemical messenger pathways in dementia brains after death in this 2025 study. Scans of living patients show decay in a cholinergic hub and its white matter routes. Those routes carry signals tied to attention and memory.

The team use postmortem MRI to check those pathways against proven diagnoses. Cases include Alzheimer's disease, Lewy body dementia, and other brain diseases. Seeing the same decay in confirmed tissue would validate the scans. It would also show whether the pattern is shared or specific. Validated markers help doctors trust scans when symptoms are mixed. Autopsy-backed imaging is the gold standard for that check.
pmc-11713706:
Sarah Gary, Reina Davis-Aoki, Prateek Verma, and Bryan McDowell charted how Alzheimer's trials measure outcomes from 1993 to today, in this 2025 study. Outcome assessments capture what matters to patients and families, and regulators now press for them and for earlier disease stages. The team mined a trials registry for nearly one thousand phase two and three studies and the measures named in them.

The share of trials using such measures rose from half in the nineties to about sixty-nine percent in recent years. The classic cognition scale stayed the top primary measure but its share is slipping. References to mild impairment and preclinical stages climb steadily. The authors read a slow turn toward patient-centered, earlier measurement.
pmc-11713806:
Clarissa Benzarti and co-authors review tools that assess sensory processing in dementia care, in work from 2025. Sensory programs are now common in dementia units, but results vary. Testing how a patient processes sound, touch, and light first could tailor the program to the person.

Such testing is routine for children, yet proof in Alzheimer disease and related dementias is thin. The review followed standard rules and searched five databases for studies from 1990 to 2023. Papers had to name both a sensory test and a dementia group. Two reviewers screened each paper on their own. The summary shows which tools have real support and where gaps remain.
pmc-11713906:
Wen Liu, Heather Suh, and Kyuri Lee review ways to improve mealtimes for people with dementia in a 2025 paper. Eating well keeps up strength, social contact, and pleasure in food. Dementia makes meals hard for patients and tiring for caregivers. The review gathers tested programs that aim to make meals safer and calmer.

The team searched five health databases for studies from 2012 to 2023. Each study was sorted by the kind of program it tested and rated for quality. Where several studies tested the same kind of help, the results were pooled. The review shows which approaches raise food intake or ease caregiver strain. Care homes can use it to pick programs with real proof behind them.
pmc-11714006:
Sampada Tamhankar and three co-authors test whether drugs that switch on a fat control switch can help rebuild myelin in Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 conference paper. Myelin is the fatty coat that speeds nerve signals, and it thins as the disease grows. The coat is rebuilt by cells called oligodendrocytes.

The switch, named LXR, steers cholesterol, a chief part of myelin. The team gave a strong switch on drug to mice bred for the disease and to a human cell line that acts like the coat building cells. Lab tests then read the cell proteins. Diseased mice showed lower levels of young and mature coat cells than normal mice. The work checks whether the drug can push those cells to recoat bare fibers.
pmc-11714306:
Chad Guilliams and Erin Abner test whether a parent's history of dementia skews the known link between low mood and thinking loss, in a 2025 conference paper. Family history can pull certain people into studies, which may bend results. Many teams now swap it for gene marks instead.

The team sorted nearly twenty-one thousand adults without dementia by mood and thinking state at their first visit. People with low mood had more than twice the odds of mild thinking loss. Adding a parent's history to the model barely moved that link, though it did shift it a touch upward. The authors also tracked who slid to worse states over time, using death as a rival outcome in the models.
pmc-11714506:
Darlingtina Esiaka and four co-authors test whether schooling links to memory area size in older Black Americans, and whether the link splits by sex, in a 2025 conference paper. Schooling is thought to build a reserve that guards thinking in old age. The memory area in question is the hippocampus, which shrinks as Alzheimer's disease nears.

The team used 38 adults from a Kentucky aging center cohort, with a mean age near 73. School years ran from ten to twenty-one. Each person had health checks, thinking tests, and a brain scan. In men, more schooling went strongly with a larger left hippocampus. The authors report no such link in women in this small group. They urge bigger studies of how schooling shapes the brain in Black adults.
pmc-11714606:
Jacob Vogel and co-authors chart in 2025 how protein cascades unfold differently in each person along the Alzheimer spectrum. Spinal fluid proteomics can read many disease processes at once, and those processes likely fire in sequence. The study drew 673 people from a Swedish cohort, from healthy to demented, all with fluid protein reads and tau scans.

Clustering distilled ten protein networks, seven of them tied to amyloid, tau, or diagnosis. A staging algorithm then sorted each person into a subtype and stage by which networks had turned abnormal in what order. The subtypes interacted with stage to shape tau spread and thinking scores, showing the cascade is personal.
pmc-11714706:
Delgado and co-authors link blood markers of brain degeneration to traits of type 1 diabetes, in a 2025 study. Cognitive problems are more common in people with this form of diabetes, yet blood biomarker work in that group is scarce. The study drew 114 adults from a project on glucose swings and cognition. Five plasma markers were measured, covering amyloid, tau, nerve damage, and brain inflammation signals.

Glucose variability came from continuous monitor readings. The team screened links between markers, demographics, and diabetes traits, then modeled the strongest pairs with adjustments for age, sex, and schooling. Kidney disease was added as a control where it mattered. The design maps which diabetes features travel with early brain change signs, guiding who might need closer cognitive watch.
pmc-11714906:
Hanna Huber and a large team of co-authors test whether a finger prick can give the same Alzheimer disease signals as a standard blood draw, in a study from 2025. A blood marker called p-tau217 is a strong sign of the disease process in the brain. Easier sampling would help early diagnosis and faster start of new treatments.

The project, called DROP-AD, enrolled 230 people at four centers. Each person gave finger prick blood so the team could measure three markers linked to the disease and to nerve damage. Values from the small samples were checked against what such tests need to be useful in clinics. If the method holds up, testing could move to simpler settings with less staff and gear.
pmc-11715006:
How a workout feels may decide whether a person keeps working out, a link shown in the young but little checked in older adults. Marta Stojanovic and three co-authors give early results in 2025 from a study of middle-aged and older adults, some at risk for Alzheimer's disease.

The team asks whether a bright mood after a single bout of exercise foretells higher day-to-day activity. Two forces may bend that link. Low mood has long been tied to less movement, and it may blunt the mood lift that exercise gives. The build-up of disease marks in the brain may also wear down the drive to move. Early data of this kind can guide plans that keep older adults active by making the work feel good.
pmc-11715206:
Kuan-Ying Li and Yuan-Han Yang profile the grown children of Alzheimer's patients, a group carrying several times the usual risk. Sixty-three adult children, aged fifty to seventy-nine, were recruited at a Taiwanese hospital for yearly clinical, cognitive, imaging, and blood follow-up alongside their parents.

The cohort skews female, tests near normal on standard screens, and carries the APOE4 risk gene at about thirty-five percent, above population rates. Of the nineteen who completed amyloid PET scanning, nearly half read amyloid-positive despite their healthy scores. The authors read that as preclinical disease already seeded in midlife, and argue this cohort is exactly where prevention strategies should be tested: old enough for pathology, young enough to intervene.
pmc-11715306:
Wei-Ju Lee and co-authors hunted a better scan mark for thought skills in a rare passed-down vessel disease. The disease, called CADASIL, stems from a flaw in one gene and harms small brain vessels. White spots on scans are its classic sign, yet they track thought skills poorly. A newer mark reads how wide the spread of water flow is in white matter tracts.

The team scanned gene carriers with no past stroke or dementia and a matched set of non-carriers. All took tests of memory, speed, planning, and space skills. Carriers showed worse white spots and a wider spread mark than non-carriers. The spread mark lined up with slower speed and weaker space skills once age and schooling were weighed. The white spot load showed no such link, which puts the new mark ahead.
pmc-11715406:
Xinyi Wang and eleven co-authors tested whether a simple at-home reaction time game can flag early cognitive decline, in a 2025 paper. Catching preclinical Alzheimer's matters for trials of protective drugs, but lab visits are costly. Nearly nine hundred older adults who reported no cognitive symptoms took reaction tests on their home computers, unsupervised, plus validated online tests of memory and thinking.

Speed on successful tries did not track cognition. Failing a trial, taking over two seconds to respond, did: more failures came with worse memory, working memory, and executive scores. The authors used models built for such zero-heavy data to confirm the links. They conclude that breakdowns, not raw speed, are the tell. A cheap home test that counts failures could help screen large groups for hidden risk.
pmc-11715606:
Jennifer Frontera and co-authors ask whether blood biomarkers of brain harm match brain volumes two years after COVID-19. Many people who had the virus report lasting brain fog and slow thinking, yet the cause stays unclear. Their 2025 study scanned and tested 90 adults. Most had laboratory proof of past infection, and a small group had never had the virus.

In the group that had the virus, high blood markers of neurodegeneration, blood-brain barrier leakage, and inflammation went with smaller volumes in mood and memory regions. The pattern was sharp in those with poor cognitive test scores and absent in those with sound scores. It also did not appear in the group that never had the virus. The team reads the blood-and-scan match as a clue to how the virus may mark the brain. More work must prove cause, not just a link.
pmc-11715706:
Zlatomira Georgieva Ilchovska, Akram A Hosseini, and JeYoung Jung test whether two brain chemicals explain the language losses of frontotemporal dementia, in this 2025 study. The disease erodes the frontal and temporal lobes, seats of word knowledge. A standing hypothesis blames disturbed balance between glutamate, an excitatory signal, and GABA, an inhibitory one.

Brain scans that read chemistry without surgery measured both chemicals in frontal and temporal cortex. Seven patients with the disease were compared with two Alzheimer's patients and twenty-three healthy peers. The dementia group scored worse on language, memory, and executive tasks, and handled a word knowledge task less well than both other groups. The excitation inhibition balance dropped in the temporal lobe. The authors present the pattern as early support for the chemical hypothesis, gathered from a small sample.
pmc-11715806:
Deng Yue-Ting traces body fat across the life course against dementia risk in this 2025 cohort study. Past work disagreed on whether body mass index in adulthood raises or lowers dementia risk, and almost nothing was known about fat in early life or where fat sits on the body.

The study followed 322,336 UK Biobank participants from 2006, recording birthweight, childhood body size, and adult measures of fat and its spread. Over about nine years, 5,083 people developed dementia. A plumper childhood body size came with twenty-two percent higher risk. Adult body mass showed a U shape, risky at both extremes, and more fat on the arms with less lean mass also raised risk.
pmc-11715906:
William Coath and co-authors measure the quiet years between two hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease. Amyloid plaques appear first; the tau tangles that track symptoms follow later, and knowing the gap matters now that anti-amyloid drugs exist. Their 2025 paper uses the Insight 46 study, a British birth cohort, whose members received amyloid scans and, for a subset enriched for amyloid, tau scans as well.

A changepoint method estimates each person's age at amyloid positivity, then asks, region by region across the brain, when tau levels bend upward relative to that personal clock. The approach turns two snapshots per person into a timeline the field usually needs decades of follow-up to see. Pinning down which regions accumulate tau soonest after amyloid turns positive could tell trial designers when treatment must start and where to look first for proof that it is working.
pmc-11716006:
Haiyun Chen and six co-authors check how stable a widely used brain scan program's readings are when the same person is scanned twice, in this 2025 study. The program, FreeSurfer, measures brain regions that shrink in Alzheimer's disease, and trials rely on it to track change. If readings jump between scans for no real reason, small true changes get lost.

One hundred adults aged sixty and older at a New York center had two scans about five weeks apart on the same machine. Measures of memory regions, cortex thickness, and total head size matched closely between the two scans. Gaps between readings did not track with age, sex, schooling, or thinking scores. The results back the program's use for following brain change over time.
pmc-11716106:
Nathan Friedman and a large Canadian expert group build a decision tool for judging when memory testing by video call is safe, in a study published in 2025. Remote assessment widens access to dementia diagnosis, but some patients should clearly be seen in person. No evidence-based guidance existed for telling the two apart.

A multidisciplinary workgroup, including neurologists, neuropsychologists, geriatricians, social workers, and people with lived experience, ran a Delphi consensus process. They catalogued red flags tied to the patient, the caregiver, the clinician, and the situation that should steer a case toward in-person care. The resulting tool gives clinics a shared checklist rather than individual guesswork, aiming to keep virtual assessment for those it serves well.
pmc-11716206:
Yuancheng Li and co-authors build a lab-made molecule that can fish a key Alzheimer's marker out of blood or spinal fluid, in a 2025 paper. Tests for the disease often rely on antibodies to grab amyloid beta, a protein fragment tied to the illness. Antibodies vary between batches and spoil in storage. The team offers a synthetic stand-in built from a chain of modified amino acid units.

The researchers made a large library of these synthetic chains and screened it for ones that grip a form of amyloid called Aβ40. They mapped the winning chains with lab instruments, then fixed them to magnetic beads. The beads can pull the target protein out of a sample for measurement. A stable, factory-made gripper like this could make fluid tests for the disease cheaper and more steady.
pmc-11716406:
Sandra Castro-Labrador and co-authors asked how Alzheimer's pathology changes thinking in Parkinson's disease, in this 2025 study. Many Parkinson's patients develop thinking problems, and added Alzheimer's change is a known risk. A blood marker can now flag that added pathology.

The team studied 88 Parkinson's patients, half with thinking problems and half without. Blood tests split the impaired group by marker status. About 28 percent of the impaired group carried the marker, versus 13 percent of the unimpaired group. Brain fuel-use scans and thinking profiles were compared across groups. The study shows the blood marker can sort patients whose decline may follow a mixed path.
pmc-11716506:
Dana Parker and co-authors test a newer brain scan method for spotting Alzheimer's damage in a key memory region. The standard scan model is too simple for the tangled wiring there. The newer method, called NODDI, splits the signal into parts that track fiber density and spread.

Scans from 199 older adults fed the study. The new measures tied far more strongly to memory scores and to the two proteins that mark the disease, tau and amyloid, than the standard measures did. One standard measure showed no link to either protein in any tract. The team reads this as proof that the finer method catches damage the old one misses.
pmc-11716606:
Blood tests that flag the brain changes of Alzheimer's disease could reshape how the illness is confirmed. That matters now that treatments aim to slow it. Aye, Handels, Winblad, and Jönsson model the money and health effects of using blood biomarkers in two places. In primary care, the test would decide who gets referred onward. In memory clinics, it would decide who needs a spinal fluid test. Their model follows patients through diagnosis and treatment over thirty years.

Used in primary care, the blood test raised referrals by eight percent and true diagnoses by about ten percent. The cost per year of healthy life gained was modest. Used in the memory clinic, it cut invasive spinal tests and saved money up front but missed some true cases, costing health in the long run. The study suggests the blood test earns its place early in the pathway.
pmc-11716706:
Bruno Hammerschlag and six co-authors test dried blood spots for Alzheimer's marks in a 2025 paper. A dried spot needs just a finger prick, ships by mail, and stores at room heat, unlike drawn blood that needs a clinic visit and cold chain. Repeat reads from spots could let trials track change in one person with fewer recruits.

They read three disease marks in spots and in matched drawn blood with fine lab tests. Work covered how to collect the spots, how to wash the marks out, and how steady repeat reads stay day to day. Samples came from a Boston aging cohort and from patients in a memory clinic workup. The team reports the tuned steps and the spread of repeat reads.
pmc-11716806:
Allison Sekuler leads a team of seven authors in 2025 in describing Defy Dementia, a Canadian public health campaign built on a hopeful fact: much dementia risk is modifiable. Age remains the biggest risk factor, but lifestyle and health habits account for a large share, and most people never hear that part.

Led by Baycrest's education academy and funded by Canada's public health agency, the campaign curates and co-designs materials with its audiences. The products aim to raise awareness of prevention and cut the stigma around dementia at once. How the campaign was mobilized is itself the lesson for other regions.
pmc-11716906:
Carlos Cordeiro Junior and co-authors study, in a 2025 paper, how swelling pathways act in the brains of mice bred to develop Alzheimer's-like disease. Plaques and tangles in the disease are tied to poor clearing of two proteins and to an overactive immune response in the brain.

Forty-eight mice were treated with lithium for three months at two dose levels, with an untreated group for comparison. Tissue from the hippocampus, a memory region, was screened for its full protein set. The team traced how sensor proteins that spark swelling connect with the disease proteins. They also asked how lithium, a long-used drug, shifts that network.
pmc-11720506:
Antibodies meant to tell apart near-twin brain proteins are put on trial by Dahlia Siano and co-authors in a 2025 study. The protein ApoE comes in three forms that differ by an amino acid or two, yet swing Alzheimer's risk hugely. Labs lean on shop antibodies to tell them apart, with shaky proof.

Control samples came from mice with no ApoE, mice carrying each human form, and human blood of all six gene pairings. Blot tests score which antibodies truly read one form only. Trustworthy tags matter since a misread form can flip a study's whole claim about risk.
pmc-11722106:
Ilya Senatorov and sixteen co-authors screen in 2024 thirty patient-derived prostate cancer organoids against 78 drugs to learn why some resist taxane chemotherapy. Castration-resistant prostate cancer is varied, and taxanes help many men but fail others without warning. Pairing drug responses with gene activity maps exposed a resistance circuit.

A transcription factor, HNF1A, switched on a program that blocks cell death through a partner protein, cIAP2. Blocking that partner with a single drug killed organoids that had shrugged off docetaxel. The circuit suggests a biomarker test to pick who needs the combination up front, turning a common failure of prostate cancer care into a targetable weakness.
pmc-11726106:
Marcio Nucci and nine co-authors issue consensus guidance in two thousand twenty-four on fever during low white cell counts. Febrile neutropenia is a dangerous side effect of treating blood diseases. Resistant bacteria are making it harder to manage, and the pattern varies by region.

Ten experts from a Brazilian hematology association built the recommendations by a structured Delphi process. The document covers the first workup of a febrile patient and preventive treatment. It sets out starting antibiotic and antifungal choices, when to change them, and when therapy can stop. The guidance is tuned to local infection patterns rather than copied from abroad. The authors present it as a shared standard for Brazilian centers.
pmc-11727106:
Akash Maurya and co-authors review nanoencapsulated essential oils for protecting stored cereals in a 2024 paper. Stored grains face attack from microbes and insects, which hurt quality, safety, and market value. Plant essential oils can fight these pests as safer, greener preservatives, but they evaporate fast, dissolve poorly, and oxidize quickly.

Wrapping the oils in tiny polymer capsules solves much of that. Nanoencapsulation gives slow, sustained release and targeted delivery without changing the taste or smell of the grain. The review weighs the antimicrobial and insecticidal strength of these systems in storage trials. For farmers and food firms, the approach promises longer shelf life with fewer synthetic chemicals.
pmc-11727206:
Shaohua Xu and co-authors present a 2024 method for designing fairer experiments to measure cause and effect. In trials with many background traits, random assignment can leave the treated and control groups uneven on those traits. The team measures that unevenness as a gap score and asks how to make the worst-case error of the standard effect estimate as small as possible.

Their design, called MODE, picks the assignment by a fixed rule built from low-clump number methods rather than by chance. It shrinks the gap score in a way that does not depend on any outcome model. Proofs show its effect estimate settles faster than those from random or re-drawn assignments. Tests on fake data back the claim, with smaller trait gaps and tighter estimates than rival designs.
pmc-11727306:
Bradley Hernlem and Reuven Rasooly report a lab study from 2024 on abrin, a toxin from the rosary pea plant. Abrin is known for blocking the making of proteins in cells, and it has been linked to nerve disease in people. The pair asked how the toxin acts on immune cells and on kidney cells.

In tests with human T-cells, low doses of abrin did the opposite of what the team expected. The toxin boosted the response of active T-cells and raised the release of signals that drive inflammation. In kidney cells, by contrast, it cut protein making as expected, and milk reduced that effect. The authors propose that this boost to immune signals may help explain how low doses could trigger harmful immune attacks.
pmc-11728106:
Grzegorz Wryk and co-authors run, in a 2024 study, a broad contest of methods that fill in missing values in protein measurement data. Such data sets can lose up to half their entries, which blurs results. Ten filling methods were tested, from simple floor values to global pattern methods, on data from two protein search tools.

Fake gaps were cut into complete data at varied rates and patterns, so each method's error could be scored fairly. The team also checked whether a log step before filling helped or hurt. Results were judged by error size and by how well true and false finds were sorted. The study gives labs a grounded pick of method by gap type.
pmc-11728206:
Kyoungwon Kwak and co-authors review progress on transistors made from atom-thin molybdenum disulfide for flexible and wearable devices, in a 2024 paper. Bending electronics need parts that keep working on curved surfaces, and this layered material offers fast charge movement, an adjustable bandgap, strength, and chemical stability that rival materials lack.

The review gathers a decade of work from leading journals on how such transistors are fabricated, structured, and built into working devices. It weighs the novel tricks that keep performance high while the device flexes. Challenges remain before these transistors reach everyday wearables, and the authors close with an outlook on what must improve, from contacts to large-area growth.
pmc-11728406:
Tatyana Li and co-authors review the puzzle of heparin resistance in patients on life-support circulation machines, in this 2024 article. ECMO pumps a patient's blood outside the body through plastic circuits, and heparin is the drug that stops that blood from clotting on contact. In some patients, standard doses simply fail, a dangerous state called heparin resistance, inviting both clots and bleeding.

The field cannot even agree on what counts as resistance: definitions quarrel over dose units and over which blood test measures the drug's effect. The machine itself muddies the picture, coating its surfaces with protein, summoning immune cells, and consuming the blood factor heparin needs as a partner. Another blood protein can also spend heparin on its own account. The review catalogs the mechanisms and pleads for shared definitions, so studies can be compared and treatment made consistent.
pmc-11728706:
Arturs Medvids and co-authors present an optical method to size tiny nanostructures in this 2024 paper. The method reads the color of light a structure emits when excited. That emission shifts toward blue as the structure shrinks. Two test objects were used, carbon nanocones and a sharp microscope tip.

For the carbon cones, the shifted spectrum gave a top size of 2.0 nanometers. For the atomic force microscope tip, green emission sat right at its apex. The spectrum gave a tip size of 1.5 nanometers, matching electron microscope measures. Time resolved readings showed how the excited state lifetime changes along the cone. The method needs no special sample preparation or costly sizing equipment.
pmc-11728806:
Saba Mudassar and co-authors prime mung bean seeds with a plant hormone to help seedlings survive cadmium-poisoned soil. Their 2024 study faces a spreading threat: cadmium from human activity is building in farm soil and cutting crop growth. The hormone, triacontanol, is known to spur plant growth and metabolism.

Seeds soaked in three hormone doses grew forty days in soil carrying 20 milligrams of cadmium per kilogram. Cadmium alone stunted germination, roots, and shoots. The middle dose performed best, lifting root and shoot length, plant weights, and germination above the other doses. Leaf pigments rose two to four times over cadmium-only plants, and gas exchange rates climbed up to sixfold. The authors present seed priming as a cheap shield for legumes on tainted land.
pmc-11729106:
Farahnaz Motamedi-Sedeh and co-authors test a fast way to make a COVID-19 vaccine in this 2024 hamster study. Fast vaccine work matters when a new virus spreads, and the team uses gamma rays to kill the virus while keeping its shape intact. A natural sugar is added to some doses to boost the immune response.

Hamsters got one of four vaccine mixes, by nose or by shot. All groups built strong virus-blocking defenses after later doses. The ray-treated mix with the sugar raised nose-level defenses the most, and spleen cell growth rose in all groups. The authors back two mixes as safe leads, while noting that a live-virus test must still prove real protection.
pmc-11729706:
Giorgio Ferriero, Irene Ferrario, and Francesco Negrini argue in 2024 that rehab plans must make room for neurodivergence in adults. The term spans autism, focus ills, and learning ills. Such traits are often spotted in youth but missed in grown and older patients, though about a fifth of people fit the term.

These adults face higher rates of stroke, long pain, weak bones, heart ills, sugar ill, and low mood. So a large share of rehab patients bring these traits, with needs standard plans can miss. The piece shows where plans clash with those needs. Rehab teams gain a push to ask, adapt, and plan with the trait in view.
pmc-11731306:
Rajkumar Kundavaram and colleagues reported a heart study in 2024 on children treated for acute lymphoblastic leukemia. A key drug in their treatment can harm the heart, sometimes soon after dosing and sometimes much later. The team used ultrasound heart scans before treatment and again three days after the first treatment dose in a small group of children. They compared many measures of how well both sides of the heart pumped and relaxed.

After the dose, both the right and left sides of the heart showed weaker pumping and slower relaxation. Several standard scan measures moved in the direction of early damage, even though the changes were modest. The authors argue that routine heart scans should be part of care from the start of treatment. Early spotting of quiet heart changes, they say, lets doctors act before the damage grows into plain heart failure.
pmc-11731806:
Fredo Tamara and co-authors pool world data on narrowing of the artery to a transplanted kidney. This narrowing, called transplant renal artery stenosis, can threaten the new kidney, yet its frequency and causes were unsettled. Their 2024 review searches three databases and keeps 31 studies out of nearly 29,000 hits, pooling both the rate and the risk factors.

Across studies, about six percent of transplant patients developed the narrowing. Diabetes, high blood pressure, longer time on dialysis before the transplant, and a deceased donor all raised the risk. So did early rejection, slow start of the new kidney, longer cold storage, and fast blood flow readings on scans. Age, sex, the original kidney disease, and one common virus showed no link. The authors note that several of the risks can be managed, and offer the list as a guide for transplant teams.
pmc-11733906:
Three dental researchers from Thailand compare how much of a protein called METTL3 shows up in jaw cysts and jaw tumors. METTL3 helps place a common chemical mark on RNA, and it has been linked to cancer growth in the head and neck. The team checked healthy dental tissue, dentigerous cysts, and two forms of ameloblastoma, a slow jaw tumor.

Stained tissue samples showed tumor tissue held far more METTL3 than cyst or healthy tissue. Levels rose step by step from milder tumor forms to the most aggressive form. The authors suggest the protein may help drive how boldly these growths behave, though they note the exact pathway still needs study. The work points to a possible marker for spotting risky lesions early.
pmc-11749006:
Sha Lai and seven co-authors study unplanned hospital readmissions among patients with mental and behavioral disorders in China, in a study published in 2024. Such returns within weeks disrupt recovery and pile costs on families and the health system. The team set out to measure the thirty-one-day rate and to find what drives it at the levels of the patient, the hospital, and the city.

Records covered over forty-nine thousand admissions at ninety-nine public hospitals in ten cities. The readmission rate came to 8.6 percent. More general practitioners in a city went with lower risk. Hospital traits such as type, size, and staffing mattered in some patient groups but not others. Patient traits (age, sex, marital and work status, diagnosis, length of stay, and cost) mattered across the board. The authors call for joint work by health systems, hospitals, and patients to cut the returns.
pmc-11757006:
Vasectomy is a safe and common form of permanent birth control, yet a small share of men later regret the choice. Degraeve and co-authors build, in a 2024 European study, a scoring system to spot men at higher risk of regret before the operation. Regret was defined by later reversal surgery or by seeking fertility treatment.

A panel of 52 experts first listed 17 traits that might predict regret. The team then checked those traits in 1,200 men who had a vasectomy in the past 15 years. Five traits proved to be strong signals, led by age under 35. The panel turned the results into a score that doctors and patients can use when they talk through the decision.
pmc-11760406:
Sandeep Shetty and co-authors present a 2024 study on a new device to pull the upper jaw forward. Some children have an upper jaw that sits too far back, a pattern called class III. The patented device, named SAVE, is meant to correct that. The team modeled the device in three dimensions and built a computer model from a patient scan.

The jaw model held a very large number of nodes and elements. Forces of three strengths were applied at a set angle on each side. The model showed the upper jaw moving forward and down, with a counter-clockwise turn. Stress peaked on the top of the frame and near the force module. The authors say the device could speed correction.
pmc-11769906:
Wei Zhang and co-authors split low mood into a passing state and a lasting trait and ask which brain marks go with each, in a study from 2024. Brain hunts for low mood have long failed to find marks that repeat, in part since state and trait are tangled in most groups. A long cohort let the team form a group in cure, a group with wild swings, and matched peers for each.

Rest scans gave fifteen broad brain nets per person. The trait group showed a louder visual net at cure than its peers, a hint of bent sight work in those prone to low mood. No net mark split the state group from its peers. The authors say sight nets earn a place in mood tales.
pmc-11781206:
Karolina Zolkiewicz and Damian Gruszka review how tuning a plant hormone could help cereals withstand drought and heat. The head of the text dates the review to 2024, though the catalog lists 2025. Brassinosteroids steer growth and development across a plant's life. Mutants that make or sense less of the hormone grow shorter, a handy trait, but the key question is stress survival without losing yield.

Studies in rice, maize, wheat, and barley show that adjusting hormone production or signaling can raise stress tolerance. Semidwarf lines with tweaked hormone pathways are a promising breeding route. The review weighs the growth-versus-survival balance that any such germplasm must strike for farmers facing a hotter climate.
pmc-11783306:
Saul Pierotti, Tomas Fitzgerald, and Ewan Birney present a software paper published in 2024 on a pipeline for genome-wide association studies. Linear mixed models handle population structure in such studies, but the usual way of setting significance by shuffling outcomes breaks down when samples are related or covariates matter.

Their tool, FlexLMM, runs inside the Nextflow workflow system. It first regresses the population structure out of the data, then shuffles only the leftover residuals, which keeps the procedure valid. The exact model can be defined flexibly by the user. The authors aim it at researchers crossing inbred lines of model organisms, farm animals, and plants, where structure is unavoidable. Code and documentation are freely available.
pmc-11786006:
Ebrahimi Chaharom, Bahari, Kimyai, and Bagban Nikzad studied how tooth bleaching changes the color of a new one-shade dental composite. The material, Omnichroma, is designed to match any tooth color, but bleaching might shift its shade or translucency. The team made 45 disks of the resin and split them among three regimens. One used strong hydrogen peroxide in the office. One used a milder gel at home over two weeks. The third paired peroxide with a dental laser.

All three regimens changed the resin's color and translucency noticeably. The home bleaching gel caused the largest shifts, significantly more than the office treatments, which did not differ from each other. The authors warn that patients with restorations in this material may see a mismatch after bleaching, especially after home treatment, and may need the work redone or polished.
pmc-11786206:
Zahra Taghinejad, Mohammad Asgharzadeh, and Ali Akbar Pourfathollah raise an urgent alert about dengue spreading through blood transfusion in Iran in a 2024 paper. Dengue is an emerging problem in the country, with close to one hundred fifty new confirmed cases noted. The virus spreads mainly by Aedes mosquitoes, which are expanding their range fast.

Donated blood is another route: a donor with silent infection can pass the virus to a patient. The authors argue for screening and vigilance in blood services as case counts climb. Their warning is brief but pointed, aimed at transfusion policy before a preventable route opens. It also flags hospital routes of spread that infection control teams should review.
pmc-11788306:
Yi Wang and co-authors study a cell-death protein in bleeding stroke in a paper whose text dates to 2024.
