The protein, MLKL, carries out a form of cell death called necroptosis and feeds swelling in tissue. Earlier work tied it to worse harm after a brain bleed, which made it a tempting drug target. How it does that harm was still unclear.

The team found the protein at high levels in brain tissue from patients, with more protein where injury was worse. In mice, removing the protein's gene did not by itself erase the damage, a result the authors report plainly. Protein mapping then listed partners the protein may act with. The study points drug hunters toward the wider network, not the single protein alone.
pmc-11794306:
Kun Zhang and co-authors study wealth, surgical delay, and survival in thyroid cancer in a paper whose journal version appeared in 2024. Papillary thyroid cancer is often slow-growing, and watching it actively has become popular. The pandemic also delayed many operations, reopening the question of how timing and social status shape outcomes.

Over fifty-eight thousand patients from a national cancer registry were analyzed with several survival models. Treatment choices, marital status, urban residence, income, and ethnicity each carried independent links to outcomes in the results. The study separates medical from social drivers. Even a 'good' cancer's prognosis is partly written by a patient's circumstances.
pmc-11794806:
Hilal Uygur studies why insomnia hits adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder so hard, in work published in 2024. Insomnia is the most common sleep problem in this group, and poor sleep can make the core symptoms worse. Uygur focuses on sleep reactivity, the tendency for stress to trigger sleepless nights, and asks how it links with symptom levels and with how severe the insomnia is.

The study compared 61 adults with the disorder and 61 matched healthy adults, all filling in scales for sleep quality, insomnia severity, and symptoms. Sleep reactivity, insomnia severity, and poor sleep quality were all higher in the patient group. In that group, worse insomnia was predicted by higher reactivity, higher symptom scores, and being female, which makes reactivity a target worth treating.
pmc-11805206:
Anand Tripathi and colleagues tested bracket bonding under different curing lights in 2024. Orthodontic brackets must stick firmly to teeth. Light curing sets the bonding glue. Sixty extracted premolar teeth were used. Three lamp types formed the groups. Two curing times were compared within groups.

Twenty seconds beat ten seconds clearly. Bond strength rose with longer curing. Lamp type also changed the results. Plasma arc and other lamps differed measurably. Both factors reached statistical significance here. Stronger bonds support successful treatment overall. Clinic choices should weigh lamp and time. Quick cures may cost holding strength.
pmc-11831906:
Meeting abstracts from SNMICON 2024 gather short reports on nuclear medicine and imaging, published in 2024. The set opens with work on brain tumor imaging. One report tests a tracer long used for kidney scans as a tool for brain scans. The team used it to look for tumor left after surgery or radiation.

In that first report, staff labeled the tracer, gave it to a small group of patients, and took scans at a cancer center. The abstracts as a set give quick snapshots of work in progress. Readers get aims, methods and early set-ups across many topics in the field, rather than one full study.
pmc-11839406:
Asma Afzal and co-authors pool studies on two non-invasive tests for bowel polyps, in work published in 2024. Polyps can turn into bowel cancer, so finding them early matters. A stool test that detects hidden blood is standard for cancer screening, but its use for polyps is less settled. Breath and stool gas compounds have also been tested.

The review gathered studies that reported accuracy for either test against advanced polyps. Twenty-two stool test papers and twelve gas compound papers entered the review, with most feeding the pooled analysis. The team checked study quality with a standard tool and computed combined sensitivity and specificity for the tests. The work aims to show whether either method, or both together, can sort patients toward timely scope exams.
pmc-11888606:
Sornamalar M and five co-authors build a scaffold meant to regrow the inside of a damaged tooth, in a 2024 laboratory study. The pulp-dentin complex, the tooth's living core, does not repair itself well after deep decay. Their scaffold blends a nano phosphorylated form of pullulan, a natural sugar polymer, into carboxymethyl chitosan gel. Five mixing ratios were made, freeze-dried, and examined with standard materials tools.

Human dental pulp stem cells were then grown on the scaffolds to check survival and growth. The best ratio was compared against plain chitosan and a bone-forming medium. A scaffold that pulp stem cells accept is a step toward regenerative fillings that rebuild living tooth tissue instead of inert plugs.
pmc-11895706:
Marius Palz examines a dugong extinction claim in Okinawan waters in a 2024 paper. In 2021, a preprint held that the local dugong stock had sunk below a viable count and should count as extinct. Feeding trails in several spots seemed to clash with that call.

Local green groups protested, and world dugong experts pushed back too. Three of the preprint's authors sat on a watch panel for a disputed military base build in prime dugong water. The animal's protected state and folk weight made its fate a political token. Palz argues that extinction talk can never be split from such settings. Caution in wording is part of the science.
pmc-11928306:
Gisèle Mukeya Mvumbi and co-authors published a 2024 study of two liver viruses, hepatitis B and C, in women who sell sex in Bamako, Mali. Both viruses are a health problem in poor countries. How often they strike this at-risk group, with or without HIV, was thin in past data. The team set out to count them.

Four hundred women took part in one year, half with HIV and half without it. Questionnaires, blood samples, and swabs were taken. Marks of the first virus ran at over six in a hundred in the HIV group, and over four in a hundred without HIV. Marks of the second virus ran higher in both. Paid sex before eighteen tied strongly to the first virus, as did the marks of the second. The team calls for a targeted prevention plan for this group.
pmc-11932406:
Malawi's health ministry set out in 2022 to build a national digital health system, and John Kar-Kin Zao and co-authors describe its design in a 2024 paper. Paper records slow care and leak privacy, so the new system aims to capture medical data on devices and manage it on a modern cloud-native platform.

The design rests on four planks. Connected devices gather the data. A Kubernetes-based setup deploys and manages services. Zero-trust communication guards data as it crosses the internet. Trusted computing lets certified software process records without breaking privacy or national control. A peer network of guard stations watches the gates of the system. The authors argue the platform can scale toward universal health coverage by 2030 while raising data quality and cutting paper.
pmc-11960306:
Lan Zhang and co-authors use gene tools to probe cause links between cell stress marks and epilepsy. The study appeared in 2024. Past work on that link gave mixed reads. The team drew gene stats from large past sets and used gene spots as stand-ins for each mark.

One metal mark tied to a raised risk of fits in both broad and wide forms. One guard mark tied to raised risk of the wide form, while a blood protein tied to less risk. In the flip read, fits tied to shifts in three marks. Wide fits also tied to drops in two food marks. Each read was checked for clumps and side paths.
pmc-11967506:
Ga-Ram You and co-authors describe a viral disease of the upper gut over ten years in Korea, in a 2023 study. The virus, CMV, mainly harms people with weak immune systems. Its gut form is a major cause of death in that group. Less was known about cases in people with normal immunity.

Records came from five large hospitals for the years 2010 to 2022. In all, 54 patients had the disease in the food pipe, stomach, or upper small bowel. Half the cases were in the food pipe. Belly pain was the top symptom. The team compared outcomes between patients with weak and normal immunity. The series gives doctors a fuller picture of a disease often tied to one patient group.
pmc-12169106:
Atharva S Kulkarni is first author on a 2025 review of mass spectrometry methods for studying host and microbiome chemistry. The microbiome is the community of microbes living in and on a body. Host and microbes trade chemical signals, including natural products, small molecules microbes make, but these are scarce amid host and food chemicals.

Covering work from twenty fifteen to twenty twenty-five, the review explains how mass spectrometers, instruments that sort molecules by weight, plus new lab and computer methods, find those signals. Examples come from human and mouse systems, with parallels from other ecosystems. The findings help researchers decode how microbes shape health and disease.
pmc-12331206:
Anna L Alves Fernandes and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 on whether slight, harmless facial asymmetry in women comes with differences in bite and chewing muscles. Subtle asymmetry is common and usually counted as normal, yet it might still track functional imbalances. Forty-two women aged eighteen to thirty were sorted by 3D face scans into symmetric and slightly asymmetric groups.

Bite force at the molars and contact patterns were measured, and ultrasound gauged two chewing muscles. No measure differed significantly between groups. The main chewing muscle was thicker than the temple muscle in both groups, and slightly thicker in the asymmetric group, but not beyond chance. The authors read slight asymmetry as functionally benign.
pmc-12439606:
Ahmad Raza Usmani and co-authors measured how bed height changes the work of getting in and out of a hospital bed, in a 2023 study. Many patient falls happen at the bedside. Low beds soften falls but force a harder rise, since the body's center starts below the knees. Twenty-four healthy adults tried heights from forty-three to eighty-six centimeters in random order, over force plates.

Height clearly mattered, the team found, for forces, balance point, and how steady and hard the move felt. Hands-on support was logged at each height too. The results give wards measured guidance for choosing bed heights that ease both moves without raising fall risk.
pmc-12490506:
Allergic rhinitis swells the lining of the nose, but the amount of swelling differs between the form triggered by seasonal pollen and the form that lasts all year. Atanas Vlaykov measured nasal openness in 2024 using acoustic rhinometry, a gentle sound-based technique that needs little cooperation and works even in small children. The study covered 139 people at a Bulgarian university hospital: 111 with allergic rhinitis and 28 healthy controls.

The test recorded the volume of each side of the nose and its narrowest point, then repeated the scan after a decongestant spray. Patients with the intermittent, pollen-driven form showed more mucosal swelling and stronger congestion than the year-round group, which the author links to pollen being a stronger immune trigger. The year-round group, though, reacted far less to the decongestant, suggesting their swelling is harder to reverse.
pmc-12660706:
Musarrat Ijaz and co-authors pack two forms of vitamin E into tiny lipid carriers in a gel, aiming at stronger skin anti-aging effects, in a study from 2025. The carriers hold fat-loving ingredients well, release them slowly, and hydrate skin by sealing it. Six versions varied the solid and liquid lipids and the surfactant, plus one placebo.

All versions trapped 66 to 93 percent of the vitamin, with particles from 68 to 290 nanometers. Release came in two phases: a burst, then a slow tail. In skin tests, the gel kept the vitamin in the skin with little passing through. On volunteers, the best gel raised moisture retention up to 68 percent and improved elasticity more than a plain solution gel. The authors credit pairing both vitamin forms in one carrier.
pmc-12661706:
Yuheng Yan and co-authors study triptolide, a natural compound from a traditional Chinese herb, as a treatment lead for small cell lung cancer. Their 2025 paper notes that this cancer is highly aggressive and has few treatment options.

Lab assays tested how triptolide affects cancer cell growth, movement, and invasion, and a network pharmacology analysis pointed to likely targets. The compound raised reactive oxygen species and triggered pyroptosis, a fiery form of cell death, through caspase-3 and GSDME. A mouse xenograft model was used to confirm the effect in living animals. The work sets out a clear mechanism that later drug studies can test.
pmc-12663306:
Mashael Maashi and seven co-authors build a deep learning model that segments lungs and screens for tuberculosis in chest X-rays, with shape aware feature blending. Tuberculosis is a chronic bacterial lung illness and a major killer. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

Chest X-rays are the main first check, and deep learning now aids spotting suspect marks. The model stacks features in layers and fuses them with shape sense, to sharpen both lung outlines and disease calls. The aim is early, exact screening that helps radiologists flag lesions and nodes. The authors frame it as a low cost aid for busy clinics.
pmc-12663406:
Véronique Gaudreault, Benoit Marchand, Raphaëlle Larcher, and seven colleagues map the neighborhoods of trafficking proteins in this two thousand twenty-five cell biology paper. RAB GTPases are the largest small GTPase family and direct membrane trafficking: cargo sorting, vesicle budding, transport, docking, and fusion. Their protein partners interact transiently, making them hard to catch. Proximity labeling solves this by chemically tagging whatever sits near a target protein inside living cells.

Using APEX2 labeling on twenty-three human RAB proteins, the team catalogued each one's neighboring proteome. Bioinformatics surfaced new connections, including a novel RAB25 partnership with DENND6A, where extra RAB25 pulled DENND6A onto recycling endosomes. Functional links also emerged between RAB14 and the EARP complex, and between SHIP164 and its relative UHRF1BP1, in endosomal recruitment. The authors offer the dataset as a resource for discovering how RAB proteins organize cellular logistics.
pmc-12671106:
Jinming Liu and co-authors published a study in 2025 on the safety of guided cancer drugs for bladder cancer. These drugs link an antibody to a poison payload, homing in on tumor cells. Their real-world harm profiles are still being mapped.

The team mined a United States harm-report system from 2004 to 2024. Of 494 reports on four such drugs, one drug made up over ninety percent. Each drug showed a distinct harm pattern: skin and metabolism ills for the main one, gut events for another. Kidney signals emerged for one drug, and bleeding and lung signals for a fourth. One mouth infection tied to the main drug was missing from its label. The authors urge drug-specific watch plans in the clinic.
pmc-12686406:
Xiaokun Hong and co-authors built a database and a deep learning predictor for how protein modifications steer phase separation in a 2025 paper. Liquid-liquid phase separation forms the membraneless droplets that organize cell chemistry, and it goes wrong in several diseases. Chemical tags added to proteins after they are built, called post-translational modifications, strongly tune that separation.

No dedicated resource gathered those effects before. The team curated a database of modification-regulated cases, then trained a model to predict new ones. Predictions can guide experiments on droplet control, a possible drug strategy for diseases of faulty droplets. The work pairs a data resource with a tool, a combination that tends to speed a young field.
pmc-12687906:
Myriam Jaam and co-authors audit heart-protective prescribing for diabetic patients with artery disease in Qatar primary care. Guidelines urge a bundle of drug classes for this high-risk group. Records from twenty-nine clinics covered 2,870 patients through 2021. Only about ten percent got high-intensity statins as advised.

About twelve percent received the newer sugar-lowering heart drugs. Blood pressure drugs of the ACE or ARB family reached fifty-six percent. Male sex, worse sugar control, and a lipid diagnosis each raised guideline use. Together such traits explained only sixteen percent of the variation. The authors call the gap wide and press for fixes against clinical inertia.
pmc-12690906:
Cécile Couchoud and co-authors map how the burden of diabetes and kidney disease varies across France, in a 2025 study. Using national health databases for 2017, before the pandemic, the team computed disability-adjusted life years for each condition and region. They then compared those rates with an index of local deprivation to see whether poorer areas carry more disease.

Diabetes cost about 685 healthy years per 100,000 people, against 251 for kidney disease, and men carried more of both burdens than women. The regional detail helps French planners aim staff and funding where the combined load of the two linked diseases bites hardest. The maps also split each region's burden by sex, so local gaps stay visible.
pmc-12692306:
Kornieieva and co-authors review whether molecular hydrogen gas could help treat heart failure. The condition, where the heart cannot pump enough blood, grows more common and still kills many patients within five years. Current drugs do not cover all its tangled causes.

Hydrogen seems to protect the heart by fighting oxidation, calming inflammation, and slowing cell death. Studies in several failure models show it easing stress on heart cells, supporting their energy factories, and limiting scarring and thickening. The reviewers call this the first summary of the field. They stress the work is young, and human value remains unproven.
pmc-12694806:
Sofie Baarnhielm and co-authors ask how migrants in Sweden made sense of official Covid advice in a 2025 study. The pandemic showed that health messages do not reach all groups with equal ease. The study focuses on residents who do not speak Swedish as a first language, in two mixed areas of greater Stockholm.

Seventy six residents were interviewed over more than a year, and their answers were grouped into five themes. People weighed rival sources, chose whom to trust, and judged official acts. Advice in a mother tongue made the content far easier to grasp. The authors draw lessons for fair, clear health messages and for readying local areas for the next crisis.
pmc-12696306:
Dimitrios Katsaros and Dimitrios Mougiakakos reviewed engineered T cells as a treatment for immune disorders of the nerves and brain, in a paper published in 2025. The cells carry a made receptor that aims them at one target type. In blood cancers they wipe the target out deeply and for long. Cell design now chases safer, cheaper, faster cells.

The same wipe-out can serve autoimmune disorders of the nerves. Early trials cover a muscle weakness illness, a cord illness, and a stiff person illness, with promising early marks. Broad B cell depletion leads; finer depletion of just the harmful B cells is in development. The pair sorts who fits the treatment, how to prepare them, and the harm watch afterward. They call nerve use a strong new front.
pmc-12696906:
Likai Pang and co-authors test a treatment for spinal cord injury based on cell packets loaded with a small RNA strand, in a research paper from 2025. Cord injury harms feeling and movement, and many new cases occur each year. Small RNA strands guide gene activity, and shifts in them shape stress, swelling, and cell death after injury.

Packets from stem cells carried the strand into tests in cells and in mice. Treated cells grew better, and stress after injury eased. Mice showed better recovery of movement. Gene data helped pick the strand and its targets. The work points to a new path for cord repair.
pmc-12699206:
Jianping Yang and co-authors published this grassland study in 2025. Shrubs are spreading across the alpine meadows of the Tibetan Plateau as the climate warms and grazing pressure grows. Tibetan herders have fought the spread for centuries by uprooting shrubs, burning patches in the dormant season, and rotating herds. The team measured encroachment across the Zoige Plateau at heights from 3,400 to 3,900 meters. They also ran experiments removing shrubs, restricting canopies, and excluding roots.

Elevation strongly limited how fast shrubs spread in the short term. The experiments showed that shade from shrub canopies does most of the damage, explaining about sixty percent of the change. Roots mattered far less, at under three percent. Canopy shade starves the grasses beneath, letting shrubs tighten their hold. Traditional herding methods strike exactly at that canopy advantage. By cutting the shade, they free the understory grasses to recover.
pmc-12699806:
Ronghong Guo and co-authors look for blood signs that flag lung damage in systemic sclerosis, in a 2025 study. Systemic sclerosis hardens skin and organs, and scarred lungs are its top cause of death. Finding the lung form early can change care, so cheap blood markers are in demand.

The team studied 177 patients, 116 with lung involvement and 61 without. They measured signs of inflammation, blood clotting traits, and the self-attacking antibodies the disease is known for. Math models then tested which signs, alone or joined as a triad, best separated the two groups. A strong combined marker could help doctors order scans and treatment sooner for the patients at real risk.
pmc-12699906:
Mohammed Tahir, Dlnya Mohammed, and Chinar Sadiq report in 2025 how common a virus linked to cervical cancer is among women in Iraq. The virus spreads by sex and can cause warts and cancer, yet data from Iraq have been sparse. The team looked back at lab cases to fill that gap.

Samples from more than two thousand married women tested over two years showed a positive rate near thirteen percent. Some carried high-risk types only, some low-risk types only, and a small share carried both. Two types stood out as most common. Most women with the virus carried a single type, and the data can guide screening and prevention plans.
pmc-12700706:
Renesa Tarannum and co-authors map, in a 2025 study, how messenger RNAs sit in the fine branches of nerve cells in the hippocampus. Nerve cells ship these RNAs out to their branch tips, so proteins can be made right where links form. RNA travels in clumps called granules. A live debate asks if many RNA types share the same granules, or ride apart. The team used a tagged-light method that can read many RNA types at once in one sample.

They tracked 15 RNA types known to sit in the branch field of rat and mouse hippocampus. The RNAs showed as dots of mixed size, spread through the field. How often two types shared a spot rose and fell with how much of each was present. Tests that copy cell-type gaps in amount gave the same pattern. Chance, set by amount, best explains the layout.
pmc-12700906:
Hebat-Allah Tohamy builds a two-in-one microbe sensor from paper industry waste in this 2025 paper. The material joins lignosulfonate, a wood derived polymer, with carbon dots, specks that glow under light. Spectroscopy and modeling confirmed the dots formed and pack more tightly than the plain polymer.

The composite killed Staphylococcus aureus and the fungus Candida albicans on contact, leaving sixteen millimeter clear zones, yet spared Escherichia coli, shielded by its outer membrane. As a sensor, it answered each microbe with a distinct glow: a blue to red shift for one, green star shapes for another, red filaments for the third, all with fading brightness. The author pitches it for food safety, drug quality checks, and protecting heritage objects.
pmc-12701306:
Xue-Yao Guo and co-authors present a 2025 review of Parkinson's disease. The disease is a progressive brain disorder with a growing global burden. Current drugs ease symptoms but do not stop the disease. Faulty clumping of one protein sits near the core of the process. The review spans spread, risk factors, molecular causes, prevention, and therapy. Newer risks include gut germ imbalance and environmental toxins.

Body-wide routes, such as gut-brain and kidney-brain axes, join the classic brain story. Molecular faults range from protein cleanup failure to iron imbalance. Prevention and therapy sections weigh what can be done now. Clinicians and students get one integrated map of a complex disease. The body-wide framing is the review's fresh angle: Parkinson's may start far from the brain, which changes where early detection should look.
pmc-12701606:
Nosair and four colleagues test a plant pigment packed in tiny bubbles against a hardy hospital germ in twenty twenty-five. The germ forms slimy layers, called biofilms, that shrug off drug care. It also talks to its kin with chemical signals to build those layers. The pigment, from a related germ, was packed into fat bubbles to help it work.

Packed pigment killed drug resistant strains in lab tests and cut biofilm growth by a wide margin. It also cut movement, iron grabbing, and the signal gene the germ uses to coordinate. In mice with lung infection, it cut germ counts and raised survival. The team sees it as a new path against stubborn infections.
pmc-12703006: Mohamed Azmi, Nur 'Aini Eddy Warman, Fatimah Mohamed Shah, and a wider team wrote this case report, published in 2025. It describes muscle breakdown caused by an underactive thyroid alone, with none of the usual triggers such as trauma or drugs. Rhabdomyolysis from hypothyroidism is rare but dangerous, since debris from dying muscle can wreck the kidneys. The authors stress it can appear without classic thyroid symptoms. They urge creatine kinase screening in puzzling presentations, so treatment starts before kidney injury sets in.
pmc-12703206:
Silas Fischer and co-authors present a 2025 natural history study of microscopic algae riding on migrating songbirds. Protists turn up in odd far-flung places, and how they travel is a standing puzzle. Waterbirds are known microbe carriers, but land birds that migrate long distances were barely checked.

The team sampled tail feathers from four thrush species with different migration styles. Every one of the seven samples held diatoms, the glass-shelled algae: 224 individuals from 25 genera in all. Most were freshwater bottom-dwellers, and some still held their green chloroplasts, a sign they might be alive. The authors suggest songbirds are overlooked ferries for these microbes. That route could help explain how pond species cross dry land between wetlands.
pmc-12703406:
Pet food flavorings need formal approval, and renewals require a fresh safety look. A European Food Safety Authority panel reviewed the renewal request for L-cysteine hydrochloride monohydrate, a flavoring compound sold for cats and dogs. The maker showed that the product on the market still matches the terms of its existing authorization.

The panel concluded the additive remains safe for cats and dogs when used under the current conditions. For the people who handle it, the picture is stricter: the substance irritates skin, eyes, and mucous membranes, and any exposure counts as a risk, so care in handling is required. Because this was a renewal rather than a first approval, the panel saw no need to test again whether the flavoring works. The opinion keeps the product authorized on its existing terms.
pmc-12703806:
A European Food Safety Authority fellowship project built a transparent way to judge the risks of eating wild boar meat, taking a One Health view that links human, animal, and environmental health. Step-by-step risk assessments are common, but they often skip clear statements of uncertainty. The fellow set out to fix that with flowcharts that show each stage of the reasoning.

Two case studies were chosen: a parasite, Trichinella, and a family of industrial chemicals called PFAS, for consumers in Latvia and Germany. For each hazard the flowchart estimates how common and concentrated it is, and adds side nodes for factors that raise or lower the final risk. The parasite chart has already been shown at two conferences. The authors offer the format as a clearer template for food risk communication.
pmc-12706206:
Nick Mamo and five co-authors improve a Dutch care network for persistent symptoms in a 2025 paper. Conditions like functional disorders need joined-up care from many professionals, yet fragmented systems leave patients and staff frustrated. Their participatory study sat inside a regional network for a year, led by an action group of patients-by-experience and local professionals. The group picked goals and ran concrete actions to improve how the network works.

The paper reports which change processes proved realistic inside such a network. It also draws lessons on the conditions that make change stick, such as shared ownership and a facilitator embedded in the group. The focus is practical know-how for other networks.
pmc-12706906:
Anderson, Tsuyuki, Fernandez DeSoto, and Stockman study medical mistrust among women who have lived through sexual violence. Their study is from two thousand twenty-five and is set in the United States. Survivors face worse health yet may shun care for fear of fresh trauma, stigma, or cost. Such mistrust has been less studied in this group.

The THRIVE study tracked women who had faced recent forced sex, and compared them with women who had not. Mistrust was scored with a group-based scale and its sub-scales. Women with past or recent rape showed higher mistrust than others, with recent cases the highest. Black women scored higher than non-Black women. The authors call for care that is trauma-aware and for routine screening for violence.
pmc-12707806:
Yoshinobu Saito and four co-authors test a free health app inside an online exercise program in a 2025 study. The app, the ME-BYO index, was built by a Japanese prefecture to turn health data into one score showing current status and future disease risk. Being free, it can reach far more people than paid apps, if users will actually measure themselves with it.

Twenty-three adults over forty who rarely did strength exercise joined an online training program, meeting twice a week. Alongside the workouts, they took their own index measurements. The study checked whether they measured as instructed, whether the routine was workable, and whether participants found the app acceptable. The authors use the answers to judge whether self-measurement with the free index can ride along with online training as a practical health habit.
pmc-12709006:
Christopher Ahmad and co-authors studied whether pre-surgery survey scores predict recovery after elbow ligament surgery in a 2025 paper. The operation, common in baseball pitchers, repairs the ligament that steadies the elbow when throwing. Return-to-sport rates are good, but each player's timeline and risk of setbacks vary.

The team drew on a multi-center registry of baseball players treated between 2019 and 2023. Of 506 screened patients, 146 had at least two years of follow-up and full survey data. The authors tested whether baseline scores and surgical details forecast recovery milestones and adverse events. Sound forecasts would help players and teams plan seasons around surgery more honestly.
pmc-12709706:
Adriana Toro and co-authors defend, in twenty twenty-five, a new surgical technique for acute cholecystitis, inflamed gallbladder, in a point-by-point response to critics. A commentary in the same journal had attacked their method. Their earlier paper presented the technique as a way to avoid subtotal cholecystectomy, a partial gallbladder removal used when full removal is unsafe. The critics questioned that claim. This manuscript answers each criticism in turn.

The authors explain why the technique deserves a place in the surgeon's toolkit for very severe cases. The title itself urges care: a new technique to use carefully. The exchange shows scientific debate in print, with the original team clarifying scope and intent.
pmc-12711206:
Gabriela Brandina Aquino de Abreu and co-authors test new mosquito control options in a 2025 cage study. One control trick lets mosquitoes carry a growth-blocking chemical to their own breeding water. Resistance to that chemical may grow, so stand-ins with different modes of action are needed.

The team compared the standard chemical with diflubenzuron, which blocks shell building, and spinosad, a bacterial toxin. Trials ran blind in large cages with dengue-carrying mosquitoes and cups of larvae. In open cups, adult emergence fell from about 90 percent in controls to 30, 56, and 75 percent across the three treatments. Spinosad also shortened adult female life. The authors judge diflubenzuron the most promising stand-in and call for field tests.
pmc-12711906:
Gentle electric stimulation of the brain is being tested against mild cognitive impairment, and dose may matter more than the device settings suggest. Jung-Won Lee and co-authors study that dose question in a 2025 paper with 55 patients. Computer models tuned the electric field strength reaching a frontal brain target for each person.

Stronger fields tracked healthier white matter in several left-side tracts, judged by diffusion imaging measures. Alzheimer's-related traits changed the size of the benefit. Amyloid-positive patients and non-carriers of two risk gene variants showed greater white matter plasticity. One gene status also governed whether stronger fields meant better executive function. The findings argue for personalizing stimulation strength rather than using one setting for all.
pmc-12712006:
Tingxu Chen and co-authors build a two-metal catalyst that cleans ammonia from exhaust in a 2025 paper. Ammonia is a major precursor of air pollutants, and burning it off selectively is hard because activity and selectivity trade against each other. Dual-atom catalysts can break that trade-off by pairing two different active sites.

Their catalyst places iridium oxidation sites and tungsten reduction sites on a ceria support. The two sites run a cascade, passing intermediates between them. The design aims to convert ammonia to harmless nitrogen efficiently, a step toward cleaner engines and industrial burners.
pmc-12712706:
Anette Væringstad and co-authors build a goal-setting interview for frail patients who live at home. Their 2025 study adapts a known interview so trial outcomes match what each patient truly wants. The new tool serves a trial on preventing crises in frail home patients across Norway.

The work runs in two parts with mixed methods. Staff in two towns helped reshape the interview through meeting notes and translation. Use tests then drew on 126 patients, 72 kin, and staff groups from 28 towns in the main trial. Checks cover whether the tool is workable, whether raters agree, and whether its content is sound. Goal focus covers both personal aims and readiness to change.
pmc-12714106:
Sultan Ahmed and co-authors report a hard treatment call in a 2025 case paper. A patient had fluid build-up around the lung tied to the liver, a state called hepatic hydrothorax. The twist was a hormone-making tumor in the pancreas, a rare growth often missed early for its vague signs.

Such tumors make up a small share of cancers in the United States and grow mostly in the gut, lungs, or pancreas. Here the fluid came from blockage, not from a worn-out liver, which is the usual cause. That split changed the care path. The case walks through how the team found the cause and chose a plan.
pmc-12714706:
Yu Liu, Yong Wan, Weimin Huang, and Zihao Zhan present a 2025 paper on spotting storage tanks in satellite and aerial images. Tanks at oil and gas sites matter for tracking methane leaks, a strong greenhouse gas. Older feature-based methods raise many false alarms, and standard deep learning detectors miss small tanks or confuse them with the background.

Their method draws circular boxes, matching the round top view of most tanks, and adds a large selective kernel that adjusts how wide the model looks. Round boxes keep the overlap score steady for small objects. The authors report fewer missed tanks and fewer false hits than the common detectors they compare against.
pmc-12715206:
Li wrote a solo study in twenty twenty-five on a smart plan to run food supply chains in a green way. Farms and food firms face waste, poor tracking, and shocks like storms or late trucks. Old plans adapt poorly when trade shifts fast.

His plan pairs a two-way memory net with a search rule drawn from sea rescue work. Sensors and market trends feed the net to forecast make and store needs. The search rule then picks plans that fit room, stock, and demand caps. In tests it cut waste by about a third and raised gains. It beat five rival tools on key scores.
pmc-12715906:
Marina Mor Shalom and co-authors track twelve years of mental health visits in Israeli community care through reform, pandemic, and war. Depression and anxiety touch about one in eight people worldwide. Their overlap with physical illness strains family doctors heavily.

Records came from a health fund serving millions of members. Adults visiting family doctors from 2013 onward were grouped yearly. Groups split into depression or anxiety, severe illness, and comparison. Visit rates and service use were compared across the groups. The window covers a national mental health reform. It also spans COVID-19 and the Iron Swords war. Trends reveal how crises reshape everyday care demand. Planners gain a rare long view of community needs.
pmc-12716506:
People with multiple sclerosis who take B-cell depleting drugs face higher risk from COVID-19, and it was unclear how well vaccines protect them. The authors followed 226 people with the disease through three doses of messenger RNA vaccine. They measured antibodies that block the virus, testing the ancestral strain and several variants from the pandemic years.

Before the third dose, people on B-cell depleting therapy had far lower blocking antibodies than healthy adults or patients on other treatments. The third dose did not lift them much. Patients whose B cells were intact matched healthy adults and gained strong boosts from the third dose. After that dose, the gap between the two patient groups widened further. No one in the study was hospitalized or died from COVID-19. The findings point to weaker vaccine protection for the depleted group.
pmc-12716706:
Nikesh Gyawali and three co-authors present a 2025 study of how vaccine talk on social media changed across a decade. The team collected English posts about vaccines from a major platform, spanning seven calm years and the three pandemic years. Public feeling toward vaccines seemed to harden in that window, but the narrative shift needed measuring.

Their data set curates 18.7 million posts from an initial 129 million, spanning 2013 to 2022. Drawing on a psychology model of how groups judge warmth and competence, they coded how speakers portray vaccines and the people tied to them. The analysis traces which story lines rose after COVID-19 arrived and which faded.
pmc-12716806:
In Ceará, Brazil, de Freitas Corpes and co-authors survey side effects among women taking hormone therapy for breast cancer. Seventy-five patients at a breast clinic were grouped by drug, tamoxifen or aromatase blockers such as anastrozole, and by whether use had passed twelve months. The team then linked symptom patterns to habits, prior treatment, and calcium use.

Every group reported some burden. Long-term tamoxifen users voiced more sexual complaints, while hot flashes, muscle and joint pain, and fatigue dominated the blocker groups. Daily habits, earlier therapies, and calcium replacement each tied significantly to symptom occurrence. The authors urge clinicians to watch for these effects early and act before women abandon a therapy that guards against relapse.
pmc-12717706:
Baranya Suprabha and colleagues examine whether stressed parents have children who cope worse, fear more, and behave worse during dental treatment. Parenting stress is known to affect children's coping strategies and behavior in non-dental settings. The cross-sectional study enrolled one hundred sixty-eight children aged eight to twelve who required dental treatment under local anaesthesia.

Parents completed a stress scale; children completed coping and fear questionnaires; behavior was rated on Frankl's scale. Contrary to expectation, no significant correlation emerged between parenting stress scores and children's use of destructive, external, or internal coping strategies. Parenting stress scores also did not differ significantly by children's clinical dental fear status. The null results caution dentists against assuming a stressed parent means a difficult child.
pmc-12717806:
Jingyi Zhao, Xinwei Wang, and Baolong Li review how uric acid levels link to Alzheimer's disease, in two thousand twenty-five. Uric acid is a waste product in the blood. Studies have found a U-shaped link, where both low and high levels go with higher risk.

At normal levels, the acid may protect the brain by fighting cell damage and swelling. It may also help clear the harmful proteins that build up in the disease. At abnormal levels, it may do the opposite and speed harm. The review also covers current drugs for the disease, and plant and standard drugs that affect the acid, to guide future work.
pmc-12718306:
Aaron Ratschow and co-authors show that flow can speed up the charging of a porous electrode. Such electrodes sit at the heart of supercapacitors, which store charge in soaked pores. The team modeled a single pore filled with a salt fluid. They solved the linked math for ion drift and fluid flow.

Their model found that the charging itself stirs the fluid. That swirl, called electroconvection, drags fresh ions in and speeds the charge. A clean math sketch predicts both the flow and the extra current it brings. The effect grows strong in long thin pores past a threshold voltage set by the fluid. The finding may guide faster energy storage designs.
pmc-12718506:
Siyu Zhu and co-authors test breath nitric oxide levels in children with allergic asthma in a 2025 study. Breath tests at set flow rates can hint where airway swelling sits, in central or outer airways. The team asked whether those levels split children by allergy type in a useful way.

One hospital gave data on 487 children, grouped by inhaled, food, mixed, or no allergy. Levels at both flow rates ran higher in the inhaled and mixed groups than in food or no allergy groups. A measure tied to outer airways did not split the groups. The central airway signal thus looks most useful for telling allergy types apart.
pmc-12719206:
Jiangfei Li and co-authors pack cannabidiol oil into porous starch to make it dissolve and absorb better, in a study from 2025. The full-spectrum oil has many noted health uses, but it mixes poorly with water and little of it reaches the body. Porous starch, full of tiny holes, can carry such oils.

The team tuned the mix and reached a packing rate near 81 percent under the best settings. The oil sat in the starch in a loose, non-crystal form and withstood more heat than free oil. The packed form dissolved about 18 times better in water and released far faster in fluids that mimic the stomach and gut. Its defense against oxidation rose by over 20 percent as well.
pmc-12719506:
Yong Wu and nine co-authors present a 2025 study on combining moxibustion with chemotherapy against stomach cancer. Moxibustion is a traditional treatment that warms acupuncture points with burning herbs. Tumors often shield themselves with an immune-suppressing environment, which blunts therapy. The team paired data analysis with mouse experiments to test whether the combined treatment reshapes that shield.

Two immune signals tied to suppression ran high in stomach tumors and linked to worse outlooks. In mice, the combination slowed tumor growth most, cutting it by nearly half. It also lowered suppressor cells and their signals in the blood while raising killer T cells inside tumors. The authors describe a two-way effect: less suppression and stronger attack at once. They present the pairing as a model for joining traditional and Western cancer care.
pmc-12720106:
Lingjiao Zhu and eight co-authors find tasty, health-active peptides in eggshell membranes, a food industry waste, in a 2025 paper. The fragments were hunted with machine learning rather than bench trial and error.

From computer-digested membrane protein, the team picked three new peptides. Made in the lab, all three tasted strongly of umami, the savory flavor, at very low levels. They also boosted umami in mixtures and fought free radicals. Quantum chemistry showed which building blocks do the work. Docking tests showed the peptides fit the tongue's umami receptor pair in a stable grip. The study turns a byproduct into a source of flavor and function, with a map of why the pieces work.
pmc-12721106:
Zoe Djajadikarta and co-authors report secondary results from a trial of home step training in multiple sclerosis, in work published in 2025. The main trial tested a computerised stepping game played at home. This analysis asked whether the training also improved ankle position sense and calf muscle performance.

Sixty-six people with the disease were split between six months of the game system and usual care. Tests measured how small an ankle movement people could detect, their reaction time, and calf strength and endurance before and after. No measure differed between the groups, and recovery after a sustained contraction was alike too. The authors conclude the step system did not improve position sense or muscle performance, even though it targets falls through other routes.
pmc-12721206:
Nathallie George and Dominique Marshall report listeriosis in a pregnant patient in a 2025 paper. Maternal listeriosis is rare but can harm mother and baby badly. Its signs mimic common viral ills, so diagnosis oft lags.

A twenty eight year old woman came in late in pregnancy with fever. Headache, light sensitivity, and muscle aches pointed toward meningitis. Blood cultures grew Listeria monocytogenes, the food borne germ. Brain scans showed no spread inside the skull. Swift antibiotics brought full recovery for the mother. A healthy baby was born weeks later by caesarean section.
pmc-12722206:
Yingxin Liu and co-authors aim a drug carrier at the brain inflammation behind nerve pain, in a 2025 mouse study. Neuropathic pain is driven by chronic crosstalk between two glial cell types. The carrier is a fat bubble decorated with transferrin and phosphatidylserine, loaded with a drug that blocks clumping of the TDP-43 protein. The design slips past the blood-brain barrier and homes to glial cells.

In dishes the carrier kept cells healthy and pushed them toward calm states. In male mice it eased pain behavior, cut inflammatory signals, and quieted the cGAS-STING pathway. The authors pitch the approach as a disease-modifying route, not just symptom relief.
pmc-12722306:
Nastaran Salehi, Olle Eriksson, Johan Hellsvik, and Manuel Pereiro model magnetism at two scales at once in a 2025 study. Some magnetic behavior needs atom-level detail, while device-scale patterns need a coarser view. Their three-dimensional hybrid simulation joins both, letting engineered defects sit inside a larger magnetic body.

They built two test defects: a double slit that splits spin waves, and a small tetrahedral cluster whose properties can be tuned. The slit produced interference patterns like those of light waves, a hint for wave-based computing. The cluster bent domain walls and could destroy or reshape skyrmions, the tiny swirls eyed for future memory. Defect design thus steers magnetic behavior.
pmc-12722606:
Cancer that has spread to the brain can sometimes be removed by surgery, and what happens around that surgery shapes survival. Peng Sun and co-authors reviewed 228 patients who had brain metastases removed at one hospital between 2012 and 2020. They tracked survival and tested which factors, including surgical technique and the order of other treatments, predicted how patients fared.

Median survival was fourteen months. A patient's functional score before surgery was the strongest predictor of outcome. Radiation after surgery stretched median survival to eighteen months, and a small group treated before and after surgery reached forty-one months. In lung cancer cases, targeted therapy also linked to much longer survival. The authors favor aggressive, combined treatment.
pmc-12722706:
Kevin Schoeffler and co-authors simulated magnetic reconnection with a cheaper numerical method that keeps the physics honest, published in 2025. In space plasmas, magnetic field lines snap and reconnect, flinging particles to high energies. Modeling that needs both huge scales and fine particle detail, a brutal combination. The team's semi-implicit particle method allows coarser grids without the instabilities that plague standard schemes.

Simulations in two and three dimensions followed a relativistic plasma sheet from first tearing to full reconnection. Particles emerged with the expected power-law energy spectra and cutoff energies, matching results from costlier explicit methods. The same quality arrived at considerably reduced resolution. The authors present the method as a bridge between planetary-scale structure and particle-scale acceleration. Astrophysical modelers, they note, can now reach regimes that were priced out.
pmc-12722906:
Zhenya Yang and co-authors test a compound from a traditional Chinese herb against colorectal cancer in cells, organoids, and mice, in a 2025 study. The compound, cryptotanshinone, had shown anti-cancer promise, but its combined effects on tumor, immune system, and gut microbes were unclear. The team used mouse tumor cells, lab-grown mini-tumors, and a mouse model where cancer is triggered chemically.

The compound slowed tumor cell growth and triggered their death in the lab. In mice it shrank tumors, eased colon damage and swelling, revived tired immune cells, and restored a healthier gut microbe mix. Metabolic faults in the tumors also eased. The authors present it as a multi-pronged candidate worth further development.
pmc-12723306:
Ryan Jonathan Sitanggang and a large team of co-authors published this commentary in 2025. It tells how HTAsiaLink, a network that links health technology assessment groups across Asia and the Pacific, wrote its first strategic plan. Such assessments weigh the value of new health tools so governments can spend wisely.

The network began in 2011 and now counts more than fifty members from twenty economies. In 2024 it ran a planning process that mixed a review of other networks' plans with wide input from members. The work produced five priorities, each with actions and signs of success. The authors share the process so other networks, above all in lower-income settings, can copy what worked. They stress that member voices shaped the plan from the start.
pmc-12723406:
Ten researchers studied how a farmed grouper responds when water oxygen drops sharply, in a 2025 paper. Oxygen in water shapes whether fish farming can stay productive and sustainable. The team held healthy blue-spotted groupers in normal water or low-oxygen water for up to nine hours and sampled their livers.

Gene activity readings found over six thousand genes whose activity shifted under low oxygen. The biggest body changes came at three to six hours of stress. Shifted genes clustered in paths for energy use, immune defense, and cell death control. Several liver enzymes also spiked at the three and six hour marks, backing the gene data. The authors say the three to six hour window is when the fish's response peaks. Their map of the response could guide breeding of hardier fish.
pmc-12724006:
Ronel T Aguilar and co-authors map a farmed seaweed in a 2025 study from the Philippines. The seaweed, sold under the name cottonii, yields a gel used in food and industry. Its farming was thought to be limited to the south of the country.

Samples from four regions across the Philippines were checked for shape and read with four gene markers from different parts of the cell. Family trees built from those markers showed the species living more widely than expected. Its gene diversity across regions was also mapped, giving growers and regulators a firmer base for trade rules and farm expansion.
pmc-12725706:
Akanksha Sharma and a large team wrote a 2025 study on predicting hamstring strain injuries in pro football players from MRI texture data. Fat inside thigh muscle holds fine patterns a scan can capture. The team asked if those patterns foresee future strains. Muscle balance and past injury data were tested as add-ons.

Scans covered just over ninety professional players, a small share of whom later got hurt. A neighbor-based classifier sorted the feature sets. Radiomic features from hamstring fat alone predicted injury fairly well. Blending them with balance measures did notably better than either alone. Injury history features added little on their own.
pmc-12727806:
Knöbel and five co-authors wrote a 2025 study asking whether mental executive functions predict soccer success in elite youth players. Executive functions, inhibition, mental flexibility, and working memory, are often touted in talent scouting. The evidence for their predictive value, however, is shaky. The team tested it three ways.

Players averaged about 15 years old. Coaches' ratings of future potential were collected for 74 players. A subgroup of 34 was tracked for age-related change, and 69 were followed toward senior performance levels. Statistical models found no significant link between executive functions and coaches' ratings, nor with later senior level. Flexibility did develop with age much as in the general population. The authors conclude the scouting enthusiasm outruns the evidence. Small samples, they note, demand bigger confirmatory studies.
pmc-12727906:
Che Chen, Qianfeng Shao, and Sheng Zhou probe how a classical Chinese formula might act against Alzheimer's disease, starting in software. Their 2025 paper studies a three-herb decoction long used for other conditions. Databases of herbal chemistry yielded thirty-seven active ingredients and 230 targets; disease gene data yielded thousands of altered genes, and forty-seven targets sat in the overlap.

Modeling pointed to three core targets and two standout plant compounds that dock neatly onto them. The enriched pathways involved inflammation signals and calcium signaling, familiar Alzheimer's territory. Cell tests then gave the software something real to answer to. In nerve-like cells injured by an amyloid fragment, the two compounds and serum from treated animals restored survival almost fully. Key pathway proteins shifted in the predicted directions. The authors present the work as a mechanism sketch with early laboratory support, not a clinical claim.
pmc-12728006:
Ignacio Marin-Jimenez and co-authors study combining two drug classes for Crohn's disease in a 2025 paper. Vedolizumab and JAK inhibitors each work through different mechanisms and help many patients alone. Combining them might offer a more integrated approach for severe or refractory disease, but the interaction needed study first.

Rather than a clinical trial, the team used systems biology and artificial intelligence in simulation. Modeling the joint action can flag likely synergy and risk before patients are exposed. Such in silico work helps prioritize which drug combinations deserve costly trials.
pmc-12728206:
Efstathios Mitropoulos and co-authors make microfluidic channels stretchy so fluids flow easier and go where told, in a 2025 paper. In blood vessels and lab chips alike, pressure drop throttles flow. Rigid walls cannot help; soft ones might, if placed with intent.

The team molded tree-like channel networks from silicone rubber in one step, swapping some wall segments for thin elastic membranes. Under pressure the membranes bulge, and the most elastic network's flow rose nonlinearly as compliance climbed. By choosing which branches got membranes, the researchers steered flow direction with pressure alone. The trick cuts pressure loss without exotic fabrication, and it turns a passive chip into one that reroutes fluid on command.
pmc-12729006:
Young patients with a dislocated, malformed hip face few good options: fix the joint they have, or replace it early. Chuan Li and co-authors report mid-term results for a modified Colonna capsular arthroplasty, a repair that reshapes the hip using its own capsule. Their 2025 study reviews nineteen patients, mostly women with a mean age of about nineteen, treated between 2017 and 2019.

After a median follow-up of nearly six years, hip function scores rose from about 59 to about 87. Leg length difference shrank from about 28 millimetres to about 11, and X-ray angles and coverage improved in every hip. One patient went on to a full hip replacement six years after surgery. Pain scores, though, barely moved. The authors call the repair favourable for this group, while asking for longer follow-up before final judgement.
pmc-12729106:
Zihao Wang and Jianchen Zhang modeled, in a 2025 study, how place shapes tuberculosis rates across China. The disease burden shifts from province to province, and national averages hide local drivers. Their aim was a factor system that respects that patchwork.

First, a two-stage screen picked the key indicators behind incidence. A plain national regression then read the broad links. Province-level models followed: one letting each factor's weight drift over space, and a multiscale version letting each factor drift at its own scale. The multiscale model fit the data best. Comparing the two showed how a factor can matter strongly in one region and weakly in another. Health planners gain a sharper lens for aiming control measures where each driver bites hardest.
pmc-12729206:
Tolesa Okuba and co-authors used linked national data to study health service use by Australian adults with cochlear implants, in a 2025 paper. How often implant users see doctors or use social services was not well known. The study drew on a person-level data asset that links health and service records.

The cohort held 6,305 adults who got an implant between 2011 and 2021. Just over half were older adults, and the rest were of working age. Older adults saw general doctors more often on average. The team modeled which traits linked to heavier service use in each age group. The results help planners fund care for a growing implant population.
pmc-12729306:
Laura Menabò and co-authors let Italian students define bullying in their own words. Their 2025 study used focus groups rather than surveys, since much bullying research leans on numbers alone. They asked how youth define bullying, what roles people play, and how victims cope.

Sixteen focus groups brought together more than two hundred students. Seven domains emerged from the talks. Power imbalance was the most shared mark of bullying, while intent and repetition were less agreed. Physical and verbal forms were widely named, and relational forms less so. Students named defender as a rare role beside bullies and bystanders. Coping ideas ranged from seeking support to nonchalance. The study gives schools a picture of bullying as students actually see it.
pmc-12729806:
Aneesha VijayaKumar and a team of co-authors reviewed crop biofortification as a fix for hidden hunger in South Asia. Their review, from twenty twenty-five, deals with micronutrient malnutrition. Lack of key vitamins and minerals stunts growth, clouds thought, and opens the door to disease. India and its neighbors bear a heavy share. The team sums the scale of the lack by age group and the traits that feed it.

They then map the ways to breed or treat crops so food holds more of the lacked nutrients. Such crops can reach far homes at low cost once in the seed line. State schemes round the plan out. Readers in food policy get a green path to a deep health gap.
pmc-12730506:
Ourania Kotsiou and co-authors read tiny RNA scraps in spit bubbles in 2025 as possible marks of chronic lung disease. COPD scars airways and limits flow, and bubbles shed by cells carry microRNAs that mirror airway change. Blood and lung-wash versions were known; spit was not. The team took induced spit from twenty stable patients and ten healthy peers, pulled the bubbles out, and read nine candidate RNAs.

Five RNAs shifted clearly in patients: two rose and three fell. One tracked symptom burden. One alone sorted disease fairly, and a trio sorted it well. Another best split mild from worse disease. The team pitches spit bubbles as a needle-free window on COPD, with larger checks owed.
pmc-12730606:
Begoña Escribano and co-authors tested whether sex hormones change how magnetic brain stimulation fights oxidative stress in a rat model of multiple sclerosis. The disease is an immune attack on the nervous system and strikes women more often than men. The team used the standard animal model and gave some rats estrogen, progesterone, or testosterone alongside the stimulation. Other rats had their ovaries removed and got hormone replacement instead.

Stimulation alone already eased the oxidative damage from the disease. In the ovary-removed rats, estrogen and progesterone replacement boosted the effect, waking up antioxidant defenses and softening clinical signs. Testosterone did not show the same help. The authors suggest that pairing stimulation with the right hormone therapy could strengthen treatment, at least in this animal setting. Human work would need to follow.
pmc-12730806:
Francesco Tona faulted modern cardiology culture in two thousand twenty-five. Technology in the field has never been stronger. Yet he sees the urge to ask why, and judgment, fading. Hands-on work often comes before thinking now. Whether a body fits the tool now outweighs whether treatment truly fits the patient. Sales pressure and set formulas reinforce that reflex.

Industry pressure shapes training settings as well. Rules can make tool-first habits seem normal. Research favors stand-in results over ones that matter. Checking current devices often beats asking new questions. Tona calls for bringing back the question why. Reforms in culture, schooling, and the system itself are needed. Technology should serve reasoning, not replace it. Values that put patients first must lead again.
pmc-12732406:
Bin Cai and co-authors describe in this 2025 paper a fellowship built to teach medical physicists the new craft of online adaptive radiotherapy. Modern systems reshape each day's radiation plan around the patient's shifted anatomy, but training programs rarely teach the skill. Their two-year fellowship immerses post-residency physicists in three commercial platforms, guided by scanner, magnet, or emission imaging.

Fellows rotate through contouring, planning, quality checks, and team decisions, judged against standard competency milestones, and each leads a research project. Twenty-two applied and two fellows joined in the first round, at home and abroad. The authors offer the design as a template for other centers. Other centers can copy the mold as written.
pmc-12732506:
Svetlana Svitko and co-authors study in 2025 how swelling in the brain from a bacterial signal worsens migraine signs in rats. Migraine brings severe pain plus sensitivity to touch and light, driven in part by a sensitized nerve system. The team gave the signal before birth or later in life, then triggered migraine with a standard drug.

Both groups showed stronger pain responses after the trigger. The early life group also showed more light avoidance. Nerve fibers answered more strongly to serotonin, and brain cells answered more to other triggers. Tests on tissue and blood showed more mast cell activity and higher pain signals. The work links early swelling to lasting nerve change.
pmc-12732606:
Bianca Tavares and co-authors followed babies born early and at term to see what shapes the age of the first tooth in 2025. Many factors have been linked to late tooth eruption. The team tested a path model that joins birth traits with social and health conditions.

The cohort held forty-three preterm and forty-eight full-term infants, checked each month from at least four months of age. Mothers answered questions on social background and health habits. Babies born early had a higher risk of later first teeth, by both plain age and age corrected for early birth. Gestational age also carried the effect of social and health conditions, which reached tooth timing through it.
pmc-12732706:
Dragica Selakovic and a large team of co-authors review brain stimulation as a treatment for major depression in a 2025 article. Depression is a leading cause of disability, and many patients do not respond to drugs or talk therapy. Two gentle methods, magnetic pulses and weak electric current applied through the scalp, have shown promise for such hard cases.

The review compares the two methods on how they work and how well they help, drawing on ten years of animal and human studies. Both may raise levels of a growth factor called BDNF, which helps brain cells form new links. That boost in brain flexibility may be part of how mood lifts and steadies. The authors call for more work on long-term effects and for care plans matched to each patient's markers.
pmc-12732806:
Dzakovich and co-authors study how spinach flavonoids change during digestion and how genes shape that change. Spinach holds a wide set of these plant compounds, which may drive its health gains. Little was known about their range, uptake, or heritability.

The team grew thirty spinach types, both hybrids and open-pollinated, under set conditions twice. They measured thirty-nine flavonoids and found the levels were shaped more by the setting than by genes. Two branches in flavonoid making may exist. How much reached the body after digestion showed stronger gene control than raw leaf content, a useful trait for breeders.
pmc-12732906:
Ratan Chaudhuri and Thomas Meyer review isosorbide diesters for skin and nerve inflammation, in work from 2025. This new compound family pairs barrier repair with immune calming in one chemistry. Two skin forms already reached blinded trials in children and adults with eczema.

The pair strengthens skin barrier, boosts surface moisture, and steadies skin cell growth. Trials showed less itch, less steroid need, and fewer staph colonies on treated skin. Sleep, severity scores, and life quality all improved under the topical pair. A newer fumarate cousin calms oxidation through a master defence switch in cells. Animal work hints at psoriasis and sclerosis uses, still awaiting human proof.
pmc-12733806:
Gaetano Ierardo and co-authors review a decade of studies on widening the upper jaw in growing patients and what it does for breathing. Published in 2025, the systematic review covers maxillary transverse deficiency, a narrow upper jaw linked to poor nasal breathing and sleep disordered breathing in children. Forty-one studies passed the screen.

Imaging consistently showed a larger nasal cavity and nasopharynx after expansion, with smaller or mixed effects deeper in the throat. Airflow tests and lung measures improved in several studies, and parents reported better sleep and quality of life across the board. Sleep study results were mixed. Certainty was graded low to very low, and the authors ask for standard outcomes.
pmc-12734206:
Guofeng Xing and co-authors characterize variants in the FLNC gene among Chinese patients with cardiomyopathy, in this 2025 Europe PMC paper. FLNC helps hold muscle structure together, and its variants are linked to several inherited heart muscle diseases and to rhythm problems. The team studied twenty-five patients at Beijing Anzhen Hospital with harmful or likely harmful FLNC variants.

Whole-exome sequencing found twenty-five variants of several types, classed by standard genetics guidelines. Dilated cardiomyopathy was the most common diagnosis. Heart scans showed reduced pumping function on average, and one variant type tracked with higher rates of a leaky heart valve. Clinical, imaging and family data round out the picture.
pmc-12734306:
Bassam Bin-Abbas and Mosleh Jabari compare weekly long-acting growth hormone against daily shots in children. Their systematic review and meta-analysis was published in twenty twenty-five. Daily injections work, but the burden wears families down and doses get missed.

The weekly form is chemically padded to linger in the body. The team searched three databases to late twenty twenty-five under standard review rules. Growth speed, height scores, and side effects were pooled across trials. Dose strength within the weekly arm was also compared, higher against lower. The question is practical: can one shot a week match seven without new harms? The synthesis gives prescribers a single evidence base for that choice.
pmc-12734806:
Turner leads a large team surveying harmful algae around the Isles of Scilly, in work from twenty twenty-five. The islands lie off the far southwest of the United Kingdom. Wild shellfish beds there are gathered for local food, but algae toxins had never been checked.

The team tested seawater and shellfish with field microscopes, lab tests, gene sequencing, and toxin kits. Local citizen scientists helped with sampling across the isolated islands. The survey design had to adapt during the national COVID period. Results give the first clear picture of which harmful species and toxins occur there. That baseline helps protect people who harvest and eat local shellfish.
pmc-12735106:
Bogdan Tarcau and co-authors count mental illness in psoriasis patients in a 2025 study. Psoriasis is a lasting skin illness that often brings a heavy mind burden. Records came from a university hospital in northeast Romania over ten years.

Over two thousand patients with the skin illness were checked for mind diagnoses in their files. The top finds were a broad depressive disorder, a mixed anxiety-depression state, and mild depression. Rates for each ran above background levels. Women showed their own pattern in the data. The authors urge skin clinics to screen minds as part of whole care, not as an extra.
pmc-12735206:
Aleksandra Małachowska and co-authors test laser treatment of titanium glasses in 2025. Titanium based glassy metals are strong and kind to the body, yet many recipes hold toxic parts. The team made five new alloys free of those elements. They then ran a laser over single tracks to mimic printed building of parts.

The study tracks how the laser changes structure, cracking, and strength. Cell tests check whether the treated alloys stay safe for body use. Such alloys could serve implants that need to be both tough and gentle. Laser steps are key because printing is how complex implant shapes get made.
pmc-12735506:
Xiaoqian Shi and co-authors hunt for mouth germ markers in a 2025 lung cancer study. The mouth opens into the airway, so its germs link closely to lung health. Radiation is a core lung cancer treatment, but no mouth germ test yet predicts who will respond well.

Mouth germs of 136 lung cancer patients and 199 healthy people were read by gene sequencing across three groups. Healthy mouths held notably more of one common germ, Streptococcus, than patient mouths in every group. The germ mix also shifted in clear ways with disease. A mouth swab test of this kind would be cheap and painless, if the markers hold up.
pmc-12735906:
Angel T Alvarado and co-authors study gene variants and drug side effects in Peruvian patients with epilepsy, in a 2025 paper. Two genes shape how the body breaks down several seizure drugs. Slow breakdown can raise side effect risk.

Eighty-nine patients at a national hospital gave blood for gene tests. Variants that slow the two genes were uncommon but present. Patients with mid or poor breakdown types had notably higher odds of side effects than normal types. Taking several seizure drugs at once also raised the odds sharply. The authors argue that gene checks could help set safer doses for this population. Larger local studies would help confirm rates, since the sample was modest.
pmc-12736006:
Dariusz Dziki and co-authors tested pasta made with flour from unroasted coffee beans in a 2025 food study. They added the green coffee flour at levels from two to eight percent of the mix. Two drying methods were compared: warm air drying and a microwave method under low pressure.

Both the added flour and the drying choice changed the pasta's texture, chemistry, and health-linked compounds. The microwave method cracked the pasta and left an uneven inner structure even at the lowest addition, while air drying showed no visible change. Cooking time also shifted between methods. Food makers get guidance on how much novelty the pasta can take before quality suffers.
pmc-12736106:
Giovanna Fernanda Vazzana and co-authors review nutrition problems in children born with heart defects in a 2025 paper. These children are especially prone to malnutrition. The causes braid together: higher energy needs, lower intake, and poorer absorption. The review gathers what is known about how common malnutrition is in this group, who is at risk, and why.

It also covers how to assess nutrition, practical feeding strategies, and care around surgery. Early screening, personal support, and team based care are presented as essential for growth and recovery. Special attention goes to feeding difficulties, micronutrient gaps, and the value of human milk and energy dense feeds. The authors call for standard, evidence based protocols and for precision nutrition tailored to each child's defect.
pmc-12736206:
Milan Senćanski, writing alone in 2025, screens drug candidates for disordered proteins. Such proteins, like the Alzheimer's-linked tau, lack a fixed shape for drugs to grip. Standard discovery struggles with them. Senćanski applies a spectrum-based computing method that reads molecules by their electron interaction patterns.

Marker patterns came from known tau ligands and from tau sequences shared across mammals. He screened an approved-drug library and a natural product trove. The screen surfaced drugs already tied to tau or Alzheimer's paths. It also flagged Bryostatin-14, a natural product that tunes enzymes acting on tau. The method offers a cheap first pass to pair with other discovery tools.
pmc-12736306:
Mariateresa Giglio and colleagues followed back-pain patients given a botanical supplement alongside their usual care. Chronic low back pain with nerve involvement resists standard drugs and tolerates them poorly. Extracts of Acmella oleracea and Boswellia serrata have anti-inflammatory and pain-relieving properties. The prospective, multicentre, real-world study enrolled 103 such patients across Italian centers. The standardized extract was added to ongoing therapy for eight weeks.

Neuropathic pain questionnaires tracked burning, tingling, and related symptoms. General pain intensity, disability, and quality of life were also scored. Painkiller use and side effects were monitored for safety. Real-world cohorts cannot prove cause like trials can, but they show how a supplement performs in ordinary practice. The twenty twenty-five study explores a gentler adjunct for a stubborn pain population.
pmc-12736506:
Dmitriy Sotnikov and co-authors turn a glow trick into a fast one-step test for a dread crop toxin. The toxin, aflatoxin B1, taints grain and nuts and is hard to catch fast in the field. Their test mixes a sample with antibodies and a glow-tagged toxin in one tube. When the pair binds, the tag glows more, not less, which is the rare heart of the trick.

Reads land in ten minutes at toxin marks as low as 200 parts per trillion. Corn mush, a hard test food, still gave true reads in their runs. Found shares in spiked corn sat in a tight band round the true dose. Fewer hand steps mean fewer slips for field crews. Kin toxins may fit the same trick.
pmc-12736606:
David Castro and co-authors tune the charge balance in films made from chitosan and a modified cassava starch, in work from twenty twenty-five. Such plant based films could shield food with less plastic waste. Plain mixes are weak and soak up water, which limits use.

Pairing the two oppositely charged polymers forms a tighter complex with smoother structure. Films were cast at a mild acidity and checked by microscopy, spectra, heat tests, and stretch tests. The complex films proved two to four times stronger than plain mixes and stretched a bit farther. They also dissolved far less in water, gut like fluid, and salt buffer. The best mix sat near a charge ratio of one.
pmc-12736806:
Guan and co-authors tailor steering feel to each driver's style. Standard steering cannot adapt to split driver tastes. Their system first reads the driver's style from motion data. A closed loop then steers the wheel feel to a target. Tests ran on a driving simulator across conditions.

The method held up across the range of trials run. Drivers reported a comfy and pleasing wheel feel. The loop kept the target feel steady as conditions changed. The authors say style-aware steering lifts the driving experience. Carmakers could use such tuning as tastes shift from volume to quality.
pmc-12736906:
Shuvo and co-authors published a 2025 study of a gut bacterium, Flavonifractor plautii, as a candidate next-generation probiotic. Standard probiotics rely on a small set of well-worn strains, so new candidates are in demand. The team isolated the strain from human feces, read its full genome, and named it PMC93. They then dosed a lab system that mimics the human gut ecosystem, daily for one week.

The strain did not disturb the overall mix of gut microbes, a good safety sign. It raised the ratio of one large bacterial group to another, a score the team tracks, beyond what standard probiotics achieved. Helpful groups that make short-chain fatty acids grew, while harmful groups shrank. The strain also passed safety tests in animals. The authors present it as a promising candidate for gut health products.
pmc-12737206:
Guillem Monrós-Andreu and co-authors assess probes for bubbly flows in a 2025 paper. Four-sensor probes measure local traits of gas-liquid flows, but their accuracy depends on probe shape and on how bubbles strike them. Classic analyses assume round bubbles and straight paths.

Their Monte Carlo framework drops those assumptions. Bubbles can be ellipsoids arriving at varied angles, and many probe shapes are tested. From synthetic signals they recover area, speeds, and chord lengths in one scheme. They distill compact correction laws and design maps for other probes. Safe ranges for probe spacing and size are given.
pmc-12737406:
Leigh Rosengren and co-authors present a veterinary economics study, published in 2025, on controlling a slow cattle plague called Johne's disease. The chronic gut infection quietly drains herd profit, and testing then culling carriers is the standard advice, though its payoff in beef herds was murky.
