The team simulated a three hundred cow western Canadian herd with an agent based model and a budget model over ten years.

Seven testing strategies, varying test type, pooled or single sampling, and testing rhythm, all cut disease spread versus doing nothing, and six made money. Yearly single animal PCR testing balanced disease control and profit best, while testing twice a year controlled most but cost more. Doing nothing let the disease grow and bled money.
pmc-12737506:
Natália Mesquita Cesnik and co-authors test doses of a reversal drug in cats under anesthesia, in this 2025 paper. The drug, sugammadex, wraps up rocuronium, a muscle relaxant used in surgery, so breathing and movement return fast. Dose data for cats were thin, so the team ran a blinded trial in thirty healthy cats.

Cats got one of three doses after deep muscle block. Recovery sped up with dose: reaching ninety percent strength took about 519 seconds at the low dose, 300 at the middle dose, and 257 at the high dose. The gap between the two higher doses was not meaningful, though the middle dose varied more between cats and one cat briefly slipped back. No heart or breathing harm appeared. The authors back the two higher doses for healthy cats.
pmc-12737606:
Jesiaman Silaban and co-authors trace bird flu lines in Australia and New Zealand in a 2025 study. Deadly H7 flu strains hit poultry farms in both lands from 2024, after years when finds sat mostly in wild birds. Where the farm strains came from was the key question.

The team pulled all public H7 gene reads from animals in the region across a decade. Family trees split the farm strains into local Australian and New Zealand branches. No tight link to Asian lines showed, which argues against a fresh import. The team urge steady gene watch on farms and in wild birds to catch new forms early.
pmc-12738606:
Liuyun Cai and four co-authors test whether ultrasound scans can help predict survival in cervical cancer. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Doctors know a lot about what drives this cancer, but the value of scan findings for outlook was still unclear.

The team drew records for four hundred twenty-eight patients from a hospital in Chongqing, China, covering twenty nineteen to twenty twenty-four. Most records trained the model, and the rest checked it. Older age and late stage raised the risk of early death. So did having no surgery, rich blood flow on the scan, and spread into nearby tissue. The authors built these factors into a chart that estimates survival at one, two, and three years.
pmc-12738706:
Azra Seyyedi, Mahdi Bohlouli, and SeyedEhsan Oskoee built a network whose nodes set their own signal range with AI in a 2025 paper. Spread-out networks need strong links and toughness, yet must save energy to live long. Each node in their model adjusts its range on its own, guided by a small neural decision model.

The decision model was trained on data from an earlier method that found near-best global states with full links at low energy. Acting locally, the nodes still reached a shared state with strong links and low waste. Simulations held up in still and moving scenes, and after damage to the web. The authors frame local AI choice as a route to networks that heal and last.
pmc-12742106:
Yadi Li and co-authors set out a plan to compare brain stimulation and acupuncture for depression across all trials at once, in a 2025 protocol paper. Depression burdens more than 300 million people, and standard antidepressants help many but leave others with weak relief or heavy side effects. Gentle electric or magnetic stimulation of the scalp and needle therapy both promise drug-free help. Direct head-to-head trials, though, are rare, and protocols vary widely.

The team will search fourteen databases for trials of these treatments and merge the results in a network meta-analysis. That method compares treatments that never met in one trial by chaining shared comparisons. The outcomes are benefit and acceptability: how much symptoms ease, and how often patients quit. The paper argues the ranking will guide choices only as far as the underlying evidence is firm.
pmc-12742306:
Gao, Li, Hu, Hu, and Su study a placental enzyme in colorectal cancer spread, in work from twenty twenty-five. Colorectal cancer is prevalent worldwide, and metastasis drives its high mortality. A process called epithelial mesenchymal transition lets cancer cells detach and spread.

The enzyme ALPP was compared between metastatic and non metastatic tumor samples from a cancer genome atlas. Cell experiments then tested its role. ALPP induced the transition by activating the Wnt beta catenin signaling pathway, a known growth route. A driver of spread that can be measured in tumors may serve as both a risk marker and a drug target.
pmc-12743206:
Qian Liu and five co-authors analyze bacterial coinfections in COVID-19 patients by illness grade, in a 2025 study from Shaanxi Province. Records covered two thousand inpatients from late 2022 to early 2023. Three hundred had bacterial coinfections on top of the virus. Two germs led the list, both known hospital threats.

Coinfected patients skewed male and older, with severe cases mostly in the seventy to ninety age band. Drug resistance ran low in mild and severe groups on most drugs. Severe cases, though, often held germs that resist key drug classes. The authors urge careful antibiotic use in severe care to slow the growth of hard-to-treat strains.
pmc-12743406:
Çınar, Demir, and Güven compared 3D-printed dental models with traditional stone models in twenty twenty-five. Accurate models matter for implant work, and printers now make them from resins of differing thickness, or viscosity. The question was whether resin choice shifts the printed positions of implant analogs.

From a reference model with eight implants, the team made stone models and printed models in low- and high-viscosity resin, eight of each. High-resolution scans fed metrology software measuring overall trueness and the three-dimensional and angular deviations of analogs. Printed models beat stone on overall trueness, ranked low-viscosity first. For analog positions, low-viscosity prints matched stone, while high-viscosity prints deviated significantly most often. Abutment-level scan bodies proved more accurate than implant-level ones in all groups. Resin viscosity, they conclude, affects positional accuracy.
pmc-12745606:
Zhu and co-authors report a rare liver tumor, a follicular dendritic cell sarcoma, and review the published cases, in this 2025 paper. The tumor grows from immune cells that present invaders to the rest of the system. It usually starts in lymph nodes, which makes a liver origin exceptional.

Their patient was a woman in her late twenties with lupus whose main complaint was fever. Scans found a liver mass, and tissue tests named the tumor. A year after radical surgery she remained free of recurrence. Pooling forty-three cases in all, the authors found patients averaged forty-eight years old, with women in the majority. Survival without disease at five years was about sixty-three percent. Early recognition guides their advice.
pmc-12745806:
Alessandro Popoli and co-authors study how repressive sequences inside an enhancer shaped leaf diversity in crucifer plants. Their 2025 paper deals with cis-regulatory sequences, which control where and when a gene is active.

They focus on the RCO homeobox gene, which arose by duplication from LMI1 and helped complex leaves evolve. Genome editing created seventeen regulatory alleles at that locus for close study. The evolved RCO enhancer turned out to be held back by repressive sequences in its genomic context. That finding shows enhancer function depends on context more than was thought. It helps explain how new expression patterns, and new leaf forms, arise.
pmc-12747106:
Ruemu Birhiray and three co-authors report a striking pancreatic cancer case in a 2025 paper. Pancreatic cancer kills about fifty thousand Americans a year and rarely allows long survival. A small subgroup carries inherited DNA repair defects that open a drug door.

The patient, a seventy-two-year-old woman, carried inherited mutations in two repair genes. Those defects leave tumors unable to fix certain DNA damage. After strong chemotherapy she reached complete remission. A maintenance pill that blocks DNA repair in cancer cells has kept her in remission for over forty months. That drug is approved for a related mutation group, not hers. The case argues for widening access to repair-targeted therapy in pancreatic cancer.
pmc-12748306:
Wai Miu Emma Liu and co-authors review whether surgical robot skills learned on one machine carry to another. Their review appeared in 2025. With several platforms now approved, training might not need to restart per machine. The team searched five databases to January 2025 and kept five studies that trained people on simulators across at least two platforms, scoring them with objective metrics or rating scales.

Beginners and experts performed consistently across machines, including the leading Da Vinci family and two newer rivals. Mid-level trainees dipped when switching. Prior robot experience, more than machine choice, predicted baseline skill and progress. The authors conclude core robotic skills do transfer, which supports shared training curricula, though evidence for early trainees stays thin.
pmc-12749106:
Heavy-duty industrial robots are built for power, but their shapes often copy each other and ignore how the machines look. Jiang, Han, and Guang propose a design method that joins Kansei engineering, which maps human feelings about form into design choices, with curve blending and content generated by artificial intelligence. The goal is a robot that works well, carries a clear brand identity through signature curved forms, and stands out in a factory.

The team applied the method to a welding robot rated at two hundred ten kilograms, walking through each step from early sketches to the final shape. A perceptual questionnaire and a fuzzy analytic hierarchy process gave early evidence that the method works and can be carried out in practice. The authors argue that the approach can lift industrial robot design past its current limits and help products compete on looks as well as performance.
pmc-12749406:
Shuang Han and colleagues read the full genome of a rare Tibetan medicine plant to help keep it alive, in this study from twenty twenty-five. Swertia przewalskii is one source of the Tibetan remedy called Zangyinchen. In Qinghai province it sits on the first list of plants with extremely small populations, a formal danger flag.

Using three sequencing methods together, the team built a chromosome-level genome of about two billion letters, anchored to twelve chromosomes. They catalogued some thirty-five thousand protein-coding genes, plus thousands of small RNA genes. Nearly nine in ten genes could be matched to known functions in public databases. The authors offer the genome as a base for conservation biology. It can guide breeding, reveal how the plant copes with its harsh home, and help managers judge which wild patches matter most for survival.
pmc-12749606:
Fatty liver disease turns dangerous when scarring joins the fat, and catching that turn without a biopsy is a standing goal. Fei Xia and co-authors trained a deep learning model on rats with diet-induced liver disease. Three versions competed: one reading ordinary ultrasound, one reading stiffness maps from elastography, and one combining both image types with clinical data.

The combined model won clearly, with the best discrimination score of the three. Decision analysis showed it would help clinicians across most risk thresholds. Calibration checks said its probabilities meant what they said. The authors present the multimodal recipe as the way forward for spotting fibrotic fatty liver early.
pmc-12749706:
Hyun-Joo Kim and co-authors present a 2025 food science study on zapping wheat with reactive air plasma to squeeze out more, and better, oil. Plasma treatment is a cold, chemical-free way to roughen plant surfaces. The team tested whether it could raise lipid yield and the anti-aging activity of wheat lipids for cosmetics.

Ten minutes of plasma gave the best extraction, lifting yield from about 1.8 to about 3.0 percent. The treated oil also blocked two skin-aging enzymes far more strongly and moisturized better at the tested dose. Two prized fatty acids rose five-fold and eight-fold. Microscopy showed the grain surface disrupted and smoothed, easing the oil's escape. The authors propose plasma-treated wheat lipids as cosmetic ingredients, pending animal and scale-up tests.
pmc-12750006:
Hui Zhang and co-authors compare the cost-effectiveness of two radiation schedules for advanced lung cancer that cannot be operated on. Their 2025 study weighs a moderately shortened schedule against the conventional longer one, both given with chemotherapy. The shorter schedule has shown better local control and survival hints in earlier studies, without clearly worse side effects.

The team built a three-stage model that follows patients over five years. It counts life years, quality-adjusted life years, and total costs for each schedule. Prior trials supplied the clinical inputs on control and toxicity. Economic value for this exact use had been largely unstudied, despite wide interest in shorter treatment. A clear cost picture helps hospitals and payers decide whether fewer, larger doses are worth adopting as standard care.
pmc-12750306:
Daniel Liu, Emily Draeger, Christopher Tien, and Fada Guan test film for pass dose in close seed care in 2025. A new film kind reads dose at 3 depth units from a flat seed cap linked to an iridium source. Eight source strengths and seven dwell spans form the test grid. Pass dose comes from a line stretch back to zero dwell.

Film reads ran straight with dwell span at all strengths, a fit mark for the use. Pass dose ran 0.3 to 4.3 percent of plan dose in the grid. Strength tied poor to pass dose, so rig shape rules the mark.
pmc-12750706:
Audrey Faveyrial and eleven colleagues published a 2025 protocol and study report on telemonitoring during injectable anticancer treatment in France. Before each treatment cycle, staff must check blood tests and call patients to confirm they are fit for therapy. Structured call programs at two French cancer centers already improved prescription accuracy and cut waiting times.

The OPTIMACURE study, a multicenter randomized prospective trial, tests whether adding the Cureety Techcare telemonitoring platform to usual care improves matters further. Patients report symptoms and results remotely between visits, so problems surface before the treatment day. The study weighs clinical benefit, safety, and workflow against standard follow-up. Its results will inform whether telemonitoring should become routine in chemotherapy services.
pmc-12751206:
Two tooth-filling materials face off over three years in a trial by Alev Ozsoy-Kaner and co-authors, reported in a 2025 paper. Thirty patients received paired fillings, one of each material, in back teeth cavities. One composite shrinks extra little as it hardens; the other uses an advanced polymer base.

Calibrated examiners, blind to material, graded the fillings at set visits up to three years. Scores cover staining, edge gaps and breaks, new decay, shine, color match, and wear. Shrinkage stresses the tooth-filling bond, so a low-shrink winner could cut the leaks that doom fillings early.
pmc-12751506:
After abdominal surgery, lungs sometimes fail, and a mask ventilator can keep patients off a breathing tube. Arthur Naudet-Lasserre and co-authors revisit a 293-patient trial of that mask support with Bayesian statistics. The reanalysis asks how the answer changes under different starting beliefs, from skeptical to enthusiastic.

Across all four belief stances, the chance that mask support truly beats plain oxygen ran from ninety-six to ninety-nine percent. The odds of needing a tube by day seven favored the mask under every prior. A meaningful benefit of at least five percentage points held with seventy-seven to ninety-three percent probability. The 2025 analysis helps clinicians weigh the trial through their own priors.
pmc-12751606:
Alisson Silva and co-authors upgraded a protein prediction tool in a 2025 paper. Proteins work in pairs and teams inside cells, and mapping those links helps explain life and design drugs. Lab mapping is slow and costly, so computer forecasts fill the gap. Their tool, GenPPi, builds such maps from bacterial genomes but leaned too much on plain sequence likeness.

The new form, GenPPi 1.5, adds a forest learning model trained on sixty traits drawn from amino acid profiles. A fresh sampling step keeps the shape of the link web intact while it trains. The gains aim for maps that catch more true links without warping the web's form.
pmc-12751806:
Yuting Li and co-authors uncover, in a 2025 study, a self-protection program inside the degenerating retina, and how to amplify it. Retinitis pigmentosa kills the eye's light sensors over time, and inflammation lit by the retina's own immune cells hurries the loss. Estrogen's role had looked contradictory. The team names its alpha receptor, Esr1, as a central brake on that inflammation, rising as degeneration proceeds.

In two mouse models, plain estrogen helped one and harmed the other, but a drug that switches on Esr1 alone protected both, saving light sensors and vision responses. The mechanism runs through the microglia: receptor activation cuts their output of a toxic signal and breaks a self-feeding recruitment loop. Blocking that signal's main receiver protected even better than broad blockers. The authors frame Esr1 activation as turning up a defense the retina already owns.
pmc-12752006:
Ali Akbari leads a team testing AI-based monitoring to cut low blood pressure during major head and neck surgery, in a 2025 trial. Low pressure during surgery raises the risk of kidney injury, heart injury, stroke, and death. The tool used predicts drops ahead of time.

Patients were assigned at random to standard care, prediction-guided therapy, or goal-directed therapy without prediction. The prediction group had far fewer low-pressure episodes and much shorter total time at low pressure. The goal-directed group without prediction did not differ clearly from control. Other outcomes were alike across groups. The authors call for larger studies on patient outcomes.
pmc-12752106:
Masahiko Okubo and four co-authors argued in two thousand twenty-five that swallowing should be checked as soon as older patients enter community care wards. They reviewed seventy-seven older patients admitted over one year. Within two days of arrival, a team of many professions tested mouth and throat function and watched patients at meals.

Many patients moved safely from tube or drip feeding to eating by mouth, and their intake scores rose a lot. The most common illnesses were aspiration pneumonia and stroke-related disorders. Linking food routes to where patients went at discharge, the study shows early swallowing checks shape safer feeding plans.
pmc-12752206:
Benoit Rallet and co-authors told in 2025 of a man whose fake heart valve was eaten by a rare germ. The germ, Actinotignum schaalii, lives in the urinary tract and is a rare cause of heart lining infection. The man, fifty-four, had a full root-and-valve swap years before and came in with repeat strokes. Blood tests first named the wrong germ, then pinned this one. Scans showed a pus pocket by the valve that had bored into the aorta wall.

Drug care could not save the graft, which had torn loose from wide rot at surgery. Repair was judged hopeless, and the man died after the team chose to limit care. The authors warn that slow blood cultures are key to catching this germ early.
pmc-12752406:
Desalegn Girma and co-authors pool past studies to estimate how often stillbirth occurs in Ethiopia and what raises its risk, in a 2025 review. Worldwide, about 1.9 million stillbirths occurred in 2021, and nearly half took place in sub-Saharan Africa. An earlier pooled study for Ethiopia looked at only two factors, so this team cast a wider net.

The team searched medical databases and regional journals, checked study quality with a standard list, and combined results with a model that allows for real gaps between studies. Factors weighed include bleeding before birth, stained birth fluid, long labor, body weight, high blood pressure, early birth, and early rupture of the waters. The pooled rate and the odds tied to each factor aim to guide care and policy.
pmc-12752506:
Rosanna Wilkins and Eva Petermann reviewed in 2025 how a mammalian enzyme keeps DNA copying from snagging on RNA scraps. As DNA is copied, stray RNA paired with DNA can stall the copying fork, and such stalls feed the genome instability seen in cancer. The enzyme they review, RNase H2, clears both looped RNA-DNA pairs and single RNA units lodged in DNA. New work has sharpened the picture of how it acts.

The review first explains how these hybrids cause stress during copying. It then details the enzyme's roles in removing them and in the wider stress response. Both too little and too much of the enzyme now appear tied to cancer growth and treatment response. The authors close with open questions the new models raise.
pmc-12752706:
Milena Hesse, Gregor Linden, and Holger Frey studied how heat and solvent shape a common plastic blend in a 2025 paper. The blend joins two oxide chains and is used widely in labs and in industry. Though it has been made for decades, how heat and the liquid it forms in sway the chain mix was not well mapped.

The team made the blend in three solvents and at heats from 25 to 60 degrees Celsius. They tracked how fast each part joins the chain, then checked the heat traits and dissolving traits of each batch. Their map links the pot settings to the traits of the end product. Makers can use it to tune the blend for a set use.
pmc-12753006:
Auden Balouch and co-authors shine multiphoton light into rat skull defects to count how many implanted stem cells survive, and where they go, in a 2024 study. Stem cell therapy for bone repair has an embarrassing secret: under five percent of injected cells remain at the site within days. The team instead delivered mesenchymal stem cells inside granular gel scaffolds, the cells tagged with fluorescent dots, into skull defects in rats.

At three and seven days, microscopy mapped the tagged cells through the scaffold at micron detail, while also counting invading host cells and identifying macrophage types. About three quarters of a million cells went in per defect. The imaging method itself is a contribution: a way to audit cell therapy honestly, quantifying survival and spread instead of assuming the dose delivered is the dose that stayed.
pmc-12753106:
Marina Medel-Plaza and co-authors present a 2025 study on a steel surface designed to resist bacterial films. Infections around bone implants are a major problem in orthopedic surgery. The team tested a treated stainless steel, anodized to change its surface, against the plain steel used as a reference.

Six bacterial species common in implant infections were grown on both surfaces. Sticking was checked after ninety minutes with a microscope, and films were grown for one to two days in a fluid like joint fluid. The treated steel cut bacterial sticking and surface coverage for every species. Film growth also fell sharply on the treated surface. Images confirmed fewer bacteria and less of the slime matrix they build.
pmc-12753406:
Wanyu Shu, Liang Chen, Jiadong Qiu, and Sung Min Kim pool the evidence on aerobic exercise for older adults with mild cognitive impairment in a 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis. Exercise is a drug-free candidate for protecting the aging brain, and trials have measured its effect on thinking skills many times. Sleep quality and overall quality of life, equally important to patients, are usually reported piecemeal.

Combining the trials statistically gives a clearer verdict on all three outcomes at once. A firm evidence base helps clinicians prescribe exercise with the same confidence they bring to medication for early cognitive decline.
pmc-12753706:
Long Qinhong and colleagues separate gravity field sources to characterise deep and shallow tectonics at the northwestern margin of the Sichuan-Yunnan block in China. Their 2025 study addresses a region with intense seismic activity.

The team refined a gravity model using measured data and a global crust model as control. Wavelet analysis separated field sources at different scales, and power spectrum analysis estimated source depths for each level. The regional gravity anomaly ran low in the north and high in the south. Several named major faults were all identified as deep, large faults at tens of kilometres depth. Results offer physical insight into crustal structure.
pmc-12754406:
Prabu Mounisamy and co-authors test a blood-based injection for long-term lower back pain in this 2025 study. The pain came from slipped discs in the lower spine that had not settled with standard care. The injection uses the patient's own platelet-rich plasma, a blood part rich in growth signals.

Seventeen patients who had failed standard care got the injection into the disc. Their results were set against twenty-two patients who had improved with standard care alone. Pain and function scores in the injected group improved clearly within six weeks. Their gains came close to those of the standard-care group, despite starting worse. The authors call the method promising but note the small group and short follow-up limit the claim.
pmc-12754906:
Love Bukola Ayamolowo and three co-authors survey students at a Nigerian university in 2025 about relationships between partners with a large age gap. Such ties can raise the risk of infections, abuse, and emotional harm for young people, and they have been linked to more HIV cases in the region. The team wanted to know how common these ties are and what students know about them.

The survey reached 390 students across 13 faculties, picked in stages, who filled out tested forms on their own. The team compared answers across groups to find links with age, sex, and other traits. Findings can guide campus health teaching and support services. The study adds local data to a topic often discussed without firm counts.
pmc-12755006:
Alston Ng, Vignesh Sivasamy, and Shirlyn Hui Shan Neo adapted a structured guide for serious illness conversations to caregivers of people with dementia in Singapore. Such talks are often delayed, yet the standard guide speaks to patients, not families, and was not written for Asian cultural norms. The team rewrote it in caregiver-facing language, then refined it through two rounds of interviews with nineteen caregivers.

Caregivers said they valued clinician professionalism and reassurance, but also wanted their own lived knowledge respected. Many could not state their loved one's wishes, because decline came first. They flinched at wording that sounded like giving up, and preferred language of continued care and partnership. In a final survey of fifty caregivers, the revised guide beat the first draft on nearly every item. The authors say the tool can help clinicians start timely, values-based conversations.
pmc-12757206:
Yan Gao and co-authors report a 2025 study of how conflict between parents links to new depression in Chinese college students. Fights at home are a known risk for teen mental health, but the paths for young adults, and any split by sex, were unclear. The team drew on more than eight thousand first-year students at two medical schools.

New depression arose in about one in forty students over the study span. Two home traits stood out in the models: rare physical clashes between parents and long-run emotional coldness in upbringing. Each more than doubled the odds of new illness, with sex splits tested as well.
pmc-12757706:
Hui Wen Lim and a team of co-authors asked health care workers what helps or blocks a smart hospital ward, in a 2025 qualitative study. Sensors and automation can ease workloads and smooth care, but new tools fail when the organization is not ready for them. Readiness rests on people, not just gear.

The team interviewed 19 staff across clinical, technical, and support roles, and sorted views under a known readiness theory. Staff saw the ward as valuable and felt driven to change, and they praised the hospital's innovation culture. Barriers stood out too: unclear timelines, uneven training, thin resources, and weak support structures for new ideas. Many also feared leaning too hard on the technology at the cost of clinical judgment. The authors say leaders must fix the basics to keep trust.
pmc-12757806:
Yoon and Zander present CRISP, a cheap and fast way to sex hemp seedlings, in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Hemp's valuable compounds come from female flowers, but growers cannot tell male plants from female ones until flowering, wasting space and risking unwanted pollination.

CRISP pairs a one-step chemical method that frees DNA at high temperature with a standard PCR test for a male-linked marker, all in ninety-six-well plates. On seedlings from two cultivars it sorted males with one hundred percent accuracy. Older methods need multi-step DNA extraction and pricier gear, so this simpler pipeline suits large breeding and farming operations that must cull males early.
pmc-12758106:
Jessica Abrams and a large team of co-authors report a 2025 study of teaching tools used inside a heart screening program in Brazil. Rheumatic heart disease can be prevented, yet it still kills young people early in poorer countries. Teaching is a key way to cut that burden, above all where reading skills are low.

The team built four flipcharts with simple text and pictures over three years. The charts were taught during screening visits in high-burden areas over three years of field work. The study checks whether patients, families, school children, and community members found the charts welcome and clear. It also measures how much knowledge people gained from the lessons. The results can help other programs teach heart health in plain, visual ways.
pmc-12758406:
Xiaoshu Zhe and co-authors test whether treating donor cells with chemicals helps cloned goat embryos divide, in a 2025 study. Cloning by nuclear transfer is inefficient, which limits its use in breeding and medicine. Donor cells were treated before their nuclei were placed into eggs, with a mix of nine small molecules at set doses.

Treated cells turned up core genes for pluripotency, the state of a cell that can form many tissues, and a gene for an enzyme that loosens DNA packing. Embryos rebuilt from treated cells split at a higher rate in early culture than untreated ones, rising from about thirty-six to about forty-six percent. The authors present the chemical step as a foundation for learning the mechanisms at play and for raising cloning efficiency in large mammals.
pmc-12758806:
Jorge Escudero and three colleagues published an insect study in two thousand twenty-five on what keeps young insects young. In flies, a protein called Chinmo holds larvae in their young state. The team studied the same protein in the German cockroach, which grows through nymph stages instead.

They tracked the chinmo gene across the cockroach's nymph stages and found it stayed active until the final stage, then dropped. Silencing the gene made nymphs change into adults two moults early. A second protein, Abrupt, acted in the opposite direction on partner genes. Together the results show both proteins help hold the young state in two very different kinds of insects. The findings inform how complete metamorphosis may have evolved.
pmc-12764306:
Yongquan Jiang and co-authors test a Chinese herbal formula against allergic rhinitis in rats in a 2025 study. The disease mixes immune imbalance with a leaky nose lining, and standard drugs often fall short or bring side effects. The formula, YuPingTongQiao, was dosed into a standard allergy model.

Symptoms like nose rubbing and sneezing eased dose by dose, and the high dose beat a common antihistamine. Under the surface, allergy driving cytokines fell, a regulatory T cell group regained balance, and a brake molecule rose. The nose lining sealed tighter and mucus output dropped, with fewer invading inflammatory cells on slides. The authors present the formula as a multi target alternative worth clinical study.
pmc-12765006:
Eleonora Anci and co-authors compare personality and impulsivity in problem online gamers and poker players. Their twenty twenty-five study recruited more than one thousand players online. Both groups can slide into problematic internet use, but their trait profiles may differ.

Players took an internet addiction test, a Big Five survey, and a short impulsivity scale. Robust models weighed how each trait linked to problem scores, holding age and gender steady. Some traits were shared across both groups, while others split them apart. Knowing the split helps clinics screen and treat each habit on its own terms, rather than as one blob of screen addiction.
pmc-12765706:
Lichun Han and ten co-authors hunt for gene marks that can tell who will gain from TNF blocker drugs in bowel disease. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. New work ties a cell mark called lactylation and germ-eater cell states to this ill. Whether those genes flag drug gain was still unclear.

Gene web and learning tools sifted past patient data for marks split by gain or no gain. Four genes split the groups before care, and a model built on them scored well in train and check sets. Five more genes split groups weeks in. Mouse gut tests backed the marks, and extra lactate boosted drug gain in mice. The team calls the marks ripe for more checks.
pmc-12766406:
Ran Zhao and co-authors publish a lab protocol for pulling two tiny cell structures out of leukemia cells together. Fat droplets and mitochondria, the cell's fuel store and furnace, are hard to isolate from blood cancer cells, which carry little fat. Yet their interplay matters: this leukemia rewires fat handling and resists chemotherapy.

The protocol walks through the separation, the checks that prove the fractions are clean, and the mass-spectrometry readout of their fats. It comes from a specialist cancer center team and is written for reuse. The authors aim to let other labs study how organelle fat chemistry is regulated in this disease.
pmc-12766806:
Meghan O'Melia and fourteen colleagues present a 2025 immunology study on why cancer vaccines underperform near the tumor. Immunotherapy rarely targets antigen presentation, the step where dendritic cells show tumor pieces to T cells. In mouse breast cancer, the team found that lymph nodes draining the tumor cripple exactly that step, while the machinery for processing antigens stays intact.

A missing cytokine, IL-1 beta, proved responsible for the presentation failure in those nodes. Nodes farther from the tumor remained competent. Delivering an immune adjuvant to those distant, antigen-bearing nodes revived T cell responses, and pairing it with checkpoint blockade produced long-term tumor control in the mice. The authors suggest aiming adjuvants at healthy nodes, not the compromised ones.
pmc-12767406:
Hongyi Zhou and co-authors build a risk score for glioblastoma, a fast and deadly brain tumor, in a 2025 study. Their focus is a set of support cells that sit around the tumor and shape how it grows, cells that had not been mapped in this tumor in a full way.

From public data and single-cell reads, the team picked out the support cells and found six genes tied to how long patients live. Those six genes form the score, which split patients into high and low risk in more than one group and held up as a sign on its own. A chart that joins the score with standard facts sharpened the calls. The score also tracked how many immune cells sat in the tumor and how well drugs might work.
pmc-12768606:
Avila Vidal and Jorge Barreto review strategies for lowering cesarean section rates in a 2025 overview. Rates have climbed worldwide and fastest in Latin America and the Caribbean, where they rose from about twenty-three to forty-two percent between the 1990s and 2014.

The authors surveyed systematic reviews and graded their quality with a standard tool. From nearly a thousand records, six reviews made the final cut. Interventions were sorted with a Cochrane taxonomy of practice and care organization. Financing steps and mixed packages were the most common types. Mixed packages, joining delivery changes with governance, cut rates the most. Success still hinged on local systems and culture, the authors stress.
pmc-12768706:
Zanfina Ademi and co-authors wrote this 2025 review on a new way to value health gains. Their measure, called PALYs, counts life years weighted by how much work people can do. It aims to show the wider social worth of staying healthy, beyond the years alone. The review asks how studies have used the measure so far.

The team gathered 34 studies from 2018 to 2024 that used the measure. Topics ranged from heart and kidney disease to dirty air. Most studies came from rich countries and used life table models. The review lists each study's setting, methods, and results. It shows where the measure helps leaders weigh prevention plans, and where gaps in the evidence remain.
pmc-12768806:
Antonella Cardone, Jose Diaz, and Martin Coombes studied whether plain language helps patient groups join health technology reviews, in a 2025 report. Such reviews judge new treatments for health systems. Patient groups often get little clear information about the treatment under review. That gap limits fair input and trust in the process.

A pilot in England tested summary sheets written for patient groups. Surveys, interviews, and an advisory board weighed the pilot. Patient groups liked the summaries whatever their past experience. The sheets cut preparation time and raised confidence. Other stakeholders valued them too. Most public respondents agreed makers should supply such summaries. Review bodies warned of extra work, timing strain, and bias checks. Eight recommendations were drawn up for wider use.
pmc-12772606:
Noelle Murphy and co-authors use design thinking to build a yardstick for paperwork in a hospital sterile compounding unit. Such units mix medicines by hand under strict cleanliness rules, yet Ireland has no national framework for how their documents should run. Design thinking starts with the users, then drafts, tests, and refines a fix.

The team read world guidelines on sterile making and drafted a first benchmarking tool. Five senior stakeholders were interviewed to sharpen its focus, and eleven end users then tried the polished tool inside a working Irish unit. Their feedback was coded into themes to guide the tool's next form. The authors offer the case as a first Irish health example of the method.
pmc-12775606:
Fusing several neck vertebrae behind one long metal plate concentrates stress at the bottom joint. Gregory Mundis and co-authors ask whether several short plates would share the load better. They built both designs in twelve donated human cervical spines. Matching foam models carried identical constructs. Rigs then flexed the spines thousands of times in bending and twisting while stiffness was tracked.

Bone quality was measured from scans. Stiff and soft specimens were spread fairly between the groups. The question matters because long single plates are linked to swallowing trouble, failed fusion, and mechanical failure at the lowest segment. Isolating the hardware in cadaver and foam tests separates the design's own behavior from patient noise. Surgeons gain cleaner evidence for a real design choice.
pmc-12775706:
Kosuke Hashimoto and co-authors test a scan measure as a warning sign for patients on a targeted lung cancer drug in a 2025 study. The drug, osimertinib, treats non-small cell lung cancer carrying a sensitive mutation in a growth gene. PET scans show how much sugar the tumor burns, and one measure, the total volume of active tumor, may reflect disease burden better than peak uptake alone.

Sixty-eight patients had scans before starting the drug. Spread to bone and liver tracked with high volume values. Response rates and side effects did not differ by scan uptake level. In adjusted analysis, the volume measure stood out as a predictor of how long patients lived without the cancer growing. The authors call it a significant marker for this treatment.
pmc-12777806:
Sofia Aragones, Ana Maria Jimenez-Garcia, and Natalia Arias pool studies on sex splits in trauma signs among refugees. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-five. War and hunt force vast folks to flee, with hard stress at each leg. The team searched four bases to late twenty twenty-four for work on trauma, worry, and low mood by sex.

Twenty-five studies fit, with most in the pooled counts. Women showed high odds and rates of trauma signs, plus more worry and low mood. Harm kinds split by sex too, with sex force high for women and kidnap high for men. Signs ran long for both sexes. The team urges sex-fit help and rules.
pmc-12780206:
Saiprasad Bhusare and eight colleagues feed black soldier fly larvae meal to a farmed catfish, Clarias magur, and watch breeding outcomes. Fishmeal is costly and strained, so insect meal is a tempting swap. The trial ran 120 days on two stocks: a farm-raised line and a growth-selected line.

Each stock ate either a fishmeal diet or one with twenty percent insect meal and no fishmeal. The selected stock grew faster and used feed better. The farm stock, though, bred better: higher fertility measures, hatching, and larval survival. Hormones and gene activity split along the same lines. The insect meal itself barely changed breeding traits in either stock.
pmc-12780406:
Munehide Nagao and co-authors use moving MRI scans of blood flow to compare two kinds of leaky heart valve. In one kind the valve itself is sound but the chamber above it has stretched, pulling the valve open; lasting irregular heartbeat is the usual cause. In the other, part of the valve physically sags. The team scanned ten surgical patients of each kind before their operations.

The stretched-chamber group pumped notably less blood per minute and lost less flow energy on the body's side of the heart, but more on the lung side, than the sagging-valve group. The authors argue these flow patterns explain how the two conditions burden the heart differently and may guide treatment choices.
pmc-12780706:
Melissa Stoneham and co-authors lay out a protocol to benchmark food security risks in very remote Indigenous communities, in a 2025 paper. For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in far-flung Western Australian communities, health gaps run widest. Food insecurity grows where kitchens fail and healthy food costs too much, but hard numbers from such places are scarce.

The mixed-methods study covers nineteen communities. Digital apps will grade whether house kitchens are fit for safe cooking. Price checks will compare food and sanitary goods against the nearest town and the capital. Residents will also judge what a proper kitchen means to them. The benchmarks aim to give governments evidence, not guesses, for closing the gap.
pmc-12782606:
Kimberly Sokol and co-authors built a practice exam course for emergency medicine residents facing a new board test, in a 2025 paper. The American board is changing its certifying exam's format, leaving trainees without matched prep materials. Their course can stretch across a residency or compress into one day that mimics the real sitting.

Eight simulation cases anchor the course, covering the case types the new exam is expected to use. The drills test skills the old written and oral exams never reached. The goal is plain: walk in knowing the format cold. The authors offer the full curriculum as a ready model for other programs.
pmc-12784706:
Laura Córdoba and a large team grow colorectal tumour organoids at an air-liquid interface to keep the tumour's immune layout intact. Most organoid systems lose the original tissue shape and immune mix. Paired tumour and nearby colon tissue from patients were grown this way and checked against the source tissue and against standard gel organoids.

The interface organoids kept the three-dimensional shape, native immune cells and mutation profile of the source. When a PD-1 blocking drug was added, regulatory T cells expanded locally inside the organoids, a possible route to immune resistance. Gel cultures mixed with blood cells did not show that response, which stresses the worth of keeping native tumour and immune contact.
pmc-12784806:
Georgea Foley and co-authors compare prostate cancer care in public and private hospitals in Tasmania, in a study published in 2025. Care in rural areas often lags behind city care. The team asked whether the type of hospital changed how men were found, treated, and how fast treatment began.

They studied records for 2,180 men diagnosed from 2015 to 2022. Public patients were more likely to live far from towns and to have higher-risk disease. Private patients most often had low-risk disease, and over half were watched rather than treated at once. Even at the same risk level, public patients were treated more often but waited about forty to fifty-nine days longer to start. The authors argue that these gaps in regional care need attention.
pmc-12784906:
Yuhang Zhu and co-authors compare the rumen microbes and blood chemistry of three deer species fed the very same diet. Sika deer, reindeer, and milu deer share the ruminant plan but range over unlike homelands. Holding the menu fixed lets the host's own hand show in the gut community.

Their 2025 study sequences rumen bacteria and reads fermentation and serum panels in small matched groups. Sika and milu deer host richer, more diverse microbes rich in carbohydrate-digesting genera. Reindeer carry fewer kinds but brew more volatile fatty acids, acetate and butyrate among them. Milu blood runs fattier, and gene network analysis ties those lipids to signaling paths. Diet equal, the species still ferment differently.
pmc-12785306:
Ultrasound with a single flat wave is blazing fast, at over a thousand frames a second, but its images suffer from clutter: stray echoes that blur contrast. Seongbin Hwang and three co-authors clean that clutter with a learning method that needs no labels. Their 2025 work shapes how alike the signals from split paths are, a trait clean tissue holds and clutter breaks.

Their loss rule adapts to how fast the scene's frames drift apart. It also picks, by physics rules, which frames best suit the loss check, given the wave's angle and pulse. Tests span simulations, a lab phantom built to fake clutter, and live tissue. Public data sets fed the training. A cleaner fast scan would widen where the method can be trusted, from heart work to quick checks at the bedside.
pmc-12785406:
Chen Wu and Lixiong Yang study how sharing outpatient costs with rural families affects children's health and household budgets in China, in a 2025 paper. Rural children face thin medical resources and insurance designs not built for them. Cost-sharing rules decide whether parents seek clinic care early or wait. Using a 2018 national household income survey, the authors matched comparable families to isolate the policy's association.

Children under the policy showed better health scores and a higher chance of reimbursement. The links seemed to run through more outpatient visits, healthier mothers, and greater spending on school food and lodging. Unlike adults, children showed no swapping of clinic visits for hospital stays, which fits care parents dare not postpone. The authors read the policy as a lever that nudges rural families toward timely care.
pmc-12785606:
Pasquale Padalino and co-authors report a fatal case of West Nile virus infection in a 2025 medical paper. The patient was a woman of forty-five with two long-term health problems. One problem left her short of a hormone from glands in the neck. The other, Sjögren's syndrome, is an immune disorder. Her illness grew into severe swelling of the brain and spinal cord.

Doctors traced damage in the thalamus, the cerebellum, and motor pathways of the cord. Stains of tissue samples showed immune cells along those motor routes, which supports spread along nerve links. Lung problems followed, and the patient died. The authors ask how her two conditions may have helped the virus invade the nervous system.
pmc-12785806:
Anne-Line Mayland Madsen and co-authors test whether scan-based markers predict outcomes for high-risk melanoma patients given immune therapy after surgery. The therapy improves freedom from recurrence but causes side effects in many. Scans that track sugar use in tissue might flag immune side effects and organ activity ratios tied to outlook.

In a Danish register cohort, over half the patients saw their cancer return and a quarter died during follow-up. Most showed at least one scan-detected immune side effect. Those side effects did not predict overall survival, and early ones were linked to higher recurrence risk, opposite to some prior reports. Ratios for spleen and bone marrow showed no prognostic value.
pmc-12786206:
Siyi Wang and co-authors published a chemistry study in 2025 on a new method to detect aldehydes in meat products. Aldehydes form during heating and matter for food safety checks. The team made tiny treated spheres and used them inside a membrane-protected extraction device. The spheres carry a reagent that binds aldehydes.

Under tuned settings, the method pulled aldehydes from varied meat samples with strong accuracy. Detection limits were very low, and recovery rates were solid across tests. The membrane blocked interfering substances, and the setup joined extraction, enrichment, and binding in one step. The authors offer the method as a promising option for meat testing.
pmc-12786706:
Ruiying Yang and co-authors test a peony flower extract against skin barrier damage in mice. Their 2025 study uses tape stripping, repeated adhesive pulls that strip the outer skin layer, as the damage model. Barrier failure raises water loss through the skin, redness, and swelling. Peony flowers are traditional medicine staples credited with calming inflammation and aging, but barrier repair was unproven.

The extract cut redness, water loss, and swelling while restoring the skin's layered structure. Protein profiling pointed to two repair programs: building the cornified envelope, the skin's tough outer shell, and assembling tight junctions between cells. Key barrier proteins all rose under treatment. Measurements spanned imaging, hydration, gene expression, and staining.
pmc-12786906:
Erik De Clercq surveyed in 2025 the long career of Thomas Merigan, a leader in treating virus infections. Work that began in 1963 with interest in interferon, a natural defense signal, grew over nearly fifty years. Merigan also found lab-made compounds that prompt the body to make that signal.

Later work moved through shingles, herpes, a virus that harms people with weak defenses, hepatitis B, and HIV. De Clercq presents Merigan as a pioneer across many of these fields. He argues that the record deserves deeper checks in patient care. Readers get a compact map of how one research path helped shape antiviral care over decades.
pmc-12787806:
Asiye Yavşan and Recep Türken present a 2025 lab study on how strongly dental crown materials stick to titanium implant posts, depending on how they are made and prepared. One hundred twenty samples of four computer-aided materials, half milled and half 3D printed, were bonded to titanium disks with resin cement. Three surface preparations were compared: primer alone, acid etching plus primer, and sandblasting plus primer.

Both material and preparation mattered greatly, and they interacted. Printed materials bonded more strongly than milled ones. Sandblasting with primer topped the table for the best material, while primer alone on another material gave the weakest bond. Microscope images confirmed rougher surfaces after sandblasting, and failures there tore through material rather than peeling cleanly. The authors advise matching the surface protocol to each material in implant dentistry.
pmc-12788006:
Zhaohua Liu and four co-authors improve a fast object-spotting model so it can find small ships at sea. Their 2025 paper starts from YOLOv11n, a light model that often misses tiny boats against cluttered waves. Small patrol boats carry few visual cues. That raises the miss rate.

The team adds three parts to the model. One blends infrared and visible-light views. A backbone block picks up fine local detail. A closing block traces small outlines with shifting filters. On two ship image sets the tuned model raised detection scores by about two points while adding few parameters. The authors say the gains matter for sea patrol and safety watch tasks.
pmc-12788606:
Jaw joint disorders blur together on examination, and Bassam Alkhalifah and five co-authors tested whether a three-dimensional scan sharpens the picture in a 2025 study. They scanned 60 clinic patients, aged 18 to 50, with cone beam computed tomography, a low-dose method that renders the joint's bone in detail.

The scans found condyle erosion in nearly half the patients, flattening in over a third, and bony spurs in a fifth. Joint space was lopsided in more than half. Patients whose scans showed arthritic change reported markedly higher pain scores than those without. In over 40 percent of cases, the scan findings changed the treatment plan the clinic had first drawn up. The authors conclude the imaging earns its place by tying symptoms to structure and steering care toward the actual damage.
pmc-12788706:
Pulling front teeth back to fix a double protrusion of the jaws might narrow the throat, or so orthodontists worry. Amelia Sugiarta, Haru Anggani, and Maria Purbiati test in 2025 that fear on forty-six treatment X-rays of bimaxillary protrusion cases. Tooth positions and upper and lower airway widths were measured before and after retraction.

Teeth moved, and the upper airway width changed, yet the changes did not correlate: patients with the biggest tooth movements were not the ones with the biggest airway shifts. The lower airway barely moved. The authors conclude premolar extraction with retraction remains a safe plan for these patients.
pmc-12788806:
Clara Paz and co-authors argue for routine outcome monitoring in Kenyan mental health care in a 2025 paper. Kenya has advanced in mental health policy and facilities, yet specialized services still lack steady, data driven habits that support outcome based care. The authors propose building routine outcome monitoring into teaching and referral hospitals first.

Done well, such systems turn hospitals into learning health systems that use daily practice data to improve care quality and accountability. The shift needs more than software, it needs digital standards, protected time for staff to reflect on data, stronger referral paths, and alignment with national health indicators. The paper frames monitoring as a deep change, not a technical add on.
pmc-12793106:
Yan Fang Cheryl Tan and co-authors test a survey tool that asks ward patients how sure they feel about falls. Falls in hospital can set back health fast, yet bold patients who shun help are hard for staff to spot with no set tool. The scale in view rates trust across fall guarding, getting up, and self-shielding. Their 2025 pilot runs in a Singapore community hospital with ninety patients and a small nurse group.

Both groups rate the tool through a known frame for new care steps, scored on ease, fit, cost, and faith to the plan. Patients rate it high on welcome and fit in the scores shown. Free-text replies add what helps and what blocks use. The pilot tells the team if the scale is ripe for wider ward use.
pmc-12795806:
Aguida Mohammed Echarif and co-authors build, in twenty twenty-five, a resource-light machine learning framework for real-time load monitoring in solar-powered aviation. Non-intrusive load monitoring infers which devices draw power from one aggregate signal. Aircraft impose strict limits on weight, latency, and compute. The team evaluated six learning models on high-rate power data, sampled two hundred thousand times per second. The data captured transients and steady states across all flight phases. Smoothing and downsampling cut noise while keeping key features.

A nearest neighbor model gave the best balance of accuracy and cost, with a score near zero point nine four and a run time of a fifth of a second. A hybrid neural model had the lowest error but took over four minutes, suiting offline analysis.
pmc-12797506:
Tongjie Zhang, Qian Xu, and Jie Zhou link a long-run blood fat marker to later dementia risk in older Chinese adults, in this 2025 study. The marker averages a fat-ratio index across years, capturing lasting exposure rather than one snapshot. The team drew on a national aging survey, following over six thousand adults into their later waves.

Higher long-run values went with higher dementia risk scores, in a straight, dose-by-dose pattern that survived full adjustment. The link ran stronger in women, in those over sixty, in rural residents, and in people with higher body weight. A standard cholesterol measure showed the same direction but more weakly.
pmc-12799506:
Yaqeen Rjoub and co-authors examined a gene change in the virus tied to nose-and-throat cancer, in a 2025 study. Nearly all such cancers link to Epstein-Barr virus. One viral gene, LMP1, helps drive the cancer, and a variant that loses a cutting site called XhoI has drawn suspicion. The team checked tumor tissue from patients in Jordan for that variant.

Virus DNA turned up in every sample. The normal form of the site appeared in about eighty-three percent of cases, and the mutant form in none, a pattern backed by gene sequencing of sample cases. The normal form showed no tie to sex, age, tumor type, or stage. Most late-stage tumors carried the normal form.
pmc-12800306:
Lydia Chougar and co-authors asked whether the brain shrinkage seen on scans in multiple system atrophy matches the biology underneath, in a 2025 study. The disease attacks support cells in the brain, but whether scan changes reflect that damage was unclear. The team measured atrophy in sixty-five patients and compared the pattern against gene activity maps from donated brains, plus maps of chemical messenger systems.

Shrinkage concentrated in the cerebellum, pons, putamen, and nearby deep structures. Those same regions overexpressed genes tied to mitochondria, the cell's power plants, and to the support cells the disease targets. The pattern differed clearly from Parkinson's disease, tested in fifty-seven patients for contrast. Shrunken areas also held lower levels of two calming messengers and higher receptor density for two alerting ones. The authors say the scan changes are biologically grounded.
pmc-12801706:
Alessandro Costa, Sharanjeet Sidhu, and Thomas Hardy present a 2025 case report on a rare bleeding emergency during eye anesthesia. Bleeding behind the eyeball can crush the eye's blood supply and blind it if pressure is not relieved fast. It usually follows trauma or surgery, and only rarely an anesthetic injection. Their patient was a seventy-five-year-old man having a routine sub-Tenon's block, an injection around the eye, before a minor eye procedure.

He had no known bleeding risk, yet bleeding began at once. He felt severe pain, his lids swelled tight, his eye stopped moving, and pressure inside the eye spiked. An emergency cut at the eye's corner released the pressure and saved his sight. The authors stress that teams must watch for this rare event even in low-risk patients. Speed, they note, is what preserves vision.
pmc-12804706: William La Cava, Glenn Cohen, and Jaya Aysola weigh a new rule on bias in health AI in a 2025 paper. A Section 1557 rule bars bias by AI tools that guide care, with a due date of May 2025. The trio flag hard parts: how to spot bias when outcomes gap, how to catch proxy bias, and how to audit high-risk tools. Shaky enforcement plans cloud long builds, so they urge strong, set guidance for health systems and tool makers.
pmc-12804806:
Hui Xue and a large consortium team report a genome-wide study of brainstem structures, published in 2025. The brainstem contains nuclei and tracts serving vital functions, but earlier genetic work drew mainly on European participants.

The team ran cross-ancestry meta-analyses in more than one hundred thousand individuals for brainstem volume, and in a smaller group for eight substructure volumes. They report hundreds of locus-trait associations, most of them new, and prioritize many genes linked to these traits. Some effects differed between ancestries, while many were similar. Results show shared and distinct genetic patterns for the midbrain, pons, and medulla.
pmc-12805706:
Siu Long Chau, Wanjia He, and Sophia Chan ask university health students how it felt to teach health topics to poor older adults at home. Their 2025 study sits inside a large Hong Kong project that trains future health workers through home visits. Book learning alone, the authors note, does not build skill with community elders.

Twenty students took hour-long interviews about their visits. Four themes stood out: limits of the elders' bodies and senses, the elders' mixed attitudes to advice, factors that shape how well elders take in health facts, and tactics that help. Some elders, students felt, had given up on seeking health facts, partly from a dim view of aging. Tailoring content to each elder's needs and readiness, the authors say, is the way to lift results.
pmc-12808106:
Xiang Tao and co-authors analyze, in a 2025 paper, why grid-forming renewable inverters sometimes fail to support the power grid as designed. Such inverters should mimic old spinning generators and steady the grid's rhythm during a jolt. Tests show their boost can rise and then fade instead of peaking at once.

The team traces the fault to how the inverter samples grid frequency. Sampling that is not in real time feeds the control loop stale news. The damping setting further shapes the odd response curve. Finding the cause matters because grids now lean on these devices for stability. The analysis points engineers toward sampling fixes that restore the intended support.
pmc-12811906:
Qing Wang and three co-authors study how soft-edged sexism shapes job dreams among Chinese college women in a 2025 paper. Benevolent sexism praises women as pure and in need of shelter, a sweet tone that can still steer them toward so-called women's jobs. The team asked how women who meet that message plan their working lives.

A survey of 427 women came first, then deep interviews with 26. Meeting the message in daily life linked to higher aims and more career search steps, through a boost in faith in one's own choices. Fitting the expected mold also won family backing, the interviews showed.
pmc-12812606:
Feng, Wang, and Zang build a yardstick for a specific worry: fear of catching an infectious disease. General health anxiety scales miss the outbreak setting. So in 2025 the team adapts an existing inventory to focus on COVID-19. They test the new scale on 1,660 adults, mostly in the United States.

The scale settles into two factors, catastrophic thinking and infection worries, with strong consistency and stability over time. Scores relate to handwashing in a curved pattern that separates healthy vigilance from excess. A five-item short form keeps most of the accuracy, and cutoffs are given for both versions. The authors offer the tools for screening during outbreaks, while urging tests in wider populations.
pmc-12813106:
Xiaofei Chen, Zhijia Zhao, Yi Liang, Yujing Zhou, Huaying Wang, and Wanjun Yu build a score to predict death risk in older pneumonia patients. The head of the paper dates the work to 2025. It joins an immune-inflammation index with a nutrition index drawn from blood tests.

Records came from a large intensive care database, with 634 patients kept after screening. A further 149 patients from a Ningbo hospital served as an outside check. Set cut points split patients into risk groups, and survival curves split clearly by score. The joined score sorted risk better than many single measures. The authors offer it as a simple bedside aid for care teams.
pmc-12815506:
Michael Char, Chuan-Chin Huang, Adit Ginde, and Peter Hou test a lung harm score in a 2025 study. A grave lung state strikes some hospital patients, and the only cures with proven gains are gentle air support and face-down care. Spotting at-risk patients early opens the door to steps that may stop the state before it starts.

A score built for ward entry was later reworked for the emergency room, where patients first arrive. The new study checks that room score on fresh patients outside its home site. Readers learn how well the score flags who will fall ill, and where it may fall short.
pmc-12815706:
Jiarong Yu and co-authors build a three-in-one virus test for pigs in a 2025 paper (head year). Three DNA viruses cause sow breeding failure with overlapping signs, and mixed infections muddy diagnosis. Standard tests miss low loads.

Their droplet test reads all three viruses at once with separate glow probes. Detection limits ran about tenfold below the standard method, and no cross-hits with other swine germs appeared. On two hundred seventeen farm samples, the new test found more positives overall and for each virus. The gain was largest for the swine fever virus. A sharper triple test can speed herd calls in outbreaks.
pmc-12815906:
Chavarin Amarase and four colleagues test a new orthopedic plate that reports bone healing through vibration, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. Judging whether a fracture has united usually means imaging and guesswork. Their plate design listens to the bone's natural frequency instead.

The physics is simple: a fractured bone strains more under load, raising frequency, while a healed bone strains less. Eight human cadaveric tibias were fitted with the plate. Fracture gaps and united states were tested under loads up to four hundred newtons. Frequency stayed flat across loads in the healed condition but behaved differently with a fracture gap. The authors argue frequency monitoring could one day track healing continuously.
pmc-12816106:
Stienstra and coauthors adapt network mapping from mass spectra to NMR spectra. NMR is a top tool to solve chemical structures. Auto workflows for NMR lag far behind mass methods, though. The team ports key network ideas to a two-axis NMR test.

That test maps carbon and hydrogen signals in one grid. A tuned distance score matches peaks across spectra. Library lookup with that score found most true kin hits. Bigger libraries did not lift that hit rate much. Full networking then links spectra into kin groups. Group links spread name tags across unknown compounds.
pmc-12816206:
Xin Tan and colleagues review how three-dimensional pancreatic models are changing drug testing. Pancreatic cancer is rising and responds unevenly to treatment, so flat cell cultures mislead. Organoids and spheroids grown from patient tissue keep the tumor's mix of cells and its neighborhood.

The review covers how these models are built and paired with engineering platforms for screening drugs. Multi-layer molecular profiling of a patient's own organoid can point to a tailored therapy. The authors weigh what stands between the bench and routine clinic use. Living tumor avatars could make pancreatic treatment far more personal.
pmc-12816306:
Jie Zhang and Weilong Yang present a framework for tracing strategy in StarCraft II games, in work published in 2025. Pro game records are messy and varied, which makes expert review slow. Their system turns raw replays into aligned state paths and learns typical strategy arcs from them.

A new deviation score shows which parts of a game stray from the typical arc and when. Deviations tended to set in early, near 8 percent of match length, and often traced to tech timing gaps. A fix module restored alignment by more than 90 percent on average. Human experts rated the auto-written game stories high for factual fit and causal sense.
pmc-12816606:
Da-In Eun and nine co-authors test whether large language models can spot delirium after surgery by reading doctors' notes, in a 2025 study. Delirium is common, harmful, and often missed or caught late.

Two models, Llama-3-70B and GPT-4o, were compared with physicians at flagging serious cases, meaning those needing drugs or a specialist's diagnosis. The models caught more true cases than physicians, about 87 to 90 percent against 72 percent, but raised more false alarms. The two models agreed with each other almost perfectly, while physicians agreed only fairly. Both models flagged cases about a day earlier than doctors. The authors suggest models as a screening aid under doctor supervision.
pmc-12817406:
Kaylin Morris, Atena Pasha, Xiaoming Li, and Shan Qiao map how health systems in poorer countries prepare for climate-driven disasters, in a 2025 review. Floods, storms, and droughts are growing stronger, and health systems with thin infrastructure and staff shortages suffer most. The team searched four databases for studies on disaster readiness in low- and middle-income countries.

Of more than five hundred records, twenty studies qualified. Preparedness rested on five common parts: trained staff, sturdy facilities, ready supplies, working communication, and coordination with partners. Some systems showed smart adaptations, such as backup resources and joint response plans. Most, though, had lasting gaps in training, policy follow-through, and resilience. The authors call for investment in people, buildings, and shared emergency plans. Stronger systems, they argue, are a frontline climate defense for the patients who depend on them.
pmc-12817506:
Xiaolu Dai and co-authors interview people who took their distress to both chatbots and human therapists in a 2025 study. Debate rages over AI as digital therapist. Critics say bots lack agency, the mind behind the words. Users' own comparisons were rarely heard.

Sixteen adults who used both forms of help gave deep interviews. Themes were drawn from their accounts by reflective analysis. ChatGPT encouraged open sharing, a first theme shows. Further themes weigh its tireless availability against the human bond. Perceived agency, theirs and the bot's, shapes what help feels real. The study grounds a loud debate in lived experience.
pmc-12817706:
Huimin Zhang and co-authors set out a protocol for a review of how stroke survivors living at home experience physical activity. Published in 2025, the plan follows a set method for reviews of qualitative research, studies built on people's own accounts. Moving more is a core part of recovery after stroke, helping survivors regain function and care for themselves.

The team will search ten databases plus hand sources and grey literature. Two reviewers will screen studies, judge quality with a standard checklist, pull out findings, and merge them. A named approach will rate trust in the merged result. The protocol promises a clear, open account of what helps or blocks activity at home.
pmc-12817806:
Gut microbes live in neighborhoods, and who sits next to whom shapes what the community does. Gurdip Uppal and co-authors present MCSPACE, a probabilistic AI tool that reads microbe co-location data and infers those neighborhoods over time. New lab methods can now sample such location data at huge scale, but the data are noisy and tangled.

To test the tool, the team built the largest data set of its kind: mouse guts tracked through diet changes over 76 days. MCSPACE also ran on two human data sets and beat existing methods in benchmarks. It found microbial groups that persist for months in the human gut, and groups that reshuffle when diet changes in mice. The authors release the software openly. They argue place, not just presence, is a missing layer in microbiome science.
pmc-12819406:
Baichen Li, Giuseppe Marrazzo, Marta Poyo Solanas, and Beatrice de Gelder trace how information about whole-body actions flows through the brain region that reads bodies. The lateral occipitotemporal cortex handles objects, bodies, and expressions, but how its subdivisions pass action information around was unclear. Their 2025 study records brain activity as people view different whole-body actions, and models the direction of flow between the region's parts. Different actions drive distinct flow patterns, suggesting the subdivisions divide the labor of reading a moving body.

Knowing who does what, from a glance, is a social survival skill, and this cortex is its hub. A flow map upgrades the picture from areas that light up to a circuit that computes. The authors use time-sensitive methods to get direction, not just activity. Their findings refine models of action perception. The work sits in cognitive neuroscience, with body language as the test case.
pmc-12820306:
Yuan-Xiang Shi and Tao Chen present a cancer bioinformatics study, published in 2025, sorting lung adenocarcinoma into new molecular subtypes. The sorting keys are genes tied to two processes: anoikis, the self destruct order given to cells that detach, and angiogenesis, the growth of new blood vessels. From public databases covering seven hundred fifty tumors, the team clustered patients by these genes and built a scoring system from the patterns.

The subtypes differed in survival, mutation load, immune cell mix, and likely response to immunotherapy and standard drugs. One cluster paired rich stroma with poor outcomes, while high scores on the new scale surprisingly tracked better prognosis. The authors offer the score as a guide for matching patients to treatment.
pmc-12820506:
Ha Ngo and co-authors examine how often family doctors prescribe anti-vertigo drugs, and for how long, in this 2025 study. Evidence that these drugs help dizziness is thin. One of them, betahistine, is still among the most prescribed off-label drugs. Doctors in primary care likely write much of that volume. The team mined records from hundreds of Dutch practices. More than a million patients' data covered the years 2018 to 2021.

They counted new and long-term prescriptions for patients with balance symptoms. Traits linked to long-term use were also sought. Long courses are the worry when benefit is unproven. The study is records-based, with identities removed. Its findings can feed prescribing guidance and review campaigns. Dizzy patients are common in primary care, so even small rates mean many people.
pmc-12821906:
Lauren Stuart and co-authors ask whether a mother's grasp of health information carries the effect of poverty on her care for her baby, in a 2025 paper. Among 168 mothers of newborns in Soweto, South Africa, most counted as socially vulnerable. The team measured vulnerability, several sides of health literacy, and two care outcomes: confidence in breastfeeding and beliefs about play.

Material hardship by itself did not predict either outcome. Three literacy skills mattered instead: engaging with health providers, finding good information, and understanding it well enough to act. The first two partly carried vulnerability's effect, while understanding predicted both outcomes directly. The authors say building these skills may lift mothers' confidence even where money stays short.
pmc-12822006:
Sherif Eid and co-authors build a sensor that tracks copper ions in water as they change, moment by moment. Their paper appeared in 2025. Copper ions are toxic and widely used in industry, yet standard tests are slow and cannot follow fast changes. The sensor is a printed electrode coated with a thin film that responds to copper alone. A layer of tiny plastic grains carries the signal.

The sensor answered within ten seconds and worked across a wide range of copper levels. The team used it to watch copper grains form in a flask, step by step. From the readings they worked out the energy terms of that process. The sensor also suited checks of water samples from the field. Fast, cheap copper checks could help both factories and water safety work.
pmc-12822206:
Phemlar Mashaba and co-authors set out a protocol for a study of what pregnant women know, feel, and do about obstetric danger signs. These signs warn of sudden problems that can harm mother or baby at any point in pregnancy. The 2025 protocol targets women at antenatal visits in one South African hospital.

The planned study uses a quantitative, cross sectional design with convenience sampling. Questionnaires will gather the data, with a statistician aiding the analysis. A pilot run will test whether the tool is sound and steady. The protocol pledges ethics care, checks on validity, and steps to guard rights and data. Findings, the authors say, should raise awareness of fast care.
pmc-12822306:
Qian Wang and co-authors track bacterial infections and drug resistance at a heart specialty hospital over seven years, in a 2025 study. Such tracking guides doctors toward antibiotics that still work. The center serves a national region for cardiovascular care in China.

From 2018 to 2024, the lab logged 9,180 bacterial isolates from patients. About two-thirds were Gram-negative types, led by three species known for hospital infections. Resistance was high across common germs. One group resisted last-resort drugs in up to about a third of cases, and resistant staph strains stayed common as well. The authors link resistant infections to more deaths and longer stays, and they urge tighter antibiotic stewardship.
pmc-12824206:
Lv Zhang, Kai Xu, and Heng Fan study a puzzle in quantum physics in this twenty twenty-five paper. Some disordered materials can hold energy in place instead of letting it spread, a state called many-body localization. Rare hot spots can break that state and spread heat to nearby regions, like an avalanche.

The authors model a chain of linked particles that keeps a basic symmetry while its parts interact. They find an in-between phase where energy does spread, set between two unlike frozen phases. By tracking the slowest rate at which the system heats up when linked to a large outside bath, they show how the hot-spot effect shifts the point where the frozen state fails.
pmc-12824306:
Antoine Boué and a large team study thinking skills in 2025 among older men treated for prostate cancer that has spread. The men receive hormone treatment, and some also get newer drugs that block the hormone path. Early work hints these drugs may affect memory and focus, but data in older adults are thin.

The team compares three groups: men on both treatments, men on hormone treatment alone, and healthy peers. At the start, about half of the first group showed thinking trouble on tests, far more than the other groups. After three and six months, the first group also reported worse thinking than the hormone-only group.
pmc-12824406:
Jadie Moon and co-authors trace how an immune signal slows healing in diabetic wounds. Their 2025 study focuses on keratinocytes, the skin cells that must crawl to close a wound. In type 2 diabetes those cells move poorly and stir excess inflammation.
