The signal IL-17A runs high in diabetic wounds. It switches on an enzyme that strips repressive marks from gene switches. The opened genes then block cell movement and feed inflammation. Removing the signal or the enzyme in diabetic mice sped healing and quieted those genes. Human wounds showed the same raised pattern. The authors name the pair as a drug target.
pmc-12827606:
Gout salt in the blood is cheap to read, and its tie to fate past a heart grip is a live ask. Zongle Sun and co-authors pool that tie in a review published in 2025. Forty sets with more than one hundred thousand grip sick form the pool.

High salt went with near twice the death odds and more than twice the heart death odds. Great heart harms, stroke, and heart fail all ran high with the salt. A fresh pipe work showed no tie. The salt's tie to death bent in a curve, not a line. The team cast the salt as a fate mark worth wide ward proof.
pmc-12827706:
Stephanie Villaire and co-authors ask whether beauty shop staff feel at ease talking with clients about sexual health. Their study surveys thirty-eight beauty workers in two Texas counties. Black women in the US face gaps in sexual health care and teaching, and shops are trusted, chat-rich places. The survey asked how at ease staff feel, how often such talks occur, and what holds staff back.

Staff felt far more at ease than the rate at which talks in fact happen. Ease in sharing health facts and a sense that clients need care access both linked to more talks. Shame, privacy fears, and low training held talks back. The authors see room for programs that back staff as health voices.
pmc-12828006:
Yingying Niu and co-authors design a layered metamaterial that absorbs terahertz waves over an extremely wide band. Stretching such absorbers to low frequencies without losing efficiency or angle tolerance is a standing challenge. Their structure couples several resonance types at once: in-plane modes, cavity modes through the layers, and waveguide modes in air gaps between cells.

Simulations predict average absorption near total across a band spanning more than a tenfold frequency range, with a peak at essentially complete absorption. Performance holds across all polarization angles and for incoming waves tilted up to a moderate angle. The authors pitch the design for terahertz sensing and electromagnetic countermeasures, and as a blueprint for future absorbers.
pmc-12830806:
Ryoma Nakao and co-authors report a 2025 mouse study of a nose-spray vaccine against pneumococcal disease. The vaccine uses membrane vesicles from a helpful strain of Escherichia coli bacteria. The vesicles carry the sugar coat of a type 14 pneumococcus on their surface. The goal is guard at the nose and throat, where these germs first settle.

Mice given the spray made strong IgG in the blood, beating two licensed shots in the test. Only the spray route switched on IgA, the guard found in mucus, and it lasted through a year of checks. A vaccine that guards the airway lining could block infection early. More work is needed before human trials.
pmc-12830906:
Xuan Han and four co-authors hunt, in 2025 work, blood proteins that cause, not just mark, the clouding of the eye's lens. Past links could not say which way the cause runs. Their method uses gene marks as natural lots, cast both ways, to sort true drivers from mere fellow riders.

Eight proteins stood out as risk raisers, from code readers to lens shards. Seven more stood out as shields. Deep data dives then mapped what those proteins do, which paths they walk, and how they touch each other. The map hints at how lens clouds are born, the team says. Fresh drug or guard ideas may grow from the named set.
pmc-12831306:
Zeynab Yousefi and co-authors test in 2025 a drug combination against liver fibrosis in rats, pairing the diabetes drug liraglutide with the antifibrotic pirfenidone. Each drug alone had shown promise, but their joint effect on cell cleanup and a key inflammatory complex was unexplored. Fifty male rats were split into five groups, including sham and bile-duct-ligated disease groups.

After twenty days, the combination cut liver injury markers more than either drug alone. Scar tissue deposition fell and tissue structure improved. Inflammatory signals dropped while a protective signal rose. Cell cleanup markers shifted favorably, and the inflammatory complex was suppressed more strongly.
pmc-12832206:
Leen Ahmed and co-authors tell of a rare germ cause of belly-fluid flare in a man with a worn liver. The study appeared in 2025. The man, in his mid-50s, came with worse belly pain, back-built fluid, and a fresh kidney hit. First counts sat low, which eased fear of the flare.

Growth tests then grew the rare germ from his belly fluid. That germ shrugs the stock first drug for the flare. Care swung to a high-dose vein drug, then a mouth pair to end the course. Fluid taps, a blood good, and vein care backed the cure. He left the ward in firm state.
pmc-12835006:
Hadiza Ado Suleiman and colleagues turn coconut shell waste into a filter for toxic metals, in this study from twenty twenty-five. Factory wastewater, such as tannery waste, often carries cadmium, lead, and other heavy metals. The team made activated carbon from the shells and treated it with potassium hydroxide to open its pores and add gripping sites.

In lab-made solutions, the carbon pulled out more than eighty percent of five metals: cadmium, lead, manganese, nickel, and copper. In real tannery wastewater its grip fell below half at first. After the team tuned the mix of contact time, dose, acidity, and warmth, removal climbed above ninety-five percent. Tests pointed to chemical bonding as the way metals stick. The carbon could also be stripped clean with acid and used again, which adds to its appeal as a cheap, local filter.
pmc-12835106:
Yi Wang, Jian Jie Zhang, and Ming Yang Zhang present a method for spotting anomalies in data streams with many channels at once. Their 2025 paper notes that real problems, from factories to networks, rarely hinge on one variable alone. Existing methods either treat channels separately and miss links, or fuse all channels and swallow noise.

Their framework, FreFilterTST, first rebuilds the input from frequency patches to learn what normal looks like. A transformer with expert sub-networks then filters channels adaptively, thinning the channel graph while keeping fine frequency detail. A frequency-domain restoration step repairs the signal. The design aims to catch subtle faults without drowning in false links.
pmc-12836906:
Tirusew Nigussie Kebede leads a large team in this 2025 review asking whether care bundles prevent infections after caesarean birth. Surgical site infections are among the commonest complications of the world's commonest major operation, and the burden falls hardest on poorer countries. The team gathered twenty-one studies covering more than thirty-two thousand women.

Pooling the results, bundles of evidence-based steps, spanning preparation, antibiotics, and wound care, cut infection risk by about seventy percent. Infection rates fell from roughly five percent before bundles to nearly zero after. The authors urge hospitals everywhere to adopt bundles as routine, with special urgency where infection rates are highest. The payoff runs beyond the mother: faster recovery supports newborn care and breastfeeding, and fewer infections mean shorter, cheaper hospital stays.
pmc-12838006:
Ahmad Tahmasebi-Ghorrabi and co-authors link nurses' spiritual health to how patients rate nursing care, in work from 2025. Stress and hard ward conditions can erode care quality. A nurse's inner sense of meaning may buffer that strain and show in patient experience.

The study paired 80 nurses with 80 of their patients in two hospitals in Ahvaz, Iran, in 2022. Standard surveys measured nurse spiritual health and patient satisfaction in matching wards. Ties between the two scores were tested with rank and regression methods. Findings can guide support programs that treat staff well-being as part of care quality. Managers get evidence for investing in nurse support.
pmc-12838406:
Catrin Jones and co-authors count the hours of care that starting kidney replacement therapy demands in a 2025 study. For patients whose kidneys have failed, the switch to dialysis or a transplant is an intense stretch: frequent clinic visits, procedures, hospital stays, and dialysis sessions fill the week. Cancer research calls this burden time toxicity, and the team borrows the idea for kidney care.

Their retrospective study follows all adults who began replacement therapy in their service, by any of the three routes. They add up the time-based workload of the transition from records. They also test which patient traits go with a heavier load. Counting time as a cost in its own right can change how services schedule the handover and support the patients who carry most.
pmc-12840806:
Yiting Yang and eleven co-authors map gene activity in pig testes before and after sexual maturity. Male fertility rests on a web of gene switches that turn sperm making on. The team used a long-read sequencing method that captures full gene messages, not just fragments. They compared young boars with mature ones and found more than eleven thousand genes whose activity changed.

Thousands of message variants and long non-coding RNAs also shifted. The changed genes clustered in sperm making and in key growth pathways. A few core genes moved in step across all levels read. The paper gives breeders and biologists a deep map of how the pig testis matures.
pmc-12841106:
Buse Sabiha Bozaslan and co-authors look for gene links to anger in athletes. Their 2025 study, framed in forensic science, picks four genes known to shape mood and conduct. Twenty licensed athletes took part, each giving a cheek swab and filling in three scales.

The scales covered sportsmanship, feelings in sport, and anger control. Lab tests then read set gene variants for each athlete. The team checked how the variants lined up with the scale scores. Early findings point to gene-wise patterns, though the group is small. The authors place the work in the wider field that ties genes to behavior and traits, a field still in its early days.
pmc-12842006:
Yan Lv and co-authors surveyed chigger mites on small mammals at a scrub typhus site in northern Yunnan, China, in 2025. Chiggers are the sole carriers of scrub typhus. A year-long study ran at one village from late 2020 to late 2021.

More than two hundred thousand chiggers were taken from over thirteen hundred mammal hosts of eighteen species. The mites sorted into one hundred fifteen species, nine of them known disease carriers. Infestation was heavy, with about seven in ten hosts carrying mites. Three rodent species were the main hosts, and three carrier mite species made up about sixty percent of all mites. Mite numbers and diversity swung with month and season.
pmc-12844106:
Ching-Mu Cheng and four colleagues present a 2025 engineering study on a humble step in contact lens making: popping the fresh lens out of its mold. The release is done with a punch, and a bad punch shape stresses the mold and ruins lenses. Using computer simulation, the team tested punch geometries for how they spread stress in the polypropylene mold.

A flat punch with a shallow arc groove in its center spread stress best and deformed the mold least. In a hundred-cycle trial, lenses released more smoothly and centered better, and the good-lens yield reached eighty-two percent, thirteen points above a plain flat punch. The authors say the small shape change cuts costs and raises throughput on the production line.
pmc-12845006:
Assem Uzakova and co-authors review advanced drug delivery systems in a 2025 paper. Smart carriers can aim a drug at the right tissue, release it slowly, and cut side effects. Yet many designs stall before clinic use, blocked by body barriers, hard manufacturing, and cost. The review asks what separates designs that translate from those that do not.

The team searched three databases for work from 2016 to early 2025 and kept 77 studies with lab or clinical data. Carrier types ranged from fat bubbles and lipid particles to polymer systems and cell-derived vesicles. For each, they logged size, surface traits, barrier crossing, and fate in the body. One lesson stood out: success hinges on matching carrier traits to the barrier at hand.
pmc-12845506:
Lewisite, a blister agent from chemical warfare, burns skin fast, and a 2025 study by Nethra Viswaroopan and co-authors builds a foam treatment for it. Good care must clean the poison off at once and keep treating the wound for hours.

The team loaded a drug called 4-PBA into tiny fat-based carriers named emulsomes, then set those carriers in a foam base. They tuned the lipid mix and drug load, then checked particle size, charge, and stability under warm and cool storage. Lab tests covered how the parts fit together and how the foam spreads. The design aims to give rescue teams one product that both decontaminates and delivers steady drug to burned skin.
pmc-12846306:
Junshu Zhu and eight co-authors test the lethal and sublethal effects of a new insecticide, cycloxaprid, on the green peach aphid, a global pest with high proofing to old sprays. The new drug keeps effect on proofed pests. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

The drug killed lab and field proofed aphids more strongly than a standard rival. In fields, the rival fell short of needed control, while the new drug cleared a far higher bar. At a low dose that does not kill outright, life table work showed shorter life and fewer young in the next adult brood for both drugs, with growth rates also cut.
pmc-12846706:
Vinícius Menezes Braga and co-authors study liver bile duct cancer driven by aflatoxin mixtures in rats, in a research paper from 2025. Aflatoxins are potent mold toxins that target the liver. Their power to cause this bile duct cancer type was underexplored, though one member toxin is well studied for liver cell cancer.

Male rats got a toxin mixture dominated by the main aflatoxin, or a control, by daily feeding tube for ninety days. After twelve months, twelve tumors were analyzed by microscopy and protein staining. Tumors showed gland-like structure and high growth rates. A tumor suppressor protein piled up in most tumors, and cell cycle control was disturbed. Wnt pathway activation was rare.
pmc-12847706:
Cervical cancer kills many women in sub-Saharan Africa, and persistent infection with cancer-causing types of human papillomavirus drives most cases. Alfred Mabika-Obanda and co-authors screened 1,524 women during three years of Octobre Rose campaigns in Libreville, Gabon. They combined visual inspection of the cervix with laboratory typing of the virus. Overall, 21 percent of women carried the virus, and 18.5 percent carried cancer-causing types.

Type 35 was the single commonest type, yet the nine-valent vaccine's target types caused 63 percent of cancer-causing infections and most detected abnormalities, led by types 16 and 45. HIV infection and high lifetime sexual exposure raised the odds of carrying a risky type. The authors argue the vaccine could prevent much of this burden, while screening must continue for types it misses.
pmc-12847906:
Yulin Sun and co-authors studied bladder cancer cells in 2025 and a route that may slow their spread. Some tumor cells shift to a loose, moving form that helps them invade new tissue. That shift also changes how the cells handle iron-linked cell death, a process called ferroptosis. The team traced a signal chain that links a growth signal to a small iron-handling protein.

In lab cells pushed toward the loose form, death-linked genes rose and the cells grew more prone to a drug that starts ferroptosis. Lowering the first gene in the chain raised iron stress and cut growth and spread. Raising the second gene undid much of that harm. Tests on patient samples backed the link between the two genes.
pmc-12848006:
Hao Hu and co-authors lock fold-up glow chains in twist by web of flat-ring grips, in a study from 2025. Foldamers are chains that fold to a set shape. Flat-ring chains glow in twist hues, a prize for screens, but their twist flips with ease since ring grips are weak.

Their build webs grips in three spans at once: face-to-face and side-shift stacks in one frame. Crystal shots and counts show the webs hold, with flip walls past the best of old twist locks. Donor and taker swaps tune the glow through the full hue band, in soup and in solid, with twist force kept high. Twist that stays, they show, can be built, not just found.
pmc-12848306:
Sofija Markovic and colleagues present the first math model of how a toxin and antitoxin pair inside bacteria can create dormant persister cells that survive antibiotics. Persisters cause infections that return after treatment, and their origin has puzzled researchers for nearly a century. In the system modeled, the antitoxin is a small RNA that keeps the toxin in check, and feedback loops link the pair. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team analyzes the equations and runs simulations to map when the circuit settles in one state or flips between two.

Two steady states appear: low toxin with normal growth, and high toxin with dormancy, with random switching between them. Stress such as antibiotics or starvation can push the system into the two-state regime. The authors chart which feedback features control the switch, offering testable guidance for experiments.
pmc-12849106:
Lijiang Zhai and co-authors review in this 2025 study a decade of work on reading mood disorders from brain waves with explainable AI. Depression, anxiety, and bipolar disorder resist easy diagnosis, and brain wave markers promise help, but black-box models stall clinical trust. One hundred forty-five studies using explainable methods passed their screen.

Wave power bands, brain region coupling, and time-domain measures carried the signal. Explanation tools confirmed known patterns, like frontal asymmetry in depression, and models scored seventy-five to ninety-nine percent accuracy. The authors weigh bias and the road to the clinic, urging designs doctors can interrogate. Clinics gain tools they can question out loud.
pmc-12849306:
Songphon Buddhasiri, Sasibha Jantrakajorn, and their co-authors studied how a gut parasite changes the microbes in young Asian seabass. Their 2025 study concerns intestinal coccidia, parasites linked to worse bacterial infections in fish, perhaps by changing gut microbes. The exact shifts in fish were not well known.

Gut samples came from seven sick young fish and five young fish that were not sick. The team read the samples by gene sequencing. Sick fish had a richer microbe mix, and the mix had shifted at several levels. Genera with a known power to cause disease grew more common, including Clostridium and Lactococcus, as did some bacteria that can infect people. The findings matter for fish farms, where a sound gut helps fish live and grow.
pmc-12849406:
Julia Szymczak and five co-authors study, in a 2025 paper, how workplace friendships and loyalties colour the way doctors read their own scorecards. The setting is an antibiotic stewardship program, where clinics get audit and feedback on prescribing to curb overuse. Such feedback works unevenly, and social context was a suspect.

The team interviewed thirty-two primary care doctors from fifteen practices in the eastern United States, a year after the program. They sampled doctors who stayed strong, who improved, and who did not. Three ties shaped how the numbers were received: trust in the health system, bonds within the practice, and the pull of patient wishes. High performers and improvers told different stories about those ties than non-improvers did.
pmc-12854806:
Harlin Kaur and Aksha Memon wrote this 2025 review of a long debate in child mental health. The topic is a class of antidepressant drugs called SSRIs, used to treat depression in children and teens. In 2004 the US drug agency put its strongest warning on these drugs over fears they raise suicide risk.

The authors searched the medical literature and chose eight studies to weigh in depth. Most found a small rise in suicidal thoughts early in treatment with these drugs. Trials were mixed on whether the drugs alone caused the rise. Care that paired a drug with talk therapy tended to do best. The review urges close watch in the first weeks of care.
pmc-12855206:
Jing Wang and co-authors study a small RNA that curbs breast cancer stemness in a 2025 paper. Breast cancer is the most common cancer among women. Micro RNAs tune gene expression and shape cancer development. One such RNA ran low in tumor cells and tissues here.

Restoring the RNA cut cell growth, migration, and shape shifting. It also reduced stem-like traits and promoted cell death. Its direct target was a signaling chemokine named CXCL12. Silencing that target mimicked the RNA's effects. Blocking the RNA reversed the silencing benefits. A Wnt pathway protein shifted with the RNA's action. Drug resistance in a resistant cell line also eased under the RNA. A stemness protein tied to resistance ran high in resistant cells. The authors propose the RNA axis as a therapy lead. Further work must test it beyond cell lines.
pmc-12855806:
Yashwanth Ramesh and co-authors presented this 2025 farm sensor shaped like a nail. Knowing how wet and salty soil is below the surface helps farmers use water and fertilizer wisely. Most sensors need batteries and upkeep, which blocks wide use. Their platform, called HARVEST, has no onboard electronics at all.

A nail probe underground couples to a three-ring antenna above the soil. Wetness and salt shift the probe's electrical traits, which move the antenna's resonant reply. A drone carrying a reader picks up that reply from as high as 1.8 meters. Lab tests and a full field season backed the design. The result is a cheap, maintenance-free way to watch soil health across large fields.
pmc-12856506:
Priyanka Verma and co-authors test whether two ultrasound measures can predict trouble for babies in pregnancies that look low-risk, in a 2025 study. The measures are the amniotic fluid index, a gauge of the fluid around the baby, and the cerebroplacental ratio, which compares blood flow in the baby's brain and cord. Both are used to judge fetal well-being, but their combined power in normal-sized, full-term pregnancies was unclear.

The study followed 236 such pregnancies between 37 and 40 weeks. One group was checked with fluid alone and the other with both measures, and outcomes were compared after birth. Delivery patterns and newborn health were much the same in both groups. Curve analysis showed both measures, alone or combined, discriminated poorly for low newborn scores, intensive care admission, and surgical delivery. The authors report the limits plainly.
pmc-12858106:
Raman Kumar writes alone in a 2025 call for a ban on gendered verbal abuse. Slurs built on the names of mothers, sisters, and daughters run through Indian film, television, social media, and public gatherings. Kumar argues such abuse is verbal violence rooted in habits that normalize disrespect toward women. It blurs the line between free speech and hate speech, he says.

The piece calls for a ban on this class of abuse in media and public spaces. It ties the language to wider humiliation of women in public life. The argument enters a live debate in India over speech limits and gender dignity. Readers get a clear, single demand backed by a survey of where the abuse appears.
pmc-12859906:
He Li and co-authors set side by side ways, in statistics, to model an outcome from multi-omics data joined as one set. Their 2025 piece asks how best to shrink more than one large set of biological data into scores that can be used as a whole.

The team sets out one univariate method, like polygenic scores, and two multivariate methods. Their test runs used data sets that were linked and spread in a normal way. They also used a mix of normal data and data in fixed groups. The multivariate ways did well in most cases. They did best with a few more parts in the score, and beat the univariate way for two normal data sets. In real data on metabolomics and genes, used to model body mass index, all ways did much the same. The piece helps staff pick a way to join data sets.
pmc-12860006:
Hendrianus Hendrianus and nine co-authors pool the evidence on a fast blood-thinning drug for the sickest heart patients, in a 2025 review. Cangrelor is given by vein and blocks platelets within minutes, unlike pills that absorb slowly in a shocked body. The patients in question have cardiogenic shock or have just been resuscitated, and all undergo stenting. Evidence for this group was extremely thin. The authors searched three databases for studies comparing the drug against standard oral therapy.

Outcomes pooled include death from any cause, heart death, stent clots, heart attack, stroke, and blood flow grades. The synthesis, registered in advance, gives intensive care and cath lab teams a firmer basis for a drug choice they currently make on habit and hope.
pmc-12866006:
Humairah Zainal and co-authors map in 2025 what would help or hinder rolling out fertility awareness programs across Singapore. Fertility rates have slid worldwide, partly because many couples learn too late that fertility falls with age. The team had run a trial of fertility health screening and awareness tools for young married couples, and this study asks how such programs could go national.

The design paired the trial with interviews of the clinicians who delivered the programs and a chosen set of couples. Talk was sorted through a standard implementation framework, hunting barriers and facilitators one domain at a time. Completion of each screening step was checked against medical records. Cost data came from time driven accounting and a productivity loss survey. With hundreds of couples in the trial, the study grounds its national rollout advice in both lived experience and hard costing.
pmc-12866406:
Qiang Zhu and co-authors sorted brain gliomas by their fuel use in 2025, blending gene, cell, and chemical data into a new grouping that tracks how patients fare. Gliomas are the most common brain tumors, and their cells do not all burn fuel the same way.

An unsupervised learning method split patients into two camps. One camp ran hot on sugar burning, a backup sugar path, and fat burning. The other leaned on a protein breakdown route. Chemical profiling and single nucleus data backed the split, inside single tumors as well as across them. One surface protein marked the first camp and, through a signaling chain, pushed tumor cells to invade and migrate. The authors propose fuel based treatment choices.
pmc-12866506:
Keshavarz and co-authors ask whether protein fragments in dairy foods link to lower risk of muscle loss in older adults. Sarcopenia, the steady loss of muscle mass and strength, raises risks of fracture, poor mobility, and death. Some dairy peptides survive digestion and stay active in the body. The team compared 80 older adults in Shiraz, Iran who had sarcopenia with 80 who did not. Diet data came from a larger survey at local health centers.

The team estimated how much of these peptides each person ate from dairy products. They then compared intake between the two groups. Sarcopenia was judged by standard diagnostic rules. The study tests whether a common food group quietly guards aging muscle.
pmc-12870006:
Hyun Jin Oh, Chung Ho Kim, Hyun-Wook Park, and Bomi Park present a study from two thousand twenty-five on the path from a stomach infection to stomach cancer. The infection is caused by Helicobacter pylori, a common stomach bacterium. The Correa pathway describes the steps: chronic inflammation, thinning of the stomach lining, cell change, growths, and then cancer.

The team used national insurance data for about six point eight million Koreans screened in two thousand eighteen. They estimated how much clearing the infection lowers cancer risk. They also measured how much of that effect flows through the middle steps of the pathway, using causal methods built for the question.
pmc-12879406:
Hien Vu and eleven co-authors document how a giant Hanoi newborn unit breathes for its smallest patients, in this 2025 study. Breathing trouble is a leading killer of newborns in lower-income settings, yet Southeast Asian intensive care practice is barely described in the literature. Their hospital handles about thirty-five thousand births a year.

Over three months, 874 babies needing respiratory support were analyzed. Respiratory distress syndrome led at forty-one percent, then fast-breathing transients and early sepsis. Non-invasive support dominated, nasal pressure methods especially, while twenty-three percent needed a ventilator. Overall mortality was three percent, but it hit thirty-six percent in the tiniest babies. A lung-opening drug, surfactant, reached thirty-seven percent of distress cases, mostly within six hours and often by a brief intubation technique. The authors flag non-invasive support and surfactant delivery as the improvement frontiers.
pmc-12881406:
Junghyun Sung and eleven co-authors achieve polariton condensation in a thick tungsten disulfide structure far from the usual exciton resonance, in a two thousand twenty-five photonics paper. Bulk layered semiconductors were long written off for polariton work because their excitons are weak and indirect.

The team built bound-state-in-the-continuum cavities from fifty-nanometer WS2 and saw a large Rabi splitting near two hundred ninety-four millielectronvolts. Condensation was driven by indirect excitons feeding photons straight into the cavity modes. Even with excitons making up only about six percent of the hybrid particles, shrinking the pump spot tuned, with light, how tightly the condensate was held. The result opens polariton physics to indirect-gap solids.
pmc-12883406:
Yuan Liu and co-authors pool trial results to rank drug plans for ovarian cancer, in an analysis whose head dates it to 2025. One drug family blocks a repair path in cancer cells, and a second family cuts tumor blood supply. The team searched major databases to the end of 2024 and merged fifteen trials with more than six thousand patients across nine plans.

All plans with the repair blocking drugs beat dummy care on time with no growth of the cancer. Pairs beat single drugs on that score, and one pair ranked first of all. A second pair ranked next. Harsh side effects ran at like rates for single drugs but rose when drugs were paired. The authors urge plans matched to each patient, since gain and harm rise together.
pmc-12892206:
Goolam and eight co-authors describe adults hospitalized with RSV in South Africa in a 2025 paper. The respiratory virus is mild for most healthy adults but dangerous for the vulnerable. Its clinical picture in African hospitals was poorly documented.

Sentinel surveillance at two urban hospitals enrolled over nine hundred patients with severe respiratory illness during 2022 and 2023. Only eighteen tested positive for RSV, far fewer than for the coronavirus or flu. Their median age was fifty, and two thirds were women. Every RSV patient carried at least one other condition, most often a weakened immune system. Chest imaging features were charted alongside symptoms. The small count itself informs vaccine and testing priorities for the region.
pmc-12903506:
Fan Zhang and co-authors present a 2025 study of a quiet gene that may help immune therapy for bowel cancer. The gene, LGALS4, runs low in tumor tissue, and a famed guard gene's mutations may drive that drop. In dishes, extra copies of the gene did not slow cancer cells directly. In mice, though, tumors with extra gene copies grew far less, which pointed to the immune setting as the lever.

The gene reshapes the tumor's immune crowd through a signal path that calls in killer cells. Paired with an immune drug that blocks the PD-L1 brake, the effect grew stronger than either alone. The work names a gene pair that could mark patients for combo therapy. It also shows a tumor gene can fight by rallying immunity, not by direct attack.
pmc-12904106:
Tiny RNAs that guard the genome also flag cancer early, if machines can spot them in sequence data. Jheremy Sebastián Reyes and co-authors review AI tools for that hunt in a 2025 paper. They sift 24 studies across four databases.

Memory-based networks led, reaching 92.3 percent accuracy. Graph networks followed at 91.4 percent and shone on disease links. Classic support vector tools hit 88 percent but scaled poorly. Plain recurrent nets trailed at 85.7 percent. The best models also led on catching true cases without false alarms. The authors back AI reads for cancer checks.
pmc-12907506:
Somayeh Vandghanooni and co-authors write an editorial on nanoparticles dressed in body like coats for immune therapy. Their piece from 2025 explains that such biomimetic particles copy real cell surfaces, which helps them dodge the flaws of plain drug carriers. Gains claimed include body fit, long blood life, tissue aim, and low toxicity.

Cell membrane coated forms lead the field, with shown power in cancer and swelling diseases. New gene tools, from mRNA drugs to CRISPR editing, are being paired with the particles for sharper immune aim. Blocks to clinic use remain: spread in the body, long term safety, stray immune firing, and scale up. The authors call for tracking tech and set making rules.
pmc-12913206:
Hanieh Sadat Hashemi Motahar and co-authors test whether copying the shape of worn cartilage cells can push stem cells toward a worn state. Joint wear, called osteoarthritis, changes the shape of the cartilage cells themselves. The team molded soft pads with the shapes of healthy and worn human cartilage cells pressed into them.

Stem cells grown on the pads took on the copied shapes. Worn cells proved larger than healthy ones, and gene activity shifted with shape, though only one key gene changed by a clear margin. Protein stains broadly matched the gene story. The authors say shaped pads can join other tools to build better lab models of joint wear.
pmc-12913706:
Edvânia Celso Manave and co-authors surveyed gut parasites in cattle in southern Mozambique in 2025. Such parasites cut cattle health and yield, above all in warm regions. Most past work in the country looked at goats or at single parasite types, leaving cattle burdens unclear.

From January to May 2025, the team took stool samples from two hundred cattle in the Limpopo district. Lab tests checked for worms and single-cell parasites, and farm data covered grazing, deworming, and animal traits. Nearly nine in ten cattle carried at least one gut parasite, and eight parasite groups were found. Two groups each appeared in close to half the animals. Some of these parasites can also infect people.
pmc-12915406:
Defu Yuan and co-authors used deep sequencing to recount HIV drug resistance worldwide, in a 2025 meta-analysis. Standard Sanger tests miss rare resistant variants hiding in a patient's virus swarm. Deep sequencing reads far more copies, catching low-frequency rebels. The team pooled forty studies covering 10,778 patients, splitting resistance present before treatment from resistance gained on it.

In untreated patients, resistance mutations showed at rates near ten percent at the usual threshold, with extra low-frequency finds below it. Treated patients carried far more, with resistance reaching about sixteen percent. The authors argue the true burden has been understated. Clinics relying on older tests may start regimens already partly beaten.
pmc-12916606:
Tahereh Firoozi, Rojin Adabdokht, and Hollis Lai review search-fed AI in dentistry in this 2025 mini-review (the catalog lists 2026). Retrieval augmented generation pairs a language model with outside sources, fixing stale knowledge and made-up answers. Dental uses are just emerging.

Early dental systems show better factual accuracy and clearer reasoning, the authors report. Yet methods vary wildly and dental text collections are thin. Progress needs shared test standards, curated knowledge bases, and image-rich resources. The review maps the foundations and parts of the approach. It closes with paths toward trustworthy AI for dental research and care.
pmc-12917506:
Faria Jaheen and co-authors model surgical imaging gear with machine learning in a 2025 paper. C-arm fluoroscopy rigs swing around a patient on an operating table, and planning safe paths for their many joints is slow by hand. The team built data sets of joint poses tagged with clash states for rigs of five to nine freedoms.

Models trained on those sets, plus fake X ray checks, hit sub millimeter place accuracy and sub degree angle accuracy in real time. That speed beats classic methods on scale, toughness, and delay. The frame could widen imaging access in theatre and cut the risk of mid surgery clashes.
pmc-12920706:
Amir Hossein Aghapour and co-authors review what is known about hepatitis E in Iran, covering both how widely it spreads and how the virus varies, in a 2025 paper. The virus inflames the liver and usually clears on its own, yet it can kill, above all in pregnant women. Worldwide it infects an estimated twenty million people a year. It spreads through dirty water and food, and through raw or undercooked meat from animals such as pigs and camels.

The review walks through the virus's biology, the illness it causes, and the routes by which Iranians catch it, including flood-driven water contamination. It surveys the four genotypes that infect humans, the tests used to find the virus, and the treatments and vaccines available. The authors close with the case for close monitoring, better hygiene, and wider vaccine use to bring the disease under control in Iran and beyond.
pmc-12932506:
Lin Zhu and a large team of co-authors test a herbal formula paired with an antibiotic in gut infection. The text is dated 2025, though the catalog lists 2026. The infection, caused by Clostridioides difficile, often returns after treatment. The antibiotic vancomycin cures flare-ups but disrupts gut microbes, while the herbal brew aids their recovery.

In mice, the team compared full dosing with two cut-down plans for the antibiotic. All paired regimens cleared the acute illness. But the cut-down plans brought worse relapse, more inflammation, and lasting gut imbalance. Only the full-dose pairing restored gut diversity and long-term stability. The finding warns that trimming the antibiotic blunts the herbal synergy it was meant to protect.
pmc-12977306:
Nancy Foldvary-Schaefer and colleagues published a 2025 review of idiopathic hypersomnia. People with this disorder sleep very long hours. They still wake unrefreshed and foggy. Daytime sleepiness dominates their days. Night symptoms are just as real, though. The authors frame it as a round-the-clock disorder.

Diagnosis is difficult and often delayed. The condition overlaps heavily with a form of narcolepsy. No reliable lab marker exists yet. A severity scale captures its distinctive symptoms. Objective sleep testing still plays a role. The review urges clinicians to assess the full day. Better definitions should reduce misdiagnosis and poor treatment.
pmc-12980106:
Tais Santana Barbosa, Natasha Cordeiro dos Santos, Millena Pereira Costa, and Roque Aras Junior review what is known about going back to work after a heart attack. Most people who have a myocardial infarction are of working age, so the event often means long absence or lasting work disability. The reviewers searched four databases and kept twelve cohort studies covering more than eighty-three thousand people.

Return rates climbed steadily with time: roughly twenty-two to forty-two percent were back within a month, and seventy-seven to ninety-three percent within a year. Studies also recorded changed duties, pay cuts, dismissals, anxiety, and depression along the way, and all twelve studies rated as good quality. The authors link successful return to physical, psychological, and social factors together. They call for faster support mechanisms and for more research across different populations and job types.
pmc-13018406:
Akshaya Rajagopal and five co-authors test, in 2025 lab work, the safety of printed plastic for clear teeth aligners. Such aligners move teeth in small steps, and new printers can now make them layer by layer. The team compared three printed resins with a heat-shaped control set.

All of the sets let more than seven in ten test cells live, which the team counts as safe. One resin was a bit harsher on cells than the rest. Germs still clung to most sets, though one resin drew fewer germs than the others. The team says the printed sets look safe for use, but their faces need work that keeps germs off if they are to serve well in the mouth.
pmc-13023406:
Chun Ding and eleven co-authors test, in work published in 2025, a herb mix for the womb's welcome in rats bred to ape a hormone flaw with insulin strain. The mix is a known aid for child-less-ness in that flaw, yet its path was murky. Web drug maps and fit sums first named its likely marks.

Treated rats cycled true again, with lower male hormone, insulin, and strain scores, and sounder ovaries. In the womb, welcome marks rose and bud forms bloomed as in health. One mark was pinned by hush tests: hush it, and welcome fell; the mix then won it back. A leaf good in the mix fit the marks tight. The team reads a womb-first path.
pmc-13037606:
Reham Karam and co-authors reviewed in 2025 the push to wipe out a deadly sheep and goat virus by 2030, and the gaps that could slow or even backfire on that goal. The virus spreads fast across borders and hits poor farming regions hardest.

The review gathers studies and agency reports from the past decade. Field tests still cannot reliably tell infected animals from vaccinated ones, vaccine roll out is uneven, and quick field diagnosis is weak. A further worry comes from history: clearing one virus can open space for a cousin virus to spread. The authors urge risk models that forecast reintroduction and spillover, built into policy before eradication is declared.
pmc-13087006:
Gui-Min Yin and three co-authors review duckweeds as a tool for green biotechnology in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Duckweeds are the smallest and fastest-growing flowering plants. They float on water and need no soil. The review pulls together recent work on their biology. Duckweeds have a stripped-down genome and great flexibility in form, traits that favor gene insertion.

Scientists have decoded that genome and built tools to change it, including gene editing. Older uses include cleaning polluted water and feeding animals. The authors stress newer aims, such as growing vaccines and medicines in duckweed. Fast growth in closed, soil-free tanks is a plus over plants like tobacco. The paper makes the case for duckweed as a clean factory for future products.
pmc-13099706:
Veronika Frehtman and eleven co-authors put twenty laboratory antibodies against bovine meat and milk factors through a specificity gauntlet, in a two thousand twenty-six immunology paper. These plasmid-like DNA elements from cattle products are suspected cancer contributors, detectable only via their replication protein.

Using an ELISA binding assay against five distinct Rep proteins plus bacterial and mammalian controls, the panel proved sensitive and specific. Peptide-consensus antibodies recognized most Reps; antibodies raised against single isolates mostly saw only their own target. None cross-reacted with bacteria from milk production or host lysates. The authenticated panel equips studies judging whether these factors truly drive cancer and chronic disease.
pmc-13101706:
Witzleben and co-authors studied two tissue markers that together forecast outcomes in head and neck cancer, in a paper published in 2026. The cancer is a common type arising in the mouth, throat, and voice box. Tumors packed with immune cells called T cells tend to do better. A second marker, a brake signal on tumor cells, has given mixed signals in past studies. The team measured both in tumor samples from 458 patients.

All patients had surgery followed by added therapy. Neither marker alone told the whole story. Patients whose tumors held many T cells but little brake signal fared best, while the reverse pattern fared worst. The pair thus carries joint value beyond either one alone. A combined score could help doctors judge risk after surgery. It may also guide who needs closer follow-up or stronger added treatment.
pmc-13114506:
A small lump in the navel can be the first visible sign that abdominal cancer has spread widely. Mohammed Abdulrasak reports such a case in this 2026 paper. A forty-seven-year-old woman had metastatic pancreatic cancer, found five months earlier. She arrived with fever, jaundice, and pain from an infected, blocked bile duct.

Antibiotics and a stent relieved the blockage. On examination, moderate fluid filled her abdomen. Only when the navel was turned outward did a small nodule show inside its fold. The lump had grown slowly over weeks. Scans confirmed the known cancer and, on re-reading, the nodule itself. This Sister Mary Joseph nodule marks advanced disease, and it hides easily.
pmc-13124606:
Qian Zhao and four co-authors report a woman whose only first sign of hidden breast cancer was a spread to a lymph node between the chest muscles, in this 2026 case report. She also carried a separate primary lung cancer, making two cancers at once. Treatment mixed chemotherapy, breast surgery, and removal of part of the lung.

She declined the advised radiation and genetic testing afterward. A year later a single brain spread appeared; surgery removed it and pathology confirmed it came from the breast side. More than fifty-six months on, she remains free of recurrence. The authors stress telling twin primaries apart, and planning for later spreads when patients skip steps.
pmc-13124706:
Zhongshan Li, Ping Wang, and co-authors scan gene use in spit gland bits from folks with a dry gland ill, in work from 2026. Long non code strings of gene text may steer gene use in that ill. Wide proof of that steer role was thin, though counts of such strings shift in cases.

Deep reads cover scores of case folks and scores of well folks. A vast net links long strings to code genes by shared tie sites and matched swings. Eight strings stand out as core, and dish tests prove three of them steer genes in gland cells. Trait ties back the lab calls.
pmc-13126606:
Schistosomiasis control has long centered on school age children, leaving preschoolers without a drug form made for them. Kijakazi Obed Mashoto and seven co-authors report in 2025 how Tanzania prepared to deliver a new child sized form of praziquantel to young children. Health leaders, workers, and community voices met at many levels to find the gaps that could slow the launch.

The group agreed to reach children in their communities, at clinics during routine visits and growth checks, and during vitamin A campaigns. They also mapped delivery models that fit the Tanzanian health system. Before the first doses go out, clinics need stronger capacity and training. The authors frame the accord as a pledge that no preschool child is left behind.
pmc-13134406:
Alkan and Ikegami review the emerging threat of Oropouche virus in a 2026 paper. The virus spreads mainly through biting midges and was long seen as a neglected tropical disease near the Amazon. Illness was usually a short fever, with rare brain inflammation.

A large recent outbreak spread into the Caribbean and brought a wider range of disease. Reported outcomes now include severe brain and nerve syndromes, lasting infection, fatal bleeding fever, fetal loss, and newborn defects. Animal models exist, but species differ in how they respond, which clouds mechanism studies. One viral protein blocks host cell transcription and is the main known virulence factor. The authors map major gaps in knowledge.
pmc-13135506:
Harun A Rashid, Tilo Kircher, and Benjamin Straube report a 2026 brain-imaging study of movement preparation timing in schizophrenia spectrum disorders. Patients often struggle with intention, planning ahead, and the sense of agency. Response strength had been studied; response timing during preparation had not.

Twenty patients and twenty controls moved hands on their own or were moved, while watching their own or another's hand. Models split preparatory from doing responses and tracked delays and durations. Patients showed late motor-area responses during preparation with their own hand in view. Timing, not just strength, is disrupted before movement begins.
pmc-13135606:
Alcântara and a large team review in twenty twenty-six how to break down melanin, the stubborn dark pigment that helps fungi infect hosts and rot materials. The review sorts attack routes into physical, chemical, and living methods across the main microbial melanin types. Sound and microwave treatments mostly loosen material as a pre-step, while chemical breakdown gives the standard fingerprints used to identify melanin pieces.

Living routes look most sustainable: wood-rot enzymes chew the pigment's tangled structure by oxidation. Newer twists pin those enzymes onto magnetic nano-carriers for reuse, pair enzyme types so they recycle their own fuel, or borrow enzymes from cell waste sacs. Toxic helper chemicals remain a snag. The authors chart fixes aimed at safe fragments for cosmetics, food, and cleanup uses.
pmc-13136206:
Shinichi Noto and co-authors present a 2026 study on a quality-of-life toolkit for family caregivers of people with Alzheimer's disease in Japan. Health economists need measures that capture what caregiving does to the carer's own life. The ASCOT-Carer toolkit was built for that, and the team tested it against the standard EQ-5D measure.

A web survey drew 705 live-in family caregivers. Scores from the new toolkit were compared with EQ-5D scores and with a short burden interview. The toolkit tracked burden more closely than the standard measure did. Factor analysis probed what each tool really captures. The authors judge the carer toolkit a good fit for Japanese evaluations. It may widen the measures available for dementia care economics.
pmc-13136506:
Marzie Reisi, Ashraf Kazemi, and Nafisehsadat Nekuei dig into how man-and-wife pairs cope as one with a lack of young borne. Their 2026 work is based on talks. It hears from thirty-six folk in Iran, with ten pairs heard as pairs.

A lack of young borne brings strain for mind and for ties with folk into a pair's life. Talks were worked on with a known talk-text method. Folk were picked for spread in age and in cause, kind, and span of the lack. Three main groups came out of the work. They took in life side by side with the lack, a find of ease for the heart, and a firm build of the pair's bond. Sub-themes took in shared load, a new shape for wed life, faith closeness, and live heart play twixt the pair.
pmc-13138706:
Kevin Fiscella and co-authors report a 2026 quality improvement project on text messages and patient portals. Portals give patients access to their health records, but low-income patients sign up less often. The team used two-way automated texts to ask about digital needs and to offer help, such as free phones or cheap internet in New York.

Texts went to 12,381 Medicaid or low-income patients at one primary care practice. About 9 percent replied, and most who did rated the texts clear and useful. Some raised privacy or trust concerns. Among those not yet enrolled, 71 percent activated a portal after the project. The authors note that texts from an unknown number drew few replies, so how a program is introduced matters.
pmc-13138906:
Katsuya Yamaguchi and eleven co-authors survey, in a 2026 study, the link between erection problems and urinary symptoms in Japanese men. The two troubles often travel together in aging men, but their tie across severity levels deserved a fresh, large look. The team ran an online survey with three standard scoring tools.

Nearly 4,800 men answered. Men with milder erection trouble had clearly lower urinary scores overall. Voiding symptoms and leakage rose in step with erection severity, and the worst group scored badly on every urinary domain. Among younger men, having no erection trouble went with the lowest urinary scores across the board. Among men over seventy, though, the urinary scores barely differed by erection status. The authors read severity of one as a signpost for the other.
pmc-13139306:
Jessica Billig, Michael Dang, Jennifer Cardin, Joseph Joo, and Joshua Liao study social risk coding in hand trauma care in a 2026 paper. Social factors such as housing and income can hurt surgical outcomes, and new Z-codes let clinics record them in a standard way. Hand trauma patients face such risks often. National data from 2015 to 2025 cover common hand trauma operations.

Only a small share of patients, under two percent, have any social code recorded, they find. Use rises about ten fold over the decade, though. Patients with codes are younger, more often Black, urban, and on public insurance. Housing and economic codes are most common.
pmc-13142006:
Rixt van der Veen, Marian Joëls, and Aniko Korosi published a 2026 methods essay on early-life adversity research. Hardship early in life raises later mental illness risk. Human studies cannot fully reveal the brain mechanisms. Rodent studies fill that gap. Yet small design choices can flip their results.

Timing of the stress matters greatly. So does the care pups receive afterward. Housing, food, and breeding details also count. Later tests must match the behavior being studied. Sex differences deserve explicit attention. The authors urge tighter, clearer experimental design. Better design means findings translate more honestly to humans.
pmc-13143506:
Emmanuelle Guérin and nine co-authors published a critical care case report in twenty twenty-six on saving a woman whose only lung was failing after emergency surgery. Massive bleeding from a lung tumor biopsy forced removal of her left lung under ECMO support. The remaining lung then developed severe ARDS with total airway closure.

Pressure measured through an esophageal probe let the team tune the ventilator against the true pressure across the lung wall. That guidance kept the fragile single lung ventilated safely while ECMO carried gas exchange. She left ECMO on day sixteen and later left intensive care. Pathology showed a benign-margin atypical carcinoid tumor. The case argues the two salvage techniques reinforce each other.
pmc-13144206:
Sara Marquard, Isabel Jalaß, and Manfred Hülsken-Giesler review digital tools for family caregivers of people with advanced cancer in this 2026 paper. The review focuses on advanced breast cancer, though it covers advanced cancer more broadly. It maps what apps and online programs exist and what support they offer.

The team searched three large databases and found fourteen studies covering ten tools. The tools gave facts, mood support, practical help, and ways to keep in touch with care teams. Most tests reported better quality of life and less anxiety for caregivers. None of the tools was built just for relatives of breast cancer patients and fully tested. The authors use the gaps to shape a new platform for that group.
pmc-13144906:
Kang Yuan and co-authors report an interim look in 2026 at a large trial of two routes for placing a neck artery stent. The standard route enters through the leg artery, while a newer route enters through the wrist. Good direct proof comparing the two for neck stenting is still scarce, so the trial spans seventy centers in China and aims for three thousand patients.

At the first planned check, 1,207 patients had been assigned to one route or the other. The wrist route met the set bar for being no worse than the leg route on a combined safety outcome at thirty days. The trial met its early stopping rule for success at this check, the authors report.
pmc-13145006:
Severity staging for a hereditary small-vessel brain disease is mapped in Portugal by Carla Morgado and co-authors in a 2026 conference abstract. The disease, CADASIL, is the most common single-gene cause of this vessel damage and a driver of early stroke and thinking decline. One hundred thirty-eight patients and symptom-free gene carriers joined the cross-country study.

Two staging systems grade how far the disease has advanced. Brain scans and gene data were reviewed beside clinical records. Most participants were women, and about one in six carried the gene without symptoms. A national severity map helps clinics plan follow-up and gives trial designers a ready cohort yardstick.
pmc-13145406:
István Szegedi and co-authors report a small study of blood clotting in people with narrowed neck arteries. Their conference abstract from 2026 asks if the degree of narrowing is linked to blood that clots too fast. They used a lab test that tracks how thrombin, a key clotting factor, forms over time.

Ninety patients were studied in three groups of thirty. One group had mild narrowing, one had severe narrowing, and one had severe narrowing with a recent stroke. Neck scans set the degree of narrowing, and blood tests gave the clotting measures. The group with severe narrowing and stroke showed the strongest signs of fast clotting.
pmc-13145506:
Pamela Galindo and co-authors present a 2026 conference study on why women join stroke trials less often than men. Women face a higher lifetime stroke risk and often recover worse, yet trial rolls skew male. The team asked whether trial design and care timing shape the gap.

Records covered close to five hundred eligible patients at one large stroke center from 2019 to 2025. About seven in ten agreed to join, but women agreed far less often than men. The gap was widest in drug trials and in long-term phase trials. The authors argue that how trials are built and timed, not patient taste alone, drives much of the gap.
pmc-13145606:
National stroke registries hold rich data, but privacy law and mismatched formats keep them apart. Alexander Salerno and co-authors describe FERES, a European project that lets registries be analysed together without moving patient-level data. Each registry is mapped to shared stroke data elements, and the same analysis runs at each site on a secure platform, with only summary results combined.

To prove the method, the team split one large harmonised registry into separate nodes and ran a set comparison of front- versus back-circulation strokes both ways. The federated run matched the pooled run almost exactly, with the same counts, the same test decisions, and only negligible gaps in effect sizes. No individual data crossed any border. The authors present FERES as a validated base for large European stroke studies and quality benchmarking.
pmc-13145706:
Min Zhao and co-authors ask why small-vessel disease spoils stroke recovery in a 2026 conference paper. Patients had clots removed from brain arteries and flow restored, yet those with heavy small-vessel damage often fared poorly. Dye leakage and brain bleeding were the suspects in between.

Records covered 243 patients treated from 2020 to 2024 at one center. About two in five carried moderate-to-severe vessel disease on MRI. Their rate of poor outcome at ninety days was fifty-eight percent, against thirty-six percent in the milder group. Leakage and bleeding were both more common with heavier vessel damage. A mediation analysis then weighed how much of the harm runs through those two events.
pmc-13145806:
Aoming Jin and Yongjun Wang set out a plan to match stroke drugs to patients in a 2026 conference abstract. Four vein drugs can dissolve the clot in an acute ischemic stroke. Which drug is best for which patient is still unclear. The team wants a tool that picks the best drug for each person.

Their plan pools patient data from four large trials of the four drugs. A machine learning model learns how each drug's effect varies by patient traits. The model then ranks the best drug for a new patient. A test group checks how well those picks would work. The abstract lays out the frame for this work and its checks.
pmc-13145906:
Zaynah Islam, Tariq Suleiman, and Farhad Huwez studied strokes in the back of the brain that standard screening misses, in a 2026 conference abstract. A quick face-arm-speech check is the usual first screen for stroke. Strokes in the rear circulation often show other signs, such as balance loss. The team reviewed all such cases at one London hospital over three months.

Eighty-one patients were found. About forty percent screened negative on the quick check. Among those patients, referral to the stroke team took a median of eight hours. Nearly a quarter waited more than two days for referral. A few were referred at once despite the negative screen. The authors urge wider screening that adds visual and balance symptoms. Faster recognition should speed time-critical care, they argue.
pmc-13146006:
In stroke care, minutes of delay cost brain, and the clock that matters runs from the hospital door to the clot-busting needle. Levca Anastasia and co-authors report a simple change at a Moldovan stroke center in a 2026 conference abstract: starting the intravenous treatment right in the emergency department instead of after transfer.

The team compared four hundred treated patients from 2019 to 2025, before and after the 2025 change. Average door-to-needle time fell from seventy-six minutes to forty-four, inside the forty-five-minute target. Patients treated under the new routine also arrived with milder strokes and left with better recovery scores and functional outcomes. Bleeding complications were tracked as well. The authors present emergency-department initiation as a low-cost organizational fix for systems with limited resources.
pmc-13146206:
Zainab Nasser, Mark Bakker, and Giulia Pederzani present this 2026 conference abstract on modeling brain aneurysm growth with genetic data. Aneurysms are bulges in brain artery walls that can burst. Personal genetic data could sharpen forecasts of growth and treatment response. Their model joins artery wall mechanics with a signal network that guides wall cell behavior.

They add settings for one gene variant that controls a growth signal in blood. More sensitive gene types gave slower growth and better response to a drug pulse in the model, though the effect was small for one gene. Work is under way to add a second gene and a broader score. The authors frame the step as a first toward gene-aware forecasts.
pmc-13146306:
Malin Woock and nine co-authors study clot-removal treatment for stroke patients who also have active cancer. Cancer raises stroke risk, and small studies suggest these patients fare worse after thrombectomy even when the artery reopens as often as in others. Their 2026 conference report uses the EVA-TRISP registry, covering stroke patients treated at eleven centers in eight countries. The cohort compares outcomes for patients with and without active cancer.

Large registry numbers can confirm or soften the worry raised by small series. If the gap is real, doctors need to know whether it comes from the cancer, its treatment, or later care. The authors supply the multicenter evidence that single hospitals cannot. Their findings feed consent talks and triage for a hard group.
pmc-13146406:
Chia Xuan Teoh and seven co-authors checked in 2026 how well one stroke center followed gene-guided blood thinner choices with slow lab testing. Certain CYP2C19 variants make one drug pair work better than another after minor stroke. Their review covered 167 patients from 2023 and 2024. Tests took a median of two days to return. Final treatment matched the gene result in about two thirds of cases.

Half the patients carried the loss-of-function variant. Repeat stroke within ninety days hit 9.3 percent of carriers versus 2.5 percent of others. Patients whose therapy matched their genotype had far fewer repeat strokes, though the gain on a combined outcome was not firm. The authors conclude that even slow lab genotyping can guide safer choices. Faster testing would likely raise adherence further. The study reports real-world friction in precision prescribing.
pmc-13146506:
István Szegedi, David Školoudík, and David Pakizer present a conference abstract on carotid web in older patients with carotid atherosclerosis. Their work is a later analysis of the ANTIQUE study, asking how common this shelf-like projection inside the carotid artery is after age fifty. It also asks what risk of stroke follows over ten years.

Three experienced sonographers rechecked ultrasound images and sorted the odd lesions into definite web, suspected web, plaque, or artifact. Among more than sixteen hundred patients, definite or suspected webs appeared in about four percent. Those patients had more strokes on the same side as the web than patients with ordinary plaque. Careful ultrasound reading, the authors argue, could sharpen stroke risk estimates.
pmc-13146706:
Iselin Syberg Dahl and co-authors report a national study of cerebral venous thrombosis in Norway in a 2026 conference abstract. This rare stroke type, a clot in the brain's veins, is mostly known from referral centers, which skews the picture. The team gathered cases from twelve hospitals covering about three quarters of Norwegian adults.

Records held five hundred eleven patients diagnosed between 2014 and 2023, with a median age of forty six and a female majority. Active cancer appeared in fifteen percent, a higher share than referral cohorts report. At six months, about a third had poor function. Cancer and seizures at arrival predicted poor outcomes. The authors call for more study of unselected patient groups.
pmc-13146806:
Valentina Tudisco and co-authors report a 2026 conference study on a scan sign that flags fading recovery right after clot removal. Some patients worsen early even when vessel pictures look like a success. A fast scan done in the procedure room can spot small clots that moved downstream.

Among close to four hundred patients at two centers, about a third showed the sign. Those patients worsened early at twice the rate of others and had lower rates of good vessel reopening. The sign foretold early decline on its own, next to stroke cause and severity. Using it regraded about half of the best-looking cases downward, and the authors suggest it can guide added drug care.
pmc-13146906:
Jinjie Liu and co-authors report a 2026 conference study that uses scan patterns to split small vessel brain disease into types. The disease harms tiny brain vessels and feeds memory decline, yet it is often lumped as one thing. The team used machine reading of brain scans to find groups.

More than a thousand adults with mild memory loss were scanned and grouped. Three types emerged: one marked by small deep strokes, one by white matter scars, and one by shrinkage of a memory area. Each type tied to its own blood fat and pressure pattern, and to its own mix of thinking faults. The groups held up in a second large data set, and the authors back type-based care.
pmc-13147006:
Sarah-Jane Byrne and co-authors survey stroke survivors about follow-up prevention care in this 2026 conference abstract. After a first stroke, patients get advice and treatment meant to cut the risk of another, a task where nurses play a growing part. The team asked patients in an early supported discharge program how that advice reached them and what they still needed.

Twenty-five patients answered the paper survey, half of those asked. Over a quarter first heard about prevention only after reaching home. Most liked the idea of an education booklet, and a fifth wanted a nurse phone line for later questions. Nearly all said they would rather get this guidance at home from a nurse specialist. The team will use the answers to build a teaching resource for those nurses.
pmc-13147106:
Luciano Sposato and co-authors present a 2026 conference abstract on a new imaging sign of stroke risk. The sign concerns the left atrial appendage, a small heart pouch where clots often form. When contrast dye fills that pouch poorly on a scan, the team argues, the pouch is likely contracting weakly and letting blood stagnate.

Data came from about five hundred fifty people in two linked studies, covering patients with and without stroke and with and without atrial fibrillation. Three preset claims were tested. The sign may track strokes that break through treatment. It may explain risk gaps between fibrillation types. It may also explain why past anticoagulant trials in unclear-source stroke failed. Scans were judged by set rules, and charts of cause helped strip out confounding factors.
pmc-13147206:
Maryline Vere and co-authors survey school children on a water-borne parasite disease in South Africa in a 2026 paper. The disease is schistosomiasis, spread through contact with infested water. Children aged 5 to 14 face high risk from play and chores in rivers. The survey took place in Nelson Mandela Bay.

They asked 759 children in early school grades about the disease. Only 11 percent had heard of it, mostly from school. Many reported risky habits such as urinating in rivers or swimming. Boys and older children scored higher on knowledge and habits. Girls scored lower on knowledge in the team's checks. The authors call for focused teaching and community action to cut risk.
pmc-13148706:
Alice Plebe studies whether large language models show a steady tendency to trust others, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Such models now work beside people in many joint tasks, where trust shapes how work is shared. Plebe tested nineteen models in two ways: a self-report scale borrowed from human research, and a set of written scenes that call for trust choices.

On the scale, all models claimed high trust, likely a habit from training to please. The scenes told a different story, showing wide gaps between models. Stronger models adjusted trust to cues about the other party, while weaker ones handed over work no matter what. Memory of past cues helped models judge better. The study shows quizzes alone cannot measure trust in these systems.
pmc-13149706:
Jupiter's four large moons, the Galilean satellites, preserve clues about how giant planet systems form. Francis Nimmo and co-authors review the evidence and the rival theories of their origin. Key facts include Callisto's possibly undifferentiated interior, the rise in ice fraction with distance from Jupiter, and the moons' present-day orbital resonance.

The favored picture is a starved disk that fed the moons slowly in cold conditions, though newer ideas invoke decretion disks and pebble accretion. Open questions concern where the solids came from and how the disk's heat and flow were set. Three incoming missions, JUICE, Europa Clipper, and Tianwen-4, should answer some of them. Later events that overprinted early features remain a core difficulty.
pmc-13150906:
The AOBERT Consortium laid out a study plan in 2026 for better use of patient questionnaires after bone breaks. Scores that patients report themselves track pain, function, and mood in recovery. Two families of such scores are in wide use, yet how they stack up in break care is not well known. The study will follow patients at fourteen centers who break an arm or leg bone.

The plan seeks fifteen hundred patients, three hundred for each of five break types, from hip to wrist. Care goes on as usual at each site. Scores are taken at the first visit and at five later points up to one year. Injury, personal, and scan data are logged at the start. The aim is clear advice for doctors on which scores to use.
pmc-13152906:
Maxime Bedez and four co-authors report a 2026 rat study on jaw bone strength after hormone loss. Bone thinning after menopause raises fracture risk, and bone density alone does not tell the whole story. Fat inside the bone marrow, and the mix of fatty acids in it, may matter too.

Rats whose ovaries were removed mimic the hormone drop of menopause. In some, the fine structure of the jaw bone stayed sound despite the loss. Those rats shared a distinct fatty acid mix in their marrow fat. The authors suggest the fat makeup of marrow ties to how well bone holds up.
pmc-13153206: Aleksandra Petrović-Fabijan and Stephen Abedon argue, in a 2026 commentary, that phage therapy must grow from striking anecdotes into a reproducible clinical tool. Viruses that kill bacteria have cured infections no drug could touch, yet results swing widely and the biology is tangled, which keeps clinics wary. The pair name three pillars for joint work across fields: getting phages to the infection, proving steady effectiveness, and staying ahead of bacterial resistance.
pmc-13153406:
Reinforcement learning is being groomed to advise sepsis care, but Shengpu Tang and three co-authors show in 2026 that a quiet bookkeeping flaw corrupts nearly half its advice. When records are aligned to the wrong clock times, the learner's picture of cause and effect slips, and its scores flatter it while its recommendations go wrong.

The flaw, they find, runs through more than eighty percent of the published literature on such systems. A simple fix restores the timing. The authors argue for problem setups that center the decision itself, its moment and its information, rather than the convenience of the data table. Sepsis, with its hour by hour stakes, is their warning case. The lesson covers clinical learning systems broadly.
pmc-13155406:
Ying Zhou and co-authors probe the role of autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system, in psoriasis. The skin disease speeds up the growth of keratinocytes and keeps skin inflamed for years. The team combined single-cell RNA data from skin samples with bulk gene data to find where self-cleaning goes wrong.

Cells with strong self-cleaning activity sat mostly among the keratinocytes. As those cells matured, two defense pathways faded, and immune signals shifted in ways tied to a hyperactive mTORC1 and weak autophagy. Protein network analysis then flagged seven candidate hub genes. Three of them held up in tests with patient samples and a mouse model of the disease. The genes offer fresh leads for drug work.
pmc-13156006:
I-Ching Chuang, Hui-Ju Wu, and their co-authors compared two ways of training older adults to do two things at once. Their 2026 study notes that aging weakens both thinking and movement, raising the risk of falls and lost independence. Training that pairs a mental task with a physical one can help, but the two styles of pairing had rarely been compared head to head.

Seventy four adults aged 60 and older, living in the community, were split at random into two groups for a twelve week group program. One style folds the mental demand inside the movement task, while the other runs a separate mental task alongside it. The team measured thinking, hand and walking skills, daily life tasks, and quality of life.
pmc-13156106:
Lifang He and co-authors map the immune scene in 2026 inside a common breast cancer type that has spread. Deaths from this cancer come mostly from spread, and immune cells in the tumor's neighborhood sway how far it goes. Using single-cell gene reads with a focus on spread to the ovary, they charted the cell mix.

Nine cell families in eighteen clusters turned up, from killer T cells to support and vessel cells, they report. The macrophage family split into tumor-linked and blood-born branches. Five genes stood out as tied to how those cells behave. In tissue from ten patients with ovarian spread, three of the five genes stained high, backing the gene-read map with direct proof.
pmc-13156606:
Yuval Milrad, Daniel Wegemann, and Michael Hippler lay out a lab method in this 2026 paper for timing a key plant protein complex. The complex helps move electrons during photosynthesis, the process plants use to make food from light. Studying it inside whole leaves mixes its signal with many other signals at once.

Their method pulls the complex out and pairs it with a partner complex in a clean lab setup. A pulsed light tool tracks color shifts at six tones at once, which reveals how fast electrons move. The steps split into flash tests and steady light tests, plus dark rest checks. Because outside factors can be added one at a time, the method can untangle paths that leaves keep mixed.
pmc-13157306:
Wu and Yang studied in twenty twenty-six how web use aims and low mood signs move each other over time in old adults in China. Past work treats low mood as one block, which hides fine links. They used two waves of a large old-age survey, from twenty eighteen and twenty twenty.

More than nine thousand old adults were in the check. News use on the web went with less of a few low mood signs later. Chat use went with more joy, and game use with less strain. Watch of clips and cash tasks on the web went the other way for some signs. The team backs aim-based web plans for old folks.
pmc-13158506:
Gomez Acosta and Chacon Pacheco map in 2026 the gaps in using entropy measures to quantify biomedical signals in clinical work. Such measures are now standard tools for judging how complex body signals are. Their scoping review asks where the methods help and where they fall short, with functional dyspepsia as a test case.

Eighty five documents were screened through a four phase review process. These quantifiers serve work on brain degeneration and heart conditions, and gastric disorders to a lesser degree. Diagnostic value in dyspepsia stays limited so far. Signal complexity and variety block integration, the authors argue, and digestive disorders remain a knowledge gap to close.
pmc-13158606:
Izzah Khairi and six co-authors build a framework for judging programs that aim to ease doctor burnout. Many such programs exist, but no shared guide tells how to weigh them. The team ran a rapid review of three medical databases and kept 105 studies that had tested a wellness program in a health care setting. For each, they noted the program type, how it was judged, and what measures were used.

From those patterns, and the gaps they found, the authors draft a data-driven framework for evaluation. The paper aims to help hospitals choose and improve wellness work on proof rather than habit.
pmc-13159506:
Jonathan Sivakumar and seven co-authors review life after surgery for esophageal cancer in a 2026 paper. Survival is improving, yet what daily life feels like after the gullet is removed is poorly charted. The review blends survey scores with survivors' own words.

The team searched four databases and kept 57 studies: 40 with quality-of-life scores and 17 with in-depth accounts. Scores were pooled to trace life quality from before surgery to five years after. The spoken accounts were woven into themes. Together the two strands give a person-centered view of eating, energy, and mood after this hard operation.
pmc-13162006:
Santosh D Ghoti and co-authors describe a hip surgery method in a 2026 case series. The patients were young adults whose hip bone head had died from poor blood flow, a problem that often needs a full hip replacement early in life. The front approach used here spares muscle and can speed healing, but it is hard to perform well.
