Five hips in young patients, with a mean age in the mid thirties, were treated with help from a leg holding and pulling system and live X-ray views. The report sets out the steps in detail and gives early results. Surgeons get a clear guide to the aids that make the front approach safer.
pmc-13163006:
Haotian Wu and co-authors study the microbes living in the gill mucus of a hardy tilapia strain in this 2026 paper. The strain was bred over generations for fast growth and resistance to a deadly bacterial disease. Gill mucus is a front line where fish meet germs, so its microbes may matter.

The team combined microbe counts, gene activity reads, chemical profiles, and a genome scan in the bred strain during a germ challenge. Six microbe genera dominated the gill mucus across the time points. Two of them tracked closely with host genes for mucus making, immune tuning, and stress defense. Mucus held rich chemical signals tied to microbe activity. A genome scan pinned down genes behind the microbe-gene links. The authors say the work clarifies how mucus helps the strain resist disease.
pmc-13166806:
Yasser Hadi and co-authors measure in a 2026 study how off center patient placement skews radiation dose in heart CT scans. Centering at the scanner's true middle is key to keeping dose lean. Scout images hold the data needed to audit that placement after the fact.

Charts for 399 adults scanned from 2023 to mid 2025 at one hospital were reviewed. Off centering past 10 mm hit 83% of scans front to back and 50% side to side. Severe front to back error past 30 mm showed in 39% of cases. Dose indices were pulled from machine reports and tied to the placement errors. Simulations then sized the dose saving that perfect centering would buy.
pmc-13167006:
Johnson and seven co-authors study how diabetes affects radiation treatment for head and neck cancer in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Diabetes is common in this patient group and may change how treatment goes. The team reviewed three hundred forty-six patients treated over a decade at their center. Eighty-four had diabetes and the rest did not. All received radiation, some with chemotherapy as well.

They compared the groups on treatment completion, breaks, side effects, and survival. A higher share of diabetic patients failed to finish their scheduled radiation. Long treatment breaks also differed between the groups. The results suggest diabetes care is part of cancer care, not a side issue. Radiation teams can use such data to plan closer support for diabetic patients.
pmc-13171306:
Balci and co-authors link heart rate to shot-by-shot tennis success in this 2026 study. Heart rate tracks physical load and arousal, but its tie to single-shot outcomes was unmapped. The team used a standardized target-based drill with camera tracking.

The dataset holds 8,197 shots from 23 players across 93 training sessions. Each shot was matched to heart rate in a ten-second window around it. Successful strokes came with lower heart rates, though the effect was small. Players hit more winners in the lower intensity zones. Mixed models that respect repeated shots agreed: each extra 10 beats per minute cut success odds to 0.957. Short-term rate swings added little extra signal.
pmc-13173106:
Polina Kukhareva and Julio Facelli use AI to map how type 2 diabetes is treated in real care. Their 2026 study draws on records for more than three million adults from 2019 to 2024. Drug, lab, and personal data were cleaned and stored in one system. People with type 1 diabetes or who were pregnant were left out.

Drug paths over time were grouped, and forty clear paths emerged. Some used one drug, some two, and some were more complex. Newer GLP-1 type drugs came second or third in line and gave the largest drops in weight and blood sugar. A basic model guessed blood sugar six months ahead quite well. The last lab value was the best clue. Work on deeper models is still under way.
pmc-13176306:
Kerala's Ernakulam district floods often, and planners need a fair way to rank which zones to protect first. Their method mixes three ranking techniques and a fuzzy number system that captures doubt from both directions.

Machine learning checks back the result: clustering and component analysis confirm the same vulnerability patterns. Kochi, Vypen, and Paravoor come out most at risk, while Kothamangalam is least exposed. The authors link the work to global climate action goals. Their 2026 study offers local authorities a tested ranking to aim flood defenses where they matter most.
pmc-13176806:
Simone Poulin, David McFarland, Stefano Rezzonico, and Natacha Trudeau follow infants over time to link early feeding trouble with later language in work dated two thousand twenty-six. Feeding is a social act as well as a motor one, and early breaks in it may echo in speech growth. The study tracks full-term, typically growing babies.

Parents rated feeding and language at eight, twelve, eighteen, and twenty-four months, with a clinic language test at fifty-four months. Poor saliva control at eighteen months tracked with smaller spoken word counts and weaker language later. Food pickiness also marked children with less advanced language at two years. The authors weigh fewer chances to practice talk and shared mouth-motor roots.
pmc-13178206:
Gao leads a team reviewing how distress over time relates to survival in cancer survivors in a 2026 scoping paper. One-off distress checks had been tied to outcomes before. How changing distress matters was less clear.

Dozens of studies with repeated distress measures were mapped across cancer types and countries. Most survivors kept low distress, while a minority stayed highly distressed. Lasting or worsening distress tracked with worse survival in study after study. Survivors whose distress eased fared about as well as those never distressed. Effect sizes varied, and not every study agreed. The authors suggest tracking distress through survivorship care. Whether easing distress itself extends life is unproven.
pmc-13179206:
Nine authors, led by Bingguo Kou, test in 2026 whether bite planes help clear aligners fix a deep overbite. Such bites are hard for aligners: front teeth sink less than planned and back teeth sink on their own. Thirty six adults were split into a bite plane group and a plain aligner group.

Digital models from before and after the sinking phase were overlaid to measure true tooth movement. Accuracy of front tooth sinking and back tooth shifts were compared between groups. Links between back tooth sinking and treatment length were checked too. Headline results follow in the full report.
pmc-13179906:
Nader Habib Bedwani and co-authors map in 2026 studies that sniff out gases given off by immune cells in lab dishes. Such gases come from cell work and can serve as pain free disease marks. How much immune cells add to that gas mix stays poorly known.

The review hunts for work on gases over primary and lab grown immune cells. It logs cell types, wake up cues, gas catch tools, and how sure each gas name call was. Eleven studies met the rules, with wide split methods. Catch tools range from fiber based to spray based high end kit. The map shows where norms are still thin.
pmc-13180106:
Siddarth Sriram and Leonard Arnolda report the case of a fifty-seven-year-old man whose heart muscle weakened badly during a period of rapid weight loss. Their 2026 case report describes his arrival with heart failure and shock after chest pain and breathlessness. He had lost twenty-six kilograms in two months while taking a low dose of semaglutide, alongside decades of nicotine replacement use.

Scans showed a stretched heart pumping at only fifteen percent strength, while artery checks and other tests found no clear cause. The authors link the harm to severe energy and nutrient stress rather than direct drug damage. They call for more study of heart risk during fast, drug-aided weight loss.
pmc-13180806:
Ten researchers chart the small-molecule chemistry of a common lichen across Europe. The team sampled the model lichen Ramalina farinacea in six European regions in winter and summer and profiled its contents with mass spectrometry.

They catalogued 187 small molecules, with a core of twelve found everywhere. Sugar alcohols dominated: arabitol alone made up about half of the measured content, joined by ribitol, sorbitol, and mannitol, all known protectors against drying. Season, region, and climate resemblance drove most of the variation, and cold sites carried more glycerol and more fluid fats, which keep membranes from stiffening in the cold. The authors call the work the first continent-scale map of lichen chemistry and name several markers tied to climate.
pmc-13181206:

If AI takes over the data chores, newcomers might spend their days only in the field and never build the analyst skills their careers will need.

The authors sketch two futures. In one, AI streamlines data work and juniors do fieldwork alone. In the other, the analyst-technician path, juniors also help run the AI-assisted pipelines. They argue firmly for the second path. Employers, they say, should set aside work time for mentees inside the data process, using the new tools. That protects skills, widens who can enter the field, and keeps careers from stalling.
pmc-13181306:
Renkun Zhao and co-authors link dietary magnesium intake to survival in people with chronic neck pain in a 2026 paper. The team drew 2,955 such patients, all at least twenty years old, from the United States NHANES survey covering 1999 to 2020. They combined survival models, subgroup checks, and a genetic mediation method to test the link.

During follow-up, 719 deaths occurred, including 180 from cardiovascular disease and 179 from cancer. Higher magnesium intake went with clearly lower cardiovascular death risk, and a threshold pattern appeared for cancer deaths. Mediation checks pointed to lower C-reactive protein, a marker of inflammation, as part of the path. The findings support attention to magnesium in diet advice for chronic neck pain patients.
pmc-13183006:
Buket Altun Özdemir and co-authors present a 2026 study asking how often two inflammatory conditions travel together: granulomatous mastitis of the breast and Hashimoto thyroiditis. The breast condition is benign but chronic, and it often appears alongside autoimmune disorders. Whether the thyroid disease is one of them, and whether blood markers shift when both occur, was unclear.

From 2019 to 2022 the team followed 179 women: fifty-two with the breast disease alone, nineteen with both diseases, and eighty-nine healthy matched controls. They compared standard blood counts and inflammation ratios across the groups. The design lets the overlap rate and any marker pattern be read cleanly.
pmc-13183106:
Weina Wang and five co-authors probed how a classic herbal mix might treat sepsis. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, looks at Qingwen Baidu Decoction. They joined two tools: network pharmacology and Mendelian randomization. First they searched herb and drug databases for the mix's active parts and their targets. They set those beside sepsis targets from disease databases.

Network maps and pathway work sketched how the mix might act. The gene based method then tested if key targets truly drive sepsis risk. Readers who study herbal care get a layered check of one mix. The work seeks firm causal ground, not just pattern links, for a sepsis remedy.
pmc-13183606:
Jiheng Zhang and co-authors review in 2026 brain lymph clearance repair as a target in Alzheimer's care. Toxic protein buildup marks the disease, and weak drainage may feed it. The review weighs modest clearance gains as a drug direction.

Routes span drugs on water channels or growth signals, light and sound methods, and surgery or lifestyle paths. An early neck vessel surgery gives proof of concept but needs care in testing. Imaging markers and timing windows lag behind the ideas. Lymph work may join multi-part care plans rather than stand alone.
pmc-13184106:
Tingting Lou and nine co-authors build and validate a lab method for measuring iomeprol, an X-ray contrast agent, along with its impurities. Older options either separated impurities poorly or cost too much to run. Their reversed-phase liquid chromatography setup uses a standard column and a tuned gradient mix. The work targets quality control for both the raw drug and finished injections.

Checks under international guidelines showed clean separation of every impurity with no interference from other ingredients. Readings stayed linear across the tested range, recoveries ran ninety-six to one hundred one percent, and repeated runs varied by under two percent. Stress tests showed the drug breaks down mainly under alkaline conditions and light. The authors conclude the method is sensitive, accurate, and sturdy enough for routine quality control, with a warning to guard the product's acidity and light exposure.
pmc-13184306:
Sara Zamzam, Ethaar Gadallah, Ahmed Henaish, and Ahmed Nosair map where ground water may lie in a dry tract of Egypt's Eastern Desert with a hard form. Their tract sits in a rift zone in the space from the Gulf of Suez to the north Red Sea. The team put in one set sixteen traits of land form, of sky and rain, of water flow, and of rocks, in a map tool.

Depth models of the rock base from pull data and fault form got prime weight through a step rank way. Form, not face shape, proved the main rule. Zones with high chance clump in low tracts with thick laid down stuff and good soak in. A chief shear zone sends set flow of new water in the space from the two rift sets. Checks showed scores staff can trust for plans for water use that can last.
pmc-13184606:
A common side effect of some mental health drugs is a rise in prolactin, a hormone tied to milk production. Marie Humbert-Claude and co-authors report a 2026 case where a second drug fixed that rise. The patient was taking paliperidone, and the hormone rise brought risks that range from missed periods to bone loss over time. The usual fix, adding a drug called aripiprazole, was not an option here.

That patient had earlier had a skin reaction to the usual fix, so the team needed a fresh plan. They added brexpiprazole, a close chemical cousin of the usual drug, which also partly activates the same brain receptor. The case shows the hormone level came under control without loss of the main drug's benefit. The authors present the swap as a new option for similar patients.
pmc-13185006:
Cuong Kim Nguyen and co-authors report a study the catalog lists under 2026. They study tuberculosis that grows inside the airways of the lung. This form can block the airway if it is found late. The study ran at a national lung hospital in Vietnam from May 2023 to May 2024. It held 91 patients aged 16 or older with lab-proven disease.

The team recorded symptoms, scan images, and what doctors saw through a scope in the airway. Lung function tests were also done. Germ tests on tissue or fluid from the airway proved each case. The goal is a clear picture of how this form looks in clinic, on scans, and under the scope. Doctors who see lung TB can use the picture to spot airway disease sooner. Early spotting gives treatment a better chance to keep the airway open.
pmc-13185206:
Moustapha Ramadan and co-authors audit infection prevention programs in Egyptian university hospitals in a 2026 study. Hospital-acquired infections are a global burden, and world guidelines give facilities a standard frame to build and grade their defenses.

Twenty-six facilities with programs running at least five years, covering over eleven thousand beds, were scored with the World Health Organization assessment tool. No facility rated inadequate, and about half reached the advanced level. Written guidelines scored highest of all core parts, while combined multimodal strategies scored lowest, just behind training and education. The authors conclude the programs stand on solid ground but need stronger teaching and bundled change tactics.
pmc-13185906:
Muffrih Mohamed Haresi reports a rare case of a giant neurofibroma on the vulva of a nineteen-year-old woman. Neurofibromas are benign tumors that grow from the sheath around nerves. They seldom appear on the vulva, and giant ones in young patients are rarer still.

The mass had grown slowly over time. MRI scans showed a large, well-edged, lobed lump whose signals fit a benign nerve sheath tumor, with no spread into nearby tissue. Surgeons removed it fully. Lab study of the tissue, backed by S100 staining, confirmed the diagnosis. The case shows how MRI helps tell such lumps apart and plan safe removal.
pmc-13186006:
Julia Götstedt and four co-authors describe a 2026 study on measuring bone strength from scans already taken to plan cancer care. People treated for cancer face a higher risk of weak bones, yet bone checks are not always done. The team wanted a way to read bone density from planning scans.

They built a simple rule that turns scan values into bone density scores. First they tested the rule on bone samples with known makeup and on test blocks. Then they used it on scans from 178 patients made on two kinds of scanner. They also checked how much scores changed when three readers marked the same spine bones.
pmc-13186906:
Dimitrios Kotzias is first author on a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of hip bone shape and fracture patterns. Hip fractures are a major cause of illness and death in older people. Beyond bone density, the geometry of the upper thigh bone and hip joint may steer where and how the bone breaks.

Pooling twenty-two studies with over four thousand patients, mostly women in their late seventies, the authors compared shape measures across fracture types. Fractures through the neck region differed from those lower down in head size, neck thickness, neck length, and angles. Angle measures separated the patterns most robustly. Simple measures from standard X-rays, they suggest, may aid risk assessment and surgical planning.
pmc-13188106:
Abdelwahed Diani and three co-authors report a pancreas case that looked like cancer but was not, in a 2026 paper. An immune form of chronic pancreas inflammation can mimic a tumor on scans and in symptoms. Their patient was a woman aged fifty three with upper belly pain and blocked bile flow.

Scans showed a mass in the head of the pancreas. Blood tests found a raised level of an antibody class tied to this immune disease. The mass shrank in response to steroid treatment, confirming the immune diagnosis rather than cancer. The authors list the clues that separate the two: certain duct patterns, kidney findings, blood markers, and tissue results. Early recognition spares patients needless major surgery, they stress. Care needs a team across specialties.
pmc-13189206:
Stela Vujosevic and co-authors test, in a 2026 eye study, whether a color-resolved glow scan of the retina can read the metabolic health of tissue hit by age-related macular degeneration. This disease is a leading cause of sight loss in older adults, and standard scans show structure better than living chemistry.

The team studied sixty-two eyes with middle or late-stage disease, classifying hundreds of scan slices into spot types: deposits, partial wasting, full wasting, and early wasting. The glow scan split its signal into red and green parts, scored by custom software. The glow measures differed clearly between lesion types, suggesting the scan could flag tissue that is stressed before it fully wastes away.
pmc-13190606:
Cecilia Ghiazza and co-authors present a 2026 study on methane-cycling microbes in two South American reservoirs. Hydro dams are seen as clean, yet their waters emit methane, a potent greenhouse gas. Microbes in the mud both make and consume that methane. The team sampled mud at three sites in each of two nearby nutrient-rich reservoirs across seasons.

Gene scans sorted the maker and eater groups, and lab jars measured their peak rates. Eater activity always beat maker activity in the tests. The two groups rose and fell together, which suggests tight coupling all year. Each reservoir held a distinct community mix, even though the same few types led in both. Makers were the more dynamic and diverse side.
pmc-13191106:
Qiang Yang and co-authors build a vaccine that wakes immune sentries dulled by surgery. Their 2026 paper targets a known slump: after tumor surgery, a signal protein cripples dendritic cells, raising relapse risk. The fault lies in broken lysosomes inside those cells. Their vaccine, BAIT, packs cell luring, antigen delivery, and activation into one self-assembling platform.

An arginine-rich backbone rebuilds the lysosomes and restores antigen digestion. Tumor lysate and a lure molecule ride along in the same assembly. Lysates from cells killed by apoptosis worked best, cutting tumor burden by over eighty-five percent in mice after surgery. The authors pitch BAIT as a personal post-surgery vaccine strategy.
pmc-13191506:
Aram Petrosyan and his team make and set out traits of two new bismuth halide salts of the amino acid sarcosine. Their 2026 study of crystal build tells of the builds of the goods, their wave reads, and their light traits.

One salt joins sarcosine parts with a frame of bismuth and iodine. The next pairs them with a frame of bismuth and bromine. The first took shape in a build where both sides match. The next took shape in a build with a set pole. Pairs of sarcosine parts with charge linked as one showed in both goods for the first time. Red-ray and Raman wave reads were read next to the builds. Light tests set the band gap of each stuff. Heat-based charge tests made the pole build of the next salt firm.
pmc-13191806:
Isabelle Kolly and co-authors headline a journal cover with an on-surface reaction that broke the expected rules in a 2026 feature. A four-armed nitrogen-rich molecule laid on gold was expected to fuse through carbon links. Instead it closed pyrrole rings first, then coupled onward.

The product is a fused framework holding both pyridine-like and graphite-like nitrogen atoms. Lab evidence and theory together favor the nitrogen path over the carbon one during the heat-driven stitching. The cover points readers to the full study inside the issue. Surface chemistry, it reminds us, still surprises.
pmc-13192406:
Russi, DiLorenzo and Relling test a rumen-protected carbohydrate feed for young beef heifers in a feedlot trial listed for 2026. The question is whether shielding the feed from rumen breakdown changes growth and blood measures.

Heifers were grouped by weight into pens and fed one of three levels of the protected feed for about two months. Weight, intake and back fat were tracked, and blood was tested at set times. The middle level ate least and used feed most efficiently, with no loss in daily gain. Blood and plasma values did not differ by the end, the authors report.
pmc-13193606:
Indira T Kudva and co-authors study how a gut germ sticks in cattle in a 2026 paper. A toxin making strain of E coli lives quietly at the end of the cow gut, in a zone called the rectoanal junction. From there it can reach food and harm people, so blocking its first grip could cut that risk.

A surface protein that appears when the germ starves, called Slp, was already shown to drive grip on human gut cells. The team now tested its role on cattle gut cells and tissue from that zone. Grip differed based on the protein's presence. The findings point to a target for keeping the germ out of herds.
pmc-13194106:
Camacho-Méndez and nine co-authors review antibiotic use in Chilean salmon farming and its risks of resistance, in a review from twenty twenty-six. Chile is the world's second-largest producer of farmed salmon. Heavy drug use fights a rickettsial disease that is always present and that vaccines hold back poorly. Most treatment is given to stop disease before it starts, through feed laced with drugs.

That path exposes healthy fish and the waters round them for no need. Resistance genes in farm microbes reach germs that can sicken people, carried on mobile bits of DNA. Export pressure and long growing cycles keep the reliance in place. Better vaccines, a close watch on genes, and care driven by data are urged. A One Health lens, which treats human, animal, and wild health as one, frames the whole problem.
pmc-13194306:
Daniel Paramythiotis leads a 2026 state-of-the-art review of gastrointestinal schwannomas, rare benign tumors growing from Schwann cells, the insulation cells of gut nerves. They form a distinct group among lumps under the gut lining, most often in the stomach, but they can appear anywhere from esophagus to rectum.

Their vague symptoms and scan and scope similarity to stromal tumors make mistaken diagnosis before surgery common. Tissue staining patterns now define them, separating them from look-alike tumors, but final proof still needs tissue examination. Removal by surgery is the mainstay for larger or complex lesions, while scope-based removal suits smaller, favorably placed ones. Accurate early diagnosis, the authors stress, avoids unneeded interventions.
pmc-13194606:
Debao Li and co-authors review fifteen years of cases of a rare birth defect in children, in a 2026 medical paper. The defect is a narrow tunnel under the skin near the buttocks, present from birth. It often causes repeat infections and is easy to mistake for other problems. The cases come from one children's hospital in China.

Twenty children were treated, and girls outnumbered boys by more than two to one. First signs ranged from a small dimple to repeat infections, and diagnosis often took over a year. Scans and dye tests helped trace the tunnel before surgery. All tunnels were cut out, and only two came back. The authors share what helps doctors spot and cure this hidden defect early.
pmc-13195806:
Praveen Kant and co-authors published this 2026 study on whether bacterial viruses help spread drug resistance. Phages infect bacteria and sometimes ferry genes between them, but how often they carry resistance genes has been argued for a decade. The team swept every phage genome collection they could reach for known resistance genes and their surroundings.

Of 38,861 phage genomes, only 82 carried any, holding 141 resistance genes in all. A few streptococcus phages carried whole clusters of four or more, and one unclassified phage held the full vancomycin resistance set. Clues in gene placement suggest temperate phages pick these genes up from their hosts by specialized transfer. The authors conclude phages do move resistance, but rarely and mostly by that focused route.
pmc-13197106:
Daniel Boris Amusin and co-authors describe CycleTrack in 2026, a platform where medical school applicants share their own admissions data. Applicants often fly blind about when interview offers arrive and what scores get in. CycleTrack pools their reports in real time to fill that gap.

From 2022 to early 2026, close to thirty-five thousand users signed up. They tracked over four hundred thousand applications across degree types. The counts per program tracked official data closely. User grades and test scores differed from national averages, so the crowd is not a perfect mirror. Still, the timing of interview offers at two schools matched well. The data show strong demand for open admissions information.
pmc-13197706:
Benjamin Wajda and co-authors review weight loss drugs of the GLP-1 class around hip and knee replacement surgery in a 2026 analysis. Obesity raises demand for joint replacement and lifts the risk of infection, wound problems, and repeat surgery. Use of these drugs before surgery is growing, but safety was unclear.

The review pooled thirteen record based studies with a very large patient count. Drug use was linked to lower odds of joint infection in the first ninety days. The authors also gathered data on other complications and care use at ninety days and at one to two years, to weigh benefit against risk.
pmc-13197806:
Yannick Vander Zwalmen and a large team test cognitive control training as an add-on for late-life depression, in a trial published in 2026. Weak cognitive control is common in older depressed patients and helps symptoms persist, yet standard care barely targets it. Ninety patients were randomized to eight sessions of control training or an active comparison training, both on top of usual care.

Over twelve months of follow-up, both groups improved by about the same amount. No edge appeared for symptoms, rumination, emotion habits or thinking scores. The authors suggest the dose may have been too light, or that ageing brains adapt too slowly for the training to bite. Dose changes and better patient matching are the proposed next steps.
pmc-13198506:
A B Paes and colleagues tested an aging mouse model for heart attack marker studies in a 2026 paper. Tiny RNA markers in blood can flag a heart attack early, but age and sex shape their levels. Fast-aging mice offer a test bed, so the team compared them with normal-aging controls after artery blockage.

Four markers rose fast in blood after injury, with four hours the best sampling time. One marker rose in fast-aging mice of both sexes but not in controls. Another rose only in aged females. Heart tissue patterns split by strain and sex as well. Starting levels differed by age in males. The model works for such studies, provided age and sex are built in.
pmc-13198606:
Eileen Dahlke and seven colleagues study how a growth signal changes the job of a kidney protein called megalin, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Megalin normally pulls useful cargo from the fluid that will become urine. A growth pathway named mTORC1 adds a chemical tag to one spot on megalin. The tag slowed megalin's cargo uptake but pulled it closer to a helper protein called ARH. Cells with the tag divided more, and the tag peaked while cells were splitting in two. Cells lacking megalin or its helper grew far less. The authors conclude the tag switches megalin from a cargo role toward a cell growth role.
pmc-13200306:
Ana Margarida Salgueiro and colleagues review the ketogenic diet for brain degeneration in a 2026 article. The ketogenic diet is a very low-carb, high-fat diet that shifts the body to burn ketones for fuel. Brain cells in diseases like Alzheimer and Parkinson struggle for energy, so an alternate fuel may help.

The review traces several paths: ketones as backup energy, less oxidative stress and inflammation, cleaner cell recycling, and shifts in gut microbes. Evidence spans five diseases, from animal work to early human trials that support feasibility. Long-term safety, sticking to the diet, and daily practicality still block wide use. The authors call for sharper trials to set dose and duration.
pmc-13200806:
Xiekun Chen and colleagues built a 2026 model for early prediction of gestational diabetes, diabetes first arising in pregnancy. Early warning could improve mother and baby outcomes, but models suffer from few early cases, lopsided data, and tangled risk factors. Their fix joins synthetic data with guided feature design.

They studied more than eight thousand pregnant women across two datasets. Artificial samples balanced the data, and a language model helped group features by medical domain and build richer combined features. A random forest model with one augmentation method scored best, catching about three quarters of cases. Explanation tools ranked the top predictors. Added data beat the baseline methods by a clear margin in recall.
pmc-13201906:
Anna Xue and Joseph Coselli commented in 2026 on whether weekend timing drives death risk in surgery for a torn aorta. Acute type A dissection still kills many patients in hospital despite faster recognition and better surgery. Debate has circled a weekend effect, the idea that weekend care is weaker.

Weekend patients died in hospital at a higher rate than weekday patients, and the gap held after statistical adjustment. Weekend patients also arrived sicker, with more liver disease and poor organ flow. Still, those traits alone did not explain the gap. The commentary weighs staffing and systems against patient mix.
pmc-13202006:
Jiagui Song and Lixiang Xue offer a 2026 commentary on a severe form of ovarian cancer. Most patients are found late, and five-year survival has stayed below half for decades. Stage alone does not explain why patients at the same stage fare so differently. The piece discusses a recent study that profiled proteins in 116 tumors from these patients.

That study found a stage point where tumor biology shifts in a sharp way. It also sorted tumors by protein and immune traits into a two-tier frame. The aim is to guide drug choice by markers, not stage alone. Immune drugs have so far helped few of these patients. The commentary sets out why protein-level maps may change that.
pmc-13202206:
Potatoes rot between harvest and market in Ethiopia, and a 2026 assessment led by Behailu Bisenebet Mossie quantifies where those losses happen. The research article surveys potato postharvest loss in the Awi and South Gondar zones of the Amhara Region, from farm gate to consumption.

Formal questionnaires reached 540 farmers, split evenly between the two zones, and nearly every farmer reported losing potatoes after harvest. Storage caused the largest share of losses in both zones, while transport caused the smallest share recorded. About nine in ten farmers still used traditional storage, and hand tools and animal plowing dominated harvesting, which frames practical targets for loss reduction.
pmc-13202606:
Aggression and suicidal thinking tangle in schizophrenia, and a 2026 one-time study led by Ruomei Fan separates their patterns in chronic illness. The research article recruits 659 patients with chronic schizophrenia from ten psychiatric hospitals in China and contrasts those with and without such thoughts.

Aggression was notably more common among patients having suicidal thoughts than among those without them, the authors report. Aggressive patients in both groups tended to be younger with more severe symptoms, though details differed by group. In patients with suicidal thoughts, stronger positive symptoms raised aggression risk while negative symptoms appeared protective, which argues for assessing aggression risk separately by thought status.
pmc-13204206:
Andrea Spagnoletti and co-authors review, in 2026, open questions in drug treatment given around surgery for melanoma, a serious skin cancer. Treatment before or after surgery has cut the return of high-risk disease and spread to distant sites. Gains have reached earlier stages too, yet many choices remain unsettled.

Open issues include how to treat the earliest high-risk stage and what to do when disease returns during treatment. The review covers immune drug pairs, personal vaccines made from tumor markers, and tests that may refine risk estimates. Stage alone still leads to over- and under-treatment, the authors warn. Better risk tools are the path forward.
pmc-13204306:
Anastasia Bezrukova and eleven co-authors probe a recycling pathway gone wrong in Parkinson's disease tied to the GBA1 gene, in this 2026 study. Cells from patients carry an overactive growth switch, mTOR, and sluggish cleanup of worn parts. The faulty enzyme at the pathway's heart, GCase, also worked better in both. The authors say mTOR blockade deserves study as a therapy tuned to mutation type.
pmc-13205306:
Min-Shu Hsieh and a large team of co-authors tested a rapid imaging method for fresh surgical tissue, in a 2026 study. Judging tissue during surgery guides key choices, but frozen sections can blur detail. The new method stains whole fresh tissue and converts the images to a familiar style. No slicing of the tissue is needed.

Specimens came from lung and breast operations. Pathologists read the new images without knowing the standard results. Their calls matched the standard fixed-tissue diagnosis at a high rate. Tissue structure and cell detail stayed clear in the images. The method also cut evaluation time sharply compared with the standard workflow. The authors judge it feasible and reliable for rapid checks. Uses during surgery are a natural next step.
pmc-13205506:
Simone Negrini and six co-authors review a brake on the immune system in a 2026 paper. The brake, a protein on immune cells, keeps attacks in check so the body does not harm itself. Its work rests on more than a plain off switch: how it grabs its partners, moves in the cell, and comes back to the surface all count.

The review joins lab proof on the brake's build with care in cancer, grafts, and immune ills. Flaws in the brake cause immune disease in some, while drugs that free it fight cancer in others. Readers get a full map of a core immune path.
pmc-13206606:
Rakesh Arya, Viplov Kumar Biswas, Hemlata Shakya, and Jong-Joo Kim hunt for gene markers of ovarian cancer tied to pyroptosis, an inflammatory form of programmed cell death. Ovarian cancer is the deadliest gynecologic cancer, often found late and prone to resist therapy. The team combined gene expression data, immune profiling, network analysis, and machine learning to find markers that hold up across data sets.

Cancer samples showed fewer helper and killer T cells and several other immune cells than normal tissue. From over a thousand changed genes, 22 were tied to pyroptosis, and nine stood out as hub genes. Machine learning methods agreed on one core marker, CEP55, which separated cancer from normal tissue with high accuracy. Higher CEP55 levels also tracked with shorter survival. The authors propose CEP55 as a candidate for early detection and as a possible drug target linking cell division with immune control.
pmc-13208906:
Qian Huang and co-authors map how sand wears away cyclone desanders at shale gas wellheads in a 2026 study. Flying rock particles scour the spinning separators that clean gas, risking leaks and shutdowns. The team measured wall loss at three points on one field unit, then built a matched computer model.

The simulation reproduced the field pattern, exposing where fast flow and pressure concentrate the wear. Nine design and operating factors were varied; six mattered most, including inlet shape, chamber size, particle size, and flow speed. A response-surface analysis then linked those factors to wear rates. The findings guide tougher desander designs for abrasive service.
pmc-13209406:
Tomasz Blachowicz, Guido Ehrmann, Elzbieta Stepula, and Andrea Ehrmann review optical biosensors in a 2026 paper. A biosensor pairs a catcher element that spots a target substance with a transducer that turns the catch into an electric signal, ready to read and store.

The review covers the main optical designs and where they are used: personal medicine, drug hunting, food safety, and plant disease checks. Pocket-sized versions often ride on tiny fluid channels or micro-machines. The authors weigh the field's limits honestly: shrinking the parts, short-lived biological reagents, and the fuss of preparing samples. The survey maps what the newest devices can do and where they still fall short.
pmc-13209506:
Nagehan Saltan and co-authors examine four Turkish species of Leonurus, a genus in the mint family known for useful plant chemicals. The team made extracts with ethanol, methanol, and water from each species and mapped their contents with liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry. They also tested the extracts for antioxidant action, effects on microbes, and effects on cancer cells grown in the lab.

Three compounds stood out across the species: verbascoside, genkwanin, and caffeoylquinic acids. One species showed the strongest antioxidant profile, matching its high phenol content. The extracts acted against Candida yeast at low doses, had weaker effects on bacteria, and slowed breast and brain cancer cell lines to varying degrees while differing in harm to lung cells. The authors say the results back the plants' folk use and point to them as steady sources for drug and supplement research.
pmc-13209906:
Misuzu Gregg, Chifuyu Hayashi, and Masami Tamada study how senior nurses support new graduates in this 2026 paper. New nurses must learn to find information fast to settle into hospital work. Managers and senior nurses guide that learning, but their methods and expectations were little documented in Japan.

The team interviewed twelve nurse managers from five hospitals and fourteen senior nurses from three hospitals. Seniors expected new nurses to show the right attitude, speak up about doubts, take initiative, and build ties with experienced staff. To help, they encouraged questions, offered needed information early, and promoted sharing among peers. Managers also worked to build a workplace where asking feels safe.
pmc-13210106:
Abdulla Albastaki and Judith Smith present a 2026 review on how to pick a DNA method for soil microbe studies. Soil holds thousands of species at wildly uneven counts, and the method chosen shapes what a study sees. Three methods lead the field: short-read gene scans, full-length gene scans on a portable device, and long-read whole-community DNA reads. Teams often pick by cost or habit, not by known bias.

The review gathers head-to-head tests that ran two or more methods on the same soil. The methods agree on the dominant species and on gaps between sites. They split on total variety counts, rare species finds, and the shares of whole microbe groups. New device chemistry has narrowed the accuracy gap. The guide helps teams match method to question.
pmc-13210906:
Fei Li and eleven colleagues argue sorghum breeding should shift from selecting traits one by one to designing the ideal plant gene by gene. Sorghum feeds people and livestock and supplies bioenergy. Traditional varieties are tall, sparse, and big-panicked, clashing with dense planting and machine harvesting. The review assembles the ideotype: canopy structure, stalk strength, panicle form, and root system suited to modern intensive farms.

Major genes controlling height, stem strength, leaf shape, and panicle type are described in mechanistic detail. Obstacles include genes with multiple effects, trade-offs between traits, and narrow genetic diversity in breeding pools. The twenty twenty-six paper is a blueprint genre: define the target plant first, then engineer toward it, rather than hoping selection stumbles onto the combination modern agriculture needs.
pmc-13211206:
Alberto Canzone and co-authors ran a small trial of foot sole training to see instant effects on balance and ankle motion, in work published in 2026. Sensory input from the sole helps the body hold posture. Twenty six active young adults were split between training and rest groups.

The training group walked on a textured mat and did balance drills on a soft pad, while controls lay still for the same time. Balance test reach improved on both feet right after training, while the rest group did not change. Ankle motion range stayed the same in both groups. The authors call the results early evidence that sole input can sharpen balance quickly.
pmc-13211706:
Liping Jia and co-authors trace, in a 2026 study, how a stomach virus evolved inside one child over a year and a half of unbroken infection. The child had Burkitt lymphoma, which weakens immune control, and shed human norovirus from twenty sixteen into twenty eighteen. Long infections like this may breed new variants that dodge population immunity. The team collected dozens of stool samples and sequenced the virus again and again.

Changes piled up in near time order across the virus's genes. The fastest change hit the outer shell region that grips gut receptors and faces antibodies, the very spots that decide immune escape. Deep sequencing even caught mixed virus populations living in the child at once. The authors say watching such patients matters, since chronic infections can seed tomorrow's outbreak strains.
pmc-13212806:
Ken Batai and colleagues study in 2026 how body fat and muscle, measured on medical scans, relate to kidney cancer features. Body composition differs across racial and ethnic groups and may shape how aggressive a tumour proves to be.

Scans from 268 patients taken before surgery supplied measures of fat under the skin, fat around organs, fat inside muscle, and muscle itself. Fat patterns varied by group, with Hispanic patients showing higher values on two measures. Fat inside muscle linked strongly to one tumour subtype, while other fat measures tied to higher grade or later stage. A low-fat, low-muscle pattern also carried higher odds of high-grade disease.
pmc-13213006:
Falconer and co-authors argue that school absence in England should be treated as a public health problem, in a paper from 2026. Lasting absence harms learning, social growth, and health at once. The authors bring in a new framework from the United States that frames absence in health terms. They ask how that frame could fit English schools and services.

The piece lays out workable steps for health services and local councils. It casts absence not as a fault of families but as a sign of unmet need. Health partners would join schools in spotting and easing the drivers of absence. Those drivers span illness, mental strain, and hardship at home. The authors say the shift in view could unlock joint action. The United States frame offers a tested start point for the change.
pmc-13213306:
Mojnu Mia and co-authors test a medicinal mushroom against Alzheimer hallmarks in worms and computer models. Their 2026 study studies Ganoderma lucidum, rich in triterpenoids and sterols. Lab assays, worm tests, and docking simulations share the work.

The extract scavenges radicals strongly at low dose. Worms under oxidative stress survive about a quarter longer on treatment. Amyloid-driven paralysis in a worm strain is delayed, with some worms still active at sixty-eight hours. Docking names three compounds as strong amyloid binders, and dynamics runs keep those bonds stable. Energy sums confirm tight binding for the lead compound. Drug-likeness predictions look clean, with good gut absorption and no flagged toxicity. The authors back the mushroom as a multi-path candidate.
pmc-13213606:
Sin Yee Lim and colleagues report in 2026 a woman whose skin sarcoma seemed to explode after repeated procedures that never fully removed it. Complete removal is the cornerstone of cure for solid cancers, yet leftover tumour is common, and its response to surgical trauma is poorly charted in humans.

The seventy-year-old patient's tumour regrew rapidly after each intervention that left visible disease behind, then spread aggressively through the body. Measuring growth rates showed marked acceleration after those incomplete procedures, a pattern the authors call hyperprogression. Inflammation from tissue injury may feed leftover cancer, they suggest. The case adds human evidence to animal data and argues for caution when clearance cannot be achieved.
pmc-13213806:
Biyan Nathanael Harapan and co-authors report a 2026 study of brain infections after brain surgery. Such infections, abscesses and empyemas, are grave and differ from abscesses that arise on their own. The team reviewed patients treated at one center between 2014 and 2024.

The study held 113 patients who had 361 surgeries in all, and most needed the bone flap removed. Infections most often followed surgery for glioma or meningioma tumors. Staph germs and Gram-negative bacteria led the causes, and mixed infections were common. Repeat scans showed infection signs fading over time, and a scan measure rose as patients healed. The authors say joint care with repeat surgery and long, targeted antibiotics is key.
pmc-13214106:
Debao Yi and colleagues published a 2026 study of sulfate transporter genes in tomato. Selenium is a nutrient people need in small amounts. Plants absorb it through sulfate pathways by chemical similarity. Adding selenium to crops could improve human diets. Tomato transporter genes were poorly mapped.

The team found twelve transporter genes in the tomato genome. Most share a common structural core. Their control regions respond to plant hormones. Selenium treatment switched on different genes in roots and leaves. Stress tests showed further response patterns. These genes are candidates for breeding selenium-rich tomatoes.
pmc-13215606:
John Sandi and co-authors sequence the first full yellow fever genome from Sierra Leone in a 2026 study. The mosquito-borne virus causes severe bleeding disease across Africa. Sierra Leone tracks cases but had no genome on record. A patient at Kailahun hospital supplied the sample.

Hybrid capture sequencing recovered nearly the whole genome. Family analysis places it in the West African II genotype. Fifty-seven changes mark it from its nearest kin, three altering proteins. Its shared ancestor with Senegalese and Dutch genomes dates to about 2001. Long hidden transmission in the region is the likely story. The genome arms surveillance with a local reference.
pmc-13217206:
Patil, Khan, and Mahyavanshi chart infections of the brain and spinal cord in children from rural western India. Such infections remain a leading cause of death and disability for children in poorer countries. Local patterns shift with vaccine uptake, environment, and how easily families can reach care, yet rural data from this region were scarce.

The study tracks which infections appeared, how their frequency changed, and what neurological outcomes children were left with. Findings like these help hospitals plan beds, tests, and follow-up for survivors with lasting damage. They also show where prevention, above all vaccination and earlier referral, could cut the toll most.
pmc-13217606:
Pongthep Wongwatcharapaiboon and four co-authors trace how Thailand put a landmark health charter into practice, in a 2026 paper. The 1986 Ottawa Charter recast health as a resource for daily life, not just the lack of disease. It named five work areas, from healthy laws to care services turned toward prevention. Thailand's answer was ThaiHealth, a fund built to push health gain across the whole society.

Later world meetings, including one in Bangkok, added fresh calls as trade and city growth widened health gaps. Poor and middle-income lands now face germ diseases and lifestyle diseases at once. The paper walks through how the Thai fund works the charter's levers: shaping laws, building settings that support health, and backing group action. It offers ThaiHealth as a working case for lands that want the charter's words to bite.
pmc-13217906:
Alice Vanneste and co-authors present a 2026 qualitative study on patient experience data: what patients report about outcomes, experiences, and preferences. The study asks why such data still struggles to enter healthcare decision-making in Europe despite wide agreement that it should.

Thirty-eight stakeholders were interviewed, drawn from industry, academia, nonprofits, regulators, reimbursement agencies, and patient groups. Three barriers recurred: no clear Europe-wide policy framework or quality bar for such data, too few proven collection tools, and little openness about how agencies weigh the data they receive. Suggested ways forward include shared guidelines, training in patient involvement, and better methods research. Views split on who should lead, which the authors say makes continued coordination across groups vital.
pmc-13218006:
Sena Gizem Arslan and Birgul Dingirdan Gultekinler test a low-cost force plate for jump and balance checks. Force plates give sound data, but their price and size keep them out of many clinics and gyms. The team tested the Meloq EasyBase plate in seventy-eight healthy young adults. Each person stood on one leg and did a jump test, then came back a week or so later to repeat the tests.

Jump height scores were highly steady across visits, and balance scores were fair to good. The plate's balance scores also matched a simple clinic balance test. The authors see it as a handy tool for field use.
pmc-13218306:
Qi Wang and co-authors test a teaching model that blends AI, case-based learning, and a flipped classroom for reproductive medicine residents, in a 2026 randomized controlled trial. Lecture teaching often fails to build clinical decision-making during residency rotations, a problem as infertility care grows more complex. The trial ran at the First Hospital of Jilin University.

Fifty obstetrics and gynecology residents were randomized to the blended model or to traditional lectures. The blended group worked through cases with virtual patients before class on one platform, reviewed cases on another, and then debated them in class. After the course, the blended group scored higher on theory tests, on observed clinical evaluations, and on structured clinical exams. They also reported stronger motivation, better clinical thinking, and more self-guided learning than the lecture group. The authors recommend the model as an effective, transferable way to train reproductive medicine doctors.
pmc-13218606:
Louise-Helene Gagnon, Humara Edell, and Patricia E. Lee review the diagnosis and management of urinary incontinence in women in a 2026 article. Incontinence is common and undertreated, because patients stay silent: many assume leaking is normal with aging or feel embarrassed to raise it. Earlier work suggests a majority of women never seek care, and it costs Canada an estimated 2.6 billion dollars a year.

The first step is classifying the problem, because treatment follows the type. Stress incontinence leaks urine when abdominal pressure rises, as with coughing or exercise, while urge incontinence follows a need to urinate, usually with frequency and night-time trips. First-line care is conservative: behavioural therapy, pelvic floor and bladder training, noninvasive options, and attention to contributing conditions. Surgery is the second-line answer for stress incontinence, and medication for urge incontinence. Matching the plan to the type is what makes treatment work.
pmc-13219706:
Amir Hossein Alipour, Fatemeh Hoda Fallah, and Bahman Abedi Kiasari build blood tests for two widespread polyomaviruses in a 2026 study. BK and JC viruses infect most people in childhood, then persist, becoming dangerous when immunity is suppressed, as in transplant patients. Reliable antibody tests are the backbone of tracking who carries them.

The team produced the viruses' VP1 shell proteins in insect cells and used them to build ELISA assays, then ran sixty-seven serum samples. Antibodies to BK virus appeared in 77.6 percent of samples and to JC virus in 34.3 percent, with both rising with age, as expected for infections acquired. Competition experiments showed the two tests did not confuse one virus's antibodies for the other's, confirming specificity. Antigens made in the insect-cell system gave stronger signals than alternatives. The authors offer the assays for population surveys and for watching at-risk patients such as transplant recipients.
pmc-13220006:
Felix Wunderlich and co-authors test whether optimism colors recovery after hip replacement. Their 2026 multicenter study tracks 846 patients with hip function scores before surgery and at three, six, and twelve months after. A standard life orientation test grades optimism and pessimism beforehand.

Optimism links significantly to better hip scores across the whole first year. Pessimism links at the six and twelve month marks. The ties are modest in size but steady. Prior work tied mood disorders to outcomes; general personality traits were the gap here. The authors suggest pre-surgery chats could flag pessimistic patients for extra support. Their registry-listed trial gives clinics a cheap lens on who may need closer follow-up after joint replacement.
pmc-13221706:
Razan Fakieh, Ranjana Kishore, Meera Sundaram, and David Reiner test what a development kinase does without its expected partner, in a 2026 study of the worm Caenorhabditis elegans. The kinase, MIG-15, is the worm's only member of a family that, in mammals, often works downstream of a switch protein called Rap2. Whether the worm pair works the same way was unknown.

Mutants missing the kinase showed severe faults in organ shaping, cell placement, and movement. Mutants missing the switch protein looked nearly normal. The split means several of the kinase's jobs run without that partner, so other switches or adhesion signals must control it. The finding redraws a wiring diagram that researchers had borrowed from mammals.
pmc-13221906:
Miriam Okorie and thirteen co-authors sweep, in 2026 work, the bars to diabetes care in poor lands. The ill weighs heaviest there, yet care stalls on many fronts at once. Their sweep of two data banks took in more than a thousand works; fourteen met the set bars and fed the tale.

Bars sort by who bears them: the sick, the healers, and the house of care. Money lack and weak care systems sat at the core. Thin staff, drug gaps, and poor teaching rode close. The team backs joined fixes: funds, staff growth, and sick-folk teaching in one push, or gains will leak.
pmc-13222006:
Ni Luh Lany Christina and co-authors review how endometriosis affects ovarian reserve, in a 2026 systematic review of studies published between 2015 and 2024. Endometriosis causes chronic pelvic pain and infertility, and cysts on the ovaries can erode the egg supply. Ten studies met the quality and reporting standards the team applied.

Women with endometriosis showed lower hormone markers and fewer visible follicles than healthy comparison groups. Chronic inflammation and oxidative stress were identified as damaging routes. Surgery to remove cysts can ease symptoms and may aid fertility, yet it can also remove healthy tissue and deepen reserve loss. Early diagnosis and personalized planning are the authors' main prescriptions.
pmc-13222306:
Hidekazu Tanaka and co-authors present updated guidance in 2026 on heart ultrasound for patients on cancer therapy. Cancer drugs can damage the heart, and longer survival makes spotting that damage early ever more important. The Japanese Society of Echocardiography first issued guidance in 2020, and this focused update reflects new evidence and imaging advances.

Two measures anchor the guidance: ejection fraction, the share of blood the heart pumps out, and global longitudinal strain, a finer gauge of muscle shortening. The document sets standard protocols before, during, and after drug therapy, plus long-term checks after chest radiation. It also covers heart inflammation linked to immune checkpoint drugs and stresses measurement quality, three-dimensional imaging, and AI support.
pmc-13222806:
Zhen Tao and five colleagues test whether narrower brain arteries mean higher stroke recurrence in older patients, in a 2026 study. They followed 527 patients aged 65 and over after a first ischemic stroke, grading the worst artery narrowing as mild, moderate, or severe on vessel imaging. Recurrence within twelve months was the outcome.

The gradient was steep: recurrence hit 8.4 percent of the mild group, 16.8 percent of the moderate group, and 27.9 percent of the severe group. After adjusting for other risks, severe narrowing still tripled the odds of another stroke, and moderate narrowing nearly doubled them. The authors advise early vessel imaging and closer follow-up for older patients with tight arteries.
pmc-13223606:
Yiheng Chi, Li Ke, Tanghai Cheng, and Xinrui Ma reviewed work on motor imagery for children with developmental coordination disorder in two thousand twenty-six. Children with the disorder struggle with movement skills. Motor imagery means picturing an action in the mind without moving.

The review pulls together theory, brain studies, and trials of training. Many children with the disorder also picture actions poorly, which may reflect weak inner models for planning moves. Training that pairs imagery with watching actions showed early promise for daily skills. The authors say proof is still early, and they call for larger trials, shared methods, and care plans shaped to each child.
pmc-13224006:
Yun Luo, Yanpuze Hao, Haochen Gong, and Bo Li reviewed human-machine collaborative decision-making in 2026, covering work in management, the military, health care, and manufacturing. In such systems, people and machines share a choice rather than one side deciding alone. The review offers a two-layer frame to sort a fast-growing field.

The first layer splits the process into four steps: set the attributes, assign weights, gather the information, and decide. The second layer names four shared mechanisms: role setup, interaction and debate, trust and explanation, and shifts of authority. A feedback loop links outcomes back to earlier steps. The authors also trace how failures spread through those mechanisms. Readers get a map for designing joint decisions and for spotting where they can break.
pmc-13225306:
Severi Santavirta and four co-authors model how people watch social scenes in films in a 2026 paper. Viewers constantly sample features from raw brightness up to the emotional tone of interactions. Over a hundred participants watched full films and clips while eye trackers recorded gaze position, pupil size, and blinking. Dozens of stimulus features were extracted, from motion and faces to pleasantness ratings.

Faces and eyes drew gaze above other content, and pupils answered brightness, scene cuts, and arousal. Blinking dropped during engaging stretches. The authors conclude social vision is steered mainly by raw and mid-level features, while high-level social signals act mostly through the pupil.
pmc-13225506:
Xiang Zhang, Miaomiao Liu, Kang Liu, and Yigang He published this 2026 study mapping blood groups in Gansu Province, in northwest China. Safe transfusion depends on knowing which ABO and RhD types the donors of a region hold versus what its patients need. The rich ethnic mix of Gansu suggested a distinctive pattern worth charting.

Records covered 71,363 donors from 2014 to 2023 and 188,827 patients from 2018 to 2023. The two groups differed clearly: type O positive was scarcer among patients than donors, while A and B positive ran higher. The rarest slot, AB negative, appeared twice as often in patients as in donors. Donation volumes also trended downward over the decade. The authors draw supply lessons for planners balancing stock against demand.
pmc-13227206:
Rogério Aires and colleagues check a 2026 mouse study of whether cyclophosphamide, a drug widely used to suppress the immune system in experiments, quietly disturbs the brain. If it did, countless neuroimmune studies could be confounded. Male mice received weekly injections for three or four weeks, then underwent behaviour batteries, brain tissue checks, and gene-expression measurement.

Immune suppression clearly took hold in the body, with slower weight gain and altered white-cell counts. Behaviour, though, barely moved, showing only mild, passing changes in strength and sickness-like signs. Brain tissue showed no structural damage and no activation of star-shaped support cells. One gene, Lgals3, rose significantly in the brain, a molecular footnote in an otherwise reassuring picture of central resilience.
pmc-13227806:
Abdulelah K Alqawlaq and colleagues report a 2026 Saudi case of a teenager with an ultra-rare skeletal disorder who went from wheelchair use to walking with support after staged joint surgery. Whole-genome sequencing confirmed spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia with joint laxity type 3, caused by a fault in the EXOC6B gene. The disorder loosens joints, invites repeated dislocations, and had severely damaged both hips and knees since early childhood.

Surgeons replaced both hips first, then both knees, tailoring the plan to her anatomy. Pain fell markedly and mobility returned step by step until she could walk with assistance. The team presents the case as the first surgically managed report of this condition in Saudi Arabia, arguing rare-disease patients deserve individualised operative planning.
pmc-13229406:
Kuang Ma and colleagues present MultiVTP in 2026, a computer method for finding human proteins that viruses target. A single host protein can serve several viruses, so the task is framed as multilabel prediction. The work uses only information inside host proteins themselves.

MultiVTP samples small graphs around each query protein and combines several kinds of protein features. A graph transformer then looks for patterns shared across viruses and patterns tied to one virus. Tests against other models showed stronger accuracy, even when training data were limited. Applied across the human proteome, the method points to new candidate targets for single viruses and for several viruses at once.
pmc-13230106:
Jessica Fay and co-authors track the rise of insecticide resistance genes in dengue mosquitoes in northeastern Argentina, in a 2026 study. The mosquito Aedes aegypti spreads dengue, and pyrethroid sprays are a main control tool. Two gene variants, called kdr mutations, blunt those sprays. The team genotyped mosquitoes from the same sites in Posadas in 2019 and again in 2024.

Both resistance variants climbed in frequency by more than fourteen percent over the five years. Over ninety percent of samples carried at least two resistance copies in the later round. Mosquitoes with three or four copies, the highly resistant class, grew by about a quarter. The authors blame heavy insecticide use during dengue outbreaks for the speed of the rise. They urge routine genetic monitoring and fresh control strategies before the sprays fail.
pmc-13230506:
Simon Hefner and colleagues test in 2026 whether photos of fingernails and eyelids can estimate hemoglobin without a blood draw. Their HeMonitor study enrolled three hundred sixty-seven patients with blood cancers plus healthy donors for comparison. Machine learning models learned to predict lab hemoglobin values from the images alone.

The best model landed close to lab values, with spread near one unit on the reported scale. A second exploratory layer combined each estimate with patient reports of overall health and fatigue. Lower estimates generally matched worse quality of life, which fits the known burden of anemia. Agreement with clinician judgment looked encouraging in borderline ranges. Home monitoring built this way still needs testing in planned follow-up studies.
pmc-13233006:
Charles Amoatey Odonkor and colleagues published a 2026 pilot study testing whether shoe-mounted sensors can measure walking as accurately as laboratory cameras. Twenty people took part, half with knee osteoarthritis and half healthy. Each person walked at a self-chosen pace, a fast pace, and an endurance pace while sensors and a motion capture system recorded more than 5,000 strides.

Sensor estimates of walking speed matched the camera system almost exactly, and stride length and cadence also agreed closely. Everyone finished the protocol with minimal problems. Participants who reported more physical activity tended to walk faster with longer strides, though the small sample makes that pattern tentative. The authors see the sensors as a practical way to track walking outside the lab.
pmc-13233406:
Koji, the mold grown on grains to start many Asian ferments, can also grow on farm leftovers. Sylvester Holt and five co-authors grew the mold Aspergillus oryzae in 2026 on wheat bran, rye bran, and the pressed cakes left from rapeseed and pumpkin seed oil. They tracked how the base food and its moisture shaped the smells the mold produced.

Each base food followed its own path as the mold worked. Grain brans soured gently and built sweet, rich notes mid course, while the oilseed cakes held sharper smells for longer. Wetter mixes pushed out sour overflow products such as acetic acid. The authors say matching base, moisture, and timing gives makers control over the final aroma.
pmc-13233806:
Miguel Castro and colleagues published a 2026 environmental study of peatland restoration in Kalimantan, Indonesia. Drained tropical peat burns readily, and Indonesia's peat fires rank among the country's largest greenhouse gas sources. After catastrophic fires in 2015, the government and partners blocked drainage canals to rewet peatlands. The team used statistical counterfactual methods to estimate what would have burned without the rewetting between 2017 and 2022.

Effects varied by place, and canal blocks whose rewetted zones overlapped performed best at preventing fire. If every block worked at that level, rewetting could avoid up to 6.4 percent of the burnt area and deliver economic returns above one hundred percent within a decade at the best sites. The authors argue restoration pays, provided blocks are placed to overlap.
pmc-13234106:
Zhixiang Jiang and colleagues published a 2026 materials study on parking helpful bacteria on biochar, charcoal made from heated plant waste. Anchored microbes survive harsh conditions better, a boon for cleaning salty or polluted soils. The team made biochars from several feedstocks at two temperatures and measured how well each loaded the soil bacterium Bacillus subtilis.

Biochars cooked at seven hundred degrees carried far more bacteria than those made at four hundred, by roughly fourteen to sixty percent. Loading changed the char surface, adding carbon and nitrogen, enriching chemical groups, and flipping it from water-repelling to water-loving. Modeling pointed to chemical, single-layer attachment driven by charge pull, hydrogen bonds, and water-shy forces together. Bacteria settled in two stages, sticking and filling pores first, then locking in with their own glue-like coatings. Anchored bacteria also tolerated salt far better.
pmc-13234806:
Tulsi Paudel and co-authors build a small power device from safe, earth-friendly films. Their twenty twenty-six paper uses a mix of polyvinyl alcohol, chitosan, and glycine. Such devices, called triboelectric nanogenerators, turn touch and motion into electric charge.

Most past devices used plastics that do not break down in soil. Here the mixed film forms one layer, cast from liquid and dried in plain air. A silicone film forms the other layer. Changing the glycine share changed the film surface, strength, and power output. Tests with scans and light tools confirm the mix, and the device can harvest small daily motions.
pmc-13234906:
Jindong Hao and Weibo Jin wrote a 2026 paper on MolFoundry, a generative design system for drug-like molecules that target a swine virus protein. The virus, PRRSV, hits pig herds hard and has no approved antiviral drug. Its nucleocapsid protein changes little across strains and is key to packaging the viral genome, so it draws drug hunters. Most design tools ignore protein shape, and so fit the pocket poorly.

MolFoundry uses the pocket shape at each step. One part scores pocket fit by shape. A second part builds compounds while it attends to the binding site. A third part weighs rival goals in a fixed way, under limits from medicinal chemistry. Trained on more than eighteen thousand complexes, it made varied, buildable compounds that fit well. It beat diffusion, transformer, and reinforcement learning baselines. Validity reached zero point nine three eight, and novelty a perfect one.
pmc-13235406:
Ariyawan Tantipongpiradet and colleagues tested in 2026 whether an olive-derived compound can protect rats against chronic stress. Hydroxytyrosol, produced through biotechnology, was given daily in an oral jelly before and during a period of unpredictable restraint stress. Rats of both sexes underwent tests of anxiety, mood, memory, and social behaviour. Brain tissue from the hippocampus was also sequenced cell by cell.

Stress alone produced anxiety-like behaviour, reduced pleasure response, memory problems, and social withdrawal in the animals. Treatment prevented those behavioural changes across the tests reported. Stress-related drops in dopamine and serotonin were also prevented, while a stress hormone rise was blunted. Thousands of gene changes across neurons and support cells were largely normalized by treatment. The authors identify hydroxytyrosol as a dietary candidate for building stress resilience.
pmc-13235706:
Perin and colleagues estimate what killed newborns and young children worldwide between 2000 and 2024. Their secondary analysis covers 195 countries. It uses a Bayesian statistical model to split deaths by cause, drawing on journal studies, health surveys, and World Health Organization mortality records, among many other sources.

Cause splits matter because the big killers of the first month differ from those of ages one to four. Fresh estimates show where past gains came from and where deaths still cluster. Governments and aid groups use such numbers to aim vaccines, newborn care, and nutrition money. The authors update an earlier round of estimates with data through the pandemic years.
pmc-13235906:
Reginato and Brandl build a new tool for naming the small, hidden fishes of coral reefs. Reefs hold more than a third of all marine species, yet many reef fishes are tiny, shy, and easy to confuse. Specialists who can tell them apart are few, so much reef life goes unrecorded in surveys.

Their tool joins deep learning with the branching structure of biological classification and very detailed images. Teaching the model the family tree, not just the final name, helps it sort look-alike species. Better identification from photos could widen reef monitoring sharply, letting cameras and computers do work that now waits on a handful of experts.
pmc-13236106:
Taro Higuchi, Hiro Nakao, and Yoshitsugu Fukuda described in 2026 a bone infection in a four-month-old girl that looked like a paralysed leg. She had stopped extending her left leg for six days and resisted during nappy changes. Early hip imaging at a community clinic had shown nothing abnormal. She had no fever, redness, swelling, or loss of appetite on presentation.

Examination in infants localizes pain poorly, so the authors stress imaging the whole affected limb early. Prompt recognition matters because acute bone infection can settle into chronic disease and form enclosed abscesses. Such abscesses near the growth plate can disturb later bone growth, requiring long follow-up. Serious disease can hide behind quiet presentations without fever or general symptoms in this age group. A systematic workup for limb disuse in infants forms the article's central practical message.
pmc-13236406:
Yoolwon Jeong, Suwan Go, Young-Hee Lee, and Yoomi Chae map in 2026 how Korean medical schools teach leadership. Doctors are expected to lead teams and keep care safe, a need thrown into relief by Korea's 2023 medical crisis, yet leadership training there has rarely been measured.

The team read the undergraduate curricula of Korean medical schools closely, counting and judging the leadership content in each. Most earlier studies came from countries where such courses are long established, so a local baseline was missing. Their analysis gives Korean schools a shared picture of what students are, and are not, being taught about leading.
pmc-13236506:
Javier Cifuentes-Quin and co-authors compared in 2026 side effects of two shortened radiotherapy schedules for prostate cancer in Colombia. More than two hundred men treated at one oncology centre between 2018 and 2025 entered the comparison. One schedule spread dose over moderately fewer sessions, while the other compressed treatment into very few sessions. Toxicity was graded with standard criteria for both early and later effects.

Early side effects occurred in about a quarter of the moderately compressed group, notably above the ultra-compressed group. Later side effects also appeared far more often under the moderate schedule in the records. Erectile dysfunction was the single most common late problem recorded in follow-up. Adjusted analysis confirmed lower odds of early toxicity with the ultra-compressed schedule independently. The authors argue the shorter course suits middle-income settings by improving efficiency and access without worse safety.
pmc-13237406:
Howard Sofen, Ranga Gogineni, Tushar Nishandar, and Jerry Bagel published a study in twenty twenty-six on whether body weight blunts a psoriasis drug's effect on the scalp. The drug blocks a single immune signal and is dosed the same for all. The team re-cut data from a blind trial of scalp disease over a full year.

Patients were split by whether their body mass index sat at or above the obesity line. Scores tracked clear skin on the scalp, itch relief, and how much scalp was clear of flakes. Near half of each arm met the weight bar. The check was a side look, not the trial's main aim, so its power is thin by design. The authors frame the read as a guide for doctors whose patients ask if weight will dull their drug.
pmc-13238106:
Zhao and co-authors interview families of disabled older adults living at home in Zhengzhou, China. Families are the main setting for guarding these elders' health. Both elders and caregivers face body, mind, and social strain as disability reshapes daily life.

The study used existence-relatedness-growth theory to frame family health needs. Twelve pairs, each an elder plus their main caregiver, took part in long interviews. Pairs were found by purposive and snowball sampling from December 2024 to February 2025. Themes were sorted with a guided analysis. Findings aim to ground family support programs in real stated needs.
pmc-13238806:
Maryam Zamani, Maryam Farhadian, Nasrin Piran, and Shiva Borzouei build a model that predicts several diabetes complications at once. Their 2026 paper notes that type 2 diabetes damages small and large vessels together, yet older models predict one outcome at a time. Joint prediction matches how the disease actually harms patients.

The team studied just under a thousand patients in retrospect. They grouped complications into small-vessel types, such as eye, kidney, and nerve damage, and large-vessel types, such as heart and brain events. Their stacked model layers three learning methods under a final combiner, in two multi-label arrangements. One arrangement clearly led on standard scores. An explanation method then surfaced the strongest risk factors, keeping the model readable for clinicians.
pmc-13239106:
Sodergren and colleagues test whether an adult quality-of-life form works for teens with cancer, in a study from twenty twenty-six. The form is the EORTC QLQ-C30, the most used cancer-specific measure in adult trials. Teens, with distinct growth needs, are often left out of trials. Lowering trial entry ages makes the question urgent.

Two hundred teens aged twelve to seventeen completed the adult form alongside a teen one. They also fed back on fit, ease, and the format they liked best, paper or screen. Filling it in took about twelve minutes on average. The teens found it acceptable and easy to finish. Score testing confirmed the subscale structure, with acceptable-to-good match. The study spans many tongues and cultures. Its verdict supports using the adult form with teenage patients.
pmc-13239306:
Samuel Gonçalves Encarnação and colleagues pooled twenty-three observational studies in 2026 on device-measured activity, sitting time, and frailty in older adults. Wearable accelerometers supplied the movement data, avoiding the rosy bias of self-report. Fourteen studies fed the activity meta-analysis and eleven the sedentary-time one.

Spontaneous physical activity correlated moderately and inversely with frailty: more movement, less frailty. Sedentary time correlated positively, with most analyzed studies agreeing.
