Pellets of marrow support cells were added to recreate direct and indirect contact. Three myeloma cell lines grew and resisted drugs inside the platform as expected. Patient marrow cells from two Spanish hospitals survived up to fourteen days, letting researchers watch the abnormal fraction over time.
pmc-13448306:
Fernandes and colleagues present in 2026, as abstract TLSB-07, a retrospective study of which breast cancer patients receiving chemotherapy before surgery go on to develop brain metastases, and how quickly. Risk factors and timing in this treatment setting were poorly defined.

Combining two Sunnybrook cohorts gave 586 patients who had received the pre-surgery chemotherapy; about twenty-six percent developed brain metastases over a median follow-up of thirty-eight months. The median time from diagnosis to brain spread was just under thirty months. It was shortest in triple negative disease at eighteen months and longest in hormone-sensitive, HER2-negative disease at about forty-nine months. Failing to achieve a complete response to chemotherapy carried the largest hazard, followed by inflammatory breast cancer and residual cancer in the lymph nodes. The authors argue brain screening for the highest-risk patients deserves study.
pmc-13448906:
Simon Vanhentenrijk and colleagues review in 2026 what is known about autoantibodies that actively disturb heart muscle function rather than merely marking disease. The review explains how B cells, helped by certain T cells, mature into plasma cells that pour out these antibodies. Imbalances in that output can disturb normal heart physiology, promote scarring of the muscle, and worsen outcomes.

Older schemes sorted such antibodies into heart-specific and non-heart-specific groups, but the authors show why that split breaks down. Many targets, including beta-1 adrenergic receptors, M2 muscarinic receptors, and ion channels, appear in many tissues, and cross-reaction is itself a functional trait. They therefore organize the findings by molecular target and by what each antibody does. The survey covers activation of complement, toxin neutralization, and recruitment of killer cells, giving clinicians a more useful map of this growing field.
pmc-13449506:
Du and team compared three years versus one year of BCG bladder therapy. BCG is the immune treatment instilled after surgery for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer. The comparison covered 140 Chinese patients treated at one center from 2017 to 2024. China's guideline recommends one year, based on local strain differences. Evidence for the longer course used elsewhere is missing.

Seventy-two patients received the three-year regimen and 68 the one-year regimen under routine clinical allocation at the center. Recurrence-free survival favored the longer course, with a hazard ratio of 0.31 in the survival analysis comparing the groups. Adjusted modeling confirmed the three-year schedule as an independent protective factor, at a hazard ratio of 0.282 in the model. The benefit held in high-risk subgroups tested. Only 27 recurrences occurred. Completion rates differed sharply, at 25 versus 51.5 percent. The authors label the findings hypothesis-generating, pending prospective trials.
pmc-13449706:
Danni Guo and colleagues explored in 2026 how skin germs relate to aging, using clinical, chemical, and DNA data at once. Skin germs shift with age, but whether germs shape aging signs was unclear. The team compared people whose skin looked young or old for their age.

A germ more common in young-looking skin, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, used the glutathione cycle to keep cell balance, and its products raised genes that make antioxidants in skin cells under stress. Models also tied it to pathways with betaine, lysolecithin, and porphyrin. A second germ, Acinetobacter guillouiae, changed skin color pathways by breaking down dopamine-like compounds. The work opens germ-based routes to anti-aging and skin-tone care.
pmc-13449806:
Matheus Santos França and colleagues write in 2026 about children and teenagers with Behçet disease who lack the genetic marker most associated with it, HLA-B51. The disease is an inflammatory disorder first described in 1937. It clusters along the old Silk Road and strikes hardest in the Middle and Far East, where the marker is common and tied to severe cases. Childhood disease is harder to pin down because symptoms arrive piecemeal, so classification criteria exist alongside judgment.

Pediatric data from Latin America are scarce, so the team analyzed 32 patients at a Brazilian tertiary rheumatology center, a multiethnic setting where 15.5 percent of healthy people carry the marker. Median age at diagnosis was four and a half years, half the patients were female, and most declared white ethnicity. Their letter investigates what HLA patterns, including B51-negative status, mean for how these children's disease presents and should be treated.
pmc-13449906:
Wang and co-authors catalogue the imaging of a rare tumour that grows inside veins. Their 2026 retrospective series reviews nineteen cases of intravenous leiomyomatosis. In that condition a benign uterine growth extends worm-like through pelvic veins and can reach the heart. One endometrial stromal sarcoma initially mistaken for it is included. Complete removal depends on mapping the tumour's full extent beforehand.

Nearly half had no symptoms, and about 58 percent were initially missed or misdiagnosed. Only three cases showed the textbook worm-like extension on imaging. MRI proved best at revealing the characteristic contours and vein filling defects. CT in its venous phase most clearly defined how far intravascular tumour reached. Both uterine and ovarian veins were involved most often. The single sarcoma stood out through much higher metabolic activity on PET-CT and a raised tumour marker. The authors recommend combining ultrasound with cross-sectional imaging.
pmc-13450006:
Chung-Kuan Wu and colleagues built a deep-learning model in 2026 to grade calcium buildup in the aortic arch from chest X-rays. Their transformer-based model, called MATM, uses multiple attention modules and a sixteen-block map of the arch to capture where calcium sits. It was tested on both the standard four-grade scale and a more detailed sixteen-grade scale, improving accuracy over manual-style grading in the authors' experiments. Radiologists gain a tool that could standardize a common chest X-ray reading and flag vascular risk more consistently.
pmc-13451206:
Hossein Khosroabadi and others introduced a beam-shaping method in 2026 that works from visible light up to hard X-rays. Tuning the undulator gap and monochromator settings lets users reshape the beam while keeping energy tunability. The approach adds flexible shaping without complex new optics or construction. pmc-13451506:
Pauline Pannenbecker and eight co-authors compared two kinds of CT scans for lung arteries in a 2026 study. A newer scanner that counts single photons can take very sharp images of the lung's blood vessels. The team set those scans against standard dual-energy scans at one center.

More than two hundred scans from 2024 were rated by three radiologists. The new scans won on seeing small outer arteries, overall quality, and reader confidence. Top confidence was near total for the new scans and far lower for the old. Two sharpness settings on the new scanner scored much the same, yet one used less than half the dose. The authors say sharp mode is a clear step up for this scan.
pmc-13451606:
Özçıbık Işık and a multicenter Turkish team asked whether lung cancer spread to multiple N2 lymph node stations worsens survival versus a single station. The N2 nodes are the middle chest nodes. Overall survival did not differ significantly between single and multiple station groups in the Kaplan-Meier comparison reported. What did predict survival was adenocarcinoma histology, overall stage, and receiving treatment before surgery. All were significant in the cohort analysis. pmc-13451806:
Wafira Wilson and co-authors ask in 2026 whether the heart rhythm at arrest shapes who gains from a heart-lung machine rescue. Those whose first rhythm could take a shock did better, at about a fifth, even though the other group had more witnessed arrests and shorter low-flow times. Survivors from the non-shock group stayed longer in intensive care and hospital. The authors say rhythm should weigh in rescue choices, pending larger work.
pmc-13451906:
Juan Sebastian Theran Leon writes in 2026 a letter that questions a study using heart-signal marks and a learning model to sort cardiology patients. The stated aim was to spot who needs top-level care, yet the model was trained on death and later heart events in people already sent to such care. That makes the task forecast, not triage, the letter argues. It also notes that no check was shown for how close the model's risk scores sit to real rates, and it urges a plain statement of intended use.
pmc-13452006:
Dou and Zhu take stock of dance based programs for mental health by reviewing the reviews themselves. Weaker review types were used to map how the field defines dance work and what it chooses to measure.

The field splits three ways, the authors find. Labels and delivery vary from formal dance movement therapy to vague group dance. Therapy reviews stress symptom relief, while others stress well being, energy, and social bonds. Most studies rely on generic mood scales rather than measures tuned to movement. On quality weighted evidence, dance programs show promise for well being, connection, and some symptoms, but low review quality and mixed groups keep confidence limited.
pmc-13452206:
Ruiming Du and co-authors build in 2026 a vision model that splits 3D scans of bare apple trees into single branches. Branch-level maps feed both breeding scores and pruning robots, yet common methods first round point clouds into blocks, which loses fine shape. Their model instead pours raw point traits into sparse block codes on the fly.

Tests showed clear gains over base models on most split scores. Those gains carried into farm tasks, with truer branch counts and pruning maps. The authors add a caution: scores tuned to plant work, not generic vision scores, should judge such tools, since a small vision gain can hide a big farm gain, or the reverse.
pmc-13452306:
Willem Geuskens and co-authors study in 2026 who gets back to work after a shoulder joint swap, and what helps. Their cohort held 103 patients under 63 with at least two years of follow-up, who filled work and shoulder forms. Two thirds made it back to work, at a mean of sixteen weeks.

Over half of those back went to their old job full time. Higher schooling, lighter physical work, sick leave under a year before surgery, and backing at work all tied to return. Age, sex, weight, swap kind, and problems after surgery did not. Returners also scored their shoulders better, a loop the authors say clinics can plan around.
pmc-13452406:
Michael J Wesley, William J McGarrigle, and Mark T Fillmore test whether rapid brain stimulation can be paired safely with a dose of alcohol in the lab. Their 2026 pilot study used short magnetic pulses aimed at the front left of the brain, a spot tied to self control. Ten healthy young adults took part in the blinded trial, which used a sham treatment for comparison.

Each person did a go and no go task sober, then again near peak blood alcohol after real or sham stimulation. Everyone finished both rounds with no serious side effects and no one quit over the stimulation. Alcohol alone raised the number of failed stops on the task. Early hints pointed to even more failed stops after real stimulation, but the group was far too small to settle that question.
pmc-13452506:
Stoess, Hannibal, and Greb show that a silicon atom's coordination number can act as a switchboard for molecules carrying two light-responsive units, a route toward multistate information storage beyond simple on-off photochromism. Their two silicon-based diarylethene Lewis acids close their rings one at a time under light, with coupling between the units changing as silicon binds four or five partners.

Adding a donor molecule let the team select single ring closure only, activate switching by wavelength, or shut photoreactivity off entirely, depending on which base was bound to the silicon center. Without donors, each closure step strengthened the molecule's Lewis acidity, culminating in the first photoswitchable Lewis superacid reported. Reversible silicon-nitrogen and silicon-oxygen bond swapping also let them reach switching-state distributions that pure photochemistry cannot exceed statistically. The authors establish valency control as a design rule for multiphotochromic systems.
pmc-13453306:
Bongiolatti and colleagues study separate lung cancers in both lungs, and ask which patients surgery on both sides helps. These cases are hard to tell from spread of one cancer, and operating twice demands a reason. Their 2026 study reviews forty five patients who had lesions removed between 2017 and 2024. It appeared in a fifth of patients. Every survival curve split on it. Patients with the feature saw survival and disease free survival collapse to zero, against strong rates without it. Adjusted risk ran several times higher. Checking for this spread, they conclude, should shape follow up after bilateral surgery.
pmc-13453506:
Benjamin W Sheffer, Verena M Schreiber, and Rachel M Thompson recount a three week traveling fellowship for children's bone surgeons across Europe in spring 2026. Every two years, the Pediatric Orthopaedic Society of North America sends three members to European centers, hosted by their European counterpart society. Their 2026 account moves through sites in the Netherlands and Belgium and ends in Sevilla, Spain.

The fellows watched new surgical methods, compared how each country's system backs patient care, and traded research ideas with host teams. Stays included a lake house near Amsterdam and a welcome dinner cooked by the European society's president. The trip closed with the European society's annual meeting. The authors frame the tour as time to think big with peers, build cross border ties, and urge the next group of members to apply.
pmc-13454206:
Heather Pathak and eight co-authors chart how Powassan virus, a tick borne virus, invades the mouse brain and what damage follows. The virus kills 10 to 30 percent of human neurological cases and leaves lasting harm in about half of survivors. Their 2026 study infects standard lab mice by four routes, from vein to skin, and tracks virus, barrier, and immune response over time.

Every route led to severe brain disease, with the virus spreading from the body into the brain in clear phases. Brain invasion came with heavy tissue change and a leakier blood brain barrier. Gene and protein reads showed interferon signaling, inflammation, and cell death programs switched on, with support cells activated and neurons dying. In survivors, viral RNA and mild inflammation lingered past the acute phase. The authors offer the full map for drug and vaccine work.
pmc-13454406:
Audrey Lavoie and Véronique Dubé built a web nurse plan in 2026 to lift activity and life quality in older heart patients. Steady activity past heart revascularisation aids second prevention and life quality, yet old-style heart rehab take-up stays low in older folk. The team built Changeons ensemble, a French web nurse plan.

Build work followed Intervention Mapping with a mixed planning group, starting from a needs trawl by book review and chats with ten older folk. Needs centred on news, drive, and self-trust, with a stress on one-to-one help. Aims and design followed the Information-Motivation-Behavioral Skills model. Nurses gain an easy, age-fit swap for old-style rehab plans.
pmc-13454606:
Abdulbasit A Darem and others optimized UAV trajectory and offloading in 2026 for intelligent mining with robust secrecy. Mining needs real-time processing of drone sensor streams under latency, safety, and energy limits, while eavesdroppers threaten data security. The team studied a dual-edge architecture with a ground base station and an aerial edge server serving aerial users, plus a protective jammer drone.

The system modeled 3GPP air-to-ground channels with probabilistic line-of-sight and passive ground eavesdroppers with bounded location uncertainty. A robust energy-efficiency maximization was solved by Dinkelbach, block coordinate descent, and successive convex approximation methods. Under urban macro calibration, the scheme reached 60.5 kilobits per joule at ten users, beating two baselines by 22.2 and 116.1 percent. Mining operators gain a secure, energy-efficient drone computing framework.
pmc-13455106:
Yuri A. Mastrikov and seven colleagues compute, in a 2026 theory study, how swapping one atom for another changes the electronics of a layered iron oxide. The material family matters for fuel cells and catalysts. Lanthanum was substituted for strontium across the full range, and the results were set against a sister material that instead loses oxygen.

Both routes raise the iron oxidation state by the same average amount. Yet the electron behavior differs sharply. The lanthanum version keeps its electrons more spread out and mobile. The oxygen-loss version distorts its lattice more, because each missing oxygen carries a double positive charge and breaks iron-oxygen bonds. A single-charge stand-in ion disturbs the structure less. The authors draw a general lesson: the kind of charged defect, not just its amount, sets a material's electronic character.
pmc-13455506:
Scott D. Wrigley, Sarah A. Johnson, Christopher L. Gentile, and Tiffany L. People with such disease often show poorer gut diversity, but cause and effect stay tangled. The combined data compared healthy volunteers with people showing early risk signs.

Simple diversity scores did not differ across risk levels. A stricter consensus method told a subtler story: as risk rose, a roster of health-linked microbes thinned out, including Akkermansia, Bacteroides, and Bifidobacterium. The authors propose that losing key microbes and their web of ties may help push early risk toward disease.
pmc-13457006:
Huixin Yu and seven colleagues report, in a 2026 case, a melanoma that began in the food pipe and reached the brain within months. Melanoma starting in the esophagus is rare, hard to cure, and quick to return even after removal. Their patient was a 47-year-old man who arrived with trouble swallowing.

Camera examination found several cauliflower-like growths in the mid-esophagus, and biopsy proved melanoma that had already reached nearby lymph nodes. Surgeons removed the esophagus. Follow-up treatment paired an immune drug with a targeted pill. Five months later, brain scans showed multiple spread spots. Doctors removed one cerebellar tumor, zapped the rest with focused radiation, and gave a chemotherapy pill. His decline was still swift, with body-wide progression, and he died ten months after diagnosis. The authors present the case as a measure of this cancer's aggression.
pmc-13457606:
Fan Lin and colleagues shine visible light on a shortcut to complex four-ring molecular structures. The reaction runs as a cascade: a light-driven [3+2] cycloaddition between the two partners, followed by a ring-closing step that locks the angular fusion in place. Earlier dearomative tricks worked within a single molecule; doing the key bond-making between two distinct molecules widens the menu of reachable scaffolds a lot. The authors present the protocol as robust and direct, giving synthetic chemists a shorter route into strained frameworks with real three-dimensional depth that medicinal chemistry prizes. The work spans photocatalysis, homogeneous catalysis, and synthetic methods.
pmc-13457706:
Lixuan Wang and colleagues go fishing for a blocker of TRPV6, a calcium channel that several cancers exploit to grow and spread. Their 2026 study lands on a candidate named AZ191 and moves it into electrical and cell-based testing.

Patch measurements put AZ191's potency against human TRPV6 at an IC50 of 3.83 micromolar, a strong showing for an early lead. In culture, the compound's anti-tumor effects tracked with its blockade of the channel, supporting the idea that shutting this calcium gateway can slow cancer cells. The authors offer AZ191 as a starting point for medicinal chemistry and further proof that TRPV6 inhibition deserves a place in anti-cancer drug development, while selectivity work remains ahead.
pmc-13458506:
Luis Posado-Domínguez and colleagues hunt blood DNA markers for immune therapy response in advanced lung cancer in a 2026 study. Immune checkpoint drugs help some patients with no-driver non-small cell lung cancer, yet blood tumour mutation load predicts inconsistently. Thirty-seven first-line patients had starting plasma ctDNA whole-exome reads through an AI-enabled workflow, with grouping by PD-L1 status and progression-free survival.

Median blood mutation load was 12.31 mutations per megabase, linked with high PD-L1 and gland cancer but not survival, and it sorted response poorly. Grouping flagged often changed genes, and in adjusted models CYP4F2 and TPSB2 flagged shorter overall survival on their own, with CYP4F2 also flagging shorter time without worsening. The early study nominates new possible markers, pending larger checks.
pmc-13458706:
Vallabh Suresh and colleagues pilot a platinum-methionine cure for lethal cyanide poisoning in pigs in a 2026 study. Cyanide, widely used at work, can kill rapidly, and approved cures need into-vein drips in hospitals, leaving mass-casualty gaps. Sedated pigs received lethal potassium cyanide drip until six minutes after breathing stopped. They then got into-vein or into-muscle platinum mix or vehicle, with vital signs and blood markers tracked beyond 90 minutes.

Into-vein cure rescued every pig in its group and reversed lactate and blood oxygen upsets. Into-muscle cure did not clearly improve survival, owing to only 7 percent body-wide uptake. The pilot proves into-vein power in a large animal model, but the field need remains a form that works fast, since into-muscle giving now fails.
pmc-13459406:
Alejandro Álvarez-Bustos and colleagues examine how muscle loss, heavy weight and their pairing shape frailty change and death in a 2026 cohort study. Muscle loss with heavy weight had been largely ignored in frailty shifts, despite both conditions predicting daily-life decline. The look-back cohort covered 1,538 home-living adults aged 65 and older, with frailty scored by two scales and follow-up medians of 2.99 years for shifts and 6.29 years for death.

Muscle loss with heavy weight always predicted frailty decline and lowered the chance of undoing early frailty, while muscle loss alone and heavy weight alone also raised decline rates. No group predicted death on its own once frailty status was counted in. Doctors gain a clearer target: keeping muscle and watching weight together may slow daily-life decline, even if death risk tracks frailty itself.
pmc-13459506:
Yike Su and co-authors built two genetic transformation systems for peach, a fruit tree whose genes have been hard to study because no efficient method existed for inserting DNA. Their 2026 work used a soil bacterium, Agrobacterium rhizogenes, on stem pieces of the Hanlumi cultivar. Tuning the bacterial strain and dose produced transgenic callus tissue and hairy roots with stable marker expression. A second, faster system delivered genes temporarily into stem and fruit callus, letting the team test flavor genes within weeks.

Both systems were put to work on the pathway making C6 aldehydes, the green, fresh smelling compounds behind peach aroma. Boosting the genes PpLOX1 or PpHPL1 significantly raised hexanal and E-2-hexenal levels in the callus. Silencing PpLOX6 or PpHPL1 markedly lowered them instead. The paired results confirm all three genes as key controls of peach flavor chemistry and give breeders working tools.
pmc-13459606:
Shuyan Qin, Nana Zhao, Lei Shen, Yanan Zhang, and Shengfang Ge survey in 2026 how language-processing tools that also read images could change eye care. Ophthalmology generates both narrative clinical text and detailed pictures, and combining the two promises better diagnosis and smoother workflows. Their review covers transformer models for text, for images, and for linking the two kinds of information together.

Uses fall into three groups: merging text and images for fuller analysis, stronger screening and prediction systems, and clearer communication with patients. Obstacles include privacy, specialized vocabulary, opaque model reasoning, uneven data formats, and regulatory proof. The authors point to few-shot learning, real-time systems, and privacy-preserving training across sites as promising directions needing joint effort from clinicians and developers.
pmc-13461106:
Georgios Karamitros and colleagues used in 2026 artificial intelligence tools to audit racial representation across plastic surgery publishing over twelve years. Web scraping gathered authorship data from twenty-four journals between 2010 and 2022, covering more than sixteen thousand publications, and a name-classification program trained on census data inferred each author's race. Patterns in first and senior authorship, mentoring pairings, and output per author were compared.

White researchers dominated throughout, holding about two thirds of first authorships and nearly three quarters of senior slots by 2022. Black authorship fell over the period while Asian representation grew on both ends of the byline. White authors also published more papers per person than Asian, Black, or Hispanic colleagues. Black senior authors mentored across racial lines most often, and the authors urge earlier pipeline support.
pmc-13461506:
Vardhan and colleagues built in 2026 an explainable decision support system that classifies flatfoot, a foot deformity where the inner arch drops or vanishes, from foot images. They compared classic machine learning fed with hand-crafted texture features against deep learning networks, testing many of each. Careful subject-wise validation kept the same person out of both training and test sets.

Vardhan found the classic random forest reached only about seven in ten correct. A deep network, ResNet101V2, averaged about 93 percent accuracy, with its best single run near 98 percent. A hybrid that fed deep features into a decision tree did better still, at 97 percent accuracy with perfect specificity in their test. Explanation maps showed the models looked at the arch and heel for flat feet, matching clinical logic. The authors back the hybrid for screening use.
pmc-13461606:
Liu and colleagues present a 2026 case report and review tackling a diagnostic puzzle between two look-alike blood cancers. Chronic myeloid leukemia in megakaryocytic blast crisis and a rare acute leukemia both carry the Philadelphia chromosome and produce the same platelet forming blasts. The first is very rare, under three percent of chronic myeloid cases.

Their patient fitted chronic myeloid leukemia in blast phase best and got a targeted kinase inhibitor plus chemotherapy induction and consolidation. Liu reports complete remission and then deep molecular remission held for thirty-five months, even though stem cell transplantation was declined for cost reasons. The review draws out signs that tell the two apart, such as prior disease history and spleen and blood patterns. A diagnostic and treatment framework is offered.
pmc-13461706:
Xiaoli Yang and co-authors present a 2026 computer method for turning brain waves into sentences. Reading language from scalp recordings is hard: the signals are weak and noisy. Rather than recovering a sentence word for word, the team argues the signal holds only core meaning points. Their system, named Brain-CLIPLM, works in two stages matched to that limited scale.

First, a learning step aligns brain patterns with a set of keywords and pulls out meaning anchors. Next, a large language model uses those anchors, guided by reasoning prompts and similar stored examples, to rebuild a sentence. On a Zurich test set, the system placed the sentence in its top five guesses two thirds of the time. Control tests showed the anchors added sentence detail beyond what the language model alone could guess. The authors frame brain-to-text work as meaning recovery first, wording second.
pmc-13461806:
Gao and colleagues pooled in 2026 the evidence on the prognostic nutritional index for liver cancer patients having part of the liver removed. The index blends a blood protein level with a white cell count to reflect nutrition and immune state. The team searched four databases to April 2026 for studies linking the index, measured before surgery, to survival after curative liver resection.

Gao included 16 studies and found patients with a higher index lived longer on every measure. Their overall death risk was less than half that of low-index patients, and disease-free and recurrence-free survival also improved. Dropping any single study did not flip the result. Signs of publication bias appeared for overall survival, but the link stayed significant after correction. Cut-off choice varied between studies and may explain some spread, the authors note, so the index suits risk checks beside standard tools.
pmc-13461906:
Giordano and co-authors analysed a 2026 cross-sectional dataset on verbal fluency, the ability to list words quickly by a starting sound, across adult ages. Fluency fades with age, but the shape of that decline and what modifies it were debated. Data came from the Look Up 8+ study of community dwelling adults.

Among 3,615 adults aged thirty to eighty, the median fluency score was ten words in thirty seconds. Giordano found performance peaked around ages forty-five to fifty and then fell progressively lower with advancing age. More education linked strongly to higher scores, as did healthy diet, physical activity, and normal blood sugar. Greater central body fat linked to lower fluency and steepened the age decline, while slower chair stand performance also tracked poorer scores.
pmc-13462006:
Fangfang Shen and co-authors used explainable machine learning on seven randomized trials to find which lung cancer patients actually benefit from immunotherapy given around surgery. Benefit varies widely, and straight line statistics miss curved relationships. In their 2026 analysis, multilevel meta regression was fused with a gradient boosting model interpreted by SHAP values, which rank each factor's contribution. The trials covered neoadjuvant and perioperative immune checkpoint treatment in resectable non small cell lung cancer.

Benefit on event free survival grew with PD-L1 expression overall. It peaked where at least half the tumor stained positive, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.44 in that subgroup. The machine learning view complicated the story: differences between trials drove most heterogeneity. The PD-L1 relationship bent into a U shape, with both very low and very high expression predicting benefit in some histologies. Squamous tumors stood out.
pmc-13462106:
Mizuki Sakai and colleagues test how assigned traits steer teamwork in language model agents in a 2026 study. Language models increasingly act as self-run agents in game settings, yet controlled evidence on trait steering was thin. Three models, GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4o and GPT-5, were scored on the Big Five quiz, then played repeat Prisoner's Dilemma games under baseline and trait-informed conditions, with each trait pushed to extremes.

Kindness led as the teamwork driver across all models, while other traits mattered little. Stated trait information raised teamwork but also raised being used risk, above all in earlier models, whereas later models cooperated more pickily. Builders gain a caution: trait steering biases conduct rather than controlling it exactly.
pmc-13463006:
Yougen Xu and colleagues report a switchable synthesis making either ring-shaped lactones or three-membered cyclopropane rings from the same starting materials. Their 2026 chemistry study uses amide-bearing sulphur compounds as one-carbon building blocks.

Both product families, especially with amide groups attached, matter in chemistry and drug work but are hard to make. Reacting the building blocks with common alkene partners delivered varied products in good yields. The method tolerated many functional groups with excellent selectivity between competing outcomes. It even modified complex natural product-like molecules at a late stage. A machine learning model predicted yields for the cyclopropane route. Both pathways start with the same addition step, then diverge by ring size.
pmc-13463506:
Yuwen Shi leads a team that tracked porcine rotavirus A in Guangxi Province, in southern China, from 2022 to 2025. The virus causes gut illness in pigs and spreads through dung. The group tested pig gut tissue and fecal swabs, then read the genes of the strains they found.

About seventeen in each hundred tests came back positive, with the G9P[13]I5 type most common. The VP4 gene varied more than the VP6 and VP7 genes, and the team also saw gene swaps and shuffled segments. Growth of the virus pool stayed flat for decades, then rose slowly after about 2016. Pig vets and health staff gain a dated gene map for tracking spread.
pmc-13463606:
David Huang and a large team ask whether hormone-primed IVF cycles change the womb lining in ways that raise blood pressure risk in pregnancy. Clinics often prime the lining with hormones rather than relying on a natural cycle. The team built a single-cell map of lining tissue from both kinds of cycle.

Primed linings differed clearly at the gene level, with fewer uterine natural killer cells and weaker signals for embryo settling and blood vessel growth. Yet in 548 tracked pregnancies, primed-cycle conceptions showed no early imbalance in vessel growth markers and no extra cases of high blood pressure disorders. The womb, the authors argue, adapts well despite the early shifts.
pmc-13463806:
Yiheng Jiang and nine colleagues published this 2026 study developing a green ultrasound-assisted extraction for polysaccharides from Banqiao Codonopsis root, a prized Chinese medicine-food plant, and testing the product against ulcerative colitis. The standard hot-water method is slow, hot and wasteful, degrading the very compounds it extracts. The team optimised the ultrasound process statistically, probed how cavitation frees them, and compared yield and energy use against the conventional method.

At the optimum, 400 watts for 34 minutes, the ultrasound process yielded 21.31 percent polysaccharide, beating hot water by 42 percent, while cutting extraction time by 43.5 percent, energy use by 38.8 percent and carbon emissions by 56.9 percent, and stripping protein and nucleic acid waste more effectively. Ultrasound shrank the plant particles by about 22 percent and loosened the cellulose structure, easing their release. The authors present the method as the scalable, low-carbon route to producing this anti-inflammatory ingredient for functional foods and medicines.
pmc-13464506:
Gerlin and colleagues model the food fight between a bacterium and a tomato plant in this 2026 paper. The bacterium Ralstonia pseudosolanacearum causes bacterial wilt, a destructive crop disease. During infection the two organisms compete directly for nutrients. The team merged a genome scale metabolic model of the bacterium with one of the whole plant, then tuned it with experimental data.

Simulations predicted the flows of matter through the infected plant. The plant's photosynthesis limited bacterial growth more strongly than its mineral supply did. Falling water flow through the plant first slowed plant growth and later starved the bacteria. The bacterium also appeared to steal resources through the stem, though only to a limited degree. Gerlin highlights water flow as central to how this disease develops.
pmc-13465006:
Sang-Ho Jeong and three co-authors review bleeding care for gastric cancer, where tumor bleeding can kill quickly and stall all other treatment. Two decades of evidence feed a stepwise plan guided by how stable the patient's circulation is. Scope-based stopping of the bleed comes first in the plan.

For unstable patients or failed scope work, artery blocking through a catheter takes over. Palliative radiation offers a non-invasive route that can slow tumor bleeding over days. Surgery waits as the last resort when other routes fail. The review reframes success: halting the bleed only opens the gate, and survival turns on getting patients back to cancer therapy fast.
pmc-13465406:
Chatterjee and co-authors investigated a 2026 regulator of disc degeneration, the enzyme PHLPP1, in the nucleus pulposus, the gel centre of spinal discs. Degeneration there drives disc related low back pain through inflammation and matrix breakdown. Earlier work tied higher PHLPP1 levels to worse degeneration in patients.

In aged mice lacking the gene, age related disc degeneration and inflammation were blunted, most clearly in males, Chatterjee reports. Silencing the gene in degenerated human disc cells sharply suppressed inflammatory and signal recruiting genes such as IL1B, IL6, and several chemokines. Matrix building gene activity rose at the same time, shifting cells toward a less destructive, less tissue eating state overall. The authors position PHLPP1 as an upstream regulator of the disc's inflammatory networks and a candidate drug target for slowing degeneration.
pmc-13465506:
Mohammad-Taghi Majnoon and colleagues report a 2026 case of a 6-year-old boy whose Kawasaki disease attacked all three main heart arteries at once. Kawasaki disease inflames vessels in children and can balloon coronary arteries, but triple-vessel disease with a giant aneurysm is rare and severe. Standard immunoglobulin on day eight settled fever, yet scans later showed a giant left anterior descending aneurysm plus widening of the other two arteries.

A clot formed inside the giant aneurysm, prompting steroids, cyclosporine, infliximab, thinners, and antiplatelet drugs. Angiography showed partial flow past the aneurysm with preserved downstream supply, so surgery was deferred. Two arteries improved while the giant aneurysm and clot persisted, yet the boy stayed stable with normal daily life, showing drugs plus close watch can carry even severe cases.
pmc-13465606:
Charles Tremblay and co-authors report early work, published in 2026, on steering drug-loaded bacteria through tumors with magnets as a cancer treatment. The bacteria move on their own and can be guided, which sets the approach apart from a simple drug injection into a tumor. Reaching deep sites such as the pancreas and rectum needs image guidance inside a new magnetic setup.

The team lays out a full guided workflow, using endoscopic ultrasound or scans through the skin to place the bacteria. They frame the report as the first complete version of this delivery chain, built to settle the technical questions that a first trial in people would raise. Pancreatic and rectal cancers are the target diseases throughout.
pmc-13466406:
Jiangtao Hu, Byoung Ryong Jeong, and Qichang Yang introduce a journal special issue, writing in 2026. Now in its second edition, the issue covers how plants respond to light at the cell and molecule level. Light feeds plants through photosynthesis, yet it also acts as a rich signal that times flowering and shapes growth, chemistry, and stress defense.

Six papers in the collection range from small RNA signaling in maize to pigment metabolism, hormone shifts, antioxidant defense, and protection of the photosynthetic machinery. Together they show light quality acting at many control levels at once. One maize study found a small RNA's free levels changing with light through binding to a partner protein rather than through new production.
pmc-13466506:
Vladislav Kozák and Jiří Vala review local approaches for predicting how cracks start and grow inside structural materials, in a 2026 article. Rather than treating a part as uniform, these methods zoom into the stressed zone near a notch or flaw and let the tiny local structure speak. Modern statistics join the finite element calculations that engineers already use.

Three material families anchor the examples: metals where cracks begin around inclusions or grain boundary particles, fiber composites with strong interfaces, and hybrids of the two. Two-scale simulations, where small-scale behavior feeds a whole-part model, get the most attention. The review weighs hierarchical schemes, where scales pass results one way, against concurrent ones.
pmc-13466806:
Yachen Liu, Xi Liu, Hongmeng Ma, and Wenxin Li report a lung cancer that changed its tissue type during targeted treatment, an extremely rare switch, in a 2026 case report. The patient, a forty-five-year-old woman, had two years of cough, sputum, and breathlessness. Her cancer began as lung adenocarcinoma carrying an ALK gene rearrangement, treated with drugs that block that signal.

Under treatment the tumor transformed into pulmonary mucoepidermoid carcinoma, a type that normally arises on its own and makes up under one percent of lung cancers. Change into small cell cancer after such drugs is known, but this destination is almost unheard of. No shared guideline covers the mechanism or best care, which the report aims to start filling.
pmc-13467006:
Erin Tresselt Murray and colleagues study how heart-lung bypass during children's heart surgery splits two neutrophil weapons in opposite directions, in a 2026 study. Thirty-nine children from one day to four years old gave blood before bypass and a day after it. Bypass sent neutrophil counts soaring more than fourfold.

One weapon, the enzyme elastase, poured out more strongly after bypass yet did not forecast organ damage. The other, web-like traps the cells cast to snare germs, fell sharply after bypass. Children whose cells answered weakly to a gentle trap trigger before surgery carried the risk signal instead. The split matters because blocking inflammation wholesale could block a useful arm along with a harmful one.
pmc-13469106:
Thibaut Bourdin and co-authors probe how a vitamin-linked enzyme places methyl marks with a chosen hand in a 2026 study. The enzyme serves a methane-making protein, adding a mark to one of its parts. Its kin can tag plain carbons and pick left from right forms, but what steers the pick was murky.

Tests on several forms of the enzyme split them by how well they grip the vitamin. The steps of grabbing a hydrogen and handing off the methyl run apart, not as one move, so the parts must shift inside the enzyme. The enzyme also made odd marks, flipped forms, and turned one small part into its mirror twin.
pmc-13469206:
Martinelli and co-authors reviewed in 2026 evidence tying hearing loss in old age to cognitive decline and dementia, under the title the sound of silence. Cognitive impairment affects about 6.5 percent of people over 65, with no treatment reversing it. Hearing loss rises steeply with age, up to 40 percent past 65 and 75 percent past 80. The review covers ear-level damage and the brain's central processing of sound, plus screening tests from questionnaires to sound-booth audiometry.

Several paths may link the two: straining to hear loads the brain's thinking budget, and deafness breeds social isolation, itself a dementia risk. Central processing faults grow more important in later stages of age-related loss. The practical message is hopeful: hearing aids may delay decline, not just ease disability, and they lighten caregiver burden by restoring communication. Paired with cognitive training, correction of hearing is presented as one of the few levers available for prevention.
pmc-13469906:
Alsanousi and Prabhu review ways to measure mental workload from body signals in this 2026 paper. Cognitive load, the mental effort a task demands, affects safety and learning in jobs like flying and surgery. Self-reports miss quick changes during a task. So the authors assessed signals that sensors can track without entering the body. These included heart activity, brain waves, eye movements, and skin conductance.

The review drew on 37 sources published between 2021 and early 2026, including 25 original studies. Heart measures appeared most often, in 16 of the 25 studies, followed by brain-wave recording in 11. Brain signals linked most directly to mental effort but were hard to use outside labs, while wearable-friendly signals reflected general arousal instead. The authors propose pairing complementary signals rather than relying on any single one.
pmc-13470206:
Tianze Zheng built a flex force field in 2026 that bridges quantum maths to liquid traits without system-specific training. Tiny-particle motion needs accurate force fields, yet cost and fit trade off and one-size models lag. ByteFF-Pol, tuned by a graph neural network on high-level quantum data alone, predicts heat and transport traits for small-molecule liquids and salts.

The model beat current old and machine learning force fields on fit across tested liquids, using physically based forms and training plans. Designers can thus test new salts and custom solvents without retraining per case. The advance opens chemical spaces once out of reach to data-driven discovery of new stuff, from batteries to green solvents.
pmc-13470406:
Vicente P. Soloviev and Michal Krompiec used gate-based quantum machines in 2026 for large fund tuning. Old methods strain under wide markets, while quantum methods usually need one qubit per asset, passing current hardware. Pauli link code packs several values per qubit, letting a trial method tackle over 250 values.

A real market graph was split step by step into sub-funds of highly linked assets, then old follow-up built a reduced, tuned fund. The code lifts reach over old trial methods and opens gate-based quantum tools to real finance. Hardware limits remain, but the approach narrows the gap to usable quantum-boosted split.
pmc-13470506:
C Arvind Kumar and colleagues tested coal bottom ash in 2026 as a partial sand substitute in eco-efficient concrete. Thermal plants landfill most bottom ash, while natural aggregate mining depletes river and quarry sand. Mixes replaced river sand or quarry sand with ash from 0% to 100%, tracking workability, compressive strength, and split tensile strength over curing.

Workability fell as ash content rose. River-sand mixes stayed within about 5% of control strength at later ages, while quarry-sand mixes lagged 6% to 25% at 28 days but closed to near control by 180 days. Gradient boosting predicted strength best at R-squared 0.99 within the dataset. Bottom ash thus offers a durable, waste-cutting aggregate option, pending broader validation.
pmc-13470606:
Louis De Wispelaere and a large team published a multicentre study in two thousand twenty-six on draining the gallbladder with an internal stent. Gallbladder inflammation is normally treated by surgery, but some patients are too frail. Ultrasound-guided drainage through the stomach wall is a growing alternative.

Eighteen Western centres contributed four hundred ninety-six patients. The procedure succeeded technically in over ninety-eight percent and clinically in about ninety-four percent. The team tracked stent-related problems, repeat biliary trouble, and deaths over a median of about six months. Practice varied widely between centres. Statistical models hunted for procedure choices tied to better or worse outcomes. The authors aim to standardise a still-young technique.
pmc-13471506:
Tian and colleagues built a finer-grained way to record skin damage in anti-MDA5-positive dermatomyositis, an autoimmune disease where skin ulcers can signal lung danger. Their 2026 retrospective study coded ulceration, itch, and scale across seven body regions in 339 patients, distilled from 513 screened at one center.

Simple presence of any ulcer already carried information: it was linked to depleted CD8 T cells with an odds ratio of 3.35 in the screening analysis, and each additional ulcer site added its own association at 1.43 per site. Location mattered too, since facial ulceration tied to pulmonary arterial hypertension with an odds ratio of 2.28, stronger than total site count. The authors stress the framework is exploratory, not yet a validated prediction tool.
pmc-13472206:
Kanchiralla and colleagues wrote this 2026 correspondence criticizing a life cycle assessment of ship exhaust scrubbers by Stathatou and co-authors. The original study used a well-to-wake analysis. It compared burning heavy fuel oil with a scrubber, a device that washes exhaust, against low-sulfur fuels. It concluded the scrubber option could match one clean fuel and beat another. These authors argue the conclusion downplays risks to the marine environment.

They point out that the original figures showed shipboard impacts for marine ecotoxicity and nutrient enrichment several times higher with scrubbers, yet those categories were set aside as too uncertain. The letter also challenges a dilution assumption used to lower those impacts, asking why dilution should apply there but not to carbon emissions. They warn the framing could sway ongoing International Maritime Organization debate about scrubbers.
pmc-13472906:
Jagannath Jena and co-authors watch magnetic whirlpools form on their own, above room temperature and with no magnet applied, in a boron doped crystal, in a study from 2026. The whirlpools, called skyrmions, are tiny stable swirls of magnetization prized for future memory and computing devices. Making them usually needs a magnetic field and a prepared starting state, which complicates devices.

Using an electron microscope that images magnetism directly, the team saw skyrmions appear spontaneously in the doped crystal. They stayed stable over a wide temperature range, in zero field, and at varied sample thicknesses. A field cooling routine could still steer their density when control was wanted. Zero field stability at working temperatures removes a practical barrier for skyrmion based hardware.
pmc-13473406:
Bonilla and colleagues present a 2026 commentary arguing that Guatemala should tap its scientific diaspora, its trained citizens living abroad, to fix weak public governance. These expatriate professionals stay linked to Guatemala but work in richer systems abroad. At home, the authors describe an administration thinned by corruption, vested interests, and dysfunctional hiring that cannot attract scarce expertise.

The commentary calls the diaspora an undervalued, publicly unrecognized asset: brain linkage rather than brain drain. Structured ways to lend diaspora expertise, short missions, remote advising, and joint projects, could strengthen institutions without requiring permanent return. The barrier is partly design: government jobs pay poorly and hire opaquely, so even willing experts cannot plug in. Building clean channels for diaspora help is the authors' central plea for Guatemala's development.
pmc-13473506:
Villavicencio-Valero and Mondavi-Sobby simulated the early history of Saturn's moon Enceladus, asking how ammonia frozen into its south polar ice shell changes the moon's internal heating. Ammonia, detected in the moon's plumes at no more than 0.5% of their composition, lowers ice's melting point, and the authors tested two solid forms, ammonia monohydrate and dihydrate, across shell thicknesses and ice stiffnesses in 2026 numerical models.

The two hydrates behaved differently. Dihydrate widened the range of conditions allowing convection, the slow churning that redistributes heat, while monohydrate zones reacted more strongly to changes in ice stiffness and shell thickness. Both promoted pockets where melting temperatures could be reached without a globally molten shell. The authors argue that small chemical patches of this kind could explain Enceladus's lopsided activity.
pmc-13474506:
A worm illness from undercooked meat has one main drug, and it falls short with side effects. El-Sayed Abdel-Hameed and co-authors screened fig leaf extracts against the worm in work from twenty twenty-six. Seven fig species gave fourteen extracts in two solvents. Adult worms from sick mice were grown in dishes and dosed with each extract.

One fig species beat the standard drug on the dose that kills half the worms, with two kin close behind. Scope views showed dosed worms lost their normal skin build. Chemical scans of the best extract named twenty-six compounds. Early screens tied the punch to plant phenol content. Computer checks backed the lab story. The work marks fig leaves as a lead worth animal tests.
pmc-13474606:
Minghui Yu and co-authors test lung washing as an add-on care in 2026 for hard-to-control allergic asthma. The wash, done through a scope, clears mucus and debris from airways. Patients treated from 2021 to 2024 got either standard inhaler-based care or the wash on top. Symptom scores, lung tests, and side effects were compared between groups.

The wash group gained more on symptom scores and on small airway measures. Gains were largest in patients whose lung scores started worst. A breath marker of airway inflammation did not differ between groups, and side effects stayed similar. Fluid from the wash also revealed which germs were present, guiding later care.
pmc-13475706:
Alejandro Ugarte Lastra led a large team comparing stomach infection treatments in a 2026 study. Cure rates for this common bacterial infection have fallen as drug resistance rises. A simplified high-dose two-drug course is a candidate to replace the standard three-drug course. Their study followed patients in routine practice at several centers, with treatment chosen by each doctor.

Among patients who completed the follow-up breath test, cure rates were nearly equal, at about four in five for both courses. Adherence was somewhat lower on the two-drug course, and side effects somewhat more common, though neither gap was firm. Extra analyses checked the effect of missed follow-up tests.
pmc-13476006:
Zhe Li and co-authors predict grave outcomes for heart and lung emergency callers from the free words in dispatch notes, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Dispatch choices rest on thin fixed fields, yet callers' own words may hold extra risk clues. Records from Nanning, China, from two thousand twenty-one to two thousand twenty-five supplied the data.

Models trained on earlier years were tested on the newest year alone. Adding note words lifted accuracy a lot over fixed fields alone, and joining both gave a small extra gain. The top tenth of flagged cases held about a third of all grave outcomes. Results held across age and sex groups. Readers see dispatch text as a rich early risk source.
pmc-13477306:
Francesco Cribari and colleagues report in 2026 on heart muscle biopsies in cancer patients with suspected heart inflammation from immune checkpoint inhibitor drugs. The patients came from a prospective fast-track cohort for people with possible heart problems during this cancer treatment. Biopsy was used when the diagnosis stayed uncertain or when results would change cancer care decisions.

Forty-eight of 175 patients had a biopsy, with tissue samples read without knowledge of their clinical details. The team compared biopsy findings with symptoms, blood tests, heart tracings, and magnetic resonance scans. Most patients were women, and breast cancer was the most common cancer in the group. The study maps how definite inflammation on biopsy lines up with scan and clinical features, which may help doctors judge when biopsy adds real value.
pmc-13477406:
Hidetaka Suzuki and coauthors present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of quick stroke scales that ambulance crews use to spot large vessel blockages. These blockages need clot-removal treatment at specialized centers, so early field detection shapes where a patient is taken. The team searched English and Japanese literature from 2016 to 2024.

Forty-three studies qualified, and eight tools had enough data for pooled accuracy estimates. The Rapid Arterial Occlusion Evaluation scale caught about three quarters of blockages while correctly clearing about three quarters of other patients. A second scale, Field Assessment Stroke Triage for Emergency Destination, performed slightly lower on both counts. The authors also weighed how the tools would perform at different blockage rates, helping services judge the trade-off between missed cases and false alarms.
pmc-13478406:
Jepma and colleagues published a 2026 study on nursing assistants and end-of-life care planning. Advance care planning records what care a person wants near life's end. Certified nursing assistants know clients' daily wishes well, yet planning often skips them. The team interviewed fifteen assistants in Dutch home care and nursing homes.

Most assistants were not routinely part of planning talks with clients. Many wanted more knowledge and skill to join those talks well. Team culture could either open the door or close it to them. Close bonds with clients and families helped assistants speak up in planning. Time pressure worked against their taking part, the assistants reported. Training offers one clear fix for the knowledge gap found.
pmc-13478606:
Mivalt and colleagues created a pig model of hippocampal epilepsy in 2026, sized so that human brain implants can be tested in a freely moving large animal. Seven pigs received MRI-guided electrodes in both hippocampi and a thalamic target, then six were infused with kainic acid, a seizure-triggering chemical, and one with saline as a control. A fully implantable stimulator-recorder, built for humans, logged brain signals continuously alongside video.

Every kainic acid pig, six of six, entered prolonged seizure activity right after infusion, confirming the induction worked in all treated animals. Four pigs survived to long-term monitoring, and three of them developed spontaneous seizures, totaling 2,733 recorded seizures averaging 27.2 seconds each in the chronic phase. Tissue checks showed patchy neuron loss in the hippocampus, and epilepsy's global burden of 50 to 60 million people frames why such a testbed matters for new devices.
pmc-13479406:
Serhat Şen and Feyza Gülgel Şen published a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of platelet-rich plasma used during cesarean delivery. Wound problems follow up to 15 percent of cesareans worldwide. The plasma concentrate, made from the patient's own blood, carries growth factors that aid repair in other surgeries, yet cesarean trials had never been pooled.

Five databases were searched through March 2026 for randomized trials comparing plasma treatment with standard care. Outcomes covered scar quality on three rating scales, early wound inflammation scores, and the integrity of the uterine scar, including niche formation and remaining muscle thickness. Pain scores served as a secondary outcome. The synthesis gives obstetric teams a first quantitative read on whether this add-on step earns its place in the operating room.
pmc-13479506:
Nobuhiro Osada and co-authors measure repeat heart event risk in Japanese patients with acute and chronic coronary syndromes, in work from twenty twenty-six. Heart disease is Japan's second biggest killer, yet real world numbers on repeat events by syndrome type were thin.

A national claims database held about twenty-six thousand acute and sixteen thousand chronic patients, followed for roughly three years. One year risk of death, heart attack, or stroke hit about eighteen percent after a first acute event. It was eight percent after a prior acute event and five percent in chronic disease. In chronic patients, older men with past acute events plus heart failure, diabetes, and kidney disease faced much higher risk. Risk sorting needs sharpening, the authors say.
pmc-13479706:
Rayan Saleh Moussa and a large team of coauthors published a 2026 qualitative study of why Arabic-speaking cancer patients in Australia rarely join clinical trials. Arabic is the country's third most spoken language, and trial underrepresentation deepens outcome inequities. Rather than asking patients alone, the team interviewed healthcare professionals about the barriers and enablers they observe.

The study deliberately looks upstream, at social determinants such as language services, transport, work, and family structures, instead of blaming individual hesitancy. Professionals described how these forces shape every step from referral to consent. Their accounts identify service-level fixes, including interpreter integration and culturally matched staff. The authors frame trial diversity as a system design problem with named owners, not a community deficit.
pmc-13480106:
Fernando Fernández-Aranda and co-authors introduce a 2026 report on a new live-in unit in Catalonia for adults with long-standing eating disorders. The unit opened in January 2024 inside the public health system. Eighteen patients with anorexia or a related diagnosis stayed three to four months on average and completed clinical interviews plus surveys on health, mood, quality of life, and satisfaction.

Patients had been ill for more than twelve years on average and had tried at least three prior treatments without lasting gain. Almost all were out of work despite varied schooling, and other mental health conditions were common. After treatment, quality of life and body mass index both improved by clear margins. Satisfaction averaged above eighty-five out of one hundred, with warm written feedback to match. Early results hint that dedicated long-stay care can help a group that standard services often miss.
pmc-13481106:
Lisandro Torre and co-authors report a 2026 trial of webinar training for vaccine advisory panels weighing a six-in-one child vaccine. National panels must judge proof across many angles before advising health ministries, and demand for coaching has surged as panels multiply. A five-part online series ran from January to June 2025 for panels weighing a switch from five-in-one plus polio shots to a combined six-in-one.

Panels from thirty-two countries joined at least one session, and nine joined three or more, mostly from the African region with support from the Gavi alliance. Surveys and interviews rated the sessions as useful, with peer stories from other countries prized most. Panels asked for more hands-on guidance on cost and feasibility angles plus pairing schemes between countries. Flexible online cohorts may scale expert coaching faster than site visits.
pmc-13481406:
Rika Tanaka and co-authors report, in a 2026 case study, an eight-year-old girl whose kidney disease was first blamed on the wrong condition. She had IgA vasculitis, a vessel inflammation that can involve the kidneys, but her kidney function kept worsening during follow-up.

Blood tests showed very high levels of antibodies against the kidney's filtering membrane, and a biopsy confirmed anti-GBM nephritis, a rare and aggressive attack. Despite plasma exchange and immune-suppressing treatment, her kidneys failed within months. The authors warn children's kidney specialists that worsening urine or function during vasculitis follow-up should trigger screening for this second disease and a prompt biopsy, not just watchful waiting.
pmc-13482206:
Mohammed Essa and co-authors review fat levels in the blood and the use of fat lowering drugs when patients reach hospital with a heart attack, in work dated 2026. Lowering one key blood fat is a base step in guarding against heart and vessel disease. The team asked how well that guard was in place at the time of the attack.

Records covered patients admitted from March 2018 to August 2022. Among those with no prior heart disease, most had fat levels above target and only a third were on statin drugs. Many who took no drug had in fact met the rules for one. Gaps also showed in patients with prior disease.
pmc-13482306:
Rathod and co-authors study a smart rubber in 2026 whose stiffness answers to both magnets and heat, a silicone filled with irregular flakes of electrolytic iron at 40 percent by weight. Unlike the round particles in standard magnetic elastomers, the flakes touch and grip more, which should sharpen the response to a magnetic field. The team swept temperature, strain, shaking frequency, and field strength across wide ranges to map the behavior.

Warming from 30 to 70 degrees Celsius softened plain silicone, dropping its storage stiffness 12.5 percent while its energy-absorbing loss measure climbed 67 percent over the same range. The filled rubber lost stiffness faster, down 18.9 percent, because heat loosened the grip that made the flakes reinforcing at cooler temperatures in the tests. The team also built a time-temperature master curve for the material and notes damping shifts with field strength too, pointing to vibration pads that can be tuned by temperature.
pmc-13482506:
Ajinkya Limkar and three colleagues reviewed in 2026 antifibrotic therapy for urinary symptoms from benign prostate enlargement. Over half of men past 50 live with these symptoms, yet drug innovation for the condition has stalled.

Searching PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov, they covered molecular, translational, and clinical work and built the case that prostate fibrosis helps drive symptoms. No antifibrotic drug is yet in use for this purpose, leaving fibrosis-driven symptoms untreated, though candidates exist for men who progress on current drugs. The review also sketches diagnostic studies that could spot fibrosis-driven cases for future trials.
pmc-13483406:
Chen and team tracked which viruses sicken Shanghai children, comparing those treated in clinics with those admitted to hospital. Their 2026 surveillance study enrolled 3,533 children under 15 in Pudong over two years, testing swabs for nine respiratory viruses. The aim was to see whether hospital and clinic cases are really the same illness stream or two different ones.

Viruses were found far more often in outpatients, at about 34 percent, than in inpatients, at about 20 percent of those tested. Flu and the COVID virus dominated clinic cases, while RSV, a virus dangerous to infants, leaned toward hospital cases. Infants filled hospital beds, while teenagers filled clinic visits. Even RSV subtypes split by setting, with different variants leading in each group. Chen argues prevention plans should be tailored separately for clinics and wards.
pmc-13483606:
Yahao Li and co-authors pool published results on deep learning for diagnosing slipped lumbar discs from medical images. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis searched major databases through March 2026 and kept ten retrospective studies with usable accuracy data. Magnetic resonance imaging is the usual standard, but human readings vary between observers.

Pooled results showed sensitivity and specificity both near 0.94, with a summary curve area close to perfect. Variation between studies was very large, so the authors treat the averages as exploratory rather than settled. Models checked on outside data lost some specificity compared with same-center checks. Differences in what models were asked to output also drove variation. At typical pretest odds, a positive result sharply raised the chance of disease.
pmc-13483706:
Qing Ye and others examine a plant compound, esculentoside A, as a possible brake on liver cancer growth. In 2026, the lab study tests the compound against hepatocellular cancer cells, testing growth, movement, spread, and stem-like actions, then checks tumour growth in animals. Computer analysis points to a protein called RORB as a likely target.

The compound raised RORB levels, dampened a growth pathway known as Wnt signal, and slowed cancer cell spread and tumour growth. Removing RORB reversed those benefits, while blocking Wnt restored them, backing a chain from compound to RORB to Wnt. Patient tumour samples showed lower RORB with stronger Wnt action and more advanced staging. The work offers a molecular route worth testing further, not yet a treatment.
pmc-13484606:
Yuye Zhang and six co-authors wrote this 2026 study on a protein pair that may drive liver injury in sepsis, and a drug that blocks it. S100A8/A9 is an alarm signal released by immune cells, suspected of feeding the neutrophil web traps that damage tissue. The team mined sepsis gene data, checked patient blood, then tested an inhibitor, paquinimod, in mice with abdominal sepsis.

Patient plasma carried high levels of the protein, highest in those with liver injury, nominating it as an early warning marker. In mice, blocking it cut web-trap formation in the liver, lowered three inflammatory cytokines, eased liver damage, and improved survival. Gene sequencing showed broad immune and metabolic shifts under treatment. The authors propose S100A8/A9 as both biomarker and target, with the caveat that the drug was given before sepsis began, a prevention scenario the clinic rarely enjoys.
pmc-13486806:
Khushi Goda and co-workers gauge how much blood pressure spread comes from genes and daily life acting as a pair. Most past work treats the two as split forces. This 2026 study uses 24,000 people of mixed roots in the UK Biobank. It sets them against 23 daily-life traits. Spread is split three ways for three pressure marks: genes, daily life, and the pair effect.

Pair effects held 7 percent of spread for the lower pressure mark. They held 4 percent for the upper mark and 3 percent for pulse pressure. The 7 percent share ran near twice the rate from a white British-only check run the same way. Still, the gap fell short of firm proof. A genome-wide hunt for pair effects found no hit past the strict bar. Mixed-root groups may show pair effects that flat groups hide.
pmc-13487306:
Hui and team tested whether a data pipeline can sort university sports departments into meaningful governance types instead of grading them on one linear scale. Sports governance juggles money, fairness, efficiency, and sustainability, which rarely peak together. Their 2026 study generated 348 synthetic schools by model run, seeded with four archetypes from resource-focused to balanced, then checked whether clustering methods could recover those types from the numbers alone.

Both clustering approaches recovered the four planted archetypes, confirming the pipeline works under controlled conditions. Nonlinear performance patterns emerged between the types that a single weighted score would flatten away. The authors stress the patterns describe their model run design, not real schools, since no actual institutional data fed the test. Hui offers the design for future use once real governance data can be gathered, positioning configuration over ranking.
pmc-13487606:
Keston Mwiwa Sinkhonde maps where Malawian households with young children fall short on protein and two key amino acids. Published in 2026, the analysis reuses the national 2019 to 2020 household survey covering 5,952 children aged six to fifty-nine months. Food records are converted through composition tables and adult-equivalent scaling, then judged against international thresholds and plotted by district.

Shortfalls in usable lysine topped 40 percent in every Central Region district, with seven of thirteen Southern districts also above that line. Usable protein inadequacy followed the same central-then-southern geography. Total amounts looked better than usable amounts, since plant-heavy diets limit amino acid availability. District-level targeting beats national averages for nutrition programs, and lysine emerges as the quiet bottleneck nutrient.
pmc-13487906:
Zsolt Molnar and fellow specialists offer a 2026 position statement on hemoadsorption for septic shock, a severe form of sepsis where blood pressure falls dangerously. The treatment passes blood through a cartridge that removes cytokines and other signals driving harmful inflammation. The authors review why the idea is appealing, given the mix of excessive and suppressed immune activity in sepsis.

Evidence so far comes mostly from small studies, registries, and mixed patient groups, so firm guidance is still lacking. The statement stresses careful patient choice, timing, and treatment intensity rather than routine use for everyone. Readers get a clear map of what is known, what remains uncertain, and where larger trials are needed.
pmc-13488206:
Gabriela Reka and colleagues review chromosome microarray results in children with autism at a hospital in Lublin, Poland, in a 2026 retrospective study. The test finds tiny missing or extra DNA segments that standard chromosome views miss. Records covered 234 children diagnosed between 2012 and 2024, and the team grouped results by type, likely importance for development, and the genes involved.

About fifty-nine percent of children had a normal result on this test. Single extra segments and single deletions were the most common abnormal patterns, and several DNA changes together appeared in about thirteen percent. Clearly disease-causing findings explained roughly nine percent of cases. Certain regions recurred, including one tied to brain signaling genes. Clustering split the uncertain findings into distinct subgroups for follow-up.
pmc-13488706:
Manar Al-Lawama and six co-authors survey how role models shape medical learners in Jordan, in a research paper from 2026. Learning from a respected clinician helps students form their professional identity and pick a specialty. The team asked whether that still holds as teaching moves online.

Nearly nine hundred students and doctors at all career stages replied. Most said they had a role model. Deep knowledge and respect for students were the traits named most often. People often chose role models in their own specialty, and male role models were common for everyone. The authors urge schools to make good role modeling more visible and more diverse.
pmc-13489206:
Zhu and a team in China traced in 2026 a chain that turns eye lining cells rogue and lays scar mats under the retina. The scar state is a grave snag of wet age linked macular disease, where sight fades fast. A fat signal dock, LPA1, sat high in scarred mouse eyes made by laser burns. The team raised or cut each link of the chain in cells and mice to test its pull.

More LPA1 drove the lining cells to shed their sheet form and crawl, the first steps of scar work. The dock acts through two aides: it lifts USP1, a tag stripper, which then shields ZEB1, a form switch, from the cell's shred bin. Cut either aide, and the rogue turn stalled. A drug that blocks LPA1, BMS-986278, curbed scar growth in mice more than it curbed leaky vessel growth.
pmc-13490506:
Maoudj and colleagues presented SPINDER, an open-source six-legged robot with eighteen movable joints built for reproducible insect-like locomotion research. Legged robot studies are hard to replicate when every lab builds its own machine. Their 2026 platform prints its body from plastic and drives legs with hobby servos. It senses the world with a depth camera, an inertial unit, and foot contact switches, while a pattern-generator controller coordinates the legs like a nervous system.

Hardware trials demonstrated stable tripod, ripple, and wave gaits, plus walking in any direction on command. The robot switched gaits smoothly, settling within about two gait cycles of each transition. It crossed structured uneven ground with height changes up to eighteen millimeters, completing every run with body pitch staying under five degrees. All designs and code are published for other labs.
pmc-13491806:
Yahao Li and five colleagues test in 2026 whether ordinary smartphone videos from clinic visits can reveal walking patterns tied to specific gene defects. The condition is osteogenesis imperfecta, a brittle bone disorder of childhood. Pose estimation software extracted step and posture measures from outpatient footage of children with IFITM5 or WNT1 gene changes, with a COL1 group kept as a comparison.

Step width and trunk lean measurements stayed consistent when the videos were artificially degraded, a check on reliability. Children with WNT1 changes walked with a wider stance and leaned their trunks further than the other groups, and the gaps survived adjustment for age, sex, medicines, and surgery. Their surgery-free survival also ended earlier. A trial classifier separated the genotypes fairly well, and the authors propose video gait checks as a low-burden monitoring tool.
pmc-13493806:
Chen and colleagues aim to speed up aircraft design by teaching a neural network to predict airflow over folding-wing aircraft. These planes change wing shape in flight to suit different missions. The usual tool, computational fluid dynamics, simulates air in fine detail but takes heavy computing time. The 2026 team generated training data with fluid simulations using moving meshes, then trained an improved PointNet++ model, a network that reads three-dimensional point clouds, to map wing shape onto surface pressure.

Once trained, the network produced pressure maps in seconds rather than the long runs full simulations need. Its predicted lift coefficient, the number describing how much upward force the wing generates, stayed within a small margin of the simulation results across test cases. The authors present the approach as a rapid screening tool that lets engineers test many wing shapes and reserve expensive simulations for the most promising designs.
pmc-13495006:
Mariana Araujo-Pereira and five co-authors review the tangled overlap of tuberculosis and diabetes, in a 2024 paper. Diabetes is a named driver of the global tuberculosis epidemic. The pairing concentrates in poorer countries. Chronic inflammation links the two diseases mechanistically. Together they worsen patient outlooks beyond either alone.

The review spans population patterns, clinical care, and inflammation biology. Transmission dynamics shift when diabetes raises susceptibility. Diagnosis gets harder as symptoms and tests interact. Treatment plans collide over drug effects and glucose control. The authors synthesize a fresh view of the combined burden. Policy should treat the pair as one problem, they argue. Integrated screening in clinics is a natural first step. Research gaps on shared inflammation pathways are flagged for funders.
pmc-13495306:
Yi Zhang and colleagues chart, in a 2026 study, multifocal germ cell tumors inside the skull, a rare form that strikes in two or more brain spots at once. Proof on this variant was thin, so the team reviewed 48 patients treated at one center across two decades. They logged symptoms, scans, tissue type, treatment, and survival.

Patients were mostly boys and young men, with a median age of thirteen. Excess thirst and urine from hormone failure was the top symptom, then weakness on one side. Two thirds had the germinoma tissue type, and over half got combined chemotherapy and radiation. Ten-year survival ran high, though freedom from return was lower, and worse than for single tumors. Germinoma type and combined treatment went with better outcomes, while immune cells inside the tumor marked worse ones. The authors back tissue-led, combined treatment for this rare disease.
pmc-13495506:
Temitayo Moyosore Adebisi and colleagues test, in a 2026 study in southwest Nigeria, whether a single teaching session can lift body and sexual functioning in women treated for cervical cancer. Care for survivors' daily quality of life lags behind prevention campaigns.
