A camera check confirmed squeezed airways. Surgeons untwisted the lobes and removed the damaged tissue. Fluid later built up and needed a second procedure, after which he recovered well.
pmc-13545406: Cao and a large group of co-authors set out general requirements for a lab test that hunts leftover stem cells in cell products grown for therapy. Even tiny traces of undifferentiated stem cells can pose a safety risk, so makers need sensitive checks. The document frames the probe-based PCR assay as an ultra-trace measurement, where the detection limit supports a yes-or-no judgment. It calls for markers specific to stem cells and proper reference controls. The requirements adapt to products grown from many stem cell sources.
pmc-13546006:
Michelle Hsu and co-authors present a 2026 study on a nanoparticle that soaks up a cancer shield in the blood. A protein called PD-L1 helps tumors block immune attack. A soluble form floats in blood, drives drug resistance, and marks a worse outlook. The team built engineered particles that capture that soluble form and remove it.

The particles cleared the protein from patient and mouse plasma in tests. In a mouse model with tumors that shed the protein, treatment slowed tumor growth a great deal. Killer T cells rose in tumor and spleen, while suppressive T cells fell. The authors say the platform could restore immune control in resistant cancers. The work is preclinical.
pmc-13546706:
Mohammed Babatunde Sadiq and colleagues ran a 2026 pilot study on whether routine hoof trimming stresses dairy cows that are not lame. Twenty healthy cows with normal gait and no hoof lesions were split into a group trimmed by the standard five-step Dutch method. A control group was only restrained as if trimmed. Blood cortisol, walking scores, time spent lying, feeding, and standing, plus milk yield, were tracked over two days.

Cortisol rose in both groups right after handling, showing restraint alone is stressful, yet trimmed cows kept higher cortisol and lay down more on the following two days. Walking scores and milk yield did not differ. The authors conclude that preventive trimming itself can cause short-term stress, and that letting cows rest matters for recovery.
pmc-13547206:
Xue Zhang and colleagues reported in 2026 a rare eye infection caused by Nocardia brasiliensis, a soil bacterium, that was first mistaken for ordinary eye inflammation. A 67-year-old man had two months of recurring pain and redness in his right eye before his vision collapsed quickly and pus appeared inside the eye. He had no known immune weakness, though testing found previously unrecognized diabetes.

Fluid from the eye plus gene sequencing identified the bacterium. Antibiotics given into the eye and by vein, followed by surgery to remove the eye's gel and fill the space with silicone oil, still could not stop the damage. The cornea clouded and his final vision in that eye was only light perception. The authors urge early microbe testing in stubborn eye inflammation.
pmc-13547606:
Ke Xu and a large team of co-authors build a space-ready sensing chip in a 2026 paper. Watching the Sun and other celestial activity from orbit needs hardware that is fast, frugal, and tough under radiation. Wide-bandgap semiconductors suit harsh space conditions, but their plain transistors cannot compute. The team set out to give one such material a brain-like computing role.

Their device uses a phase of gallium oxide whose internal polarization can flip by atomic sliding. Built into a transistor, it senses deep ultraviolet light, stores states, and computes in one unit. The chip held up from deep cold to strong heat and under ion bombardment. A reservoir computing system built on it recognized celestial activity with up to 95 percent accuracy.
pmc-13547706:
A large team of co-authors reports a study dated two thousand twenty-six on gene silencing inside a crop pathogen. The pathogen causes clubroot, a disease that swells the roots of cabbage-family crops. It belongs to the rhizarians, a major branch of life where gene silencing by RNA interference was barely studied and might even be lost.

Sequencing small RNAs across five life stages found many silencing RNAs of a characteristic size and pattern. The genome held two working copies of a key silencing protein but no copy of the usual cutting partner. A stand-in protein with a related part seems to fill that role, making the pathway unusual.
pmc-13548006:
Khanin Iamthanaporn and co-authors ask whether the second of two staged knee replacements hurts more than the first. Some earlier work blamed a sensitized nervous system for extra pain the second time. The team reviewed 155 patients who had both knees replaced in stages at one Thai hospital.

Pain scores came every four hours for three days after each operation. A mixed-effects model adjusted for opioid use and nerve block type. The second knee scored no higher than the first; the difference was tiny and not significant. Pain fell steadily over time in both stages. A femoral nerve block lowered pain. The finding calms a common patient worry.
pmc-13548206:
Ana Maria Sandoval Barrantes and co-authors study an online course that teaches Peruvian health workers about diabetes and insulin, in this 2026 paper. Weak training limits insulin use across the country. The state launched the course in late 2021 for staff in public clinics.

The mixed study surveyed all enrollees, then interviewed a sample in depth. Five hundred thirty-six workers joined nationwide, and about sixty-three percent finished. Acceptability answers and completion patterns were read together. The authors judge whether flexible, cheap online training can close a national skills gap, and what keeps workers from finishing their modules.
pmc-13548706:
Stanslas Avaga and colleagues measure how often chemotherapy damages the nerves of cancer patients at a Ugandan regional center, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Nerve injury from platinum drugs, vinca alkaloids, and taxanes can progress to weakness and disability. Over two months, the team enrolled 235 adults on chemotherapy at Mbarara Regional Cancer Centre, interviewing patients, reviewing files, and scoring symptoms with a standard twenty-item tool.

Nearly a third of patients had chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy. Odds rose with age past sixty, with a past episode of nerve trouble that had resolved before chemotherapy, and with taking other nerve-toxic medicines alongside. Only about thirty percent of affected patients received any treatment, usually nerve pain drugs or vitamins, while guidelines recommend a specific antidepressant the center rarely used. The authors urge closer monitoring of high-risk patients so treatment starts promptly.
pmc-13549306:
David Weinberg and colleagues report syntheses and structures of gold(III) complexes with bulky nitrogen ligands. Their 2026 paper covers three new complexes in the family. One ligand is a tert-butyl phenanthroline, the others quinolinyl amides. Mixing gold salt solutions with ligand solutions formed the products. Two complexes required loss of a proton from the amide.

Adding a mild base improved yields for two of the three. Crystal structures were assessed for each complex. Properties of the solids were characterized alongside. Reactivity patterns were examined for the new compounds. Such gold complexes interest chemists for catalysis and materials. Ligand bulk shapes how the metal center behaves. The work extends the map of stable gold(III) chemistry.
pmc-13549706:
Ryota Kitano and his seven co-authors report, in a 2026 case study, a young man's rare brain tumor that spread through the fluid around his spine. It then answered, for a while, to targeted drugs. The tumor type often carries a mutation called BRAF V600E. His also carried a second mutation linked to spread and poor outcomes. After three operations, radiation, and chemotherapy, the disease seeded his spine.

Spinal radiation came first. Then the team started a paired drug treatment that blocks the mutated pathway at two points. Scans showed the spread shrinking, and his symptoms eased. The reprieve lasted ten months before regrowth. He was still alive when the report was written. The authors present the pairing as a real option where no standard treatment exists, and they flag the second mutation as a possible marker for spread risk.
pmc-13550006:
Yunhee Kang and co-authors present a 2026 study of new mothers' sleep in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. Sleep in the first month after birth is shaped by feeding and night care demands. The results suggest new mothers' short sleep is near universal, not a feeding-style effect.
pmc-13550306:
Guang Zhang and colleagues dissect how the oyster mushroom defends itself against heat, in a 2026 molecular study. The team studied a gene for glutathione peroxidase, an antioxidant enzyme, and found it quiet during mushroom formation but switched on by stresses, heat above all.

The silenced strains stockpiled more trehalose, a protective sugar, and a scavenger that mops up reactive oxygen erased that buildup, tying the effect to oxygen signaling. pmc-13550406:
Ilaria Stanisci and colleagues gather the recent European evidence on air pollution and death from specific causes, in a 2026 review combining meta-analysis and meta-regression. Thirty-one studies from 2020 to 2025, including two large Italian projects, were screened, with pooled analysis possible for the fine particle studies. The team graded bias risk with an international tool.

Long-term exposure hurt more than brief spikes. Nitrogen dioxide tracked with the same three outcomes under long exposure, while coarse particles looked weaker and ozone evidence was mixed. pmc-13550706:
Erin Daly and co-authors measured how smarter nitrogen fertilizers and timing cut laughing gas from wheat fields, in a 2026 study. Nitrous oxide from fertilizer is a potent greenhouse gas. Soil nutrient supply rates were tracked alongside emissions.

Enhanced products cut emissions without costing yield. Inhibitor-based ones led: the nitrification inhibitor alone cut yearly totals eight to fifty-four percent, and the dual inhibitor cut thirty-six to sixty-four. The coated urea, by contrast, lagged. pmc-13551006:
Li Wan, Chao Huang, Tianlan Li, and Yanfei Ma study presenteeism among rotating nurse managers in western China. Their 2026 survey covers 97 managers across fifteen hospitals who recently rotated posts. Presenteeism means working while unwell, with productivity quietly leaking away.

The mean score on a six-item scale sits near sixteen, a mid-level impairment. Hospital tier, rotation frequency, health status, views of the rotation system, and prior consent all split scores significantly. Correlation and regression steps hunt the drivers. A sensitivity check adjusts for years in management. The authors aim the results at nursing practice: rotation schemes that ignore health and consent may cost the very output they seek to build.
pmc-13551206:
Venja Musche and co-authors report the making of a quality-of-life questionnaire in a 2026 German-language paper. The tool, called EMQoLI, is built for patients with melanoma, a serious skin cancer. Burdens range from drug side effects to money worries, and they differ by stage. A tailored inventory lets clinics track how patients actually feel through treatment and beyond. The study covers the tool's development and its validation tests.
pmc-13551306:
Bíró and colleagues present a 2026 longitudinal case study of how dreams changed during one year of psychotherapy with a 28-year-old patient. The patient had anxiety and depressive symptoms alongside ulcerative colitis, a chronic bowel inflammation. Five dreams judged clinically important were analyzed together with session notes and the patient's own associations.

Early dreams showed helplessness and sharp sensitivity to danger. Later dreams cast the dreamer as able to notice danger and respond in a more adaptive way. The authors suggest dream content can act as a sensitive window on improving emotion regulation during therapy, especially in psychosomatic care.
pmc-13551506:
Masahiro Asaka and co-authors track stomach cancer trends after a Japan policy shift in a 2026 study. In 2013 national insurance widened cover for wiping out Helicobacter pylori to patients with chronic gastritis found by scope. The team read national death and case data around that turn.

Yearly stomach cancer deaths fell from near forty eight thousand in 2013 to near thirty seven thousand in 2024. New cases also ebbed after a later peak in the national registry counts. Drops ran steepest under age 80. The authors treat the policy as context, not proven cause, and weigh screening and uptake shifts beside it.
pmc-13551606:
Ashleigh Bull and co-authors test, in 2026, whether an unfunded network of burn centers can jointly study older burn patients. Older adults are a growing share of burn cases and need special care, yet single centers are too small to answer key questions. Twelve North American centers agreed to pool standardized data on patients aged sixty and older.

The shared database holds more than sixteen hundred patients treated over three years. Typical burns were small, yet one in ten patients died in hospital and healing took a median of forty days. Most had one operation within days. The pilot shows volunteer collaboration can produce useful shared data without grant money.
pmc-13551706:
Liyuan Zhang, leading six colleagues, published a 2026 retrospective study linking a simple insulin resistance marker to death after bleeding in the basal ganglia, a deep brain region. The triglyceride-glucose index had no established relation to prognosis in this stroke type. The single-center study followed 282 patients for one year, confirming deaths by standardized phone follow-up and modeling risk with survival methods.

Forty-nine patients, about one in six, died within the year. Each standard deviation rise in the index carried a notably higher mortality risk in the reported model, with risk climbing roughly linearly past a cutoff value the authors identified. Adding the index to a basic model improved some accuracy measures but not others, a mixed result the authors report plainly alongside robustness checks.
pmc-13551806:

The finding refines the hormone control model.
pmc-13551906:
Pengfei Zhang, Wanning Huang, Qiang Li, and Xiuyun Wu published a 2026 study of men's curling at the 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics. They then modeled which signs predicted a win.

China leaned on attacking shots such as draws and hit-and-rolls. Medal teams mixed attack and defense with wider range. Medalists also landed key shots more often. One takeout type predicted winning strongly in the models. Sweeping success predicted losing, oddly. The team reads sweeping as a rescue move used under pressure, not a cause of defeat.
pmc-13552306: Filippo Migliorini and Nicola Maffulli wrote a 2026 editorial that pushes back on letters to the editor used as a main form of scholarly output. The authors see a shift: journals now field harsh letters from writers with thin or no record of first hand research. Such letters, they argue, pad a publication list at low cost while adding heat more than light.
pmc-13553506:
Dan Qi and six colleagues target nucleolin-driven cancer stemness in high-risk neuroblastoma. Event-free survival for high-risk disease stays near 40 to 50 percent, and relapse is typically fatal.

The team's earlier work tied nucleolin to upkeep of CD34-positive stem cells. Their 2027 paper reports that targeting nucleolin-driven stemness suppresses high-risk neuroblastoma in living models. The work points to nucleolin as a lever against relapse and resistance.
pmc-13554906:
Karl Chan, Louis Choi, and Kevin Kam write a commentary from 2026 on a striking case of a heart attack at age twenty. The young man they discuss had a blocked main heart artery and disease in three vessels. He also had a narrowed heart valve outlet and a genetic disorder that keeps blood cholesterol very high from birth.

The disorder, in its double gene form, is rare and often missed. With little working receptor to clear cholesterol, fatty deposits build up from childhood. Attacks can then strike in the second or third decade of life if the condition goes untreated. Chan and co-authors use the case to stress early diagnosis and firm treatment. They also note the care choices that such a severe, early case forces on a heart team.
pmc-13555506:
Clara Bueno Lopez and co-authors test whether a gas in exhaled breath tracks Parkinson disease risk, in a study of smoking. Their paper from 2026 uses a China cohort of over half a million adults aged thirty to seventy nine, signed up from 2004 to 2008 across ten areas. Smoking has long tracked with lower Parkinson rates, but the mechanism is murky.

Over about twelve years, 1,131 Parkinson cases and 2,949 cases of other nerve decay diseases were logged through death and health records. Breath carbon monoxide was measured at entry, alongside self told smoking. Risk models compared smokers and, among never smokers, breath gas levels, against Parkinson and other diseases. Known smoking linked diseases serve as a sanity check set.
pmc-13555606:
Sen Yan, Xiaohong Wang, Cai Li, and Rong Wang review smart gel systems for stroke treatment in a paper from 2026. Ischemic stroke unfolds in fast-changing phases, from oxygen burst to inflammation to repair. Single-dose protectants match that timeline poorly. Designs vary in how particles are trapped, anchored, or assembled in place. The goal is phase-matched care of the vessel and brain tissue together. pmc-13555706:
Alice Fraser and co-authors (2026) hunt for new antibiotics inside snake venom, as drug-resistant bacteria outpace the pharmacy. Venoms are cocktails of proteins and peptides refined by evolution to act on other animals' bodies, and some components kill microbes. The team screened fourteen venoms against two problem bacteria, Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae. Six venoms nearly shut the bacteria down. Filtering through dialysis showed the active agents in four were large molecules, above the cutoff size, not small chemicals.

The method is iterative: screen, split, test again, narrowing from whole venom toward single active proteins. Each round concentrates the search. The authors present the pipeline as a practical route from a feared natural product to candidate drugs.
pmc-13555906:
Abdirezak Mawlid Abdi and three colleagues analyse what Somalia needs to fold chronic disease and mental health care into basic clinics in a 2026 review. Medicines and supplies form the largest cost driver in the expansion model, reflecting years of chronic care. Gaps in financing and service delivery remain structural. The authors judge integration workable and frame it as the route toward universal coverage.
pmc-13556006:
Pelin Kiyat and Melis Palamar studied 524 healthy volunteers in 2026 to see how eye dominance lines up with hand dominance and eye structure. Detailed scans measured the cornea, retina, and choroid, while a separate device measured the length of each eye.

Dominant eyes also showed a thicker central cornea once strict statistical corrections were applied, with some retinal measures trending the same way. Choroid measures did not differ. The findings matter for clinicians who plan surgery or interpret scans one eye at a time.
pmc-13556106:
Xiaoyong Xiao and thirteen colleagues identified in 2026 a protein, tenascin C, that helps drive abdominal aortic aneurysm, the dangerous ballooning of the body's main artery. pmc-13556306:

pmc-13556406:

pmc-13556506:
W R Earley and co-authors analyze patient reported symptoms in a 2026 conference abstract on a depression treatment. The drug, lumateperone, is approved for schizophrenia and bipolar depression, and as an add on for major depression.

Eligible adults had moderate to severe depression and weak response to one or two prior drugs. Half received the add on drug and half a placebo for six weeks. pmc-13556606:
A large team studies genetic risk for a menstrual mood disorder in bipolar patients in this 2026 conference abstract. Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is more common in women with bipolar disorder and tracks with a harsher illness course, and its cyclic pattern echoes bipolar mood swings.

pmc-13556706:

pmc-13556806:

pmc-13556906:

pmc-13557506:

pmc-13558306:

pmc-13558506:

pmc-13558906:

pmc-13559106:

pmc-13559206:

pmc-13559606:

pmc-13559806:
Akrem Ahmed and co-authors reported in 2026 a case of a rare condition in which one side of the face slowly wastes away. The report also reviews one hundred cases from the past two decades. Brain and nerve signs, such as seizures and headaches, appeared in a share of those cases.
pmc-13560206:

pmc-13560406:
Exercise classes moved online during the pandemic years and never fully moved back, but what the people involved think of the shift was unrecorded. Convenience, flexibility, and company head the benefits, and leaders see a bridge for people the gym never reached. Training, guidance, and a sound business case head the enablers. The authors conclude online classes complement the hall rather than replace it.
pmc-13560506:

Keeping it active in young muscle was enough to impair contraction before much mass was lost, and over time it drove further loss. It also disturbed cell powerhouses and shifted gene activity toward an aged pattern. Blocking the protein in aged muscle improved some measures in their tests.
pmc-13560606:

Patients with the tick-borne fever were older, more often women, and showed more nerve symptoms and blood changes. The authors call the models proof of concept and say outside checks are needed before clinic use.
pmc-13560706:

The team catalogued the strain's antibiotic resistance genes as part of the characterization. The isolate now rests in a national culture collection for other researchers. pmc-13561006:
Cécile Bessat and co-authors study lung ultrasound training in Swiss emergency rooms in 2026. Lung ultrasound can spot pneumonia fast, but standard training takes long and slows uptake. After the course, the team tested how well the doctors could read lung scans. They also asked what blocks wider use of the method in daily work. Sites across many centers took part in the stepped trial design. Short training that truly works could spread a handy bedside tool to more emergency teams.
pmc-13561306:
Ruolin Wang and co-authors benchmark methods that merge single-cell gene data across species, a step toward comparing how cells work in humans and other mammals. pmc-13561606:

The United States dominates output, citation impact, and international collaboration in the country analysis. Themes shifted visibly from wire-guided localization and basic imaging toward precision approaches tied to chemotherapy before surgery. The most cited work is clinical, showing guidance improving surgical precision and margin control. The authors call for rigorous comparative trials and wider collaboration to standardize the new methods.
pmc-13561706:
Ling Du and Lei Wang present this 2026 case report on a rare kidney cancer, primary renal squamous cell carcinoma. It makes up under one percent of kidney tumors and has no standard treatment path. Their patient was a fifty-six year old man whose cancer returned soon after kidney removal.

pmc-13562006:

pmc-13562306:

pmc-13562406:

Trust in a gene test rests on how well the read covers the zones that drive care calls. The frame lets users set gene lists, cover floors, and variant sets. It then scores cover, pass rates, and call skill across test types.

Trials ran on a standard sample and on 665 clinic samples across six platforms. Two whole-exome sellers led on cover of known disease zones. One seller and the whole-genome run led on call skill. Labs can use the frame to pick platforms with proof in hand.
pmc-13562506:
Ahmad Sulaiman, writing alone, develops a volcanic rock into a copper filter for polluted water, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Copper from industrial effluent is toxic. It never biodegrades once it is in the ground or the streams. Adsorption can clean it up. But commercial adsorbents for the task are expensive to buy.

Pumice is porous, abundant, and cheap. Yet raw pumice adsorbs in a weak way on its own. Sulaiman prepared and characterized an ion exchanger based on Syrian pumice specifically. The review of past work shows chemical activation can raise capacity in such a stock. Local materials count for a lot in lands where imported resins strain budgets. The study sets Syrian deposits in place as a remediation resource for the land. Affordable water treatment often hinges on geology. It hinges on what rock a region has in the ground as it stands.
pmc-13562606:
Kun Yang and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, whether secondary-type mutations darken the outlook in a leukemia subtype usually considered favorable. NPM1-mutated acute myeloid leukemia often responds well, yet patients vary widely, and these extra mutations were suspected culprits.

The team reviewed 179 patients, weighing age, common partner mutations, and the secondary-type set together. Only age sixty or more and the FLT3-ITD mutation independently predicted worse survival. Patients carrying NPM1, FLT3-ITD, and DNMT3A together fared worst. Secondary-type mutations showed no survival link in the whole group or in risk and age subgroups, though few carriers limits certainty.
pmc-13562806:
Jianwei Wang and co-authors decode what drives people to pay for cancer screening in a 2026 study from China. Willingness to pay is a common lens on why screening uptake lags: if people will not pay, cost or perceived value may be the block. The team joins two classic behavior models, one built on health beliefs and one on planned action, into a single frame.

A staged survey in a cancer screening demonstration zone enrolled more than forty-five hundred residents, most around seventy years old. Questionnaires covered background, both models' measures, and willingness to pay. Layered models picked out the correlates, and a path analysis tested how the beliefs and intentions link in a chain. The map shows where health messages and pricing could move uptake together.
pmc-13562906:
Allege-Cudjoe and co-authors ask how ready Ghana's animal health services are for African swine fever, in a 2026 study. The virus has haunted Ghanaian pig farms since 1999, wiping out herds and livelihoods in wave after wave. The team surveyed and interviewed veterinary officers, farmers, policy makers, and community animal workers across the country's three belts.

Preparedness came out patchy: strong central laboratories, weak regional facilities, and farmers left too far out of the loop. Awareness of the disease varied, and misconceptions persisted. A fever this fatal leaves no slack; the gaps named here mark where money and training should land first.
pmc-13563206:
Rashmi Neginhal and Rebecca Rejo George review how the lack of gravity wears the whole body down, read as a web of systems. Their short review, from two thousand twenty-six, draws on flights, ground tests, and cell work.

No weight lifts the load that sets fluid spread, force sense, balance, and blood calm. The shifts do not come organ by organ; they spring from fouled talk across organs. Muscle waste starts in days, with strength lost first. Bone thins at a set pace each month at load sites, and does not fully come back. The heart reshapes, blood bulk shrinks, and stance calm fails on return.
pmc-13563906:
Sheng Zhang and co-authors tested a protective enzyme in retinal pigment cells under low-oxygen stress in two thousand twenty-six. These cells support the retina and are prone to damage from poor oxygen and oxidative stress. A chemical, cobalt chloride, is often used to mimic low oxygen in the lab.

They exposed a cell line to rising doses and tracked wound recovery and metabolic activity. A mid dose gave clear injury without the worst damage, so they used it for deeper tests. Stress markers rose and the enzyme's level fell. A drug that activates the enzyme improved recovery and restored its level, while a blocking drug made injury worse. The enzyme's detox role looks protective.
pmc-13564106:
Rodrigues and colleagues published in twenty twenty-six a genomics study of a burrowing bug damaging peanut crops in the United States. Knowing a pest's identity, diet, and movement usually takes slow field work. New threats, though, demand fast answers. The team combined gut-content DNA tests with population gene sequencing. They examined bugs caught in light traps near peanut fields. Two look-alike species turned up, not the single expected pest.

One species had never been counted a peanut pest before. Gut tests showed both species eat many plants, with somewhat different menus. Peanut itself was a rare item in either diet. Gene data showed weak spread over distance for both species. The authors frame the problem as a pest complex, not a lone species. Genomic shortcuts can speed responses to emerging pests.
pmc-13564506:
Eun Ha Kim, Jung Jun Park, Chang-Moon Lee, Hyeon Jin Kim, and Jung Sick Lee describe a sand dollar's feeding apparatus in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Aristotle's lantern is the jaw-like structure sea urchins use to eat; in Scaphechinus mirabilis its fine structure was unmapped. The team combined light microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and three-dimensional X-ray microscopy.

The lantern is a star-shaped calcareous assembly of pyramids, joints, and teeth on the shell. Each pyramid splits into two demi-pyramids with an epiphysis and a bump; joints combine ligaments and a rotula. A tooth is an elongated trapezoid, about four millimeters long, with an embedded part tied to ligament and muscle and a projecting part meeting the food. Its fifteen to twenty calcareous layers end in a worn tip. The authors read the tooth as specialized for crushing sediment and food particles internally.
pmc-13564706:
Roberto Castro-Gutierrez and co-authors probe how stem cells become insulin-making beta cells in a 2026 study. Grown beta cells could one day replace lost cells in diabetes, but labs still struggle to make them well and at scale.

Working in 3D floating clusters, the team varied the starting cluster size and each growth signal in turn. Cluster size alone strongly shaped how many beta cells formed. Some signals kept early pancreas cells alive without pushing them to mature. Others forced hormone traits but mostly yielded glucagon cells, not insulin cells. A few, among them retinoic acid and thyroid hormone, kept a key marker high while still giving insulin cells, a recipe clue for better batches.
pmc-13565006:
Xiao Lei and co-authors test recipes for better buckwheat noodles in a 2026 study. Buckwheat has strong nutrition value but no gluten, so its dough is weak and noodles are hard to sell at scale. Adding wheat flour and gluten may give the dough the structure it lacks.

The team compared six blends using two buckwheat types. They measured dough stability, stretch behavior, water binding, flour pasting traits, and the cooking and texture quality of the noodles. Wheat and gluten clearly improved dough strength, above all for the weaker Tartary type. One Tartary blend, half wheat flour with the higher gluten dose, gave the best cooking and texture results. The authors offer the recipe as a practical route to quality buckwheat noodles.
pmc-13565106:
Tara Coreanu and nine colleagues published a 2026 study on a blood score that may foretell outcomes in skin cancer care. The cancer is cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, a common skin malignancy. A drug called cemiplimab has changed its treatment, but doctors lack a good test to sort patients by risk before therapy.

Their score, called GINI, blends immune strength, nutrition, and inflammation into one number. The team checked whether the score, taken before treatment, tracks how patients fare on the drug. Patients across all disease stages were included. A cheap blood-based score could help teams choose who needs closer watch or stronger care. The study tests GINI as that sorting tool.
pmc-13565506:
Sándor Pál, Margit Solymár, and Hussain Alizadeh published a 2026 study of the long-term health of children whose parents took tyrosine kinase inhibitors for chronic myeloid leukemia. These drugs transformed the outlook for this blood cancer, but evidence about offspring exposed before conception or during pregnancy has been limited. Nervous parents need follow-up measured in decades, not months.

The single-centre study followed patients with chronic-phase disease who had a pregnancy, or whose partner did, in association with drug exposure. Offspring health was tracked through adolescence and early adulthood, with follow-up reaching 24.6 years. The authors describe pregnancy outcomes and later health in this cohort. Long-term data of this kind directly inform counseling for patients who want children during treatment.
pmc-13565606:
Qian Zhang and co-authors work out how to make antioxidant peptides from quinoa, in a 2026 study. Peptides are short protein chains, and some can mop up harmful oxygen radicals. The team used black, red, and white quinoa from one region of China. They extracted the protein, then cut it with enzymes to free the peptides. Eight candidate enzymes were compared head to head.

Black quinoa and one enzyme, alcalase, won the comparison. Fine-tuned settings of dose, time, heat, and acidity pushed the radical-clearing rate near eighty-seven percent. After cleanup, one fraction showed the strongest activity. Gene-style sequencing named more than fifteen hundred peptide chains with high confidence. Most held two or more water-shy building blocks, a trait common in such peptides. The authors offer the process as a base for quinoa health ingredients.
pmc-13565706:
Tingting Shen and co-authors test a fast light-based scan to grade Chinese yam before it is dried into slices. Yam types differ in sugar, plant compounds, and firmness, and those traits shape the dried product. Picking the right raw yam by slow lab tests is costly. Their 2026 study compares ten yam types.

The types differed in sugar levels, plant compounds, and texture, and traits linked to dried quality in type-specific ways. Models built from the light scans predicted sugar, plant compounds, and firmness with high accuracy. The best model pairings differed by trait. The authors say farms and factories could use the scan to sort yam lots quickly before drying.
pmc-13566106:
Raniah Aldekhyyel and co-authors ask smartwatch owners in Riyadh how willing they are to share the health data their watches collect, in a 2026 study. Sharing could tighten follow-up care, but trust decides whether patients agree. A questionnaire at a large public venue drew 391 adults, of whom 168 owned a smartwatch.

Among owners, 62 percent said they would share their watch data with care providers. The team modeled which traits tracked with willingness, from age and education to how the watch is used. The authors say clinics in Saudi Arabia can build sharing programs on this openness, provided privacy terms stay plain and consent stays real.
pmc-13566506:
Osman Görkem Muratoğlu and co-authors examine in 2026 whether flexible nailing restores the natural bow of the radius bone in children's forearm fractures. Union alone is not enough; the bow's size and peak location both shape forearm rotation. They reviewed sixty-one children treated with elastic nails, measuring bow size and position on X-rays taken after surgery.

Average bow size sat near the low end of the reference range. Bow position fell inside its range in about eighty-five percent of cases. Both measures were in range together in about half the children. Regression hunted factors tied to that combined result. Most patients were boys around eleven years old.
pmc-13566606:
Qianyi Dai and co-authors review microproteins, a hidden class of tiny proteins, in breast cancer in a 2026 paper. Breast cancer remains a top killer of women, and treatments are blunted by side effects and resistance. New scanning and computing tools have revealed small proteins coded by stretches once dismissed as non-coding.

Evidence now shows several of these microproteins steer how breast cancer grows and spreads. The review gathers what is known about their biology and catalogs those tied to the disease. It then weighs their use as diagnostic signs, outlook markers, and drug targets. The authors frame microproteins as an overlooked layer of cancer control with real clinical promise.
pmc-13566706:
Robert Balan and co-authors report early experience with an automated suturing device in heart valve surgery in a 2026 study. Minimally invasive valve replacement offers patients real gains, but stitching the new valve's ring in place through small openings is demanding. The device aims to place those stitches in a standard way.

The team reviewed the first 43 patients treated with the device from 2021 to 2025, covering mitral and aortic valve jobs. Every case was completed with the device, with no mechanical failures or stitch line breaks during surgery. Two patients died within thirty days from medical problems not tied to the device, in a group with high baseline risk. The report judges the tool feasible and safe in early use.
pmc-13566906:
Lingling Xing and twelve co-authors present a 2026 study of a prenatal screening failure flag and its link to poor fetal growth. The screen reads free DNA in the mother's blood. In about 0.2 percent of cases it fails because the mother's own DNA level runs too high, even after a second extraction.

From more than seventy three thousand pregnancies at a large center in China, the team found 102 single pregnancies with that failure flag. They matched them with 396 controls whose DNA level was normal. The main outcome was fetal growth restriction, where the baby grows too slowly. The study weighs whether the flag should prompt closer growth checks.
pmc-13567506:
Shuai Kuang and co-authors build in 2026 a membrane from a common water-soluble plastic blended with a salt made from humic acid, a natural material rich in chemical handles. A crosslinking agent ties the mix into a firm network. Such films could serve as farm mulch that breaks down and releases useful matter slowly.

Changing the blend ratio let the team tune strength and stretch. At a humate share of seven and a half percent, the film reached its best balance, with high tensile strength and good stretch before breaking. After two days, about two thirds of the humate had seeped out, showing it was held fast yet released in a sustained way. A standard release model fit the seepage curve well. The authors propose the film for further testing as a mulch material.
pmc-13567606:
Layla El Moussaoui and co-authors built a catalyst on biochar to clean a toxic pollutant from water, in a 2026 paper. The pollutant, 4-nitrophenol, can be turned into a useful drug making intermediate by a reduction reaction. Their support material was porous biochar made by heating sewage sludge and washing it with acid. Cobalt oxide particles were then loaded onto it at several levels.

Many lab methods confirmed the makeup and pore structure of the combined material. A statistical design varied catalyst dose, reducer strength, and cobalt oxide content to find the best mix. At the best settings, a small dose cleared the pollutant fully within five minutes. The tuned catalyst was porous, spread its active particles well, and stayed stable across reuse. The authors present it as a low cost option for this cleanup task.
pmc-13567806:
Zhuwen Yan and co-authors published a research paper in 2026 on keeping steel strip flat when a rolling mill squeezes it with extreme force. Under very high force, flatness control on a six-stand cold mill breaks down and wavy edges appear. The team replaced slow physics simulations with two fast learned stand-ins, trained on sampled process settings.

A combined search then tuned the bending forces on two roller pairs at once, balancing thickness spread, crown shapes, flatness error, and pressure balance. At the highest force tested, thickness spread fell from eighteen to six micrometers and pressure unevenness dropped by three quarters. Edge waves nearly vanished. The recipe offers mills a fast fix under crushing loads.
pmc-13568006:
When a power plant's sensors cry wolf, operators must guess fast: is the process broken, or is the data lying? Fuliang Ma and co-authors build a triage framework for that fork in a 2026 paper on energy systems.

A fixed detector first flags anomalies. Nine consistency checks, grounded in physics, then sort physical faults from measurement-integrity problems. On a chemical process benchmark and a wind farm simulator, cause attribution scored well above chance. Weighing the cost of each wrong response, the framework cut expected losses by up to about twenty-nine percent against blanket reactions. Matched pairs designed to be indistinguishable stayed at chance, an honest boundary: some causes cannot be told apart from data alone, and those cases go to human review.
pmc-13568206:
Zhengxuan Chen and Junming Chen recalibrate differential privacy for sensor streams that leak through their correlations, in a 2026 paper. Internet of Things data braid time, place, and channels together, so a release that is private on paper can still betray an attribute through the braid. Standard privacy guards a declared unit, which may be narrower than the secret that matters.

Their graph-calibrated scheme ranks each component's exposure on a lag-aware graph, then spends the privacy budget accordingly, with certified sensitivity bounds per coordinate. Tests on four public data sets show better task utility and weaker attribute inference than baselines. Correlation, long privacy's blind spot, gets priced in.
pmc-13569106:
Geovana Rocha Marzochi and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether essential oils from orange and citronella can act as natural weed killers, as herbicide-resistant weeds push farmers to seek alternatives. Oils made by two extraction methods were applied at several doses to seeds of four major weeds, and sprouting and early growth were measured.

Citronella oils nearly stopped seedlings from the middle dose upward, driven by compounds such as citronellol and geraniol. Orange oils weakened germination more gently and unevenly across weed species. The contrast positions citronella oil as a strong bioherbicide candidate and orange oil as a supporting tool in greener weed control.
pmc-13569206:
Javier Caviedes-Bucheli and colleagues review a little-studied brake on tooth pain: neuropeptide Y, a signalling molecule inside the dental pulp. The pulp is a densely wired, rigid tissue where inflammation can quickly raise pressure, choke blood flow, and cause pain. While two excitatory messengers, substance P and CGRP, are well known drivers of that spiral, neuropeptide Y's counterbalancing role has been underexplored. Their 2026 review synthesised 92 studies.

Across models, neuropeptide Y emerged as a master regulator that damps excitation, constricts vessels, and quiets pain-sensing nerves, partly by suppressing CGRP release. In decayed teeth its levels shift with disease stage, hinting at an early protective program that fails as damage advances. The authors frame pulp outcomes as a balance between excitatory and inhibitory signals, with neuropeptide Y as a potential therapeutic lever.
pmc-13569406:
Carla Teresa Palleis, Alexander Bernhardt, and Gunter Hoglinger review two brain diseases in a 2026 paper written in German. Both diseases are marked by clumps of a protein form called 4-repeat tau in the brain. Both slowly harm movement, balance, speech, thinking, and daily life.

One disease tends to strike the body axis and shrink a mid brain region, with a telling loss of up and down eye movement. The other tends to affect one side more, with shrinkage at the front and side of the brain. Since signs overlap with other diseases, telling them apart in clinic is hard. The review sorts the tissue facts from the bedside signs.
pmc-13569506:
Alayna Carrandi and six co-authors follow women's quality of life from late pregnancy through the first weeks postpartum, comparing paths by birth mode. It reuses data from a Queensland cohort of nearly twenty-nine hundred pregnant women. Each woman rated her quality of life at thirty-six weeks of pregnancy and again at six and twelve weeks after birth; ratings were converted to a standard utility score.

Scores rose on average from late pregnancy to twelve weeks after birth, whatever the birth type. Women headed for a planned caesarean reported lower quality of life late in pregnancy than women headed for a natural birth, even after accounting for social and economic traits. After birth, though, no clear differences by birth type appeared at either check. The authors call for work on supporting women at risk of low quality of life around birth.
pmc-13569606:
Xiao Wu, Duo Jiang, and Bin Li build, in a 2026 retrospective study, prediction models for complete tumor disappearance after immune therapy given before lung cancer surgery. Two established markers, a tumor protein level and the number of tumor mutations, were combined with clinical features in 232 surgical patients, then checked in 115 later patients at the same hospital.

Combined immune therapy with chemotherapy strongly raised the odds of complete response, as did higher marker levels, while nodal spread lowered them. A paper chart and a machine-learning model were both built and graded for accuracy and calibration. Such tools could help surgeons and patients judge who gains most from pre-surgery immune treatment.
pmc-13570106:
Bryan Khoo and a team of co-authors model how the kneecap groove in the thigh bone grows during the teen years in a 2026 paper. A shallow groove is a main risk factor for kneecap dislocation, and fixing it by surgery can harm the growth plate in young patients. Safer choices need a clear map of how the groove and growth plate change with age and sex.

The team study hundreds of knee scans from people aged eight to twenty-two, using a learning model to outline the bone. Between the early and late teens the growth plate moved upward and the groove deepened in both sexes. After the mid teens, boys showed a deeper outer groove than girls for their size.
pmc-13570906:
Susan Mayes and co-authors chart how four child problems overlap in a 2026 study. ADHD, autism, defiant disorder, and school impairment bring most children to mental health checks, yet they are often weighed one by one. Mothers rated symptoms on a standard behavior scale in clinic and community samples.

The clinic sample held 1601 children with autism or ADHD, and community samples held more than a thousand more. Nine in ten clinic children showed signs of two or more of the four problems. Most children with autism also met ADHD and defiant signs. Inattention tied most to school harm, while hyperactive traits tied most to defiant signs.
pmc-13571006:
Seven physicians describe a man in his mid-fifties whose lungs were slowly filling with tiny calcium stones. He had ten years of worsening breathlessness and cough that standard treatment never relieved, and he was first managed as emphysema. When he returned two months later with blue discoloration from low oxygen, scans and tissue samples confirmed pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis. It is a rare inherited disorder in which calcium phosphate grains settle inside the air sacs.

Gene testing found a new pairing of faults in the SLC34A2 gene: a stop-sign change in one copy and a deletion of about 5,500 DNA letters removing several sections from the other. Together they block the phosphate transport the gene normally provides. The man received a double lung transplant, and no disease returned in the first year. The authors add the variant pair to the catalogue of causes for this condition.
pmc-13571106:
Priscilla Chong, Kulsoom Bilal, Imran Ahmed, and Haji Sheeraz Khan report a brain tumor in a baby that hid behind feeding problems, in a 2026 case report. A seven-month-old boy fed poorly, lost weight, and vomited again and again for three months, with no early nerve signs. Feeding checks, team reviews, and drug trials found no cause.

A brain scan at last showed a large mass above the pituitary area, with spread along the brain's lining. Tests on tissue and genes confirmed a pilocytic astrocytoma, a common childhood tumor that more often causes headaches or vision trouble. Treatment with two chemotherapy drugs began. The case urges doctors to scan infants whose vomiting and poor growth will not explain themselves.
pmc-13571206:
Wei Dong, Xin Zhao, and Qiuxia Gao examine patients receiving continuous blood purification, a demanding dialysis-related treatment. Their cross-sectional study, published in 2026, asks how depressive mood relates to treatment compliance through sleep quality and family resilience.

The authors surveyed one hundred ninety-five patients using scales for depression, sleep quality, family resilience, and dialysis adherence. Depressive mood was linked to poorer sleep and lower family resilience, and both were linked to lower adherence. The chain path from depression through sleep and resilience to adherence contributed a small share of the total effect. The findings point to sleep and family support as possible routes to better compliance.
pmc-13571306:
Beatrice Anfuso and co-authors give in 2026 a protocol to model bile duct cell activation in thin slices of human liver. Lasting duct reaction marks chronic liver harm, with duct cells that grow and drive swelling. Live human tissue slices keep native layout and cell mix for study.

Steps cover sample taking, slice making, culture care, and waking duct cells outside the body. A growth marker count grades how strongly the cells wake. The setup supports both mechanism study and drug screening in a near-real liver setting. Full run details point to a linked full study by the same group.
pmc-13571506:
Yasha Taimuri and Riaz Ahmad review low-oxygen signals in liver scarring in a 2026 paper. Scarred livers form when injury keeps laying down stiff matrix until the organ's shape is lost. Damaged tissue also runs short of oxygen. Proteins that sense low oxygen then switch on genes that drive more scarring, swelling, and abnormal blood vessel growth.

One lead protein in that sensing system activates the liver's scar-making cells. The review also covers fresh links to a form of cell damage driven by iron and rust-like chemistry. Drugs that block the oxygen-sensing path are weighed as future treatments. The authors map where proof is strong and where it is still thin.
pmc-13571806:
Patrik Šimják and colleagues report, in a 2026 prenatal case, blocked nasal passages on both sides spotted in the first trimester. The finding was the first sign of a severe new syndrome in one twin. The pregnancy was a naturally conceived twin pair. Screening at thirteen weeks was normal for both, yet one fetus showed a gap at the upper jaw that prompted a closer look.

Three-dimensional imaging showed both nasal cavities symmetrically widened with clean bony edges and a prominent central bone, suggesting choanal atresia, a blockage never before reported this early. Genetic testing later found a new harmful variant in the KMT2D gene, giving the first prenatal diagnosis of BCAHH syndrome. Early nasal imaging may flag this condition before birth.
pmc-13572106:
Spotting walking limits early helps older adults stay free. Yet front-line clinics in China lack a shared way to test for them, so Linbing Chen and co-authors asked clinic staff what they need, in work from twenty twenty-six. Fifteen staff in Dongguan, from doctors to public health staff, gave long talks.

Four themes came out of the talks. Staff told how testing runs now and what it is worth. They gave views on tuning forecast models and named blocks that stall clinic use. They also wished for a full loop of support built around the older adult. Their asks shape how a forecast tool could earn a place in busy front-line care.
pmc-13572206:
Xiaoyu Zhao and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, whether curcumin, the yellow compound in turmeric, protects chick livers against a common plasticizer called DEHP that leaks from plastics into the environment. Cell experiments and live chick exposures traced damage through oxidative stress, energy production, and a mixed cell-death program.

In cells, curcumin restored mitochondrial power, calmed calcium imbalance, and eased internal stress while suppressing a sugar-burning pathway that the plasticizer switched on. Blocking that pathway lowered death markers too. In live chicks, the plasticizer shrank body weight and swelled and scarred the liver, while curcumin feeding largely reversed those changes. The findings support turmeric compounds as a feed defense where plastic contamination reaches poultry.
pmc-13572306:
Four surgeons survey Dutch specialists on elbow nerve surgery in a paper from 2026. The condition, ulnar neuropathy at the elbow, pinches the nerve that serves the hand. Several operations exist, and no single one is agreed best. Follow-up care also varies. The team sent a questionnaire to Dutch plastic, neuro, and orthopedic surgeons with hand expertise.

One hundred sixty-three surgeons replied. Open decompression was the clear favorite for first operations. For repeat operations, moving the nerve under the skin was most chosen. First check-ups usually came four to eight weeks after surgery. Hand therapy was advised by two thirds of surgeons. The authors call for standard, evidence-based protocols.
pmc-13572406:
Somayeh BeyranvandRaad, with two colleagues, presents a 2026 computer study of a nano sheet that might carry the gut drug mesalazine. The drug calms swelling in the bowel, but poor delivery can blunt its effect and raise side effects. The carrier in focus is graphitic carbon nitride, a flat sheet of carbon and nitrogen.

Quantum chemistry calculations compared the drug on the sheet in gas and in water. Binding was favourable in both, at about minus 19.68 and minus 21.50 kilocalories per mole for the most stable pose. Weak forces, not strong bonds, held the pair, which should let the drug come off at the target. Charge flowed from the drug to the sheet. Light absorption peaks shifted in each medium. The authors rate the sheet as a strong carrier prospect.
pmc-13572506:
Maryam Malekpour and four co-authors published a review in twenty twenty-six on copper ferrite, a magnetic speck of matter with real range in medicine. One tiny grain can heat up in a magnetic field, carry drugs, sharpen scan images, and kill germs. The review asks how the way these grains are made steers what they can do.

The authors sort the levers: how the grains are cooked, what atoms are swapped in, how the coat is built, and how they are joined with other stuff. Each choice shifts size, pull, and safety in the body. They then map those traits onto uses, from cancer care to germ control. Gaps in proof of safety get plain words. The piece reads as a builder's guide, not a mere list.
pmc-13572706:
Dorrie Rizzo and co-authors ask whether sleep apnea risk or insomnia tracks more strongly with weaker thinking in older adults, in a 2026 study. Both sleep problems are common late in life and both have been tied to decline. The team drew on a large Canadian aging study, taking 473 people who reported a doctor-diagnosed memory problem and 473 matched peers without one.

Apnea risk was scored with a standard checklist, and insomnia was judged by how long sleep takes to start, waking in the night, and total sleep length. Thinking speed was timed with a choice reaction task. Models weighed age, sex, body mass, income, and diabetes. The paper's title states its thrust: higher apnea risk went with a weaker thinking profile.
pmc-13573006:
Xi-Jing Zhuang and four co-authors tracked gene changes in hearts injured by severe pancreatitis in a 2026 rat study. Pancreatitis can wound the heart as it rages, but the moving molecular picture was unclear. Rats were given a bile salt infusion to trigger severe disease, and heart tissue was profiled over time. About 1,800 genes shifted, clustering around oxygen shortage, cell death, and oxidative stress.

One gene, FKBP4, sat at the center of the co-expression network and fell at every time point. Restoring it in heart muscle cells cut injury, inflammation, and cell death, and steadied the heart's contraction. It worked by raising two protective partners and quieting a fission driver and an inflammation switch. The authors name FKBP4 a candidate shield for the heart in this disease.
pmc-13573506:
Ruth Muchiri, Natalie Thun, and Richard van Breemen report how to measure the active compounds in a kava extract in a paper from 2026. Kava is a South Pacific plant used in ceremony and sold as a supplement said to calm anxiety.

Safe use of kava products depends on knowing how much of each active compound they hold. The team profiled a checked sample of the extract with a high-end lab method and named its main kavalactones and flavokavains. They then built two ways to measure those compounds and compared them. One approach, adding known amounts to the sample itself, corrected for the way the extract can distort readings. The work supports safety testing of kava products by the Botanical Safety Consortium.
pmc-13573606:
Miles Martinati and co-authors watch salt steer the self-assembly of a dye molecule in water, in a research paper from 2026. The dye, a perylene bisimide, is a prized building block for layered molecular structures. Its clumping is fast and its glow blinds normal probes.

Two light methods, one tracking glow changes and one using Raman scattering, followed the process. Pairs of molecules formed quickly regardless of salt. Chain growth, though, leaned hard on salt: chloride ions slowed the escape of single units, steadying the chains. Raman signals tied these steps to structural shifts inside the stacks. The findings clarify how electrolytes sculpt molecular assembly.
pmc-13573706:
Marie Catherine Tiveron and co-authors combine three dimensional and multiplex imaging to profile a mouse glioblastoma model, in a 2026 paper. Survival in this brain cancer has barely moved in decades, so better models and tools are needed. Stem cell based somatic models exist and are well read by sequencing, but their tissue study lagged.

Whole brain light sheet imaging showed the model grows in a highly repeatable way, letting tumor growth be measured across groups. Cyclic staining then mapped the cell types and molecular layout of the tumors and their setting, with a vetted antibody set for mouse tissue. The two imaging modes join smoothly, giving spatial protein data in three dimensions.
pmc-13573806:
Haipeng Xu and co-authors grade the models that predict pain after cancer surgery, both fresh pain and pain that lingers for months. They searched four databases through February 2026 and scored each model's bias risk with a standard tool.

Twenty-nine studies held 53 models. Pooled accuracy was decent: about 0.83 for acute pain models and 0.79 for chronic pain models in training data, a bit lower in fresh validation data. Spread across studies was wide, and only eight studies ran a low bias risk. Cancer-specific results varied, with lung cancer models for chronic pain doing best on thin data. Better-built models are still needed.
pmc-13574206:
R Elilarassi and co-authors review AI for magnetism in a 2026 paper on spintronics, electronics that use electron spin. New devices need magnetic materials with exact traits: strong spin alignment, large moments, and stability under heat. The search space of mixtures and structures is vast, which is where learning models come in.

The review covers models that predict magnetic traits from data, fed by quantum calculations and lab databases. It explains how features are built from composition, structure, and electron behavior. Graph-based networks and physics-guided learning get special attention. Alloy families, topological systems, and atom-thin magnets are surveyed as hunting grounds. The authors look ahead to self-driving discovery loops that mix prediction with testing.
pmc-13574306:
Marshall and co-authors draw up design guidelines for online health forums, grounded in user experience. Such forums are widely used, yet proof of their benefit is mixed. Better design, tied to theory and lived experience, could improve results. The team ran 54 interviews, with 36 forum users and 18 forum staff. Four design workshops with staff added more input.

Ideas also came from past design research and from self-determination theory. A structured analysis sorted the material into a well-being support frame. The output is a set of guidelines for safe forums that support well-being. The authors hope builders will test the guidelines in live services.
pmc-13574506:
Paolo Compagnucci and fifteen co-authors pool evidence on a heart procedure in a 2026 review. Pulsed field ablation zaps faulty heart tissue with electric pulses. It is well studied in upper heart chambers, less so in the lower ones. Faulty rhythms there can be deadly and hard to treat.

The team gathered seventy five studies, split between lab and clinic work. Just over three hundred fifty patients appeared in the clinical set. Lab lesions reached about six millimeters deep on average. Depth held up even in scarred heart muscle. Full wall penetration varied, running higher inside scar. The review maps how lab measures line up with patient outcomes. It also flags where proof remains thin for wider use.
pmc-13574606:
Rie Kudoh and Taiga Shibayama review social factors that shape diabetes self care among immigrants in a 2026 paper. Migrants face language, cost, and food hurdles that complicate daily diabetes care. The pair screened studies from 2020 to 2024 in two databases. Twenty-five studies passed, mostly from North America and the Caribbean.

All six social domains tied to at least one care habit, from diet to clinic visits. Community and social context touched every habit studied. Money strain and language gaps recurred across domains. Food setting shaped diet most, while neighborhood shaped activity and visits. No studies came from Southeast Asia or Africa, a gap the authors flag for urgent work.
pmc-13574906:
Gergely Csáji and co-authors study matching doctors to hospitals when couples apply together, in a 2026 paper. In the hospitals and residents problem, each side ranks the other and a stable match is sought. Couples state joint choices, which makes the puzzle much harder. A solution may be a stable matching or a proof that none exists.

Under set limits on how couples rank pairs, the team gives fast methods with a twist. One finds a near-feasible stable match by shifting hospital capacity by at most one place. Other fast methods cover special market forms and couple types. Hardness results then mark where no fast method can work. Readers get a clear map of what is solvable here.
pmc-13575106:
Nate Christensen sets out a 2026 physics paper linking stability boundaries across fields, from quantum systems to the expanding universe. His organising idea is a damping ratio, a unit-free number that marks where a system's behaviour changes class. At a value of one, the system reaches a special boundary called an exceptional point.

Christensen shows an exact algebraic link between the start of cosmic acceleration and a critical damping point for the growth of structure. He is clear that the link restates known equations rather than adding a new law. Its value, he argues, lies in a testable forecast: models beyond the standard flat cosmology should show a small offset that the standard model lacks. Particle lifetimes are also sorted into stability bands under his scheme.
pmc-13575506:
Ying Tian and six co-authors fed overweight mice in a 2026 study to see how short-term calorie cuts, at three levels, change liver fat handling and gut microbes. Protein stayed normal while energy was cut by twenty, thirty, or forty percent. Blood, liver, and stool tests tracked the effects in males and females apart.

High-fat feeding alone harmed blood sugar control and blood fats in both sexes, but liver fat handling broke down only in males. Females showed harm mainly in cholesterol handling. Calorie cuts then shifted these patterns by level and by sex. The study warns that diet advice from male-only data can mislead.
pmc-13576006:
Albaladejo-Carrasco and co-authors review models of hormone effects in type one diabetes in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Women with this condition often find blood sugar harder to control at certain points in the monthly cycle. Hormones from the ovaries seem to affect not just insulin sensitivity but several control processes at once.

The review surveys math models that try to link hormone cycles with glucose and insulin control. It finds only a few that join the two systems in an explicit way. The authors say this gap matters as automatic insulin systems grow more common. Better models could lead to tools and dosing methods designed for women.
pmc-13576106:
Mia L Barron leads a 2026 scoping review of communication between clinicians and African American adults living with lupus. Lupus is an autoimmune disease that damages many organs, and outcomes run worse for African American patients. Weak communication and missed screening for changeable risks add to that gap.

Searches of four databases covering 2012 to mid-2025 yielded 214 papers, of which 20 met the review's rules. Helpful habits included involving family, speaking more slowly, and showing empathy. Several papers pushed for decision aids with communication built in. None tested a communication tool aimed at cutting changeable risks or improving outcomes in this group. The authors flag that absence as the key gap for future work.
pmc-13576206:
Chang-Zhu He and five colleagues test whether combining structural and blood flow eye scans improves spotting normal-tension glaucoma in very short-sighted eyes, in a 2026 diagnostic study. High myopia and this glaucoma type can look alike, making diagnosis tricky. Structural scans map tissue layers, while a related scan maps tiny vessels.

The study enrolled 87 patients, 42 with high myopia alone and 45 with glaucoma added. Structural measures beat vessel measures overall. One layer measure at the lower macula scored best, at 0.85 on the ranking accuracy scale, while the best vessel measure sat lower. Machine learning and standard regression models were built from the chosen features and checked with resampling and calibration tests. Explanation tools showed how each feature pushed individual predictions. The authors see combined data as useful support for a hard distinction.
pmc-13576306:
Giuseppe Migliaretti and Paolo Giacomo Arduino test whether entrance exam scores forecast success in dental school, in a 2026 study from the University of Turin. Italy long admitted dental students by national exam, and a recent reform scrapped that route. The team looked back at 431 students enrolled between 2009 and 2018.

Higher admission scores tracked with earning credits on schedule and graduating on time. The test predicted first-year performance with a ranking score of 0.71, and degree completion at 0.70 in the same units. A cut-off of 40 out of 90 separated strugglers: students below it had five times the odds of falling behind on first-year credits. The authors argue the findings should inform the debate on removing the exam, given the risks for dropout rates and wasted resources.
pmc-13576606:
Chiu and colleagues published a 2026 trial on a magnetic tracer for breast cancer surgery. Surgeons check the first lymph node, the sentinel node, to stage early breast cancer. The standard method pairs a radioactive tracer with a blue dye. The trial tested iron oxide particles that a magnet probe can find instead.

Nearly 300 patients were split between the magnetic tracer and the standard pair. The magnetic method found the sentinel node in over 99 percent of cases. The standard pair scored a perfect rate, a gap within the set limit. One failure occurred in the magnetic group across 153 procedures. The authors back the magnetic tracer as a sound stand-in option. The trial ran from 2021 to 2024 across several hospital centers.
pmc-13576706:
Matthew Susko and co-authors review one center's results using focused radiation for benign spinal tumors. These growths are uncommon but can cause real harm by pressing on the cord or nerves. Surgery is the usual fix, yet some patients cannot have it or relapse afterward. Their 2026 paper covers patients treated with stereotactic body radiation, a few high-dose, tightly aimed sessions, from 2010 to 2021.

The series held 31 patients and 36 tumors, most in the neck and chest parts of the spine. Schwannomas and meningiomas made up the bulk, with blood-vessel tumors next. The median dose was 25 gray, split over five sessions. The authors track how well the tumors stayed controlled, whether symptoms eased, how scans responded, and what side effects appeared. Their account adds rare long-run data for a treatment used when surgery falls short.
pmc-13576806:
Fjorda Kazazi and Peter Howell tested in 2026 whether virtual reality tasks can reveal attention differences tied to ADHD traits. Lab tasks for attention often feel artificial, and past virtual reality work covered mainly sustained attention. Their study used ten virtual tasks spanning four forms of attention: sustained, selective, divided, and switching.

Adults with self-reported ADHD traits scored lower on attention measures and working memory than a comparison group. In the virtual tasks, group gaps showed up mostly on the sustained attention task modeled on a classic test, with more missed targets and lower accuracy. Nearly all measures predicted group membership. Participants reported feeling present in the tasks, supporting virtual reality as a realistic testing tool.
pmc-13576906:
Zhenzhen Zhao and co-authors hunt in 2026 gene variants tied to liver harm from tuberculosis drugs in western China. More than thirteen hundred patients on treatment join the study. Four variants in one gene and five spots in another face genotyping.

Liver harm strikes near three in ten patients in the cohort. One variant in the first gene nearly doubles harm risk under a recessive pattern. Three spots in the second gene instead look protective against harm. The gene map may help flag patients who need closer liver watch on therapy.
pmc-13577306:
Three authors, Bilgi Isler, Ahmet Murat Bayraktar, and Matthew Balcarras, offer a short comment from 2026 on a study of chatbots. The study they discuss looked at how chatbots talk with men about sex health after prostate cancer care. The comment team reads the chat logs as urology doctors and asks if the facts in the replies were right.

They find three gaps that the first study did not score. None of the four chatbots fixed a wrong claim in the prompt about hormone care with surgery. The replies also blurred key ways that surgery and radiation differ for sex life. One link was tied to the wrong group, which the team calls a kind of made-up fact. They urge a set urology check in future work.
pmc-13577806:
Justin Eastwood and co-authors show that heat harms wild birds in quiet ways in this 2026 study. Their subjects are cooperatively breeding birds in the hot savannah of Australia. The team tracked telomeres, the caps that protect chromosome ends and shorten with wear, across the birds' lives.

Hotter weather sped up telomere loss at two key stages: young birds leaving parental feeding, and adults entering breeding. Neither social help nor better luck softened the wear, except for adults living in dense plant cover. The wear signals a worn body state that can cut breeding success. The authors say hidden heat harm may be widespread, and that shaded refuges deserve protection.
pmc-13577906:
Arsela Prelaj and co-authors test AI tools that help doctors pick immune therapy for lung cancer, in a 2026 study. For non-small cell lung cancer, the choice of immunotherapy still leans on one protein score and rough clinic grades. The I3LUNG project gathered real-world data on nearly twenty-four hundred patients across many lands. Records, blood tests, scans, tissue images, and gene reads all fed the models.

Blood and clinic data alone gave steady scores across outcomes. Richer mixes that added scans and tissue looked better in training but did not hold the edge in fresh tests. Still, the AI beat the standard scores by a clear margin. In a usability run, both expert and general doctors sharpened their calls with the tool's explained output. A forward trial in more than two thousand patients is now under way.
pmc-13578506:
Konsta Kukkonen and six co-authors compare how male hormone signals reshape DNA access in healthy and cancerous prostate cells, in this twenty twenty-six study. The hormone switch, the androgen receptor, opens and closes stretches of DNA. Its effect in healthy prostate cells was poorly known, for lack of good cell models.

The team used lab cell lines of both types, with and without the hormone. Even before the hormone, the two cell types differed widely in which DNA lay open. The hormone widened the gap, opening distinct sets of sites in each type. The maps show why the same hormone can drive growth in cancer yet act calmly in healthy tissue.
pmc-13578606:
Ervin Toth, Wojciech Marlicz, and Anastasios Koulaouzidis write a letter to the editor on wide-view camera capsules for examining the small bowel, published in 2026. A recent review had compared panoramic capsules with standard forward-view ones in patients with suspected bleeding.

The letter praises the question but warns against reading too much into the results. Most studies measured detection yield, not true accuracy, and yield depends on patient choice, timing, and reading habits. Definitions of a found lesion also varied between studies. A wider view is attractive, they grant, but it should not be confused with proven benefit. What counts is better decisions and better patient outcomes. Stronger comparative evidence is still needed.
pmc-13579306:
Flavio Miura and eight co-authors published an education research study in twenty twenty-six on how well exams actually measure doctors' retained ethics training. Residents took interactive courses on practical ethics and professional conduct, then sat twenty-question retention tests. The team subjected both exams to classical psychometric analysis.

The first exam was easy and weakly reliable; nearly everyone answered nearly everything correctly, leaving little spread to measure. The second improved markedly on reliability and discrimination. The authors argue easy items after good teaching can signal genuine short-term retention, not just a bad test. Still, ceiling effects limit what such exams can prove. The paper presses medical schools to design ethics assessment as carefully as ethics teaching.
pmc-13580006:
Yuteng Wang and a large team of co-authors link social isolation and loneliness to early menopause and death in women, in a 2026 study of the UK Biobank. Nearly eighty thousand women were classed by when menopause came, early at forty to forty five or in the normal band after that. Isolation was scored from living setup, contact, and group life; loneliness from felt loneliness and having someone to confide in.

Both hardships tied to higher odds of early menopause, modestly but steadily. The survival penalty hit far harder in the early group: high isolation raised death risk by over half there, against a far smaller lift in the normal group. Survival curves split wider as hardship rose. The authors urge menopause care to screen for social strain.
pmc-13580606:
Arif Ahmed and a team of co-authors test trust in AI health answers, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Two randomized experiments asked whether habit-like reliance on AI skews how people judge its output. Highlight cues in the text were tested as a counterweight.

The first run used 338 college students; the second, 563 online workers. Each split people by answer accuracy and by whether key text was highlighted. Trust was scored on a multi-item scale. The design separates blind trust from earned trust and checks whether simple cues can curb overreliance on wrong answers.
pmc-13581106:
Na Liu and co-authors present a 2026 survey study of bowel cancer patients in China who had a temporary stoma. After stoma reversal, many face a cluster of bowel troubles known as LARS. The team asked two hundred patients across twenty hospitals what they knew, felt, and did to prevent it.

Scores showed fair attitudes but middling knowledge and weak daily practice. Schooling level, home setting, and who cared for the patient shaped scores most. Attitude carried about a quarter of the path from knowledge to action. People who knew more did more, in part because they cared more. The authors urge teaching that builds both facts and motivation before reversal surgery.
pmc-13581506:
Luke Dreher and co-authors reviewed in 2026 how connective tissue disorders can disturb heart rhythm. Disorders such as Marfan syndrome and the Ehlers-Danlos group are known for weak vessels and aorta problems. Growing evidence shows they also raise the risk of atrial and ventricular rhythm faults, often without clear muscle or valve disease.

The review draws together data on the tissue changes that set up those faults. It stresses four bridges. One is widespread heart scarring driven by a growth signal. Others are valve and ring faults such as mitral prolapse, and altered force sensing that links loose matrix to cell signaling. Gene routes behind the disorders are mapped as well. Readers get a guide for spotting rhythm risk in patients often watched only for aorta trouble.
pmc-13581606:
Shimeng Wu and co-authors improve liquid state machines for time prediction in a 2026 paper. These spiking reservoir systems suit low power, online forecasting, since only a simple readout layer is trained. Standard training reads a single instant of reservoir state, which misses evidence spread over time.

Feeding the readout a sliding window of recent states changed results sharply. On a standard benchmark, error for a ridge readout fell by about eighty five percent as window length grew, and a transformer readout improved by a similar share. The same trend held on two harder tasks. The lesson is that recent reservoir history, shown at the decoder, lifts cheap temporal prediction.
pmc-13581706:
Meng Sun, Zhixiong Gao, Fengyan Hu, and Guo Chen review an enzyme as a treatment target for heart damage after restored blood flow, in a 2026 paper. When a blocked heart artery reopens, the returning blood itself injures heart muscle. Toxic aldehydes built up during that phase are a key part of the harm.

The enzyme ALDH2 clears those aldehydes and calms several injury pathways, from cell death to inflammation. Animal studies show that lacking the enzyme worsens damage, while boosting it protects the heart. A common gene variant that weakens the enzyme, frequent in East Asian populations, may shape risk and treatment response. The authors stress that most evidence is still preclinical.
pmc-13581906:
