The authors urge doctors to suspect the syndrome when eye disease, obesity, extra digits, and kidney trouble appear together, especially in families where parents are related. Early naming allows monitoring that can delay lasting damage and improve daily life.
pmc-13634306:
Jiexun Cai and eight colleagues built a blood score meant to capture the body-wide inflammation behind COPD, a chronic lung disease. Breathing test results often fail to match how burdened patients feel. The team measured eleven cytokines, small immune signaling proteins, in the blood of sixty-two patients with stable disease. They combined the readings into one score using an automated selection method that kept only the most useful markers.

The final score rests on three cytokines. It tracked breathing-based severity better than any single cytokine and separated severity grades reasonably well. Breathing scores still explained effort-related symptoms such as breathlessness more strongly. The new score leaned toward sleep and energy complaints, though those links stayed short of firm statistical ground. The authors present the score as a companion to breathing tests, not a replacement, and call for outside validation in larger, longer studies.
pmc-13634706:
Zahra Hamzehee and co-authors test two plant powders in feed for older laying hens in a 2026 study. The powders come from oleaster fruit and ginger root. The team looked at laying performance, egg quality, blood traits, gut shape, and organ traits in late-phase hens.

One hundred forty-four Lohmann hens, ninety-two weeks old, were split into four diet groups for eight weeks. Each group had six pens of six birds. The factorial design shows the effect of each powder and of both together, useful for farmers seeking natural feed additives for aging flocks.
pmc-13635406:
Jolanta Kowalska and co-authors track ground beetles in a flower strip and nearby crops in a 2026 study under organic farming. Farm intensification has simplified landscapes and harmed biodiversity. Flower strips can offer habitat and resources, and ground beetles help by eating pests and weed seeds.

The strip held richer beetle communities than wheat or oilseed monocultures, including rare species absent from the crops. Its community was more even, suggesting greater stability. Beetle numbers rose in May and June in both years, most sharply in the strip. The authors conclude strips serve as stable habitat for these helpful insects.
pmc-13635506:
Rui Qi and a large team of co-authors engineer messenger RNA tails that switch expression by cell type in a 2026 paper. RNA medicines need to act in target cells and stay quiet elsewhere, yet control after delivery is hard. The tail at the end of an RNA strand is a promising control site that leaves other control regions intact.

They insert target sites for small regulatory RNAs at varied spots in that tail. Certain layouts muted a test protein in three non target liver cell types while keeping strong expression in liver cells proper. The order of the inserted sites mattered a lot. The authors present the tail as a programmable platform for selective RNA medicines.
pmc-13636006:
Kevin Horton and five colleagues published a registry study in two thousand twenty-six on survival after ALS in military veterans. Service members face a higher risk of this fatal nerve disease. Whether they also die sooner after diagnosis was less known.

The United States National ALS Registry supplied over eight thousand six hundred participants with survey and death records. About a fifth were veterans. Veterans were older at diagnosis and reported more smoking and drinking. Their median follow-up to death was about a year shorter, and five-year survival was lower. After adjustments, veteran status still linked to a higher death risk. The authors say the survival gap deserves attention in care planning.
pmc-13637106:
Demet Çelik and Orkun Erkayiran published this 2026 interview study on how hemodialysis reshapes family life in Türkiye. Dialysis patients spend long hours tied to a machine several days a week, and the treatment reorganizes the whole household around it. The pair interviewed fifteen patients at a hospital in Central Anatolia during mid 2025. They analyzed the conversations with a mix of ready-made family-systems themes and new themes drawn from the interviews themselves.

Six themes emerged. Families pulled closer in solidarity, yet roles and care burdens shifted onto particular members. Exhaustion and rest formed a repeating cycle, and daily routine bent around dialysis appointments. A line appeared between emotional loyalty and practical help. Faith-based acceptance helped long-term patients normalize their situation, a theme stronger in veterans of treatment than in newcomers. The authors recommend family-centered planning that builds rest into daily life and fixes transport headaches.
pmc-13638006:
Shtaitz and co-authors report the making and crystal structure of a complex ring compound built by a new route. The route reworks a nitrogen-rich ring by swapping one of its groups for a second ring unit. Such swaps give chemists fresh ways to build drug-like frames.

In the crystal, the molecules link into ribbons through bonds between nitrogen, hydrogen, and oxygen. Flat ring faces also stack on each other at a set distance. The team mapped the surface contacts of the molecule to show which atoms touch neighbors. Full shape data help others judge how the compound might bind metals or proteins. The report adds one more proven product to a young synthetic method. It also gives growers of crystals a packing pattern to expect.
pmc-13638906:
Stefano Cacciatore and ten colleagues published a 2026 network analysis of intrinsic capacity and death in very old adults in Italy. Intrinsic capacity combines five areas of healthy aging: movement, thinking, vitality, mood, and the senses.

The study used the ilSIRENTE cohort of 319 people aged eighty and over living at home. Vitality, mood, and thinking clustered closely together, while hearing and vision sat at the edges and connected through movement. Better movement scores and higher overall capacity each predicted lower death rates over four and seven years. The authors suggest routine assessments could flag older people most at risk.
pmc-13639206:
Lisa Dasen and eight colleagues published a 2026 study of stress and mental health among forcibly displaced people living in Switzerland. Earlier work treated trauma exposure as a single scale, which can hide very different individual patterns.

Survey data from 437 people were sorted into five profiles, from very high stress with very high symptoms down to low stress with none. Men, people with stronger social support, and people with secure visa status were more likely to sit in lower-symptom groups. The authors say such profiles can help services spot both vulnerable and resilient people and tailor support accordingly.
pmc-13639606:
The GBD 2023 Tetanus Collaborators report a systematic analysis of tetanus burden across 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023. Tetanus is deadly yet vaccine-preventable, and global campaigns have cut it sharply without eliminating it.

Standardized incidence fell from about eleven cases per hundred thousand people in 1990 to under one per hundred thousand in 2023. The remaining burden concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, while wealthy regions approached zero. Burden tracked closely with a social development index, falling as development rose. The group presents the estimates as a guide for closing the last gaps in vaccination.
pmc-13642306:
Zhongming Chen and two colleagues present a 2026 method for reading the past paths of migrating cells inside living tissue. Watching cells move deep in the body over long periods is nearly impossible with ordinary live imaging.

Their trick is to engineer cells to release fluorescent protein fused to collagen, leaving glowing trails in the tissue as they travel. In mice, the team found trails in healthy organs, primary tumors, and sites where cancer had spread. Some trails ran together along blood vessel walls, hinting at group travel. Reading the trails after death reconstructs migration history that cameras could never capture.
pmc-13642506:
Helena Barrasa and colleagues propose a 2026 viewpoint for catching the drug's brain side effects earlier in brain critical care, where the antibiotic's brain side effects remain under-recognized. The drug is widely used for its broad coverage and brain penetration. Toxicity often appears as shifting confusion, inattention, muscle jerks, or speech trouble within days, easily mistaken for sepsis or underlying brain injury. Because sedation and critical illness hide early signs, the drug is often continued too long, delaying the most effective step, stopping it.

The authors argue toxicity is largely exposure-driven and therefore preventable, with risk raised by unstable kidney function, prior brain disease, white-matter change, older age, higher weight, and other health problems. Their framework pairs early spotting of at-risk patients with simple brain monitoring and timely drug-level testing to spot harmful exposure before severe confusion or silent seizures develop.
pmc-13642606:
Yuxuan Zhou presents a 2026 design for wide-angle perfect absorption of terahertz waves using a thin Tamm-type structure built from a Lorentz dielectric and a Bragg reflector. Perfect absorption matters for sensing and integrated photonics, yet existing designs need thick layers, complex patterning, or narrow angles. The new approach balances phase and amplitude: the Lorentz layer supplies frequency-dependent phase and controlled loss, while the reflector supplies cavity feedback.

The result absorbs above 92 percent for entry angles up to eighty degrees, with a top layer only about one twenty-second of a wavelength thick. Tuning the Lorentz parameters or layer thickness changes the absorption range without rebuilding the stack, enabling multi-channel use with less than 5.7 percent frequency shift under oblique incidence. Photonics engineers get a route to simple, tunable, on-chip absorbers that hold up at steep angles.
pmc-13643506:
Ie and co-authors survey older adults in the United States and Japan about trust in their doctors and readiness to stop unneeded medicines. Many older adults take five or more drugs. Cutting back safely, called deprescribing, works best when patients agree to it.

The Japan group held 185 patients from a community hospital and clinic in Kawasaki City. The American group held 107 adults from a research registry in Pittsburgh. All took at least five medicines and had stable routines. Each filled short surveys on readiness to cut back and on trust in their care team. The team compared how trust tracked with readiness across the two lands. Trust may be a lever clinics can use to start hard talks about stopping drugs.
pmc-13644906:
Nicholas Streicher checks whether a hospital's routine blood test platform can carry a proven ALS warning marker, in a 2026 study. In motor neuron disease, the protein neurofilament light chain leaks from damaged nerves into blood, and its level predicts how fast function will decline. Most evidence used a research-grade platform; routine hospitals use a different commercial system that reports values about six times lower. Streicher reviewed fifty-eight confirmed patients at one academic centre.

Their blood levels on the routine platform correlated strongly with the rate of functional decline, matching the research platform's behaviour. Repeat samples in the same patients were also examined. Two companion markers were tested for extra value. The study supports using the test hospitals already own for prognosis conversations and trial screening, instead of sending samples to specialist labs.
pmc-13647906:
Linna Ma and seven colleagues chart the conversation between switch genes and defense genes in rice under attack by the blast fungus, in a 2026 study. Rice blast is among the most destructive crop diseases on Earth. Drawing on the rice pan-genome and gene activity measured across an infection time course, the team built interaction networks with two independent methods. One switch family, the bHLH factors, lit up across the response.

To test the network, the team knocked out three bHLH genes in rice lines. Each knockout left the plants clearly more susceptible to the fungus, which confirms the family defends rather than merely watches. Two of the genes are entirely new candidates for blast resistance. The authors present the first pan-genome-based map of its kind for this disease. Breeders gain both a wiring diagram of rice immunity and fresh genetic material for resistant varieties.
pmc-13650306:
Moradi and co-authors map in 2026 the HER family of growth receptors in advanced bladder cancer of the urinary tract. That family counts four kin receptors, and one of them has long been a drug target in breast and stomach cancers. In bladder cancer, the gains from such drugs stayed less clear.

New drug pairs that carry poison to receptor marked cells have revived the field. The lead target stays the best backed one, but trials now test pairs that hit two family members at once. The piece weighs a new study in the same issue and sets out why the whole family merits a fresh look.
pmc-13650606:
Xingxing Wang and thirteen colleagues build a way to read pancreatic cancer's makeup from scans instead of surgery. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma mixes tumor cells with supporting stroma in widely varying proportions. That ratio shapes recurrence and drug response, yet it has only been measurable on tissue removed in an operation.

Using enhanced magnetic resonance images from 737 patients across several centers, the team trained a scoring model. It predicted the tissue-measured ratio with strong accuracy in training and solid accuracy in outside validation. The score separated patients by recurrence risk on its own and sharpened early recurrence forecasts when combined with clinical facts. Tumors scoring high on stroma fared better under standard systemic therapy and under immune-based combinations. Gene and single-cell analyses tied low-stroma tumors to matrix remodeling pathways and distinct immune cell states, giving the scan score a biological footing.
pmc-13650806:
Bingchen Wu and co-authors coat tiny brain electrodes with a special polymer so they can track dopamine and brain waves in mice for weeks. Watching both signals in free moving animals is hard: proteins foul the sensors, and the reference electrode flakes apart. Their 2026 study centers on the striatum, a hub for reward and daily rhythms.

The coating, a zwitterionic polymer, blocks protein fouling and calms inflammation around the array. A gel form of it also shields the reference from peeling. The team logged stable dopamine and signal reads over four weeks in moving mice. Weekly checks confirmed the electrodes stayed sound, which opens joint study of behavior, signals, and dopamine.
pmc-13651106:
Guiomar Mendieta and eleven co-authors interview doctors across six European countries about inflammation's place in cardiovascular care. Evidence more and more ties smoldering inflammation to the progression of artery disease combined with kidney disease or heart failure, yet nobody knew whether front-line physicians believe it or act on it.

Sixty-two cardiologists, kidney specialists, and general doctors with substantial experience joined hour-long interviews in early 2024. Most accepted inflammation's importance in theory, but only about a quarter routinely ordered the sensitive blood test that measures it. The barriers were practical: unclear meaning of a result and no proven treatment to offer when the value runs high, leaving doctors feeling unable to change management. The authors conclude that inflammation remains a neglected target for want of evidence-backed treatments and clearer guidance, not for want of awareness among physicians.
pmc-13651706:
Mario González-Gutiérrez and ten co-authors fix a subtle artifact in fluorescence lifetime imaging, a microscopy method that maps molecular settings by how long fluorophores glow. Because the microscope's blur spot mixes light from neighboring molecules into one pixel, blended decay curves masquerade as intermediate environments that do not exist.

Their workflow sharpens the raw intensity image with a mean-shift super-resolution method first, building spatial masks that keep each pixel's photons honest. Only then does it run the lifetime analysis, leaving the timing data untouched. In human cells carrying two overlapping dyes, the phantom in-between group sat exactly at blur interfaces and vanished under masking, while each dye's true signature survived. Simulations showed blending persists at separations ordinary resolution rules call safe. A three-dye test also separated cleanly. The authors argue spatial refinement, not temporal tinkering, is the honest cure.
pmc-13651806:
Peng Qin and four colleagues speed up ions trapped inside nanoporous crystals by applying a sideways gate voltage, a trick borrowed from transistor thinking. Ion mobility inside porous electrode materials limits batteries and supercapacitors, and the team used ionic liquids inside metal-organic framework films as a clean model system.

Conductivity rose by up to about a third when the gate field was switched on. Simulations explained why: the field sorts ions into parallel layers of higher and lower concentration running along the transport direction. Ions inside the favorable layers moved up to two and a half times faster than in the bulk liquid. The authors dub these strata ion highways. A general link between local concentration and mobility emerged from the data. The study offers both insight into confined ion dynamics and a practical method for squeezing more speed from porous devices.
pmc-13652406:
Dorra Chiboub, Chiraz Mbarek and their co-authors report a rare case of large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma arising in the submandibular gland, listed for 2026. This aggressive cancer usually starts in the lungs, so a primary salivary case is exceptional and hard to tell from spread of lung disease.

Their patient was an older man whose neck mass had stayed stable for many years before growing fast. Scans showed a large, partly dead tumor plus spread to lungs and liver. Tissue tests showed a high-grade neuroendocrine tumor beside a benign component. The history pointed to change within the long-standing benign lesion.
pmc-13653906:
Milian, Geindreau, Pignol, and Vegran review how killer immune cells enter tumors, spread within them, and why they so often fail to finish the job. These cells are the main weapon behind immune therapy for cancer. Their presence in a tumor, though, does not ensure control.

The review follows the cells step by step: waking in lymph organs, travel in blood, entry through tumor vessels, and movement inside the tumor. At each step, barriers block them: scrambled signal chemicals, faulty vessels, dense tissue glue, and suppressive signals. The result is tumors that shut the cells out at the rim. The authors gather ways to breach those barriers. Their map joins steps that older reviews treated apart.
pmc-13654006:
Marco Turati and co-authors review ankle bone and cartilage harm in children and teens, in a 2026 paper. Such harm in the talus bone is a key cause of lasting ankle pain after a fall or twist, though it can arise with no clear event. Plain X rays may miss the harm or play down its depth.

The review sets out how scans help judge if a loose fragment is stable, and when rest based care may heal it. If surgery is needed, choice turns on fragment stability, cartilage state, and bone harm. Ankle ligament state also counts. The authors call for more even care plans and for studies that track young patients over time.
pmc-13654106:
Xu and co-authors review their use of a slim, flexible stent in narrowed brain arteries. Narrowing of these arteries is a major cause of stroke, with high odds of a second stroke. The risk runs highest in East Asian groups, the authors note.

The stent was first made to treat bulges in brain arteries, not narrowing. Its slim profile may suit bent and twisted vessels better than stiffer rivals. An older stent for this use raised worries about the artery narrowing again. The team studied patients whose narrowed stretch sat in a key middle brain artery and caused symptoms. They weigh how safe and how well the stent worked in daily practice. Their results may support tailoring the device choice to each vessel's shape.
pmc-13654506:
Jean-Michel Halimi and seven co-authors reply to a letter about their study of kidney risk after pregnancy hypertension. Their original work used national health records to compare later kidney outcomes after ordinary pre-eclampsia and after the severe HELLP form, which adds blood and liver breakdown. The critics questioned the handling of women who already had kidney disease. The reply notes such disease was documented in well under one percent of both groups.

The authors explain that kidney disease is under-recorded in the database, so removing only the flagged women would leave others in and bias the groups. They accept one correction: the first follow-up window is better described as six weeks to one year after birth, not the whole first year. They also defend comparing each disorder against healthy pregnancies, since their aim was clear risk figures for counseling.
pmc-13655206:
Nikki Kerdegari and co-authors tell in a 2026 report how a trainee-led urology research network in Britain went digital to run studies across many hospitals. Such studies can answer big questions fast, but herding many sites is the hard part. Their network, called BURST, has over a decade of shared work.

With database builders they shaped tools that ease site sign-up and data entry while keeping quality high. One study they cite drew near eleven thousand patients from one hundred ten hospitals. The report shares what worked, in a field where many trials fail to recruit.
pmc-13655406:
Eunse Kim and a large team sort asthma into blood gene clusters from two Korean groups. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Asthma splits in both signs and cell paths, which clouds cure picks. Blood cell gene reads from more than four hundred adults in one group were sifted for clusters tied to flare kinds.

Three clusters came out. One was a clear type-two high kind, one mixed type-two with non-type-two traits, and one low type-two with burst path traits. A check group of more than one hundred grave cases held the first two clusters firm. The mixed group used less biologic cure and fared less well. The team sees fit cure clues.
pmc-13656306:
Yonatan Degefu and three co-authors built a model of a protein network that shapes skin cancer cell states, in a 2026 paper. The network, called AP-1, helps cells switch states and adapt to drugs. Cells in one group show only some of the many possible network states. Why states are limited, and why mixes differ between groups, was unclear.

The model captures how network parts pair up, compete, and are jointly controlled. It was tuned to single-cell protein data from many melanoma groups. Settings that explained each group's state mix also tracked a key growth signal. The model forecast state shifts after that signal was blocked. Lab tests confirmed a shift toward a drug-resistant state. Guided tweaks blunted that shift, offering a route to control cell switching.
pmc-13657506:
Ankur Bhandari and co-authors report in 2026 a rare skin growth on a young woman's elbow, with a sweep of past work. The growth is a low grade flesh tumor of thread cells, slow yet prone to creep back at the spot. Far spread is rare, and rates run a few per mil lion a year.

At thirty three, the woman bore a lone dark lump on her elbow's out side for most of a year, with now and then pain. Cloth tests named the growth. Wide cut with a vein flap and skin graft closed the wound. Long watch for creep back is the close note.
pmc-13657606:
Bhawana Bastola and three co-authors report an odd case of a chromosome syndrome in a young man in Nepal. The syndrome adds an extra X copy in males and often stays hidden till adult years. His main gripe was lasting nausea and vomiting, a rare first sign.

Checks found classic marks too, from tall build and small testes to breast growth, thin hair, and no sperm despite normal desire. Early tooth loss was a rare extra mark. Hormone tests and a chromosome scan confirmed the call. Early spotting can lift health and life quality, they stress.
pmc-13657706:
Kaung Hset Tun and co-authors review treatment choices for high risk prostate cancer in 2026. They compare three main paths: surgery to remove the prostate, beam radiation, and radiation plus hormone blocking drugs. This type of cancer is more likely to spread and cause death. No large trial has tested the three paths head to head, so the best choice stays unclear.

The review pulls together past studies on survival, side effects, and quality of life. Surgery and radiation each won in some studies. For radiation, adding hormone drugs for a long stretch helped survival. Surgery harmed bladder control and sex life more, while radiation harmed the bowel more.
pmc-13659006:
Plant-based meats now come in two waves, traditional staples like tofu and tempeh and engineered products that mimic beef, and families judge them very differently. Ai Ting Goh and co-authors scoped the research on what parents and children think of these foods, searching five databases for studies of perceptions and attitudes. Their interest is practical: children form food preferences early, mostly at the family table, so parents act as gatekeepers for anything new.

The review maps what draws families toward these products and what holds them back, from taste and health beliefs to price and habit. The authors aim the map at makers and educators trying to fit plant-based options into everyday meals.
pmc-13659106:
Yoon Shin and five colleagues compare two hepatitis B drugs on the outcome patients fear most: liver cancer. Besifovir is a newer option for chronic hepatitis B, while tenofovir has a long track record, and besifovir's long-term effect on cancer risk was unproven. Using Korean national insurance records covering more than thirty thousand patients, the team matched besifovir users with similar tenofovir users to make the comparison fair.

Liver cancer developed less often in the besifovir group, with cirrhosis tracked as a second outcome. Because the data come from routine care nationwide rather than a selected trial population, the result carries real-world weight, though records-based studies cannot erase every difference between groups. For doctors choosing between two daily antivirals meant to be taken for years, cancer risk is exactly the kind of long-horizon evidence that should steer the choice.
pmc-13660706:
E Cole Green and co-authors study Black teens, school life, and mental health in a 2026 paper. They ask whether a good school climate can soften the harm of racial bias. Bias is linked to low mood, worry, and acting out in teens. The data come from a large national study of brain growth in youth, with over a thousand Black teens tracked over time.

Teens who saw their school climate in a good light showed a weaker link over time. For them, bias tied less strongly to later low mood and problem acts. The authors say schools should cut bias and also build fair, safe places to learn. Both steps matter for teen health and growth.
pmc-13662406:
Sebastien Hayoz and Christopher Banek test whether a hormone linked to blood pressure makes kidney nerves fire more easily. Kidney sensory nerves run hot in models of high blood pressure and polycystic kidney disease, and cutting them slows both diseases. The hormone vasopressin also rises in those conditions, but its direct effect on the nerves was untested. Their 2026 paper checks that link in rat nerve cells.

The team isolated kidney-linked nerve cells from male and female rats and measured their firing with patch-clamp tools. Vasopressin raised firing rates and lowered the current needed to trigger spikes in both sexes. The effective dose range ran wider in female cells than in male cells. The results support the idea that the hormone directly excites kidney sensory nerves, which may help explain their overactivity in disease.
pmc-13662706:
Yuwei Wu and co-authors track birth defect burden in China in a 2026 report. Neural tube defects are severe faults in early spine and brain formation. Rates have fallen with folic acid programs, but whole life burden data were lacking. The team used a global burden study to cover all ages over three decades.

New cases, deaths, and disability rates all fell sharply in China over the span. Among adults over fifty, though, the share living with these defects grew. Disability rates also rose among the oldest adults in the data. The authors urge life long care that pairs prevention with rehab and team based support.
pmc-13663306:
Yuriko Fukuta and a large team look for blood markers that predict which mild COVID-19 patients will end up in hospital, in a research paper from 2026. The data come from an outpatient trial of convalescent plasma. Two markers were tested: a general inflammation protein and virus RNA in the blood.

Among nearly five hundred patients, each marker alone gave modest warning. Together they did better: when both were raised, more than a third of patients were later hospitalized. At very high virus levels, that share rose much higher. When both markers were normal, high-risk patients rarely worsened. The authors say the pair can guide who needs close watching.
pmc-13669206:
Seven authors, led by Jiaxian Zheng, present a 2026 paper on a solar evaporator that turns seawater into fresh water. Standard evaporators for desalination often fail in brine: they are weak, grow salt crusts, or degrade. The team's device is built from a silicone material chosen for its toughness.

Silicone resists chemicals and corrosion, bends without breaking, and shrugs off fouling. The white surface, joined with a reflector, scatters light well and keeps heat where it is needed. With the reflector, the device evaporated 4.344 kilograms of water per square meter per hour under one sun of light. Under three suns, the rate rose to 8.087. It ran for eight hours with no salt build-up and kept stable cycles for 53 days. It also sat in seawater for 197 days without damage.
pmc-13669806: Jiacan Sun and three co-authors test whether root nodules change how pea roots move water, in a short 2026 report. The team compared normal peas with two mutant types, one that forms no nodules and one that forms extra nodules. Water flow was scaled by root dry mass, nodules counted, and plants were tested both well watered and under dry soil. The finding is plain: forming nodules did not change the water flow rate.
pmc-13670806:
Fjallstrom, Coe, Lilja, and Hajdarevic study how Swedish primary care handles possible cancer symptoms, in work from twenty twenty-six. Most cancer patients start their path in primary care. Alarm symptoms are often vague, though, and usually signal something else.

Sweden introduced standardized cancer patient pathways to speed diagnosis. The study explores strategies providers use when patients present with potential cancer symptoms under the new system. When to refer fast, when to watch, and how to safety net are daily judgments. Understanding real strategies helps refine the pathways so speed does not flood specialists with low risk referrals.
pmc-13672706:
Jad Madani and co-authors report a single hard case of macular hole repair using a graft of the patient's own retina. The hole sat at the center of vision and had resisted a prior repair with membrane peel and gas. When standard surgery fails, surgeons may move a small piece of retina into the gap.

The patient, a man in his early seventies, had the graft placed during a vitrectomy with heavy liquid support, then a gas fill. Scans after surgery showed the hole fully closed. Dye and vessel imaging found new blood flow inside the graft at the surface layer. Vision rose from counting fingers to a far clearer level over the next year. Four years of follow-up support grafting as a fallback for large, stubborn holes.
pmc-13673506:
Wasin Tiarawut, Gabriel Saenz, Jinyi Yang, and Ronald Raines ask whether plain glycine strands can fold into a collagen triple helix. Their 2026 study targets the most common protein motif in animals. Collagen demands glycine at every third spot, while proline-rich strands normally pre-fold to ease assembly.

The team embeds a six-glycine run between proline clamps and compares it with a matched flexible spacer lacking the glycine backbone links. Light spectra show the helix signature for both. The spacer version reaches about eighty-six percent of the glycine signal, matching the share of helix-capable residues. Melting points land near forty-seven degrees for the glycine peptide. The result says the helix is sturdy enough to recruit even unprepared glycine runs.
pmc-13674406:
Marine fish are rich in healthy polyunsaturated fatty acids even though fish themselves make few of them. Ruojing Li and co-authors trace that supply to the gut in a 2026 study. They profiled the gut microbes of a fatty-acid-rich fish, then tested promising strains in zebrafish.

One bacterium stood out, and its key product was a small molecule called indole-3-butyric acid. That molecule switches on a master fat regulator in fish cells, much like a known drug does. Fed to zebrafish over time, it raised weight gain, liver fat storage, and the level of DHA, a prized fatty acid, in muscle. It also reshaped the gut community itself. The findings suggest a route to richer fish through managing their microbes rather than their feed alone.
pmc-13674506:
A large research team reports, in a 2026 study, a gene screen that maps how cells survive when their protein-tagging system is blocked. The tagging system marks worn proteins for disposal and keeps cell division in order. Blocking its first step stresses cancer cells in useful ways.

The team switched off genes one by one across the genome while a blocking drug was present. Loss of 239 genes made cells far more sensitive to the block. Follow-up work singled out a partner pair of proteins that guard the cell's DNA packaging. When that guard fails, tagged proteins pile up where they can do harm. The findings name new pressure points where cancer drugs might push next.
pmc-13675406:
Atef Hulliel and co-authors present a 2026 nationwide study of long-term opioid use before lower back fusion surgery. Many patients having this operation already take such pain drugs for months. Past work linked that use to worse results after surgery, but often lacked good data on mental health.

The team used a large national research program that links health records with survey data. Adults were classed as long-term users if they filled at least three opioid prescriptions over ninety days or more in the year before surgery. The study then compared outcomes after the operation between users and non-users. Its design lets readers judge how much of the risk comes from the drugs and how much from other health factors.
pmc-13675506:
Birao Fan and Ruixing Yu compare, in a 2026 real-world study, two skin treatments for a redness-heavy form of rosacea. One group got a salicylic acid peel plus pulsed light therapy. The other group got the light therapy alone. Proof that the peel adds anything has been thin so far.

The study drew on routine care at one center, covering adults treated from 2022 through 2025. Results were checked at the start and three months after the last session. Imaging tools measured redness and dark patches in a standard way, and patients reported their own views. Comparing both kinds of measures shows whether the added peel is worth its cost and effort. The design mirrors choices clinics face every week.
pmc-13675706:
Yarou Hu and co-authors use wide scans of the back of the eye to map the signs of Stickler syndrome, a condition that can lead to a torn retina. Past imaging work left gaps in what the full set of signs looks like.

The study covered twenty-five eyes from thirteen patients seen at a clinic over a year. Three eye doctors read the scans and agreed on fifteen clear signs. Changes in the clear gel of the eye were the most common, seen in nearly all eyes. Most signs in the retina and its junction with the gel showed in over three quarters of eyes, while breaks and tearing were less common.
pmc-13675806:
Therese Murphy and co-authors report a stubborn fungal skin infection in a man with a weakened immune system, in this 2026 case report. The patient, in his sixties, had survived leukemia and a stem cell transplant, and took immune-suppressing drugs for graft-versus-host skin disease. A red, crusted bump grew on his forearm over a month, without pain.

A biopsy found pigmented fungal bodies, the classic copper-penny cells of chromoblastomycosis, a chronic infection seeded by fungi entering through skin breaks. The fungus proved to be Exophiala bergeri. The authors note such infections can look deceptively plain in suppressed patients.
pmc-13676406:
Cavallari, Bitonto, Giachello, and Bifone add manganese to a molecular MRI method so the signal can be split by cell type. The base method senses faint metabolite pools but mixes contributions from neurons, support cells, and structural material. Manganese slips into active excitable cells through calcium channels and shortens a relaxation time there, dimming their share of the signal.

Comparing spectra with and without manganese isolates the sensitive share. In the cerebellum of living chick embryos, manganese cut the relaxation time by about twenty-eight percent and reshaped the spectrum at spots matching neuron-linked pools. Their 2026 paper presents the trick, MangaCEST, as a route to cell-weighted molecular imaging.
pmc-13676506:
Caner Kara and co-authors trace brain drain catheters through the skull's common entry points in this 2026 paper. Placing such catheters freehand is a daily emergency skill, yet each entry point threads different anatomy. The team inserted catheters in six donated heads under navigation, then dissected along each path. Angles and lengths were also measured in fifty patients with hydrocephalus.

Two entry points crossed dense vessel fields and speaking cortex. A third threaded the richest mix of white matter paths. Two others, Kocher's and Dandy's points, passed through quieter cortex with fewer vessels and tracts. Magnetic resonance tract maps turned each route into a 3D model for teaching.
pmc-13677306:
Sanz-Cabanillas and co-authors reviewed other health problems that travel with two scarring hair loss conditions, in a paper published in 2026. Both conditions destroy hair follicles and leave bare, scarred skin. They were long treated as one disease. New evidence on their looks, tissue signs, and gene activity suggests they are close cousins rather than twins. The team pooled past studies to compare the illnesses each one keeps company with.

They searched two large medical databases for all studies on the topic. By combining results across studies, they could spot patterns too faint in single clinics. The review asks whether the two conditions link to different sets of thyroid, hormone, or immune problems. An answer would support or weaken the case for splitting them. It would also tell doctors which screening tests each group of patients needs most.
pmc-13677706:
Poon and fifteen co-authors uncover a helper protein that drug-resistant staph bacteria need to sense antibiotics and switch on their defenses. In MRSA strains, a membrane sensor called BlaR1 spots beta-lactam drugs and triggers production of the resistance machinery. The team shows a kinase, Stk1, must first tag the sensor.

That tag holds the sensor steady in the membrane so it can do its job. Blocking Stk1 made most natural MRSA strains die when beta-lactams were added, a synthetic lethal pairing. The authors also solved the structure of the kinase bound to a blocker. They offer it as a blueprint for new anti-MRSA drugs.
pmc-13678406:
Silvia Schaefer, Adolfo Luna, and Maik Behrens study bitter compounds from cocoa in a 2026 paper. Cocoa carries cyclic dipeptides formed when proteins break down under heat. These compounds drive much of the bitter taste in chocolate foods.

Humans detect bitterness through about twenty-five receptor types. Which receptors answer these cocoa compounds was unknown. The team tested the compounds against the receptor family in cells. Bitter taste warns against toxins, yet mild bitterness is enjoyed. Mapping receptors to foods helps explain that balance. Readers learn how a chocolate note reaches the tongue at the molecular level.
pmc-13679806:
Ezequiel Dantas and a large team report a 2026 feeding trial on diet and immune marks after weight loss. All members first lost 15 percent of their weight on a very-low-carb diet. They were then split by lot among three set diets for ten weeks: the same low-carb plan, a high-carb plan rich in starch, or a high-carb plan rich in sugar.

Blood immune marks were tracked in 44 members with a blend of lab tools. The starch-rich plan shifted some immune cell marks in ways the other plans did not. Readers learn how the kind of carb, not just its amount, may sway the immune system after loss.
pmc-13679906:
Ipsit V Vahia and co-authors tested, in a 2026 trial, whether feeding patients' own texts and emails into therapy improves outcomes. Digital traces surround modern care, yet few studies ask if a therapist reading message patterns actually helps. The EMAP trial randomized 101 adults in therapy for depression or anxiety.

Half got enhanced care: staff scanned their texts with personal mood keywords before sessions and charted findings on a private dashboard for the clinician. The other half got usual therapy. Mood, anxiety, quality of life, and trust in the therapist were tracked in both arms. The trial also watched whether extra insight changed clinical choices. Whatever the verdict, the study sets a careful template for using private messages in care, consent and privacy included.
pmc-13680606:
Fei He and co-authors correct figure data in their study of a histone-modifying enzyme pair, in a 2026 notice. The original paper reported that SESAME-driven phosphorylation blocks a second enzyme's methylation mark, jointly steering autophagy and telomere silencing. Three figure panels and their source data contained errors. Data for three autophagy genes were wrong in one panel.

Elsewhere, one replicate's data had been duplicated into another's slot, in both a main figure and an extra one. Two more genes suffered the same copy slip in the supplement. The notice supplies the original figures for comparison. Corrected figures and source data now stand in the article's online and PDF versions. The amendment keeps the published record straight.
pmc-13681206:
Lisa Doan and four colleagues published a cohort study in two thousand twenty-six on first treatment for acute low back pain and later opioid harm. Care that ignores guidelines is common in this condition. The study asked which starting treatments track with later opioid use disorder or overdose.

Nearly four hundred thousand opioid-naive Medicaid patients in twenty-five states were followed for thirteen months. New disorder or overdose diagnoses reached two point three percent by the end. Starting on higher-dose opioids was linked with higher later risk in the analysis. Other drug and non-drug starting options were compared in the full results. The authors argue first-choice prescribing shapes long-term opioid outcomes.
pmc-13681506:
Jiemei Gu and co-authors reply to a critical letter about their phase three trial of a once-weekly bone drug, defending their reading of the data point by point. The drug is a biosimilar of weekly teriparatide for osteoporosis. The critics raised four charges: how bone turnover markers were read, whether adherence and persistence were confused, the statistics, and how fracture benefit was framed.

The reply explains why one marker barely moved at week twelve while an earlier study saw a jump at week four, and it supplies background the original report had compressed. Trial methodology is the real subject: what weekly snapshots of bone markers can and cannot say. Bone researchers get a public audit of a trial's soft spots, answered in the open.
pmc-13682406:
Wei Wang and co-authors chart, cell by cell, how pig lungs answer infection in a 2026 study. The strain is Klebsiella, and it resists drugs. It is a leading cause of lung infection. Yet how lung cells respond was poorly mapped. The team used single-cell sequencing, flow cytometry, and imaging. They compared healthy pig lungs with infected ones.

Infection rapidly activated neutrophils, monocytes, and interstitial macrophages. Their migration and interferon signatures rose. Alveolar macrophages split into subsets. Several subsets died off, which upset the balance. New subsets presented antigens, were inflamed, and leaned toward scarring. T cell groups rewired how they talked with myeloid cells. Fibroblasts began to multiply toward fibrosis. The atlas gives vaccine and drug hunters a cell map of a serious infection in a large animal lung.
pmc-13682606:
Devin Clegg, Amanda Bentley-DeSousa, Agnes Roczniak-Ferguson, and Shawn Ferguson traced how stress on a cell's recycling centers switches on a Parkinson's-linked enzyme, in a 2026 paper. The enzyme, LRRK2, becomes risky when overactive, and it gathers at lysosomes under stress. The team blocked a fat-making enzyme in the lysosome called PIKfyve and watched what followed.

Blocking PIKfyve drew LRRK2 to lysosomes and turned on its signaling. That response needed a chloride channel named ClC-7, which in turn piled several Rab proteins onto the lysosome surface. LRRK2 latched onto those Rabs, with Rab12 playing a large part. A different stress route, called CASM, used a different mix of helpers. The authors conclude that distinct lysosome troubles reach the same enzyme through different wiring, a map that may guide future drugs.
pmc-13682906:
Tae Jung Kim and five co-authors survey South Korea's intensive care specialists on palliative care inside the ICU, where integration lags other countries. Two hundred forty-one certified intensivists and fellows answered the nationwide online survey in spring twenty twenty-four, a response rate near twenty-four percent. Near-unanimous majorities agreed palliative care belongs in ICU care and said they would refer patients.

Advance care planning, symptom management, and family decision-making were the most expected supports. Involvement in psychological support, end-of-life care, and bereavement was rarer. Referrals flowed more where palliative teams existed; lack of resources, unsupportive culture, and unclear processes were the common barriers. Willingness, the survey suggests, is not the bottleneck.
pmc-13685606:
Liujiazi Shao and co-authors trace an enzyme that stalls immune cells in sepsis in this 2026 study. Sepsis is a runaway inflammatory state that can shut organs down. The enzyme PAD2 tags proteins with a chemical edit called citrullination, and its role in immune metabolism was unclear.

Single-cell reading of lung wash fluid from septic mice gave the first clues. Mice without PAD2 shifted their macrophages toward a healing type, with less lung injury and better survival. A protein census found the enzyme's target: a channel in the cell's power units. Editing that channel chokes glutamine use. The work names a lever on sepsis immunity.
pmc-13688406:
Takamichi Ishii and a large team of co-authors published this study in 2026. It concerns cholangiolocarcinoma, a rare liver cancer defined by a duct-like growth pattern that fills most of the tumor. Because the cancer is so rare, doctors still debate whether it is truly its own disease.

The team collected cases from forty-nine hospitals in Japan and had experts recheck every sample under one standard. Of 196 patients, 56 had the cancer in its pure form. These tumors often showed bright images on scans and a low rate of viral hepatitis. Half the patients lived more than ten years after surgery, far better than related cancers. The authors argue the cancer deserves its own class, while calling for gene studies to settle the borders.
pmc-13689106:
Sepehr Bardi, Mercedes Nieves-Morión, and Rachel Foster studied in 2026 how cells in a chain-forming bacterium pass molecules to each other. These bacteria share food and signals through tiny junctions between cells. The strain they studied lives with algae and forms its special nitrogen-fixing cells only at the chain's end. The team compared it with a free-living relative and a mutant with broken junctions.

Using light methods that bleach a dye and watch it return, they found exchange rates much like the relative's. The mutant, by contrast, showed weak and uneven exchange. Chain shape and cell type shaped how exchange spread along the filament. Pore counts in the walls varied, which may explain some of that spread. The work offers a way to map talk between bacterial cells.
pmc-13694106:
Ulugbek Mirzaev and co-authors track cervical cancer in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, from 2014 to 2024 in a 2026 registry study. The cancer kills many women in the country, school vaccine cover began in 2019, and screening still reaches few women.

More than two thousand cases fill the city register. Early, pre cancer finds jumped more than threefold after two screening projects began, while late stage shares fell steeply. Five year survival ran from near full for the earliest stage to under a third for the latest. Death rates fell hard across the decade. The team credit planned screening for the shift.
pmc-1629006:
Staff of the United States Food and Drug Administration issue draft guidance on patient-reported outcome measures. Such measures capture how patients feel and function, as reported by patients themselves. Drug makers may use them as endpoints in trials to support claims on product labels.

The guidance explains how the agency judges these tools and what it currently expects from sponsors. It covers how a measure should be built and how trial results may back a label claim. Clear rules help firms design trials that truly reflect patient experience, not only lab values.
pmc-2270306:
Mossong, Hens, Jit, and co-authors measure social contacts that matter for spreading infectious disease. Models of diseases passed by breath or close contact, such as pandemic flu, guide choices about vaccines and closures. Contact patterns are known to drive what those models predict.

The team gathered real data on who meets whom, by age and setting, across everyday life. Such data replace guesses in models with observed mixing. Better contact data lead to better forecasts of how fast an outbreak grows, which groups drive spread, and which interventions help most.
pmc-3111406:
Boulkedid, Abdoul, Loustau, and co-authors review how the Delphi method is used and reported for choosing healthcare quality indicators. The Delphi technique is a structured process in which experts answer rounds of questions until views converge. It is commonly used to build quality indicators, yet guidance for users was thin.

The authors describe how studies report their Delphi work and discuss its strengths and gaps. Inconsistent reporting makes indicator sets hard to judge or copy. Their review pushes for clearer standards, so measures used to grade hospitals rest on a sound process.
pmc-3995906:
Assarsson and co-authors reported a new protein test in 2014 that can measure many targets at once. Care that is tailored to each patient needs large amounts of high-quality data on markers in blood and tissue. Older tests often measured one protein at a time, which was slow and costly.

Their proximity extension assay measures ninety-six proteins in a single run, all in one format. The method uses pairs of probes that must bind side by side, which keeps the signal specific. Tests showed high sensitivity and good scaling to large sample sets. Such panels can speed the search for marker patterns that warn of disease early.
pmc-4086106:
Robert and Gouet presented a new version of ENDscript in 2014, a web server for studying protein structure. Proteins have levels of structure, from their amino acid chain up to folded units and complexes. Pulling all that information together by hand is slow and error prone.

ENDscript two gathers and draws a full analysis in an automated way, from the basic sequence to the assembled form. The upgrade was rebuilt to improve speed, accuracy, and ease of use. It also adds interactive three-dimensional viewing. Structural biologists use such views to spot the features that govern how a protein works.
pmc-4987906:
Afgan, Baker, van den Beek, and their colleagues updated the Galaxy platform in 2016. High-throughput technologies, above all next-generation DNA sequencing, had brought disruptive change to biomedical research. Reading the huge datasets they produce takes sophisticated statistical and computing tools.

Galaxy offers those tools through a web platform designed to be accessible, reproducible, and collaborative. Users run complex analyses without programming, and every step is recorded so others can repeat it. Sharing workflows helps teams check and build on each other's work. Galaxy brought data-heavy biology within reach of labs without dedicated computing staff.
pmc-5081106:
The NCD Risk Factor Collaboration pooled data in 2016 on worldwide trends in diabetes since 1980. One global target for non-communicable diseases is to halt the rise in adult diabetes prevalence by 2025 at its 2010 level. The team estimated trends and judged how likely countries are to meet that target.

Their pooled analysis covered hundreds of population-based studies with millions of participants. Such scale reveals which regions drive the global rise and where progress stalls. The results show the scale of change needed in diet, activity, and care. Governments use these trend estimates to set and check national diabetes plans.
pmc-517706:
Edgar presented MUSCLE in full in 2004, a program for multiple sequence alignment of proteins. Aligning many protein sequences side by side reveals which parts are conserved and how proteins are related. In an earlier paper, Edgar had shown MUSCLE reaching the highest scores then reported on four accuracy benchmarks.

This paper presents the algorithm in more detail. MUSCLE was designed to cut both the time and the memory that alignment takes, without losing accuracy. Faster alignment matters because sequence collections were already growing quickly. MUSCLE became one of the most used alignment tools in biology, a base step for trees, structure work, and gene family studies.
pmc-5491406:
Roth, Johnson, Abajobir, and many colleagues measured the global burden of cardiovascular diseases in 2017 for the GBD 2015 study. In many world regions, the true burden of these diseases was still murky. The team merged data on new cases, total cases, and deaths into consistent, current estimates.

Cardiovascular diseases cover heart attacks, stroke, heart failure, and other causes, ten of which the team tracked from 1990 to 2015. Their estimates show where death rates fall with treatment and prevention and where they still climb. Consistent methods across countries make the comparisons meaningful. Health ministries use such figures to plan cardiac and stroke services.
pmc-549606:
Pao, Miller, Politi, and their team reported in 2005 on why some lung tumors stop responding to targeted drugs. The drugs gefitinib and erlotinib block EGFR, a growth switch. Tumors that respond at first tend to carry changes in the EGFR gene that make the switch easy to block.

Most such tumors grow back in time as resistance sets in. The team found that tumors which had become resistant often carried a second change in the same part of EGFR. That second change lets the switch dodge the drug. The find explained a chief route of resistance and pushed the design of new EGFR drugs built to beat it.
pmc-5642006:
Stephen Burgess, Dylan Small, and Simon Thompson wrote this methods review in 2015. Their topic is Mendelian randomization, a way to test cause and effect using genes as stand-ins for a risk factor. The review compares the main statistical tools researchers use for that job.

Each method rests on assumptions about the gene variants, and the authors explain when those assumptions can fail. They weigh strengths and limits side by side so readers can pick a tool that fits their data. For anyone using genetic data to judge whether a habit or trait truly causes disease, the guidance here helps avoid false claims.
pmc-5753206:
Daniel Zerbino and a large team at Ensembl published the 2018 update of the Ensembl genome resource. Ensembl has collected and shared genome data since the first draft of the human genome. Its aim is to speed research by giving public data away fast and free.

The update reports new genomes, richer gene annotation, and better tools for comparing species. Users can browse genes, variants, and regulation data in a web browser or pull data in bulk. Most genomics papers rely on Ensembl at some step. The yearly updates keep the resource matched to fast-growing data volumes.
pmc-6227606:
The GBD 2017 Causes of Death Collaborators published this mortality analysis in 2018. Countries need cause-of-death figures they can compare to judge their own progress. The study estimates deaths by age and sex for a long list of causes.

Coverage spans nearly two hundred countries and territories over almost four decades. Heart disease and stroke lead the global totals, while child deaths from infection keep falling. The authors flag places where death records are weak and estimates lean on models. Even with those limits, the release is the standard yardstick for global mortality.
pmc-6441206:
Yang Mou, Jun Wang, Jinchun Wu, and coauthors reviewed ferroptosis in cancer in 2019. Ferroptosis is a recently named form of cell death driven by iron and fat oxidation. It looks and behaves quite unlike the classic apoptosis pathway.

Fast-growing work links ferroptosis to many cancers. Some tumors resist standard drugs yet stay sensitive to ferroptosis triggers. The review gathers the core machinery, from iron handling to lipid repair failure. It also lists the hard problems, such as finding markers in patients. The field hopes this death route can kill cancers that evade other treatments.
pmc-7182206:
Bui Quang Minh, Heiko Schmidt, Olga Chernomor, and coauthors presented IQ-TREE 2 in 2020. IQ-TREE builds evolutionary trees by maximum likelihood and is popular for its speed and ease of use. The first version had gathered many features since its release years earlier.

The second version adds new models, including ones for mixed and partitioned data, and faster search methods. It handles the huge alignments of the genomic era without special hardware. Benchmarks show accuracy on par with or better than rival tools. Phylogenetics courses and labs worldwide treat it as a default choice.
pmc-7618106:
Cryptosporidium, a gut parasite, is a leading killer of young children in poor regions and has no vaccine or good drug. Muralidhara Rao Maradana and co-authors uncover a diet-linked defense in this 2023 study using a mouse-infecting cousin of the parasite.

Killer T cells living in the gut wall held the parasite down, and they depended on a sensor protein that answers to plant compounds in food. Without the sensor, these cells thinned out and infections worsened. Feeding newborn mice a cabbage-family compound that switches the sensor on made them resist infection. The findings point to food-based support for gut immunity.
pmc-7719906:
Fiona Bull and co-authors set out the World Health Organization's 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behavior. The guidelines were built following the organization's standard process, with an expert group reviewing the evidence. That evidence covered how activity and sitting time relate to health in children, teenagers, adults, and older people.

The document states how much activity each age group should aim for each week, and advises cutting down long stretches of sitting. It also speaks to people living with chronic conditions and disabilities, groups often left out of such advice. National health agencies around the world base their own recommendations on these guidelines, so the numbers chosen here shape public advice for years.
pmc-7764106:
Zeinab Breijyeh and Rafik Karaman wrote a comprehensive review in 2020 on Alzheimer's disease, the main cause of dementia worldwide. The disease slowly breaks down brain cells, and with them a person's thinking, memory, and independence in daily life. It is understood as a condition with many contributing causes rather than a single one.

The review lays out the leading explanations for how the disease begins and advances, including the long debated roles of abnormal protein deposits in the brain. It then surveys the treatments in use and under study, and what each can and cannot do. For readers seeking one clear account of a complex illness, the review gathers causes, symptoms, and therapy in a single place.
pmc-8010506:
Laith Alzubaidi and colleagues wrote a broad review in 2021 of deep learning, the approach that had come to dominate machine learning. Deep learning trains layered networks on large amounts of data, and it had recently produced standout results in fields from image recognition to language. The authors set out to give newcomers and specialists one shared map of the field.

They explain the core concepts, then compare the main network designs built around convolutional networks for images. They also take stock of open problems, survey real applications, and sketch where the field may head next. A review of this scope serves as an entry point for students and as a checkpoint for researchers measuring how fast the ground is shifting.
pmc-8617206:
Xiaojia Hu and co-authors reviewed in 2021 the JAK/STAT signaling pathway, a fast route by which cells pass messages from their surface to their nucleus. The pathway was discovered more than twenty-five years ago and has since proved central to many vital processes, including immunity and blood formation. It works as a rapid module: a signal at the membrane switches on transcription factors that head straight for the genes.

The review traces the pathway from laboratory discovery to the clinic, where drugs blocking its Janus kinase enzymes now treat several diseases. The authors also cover what goes wrong when the pathway is overactive or broken. Few signaling routes have traveled so completely from basic biology to the pharmacy shelf.
pothier-obligations-contracts-1806:
Robert Pothier, a French judge and scholar, wrote his Treatise on Obligations in the 1760s. William Evans's English translation of 1806 is the version here, with notes on English law. Pothier's book is the French civilian foundation of modern contract law.

He defines contracts, consent, error, and fault in clear, ordered chapters. His rules passed almost whole into the French civil code and from there worldwide. English and American judges cited the translation in court for decades. Anyone tracing where modern contract ideas came from will land on Pothier, the quiet professor from Orléans who organized a whole field.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-159-19:
October 6, 1920, in Punch, volume 159, opens with Charivaria, the standing column of short jokes on the news. Motors, servants, and literary quarrels supply this week's material.

A London magistrate rules that motorists cannot go about knocking people down every day, and the column agrees once should be enough for any walker. A Kensington lady hires a parlourmaid three feet seven inches tall, a sign of the servant shortage. A play called The Man Who Went to Work is treated as a farce by its title alone, an Ealing sergeant has summoned six hundred motorists since March, and Mr. H. G. Wells and Mr. Henry Arthur Jones agree to shake hands and stay enemies.
ramusio-navigationi-et-viaggi-vol-3-1606:
Giovanni Battista Ramusio's Delle Navigationi et Viaggi closes with volume three, here in the Venetian printing of 1606. The collection itself dates to 1550 through 1559, when Ramusio issued its volumes in Italian at Venice. He worked from reports sent home by travelers, merchants, and ambassadors of many nations.

Ramusio's three volumes formed the first great voyage collection, the pattern for Hakluyt's and Purchas's later English sets. Marco Polo's travels found their first complete printed home in its pages. Voyages to Africa and Asia fill out the survey. With volume three, the work that taught Europe to read the world as one map stands complete.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: A publisher's header, and a publisher's header only, fronts volume six of Constant's Private Life of Napoleon Bonaparte in these pages. From it a reader gathers the title, the author Constant, and that the work is in English. No page of the valet's account of his master follows in what is shown: neither an opening chapter nor a contents page is present. Which years or scenes of Napoleon's life this sixth volume holds is therefore a question these pages leave unanswered.
richard-carvel-volume-06:
Winston Churchill's Richard Carvel opens its sixth volume with His Grace Makes Advances, as Richard casts about for his next move. Jack Comyn blows in like a gust of wind, rating him for moping and ignoring his calls. Comyn swears Dorothy loves him, for there were no tears when Comyn made his own avowal.

Mr. Manners, Comyn holds, had appealed to Dorothy to save him, and her tears point one way only. Richard laughs and recalls Comyn's earlier counsel, spoken when he got Richard out of the sponging-house. The volume's list runs from Lord Baltimore and a glimpse of Mr. Garrick to Holland House and Vauxhall.
rivers-the-todas-1906:
W. H. R. Rivers went to the Nilgiri Hills of southern India to study the Toda people, and his 1906 book reports what he found. The Todas were few in number, pastoral, and organized around the buffalo in a way no outsider had fully recorded.

At the center stands the sacred dairy, where buffalo milk is handled as a ritual by priest-dairymen under strict rules. Rivers also documents polyandry, in which brothers share a wife, and works out Toda kinship with new care. His genealogical method, built for this study, changed fieldwork itself. The book launched British social anthropology's classic period.
san-francisco-during-the-eventful-days-o:
James B. Stetson wrote San Francisco During the Eventful Days of April 1906 as personal recollections, written in June 1906. A note adds that, the first edition being used up and a new one required, he has included some events that occurred later, without changing the original date. Stetson says the earthquake and great fire of 1906 were events of such unusual interest that he jotted down incidents he personally observed while they were fresh. He laid the notes away so he could refer to them later with some assurance of their accuracy, knowing how faulty memory grows after time passes.

On the morning of April 18, 1906, at 5:13, in his residence at 1801 Van Ness Avenue, Stetson was awakened by a very severe shock. The shaking nearly threw him out of bed.
santayana-life-reason-vol-5-1906:
Reason in Science, published in 1906, closes The Life of Reason as its fifth and crowning volume. Santayana turns last to science, the pursuit his whole system had to honor without worshiping.

He treats science as reason's most disciplined form: a method for mapping nature's order, powerful exactly because it describes rather than consoles. Against it he sets the claims of history and of the inner life, which science cannot replace. The volume rounds the five books into one vision: reason as man's one guide in every sphere. Santayana was thirty-nine when he finished; few systems begin so complete.
scheible-das-kloster-vol06:
Johann Scheible closed the year 1846 with band six of Das Kloster, cells twenty-one through twenty-four. Halfway through the set, the shape of his work stood clear. He meant to save the whole range of German folk print, high claims and low alike, in full reprints.

The grimoire shelf stays heavy here: spell books, Faust books, and Höllenzwänge in their full, stark text. Beside them sit folk charms and popular chapbooks, the small books that passed from hand to hand. A modern reader meets magic here as it was sold, not as later ages cleaned it. That plain honesty gives the band its lasting use.
schlussel-zu-dem-cabinet-der-geheimen-sc: A 1706 German key unlocked nature's secret treasure chamber. The cabinet of hidden riches. The natural secrets. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care for all readers. Scholars prize such firsthand sources from long ago.
serapis-volume-06:
Georg Ebers wrote this historical novel of Alexandria; volume six opens at chapter twenty-five in the vast Hippodrome. Thousands fill the seats on race eve, though a night storm and fear have kept many home. Word spreads that the statue of Serapis came through the siege of his shrine unharmed.

Imperial legate Cynegius and city prefect Evagrius enter with great pomp, followed by senators and ranked ladies and men. Christians, heathen, and Jews sit together as the games, put off by panic, begin at last. This closing volume stages a city's relief and dread in one bright, tense public scene.
shahnama-warner-vol-2-1906:
Arthur George Warner and Edmond Warner published Volume 2 of their Shahnama of Firdausi in 1906. The Shahnama, or Book of Kings, is the Persian national epic, written by Firdausi around the year 1000. The Warner brothers set out to give English readers the whole poem, in nine volumes.

Volume 2 carries the epic's early kings and heroes onward, through wars, hunts, and court tales told in verse. Their translation kept the poem's shape while making its stories plain to English readers. No full English Shahnama existed before theirs. The volume continues a vast record of Persian myth and memory, where legend and early history flow together without a clear break.
shahnameh-warner-vol2-1906:
Ferdowsi wrote the Shahnama, the Book of Kings, the great epic poem of Persia. Arthur George Warner and Edmond Warner turned it into English verse. Theirs was the first full English verse version of the whole poem. Book two of their set came out in 1906.

Kings rise and fall in long tales of war, love, and fate. Heroes fight beasts and rival lords while wise men warn of pride. The Warners kept the sweep of the tale in plain, strong verse. For most English readers, this set was the first door into Persia's best loved book.
shaku-sermons-buddhist-abbot-1906:
Soyen Shaku was the Zen abbot who spoke for Buddhism at the Chicago Parliament of Religions in 1893. His Sermons of a Buddhist Abbot, published in 1906, gathers the addresses he gave on his American tour of 1905 and 1906. His student Suzuki translated them into English.

Shaku explains karma, rebirth, and the Buddha's enlightenment in a calm, gracious voice shaped for Western hearers. He presents Buddhism as a way of waking, not a set of dogmas to be believed on command. The sermons mark the moment Zen first addressed America through one of its own masters. His dignity did much to win Buddhism a fair hearing in America.
sherrington-integrative-action-1906:
Charles Sherrington was a British physiologist whose lab work mapped how nerves join muscles into working systems. His 1906 book The Integrative Action of the Nervous System sums up years of trials on reflexes. It is often named the founding text of modern neuroscience.

Sherrington names the synapse, the tiny junction where one nerve cell hands its signal to the next. He shows how reflex arcs combine, compete, and yield so that an animal acts as one whole. Later brain science built directly on his terms, his maps, and his careful method. He coined much of the language that nerve science still speaks.
sinclair-jungle-1906:
Upton Sinclair went undercover in Chicago's stockyards in 1904, living among the packinghouse workers for seven weeks. He published The Jungle in 1906, intending a socialist indictment of wage slavery. Sinclair later joked that he aimed at the public's heart and hit its stomach instead.

Jurgis Rudkus, a Lithuanian immigrant, arrives strong and hopeful, then is ground down by injury, layoffs, and the loss of his family. Around his story Sinclair documents the meatpacking industry in revolting detail: spoiled meat, filth, and worse sold as food. Congress rushed through the Pure Food and Drug Act and meat inspection within months. The Jungle remains the most consequential protest novel in American history.
spr-proceedings-vol20-1906:
Volume twenty of the Proceedings, from 1906, consists of part fifty three alone. The Society for Psychical Research often filled a whole part with one great report. Telepathy and trance work dominate the society's business in this period. Long sittings with mediums appear in near verbatim form.

Investigators weigh the Piper material and its rivals with care. Spontaneous cases of apparitions arrive in smaller numbers, well documented. The volume's single part format suits readers who want depth over range. It forms one brick in the archive wall built between 1882 and 1930. The society's standards, set early, hold firm here. Evidence first remains the rule.
suess-face-of-earth-vol2-sollas-1906:
Volume 2 of Sollas's translation of Suess's Face of the Earth appeared in 1906. Eduard Suess turned in this volume to the oceans, their history and their floors. The work surveys the Atlantic and other seas as archives of the Earth's past.

Suess traced marine transgressions, the long advances of sea over land recorded in layered rocks. He compared coastlines and fossil seas across continents to rebuild vanished oceans. One of them, the Tethys, became a lasting term of geology from his pages. Sollas's translation kept pace with the German original's ambition. The volume shows geology thinking at planetary scale a generation before plate tectonics gave it a new engine.
tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontaine-vol:
The Magick Cup stands alone in the sixth volume of La Fontaine's Tales and Novels. It tells of a husband who tests his wife's faith with an enchanted cup. The cup spills on the unfaithful. Jealousy is the volume's whole subject.

The poet begins by calling jealousy the worst of ills, beside which all other torments are trifling. He pictures the jealous fool as suspicion's easy tool, finding no repose by night or day, forever dreaming that his forehead sprouts, and never doubting the truth of his dreams. Against that portrait the tale sets its test: a cup that promises certainty, and the misery certainty brings. La Fontaine treats the green-eyed passion with pity and mockery in equal measure.
tales-and-novels-volume-06:
Volume VI of Maria Edgeworth's Tales and Novels holds The Absentee, her novel of an Irish landlord's son who comes home from London fashion to face the estate his family has drained. The tale opens in the crush-room of the opera-house, where carriages are waited for and gossip does the work of news.

Lady Langdale and Mrs Dareville trade word of Lady Clonbrony's coming gala. The rooms are to be furnished at prodigious expense. The style will be most magnificent. Colonel Heathcock marvels at the rate the Clonbronies are dashing on. Then her grace asks a simple question. Who are these Clonbronies, that one hears of so much of late? The novel's question is set by it. New money apes old rank here. The Irish tenants pay for the show.
the-amateur-cracksman-pg706:
Eight linked tales by E. W. Hornung make up this volume, all circling Raffles, a gentleman thief at ease in smart London rooms. Its contents run from The Ides of March and A Costume Piece through Gentlemen and Players and Wilful Murder to The Return Match and The Gift of the Emperor.

The opening story finds the narrator back at the Albany after midnight, facing a table strewn with baccarat counters and glasses. Raffles, now in a blazer, raises his brows at the late visit. The younger man admits he barely knows his host, yet reminds him they met at school and asks to be heard.
the-bride-of-the-nile-volume-06:
Volume 6 of The Bride of the Nile, by Georg Ebers, opens at Chapter XXII with a girl in swift change. Till a few days back Katharina was a docile child. She held it a point of honor to obey at once her mother's lightest word, Dame Neforis, and even the sour Eudoxia. She hid nothing, and could not rest till, before evening prayer, she had confessed each small fault and been forgiven. Night after night the Water-wagtail slept with a conscience as white as her whitest dove.

The change came after Orion's kiss among the flowering trees. Since then each hour has waked new hopes and new views in her. A barrier, too, stands between her and Paula. Paula, she is sure, is that other one of whom Orion spoke. With the governor's house shut to her, Katharina has no one left to trust.
the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume-06:
The sixth part of The Caxtons keeps the son, Pisistratus, as its teller. Readers hear the family from inside, in his own words. At the center sits his father, learned, retiring, and fond of a good argument after tea.

Mr. Trevanion sits in the family drawing room on a warm night, at ease after two cups of tea. With him comes Sir Sedley Beaudesert, a college friend his father has not seen for years. Talk turns on whether happiness is the end and aim of human life. The narrator's father answers the common claim with plain doubt, and the talk sets the tone for the part.
the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rousseau:
Book VI of Jean Jacques Rousseau's Confessions stands here as volume VI of the twelve-book set, privately printed for members of the Aldus Society at London in 1903. A Latin tag from Horace heads the book, wishing for a modest plot of ground, a garden, a spring near the house, and a little wood beyond.

 He had no need to own the place; enjoying it was enough. Proprietor and possessor, he remarks, are two very different people, even leaving husbands and lovers aside. At this moment, he writes, began the short happiness of his life, those peaceful and rapid moments that give him a right to say he has lived. He begs those precious, regretted moments to run their course again, more slowly, through his memory. Book VI is the idyll of the set, the still center against which the later misfortunes are measured.
the-crisis-volume-06:
Volume 6 of Winston Churchill's The Crisis opens Book III with Chapter I, Introducing a Capitalist. A cordon of blue regiments rings the city from Carondelet to North St. Louis like an open fan. Crowds favor Compton Heights, where German citizen-soldiers' tents spread like slices of white cake beside the reservoir.

Inside the ring lies the peace of martial law. Beyond it, an angry governor gathers his forces and trades letters with Jefferson Davis. Young men of St. Louis slip away at night to Glencoe, and Union officers search Colonel Carvel's house there from garret to cellar more than once. Headquarters marks the house in red ink as a place where young men's feet stray, and councils of war debate seizing it.
the-disowned-volume-06:
