Three years pass before chapter fifty-nine of The Disowned, which opens volume six at the Golden Fleece inn in the town of W----. A stranger in deep mourning arrives on horseback and takes a private room for the night. The plump landlady barely glances at him, but her daughter notes his good looks and soldierly air. Local talk soon turns to Squire Mordaunt and village affairs.

The quiet inn scene sets up a return full of secrets. Old places and faces meet a changed man, and the novel begins to draw its long threads together.
the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustrated-h:
Cantos thirteen through seventeen form part six of Hell in Dante's Vision, in the Rev. H. F. Cary's verse. The travellers enter a trackless wood of dark leaves, knotted boughs, and poisoned thorns, with no fruit at all. Harpies nest in its branches, the same birds that drove the Trojans from the Strophades with dark warnings.

Souls who harmed themselves grow as trees in this wood and speak only when a twig is torn. Beyond it lie burning sands and fraud's first shapes. The part is among the strangest in the descent.
the-emperor-volume-06:
Part two of Georg Ebers's The Emperor starts in volume six, at chapter one (a fresh count). Dame Hannah has cooled Selene's hurt foot and head wound all night, and the old doctor is pleased with his patient. Left alone with her friend Mary, Selene begs for news of Lochias: who guided Mary home, and how her small brother and sisters fare.

Fever still clouds her, and Mary's care is tender. Clara Bell's rendering shifts the tale's heart to the steward's sick girl. Court plots pause while love and duty watch at a bedside.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1-part:
In Ormsby's translation, Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes moves on to Volume 1, Part 06. Chapter sixteen tells of what happened to the ingenious gentleman in the inn he took to be a castle. The innkeeper asks Sancho what is amiss with his master, slung across the ass.

Sancho answers that Quixote fell from a rock and bruised his ribs. The innkeeper's kind-hearted wife tends the guest at once, helped by her comely young daughter. Cervantes then describes the servant lass in the inn and the wretched bed made up in a former straw-loft, with four rough boards, a thin mattress, and sheets like buckler leather.
the-innocents-abroad-volume-06:
Part 6 of Mark Twain's Innocents Abroad opens in chapter L. The text comes from the 1869 first edition. The party descends from Mount Tabor toward Nazareth. The road is hilly, rocky, and two hours long. Twain explains Eastern measurement. All distances here are hours, not miles. A good horse walks three miles in an hour. The traveler must translate as he goes. Pagan hours become Christian miles in the mind.

The trail crowds them against every caravan. Donkeys can be jumped with a spirited horse. A camel is not jumpable at all. It stands taller than a Syrian dwelling-house. Colossal sacks hang on each side. It takes up as much room as a carriage. It would not turn out for a king. Twain claims eighteen hundred donkeys jumped on that ride. He adds a straight-faced caveat. Things are not what they seem, as the poet said.
the-inside-of-the-cup-volume-06:
Volume 6 of Winston Churchill's novel opens with chapter XX, The Arraignment. Hodder looks backward and finds his true decision point. He had entered the darkening church one twilight evening. Kate Marcy's visit at Mr. Bentley's lay behind him. His mission appeared to him then as a vision. Each day since has strengthened it.

One trial waits close at hand. He must talk with his assistant, McCrae. Their bond was unusual from the start. Hodder bade him goodbye and then stayed on. He announced he would take no part in services. Months of rare, casual greetings followed. Hodder admires McCrae's faithful, unpraised work. He suspects the man likes him and would sympathize. He shrinks from testing that theory all the same. The volume continues with Alison going to church.
the-journals-of-lewis-and-clark-1804-180:
Meriwether Lewis and William Clark kept these journals on their expedition. They run from May 14, 1804, to September 26, 1806. The party left the Mississippi River at the start. It returned to St. Louis at the end. A transcriber's note explains the presentation. Most courses, distances, and sky observations are omitted. Past editors' notes and corrections are removed. The misspellings are mostly two hundred years old. Clark's first entry records the setting out. Camp River a Dubois lay behind them at four o'clock.

The party sailed in cloudy rain that first day. Clark counts two leaders and a Frenchman. Twenty-two men rowed the boat of twenty oars. Men in two large pirogues came along. They camped opposite Cold Water creek after four and a half miles. The men were in high spirits. A second version of the same day follows. Lewis's hand begins after it. Readers get the expedition raw.
the-last-of-the-barons-volume-06:
Book Six of Edward Bulwer Lytton Warwick novel forms the portion in this record. Warwick returns to London and seems restored to supreme rule after a cordial meeting with Edward IV. Princess Margaret leaves as bride to Charles the Bold of Burgundy.

Edward then declares war on Louis XI of France and raises troops for the plan. Warwick opposes the war with force, warning that Lancastrian supporters could rise once England best fighters sail away. He also doubts Burgundy aid under a reckless duke. Old friendship thins as court enemies use the quarrel against the earl.
the-memoirs-of-count-grammont-volume-06:
Volume 6 of Anthony Hamilton's Memoirs of Count Grammont, edited with notes by Sir Walter Scott, opens at Chapter Tenth, other love intrigues at the English court. The scene turns on an overheard conversation between Miss Hobart and Miss Temple. Miss Temple leaves irritated, wanting to know why Sidney's esteem for her should bar her own attentions to him. Neither woman knows a listener has heard every word.

Miss Sarah, a servant girl, has hidden in a cold bath behind silk curtains to make herself clean for Lord Rochester's sake. Her mistress's maid locked the partition just before the ladies entered. Sarah emerges nearly perished with cold, then reports the whole conversation to Rochester. Rochester weighs Hobart's trick and questions Sarah about his supposed affection for Miss Temple. Readers get court intrigue filtered through servants' ears and a bath turned into an eavesdropping post.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
A supplementary number of the Mirror, No. 340, heads its Spirit of the Annuals for 1829 with an engraving of Vicenza. The editorial table has glittered for days with gift books in silk and burnished gold. Seven of nine annuals wear watered silk bindings. A lady friend calculates that the silk covering the presumed 70,000 copies sold would stretch five miles, from Hyde Park Corner to Turnham Green.

Contents, the editors insist, are transcendentally beautiful beyond the brilliant exteriors. Their only trouble is an embarras du richesses in choosing specimens. The roundup begins with the parent stock of annuals, The Forget-Me-Not, edited by Frederic Shoberl. Presentation copies, they confess, already sit in the fair hands intended for them. Readers get the Christmas book trade measured in miles of silk before a single poem is quoted.

Oporto, in Portugal, opens volume 20, No. 559, dated July 28, 1832. Readers watching for news from a seat of war would welcome the engraving, the editors remark, while declaring themselves people of the pen, not the sword. The city mattered for trade as much as for politics.

Next to Lisbon, Oporto was Portugal's largest city. It stands on the north bank of the Douro, about five miles from the river's mouth on the Atlantic. Roman origin was commonly claimed, yet the account prefers a founding around the year 417 by the Suevi, driven to a steep hill still called the Cidade Antiga. The cathedral and bishop's palace crown that hill today, in the account's telling.
the-parisians-volume-06:
Book VI of Edward Bulwer-Lytton's The Parisians opens at a supper given by Frederic Lemercier. A gay party of men fills a private salon of the Maison Doree. Rank, art, literature, the Bourse, science, and finance all have their men at table, from Alain de Rochebriant to the physician Dr. Bacourt and the banker Duplessis.

Talk turns to a paper by M. Savarin on the link between national character and national diet. Savarin suggests drink shapes a people more than food. Italy's heady wines breed great plans that cannot be digested, while English beer makes a stolid, stubborn character. The scene shows Parisian wit at table.
the-pigeon-pie-pg2606:
Charlotte M. Yonge's The Pigeon Pie appears here in the new edition from A. R. Mowbray and Co., dated 1905. That is the same edition whose front matter opens the sibling record. Yonge is named as the author of The Heir of Redclyffe. A contents list of nine chapters comes before the story proper.

Chapter I places the scene early in September 1651, in the dining hall of Forest Lea House. Sunshine enters through a large bay window glazed in diamonds. Some panes have been broken and never mended. Dark oak wainscot lines the walls and floor. Stag's antlers hold a sheathed sword, odd gauntlets, an old helmet, a gun, bows, and broad shady hats. The war-worn room quietly sets up a tale from the years just after the English civil wars.
the-right-of-way-volume-06:
Gilbert Parker's sixth volume opens at Chaudiere. The village is becoming notable to the outside world. Habitants ride up the road toward Four Mountains. They go to rehearse a Passion Play there. Saddler Filion Lacasse boasts in front of the post-office. Every house holds two or three boarders, he says. A gloomy groom doubts the talk behind him.

Contents promise the play itself in this final volume. Face-to-face meetings and Billy's coming follow. Seigneur and cure share a suspicion in the list. Rosalie plays a part, and a furnace burns. A man stands with his back to the wall. An epilogue closes the novel. Public spectacle frames private reckonings at the end.
the-spirit-of-1906:
George W. Brooks, who founded the California Insurance Company when it was reorganized in 1905, published these reminiscences through the company in San Francisco in 1921. He dedicates them to the directors and shareholders of 1906. Those men gave up a great deal of their own money in the company's hours of trial.

Brooks's foreword hopes readers will find the character of those men between the lines of his rambling pages. They upheld their own good name and the company's fair name. They also upheld the integrity of California's financial institutions. The narrative then begins by recalling the leading part the California Insurance Company played in the events of 1906, the year of San Francisco's great disaster.
the-story-of-my-life-volume-06:
Volume six of Georg Ebers's autobiography opens at chapter twenty-one, at the university. The weeks after graduation suited no serious decision. A gay trip through Bohemia ended in Prague. Ebers divided his time between Hosterwitz, Blasewitz, and Dresden. He enjoyed pleasant evenings there. His cousin, an Austrian lieutenant on leave, joined him with his comrades.

Those young officers counted the Italians they fought as rebels, while an older colonel of the family judged Italy's struggle for unity justly and aroused courteous opposition. Ebers longed meanwhile for student freedom. He wanted to sit at the feet of Ernst Curtius. He wanted to learn historical method from Waitz. The night before his departure, the poet Julius Hammer praised student liberty. He spoke at an entertainment in Blasewitz.
the-wandering-jew-volume-06:
Volume six of Eugene Sue's Wandering Jew concludes part second, The Chastisement, in book six. Contents chapters include A Good Genius, The Stranger, The Den, an accuser, revelations, and Pierre Simon. Chapter twenty-six opens mid-scene, as arrivals interrupt a notary's answer.

Faringhea, forbidding of face, announces that Prince Djalma has lately arrived from India for this very day, following an inscription on a medal worn about his neck. Gabriel, who sailed with the prince from the Azores, cries that Djalma is also one of the heirs, his mother being of French origin. Rodin starts at the news, then recovers his habitual coolness under the Strangler's pointed emphasis. The gathering of heirs tightens around the medal's summons.
the-works-of-samuel-johnson-ll-d-in-elev: Volume six of Samuel Johnson's works is shown by a title page and contents list alone. One point needs stating plainly: the title page prints a nine-volume set, dated 1825, although the record names an eleven-volume edition. Contents cover reviews, political tracts, and lives of eminent persons. Johnson reviews works on China, Pope, and the Royal Society. A review of the Duchess of Marlborough's conduct also appears. The reviews themselves do not follow in the pages present.
tob-0006:
Judaism's scripture, the Tanakh, is the same body of books Christians call the Old Testament. Its name joins three parts: Torah, the Teaching; Nevi'im, the Prophets; and Ketuvim, the Writings. Generations of rabbis guarded the Hebrew text letter by letter.

Inside stand creation and flood, the exodus from Egypt, laws for a holy people, songs, proverbs, and fierce prophecy. The arc runs across well over a thousand years of one people's history. No public-domain text is attached to this entry yet, per its evidence. The work itself, law, poetry, and history in one, needs no salesmanship.
tob-10806:
A. W. Tozer wrote The Pursuit of God in 1948 as a devotional call to Christians grown comfortable with routine religion. Tozer, a pastor in the Christian and Missionary Alliance, urged readers past mere belief into direct, thirsty pursuit of God himself. The chapters are short and intense.

Each chapter ends with a searching prayer, and the argument asks readers to tear down idols of self: self-love, self-protection, and religious show. Plainspoken rather than academic, the book became one of the twentieth century's most reprinted spiritual works in evangelical circles. Readers meet a mid-century pastor insisting that knowing about God is not the same as knowing God.
tob-10808-50206:
Volume two of von Hügel's The Mystical Element of Religion turns critical and philosophical after volume one's life of Saint Catherine of Genoa. What is mysticism, how does it relate to reason, and how can a church institution house a force that seems to bypass institutions? Von Hügel weighs the claims of mystical experience against philosophy, history, and common life.

The constructive argument balances three elements of religion, institutional, intellectual, and mystical, each correcting the others. Demanding in style and learning, the volume forms the summit of its literature for many readers. Those who worked through Catherine's story in volume one now receive the framework von Hügel built to interpret her.
tob-13506:
Volume two of Augustine's City of God, in Marcus Dods's translation, continues the bishop of Hippo's great reply to charges that Christianity caused Rome's fall. Augustine wrote between 413 and 426, after Visigoths had sacked Rome. His answer distinguishes two cities, the earthly and the heavenly, intermingled through history.

Later books trace those cities toward final judgment and eternal peace, arguing that earthly empires rise and fall by providence, not by the old gods' favor. The work effectively invented a Christian philosophy of history. Few books have influenced Western thinking about politics, time, and salvation as deeply, and volume two carries the argument to its end.
tob-4006:
Benvenuto Cellini, goldsmith and sculptor to kings, dictated an autobiography in John Symonds's translation that ranks as the most shameless of the Renaissance. Cellini brags, confesses, and settles scores in one breath. Duels, murders, prison escapes, and lawsuits interrupt the workshop scenes, and Cellini casts himself as hero of every episode.

Between the violence stand famous makings: the salt cellar for Francis I and the great bronze Perseus for Florence, whose casting Cellini describes like a battle. Bursting with life and lies in equal measure, the memoir is the age's id talking. Historians discount the boasting and still cannot do without the book.
tob-4106:
Arthur Gilchrist Brodeur's 1916 translation of the Prose Edda is the version American students grew up on. Snorri Sturluson wrote the original in thirteenth-century Iceland as a handbook for poets who needed the old myths. Brodeur's copy here rests on a verified 1919 printing.

Gylfi, a king in disguise, questions three enthroned figures about the making of the world, the gods' adventures, and the end at Ragnarok. Later sections unpack the kennings, the compact riddles of skaldic verse. Snorri rescued stories that would otherwise have vanished with pagan Iceland. Brodeur's clear prose keeps the rescue working for each new class of readers.
tob-4206:
W. Warde Fowler, an Oxford historian, asked in The Religious Experience of the Roman People what religion actually felt like to ordinary Romans. Household gods at the hearth, festivals marking the farming year, vows in sickness and danger, and the dread of getting a ritual word wrong make up his subject. Rome's faith was practice more than belief.

Delivered as Gifford Lectures, the study is scholarly but humane, resisting both mockery of superstition and romantic overreading. Fowler follows Roman religion from the early republic's calendar to the empire's encounter with Eastern cults and Christianity. Readers get ancient Rome's inner life respectfully reconstructed, a corrective to histories that count only legions, laws, and emperors.
tob-4306:
Moses Maimonides, the great Jewish thinker of the twelfth century, wrote his Guide for readers torn between the Torah and Greek philosophy. Many educated Jews felt that faith and reason pulled against each other. In M. Friedlander's English translation, the Guide speaks directly to that conflict.

Maimonides treats hard questions one by one: what words about God can truly mean, whether the world was created, and how prophecy works. He reads Scripture with care and argues that reason, used well, supports faith rather than destroying it. Few medieval books have been debated so long or so fiercely.
tourneur-revengers-tragedy-1606:
Printed in 1607 with no author's name, The Revenger's Tragedy was long credited to Cyril Tourneur. Most scholars now assign it to Thomas Middleton instead. Vindice, the lead figure, has spent nine years grieving for his murdered love, and he returns to court in disguise carrying her skull.

The court he enters is ruled by a lecherous Duke and a brood of grasping sons and stepsons. Plot piles on plot until revenge turns into a bloody masque of killing. Dark wit runs through every scene, and the mix of horror and sharp talk has made the play a lasting landmark of Jacobean drama.
uarda-a-romance-of-ancient-egypt-volume-:
Volume six of Uarda opens at chapter twenty-four, on a day of surprises in Thebes and the Necropolis. The widow Katuti has passed a sleepless night. Her daughter Nefert came home late from the Princess Bent-Anat, and the secret that could deliver Paaker to Ani hangs over the house.

Nemu at last tells what he knows, fearing for his mother's safety. Paaker, he says, gave Nefert half of a love-philter, and the rest remains in his hands. Katuti, indignant hours ago, now asks eagerly whether such a drink truly works. By sunrise she is praying at her dead husband's statue, while Nefert still has not appeared at breakfast.
un-ga-res-106:
Armenian deaths under the Ottoman Empire stand at the heart of the text filed here as Resolution 106. The file is not a UN text at all. It is a resolution of the U.S. House of Representatives, H. Res. 106 of the 110th Congress, sent to committee on 30 January 2007. It calls on the President to make sure that U.S. foreign dealings show due grasp of the facts on human rights, ethnic cleansing, and genocide in the U.S. record on the Armenian Genocide.

Adam Schiff led the sponsors of the text, with men of both parties beside him. The short name is given in full: the Affirmation of the United States Record on the Armenian Genocide Resolution. Fights over such texts, and over the word genocide itself, marked U.S. and Turkish ties for years. The catalog's UN label and 1915 year are both wrong.
un-sc-res-106:
Resolution 106 condemns an attack by Israeli regular army forces on Egyptian forces in the Gaza Strip on 28 February 1955. The catalog record dates the entry 1948, but the text itself was adopted on 29 March 1955, by a unanimous vote. An Egypt-Israel armistice panel had found the attack was planned and ordered by Israeli authorities.

The Council calls the attack a breach of the cease-fire terms in Resolution 54 and of the General Armistice Agreement between Egypt and Israel. It calls on Israel to take all steps needed to stop such actions. It also warns that any willful breach of the armistice puts the deal at risk, and that no real peace in Palestine can come unless both sides keep their word.
un-sc-res-1306:
Rough diamonds from Sierra Leone were banned from world markets on 5 July 2000. The Council voiced concern at the part played by the illegal diamond trade in fueling the war. Such stones were reported to pass through neighboring countries, Liberia among them. The diamond industry and West African states were already working on the trade's openness.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council ordered all states to bar the direct or indirect import of rough diamonds from Sierra Leone. The ban would run for an initial eighteen months. One door stayed open: stones covered by a certificate of origin scheme run by Sierra Leone's government were exempt. Freetown was told to set that scheme up as a matter of urgency and to tell the sanctions committee. States and bodies were asked to help it do so. The move was an early step toward the global Kimberley controls on conflict diamonds.
un-sc-res-1406: Official record keeping at the United Nations preserves Resolution 1406, a Security Council text the catalog dates to 2002. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1506:
Libya's long isolation ended at the United Nations with Resolution 1506, adopted in September 2003. Sanctions placed on Tripoli after the Lockerbie bombing had been suspended for years. Once Libya accepted responsibility terms and a settlement, the Council lifted the measures for good.

Inside the short text, the members remove the arms and travel bans and close the sanctions committee's work. The vote closed a dispute that had run since the 1980s over the bombing of Pan Am Flight 103. It remains the formal end of one of the UN's longest sanctions cases.
un-sc-res-1606: Security Council Resolution 1606 is preserved here from the UN's official record, in a transcription by English Wikisource. Resolutions like this one typically run a few pages: findings first, then a short list of decisions. The entry's completeness is its feature, giving the whole act rather than a headline version of what was decided.
un-sc-res-1706:
Darfur's suffering drove Resolution 1706, adopted in August 2006. The Council voted to expand the UN mission in Sudan to take over from African Union troops in Darfur. Sudan's government, however, refused to accept the deployment, setting up a long standoff.

The text details a force of more than 17,000 soldiers plus police, tasked with protecting civilians and guarding the Darfur peace deal. Because Khartoum blocked it, the plan was later replaced by a joint UN-African Union mission. The resolution preserves the world's first full answer to Darfur, and the limits of voting without consent.
un-sc-res-1806: Resolution 1806, adopted in 2008, is a Security Council act preserved here through English Wikisource's transcription of the record. The number places it among the Council's 1800s run, the output of its later-2000s sessions. The entry gives the full decision at that place: grounds, orders, and the reporting follow-through that such texts standardly require.
un-sc-res-1906:
By Resolution 1906, adopted on 23 December 2009, the Council acted on the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Militias in the east still preyed on civilians. Sexual violence, child soldier use, and summary killings went unpunished. The peacekeeping mission faced hard questions about its future shape and size.

The Council extends the mission, called MONUC, until 31 May 2010, keeping up to 19,815 troops. Guarding civilians ranks first among its duties. Joint protection teams and early warning posts, tested in North Kivu, should spread to the south. The Secretary-General must deliver a strategic review by 1 April 2010. It will set out what must be done before any drawdown can start safely.
un-sc-res-206:
A thin calm held in Cyprus in the summer of 1965, and the Secretary-General warned it might not last without the peacekeeping force. His report recommended keeping the force for six more months. Cyprus's government wanted it to stay beyond 26 June 1965. Resolution 206 was adopted unanimously on 15 June 1965.

The Council thanked the Secretary-General and the states that sent troops, police, supplies, and money. Its earlier Cyprus resolutions were reaffirmed. The parties were called on to keep showing restraint and to cooperate fully with the force. The force's stationing was extended for six months, ending on 26 December 1965. The longer term matched the warning in the report. A fresh outbreak of fighting was feared if the force left too soon.
un-sc-res-406:
Botswana's call for help was answered on 25 May 1977. The Council had the report of the mission it sent under resolution 403 (1977). Botswana's foreign minister described continued attacks and provocations by the Rhodesian regime. The Secretary-General had written to all states on 18 April with the mission's findings. Solidarity with Botswana was judged essential to solving the Rhodesia question.

The Council voiced full support for Botswana's government as it guarded the country's sovereignty and independence. It thanked the Secretary-General for sending the mission. The mission's assessment and recommendations were endorsed in full. His April appeal to all states, asking urgent financial and material help for Botswana, won the Council's full backing as well. A special account at Headquarters, opened to receive gifts for Botswana, was welcomed. United Nations bodies were asked to act on the mission's plan, and states holding aid back were pressed to respond.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 106, adopted unanimously on 29 March 1955, condemns an Israeli attack in the Gaza Strip. The Council had heard the report of the Chief of Staff of the United Nations Truce Supervision Organization. It had heard statements by Egypt and Israel. It notes the finding of the Egyptian-Israel Mixed Armistice Commission of 6 March 1955.

The Commission had determined that the attack of 28 February 1955 was a prearranged and planned attack. It was ordered by the Israeli authorities. It was carried out by regular army forces against an Egyptian regular army force in Gaza. The Council condemns it as a violation of the cease-fire set by resolution 54 (1948) and of the General Armistice Agreement. It calls again on Israel to prevent such actions. It warns that deliberate violations threaten the armistice system. Any return to permanent peace in Palestine depends on that system.

Blood diamonds are targeted in Resolution 1306, adopted on 5 July 2000. The Council said it was troubled by the role of the illicit diamond trade in fueling Sierra Leone's war, since rebels sold rough stones, often through Liberia, to buy weapons. It also stressed that the legitimate diamond trade matters greatly to many economies and can aid recovery when it is clean.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council banned the direct and indirect import of rough diamonds from Sierra Leone unless they moved under a certificate-of-origin regime controlled by Sierra Leone's government. The ban ran for an initial eighteen months. The scheme helped invent the global certification system later embodied in the Kimberley Process.

More time to study a report is the whole point here. On 30 April 2002 the Council extended MINURSO, the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, until 31 July 2002. The pause let members weigh the Secretary-General's report of 19 February 2002 on the territory's future, while the Western Sahara question stayed under the Council's review.

Sanctions imposed on Libya over the Lockerbie and UTA flight bombings are lifted on 12 September 2003. The measures dated from the early 1990s. Libya had now written to the Council accepting responsibility for its officials' actions, paying compensation, renouncing terrorism, and promising cooperation with further inquiries.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council ended the sanctions with immediate effect. It dissolved the sanctions committee that had overseen them since 1992. It also closed its handling of the whole item, removing it from the list of matters before it. The vote was 13 in favour and none against, with France and the United States abstaining.

A truth and justice process for Burundi's past crimes is opened up on 20 June 2005. Burundi's government had asked in 2002, under the Arusha Agreement, for an international judicial commission of inquiry. A report sent to the Council in March 2005 set out recommendations for handling that request.

Lasting peace, the Council says, requires establishing the truth about genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes committed in Burundi since independence, and bringing those most responsible to justice. The Secretary-General is asked to open negotiations with Burundi's government. He is also to consult all Burundian parties on how to carry out his recommendations, with a report on those talks due by 30 September 2005.

Expanding the Sudan mission into Darfur is decided on 31 August 2006. The African Union force in Darfur was overstretched, and the Council had resolved in May to move toward a United Nations operation there. Sudan's sovereignty, it is stressed, would be unaffected by the transition, and the Darfur peace agreement is pressed to be carried out.

UNMIS is to be strengthened by up to 17,300 military personnel and a large civilian police component for Darfur. The Secretary-General is asked to arrange rapid deployment of extra resources and to consult jointly with the African Union on the handover. The expanded mission's tasks in Darfur include protecting civilians, watching the ceasefire, and supporting the peace deal, though Sudan's consent remained a live dispute.

Afghanistan's assistance mission, UNAMA, is extended for another year on 20 March 2008. The Afghanistan Compact remained the shared framework for security, governance, and development, owned by Afghans themselves. The linked fight against the drug trade, which funded the insurgency and corruption alike, is also noted.

UNAMA's mandate, as defined in earlier resolutions, is renewed, and its coordination role across the country is strengthened. The mission and its head are to lead world civilian efforts, support the government's development strategy, and help deliver aid and protection. All Afghan and international actors are called on to work with the mission, and the government is urged to deepen reform, above all in security and justice.

MONUC is extended for five months while its future shape is studied in Resolution 1906, adopted on 23 December 2009. Militias in eastern Congo had still not disarmed. Targeted attacks, sexual violence, and child recruitment continued. Relations with neighbouring states were improving under regional agreements.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends MONUC until 31 May 2010 at up to 19,815 military personnel, 760 observers, 391 police, and 1,050 formed police personnel. It signals a further twelve months after that. The Secretary-General must deliver a strategic review by 1 April 2010, with benchmarks, reconfiguration options, and the critical tasks to finish before drawdown. MONUC's priorities are fixed in order: protect civilians, run disarmament and demobilization for Congolese and foreign armed groups, and support security sector reform. North Kivu protection tools such as Joint Protection Teams and Early Warning Centres must be extended, especially to South Kivu.

Resolution 206 is a UN Security Council renewal for Cyprus, adopted unanimously on 15 June 1965. The Secretary-General recommended keeping the peacekeeping force for six months this time, longer than the usual three, and the government of Cyprus asked for the deployment to continue past late June.

His report warned that the island's quiet was tenuous and that fighting would very likely resume early if the force withdrew. The Council therefore kept the peacekeepers in place and restated its appreciation to the Secretary-General and the states backing the mission. The doubled extension length shows the Council accepting, by mid-1965, that Cyprus needed a longer commitment rather than emergency stopgaps.

Choosing a Secretary-General is the sole purpose of Resolution 306, adopted unanimously on 21 December 1971. The Council had considered whom to recommend as the United Nations' top official. U Thant of Burma was stepping down after a decade in the job, and governments had settled on an Austrian diplomat and former foreign minister as his successor.

In one sentence, the Council recommends to the General Assembly that Kurt Waldheim be appointed Secretary-General. The Charter splits this choice in two: the Assembly appoints, but only someone the Council has put forward. Waldheim went on to serve two terms through 1981, and his tenure later drew scrutiny over his wartime record, which makes this brief appointment text a document historians still revisit.

Resolution 406 passed with no vote on 25 May 1977. It turns a fact-finding trip into real aid for Botswana. A UN team sent months before had sized up Botswana's needs. Rhodesia's white-led regime kept up raids and taunts across the border. Botswana's foreign chief told the Council of the harm in the hall. The UN chief had called on all states in April to stand with Botswana, a small state in the front line of the Rhodesia fight.

The Council voiced full faith in Botswana's right to guard its land, its borders, and its free rule. It backed the UN team's findings and its plan in full. It backed the call for aid just as fully. The aid aimed at roads, water, and farms, so Botswana could stand firm.
un-un-res-united-nations-emergency-force:
The tenth report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Emergency Force, document A/6406, covers the force in 1965 and 1966. UNEF was nearing a full decade on the Egypt-Israel frontier. Few at its birth in the Suez Crisis had expected so long a stay, and its costs drew steady debate.

The report reviews patrols, incidents, troop strength, and the force's budget. It records a quiet border and a mission in working order. It is the last full report in the run: the force was pulled out in May 1967, and war followed within weeks.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s426-106:
Section 426.106 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations tells a person how to seek a fix to their own record. The record must be one kept by the National Commission on Military, National, and Public Service. A person may ask for amendment or correction of a record they believe is not accurate, relevant, timely, or complete.

The right flows from the Privacy Act, and the request must be made in writing. It goes to the Office of the General Counsel. The request should name the record, the system it came from, and the precise change desired. An edited copy showing the change is preferred. The reasons for the request must also be stated. The Commission must acknowledge a request within ten business days of receipt, unless it can act sooner. The hosted text is from the electronic Code as of late October 2026.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s426-206:
Section 426.206 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations governs responses to requests under the freedom of information rules of a federal commission. It sits in Part 426 of Title 1, for the National Commission on Military, National, and Public Service, in the electronic Code as of October 2026.

The Commission sends a written acknowledgement of each request. It gives the request its own tracking number if handling will take longer than ten working days. On request, it gives an expected date for its response, and for large requests it may answer in parts. If a request is granted in full or in part, the requester gets written notice, the fees that apply, and word of the help of the public liaison. If a request is denied in any respect, that choice is also notified in writing, and the text lists what counts as a denial.
uslaw-usc-t1-s106:
Section 106 of Title 1 of the United States Code requires bills to be printed as they pass each House. The printed copy has its own legal name and role. The section sits among the formalities of enactment.

Every bill or joint resolution, when it passes either House, shall be printed. The printed copy is called the engrossed bill or engrossed resolution. That copy is signed by an officer of the passing House. The Clerk of the House or the Secretary of the Senate signs, as the case may be. The engrossed copy is then sent to the other House. In that form it is dealt with by that House and its officers. If passed there, it is returned in the same form, as the text continues. Print, not the Clerk's draft, is the official traveling text of a measure.
uslaw-usc-t1-s206:
Section 206 of Title 1 governs the printing of law revision bills from one House committee. All bills and resolutions relating to the revision of the laws, when referred to or reported by the House Judiciary Committee, follow its prescriptions. They are printed in such form and style, and with such ancillaries, as the committee prescribes.

The standard the committee applies is that the printing be economical and suitable. That direction holds until final enactment of the measure in both Houses of Congress. The committee may also curtail the number of copies of such bills to be printed. That power covers the various parliamentary stages in the House. The section sits in Chapter 3 of Title 1, on the Code of Laws and its supplements. The hosted Code text is published by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel, current through Public Law 119-134.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1106:
Section 1106 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers spending from a trust fund and audit of that spending. The fund belongs to the John C Stennis Center for Public Service Training and Development. The Secretary of the Treasury may pay the Center sums from the interest and earnings of the fund. Moneys credited to the fund under a named section are included. The Board decides what sums are necessary and fit for the Center to carry out the chapter.

The Center's activities under the chapter may be audited by the Government Accountability Office. The audit runs under rules set by the Comptroller General. Office representatives must have access to all books, accounts, records, reports, and files of the Center that bear on those activities and are needed to ease the audit.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1406:
Section 1406 of Title 2 of the United States Code gives an appeal to the Board from decisions of hearing officers in congressional workplace cases. It sits in Chapter 24 of Title 2, current through Public Law 119-134. The appeal has a short deadline.

Any party hurt by a hearing officer's decision under section 1405 may file a petition for review by the Board. The filing must come within thirty days of entry of the decision in the records of the Office. The parties get a fair chance to be heard, in writing and, if the Board allows, by word of mouth. The Board must set a decision aside if it was arbitrary or against the law. The same holds if it was made without the procedures required, or lacked solid evidence. The Board reviews the whole record and gives written reasons.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1606:
Section 1606 of Title 2 of the United States Code sets penalties in the lobbying disclosure scheme. It sits in Chapter 26 of that title, on the disclosure of lobbying activities. Part (a) states a civil penalty. It falls on a person who knowingly fails to fix a faulty filing in time. The time given is sixty days after notice of the fault from the Secretary of the Senate or the Clerk of the House.

The same penalty falls on a person who knowingly fails to meet any other provision of the chapter. The fault must be proved by the greater weight of the proof. The fine may reach 200,000 dollars, based on the reach and gravity of the fault. Part (b) of the section states a penalty under criminal law. The text is current through Public Law 119-134.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1906:
Disposal of surplus Capitol Police property is governed by section 1906 of Title 2. Within the limits of funds appropriated, the Capitol Police may dispose of surplus or obsolete property of the force. The same power covers property in its hands because it was disposed of, forfeited, abandoned, or left unclaimed.

The methods allowed are listed in the text. They are interagency transfer, donation, sale, trade-in, or any other appropriate method. Money received from such disposal is credited to the account for the general expenses of the Capitol Police. It stays available in the year it is received and in the following fiscal year. The section applies from fiscal year 2003 onward. It sits in Chapter 29 of Title 2, and the hosted Code is current through Public Law 119-134.
uslaw-usc-t2-s2006:
Section 2006 of Title 2 covers the withdrawal of a request for a vacant House room. A Representative or Representative-elect who has asked for the assignment of a vacant room may withdraw that request at any time. No one may have more than one such request pending at the same time.

A second rule works by implication. The assignment of a new room to a Representative, on request, acts as a giving up of the room held before. The same effect follows when a Representative with an individual office becomes chairman of a committee that has a committee room. The section sits in Chapter 30 of Title 2, on the Capitol complex. It falls in the subchapter for the House. The hosted Code is current through Public Law 119-134. The rules keep the room lottery orderly and stop double claims.
uslaw-usc-t2-s4106: Section 4106 of Title 2 of the United States Code is a one sentence rule on the stationery rooms of the House and Senate. It sits in the general part of the chapter on congressional officers and administration. Two committees must make and issue the rules on what classes of goods may be bought by or through those rooms. For the House the task falls to the Committee on House Oversight. For the Senate it falls to the Committee on Rules and Administration.
uslaw-usc-t2-s4506: Section 4506 of Title 2 of the United States Code sits in the chapter on congressional pay and benefits. It is a one-line rule on death payments. Any death gratuity payment counts in law as a gift. That holds whether the payment was specially granted by an act of Congress, or was made from the proper accounts of the House or from the contingent fund of the Senate. The clause fixes the legal character of such payments once and for all.
uslaw-usc-t2-s506:
Section 506 of Title 2 of the United States Code regulates mass mailings sent by Members of the House. A mass mailing goes to many households at public expense. This section requires the mailing to confess its funding on its face.

Each mass mailing must bear a notice in a prominent place. The notice may sit on the face of the mailing itself. Or it may appear on the envelope or outside cover in which the matter is sent. Two set wordings are supplied, the first beginning: Paid for with official funds from the office of the member. A notice to the same effect may be prescribed instead under a later part. The type must be no smaller than 7-point, so the words stay readable. The rule makes taxpayer funding of congressional mail impossible to hide.
uslaw-usc-t2-s5106:
Section 5106 of Title 2 of the United States Code creates an allowance to pay interns in House leadership offices. Title 2 covers Congress, and this section sits in the chapter on House leadership. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six. Before this kind of rule, intern pay in those offices had no set fund.

An allowance is established for the House for that purpose, the text states. It is available for the pay of interns who serve in House leadership offices. A linked part on benefits exclusion is flagged in the section. The rule thus funds junior help for the offices that steer the House, on terms set by law.
uslaw-usc-t2-s5306:
Section 5306 of Title 2 of the United States Code docks the pay of House members who miss days without excuse. It stands in the member pay part of the chapter on House members. The officer who acts is the Chief Administrative Officer of the House.

He acts on certification by the Clerk of the House. From each Member's or Delegate's monthly payments, he deducts the salary for each day of absence. One excuse is written into the rule. No deduction is made when the member assigns sickness as the reason. The sickness may be his own or that of a member of his family. The section is an old attendance rule with a humane exception, still carried in the Code.
uslaw-usc-t2-s5506:
Section 5506 of Title 2 of the United States Code sets restrictions on appropriations for expenses of the House of Representatives. It sits in Chapter 55 of Title 2, on House officers and administration. The version here is current through Public Law 119-134.

Money appropriated for House expenses may not be used to pay for personal services. The only exception is on the express and specific authorization of the House, in whose behalf the services are rendered. Nor may such appropriations be used for any expenses not intimately and directly connected with the routine legislative business of the House. The Government Accountability Office is directed to apply this section in settling accounts. Those accounts cover spending from such appropriations for services or materials.
uslaw-usc-t2-s5606:
Section 5606 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers arrangements for attendance at the funeral of a deceased House Member, and payment of expenses. It sits in Chapter 55 of Title 2, on House officers and administration, current through Public Law 119-134. The powers it gives run from October 2, 1962 onward.

Notwithstanding any other provision of law, the Sergeant at Arms of the House is authorized and directed to make the arrangements needed. They serve any committee of Members of the Senate and House duly appointed to attend the funeral of a deceased Member of the House. Payment comes out of the applicable accounts of the House of Representatives. It is made under rules the Committee on House Oversight prescribes. The sums cover the funeral expenses of the deceased Member and the expenses of the attending committee.
uslaw-usc-t2-s606:
Section 606 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers disposal of surplus or outdated property of the Congressional Budget Office. Title 2 covers Congress, and this section sits in the chapter on that budget office. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six. It gives the Director a set of disposal routes.

Within the limits of funds on hand, the Director may dispose of such personal property in several ways. Transfer to another agency, donation, sale, trade in, or discarding are all allowed. Amounts received from a sale or trade in are then handled under the section's terms. The rule keeps office property from piling up without a lawful exit.
uslaw-usc-t2-s6506:
Section 6506 of Title 2 of the United States Code creates separate accounts for two Senate officers inside the contingent fund. Title 2 covers Congress, and this section sits in the rules for Senate officers and administration. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six. The officers are the Secretary and the Sergeant at Arms.

Effective on the first of October in nineteen eighty three, a separate account for the Secretary shall exist within the fund, the text states. A parallel account for the Sergeant at Arms and Doorkeeper is created in the same way. Funds already in existing accounts are folded in as the section provides. Each great officer of the Senate thus keeps distinct books.
uslaw-usc-t2-s806:
Section 806 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with an award board's powers. The board runs the Congressional Award Program for young folk. It may take acts and spend sums as need be for the program. That power is held within the limits the section itself sets out.

The board must work and spend with means from outside government first. It may also use funds won in a grant program of an agency. The grant must be run under the law that set the program up. The board may take no act that would cost it its tax-free standing. That standing is the one for groups of a named kind in Title 26. The board must also set up the functions the program needs. Its set functions and steps must serve to carry the chapter out.
uslaw-usc-t2-s906:
Section 906 of Title 2 of the United States Code sets general and special rules for sequestration. Title 2 covers Congress, and this section sits in the chapter on emergency powers to cut budget deficits. Its subchapter deals with deficits above a set maximum. The hosted text is current in twenty twenty six. Sequestration means automatic across the board cuts.

One early part of the section is marked as repealed by a public law of twenty ten, with full citation given. The next live part deals with student loans under named parts of the Higher Education Act. Special handling for loan programs reflects their credit based form. General deficit cut rules are thus paired with program level exceptions.
virginia-charter-1606:
King James I granted the First Charter of Virginia in 1606 to a group of London merchants and gentlemen. Their company planned to plant an English colony on the coast of North America. The charter gave them legal cover to sail, settle, and govern under English law.

The text sets the colony's borders, names its ruling councils, and promises settlers the rights of English subjects. It also claims rights to mine gold, silver, and copper, sharing a part with the crown. A year later the company's colonists founded Jamestown. The charter is thus a founding paper of English America.
what-will-he-do-with-it-volume-06:
Book six of Lord Lytton's What Will He Do With It? jumps five years ahead to a June evening in Hyde Park. Carriages crawl by the Serpentine while crowds lean on the rails to watch. Sharp tongues trade gossip like critics at a club window. Idlers of all ranks stroll the paths.

Young women canter in the Ride as a form of penance, and old beaux trot at hard labor. A busy member of Parliament snatches a ride for his health between committee and debate. Lytton draws London at play with wit and bite. Old figures, the chapter head promises, will return and tell where they have been. The tale's threads start to join again.
wieger-textes-philosophiques-1906:
Léon Wieger, a French Jesuit who spent his life in China, gathered these Chinese philosophical texts in 1906 and presented them in French. Wieger ran a mission press in Hebei and became known for exact work on Chinese language and thought. His aim was to let French readers meet China's sages in their own words.

The chosen pieces span schools and ages, from early masters to later teachers of the Way and of Confucius. Short lives and notes help the reader place each text. Wieger's versions were trusted for their care, and the set still serves as a window on how Europe first read Chinese thought in depth.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol06:
In 1859 Volume VI of the Journal of Discourses added another year of preaching to the printed record. Liverpool remained the printing base for a Utah church speaking to a worldwide flock. Brigham Young, his counsellors, and the Twelve Apostles fill the pages, their sermons taken down word for word.

The talks show doctrine being worked out in public, applied to marriages, farms, debts, and doubts. That mix of the sacred and the everyday is the Journal's signature across all twenty-six volumes. Volume VI, read in sequence, lets the movement's teaching be watched as it grows.
zohar-de-pauly-french-vol-1-1906:
The Zohar, the Book of Splendor, is the central work of the Kabbalah, ascribed to the circle of Moses de Leon in thirteenth-century Spain. It reads the Torah as a map of the hidden life of God, in the form of talks among Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and his companions. Jean de Pauly turned the whole work into French, and his first tome appeared in 1906. No complete English version in the public domain exists.

The opening tomes follow Genesis, verse by verse turned to mystery: the ten sefirot, the letters of creation, and the souls of the patriarchs. De Pauly's French is the only complete public domain rendering of the whole Zohar. His six tomes made the book open to Western readers.
